en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Book of Twos in the Aṅguttara Nikāya.
1. The First Fifty-Section (Paṭhamapaṇṇāsaka) 1.
The Chapter on Punishment (Kammakāraṇavagga) 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on Faults (Vajjasuttavaṇṇanā)

1. In the first chapter of the *Duka-nipāta*, "faults" (*vajjā*) refers to defects or transgressions. "Belonging to this very life" (*diṭṭhadhammika*) means having its fruit arise in this very present existence, in this very selfhood.
"Belonging to the future life" (*samparāyika*) means having its fruit arise in a future existence, in a subsequent selfhood.
"One who behaves wickedly" (*āgucārī*) refers to an evildoer, a perpetrator of transgression. Kings, having seized such persons, inflict upon them various forms of punishment.
Having seized a thief, the king’s men carry out various forms of punishment; however, it is the kings who are said to "carry them out.
He sees that thief being subjected to such punishments as he is being executed. Therefore it is said:
“He sees a thief, a wrongdoer, whom kings, having seized him, are subjecting to various forms of punishment. *Addhadaṇḍakehi* means with clubs.
Or, for the purpose of inflicting blows, they take sticks four cubits long, split them in two, and use the handles thus held. "Bilaṅgathālikā" refers to the punishment of the rice-pot gruel;

while undergoing it, they have the skull removed, seize a red-hot iron ball with tongs, and thrust it therein, whereby the brain boils over. "Saṅkhamuṇḍikā" [refers to the punishment of the conch-shell shaven].
The "conch-shell shaving" torture: while performing it, they cut the skin along the boundaries of the upper lip, both ears, the crown of the head, and the nape of the neck;
having gathered all the hair together into a single knot and bound it with a stick, they tear it out, whereupon the skin comes away with the hair.
Then, rubbing the skull with coarse gravel and washing it, they make it the color of a conch shell.
They perform [this torture]. "Rāhu’s mouth" refers to the judicial punishment of being cast into Rāhu’s mouth.

While performing it, they force open the victim's mouth with a wedge and set a lamp on fire inside; or, starting from the ears and the back of the head, they gouge the mouth with a chisel until blood flows out and fills the mouth.
*Jotimālika*: They wrap the entire body in an oil-soaked cloth and set it on fire. *Hatthapajjotika*:
They wrap the hands in an oil-soaked cloth and set them ablaze like a lamp. *Erakavattika*: This is the punishment of the *erakavatta* (grass-cord) torture.
While performing it, they slit the skin starting from the neck and wind it down until it reaches the ankles; then, [they... him.
Having bound them with ropes, they drag them along. He falls down, repeatedly stepping upon his own skin-cord.
"The bark-garment punishment" refers to the penal practice of wearing a bark garment. While performing that, they cut [the skin] in that same manner and place it around the waist;
starting from the waist, they cut it further until it reaches the ankles, so that the lower part of the body is clothed in a bark-garment.

It is as if [it were] so. "The Eneyyaka" refers to the Eneyyaka punishment. Those who inflict it place iron rings on both elbows and both knees and drive iron spikes through them. He stands upon the ground supported by four iron spikes.
Then, surrounding him, they kindle a fire. This is also mentioned in the passage where it says, "The Eneyyaka, like one enveloped in flames."
This very thing has been stated. From time to time, having removed the spikes, they leave [the victim] standing on its four bone-ends alone;
there is no such thing as a punishment like this.
"The hook-and-flesh" means that after striking with hooks from both sides, they tear away the skin, flesh, and sinews. "The kahāpaṇa coin" means...
"Entire-body": they cut the whole body with sharp adzes, starting from the top of the head, driving them in piece by piece the size of a *kahāpaṇa* coin.
"The caustic-scorcher": having struck the body here and there with weapons, they rub it with caustic using brushes;
when the skin, flesh, and sinews have melted away, only a skeleton remains. "The revolving bar": [they force the victim to turn on a heated iron bar].
Having laid him down on one side, they drive an iron spike through his ear-hole and fix it firmly into the earth.
Then, seizing him by the feet, they drag him along. As for the "straw-mat" torture:
a skilled executioner strips off the skin and hide, breaks the bones with small hammers, and lifting him up by the hair, he leaves behind nothing but a heap of flesh.
Then, having completely wrapped him in his hair, they seize him; making him like a bundle of straw, they bind him again.
"By dogs" means that for several days they provide no food and have him devoured by hungry dogs;
in a mere moment, they reduce him to a mere skeleton of bones. "Impale on a stake" means they place him upon a stake.

"He does not wander plundering what has been brought by others" means that even if he sees another's property or goods brought in their absence—even down to a thousand coins dropped in the middle of an alleyway—he does not wander about plundering them with the thought, "I shall live by this.
Thinking, "What is the use of this? he either rolls it away with his heel and goes on his way.
“Evil” means base. “Suffering” means undesirable. “And what might that be? means: what indeed could be the cause? “By which” means by which [cause] I [experience it].

“Bodily misconduct” refers to the threefold unwholesome bodily action, beginning with the destruction of life. “Bodily good conduct” refers to the threefold wholesome action that serves as its opposite.
“Verbal misconduct” refers to the fourfold [unwholesome verbal action], beginning with false speech.
Unwholesome verbal action (*vacīkamma*). Wholesome verbal conduct (*vacīsucarita*) is the fourfold wholesome action that serves as its opposite.

Mental misconduct (*manoduccarita*) is the threefold unwholesome action consisting of covetousness and so forth. Mental good conduct (*manosucarita*) is the threefold wholesome action that serves as its opposite.
Regarding the phrase "he preserves himself purely," here purity is twofold: in a figurative sense (*pariyāyato*)...
And [it is purified] both figuratively and absolutely. For by means of the figurative method, one maintains oneself as pure through the act of going for refuge;
likewise through the five precepts, the ten precepts—the fourfold purification of virtue—through the first jhāna... pe...

up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, through the path of stream-entry, the fruit of stream-entry... pe... and through the path of arahantship, one maintains oneself as pure by the figurative method.

He is said to "maintain" [himself]. However, one who has attained the fruit of arahantship and whose taints are destroyed—whether he causes the five aggregates, whose roots have been severed, to be washed, fed, nourished, seated, or laid down—he maintains, looks after, and preserves his own self as truly pure and stainless in the absolute sense; this is how it should be understood.
Therefore (*tasmāti*): because these two are indeed faults (*vajja*), and not non-faults, for that reason.

"Those who fear faults" (*vajjabhīru*) means those who are afraid of faults. "Those who see faults as danger" (*vajjabhayadassāvī*) means those whose nature it is to view faults as a source of fear. "This is to be expected" (*etaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ*) means this is to be desired;
the meaning is that this is bound to happen. *Yaṃ* is merely a particle, or it is a statement of cause, meaning "by which cause" one will be liberated.
From all faults. But by what cause will he be liberated? By the fourth path and the fourth fruit.
For it is by the path that one is said to be liberated, and having attained the fruit, one is said to be liberated.
But does unwholesome karma not ripen for one whose taints are destroyed? It does ripen; however, that was performed prior to the state of one whose taints are destroyed. And that—
"He [claims] that there is no such thing as the fruit of kamma for him in this very life, but only in the future life. First. 2.
Commentary on the Discourse on Exertion (Padhāna-sutta).
Second. Regarding "exertions" (*padhānāni*), they mean energies (*vīriyāni*). For energy is called "exertion" (*padhāna*) because it must be exerted, or because it brings about the state of exertion.

It is said: "Difficult to accomplish" means difficult to endure and difficult to fulfill; the meaning is that they are hard to perform. "For one living in a household" means for those dwelling in a home.

"Exertion for the purpose of providing robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick" means that exertion is indeed for the sake of providing these four requisites, beginning with robes.

This shows that they are difficult to accomplish. For it is as difficult to bring forth and give to others even a scrap of ragged cloth four spans in size, or a meal consisting of only a handful of rice, or a leaf-hut four spans in size, or even a small amount of medicine such as oil, ghee, or butter—as it is to enter a battle with both flanks arrayed; thus the Blessed One said:
“Giving and battle are said to be alike:
even a few, being united, conquer many.
Even if one gives but little with faith, [it brings great fruit].”
"By that very [means] he becomes happy for the sake of others.

Regarding those who have gone forth from the home to the homeless life: having departed from the household, they have entered the homeless state (*anagāriya*), which is the going-forth (*pabbajjā*) devoid of agriculture, cattle-rearing, and other such activities conducive to the welfare of a householder’s life. For the purpose of relinquishing all acquisitions (*upadhi*).

"Exertion" (padhāna) refers to the energy that arises simultaneously with insight and the Path for the sake of Nibbāna—which is defined as the relinquishing of all acquisitions (upadhi), namely those consisting of the aggregates, the defilements, and volitional formations.
"Therefore" means because these two types of exertion are difficult to accomplish; therefore [it is said]. This is the second [section].
3. Commentary on the Tapanīya Sutta Third:
"Tapanīya" means those things which burn both here and in the future life; thus they are called *tapanīya*.
One "is burned" (*tappati*) means one is tormented by mental anguish and grieves after having committed bodily misconduct, like the yakkha Nanda, the student Nanda, or the ox-slaughterer Nanda.

It was like Devadatta and like the two brothers. It is said that after they had slaughtered a cow and divided the meat into two portions, the younger brother said to the elder, "I have many children; give these entrails to me.
Then the elder struck him and brought about his death, saying, "All the meat has been divided into two parts; what more do you seek?"
He sent him back. Turning back and looking at him, he saw that he was dead and thought, "I have committed a grievous deed.
Then a powerful sorrow arose within him. Whether standing or sitting, he kept reflecting on that very deed and found no peace of mind.
Even the food he ate, drank, chewed, and tasted failed to provide nourishment to his body.
It was nothing but skin and bone. Then an elder, seeing him, said: "Lay follower, you were once possessed of abundant food and drink;
now only skin and bone remain. Have you perhaps committed some deed that brings remorse? He replied, "Yes, venerable sir," and related everything.
Then the elder said to him: "Lay follower, you have committed a grave deed; it was in a place where there was no fault..."
"I have erred," he said. Having died because of that very deed, he was reborn in hell. Through verbal misconduct, one burns like Suppabuddha the Sakyan, Kokālika, Ciñcamāṇavikā, and others.
The rest here, as well as in the fourth [sutta], is of obvious meaning. The third [is concluded]. 5.
Commentary on the Upaññāta Sutta.
5. "Of two" means of two things. "I understood" (*upaññāsiṃ*): having approached [them], I recognized their quality;
the meaning is that I knew and penetrated them. Now, showing those qualities, he said: "And non-contentment," and so forth.
For it was by depending on this pair of qualities that the Teacher attained omniscience; therefore, demonstrating their power, he spoke thus. Therein, "non-contentment" (*asantuṭṭhitā*)...
By the phrase "regarding wholesome states," he illustrates this:
"Being dissatisfied with mere jhāna or even with the mere sign of light, I brought forth the path to arahantship itself. As long as that had not arisen, I was not satisfied.
And remaining without shrinking back from exertion, I performed the work of striving without weariness."
Showing this meaning by saying “he did,” he spoke the passage beginning with “and that which is unyielding.
Therein, “unyielding” (*appaṭivānitā*) means non-retreating and non-withdrawing. Regarding the phrase “Indeed, monks, I strove unyieldingly,” here *sudaṃ* is merely a particle.
Monks, standing in non-withdrawal during my time as a Bodhisatta, aspiring for omniscience—
"I exerted myself"—this is the meaning here.
Now, showing how he performed that exertion, he said, "Willingly, even my skin," and so forth.

In this context, by the word "attainable" (*pattabba*), he shows the collection of qualities to be attained. By the phrase "with manly strength" (*purisathāmena*) and so on, he indicates the man's power of knowledge.
Knowledge and energy, as well as knowledge and exertion, have been explained. "Steadfastness" means establishing, non-occurrence, and withdrawal;
the meaning is "tranquillization. Up to this point, he has explained what is called the foundation of energy endowed with four factors.
For here, although "skin" is one factor, "sinew" is one, "bone" is one, and "flesh and blood" is one—
These are the four factors. "With manly strength" and so forth are synonyms for supreme energy.
Thus, when one is endowed with these four preceding factors, this energy thus resolved should be understood as the "Foundation of Energy Endowed with Four Factors.
Up to this point, he has described the path by which he arrived at the seat of enlightenment.
Now, in order to describe the qualities obtained by that practice, he said, "To me, O monks," and so forth.
Therein, "attained through diligence" means attained through diligence characterized by the non-forgetting of mindfulness;

it was not obtained by one who is drowsy or negligent. "Enlightenment" refers both to the knowledge of the four paths and to omniscience. For this cannot be achieved by one who is drowsy or negligent.
"To be attained" means: therefore he said, "Enlightenment is attained through diligence.
Not only is enlightenment [attained thus], but the unsurpassed security from bondage—consisting of the fruit of Arhatship and Nibbāna—is also attained solely through diligence.
Now, encouraging the Saṅgha of bhikkhus to adopt the qualities he himself has realized, he said, "If you too, O bhikkhus," and so forth.
In that context, "for the sake of which" means for the purpose of which; the sense is: having become desirous of entering and dwelling therein.
"That unsurpassed" means that which is unsurpassed. "The culmination of the holy life" refers to the noble fruit, which constitutes the culmination of the holy life of the path.
"Having realized through direct knowledge" means having made it manifest through *abhiññā*, that is, through supreme wisdom. "Entering and dwelling" means...
Having attained and reached it, you shall dwell [in it]. Therefore—because this "unyielding striving" (appaṭivānapadhāna) is of great benefit and accomplishes the supreme goal—therefore. The fifth.
6. Commentary on the Saṃyojana Sutta.

6. In the sixth [section], "regarding phenomena conducive to fetters" (*saṃyojaniyesu dhammesu*) means regarding the phenomena belonging to the three planes that serve as conditions for the ten fetters (*saṃyojana*).

"Contemplating gratification" (*assādānupassī*) means one who contemplates by way of gratification; the sense is the state of contemplating. "Contemplating disenchantment" (*nibbidānupassī*) means the state of contemplating by way of disenchantment, that is, by way of weariness.
"By birth" (*jātiyā*) means from the production of the aggregates (*khandha*). "By aging" (*jarāya*) means from the maturation of the aggregates.

"By death" means by the breaking up of the aggregates (*khandha*). "By sorrows" means by sorrows characterized by inward brooding. "By lamentations" means by lamentations characterized by the outburst of wailing dependent on that [sorrow].
"By pains" means by bodily pains consisting of oppression. "By mental distresses" means by mental distresses consisting of the frustration of the mind.
"By despairs" means by despairs characterized by excessive exhaustion. "From suffering" means from the entire suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
"He abandons" means he abandons by means of the Path. "Having abandoned," however, refers here to the moment of the Fruit (phala).
In this sutta, the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) and its cessation (vivaṭṭa) are explained. The sixth [sutta]. 7. Commentary on the Kaṇha Sutta.
7. Seventh: "Black" (*kaṇha*) does not mean black by way of color; rather, they are called "black" because they lead to blackness—that is, to the state of being produced as dark.
Or, according to the commentary (*sarasena*), all unwholesome states (*akusaladhamma*) are indeed black, for the mind does not become luminous through their arising.
"Shamelessness" (*ahirika*) is the state of being shameless. "Fearlessness of wrongdoing" (*anottappa*) is the state of being fearless of wrongdoing. This is the seventh.

8. Commentary on the *Sukkā-sutta* In the eighth [verse], "bright" (*sukkā*) does not mean bright by way of color; rather, they are called "bright" because they lead to what is bright—that is, they are bright by way of their result.
Alternatively, all wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*) are indeed bright by their very nature. For through their arising, the mind becomes luminous (*pabhassara*).
...exists. Regarding the phrase "conscience (*hirī*) and shame (*ottappa*"): here, conscience has the characteristic of disgust for evil, while shame has the characteristic of fear [of it].
Whatever further detail might need to be stated regarding this has already been explained in the *Visuddhimagga*. This is the eighth [chapter]. 9.
Commentary on the *Cariyāsutta*.
9. "They protect the world" means they sustain, establish, and guard the world.
"One’s mother would not be known here" means that in this world, one's biological mother would not be recognized as "this is my mother" by way of respectful esteem.

The same principle applies to the remaining phrases as well. "Confusion" (*sambheda*) means a mixture or a breaking of boundaries, as in the case of [the confusion between] goats and sheep, and so forth.
For these beings do not recognize one another with a sense of reverence, thinking, "This is my mother," or "This is my maternal aunt.
Instead, they act with hostility toward the very source from which they were born. Therefore, bringing forward a simile, he said, "Just as goats and sheep," and so forth.
This is the ninth [chapter].
10. Commentary on the Vassūpanāyika Sutta.
The tenth [sutta] was spoken on account of a specific occasion (aṭṭhuppatti). On what occasion? On account of the complaints of the people.

For during the first twenty years after his enlightenment, the observance of the rains-retreat (vassūpanāyikā) had not been prescribed by the Blessed One. Consequently, the bhikkhus lived without a fixed residence.
They wandered about at their pleasure during the winter, the summer, and the rainy season.

Seeing them, people said, "How can these recluses, sons of the Sakyans, wander on tour during the winter, the summer, and the rainy season, trampling upon green grass, harming one-sensed living beings, and bringing many small creatures to destruction? For these [other] members of other sects..."
“They will settle and roost for the rains-retreat where the Dhamma is poorly proclaimed;
these very birds, having made their nests on the tops of trees, will settle and roost for the rains-retreat,” they said, and thus they complained.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One. Taking that as the occasion, the Blessed One spoke this discourse.
First, the Teacher said only this much: "Monks, I allow you to enter the rains residence.
Then, hearing the thought that had arisen among the monks—"When, indeed, should the rains residence be entered?"—he said:
"Monks, I allow you to enter the rains residence during the rainy season. Thereupon, it occurred to the monks: "How many..."
"Is this now the time for entering the rains-retreat? They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Having heard it, while teaching this entire discourse, he said, "Bhikkhus, there are these two," and so forth. In that context, *vassūpanāyikā* means the entries into the rains-retreat.
*Purimikā* refers to the first [entry], which should be undertaken on the day after the full moon of Āsāḷha and concludes with the full moon of the first Kattika month.

The three-month period. "The latter" means the latter three-month period beginning from the month of Āsāḷhī when it has arrived, ending with the last day of the month of Kattika; this is the latter [period]. Tenth.
The first chapter on disciplinary actions is concluded.
2. Explanation of the Chapter on Legal Issues (Adhikaraṇavagga).

11. Regarding the first [section] of the second [chapter], "The Powers": in what sense are they called powers? They are called powers in the sense of being unshakable, as well as in the sense of being difficult to overcome and in the sense of being unsubduable. "The power of reflection" is the power of reviewing. "The power of development" is the power of cultivation, the power of increase.
"A pure self"—this is according to the method already explained below.

It should be understood. "Therein" means in those two powers. "This which" means this very [power]. "This power of the trainees" means this power of knowledge (*ñāṇabala*) belonging to the seven types of trainees (*sekha*).
For it is said: "By relying on that power of the trainees, monks," referring to and depending upon the power of knowledge of the seven trainees.
"Abandons" means he abandons by means of the Path (*magga*). Furthermore, by the word "having abandoned":

The fruit has been explained. "That which is evil" means that which is wicked and base. However, because one attains arahantship by increasing both of these together, it should be understood that this [specific] "foremost" status does not apply here. 12.
Regarding the second [set], in the passages beginning with "he develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor," this [explanation] follows from the perspective of the terms not yet mentioned below.
Commentary on the meaning: *Vivekanissitam* means dependent upon seclusion (*viveka*). Seclusion (*viveka*) is the state of being secluded.

This seclusion is fivefold: seclusion by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga-viveka*), seclusion by suppression (*vikkhambhana-viveka*), seclusion by eradication (*samuccheda-viveka*), seclusion by subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi-viveka*), and seclusion by escape (*nissaraṇa-viveka*). Among these five kinds of seclusion, "dependent upon seclusion" refers to that which is dependent upon seclusion by substitution of opposites, dependent upon seclusion by eradication, and dependent upon seclusion by escape.
"One develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor"—this is how the meaning should be understood.

For when a yogi is devoted to the development of the mindfulness enlightenment factor, at the moment of insight (vipassanā), it is based on seclusion by way of function (*kicca*) and based on seclusion as escape (*nissaraṇa*) by way of aspiration (*ajjhāsaya*);
but at the time of the path (*magga*), it is based on seclusion by way of cutting off (*samuccheda*) through its function, and based on seclusion as escape through its object (*ārammaṇa*).
One develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness. Some say it is based on fivefold seclusion.

For they extract the enlightenment factors not only at the moments of powerful insight, the path, and the fruit, but also in the kasiṇa-jhānas, the ānāpāna-jhāna, the asubha-jhāna, and the brahmavihāra-jhānas that serve as the basis for insight;
nor have these been prohibited by the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathās. Therefore, according to their opinion, in these jhānas—
At the moment of its occurrence, it is based on seclusion by suppression solely by way of its function.

And just as it is said that "at the moment of insight it is based on seclusion by escape through aspiration," so too it is appropriate to say that "one develops [the path] based on seclusion by tranquillization.
This same method applies to the phrases "based on fading away" and so forth; for fading away and the rest have seclusion as their very meaning.
In this context, relinquishment (*vossagga*) is twofold: relinquishment as giving up (*pariccāga-vossagga*) and relinquishment as leaping forward (*pakkhandana-vossagga*).

Therein, relinquishment as giving up refers to the abandoning of defilements through their suppression at the moment of insight (*vipassanā*) and through their eradication at the moment of the path (*magga*).
Relinquishment as leaping forward refers to the state of being inclined toward that [nibbāna] at the moment of insight and at the moment of the path.

Furthermore, there is the leaping forward toward Nibbāna by making it the object. Both of these are appropriate within this method of explaining the meaning, which is a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane.
For in the manner already described, this mindfulness enlightenment factor abandons the defilements and leaps forward toward Nibbāna.
By the entire expression "resolving upon relinquishment," however—
This means: maturing for the sake of relinquishment and having matured;

ripening and having ripened. For this monk devoted to the development of the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), just as the mindfulness factor of enlightenment (satisambojjhaṅga) ripens for the sake of relinquishing defilements and for the sake of relinquishment that leaps toward Nibbāna, and just as it becomes fully ripened, so he [should develop it].
"He develops": this same method applies to the remaining factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*).
However, in this context, it is said that Nibbāna itself is "seclusion" (*viveka*) because it is secluded from all conditioned things (*saṅkhata*);

it is "dispassion" (*virāga*) because of the state of dispassion toward everything; and it is "cessation" (*nirodha*) because of the state of cessation. And the Path itself is "tending toward relinquishment" (*vossaggapariṇāmī*); therefore, [one develops] the mindfulness factor of enlightenment (*satisambojjhaṅga*).
One develops it by making seclusion the object, such that it occurs dependent on seclusion; likewise, it is dependent on dispassion and dependent on cessation.

Furthermore, this should be understood as meaning that it has matured and reached full development through the abandonment of the defilements by their total eradication at the moment of the arising of the Noble Path, and through its state of leaping forward toward Nibbāna.
This same method applies to the remaining factors of enlightenment. Thus...

These seven factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) are explained as being a mixture of mundane and supramundane. Regarding these two [sets of] powers (*bala*) as well, their state of being "foremost" (*etadagga*) should be understood in the same manner already described. 13.
Third: The meaning of the text and the method of cultivation for the four *jhānas* beginning with "quite secluded from sensual desires" (*vivicceva kāmehi*).
All of this has been explained in detail in every aspect in the *Visuddhimagga*.

However, these four jhānas are developed by one bhikkhu for the sake of one-pointedness of mind, another for the sake of providing a basis for insight (*vipassanā*), another for the sake of providing a basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), another for the sake of providing a basis for cessation (*nirodha*), and another for the sake of a particular state of existence. Here, however, those that provide a basis for insight are intended.
For this bhikkhu, having entered these jhānas and emerged from them,
contemplates formations, performs an investigation of causes and conditions, defines name-and-form together with its conditions, and coordinates the faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment,
thereby attains arahantship. Thus, these jhānas are described as being a mixture of both mundane and supramundane.
In this pair of powers as well, the state of being "foremost" (etadagga) is to be understood in the same manner already described. 14.
Regarding the fourth [power], the phrase "both in brief and in detail" indicates that there are only two types of Dhamma-teachings:
the teaching of the Dhamma in brief and the teaching of the Dhamma in detail. Therein, a teaching delivered after having set forth a summary outline (mātikā) is a teaching in brief.
The brief teaching is so called because it explains that very same matrix (mātikā) by way of its essential meaning.

The detailed teaching is so called because it explains that same matrix by analyzing it in detail. Alternatively, the detailed teaching is so called whether or not the matrix is first established; it is explained by analyzing it in detail.
Among these, the brief teaching is given for the sake of a person of great wisdom, while the detailed teaching is for one of duller wisdom. For one of great wisdom—
For a detailed exposition becomes like excessive prolixity. To one of dull wit, a concise exposition is like the leaping of a hare;
it is unable to reach either the end or the limit.

Furthermore, the concise exposition is taught for the sake of one who gains knowledge through a brief summary (*ugghaṭitaññū*), while the detailed exposition is for the sake of the other three types. Indeed, even the entire Tipiṭaka is a concise exposition.
"An exposition in detail" is understood here as referring to this very point.

15. In the fifth [section], "in whatever legal issue, monks"—that is, in whichever among these four legal issues: a legal issue arising from a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), a legal issue arising from an accusation (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*), a legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*), or a legal issue arising from business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*).
"And a monk who has fallen into [an offense]" means a monk who has incurred an offense. "In that regard" means in this matter.

"For the sake of long duration" means for the purpose of remaining for a long period of time. "For the sake of harshness" means for the purpose of causing the utterance of harsh speech such as "slave," "outcaste," "Caṇḍāla," or "Ven.
"For the sake of ferocity" means for the purpose of a state of cruelty by means of striking with hands, clods of earth, sticks, and so forth. And monks...
Thinking, “They will dwell in comfort,” those who— when the Saṅgha of bhikkhus has fallen into mutual dispute— are desirous of receiving the recitation or the interrogation,
or are desirous of devoting themselves to striving, they will not dwell in comfort.
For when the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies have been suspended within the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, those who need the recitation and so forth are unable to receive the recitation and so forth.
The mental state of those who practice insight (vipassanā) does not become one-pointed; consequently, they are unable to produce further distinction.
Thus, the bhikkhus will not dwell in comfort. Regarding the phrases "not for long life" and so forth, the meaning should be understood by way of the opposite of what was stated previously.
"Here" means in this teaching. "Reflects thus" means he reviews in this manner. "Has fallen into unwholesomeness" means...
Here, "unwholesome" (akusala) refers to an offense; the meaning is that he has fallen into an offense.

"A certain part" means not every single offense, but rather a certain portion of an offense, that is to say, one particular offense. "With the body" means with the physical body composed of the four elements.
"Displeased" means having a mind that is not satisfied. "Displeased speech" means speech uttered when one is dissatisfied. "Only for me" means only toward me. "Therein" means...
"In that legal matter": "Transgression has overtaken me" means that the offense has passed over and crushed him;

"I alone am the offender here. "As with a tax-payer regarding his goods" means that just as when goods are carried away by avoiding the place of taxation, the offense of the tax-payer prevails, and he alone is the offender there—not the kings, nor the king’s men—this is the meaning.
This is what is meant: Suppose a man avoids a toll-station established by a king and carries away his goods;

they bring him back together with the cart of goods and present him to the king. In that case, there is no fault on the part of the toll-station, nor on the part of the king, nor on the part of the king’s men;
rather, the fault lies solely with the one who went by way of evasion. Even so it is with that bhikkhu.
When one has fallen into an offense, there is neither fault in the offense itself nor in the accuser. However, for three reasons, the fault lies with that very bhikkhu:

first, there is fault because he has fallen into the offense; second, there is fault because he is displeased with the accuser; and third, there is fault because, being displeased, he reports it to others. As for the accuser, when that [bhikkhu] falls into such an offense...
There is no fault in seeing [the offense]; rather, there is a fault in reproaching [another] out of displeasure.

Disregarding even that, this bhikkhu, reflecting upon his own fault, contemplates thus: "In this matter, transgression has indeed overtaken me, just as it did for the one who paid the toll regarding the goods.
This is the meaning. In the second instance, there is also the displeasure of the reproacher.

There are two faults: the state of being reproved due to dissatisfaction. By means of these, the application of the phrase "transgression has overcome me" should be made here. The rest here is self-evident.
In the sixth [sutta], "a certain one" refers to a brahmin whose name was not well-known. "Went to where the Blessed One was": as for "where,"...
The instrumental case is used in the sense of the locative. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: "He approached where the Blessed One was.
Or, the meaning should be seen as: "He approached for that reason by which the Blessed One is to be approached by gods and humans. And for what reason is the Blessed One to be approached?
It is like a great tree that bears fruit constantly because it is frequented by flocks of birds who desire to obtain its various excellent qualities and to enjoy its sweet fruit.
"Upasaṅkami" (he approached) means "he went. "Upasaṅkamitvā" (having approached) indicates the completion of the act of approaching.
Alternatively, it also means that having gone in this manner, he proceeded to a place even closer than before, which is reckoned as the vicinity of the Blessed One.
"He exchanged greetings with the Blessed One" means that just as the Blessed One was asking him about his health and well-being, so too did he share a mutual joy with the Blessed One;
like cold water meeting hot water, they mingled and attained a state of unity.
And by that [greeting], "I hope, Master Gotama, you are faring well? I hope you are keeping well? I hope, Master Gotama... [he asked].
He exchanged greetings with him through such conversation as, "May you and your disciples be free from illness, free from affliction, physically light, strong, and living in comfort.
This [discourse] is called *sammodanīya* (conducive to greeting) because it generates *sammoda*—which consists of joy and gladness—and because it is appropriate for greeting.
Furthermore, due to the sweetness of its meaning and phrasing, it can be sustained and maintained continuously for a very long time.

It is "conducive to recollection" (*sāraṇīya*) because it is worthy of being remembered and because its nature is to be recalled. Alternatively, it is "delightful" (*sammodanīya*) because it is pleasant while being heard, and "conducive to recollection" because it is pleasant when being recollected;
likewise, it is "delightful" due to the purity of its phrasing (*byañjana*), and "conducive to recollection" due to the purity of its meaning (*attha*).
Having thus exchanged such delightful and memorable discourse through many such methods, having brought it to a conclusion and finalized it—
Desiring to ask about the purpose for which he had come, he sat down to one side.
The term *ekamantaṃ* is a neuter locative designation, as in such expressions as "the moon and sun move unevenly.
Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: he sat down in such a manner that he was seated to one side.
Or rather, this is the accusative case used in the sense of the locative. "He sat down" means he entered [the presence].
For wise men, having approached one who occupies a position of honor, sit to one side due to their skill in the etiquette of seating. And since he was one among them, he sat down to one side.
But how does one sitting become "sitting to one side"? By avoiding the six faults of sitting. Namely as follows:
—Too far away, too close, in the wind, on high ground, directly in front, or directly behind.
For if one sits too far away and wishes to speak, one must speak in a loud voice.
If one sits too close, one causes physical contact. If one sits in the wind, one is troubled by the odor of the body. If one sits on high ground...
He displays a lack of respect. If he sits too close and wishes to see [the teacher], he must gaze directly from eye to eye;
if he sits too far back and wishes to see, he must stretch out his neck to look.
Therefore, he sat having avoided these six faults of sitting. Thus it is said: "He sat to one side."
"He spoke thus": for there are two kinds of questions—the question of a householder and the question of one who is homeless. Among these, the question of a householder comes down in the manner of:
"Venerable sir, what is wholesome? What is unwholesome? The question of one who is homeless comes down in the manner of: "Venerable sir, are these the five aggregates of clinging?
But this [questioner], asking a question appropriate to himself as a householder, said:
He spoke these words beginning with, "What, Master Gotama, is the cause, what is the condition? In this context, both "cause" (*hetu*) and "condition" (*paccaya*) are merely synonyms for a reason.
"With unrighteous conduct and improper conduct as the cause" means with the cause consisting of improper conduct known as unrighteous conduct;
the meaning is: having that as its cause, having that as its condition. Herein, the word-meaning is as follows: of unrighteousness (*adhamma*)...
*Adhammacariyā* means conduct contrary to the Dhamma; that is, unrighteous conduct. *Visamacariyā* means uneven conduct, or the practice of uneven (improper) action.
Thus, it is "unrighteous and uneven conduct" (*adhammacariyāvisamacariyā*).
By this same method, the meaning should be understood for the bright side as well. As for the actual meaning here, it is unrighteous and uneven conduct.

The ten unwholesome courses of action (akusalakammapathā) should be understood as such; the ten wholesome courses of action (kusalakammapathā), namely the practice of Dhamma and the practice of equanimity (dhammacariyāsamacariyā), should be understood as such.

Regarding the phrase "Excellent, Master Gotama," here this word *abhikkanta* is seen in the senses of excellence (*khaya*), beauty (*sundara*), loveliness (*abhirūpa*), and rejoicing (*abbhanumodana*). For example, in such passages as:
"Venerable sir, the night has passed; the first watch has ended; the community of monks has been sitting for a long time."

For it is seen in the sense of destruction (*khaya*): “This one is more excellent and more sublime than these four persons,” and so forth. It is used in the sense of beautiful (*sundara*) in such passages as:
“Who is saluting my feet, shining with the glory of psychic power, illuminating all directions with his most excellent complexion?”—thus it is said.

In such contexts as these, it means "excellent. In expressions such as “It is excellent, venerable sir” (*abhikkantaṃ, bhante*), it signifies approval. Here too, it is used specifically for approval. Since it is used for approval, it should be understood that what is being said is: “Excellent, excellent, Master Gotama!
“A wise person should employ repetition (*āmeḍita*) in cases of fear, anger, praise, haste, curiosity, distress, laughter, sorrow, and faith.”

And by this characteristic, it should be understood that this [word] is stated twice here: once by way of confidence and once by way of praise. Alternatively, "abhikkanta" means "excellent," "very desirable," "very agreeable," or "extremely beautiful.
In this context, he praises the teaching with one instance of the word "abhikkanta" and his own confidence with the other.
This is the intended meaning here: "Excellent, O Gotama, is this Dhamma-teaching of Master Gotama; excellent indeed!"
"That is, my confidence has arisen by coming to Master Gotama’s teaching of the Dhamma.

Or rather, he praises the Blessed One’s own words by referring to two pairs of meanings: "Master Gotama’s word is excellent" because it destroys faults and because it brings about the attainment of qualities;
likewise, because it generates faith and because it generates wisdom, and because it is meaningful and well-phrased.
It should be applied by means of such qualities as: having clear words, profound meaning, being pleasant to the ear,
reaching the heart, not exalting oneself, not disparaging others, being cooled by compassion, being purified by wisdom, being delightful upon first hearing,
being able to withstand scrutiny, being pleasant while being heard, and being beneficial when investigated.
Beyond that, he further extols the teaching itself by means of four similes. In this context: "upturned" (*nikkujjita*) means placed face-downward or having its opening turned downward;
"he would turn up" (*ukkujjeyya*) means he would make it face upward. "Concealed" (*paṭicchanna*) means covered over with grass, leaves, and so forth;

"he would uncover" (*vivareyya*) means he would remove [the covering]. "Of one who is lost" (*mūḷhassa*) means of one who is confused about the directions; "he would point out the path" (*maggaṃ ācikkheyya*) means [pointing it out] while taking him by the hand.

“He would say, ‘This is the path. Regarding “in darkness”: this refers to the fourfold darkness consisting of the dark fortnight, the fourteenth day of the lunar month, midnight, and dense forest thickets or masses of clouds. This, first of all, is the literal meaning of the words.

However, this is the interpretation according to the underlying intention: just as someone might set upright what had been overturned, so too [the Buddha] [sets upright those who were] turned away from the True Dhamma.
By raising me up from unrighteousness (asaddhamma) to which I had fallen;
by revealing the teaching that had been concealed by the thicket of wrong views since the disappearance of the Blessed One Kassapa’s dispensation, just as one would uncover what is hidden;
and by pointing out the path to one who is lost, just as one would show the way to one who has entered upon a bypath or a wrong path.
By revealing to me the path to heaven and liberation— just as one might hold up an oil lamp in the dark—

my Lord Gotama has revealed the Dhamma in many ways, because he has manifested it through these various methods for me, who was submerged in the darkness of delusion and unable to see the forms of the Jewels beginning with the Buddha, by holding aloft the lamp of the teaching that destroys the darkness of delusion which obscures them.
Having thus praised the teaching, and manifesting his confidence in the Triple Gem through this teaching, he said, "I go to him for refuge," and so forth.

Therein, "I go to him" (*esāhaṃ*) means "this I. "I go to the venerable Gotama for refuge" (*bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi*) means that the venerable Gotama is my refuge and ultimate resort, with the intention: "He is the protector from suffering and the provider of welfare. The venerable...
"I go to Gotama; I resort to him, I serve him, I attend upon him; thus I know, thus I awaken.
For those verbal roots whose meaning is "going," their meaning is also "awakening. Therefore, for the word "I go," the meaning "I know, I awaken" is stated.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the Dhamma and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus," here [it refers to] one who has attained the path and realized cessation.
It is called *dhamma* because it sustains one who practices according to the instruction and prevents one from falling into the four states of misery.

In its essential meaning, it consists of both the Noble Eightfold Path and Nibbāna. For this has been said in detail: "Bhikkhus, to whatever extent there are conditioned phenomena, the Noble Eightfold Path is declared the foremost among them. And it is not only the Noble Path and Nibbāna that constitute it.
Moreover, the Dhamma of the scriptures is also included along with the Noble Fruits. For this has been said in the *Chattamāṇavaka-vimāna*:
“Seek refuge in this Dhamma—sweet, skillful, well-expounded, stainless, free from passion, griefless, unconditioned, and not repulsive.”
Here, "freedom from passion" refers to the Path. "The stainless and griefless" refers to the Fruit. "The unconditioned Dhamma" refers to Nibbāna.
"This non-repulsive, sweet, skillful, and well-analyzed" refers to all the aggregates of Dhamma analyzed by means of the Three Piṭakas.

"United by the combination of view and virtue" refers to the Saṅgha; in its actual meaning, it is the assembly of the eight noble persons (ariya-puggala). For this has been stated in that very same Vimānavatthu:
“And where they say a gift yields great fruit, among the four pure pairs of persons;
those eight individuals who are seers of the Dhamma—to this Saṅgha, go for refuge.
Here, the community of monks is the *bhikkhusaṅgha*. At this point, the brahmin had declared his threefold going for refuge.

Now, for the sake of proficiency regarding those acts of going for refuge, this method should be understood: namely, refuge, the act of going for refuge, he who goes for refuge, the classification of going for refuge, the fruit of going for refuge, its defilement, and its breach.

To explain: first, in terms of the meaning of the words, it "destroys" (saraṇa), which means that by that very act of going for refuge, it destroys and eliminates fear, terror, suffering, and the defilement of miserable rebirths for those who have gone for refuge; this refers specifically to the Triple Gem.
This is a synonym. Alternatively, he is called the Buddha because he destroys (*hiṃsati*) the fear of sentient beings by promoting their welfare and withdrawing them from what is harmful;
the Dhamma because it delivers the world from the wilderness of existence and bestows consolation;
and the Saṅgha because it causes one to obtain vast fruits even from small deeds. Therefore, by this method as well, the Triple Gem is a refuge.

The arising of consciousness that proceeds in the mode of taking those [Three Jewels] as its supreme object—having dispelled the defilements through faith, satisfaction, and reverence—is "going for refuge.
The being endowed with that [consciousness] goes for refuge; the meaning is that he approaches them with such an arising of consciousness, thinking: "These Three Jewels are my refuge;
these are my supreme resort. Thus, first of all, the refuge and the going for refuge are defined.
And when one goes for refuge, this should be understood as follows.
Regarding the classification of going for refuge, there are two kinds of going for refuge: supramundane (*lokuttara*) and mundane (*lokiya*).

Therein, the supramundane occurs at the moment of the path for those who have seen the Truths; through the complete eradication of the defilements of going for refuge, it has Nibbāna as its object (*ārammaṇa*).
Having performed it according to its function, it succeeds even with respect to the entire Triple Gem.

For worldlings, the mundane going for refuge succeeds by way of its object through the suppression of the defilements, having the qualities of the Buddha and the others as its object. In terms of meaning, this is the acquisition of faith in the bases such as the Buddha;
and right view rooted in faith is called "rectification of view" (*diṭṭhijukamma*) among the ten bases of meritorious action.
That [going for refuge] occurs in four ways: by surrendering oneself, by making that one’s ultimate resort, by entering into the state of a pupil, and by prostrating.
Therein, "surrendering oneself" means the relinquishing of oneself to the Buddha and the others, thinking:
"Starting from today, I surrender myself to the Buddha, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha. "Making that one’s ultimate resort" [is as follows]:...
“Taking today as the beginning, consider me one who has the Buddha as his ultimate resort, the Dhamma as his ultimate resort, and the Saṅgha as his ultimate resort”—
this is the state of having them as one’s ultimate resort. “Taking today as the beginning, consider me a pupil of the Buddha,
a pupil of the Dhamma, and a pupil of the Saṅgha”— this is the entering into the state of being a pupil.

Prostration (*paṇipāta*) means: "Starting from today, may you consider me as one who performs only the three acts of homage—namely, salutation, rising to greet, joining the palms, and respectful service—toward the Buddha and the other two [the Dhamma and the Saṅgha]. Such is the supreme act of self-surrender toward the Buddha and the others.
For by performing even one of these four modes, the going for refuge is indeed taken.
Furthermore, "I surrender myself to the Blessed One; I surrender myself to the Dhamma;
I surrender myself to the Saṅgha; I surrender my life; my very self is surrendered, my very life is surrendered;
for as long as life lasts, I go for refuge to the Buddha; the Buddha is my refuge, my shelter, my protection"—this too is the surrendering of oneself.

It should be understood that entering into discipleship is to be seen as being like Mahākassapa’s going for refuge, [expressed] thus: “If only I might see the Teacher, I would see the Blessed One; if only I might see the Sugata, I would see the Blessed One; if only I might see the Perfectly Enlightened One, I would see the Blessed One.”
“Thus I shall wander from village to village, from town to town, paying homage to the Fully Enlightened One and to the sublime nature of the Dhamma.
In this way, one’s taking of refuge should be understood as having that as one’s ultimate goal, just like the taking of refuge by Āḷavaka and others. Then Brahmāyu...

The brahmin rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, prostrated with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, kissed the Blessed One’s feet with his mouth, stroked them with his hands, and announced his name:
“I am Brahmāyu, Master Gotama, a brahmin; I am Brahmāyu, Master Gotama, a brahmin. In this way, too, prostration is to be understood.

Furthermore, this [going for refuge] is fourfold, according to relatives, fear, teachers, and those worthy of offerings. Among these, going for refuge occurs through prostration to one worthy of offerings, and not by the others.
For one takes refuge on the basis of what is supreme, and one breaks [the refuge] on the basis of what is supreme.
Therefore, if a Sākiyan or a Koliyan pays homage thinking, "The Buddha is our relative," that [refuge] is certainly not taken.
It becomes a refuge. Or, if one pays homage out of fear, thinking, “The ascetic Gotama is honored by kings and possesses great power;

if he were not saluted, he might even cause me harm,” that refuge is not truly taken. Or, if one remembers something learned in the presence of the Blessed One during his time as a Bodhisatta, or [remembers it] at the time of his Buddhahood—
“One should enjoy wealth with one part, employ two parts in work, and set aside the fourth as a reserve for times of misfortune.

Having received such instruction and thinking, “He is my teacher,” one pays homage; yet the taking of refuge has not actually occurred. However, if one pays homage thinking, “This one is the foremost person worthy of offerings in the world,” by that very act the taking of refuge is accomplished.

For a lay follower (upāsaka) or a female lay follower (upāsikā) who has thus taken refuge, the taking of refuge is not broken even when they pay homage to a relative who has gone forth among other sects, thinking, "This one is my kinsman," let alone one who has not gone forth.
Likewise, it is not broken when paying homage to a king out of fear; for since he is honored by the whole kingdom, if he were not paid homage, he might even cause harm. Likewise...
Even for one who pays homage to a teacher of any craft or to a member of another sect (titthiya), thinking, "This is my teacher," the refuge does not fail;
thus should the classification of going for refuge be understood.

And herein, regarding supramundane going for refuge, the four fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala) are the fruit of ripening (vipākaphala), while the destruction of all suffering is the fruit of benefit (ānisaṃsaphala). For this has been said:
“But whoever has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha,
sees the Four Noble Truths with right wisdom:
suffering, the origin of suffering, and the transcending of suffering.”
And the Noble Eightfold Path, which leads to the stilling of suffering.
"This indeed is the secure refuge, this is the supreme refuge;
by coming to this refuge, one is liberated from all suffering."
Furthermore, its beneficial fruit should be understood by way of not falling into [the view of] permanence and so forth. For this has been said:

"It is impossible, monks, it is out of the question, that a person endowed with right view should regard any conditioned phenomenon as permanent, should regard anything as pleasant, or should regard any state as a self; or [that he would deprive his mother of life]..."

“...to kill one’s mother, to kill one’s father, to kill an arahant, with a malicious mind to draw blood from a Tathāgata, to cause a schism in the Saṅgha, or to acknowledge another teacher—this is impossible.
However, for the mundane going for refuge, even the attainment of existence and the attainment of wealth are indeed its fruits. For it has been said:
“Whoever has gone for refuge to the Buddha will not go to the plane of misery;
having cast off the human body, they will attain the state of the devas.”
“They will fulfill the body of a god.
Furthermore, it is said:
“Then Sakka, lord of the devas, together with eighty thousand deities, approached the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna...”
He approached him... [as before] ...and stood to one side. As he was standing there, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this to Sakka, lord of the devas:
“It is good, lord of the devas, to go for refuge to the Buddha.
It is because of going for refuge to the Buddha, lord of the devas, that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.”
“They are reborn there. They surpass other devas in ten respects:
in divine lifespan, divine beauty, happiness, fame, sovereignty, and divine forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles.

This same method applies to the Dhamma and the Saṅgha as well. Furthermore, the specific fruits of going for refuge should be understood by way of the Velāma Sutta and others. Thus should the fruit of going for refuge be understood.
In that regard, the mundane going for refuge is defiled by ignorance, doubt, wrong knowledge, and so forth regarding the three objects;
it is neither of great radiance nor of great extension. For the supramundane [going for refuge], there is no defilement.
Furthermore, the mundane going for refuge has a twofold breach: blameworthy and blameless. Among these, the blameworthy occurs with respect to other teachers and so forth.
It occurs through such acts as surrendering oneself; that has an undesirable fruit. Death while free from fault is without fruit because it lacks karmic ripening.
However, for one who has transcended the world (lokuttara), there is no schism at all; for even in another existence, a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka) does not designate another teacher.
Thus should the defilement and the schism of going for refuge be understood.
"May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower"—the meaning is that Master Gotama should hold me as "this one is a lay follower," and thus know me as such.
Furthermore, for the sake of proficiency in the rules for lay followers, this supplementary matter should be understood here: who is a lay follower? Why is he called a lay follower?
What is his virtue? What is his livelihood? What is his failure? And what is his success?
In this context, who is a lay follower (*upāsaka*)? Any householder who has gone for refuge. For it is said:
“Mahānāma, when a lay follower has gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and gone for refuge to the Saṅgha—it is by this much, Mahānāma, that one is a lay follower.

Why is he called a lay follower? Because of his attendance upon (*upāsana*) the Triple Gem. For he attends upon the Buddha, thus he is a lay follower; he attends upon the Dhamma and the Saṅgha, thus he is a lay follower.
"What is his virtue? It consists of the five abstinences. As it is said:

"Insofar as, Mahānāma, a lay follower abstains from the destruction of life, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence—to this extent, Mahānāma, a lay follower is virtuous."
What is right livelihood? It is the maintenance of one’s life by means that are lawful and righteous, having abandoned the five kinds of wrong trade. For this has been said:
“Monks, there are these five trades that should not be practiced by a lay follower. Which five?
Trade in weapons, trade in living beings, trade in meat, trade in intoxicants, and trade in poisons. These, monks, are the five trades that should not be practiced by a lay follower.”
"What is failure? It is the failure of that very virtue and livelihood; this is his failure.
Furthermore, it should be understood that whatever makes him an outcaste (*caṇḍāla*), as well as impure and contemptible, is also his failure.
And in terms of their actual nature, these consist of five factors, beginning with lack of faith (*assaddhiya*). As it is said:

“Bhikkhus, possessing five qualities, a lay follower is a candāla among lay followers, a stain among lay followers, and one who is despised among lay followers. What are the five? He is faithless; he is immoral;
he is superstitious and believes in omens rather than in kamma; he seeks outside this teaching for those worthy of offerings. Therein...”
“And he performs meritorious deeds.

What is success? That which consists of his perfection of virtue (*sīlasampadā*) and perfection of livelihood (*ājīvasampadā*) is success. And there are the five qualities beginning with faith (*saddhā*), which produce the state of being a jewel and so forth. As it is said:
“Bhikkhus, an upāsaka endowed with five qualities is a jewel among upāsakas and a lotus among upāsakas.”
And the *Upāsakapuṇḍarīka*. By which five? He is endowed with faith; he is virtuous; he does not regard superstitious omens as auspicious;
he has conviction in karma rather than in omens; he does not seek those worthy of offerings outside this [Dhamma];
and he performs meritorious deeds here first.”

In the phrase *ajjatagge*, this word *agga* is seen to mean "beginning," "extremity," "portion," and "best. For instance, in such passages as, "From this day forward (*ajjatagge*), friend gatekeeper, I close the door to the Nigaṇṭhas and Nigaṇṭhīs," it is used in the sense of a beginning.

In such passages as, "He might touch that tip of the finger with that very tip of the finger; the tip of a sugar-cane, the tip of a bamboo," it is used in the sense of an extremity. In [the passage], "The tip of a mango... [it is used in the sense of a portion].

In such passages as, "I allow you, monks, to divide it by the portion of the monastery or by the portion of the cell—whether it be the sweetest part or the bitterest part," *agga* refers to a portion (*koṭṭhāsa*).
In such passages as, "Monks, whatever beings there are, whether footless... the Tathāgata is declared the foremost among them," *agga* refers to the best (*seṭṭha*).
However, here it should be understood in its first sense. Therefore, *ajjatagge* means "from today onwards" (*ajjatan-taṃ*).

"Taking this as the beginning"—this is how the meaning should be understood here. "Ajjatan" (today) means the state of being today. Alternatively, the reading is "ajjadagge," where the letter *da* is used for euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*); the meaning is "taking today as the limit.
"Pāṇupetaṃ" means accompanied by life; that is, as long as my life continues, it remains so, with no other teacher.
"May the venerable Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge with the threefold going-for-refuge, knowing me as one who makes what is allowable.

For even if someone were to cut off my head with a sharp sword, I would never say of the Buddha, 'He is not the Buddha,' or of the Dhamma, 'It is not the Dhamma,' or of the Saṅgha, 'It is not the Saṅgha. Thus [he spoke] by way of surrendering himself.

Having gone for refuge and having invited [the Blessed One] to accept the four requisites, he rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him three times keeping him to his right, and departed.
17. Regarding "Jāṇussoṇī": it is said that immediately after the position of Jāṇussoṇī there is another position; by which family [that name originated].
That which was obtained is called the *Jāṇussoṇi* clan. This [person] is called *Jāṇussoṇi* because he was born into that clan and because he received honor from the king [named] Jāṇussoṇi.
“He approached him” means: having heard that “the ascetic Gotama is indeed wise, competent, and learned,” [he thought], “If he knows the distinctions of gender, case, and agent...”
"He will know only what we already know; what will he know that is unknown? He will speak only of what we already know; what will he say that is unknown?
Having thought thus, raising the banner of pride and lifting his horn, surrounded by a great retinue, he approached the Blessed One.
And when the Teacher [spoke] those words, "Because of what has been done, O Brahmin, and because of what has not been done... [the Brahmin departed].
Having heard this, [the Blessed One] thought: "This brahmin did not come here desiring to know or seeking the goal;

rather, he came having taken up pride and raised his banner. Now, will there be growth for him if I speak according to how he understands the meaning of the question, or rather, if I speak according to how he does not understand it? Thinking thus, [he concluded]: "Since he does not understand..."
When this was said, [the Blessed One], knowing that "growth will come about," replied, "It is, O brahmin, both because of what has been done and because of what has not been done.
Having heard this, the brahmin thought, "The ascetic Gotama speaks of rebirth in hell both because of what has been done and because of what has not been done;
since he speaks of rebirth in one place due to both these causes, it is a profound darkness difficult to understand. There is no..."
This is my standing ground. However, if I were to remain silent after this much, even while speaking in the midst of the brahmins, they would say to me:
"You went into the presence of the ascetic Gotama having taken up pride and raised your horn;
yet, at the very first word, you became silent and were unable to say anything—why do you speak now at this place?"
"Therefore, though I have been defeated, I shall act as if undefeated and ask again about the question of going to heaven," he thought, and thus he began this second question:
"Sir Gotama, who is it? He also reflected:
"By means of the subsequent question I will know the preceding one, and by means of the preceding question the subsequent one."

For that reason as well, he asked this question. The Teacher, reflecting in the same manner as before, spoke again, saying, "Because of what has been done, O Brahmin, and because of what has not been done," even while speaking in such a way that [the Brahmin] did not understand.
Unable to establish himself even on that point, the Brahmin said, "Enough, sir! It is not fitting for one who has come into the presence of such a person to depart without having understood."

Having made the resolution, “Abandoning my own doctrine and following the ascetic Gotama, I shall seek my own welfare and clear the path to the world beyond,” he addressed the Teacher, saying, “It is not I, indeed,” and so forth.
Then, perceiving that his pride had been humbled, the Teacher, expanding upon the teaching, said, “In that case, Brahmin,” and so forth. Therein:
"By that" (*tena hi*) is an indication of the reason. The meaning is: "Because you, not understanding the meaning of what was spoken in brief, request a detailed exposition.
The rest here is of obvious meaning.
In the eighth [lesson], "Venerable" (*āyasmā*) is a term of endearment. "Ānanda" is the name of that elder. "Unilaterally" (*ekamsena*) means "absolutely."
*Anuvicca* means having entered into [the matter]. *Viññū* means wise ones. *Garahanti* means they censure; they speak dispraise.
The rest here, as well as everything in the ninth [chapter], is of plain meaning.
In the tenth, regarding the phrase "words and syllables ill-placed": for it is precisely the textual passage (*pāḷi*) taken out of its proper sequence that [constitutes] the meaning.
Because it consists of phrasing, it is called "phrasing. Both of these are names for the *pāḷi* itself.
The commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) has been taken out of order by being reversed; thus, it is said: "Monks, when the words and phrasing are poorly set down, the meaning is also wrongly interpreted.
The commentary on the *pāḷi* that has been taken out of order by being reversed is what is meant by "wrongly interpreted."
It is called "difficult to bring out" and "badly spoken. The meaning should be understood according to the method stated as the opposite of that in the eleventh [chapter].
The second section, the Chapter on Legal Issues (*Adhikaraṇavagga*), ends here.
3. Commentary on the Chapter on Fools (*Bālavagga*).

22. Regarding the first [offense] of the third [category]: "He does not see his transgression as a transgression" means that he does not see his own fault, thinking, "Though I have offended, I have not offended.
The meaning is that having said, "I have offended," he brings forth a punitive act and does not ask for forgiveness.
"Of one confessing a transgression" means of one who, having spoken thus and brought forth a punitive act, asks for forgiveness. "In accordance with the Dhamma" (yathādhammaṃ).
"He does not accept" means that when being told, "I will not do this again;
forgive me," he does not accept this transgression according to the Dhamma and according to its true nature. He does not say, "From now on, do not do such a thing again;
I forgive you. The white side (the virtuous course) is to be understood by the method of the opposite of what has been stated.
23. "In the second [case], 'misrepresenting' means they speak having overcome [the truth]; they speak what is untrue.

'One with internal hatred' means one in whom hatred has fallen within. For such a person, like Sunakkhatta, who says things such as 'The ascetic Gotama possesses no superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma),' misrepresents the Tathāgata. Or, 'one who is faithful but misapprehends' refers to one who..."
One who possesses excessive faith based on a faith devoid of knowledge is blindly devoted;

he, having grasped things wrongly by such lines of reasoning as, "The one called Buddha is supreme over the whole world, and all his thirty-two parts, beginning with the hair, are likewise supreme," misrepresents the Tathāgata. The third [section] is of plain meaning.
25. Regarding the fourth point, "a discourse of interpretable meaning" (*neyyattha-suttanta*): that whose meaning must be led [to its conclusion] is a discourse of interpretable meaning.
"A discourse of definitive meaning" (*nītattha-suttanta*) means it is explained that the meaning stated here is the discourse itself.
In this regard: "There is one person, monks; these two persons, monks; these three persons, monks; these four persons, monks..."
A discourse such as this, beginning with "individuals," is called *neyyattha* (of interpretable meaning).

For although it was spoken by the Perfectly Enlightened One, saying "Bhikkhus, there is one individual," and so forth, its meaning must nevertheless be led [to its true sense] in this way: that from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*), no such thing as an "individual" exists.
Yet, due to his own ignorance, he claims, "This discourse is of direct meaning (*nītattha*). For, from the perspective of ultimate reality—
If the person (*puggala*) did not exist, the Tathāgata would not have said such things as, "Bhikkhus, there is one person...

Since he has indeed spoken thus, one who grasps that the person exists in the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*) demonstrates that this sutta of indirect meaning (*neyyattha*) is actually a sutta of direct meaning (*nītattha*).
"Of direct meaning" means having a meaning explained in such terms as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self. Herein—
The meaning is: "Indeed, it is only impermanent, only suffering, and only non-self. However, due to his own foolishness, one who grasps this sutta—thinking, "This sutta is of interpretable meaning;

I shall bring forth its meaning"—and asserts that "there is such a thing as permanence, there is such a thing as pleasure, and there is such a thing as a self," is merely illustrating that a sutta of definitive meaning is actually a sutta of interpretable meaning. The fifth [point] has its meaning already explained.
27. In the sixth [verse], "one of concealed conduct" (*paṭicchannakammanta*) refers to one of evil deeds. For they perform evil deeds while concealing them.
Even if they do not conceal them while performing them, the evil deed is still said to be "concealed. "Hell" (*niraya*) refers to the aggregates (*khandha*) that share a common location.
Only the aggregates are found in the animal realm (*tiracchānayoni*). The seventh and eighth [verses] have meanings that are self-evident.
30. In the ninth [section], "receivers" (*paṭiggāhaka*) means those who receive; the meaning is that they receive two things from an immoral person (*dussīla-puggala*).
31. In the tenth, "for a purpose" (*atthavasena*) means for reasons. "Forest and jungle-thickets" (*araññavanapatthāni*) means forests (*araññāni*) and jungle-thickets (*vanapatthāni*).

Regarding this, although in the Abhidhamma it is stated in the non-figurative sense (*nippariyāyena*) that "having gone out beyond the threshold of the gate, all this is forest," [the term is used here in its conventional sense].

Although it has been stated thus, nevertheless, it should be understood that what is intended is precisely that lodging which produces the "forest-dweller's" status, described as "fifty cubits from the village boundary.
*Vanapattha* means a place beyond the vicinity of a village where people do not frequent, where there is no plowing or sowing. *Pantāni* means remote, being far away and on the outskirts.
“A dwelling in happiness in this very life” means a comfortable dwelling, both mundane and supramundane.
“Out of compassion for future generations” means out of compassion for my future disciples.

32. In the eleventh [section], “pertaining to true knowledge” (*vijjābhāgiya*) means belonging to the category of true knowledge. “Tranquility” (*samatha*) is one-pointedness of mind. “Insight” (*vipassanā*) is...
The knowledge that comprehends formations: what benefit does it experience? That is to say, what purpose does it achieve, accomplish, and fulfill?
"The mind is developed" means the path-consciousness is developed, cultivated, and increased.
"Whatever lust there is, that is abandoned" means whatever lust exists by way of passion, that is abandoned; for lust is the adversary of path-consciousness, and the path-consciousness...
And regarding lust (*rāga*): at the moment of lust, the path-consciousness (*maggacitta*) does not exist; at the moment of the path-consciousness, lust does not exist.
When lust arises, it prevents the arising of the path-consciousness and cuts off its progress.
But when the path-consciousness arises, it arises only while uprooting and utterly eradicating lust along with its very root.
Therefore it was said: "Lust is abandoned.
When it is said, "Vipassanā, bhikkhus, has been developed," this means that the knowledge of vipassanā has been cultivated, increased, and expanded.
When it is said, "Wisdom is developed," this means that path-wisdom is developed, cultivated, and increased. That which is ignorance is abandoned in these eight instances.
The great ignorance rooted in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is abandoned. For ignorance is the adversary of path-wisdom (*maggapaññā*), and path-wisdom is the adversary of ignorance.
At the moment of ignorance, path-wisdom is absent; at the moment of path-wisdom, ignorance is absent.
When ignorance arises, it prevents the arising of path-wisdom and cuts off its footing. When path-wisdom [arises...]
When it arises, it arises as if uprooting and utterly eradicating ignorance along with its root. Therefore it is said:
"Ignorance is abandoned. Thus, both the path-consciousness and path-wisdom are spoken of as two co-nascent states (*sahajātadhamma*).
"Bhikkhus, a mind defiled by lust is not liberated"—because it is defiled by lust, the path-consciousness...
He shows that one is not liberated. Or, "wisdom defiled by ignorance is not cultivated" means he shows that because it is defiled by ignorance, the wisdom of the path is not cultivated.
"Thus indeed, monks"—that is, in this way, monks.

"The liberation of mind through the fading away of lust" means that through the destruction and fading away of lust, there comes to be what is called liberation of mind; this is a name for the concentration of fruition (*phalasamādhi*).
"Liberation through wisdom by the fading away of ignorance" means that liberation through wisdom comes about through the destruction and fading away of ignorance.
In this sutta, concentration and insight are described as occurring at different moments.
This is the third chapter, the Chapter on the Fool.
4. Explanation of the Chapter on Even-mindedness (Samacittavagga) 33.

Regarding the first [sutta] of the fourth [chapter]: "The plane of the bad person" (*asappurisabhūmi*) means the place where bad persons are established. The same method applies to "the plane of the good person" (*sappurisabhūmi*).

"Ungrateful" (*akataññū*) means one who does not recognize what has been done for them. "One who does not acknowledge what has been done" (*akatavedī*) means one who does not recognize what has been done by making it manifest.
"Upaññātaṃ" means praised, extolled, lauded, and commended. "Yadidaṃ" means this which.
"Akataññutā akataveditā" refers both to the lack of recognition of a benefit conferred by another and to the failure to acknowledge it openly. "Kevalā" means entire.
The meaning in the white category (the wholesome side) should also be understood according to the same method already stated.
34. "In the second [case], 'mother and father' means the biological mother and the biological father.
'With one shoulder, monks, he should carry his mother,' means that having placed his mother on one shoulder-peak, he should attend to her.
'With one shoulder, he should carry his father,' means that having placed his father on one shoulder-peak, he should attend to him. [Even if] he were to live for a hundred years..."
"One who lives for a hundred years" means one born at a time when the lifespan is a hundred years, living out that full century. This is what is meant:

even if a son were to rise up again and again with the thought, "I shall repay my mother and father," and were to carry his mother on his right shoulder and his father on his left, living for a full hundred years with a lifespan of a hundred years—if he were to carry them in this way for the whole of that century.
"And by anointing, massaging, bathing, and rubbing them": that son, while standing right on the shoulders of his parents,
[provides] anointing with fragrant substances for the purpose of removing foul odors, massaging with the hands for the purpose of dispelling fatigue,
and bathing with warm water and cold water during times of cold and heat respectively.
One might attend to them by massaging their hands, feet, and so forth—
what is known as pulling and rubbing. And even if those parents were to void urine and excrement right there while sitting upon his shoulders,
monks, even by this much, one has not done or repaid what was done for one’s mother and father.

He spoke thus with reference specifically to the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti-rājya*) among the lordly dominions. "Nourishers" (*āpādaka*) means those who cause growth and protectors;

for sons are indeed caused to grow and protected by their mother and father. "Sustainers" (*posaka*) means those who sustain them by developing their hands and feet and feeding them the blood of their own hearts;
for sons are indeed nurtured, supported, and cared for by their mother and father with food, drink, and so forth. Of this...

"Showerers of the world": for if parents were to take their child by the feet on the very day of birth and throw him into the forest, a river, or a precipice, he would not see the desirable or undesirable objects in this world.
Because they did not do so, but instead nurtured and supported him, it is the parents who [show him] the desirable and undesirable objects in this world.
"He sees by depending [on them]" means that they are his guides who show him this world. "He encourages" means he causes them to take up [the practice].
In this sutta, faith, virtue, generosity, and wisdom are spoken of as a mixture of mundane and supramundane.
It should be understood that a monk similar to the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, is the one who establishes others in these qualities.
35. Regarding the third [question], "he approached him": that brahmin, thinking, "It is said that the ascetic Gotama answers what is spoken;
there is no failing in his responses. I shall compose a question for which he will fail," ate choice food, closed the door of his chamber, sat down, and began to reflect. Then, to him...
