It occurred to him: "In this place there is loud noise and great clamor; the mind does not become one-pointed. I shall have an underground chamber built.
Having had an underground chamber built, he entered it and thought: "When questioned thus, he will speak thus;
when questioned thus, he will speak thus. Grasping one [word] and releasing another, he spent the entire day [reciting], but nothing...
He was unable to see him. In this very manner, four months passed for him.
At the end of those four months, he saw what is called a "double-pronged question. It occurred to him thus:
"I shall approach the ascetic Gotama and ask, 'What is your doctrine? If he says, 'I am a proponent of action (kiriyavādin),' [then I will ask: 'Of all unwholesome states..."
If he says, “I am a proponent of action,” I will refute him by saying, “You claim that there is no action regarding deeds.
If he says, “I am a proponent of non-action,” I will refute him by saying, “You claim that there is no action regarding wholesome states.
For when questioned with this dilemma, he will be unable either to spit it out or to swallow it down; thus, my victory will be secured.
“The ascetic Gotama has been defeated! Having said this, he rose up, clapped his hands, and emerged from the underground chamber.

Thinking, “It is not fitting to go alone when asking such a question,” he had a proclamation made throughout the city and, surrounded by all the people of the city, approached the Blessed One. *Kiṃvādī* means “what is his doctrine?”; *kimakkhāyī* means “what does he proclaim? (i.e., what is his name?).

He asked, "Has he declared the path for his disciples? Then the Blessed One, having prepared an answer over four months and thinking, "I have found the question that will defeat the ascetic Gotama," and having assumed an air of pride upon learning that [the Brahmin] had come, he shattered that very question with a single word, saying, "And I, O Brahmin, am one who maintains the doctrine of action (kriyāvādin)," and so forth. Then the Brahmin—
Having set aside his pride, he addressed the Blessed One with the words beginning, “But how...,” and so forth. The rest here is of plain meaning. 36.
In the fourth [question], “those worthy of offerings” (*dakkhiṇeyya*): “offering” (*dakkhiṇā*) refers to a gift; he asks how many persons are fit to receive it.
By the word “trainee” (*sekha*), he indicates the seven types of trainees. And herein, even a virtuous worldling (*puthujjana*) is included by way of the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*).
"Is included. "They become worthy of offerings for those who sacrifice" means that for those giving gifts, they are called recipients of the offering (*āhuna*) and thus worthy of it;
this is the meaning. "A field" means a site or foundation; the meaning is a place for the growth of merit. 37.
In the fifth [sutta], "in the Eastern Monastery" means in the monastery situated in the eastern direction from Sāvatthī. "In the Palace of Migāra’s Mother" means...

In the mansion of the laywoman Visākhā. For she is called Migāramātā both because she was placed by the merchant Migāra in the position of a mother, and because she shares the same name as the merchant Ayyaka, the eldest son’s grandfather.
The thousand-pillared mansion built by her is known as the Migāramātupāsāda. The Elder dwells there. There, the Venerable Sāriputta...
While dwelling in that palace, the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, addressed the bhikkhus. At what time did he address them?
For some suttas were spoken before the meal, some after the meal, some during the first watch of the night, some during the middle watch, and some during the last watch.
This *Samacittapaṭipadā-sutta*, however, was spoken after the meal; therefore, he addressed them in the evening.
This was not spoken by the Elder alone, but was also spoken by the Tathāgata.
Where did he sit? He sat in Visākhā’s Jewel Palace (*Ratanapāsāda*). For during his first period of enlightenment, the Tathāgata lived for twenty years without a fixed residence.
Having offered [the sacrifice], he went wherever it was convenient and dwelt there.

For during the first rainy season, having set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion at Isipatana and having caused eighteen koṭis of great Brahmās to drink the draught of the Deathless, he dwelt at Isipatana in dependence on Bārāṇasī.
During the second rainy season, he dwelt in Veḷuvana in dependence on Rājagaha; and so too for the third and fourth.
In that very place, during the fifth rainy season, he stayed at Vesālī, in the Mahāvana, at the Gabled Hall;
during the sixth rainy season, at Mount Makula; during the seventh, in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven; during the eighth, at Susumāragira in the Bhagga country, in the Bhesakaḷā Grove;
during the ninth, at Kosambī; during the tenth, in the Pālileyyaka forest grove; and during the eleventh—
The eleventh was at Nālā in the Brāhmaṇa village; the twelfth at Verañjā; the thirteenth on Cāliya Mountain;
the fourteenth in Jeta’s Grove; the fifteenth at Kapilavatthu; the sixteenth at Āḷavī, after taming the Āḷavaka demon and causing eighty-four thousand beings to drink the drink of the Deathless;
the seventeenth right here at Rājagaha; and the eighteenth on Cāliya Mountain itself.
Likewise, he spent the nineteenth and twentieth rains retreats residing right at Rājagaha.
Thus, for twenty years, he lived without a fixed residence, staying wherever it was convenient.
From then on, however, he made two resting places his permanent abodes. Which two? The Jeta Grove and...
And the Eastern Monastery. Why? Because of the greatness of the virtues of two families.
For it was with reference to the virtue of Anāthapiṇḍika and that of Visākhā, and depending upon their virtue, that the Teacher made use of those lodgings as his permanent residence.
Even after wandering on tour during the season for travel, he would dwell in only these two monasteries during the rains retreat. While dwelling thus—
But having stayed the night at Jetavana, on the following day, surrounded by the community of monks,
he entered Sāvatthī for alms through the southern gate, departed through the eastern gate, and took his midday rest at the Eastern Monastery (Pubbārāma).
Having stayed the night at the Eastern Monastery, on the following day, he entered Sāvatthī for alms through the eastern gate and [departed] through the southern gate.
Having gone out, he would take his midday rest in Jeta’s Grove. On that particular day, however, the Perfectly Enlightened One stayed right there in Jeta’s Grove.
Wherever he might dwell, the fivefold duty remained unforgotten; this has already been explained in detail above.
Among those duties, at the time for the duty of the final watch of the night, the Blessed One, surveying the world, [beheld] the inhabitants of Sāvatthī...
And he saw that within a radius of four, six, or eight *yojanas* all around Sāvatthī, immeasurable beings had attained clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
Then, looking to see at what time the realization would occur, he perceived it would be at the evening hour. He then considered:
"Will the realization occur while I am speaking, or while my disciples are speaking? [He then looked toward] the Elder Sāriputta...
He saw that they would be conversing. Then, looking about to see where they would sit to converse, he saw that they would be sitting in Visākhā’s Jewel Palace.
He thought: "There are three assemblies of disciples for the Buddhas, and one for the Chief Disciples.
Of these, today there will be an assembly of disciples for the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma."

He saw him. Having seen him, early in the morning, after attending to his physical needs, he dressed himself in his lower garment and upper robe, put on the Sugata’s outer cloak, took up a stone bowl, and, surrounded by the community of monks, entered the city through the southern gate.
While wandering for alms, he ensured that the community of monks obtained food easily; then, like a ship struck by the wind, he turned back.
Having departed through the southern gate, he stood outside the gate.
Then the four assemblies—the eighty great disciples, the assembly of bhikkhunīs, the assembly of upāsakas, and the assembly of upāsikās—surrounded the Teacher.
The Teacher addressed the Elder Sāriputta: "Sāriputta, it is fitting for you to go to Pubbārāma; it is yours..."
“...and taking your retinue, go. “Very well, Bhante,” the Elder replied, and surrounded by his own retinue of five hundred bhikkhus, he went to the Eastern Monastery.

Following this same method, having sent the eighty great disciples to the Eastern Monastery, he himself went to Jeta’s Grove accompanied only by the Elder Ānanda. The Elder Ānanda also [entered] the monastery.
Having performed his duties toward the Teacher and paid homage, he said, "Venerable Sir, I am going to the Eastern Monastery. "Do so, Ānanda," [replied the Teacher].
Having paid homage to the Teacher, he departed from that very spot. The Teacher remained alone behind in Jeta’s Grove.
For on that day, the four assemblies were desirous of hearing the Dhamma discourse from the Elder alone. The Great King of Kosala, too—
Surrounded by his army, he went to the Eastern Monastery. Likewise did Anāthapiṇḍika go, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred lay followers.
But the great female lay follower Visākhā went, surrounded by two thousand foot-soldiers.

In the city of Sāvatthī, the dwelling place of seven million five hundred thousand families, everyone except the household-keeping children left behind perfumes, powders, garlands, and other offerings.

Having taken it, he went to the Eastern Monastery itself. In the four gate-villages, all the people within a distance of up to four, six, or eight *krośas* went to the Eastern Monastery with perfumes, powders, garlands, and other offerings in their hands.
The entire monastery appeared as if strewn with a mixture of flowers.
The Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, also went to the monastery and stood in the courtyard of the monastery’s precincts.
The monks prepared a seat for the Elder. Having sat down there, and after the attendant elder had performed the duties of hospitality, the Elder gave exhortation to the community of monks;
then, entering the Perfumed Chamber, he sat down having entered into meditative absorption.
Thus, having emerged from attainment according to the predetermined time, he went to the Aciravatī River. Having washed away the dust and dirt from his body, his fatigue subsided;
he crossed back up at the very same ford where he had descended, put on his lower robe, donned his upper robe, and stood there.
The community of monks also descended one after another, washed the dust and dirt from their bodies, and [stood there].
Having stepped down, they surrounded the Elder. Inside the monastery, they prepared the Dharma-seat for the Elder.
Each of the four assemblies, having identified their respective places and cleared a path, sat down.
The Elder Sāriputta also arrived at the Dharma-hall accompanied by a retinue of five hundred bhikkhus, and stood upon the lion’s head with a white parasol raised high above him.
Taking a fan made of peacock feathers upon his jeweled couch, he sat facing the east. Having sat down and surveyed the assembly, he thought:
"This is indeed a great assembly; a mere trifling and limited teaching of the Dhamma is not suitable for it.
What kind of Dhamma teaching would be appropriate? As he reflected upon the Three Piṭakas, he [saw] this...
He saw the teaching on the Dhamma concerning the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Having observed this teaching and wishing to teach it himself, he addressed the monks, saying, "Friends, monks.
For instead of saying "friends," the address "monks" is what is called the Buddha’s mode of address; yet this Venerable One [used it] as if he were equal to the One of Ten Powers.
Thinking, "I shall not engage in conversation," yet out of reverence for the Teacher, he addressed his disciples, saying, "Friends, monks.
He spoke this: he uttered this phrase of Dhamma teaching, "Friends, I will teach you the person bound internally and the person bound externally."
Now, there was a certain son of the gods, a stream-enterer, residing in that jewel palace;
he knew as soon as the Buddhas or their disciples began a teaching: "This teaching will be superficial; this one will be profound.
This one will be based on meditative absorption (jhāna); this one will be based on insight (vipassanā); this one will be based on the path (magga)."
“This one is dependent on the fruits; this one is dependent on Nibbāna. On that very day, as soon as the Elder had begun his teaching, he understood thus:

“The manner in which my noble master, the General of the Dhamma, the Elder Sāriputta, has commenced his teaching indicates that this discourse will be steeped in insight (vipassanā); he will explain insight through six aspects.”
"At the conclusion of this teaching, one hundred thousand times ten million deities will attain Arahantship;
as for the number of gods and humans who become stream-enterers and so forth, there will be no limit. Having acted in a manner worthy of this teaching, I shall give my master a cry of 'Well done!
With the power of a deity, she made a great sound and said, "Excellent, excellent, Master!"
When the King of the Devas gave his applause, all the deities dwelling in the thousand surrounding palaces likewise gave their applause.
By the sound of their applause, all the deities dwelling in the Eastern Monastery (Pubbārāma) heard it; by their sound, those at a distance of one *gāvuta*;
from there, at half a *yojana*, then a *yojana*—by this means, throughout one world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), two world-systems, and three.
"In the world-systems" means that in the ten thousand world-systems the deities gave their approval.
By the sound of their approval, the earth-dwelling nāgas and the space-dwelling deities [responded].

Then the cloud-deities, the heat-deities, the cold-deities, the rain-deities, the four Great Kings of the Cātumahārājika realm, the deities of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, and Sakka, the king of the gods, [responded].
The Yāma devas, Suyāma the king of gods; the Tusita devas, Santusita the king of gods;
the Nimmānaratī devas, Sunimmita the king of gods; the Vasavattī devas, Vasavattī the king of gods; the Brahmapārisajja devas, the Brahmapurohita devas, the Mahābrahmā devas;
the Parittābha devas, the Appamāṇābha devas, the Ābhassara devas; the Parittasubha devas, the Appamāṇasubha devas, and the Subhakiṇha devas.

The Vehapphala, Aviha, Atappa, Sudassa, Sudassi, and Akaniṭṭha deities—all these deities, with the exception of the non-percipient beings and the beings of the formless realm, gave their applause in the place where the ear-sphere was functioning.
Then the Great Brahmas whose taints were exhausted [cried out]: "Oh, how great indeed is this sound of applause! Starting from the surface of the earth..."
Having ascended as far as the Akaniṭṭha realm, they wondered, "For what purpose has he come? While reflecting thus, they perceived:
"The Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, is seated in the Eastern Park at Visākhā’s Jewel Palace and has begun a discourse on the sequence of the fetters;
it is fitting that we too become witnesses of the body there. Thinking this, they went there. [This was] the Eastern Park.
It was filled with deities for a quarter-league all around the eastern grove, for half a league, and for a full league;
indeed, from the surface of the earth below to the boundary of the world-system (cakkavāḷa) across, it was packed without any gaps by deities who had assembled from ten thousand world-systems.
Even in a space the size of the tip of an awl, there were sixty [deities] at the upper limit.
The deities, having fashioned subtle bodies, stood there.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta, reflecting, "What indeed is this great clamor? What could it be?

saw that the deities stationed throughout ten thousand world-systems had assembled within a single world-system. Then, because of the Buddhas' power of resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna-kicca*), [the assembly was made visible].
It is not so; they see and hear the sound by means of the very measure of the assembly. However, for disciples, a formal resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*) is permissible.
Therefore, the Elder, having entered into meditative attainment and emerged from that attainment, made a resolve with a sublime consciousness:
"May the entire assembly, as far as the limits of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), see me, and may they hear the Dhamma as I teach it."

“Let him hear the sound. From the moment he made this resolve, he sat upon the right knee and at the rim of the world-system (*cakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭi*), and there was no reason for anyone to say, “What is the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, like? Is he tall or short, dark or fair?
For everyone seated in every direction, he appeared as if right in front of them, even in the midst of the sky.
He became like the moon standing still. As he taught the Dhamma, everyone seated on his right knee and at the edge of the world-system heard his voice with one and the same sound.
Having thus resolved, the Elder began this Dhamma teaching, starting with the words: "Friends, [this is] the internal fetter."
In this context, "internal" refers to existence in the sense-sphere (kāmabhava); "external" refers to existence in the fine-material and immaterial spheres (rūpa- and arūpabhava).

For although beings dwell for only a short time in the sense-sphere existence—occupying only the fourth division of an eon—the sense-sphere existence remains empty and void during the other three divisions;
whereas they dwell for a long time in the fine-material existence, nevertheless, because their deaths and rebirth-linkings occur within the sense-sphere existence...

They are numerous in the sense-sphere existence and few in the form and formless existences. Where there are many instances of death and rebirth-linking, there attachment (*ālaya*), aspiration (*patthanā*), and longing (*abhilāsa*) are also numerous; where they are few, these too are few.
Therefore, sense-sphere existence is called "internal," while form and formless existences are called "external. Thus, desire and lust for sense-sphere existence, which is reckoned as internal—
The "internal fetter" (ajjhattasaṃyojana) is the desire and lust for those states reckoned as external, namely for existence in the fine-material and immaterial realms;

this is called the "external fetter" (bahiddhāsaṃyojana). Alternatively, the five lower fetters (orambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni) are the internal fetter, and the five higher fetters (uddhambhāgiyāni) are the external fetter.
Herein, this is the etymological explanation: "lower" (oraṃ) refers to the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu); therein...
They are called "lower-fettering" (*orambhāgiya*) because they lead to rebirth in the lower realms; thus, those that pertain to the lower are the lower-fettering.
"The higher" (*uddhaṃ*) refers to the form and formless realms; because they lead to rebirth there, those that pertain to the higher are the higher-fettering (*uddhambhāgiya*).
Thus, a person who is bound by the internal fetters is one "possessed of internal fetters," while [one bound] by external fetters...
A person who is fettered is one whose fetters extend outward. Both of these terms are not names for the worldly masses who are dependent upon the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
Rather, they are names for those noble disciples—the stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners—for whom existence has been cut off in two ways.
For just as in a great forest, specific groves such as acacia thickets or sal forests receive names such as "pillar," "beam," or "framework."
They do not obtain [that name]; they receive only the name "Khadira forest" or "Sāla forest.
But when those trees are cut down with a sharp axe and carved into the shape of pillars and so forth, then they receive the names "pillar," "beam," or "framework.
In the same way, the worldling (*puthujjana*), whose existence is undetermined and whose defilements are thick, does not receive this name.
It is only those who have attained the stage of stream-entry (sotāpanna) and beyond—who have delimited [the path] and attenuated the defilements—who obtain it.
To clarify this point, the simile of the calf-pen should be understood.
For having constructed a calf-pen, they knock a post into the ground inside, tie the calves with ropes, and fasten them to those posts; then, to the ropes...
When even the ears were insufficient, they would seize the calves and force them inside;
when there was no room within the hall, they would even drive stakes into the ground outside and do the same.
Among them, some calves tied inside lay outside; some tied outside lay inside; some tied inside remained inside; and some tied outside [remained outside].
It lies outside. Some [cattle] wander neither tied inside nor tied outside. In that regard, for one tied inside and lying outside, the tethering-rope is long;
for when oppressed by heat and so forth, it goes out and lies down among the calves outside.
The same principle applies to one tied outside and lying inside. But as for one tied inside and lying inside, [the rope is short].
His tethering rope is short. The same principle applies even when he is tied outside or lying outside;
for both of them spend the whole day walking around the stump and lie down right there. But he who is not tied inside wanders among the calves right there.
This virtuous calf, having been caught by the ear, was released among the calves.
Even during the day, it does not go elsewhere but wanders right there. The same principle applies even when [a calf] is not tied outside but wanders right there.
In this context, the three realms of existence (bhava) should be understood as being like a calf-pen; the pillar of ignorance (avijjā) is like a post in the calf-pen;
the ten fetters (saṃyojana) are like the rope that binds the calf; and the beings reborn within the three realms of existence are like the calves.
Those who have entered the stream (*sotāpanna*) and those who return once more (*sakadāgāmin*) are like calves tied inside while standing outside;

they dwell within the realms of form and formlessness (*rūpārūpabhava*), yet their fetters (*saṃyojana*) are still bound specifically to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*). In what sense? In the sense that they have not yet been abandoned.
Even the worldling (*puthujjana*) is included among these in the realms of form and formlessness; for although he dwells there, his fetters...
For him, [the fetter] is bound only to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara). An Anāgāmī in the sense-sphere is like a calf sleeping inside while tied outside the pen;
for although he dwells in the sense-sphere, his fetter is bound only to the fine-material and immaterial existences (rūpārūpabhava).
Sotāpannas and Sakadāgāmins in the sense-sphere are like those tied inside and lying inside the pen; for they themselves [dwell] in the sense-sphere.
They dwell [there], and their fetter is likewise bound only to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara).

Like one tied outside and lying outside, the non-returner (anāgāmī) dwells in the fine-material and immaterial realms (rūpa- and arūpabhava); for he himself dwells there, and his fetter is also bound only to the fine-material and immaterial realms.
Like a calf tied inside and wandering inside, the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) dwells in the sense-sphere. Like a calf tied outside and wandering outside...
Just as one whose taints are exhausted [does not go] to the realms of form and formlessness, so too these three fetters— personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), doubt (*vicikicchā*),

and adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*)— prevent one from going and cause one who has gone to return. However, these two fetters— sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and ill-will (*byāpāda*)—
[lead one to] the realms of form and formlessness, unless they are suppressed by meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) or eradicated by the Path (*magga*).
He is unable to be reborn.

"And which one, friend?"—this [question] was like a man who, having placed two caskets of jewels before his eyes, might fill the hands of the assembled crowd and distribute seven kinds of jewels; thus [the Elder spoke of] the first casket of jewels.
Having given [the first], one should give in the same way a second time as well.
In this very manner, having established these two phrases— “Friends, I shall teach the person with internal fetters and the person with external fetters”— as a summary outline (mātikā),
he now began the detailed exposition in order to demonstrate them by dividing them according to the eightfold assembly.
In this context, "here" means in this teaching. "He is virtuous" means he is endowed with virtue through the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*).

Thus, the Elder Summa, who dwelt at Dīpa Monastery, said that the Elder [Mahākaccāna], having first indicated the fourfold purification of virtue by this much, then demonstrated the preeminent virtue therein by means of the phrase "restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha."
However, his pupil, the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷanāga, said: "In both cases, only restraint by the Pātimokkha is mentioned.
For restraint by the Pātimokkha alone is virtue; as for the other three, there is indeed a place where they are called 'virtue'.
Not accepting this, he further said: "Restraint of the faculties is merely the guarding of the six doors."

Purity of livelihood consists merely in obtaining the basic requisites through righteous and equitable means, and merely in using those requisites obtained after reflecting upon them as "this is for this purpose.
However, in the ultimate sense, virtue is simply the restraint of the Pātimokkha.
For one whose [restraint] is broken, it is as if a man with a severed head were to try to protect his remaining hands and feet.

It should not be said [that he is unvirtuous]. However, for one who is healthy, this person—like a man whose head has been severed—is able to restore the remaining faculties to their natural state and protect them.

Therefore, having indicated the restraint of the Pātimokkha by the term "virtuous" (sīlavā), he spoke the passage beginning with "restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha" (pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto) in order to explain it in detail.
In this context, "restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha" means endowed with the restraint of the Pātimokkha.
"Perfect in conduct and resort" means perfect in both conduct and resort. "In even the slightest" means in those that are very minor.
"Offenses" means unwholesome states. "Seeing danger" means seeing them as fearful. "Having undertaken" means having correctly adopted. "He trains in the rules of training" means that...
Having undertaken that training precept, one trains in it. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "having undertaken, one trains in the training precepts":
whatever is to be trained in among the training precepts—the various divisions of training, whether physical or verbal—all that one undertakes correctly and trains in.
This is the summary here; however, in detail, all these [precepts] beginning with the restraint of the Pātimokkha...
The steps have been stated in the *Visuddhimagga*, and the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*) has been demonstrated by analyzing it in all its aspects.
"One of the classes of gods" means one of the classes of gods among the six groups of sense-sphere gods (*kāmāvacara*).
"He is a returner" means he is a returner to the lower realms. "A visitor to this state" means a visitor to this very state, namely, the condition of the five human aggregates (*pañcakkhandha*).
It does not lead to rebirth there or to a higher rebirth; rather, it shows that one goes only further downward.

By this factor, both the lower two paths and the lower two fruits for a dry-insight practitioner (*sukkha-vipassaka*) who takes the meditation subject of the elements (*dhātu-kammaṭṭhāna*) are explained.
"A certain peaceful liberation of mind" refers to any one of the eight attainments, namely the attainment of the fourth jhāna.
For that is called "peaceful" because it is tranquil due to the subsiding of adverse defilements, and it is called "liberation of mind" because the mind is liberated from those very defilements.
"A certain order of devas" refers to any one of the five orders of the devas of the Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*). "One who does not return..."
"Not returning to this state" (*itthattaṃ*) means that one does not come again to this condition of the five aggregates;
it shows that one is neither reborn in a lower realm nor reborn in a higher realm, but rather attains final nibbāna right there.
By this factor, the three paths and the three fruits are explained for the monk who practices through concentration (*samādhi*).

"Out of disenchantment with sensual pleasures alone" means for the purpose of becoming disenchanted with and weary of both kinds of sensual pleasures. "For the fading away of lust" means for the purpose of the fading away of lust.
"For cessation" means for the purpose of bringing about non-occurrence. "One who has entered upon the way" means one who has entered upon the practice.

Up to this point, it is the insight into the path of the non-returner (anāgāmi-magga-vipassanā) for the sake of the destruction of lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure of both the stream-enterer (sotāpanna) and the once-returner (sakadāgāmin).

"It has been explained. "Of existences alone" means of the three existences (*bhava*). By this, the insight (*vipassanā*) of the path to Arhatship for the sake of the destruction of craving for existence (*bhavarāga*) in a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) has been explained.

By the phrase "he is practicing for the destruction of craving," the insight of the path to Non-returning for the sake of destroying the craving for the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañcakāmaguṇika-taṇhā*) in Stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) and Once-returners (*sakadāgāmī*) alone has been explained. "He [is practicing] for the destruction of greed... [and so forth].
By this [statement] as well, only the insight into the path of arahantship for the sake of the destruction of craving for existence by a non-returner is described.

"Into one or another order of devas" means into one or another order of devas within the Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa) themselves. "One who does not return to this state" means one who does not return to this condition of the five aggregates;
such a person is not reborn in a lower realm, but is either reborn in a higher realm or attains final nibbāna right there.
Thus, by the first factor, the two lower paths and fruits are explained for the dry-insight practitioner (sukkha-vipassaka) who takes the elements as his meditation subject (dhātu-kammaṭṭhānika).
By the second, the three [higher] paths and fruits are explained for the one who practices through concentration (samādhi-kammika).

With the phrase "he [is detached] from sensual pleasures," the insight into the higher path of non-returning (anāgāmi-magga) is indicated for the purpose of destroying the lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure belonging to stream-enterers (sotāpanna) and once-returners (sakadāgāmin).
By the phrase "for the destruction of becoming," the insight of the path to Arahantship above that of the Non-returner is indicated;

by the phrase "for the destruction of craving," the insight of the path to Non-returning above the destruction of craving for the five strands of sensual pleasure belonging to Stream-enterers and Once-returners is indicated;
and by the phrase "for the destruction of greed," the insight of the path to Arahantship above the destruction of greed for existence belonging to the Non-returner is indicated.
Having thus explained insight (vipassanā) through these six aspects, he brought the teaching to its proper conclusion.
At the conclusion of the discourse, one hundred thousand times ten million deities attained Arahatship; there was no limit to those who became Stream-enterers and the other stages.
And just as it was in this assembly, so it was in the Mahāsamaya Sutta, the Maṅgala Sutta, and the Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta.
One hundred thousand million deities attained Arahatship; there was no limit to the number of gods and humans who became Stream-enterers and so forth.
"Deities of even mind" means they were of even mind due to the evenness of the subtlety of their minds.
For all of them had fashioned their own bodies by making them subtle and similar to the mind; therefore, they were called "of even mind. Furthermore...
They were of even mind for the following reason: “The Elder has indeed spoken of the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), but he has not yet spoken of the power of those attainments.
Let us summon the One of Ten Powers and have him speak of the power of the attainments. Thus they all became single-minded and of even mind.
Furthermore, there was another reason: “By this one method, the Elder has spoken both of the attainments and of the power of the attainments...”
As they looked about, wondering, "Who indeed has arrived at this assembly, and who has not?", they saw that the Tathāgata had not yet arrived.
Thinking, "Let us have the Tathāgata summoned so that we may complete the assembly," they all became single-minded and even-hearted.
Furthermore, there was another reason: lest some bhikkhu in the future...

Or if a bhikkhunī, a deva, or a human were to show disrespect, thinking, "This teaching was spoken by a disciple," [the assembly] would summon the Perfectly Enlightened One and declare, "We shall establish this teaching as spoken by the Omniscient One.
Thinking, "In this way, it will be held in high esteem and revered in the future," they all became of one mind and even-minded. There is yet another reason.
For all of them were either attainers of the same meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) or attainers of the same object (*ārammaṇa*); thus they were even-minded.
"Joyful" (*haṭṭhā*) means satisfied, exultant, gladdened, and delighted. "Sādhu" is a particle used in the sense of a request.
"Out of compassion" (*anukampaṃ upādāya*) means not out of dependence on the Elder’s compassion, pity, or tenderness; nor was there any need for the Elder to be shown compassion in this instance.

It is so. For on the day when the Elder stood at the entrance of the Sūkarakhatā Cave fanning the Teacher with a palm-leaf fan while he was teaching the meditation subject of feelings to his nephew, the wanderer Dīghanakha—
just as one dispels hunger by eating another’s extra meal, or as one puts on another’s prepared ornament upon one’s own head— so it was then.
Having reached the very pinnacle of the knowledge of the perfections of a disciple as if it were his own, he was named "Anukampita" (The Compassionate One) by the Blessed One on that very day.
Furthermore, the rest of the gods and humans who had gathered at that place entreated the Blessed One, saying,
"May the Blessed One go out of compassion for us."
"A strong man": for one who is weak is not able to perform the bending and stretching quickly, whereas only a strong man is able;
therefore this was said. "Appeared before his face" means he became manifest right there in front of him.
"The Blessed One said this" means he stated the reason for his own arrival in the manner beginning with, "In this case, Sāriputta."
It occurred to him: "If some foolish person—whether a monk, a nun, a lay follower, or a female lay follower—should think thus: 'The Elder Sāriputta has obtained a great assembly;
the Perfectly Enlightened One, being unable to endure such a crowd, has come out of envy to disperse the assembly,' then he would harbor this mental corruption toward me."
“Having done so, one might be reborn in a state of misery. Then, explaining the reason for his own arrival, he spoke these words beginning with, “Here, Sāriputta.

Having thus explained the reason for his arrival, he now spoke the passage beginning with, “But those deities, Sāriputta, even when they were ten,” in order to describe the power of his meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
In this context, it is appropriate to bring forth the meaning by way of its significance (*yasa*).
Or by way of attainment (*samāpatti*). First, by way of fame (*yasa*), deities of great power stood ten by ten in one place;
those of lesser power than them stood twenty by twenty in one place; those of still lesser power...
[and so on] ...stood sixty by sixty in one place. But by way of attainment, those by whom a sublime attainment has been developed—
Sixty each stood together in one place. Those who had cultivated attainments inferior to those [sixty] stood fifty each... pe...
those who had cultivated attainments even more inferior than those stood ten each in one place.
Or, those by whom inferior [attainments] were cultivated stood ten each in one place; those by whom more excellent [attainments] than those were cultivated stood twenty [each].
Twenty. Those which were even more refined than those... [as before] ...stood sixty by sixty in one place.
"In a space no larger than the point of a needle" means in a space just sufficient for the tip of a needle to fall.
"And they do not obstruct one another" means that although they stand in such a crowded place, they do not obstruct or strike one another; they are without pressure.
They were without obstruction. There was no reason for her to say, "Your hand oppresses me," or "Your foot oppresses me," or "You stand pressing against me.
In that context, *nūna* means "surely" in that existence.
*Tathācittaṃ bhāvitaṃ* means the mind was cultivated in that manner. *Yena tā devatā* means by means of that mind so cultivated, those deities...
"Even though they are ten [in number]... they remain without harming one another.
Here, "right here" (*idheva*) refers to the Dispensation (*sāsana*) or the human world (*manussaloka*); the meaning is: "in this very Dispensation" and "in this very human world.
For it was in this very human world and in this very Dispensation that the minds of those deities were developed, by means of which—
Thus they were reborn in the realm of form (*rūpabhava*); and having come from there, they remained after fashioning such subtle bodies for themselves.

In this regard, although there are indeed deities who, having realized the three paths and fruits under the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, were reborn in the Brahma-world, nevertheless—considering that the instruction of all Buddhas is one and the same dispensation—[this applies to them as well].
“Right here indeed, Sāriputta”—saying this, he spoke while making the teachings of other Buddhas identical to this very teaching.
Up to this point, the Tathāgata has described the power of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
Now, addressing the Elder Sāriputta, he speaks an instruction according to the tradition: “Therefore, Sāriputta...”

He said: "In that regard, 'therefore' means because those deities, while remaining right here, having produced meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), were reborn in a peaceful existence; therefore [it is said].
'With peaceful faculties' (*santindriyā*) means they have peaceful faculties due to the peace, the extinction, and the refinement of the five faculties.
'With peaceful minds' (*santamānasā*) means they have peaceful minds due to the peace, the extinction, and the refinement of the mind."
"Thinking, 'We shall offer only what is peaceful,' we shall offer only that which is peaceful, extinguished, and sublime—the offering of body and mind.
Regarding 'fellow practitioners of the holy life' (sabrahmacārīsū), this refers to those who share the same Dhamma and practice the holy life together, such as by studying the same teachings.
'In this way, Sāriputta, you should train yourselves'—by this much, the Blessed One has concluded his teaching spoken with omniscience."

"Anassuṃ" means they have perished, been lost, and ruined. "Ye imaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ nāssosuṃ" means those who, relying on their own evil, empty, and useless views, did not obtain the opportunity to hear such a teaching of the Dhamma.
Thus he concluded the instruction according to the sequence of the narrative.
38. "He dwells at Varaṇā" means there is a city named Varaṇā; he dwells depending upon it.
"On account of adherence, bondage, cleaving, obsession, and clinging to sensual lust" means:

on account of adherence to sensual lust, on account of bondage to sensual lust, on account of cleaving to sensual lust, on account of obsession by sensual lust, and on account of clinging to sensual lust.
The meaning is as follows: This refers to that sensual lust which arises depending upon the five strands of sensual pleasure.

Because one is obsessed by, bound to, and submerged in that very sensual lust—as if stuck in a great mire—and because one is gripped by it and has become addicted to it through that very sensual lust.
"Because it has been swallowed and fully digested, it is said to be 'taken. The same principle applies to the terms "lust for views" (*diṭṭhirāga*) and so forth.
Here, however, "lust for views" should be understood as the lust that arises based upon the sixty-two types of views. Regarding the phrase "in the eastern countries":
from the Elder’s place of residence, the country of Sāvatthī lay in the eastern direction; and when the Elder sat down...
Sitting as if facing that very [truth], he spoke thus. He uttered an *udāna* means he uttered an exclamation.

For just as oil that cannot be contained within a measure and flows over is called "residue" (*avasesaka*), and water that cannot be contained within a pond and flows over it is called a "flood" (*ogha*), even so—
That which is a word of joy (*pītivacana*) which the heart is unable to contain, and being excessive, not remaining within but emerging outwardly, is called an *udāna*;
the meaning is that he uttered such a word consisting of joy. 39.
In the seventh [section], "in the Gundavana" means in the forest so named. "He approached" means: "It is said that the Elder Mahākaccāna..."
Having heard that he neither saluted, nor rose up for, nor invited with a seat even his own father or grandmother, [the king thought]:
"One cannot reach a conclusion based on this alone; I shall go to him and examine him closely.
Having finished his breakfast, he approached the Venerable Mahākaccāna. *Jiṇṇe* means aged by old age. *Vuddhe* means advanced in years.
"An elder" means one who is advanced in years. "One who has reached a stage of life" means one who has passed through a long period of time.
"One who has arrived at the final stage of life" means one who has entered the last phase of existence. "This is indeed so, Master Kaccāna," [said the other].
"Master Kaccāna, that which we have merely heard accords with this which has now been seen. Therefore, it is exactly so and not otherwise. For..."
“Sir Kaccāna, the brahmin”—this he says referring to himself. His intention, it is said, was this:

“Seeing us so elderly, there is not even a mere salutation, nor a mere rising up, nor even an invitation to sit for the venerable Kaccāna. “Not at all fitting” means not at all appropriate, not at all suitable.
Having heard the words of the brahmin, the Elder thought, "This brahmin knows neither the old nor the young;
I shall explain both the old and the young to him. Expanding his teaching, he said, "There are, O brahmin," and so forth.

In that context, "by one who knows" means by one who knows all that is to be known (*neyya*); "by one who sees" means by one who sees it as if it were an *āmalaka* fruit placed in the palm of the hand.
"The stage of the grown" refers to the reason by which one is called "grown. "The stage of the young" refers to the reason by which one is called "young.
"Eighty years old" means an age of eighty years. "Ninety years old" means an age of ninety years.

"He enjoys sensual pleasures" means that he enjoys both kinds of sensual pleasure—the sensual pleasure of objects (*vatthukāma*) and the sensual pleasure of defilements (*kilesakāma*)—by way of desiring them.
“He dwells in the midst of sensual pleasures” means that he lives and resides in both kinds of sensual pleasure like a householder in his own home.
“He is eager for the pursuit of sensual pleasures” means that he has become intent upon seeking after both kinds of sensual pleasures.
“The fool is not reckoned as an elder” means that he is not an elder; rather, he is reckoned simply as a fool, a dullard. For it has been said:
“One does not become an elder merely because one’s head is grey;
his age is fully ripe, yet he is called ‘vainly aged.
“Dahara” means young. “Yuva” means endowed with youth. “Susukāḷakeso” means having very black hair. “Bhadrena”...
"Endowed with youth" means that he shows how the youth who is endowed with such youth has obtained what is excellent.
"By the first stage of life": the first stage of life consists of thirty-three years; the meaning is that he is endowed with that.
"The wise man is reckoned as an elder": such a person is reckoned as both "wise" and "an elder."
And he does not count as one [who is truly venerable]. For it has also been said:
“In whom there is truth and the Dhamma, non-violence, self-restraint, and self-mastery— he indeed is called a wise elder, one whose taints have been cast out.”
40. In the eighth [case], "the thieves are powerful" means they are endowed with allies, endowed with a retinue, endowed with wealth, endowed with a place of residence, and endowed with vehicles.
"The kings are weak at that time" means that at that time the kings are weak due to the absence of those aforementioned endowments. "To overstep" means beyond [the boundary].
Having traveled on tour through the countryside, they may wish to enter the city at any desired moment.

To "set out" means that it is not convenient for them to depart during the first watch, the middle watch, or the last watch of the night, thinking, "Thieves are plundering and crushing the countryside;
we shall stop them. Then, having risen, the thieves beat the people.
They go away having seized [the property]. Or, "they are well-known in the border regions":
it is not easy even to travel through the border regions for the purpose of establishing villages, building bridges, digging lotus ponds, or constructing halls and such.
"Of the brahmins and householders" refers to those dwelling within the city.
Of the brahmins and householders. "Or external works" means agricultural works in fields located outside the village or in monasteries.

"Evil monks are powerful" means they have superior factions, superior fame, possess merit, are attended by many male and female supporters, and are supported by kings and royal ministers. "Virtuous monks in that [place]..."
"At that time they are weak" means that at that time, the monks of lovely virtue are weak due to the absence of those [expected] accomplishments.
"Remaining silent, they waver in the midst of the Saṅgha" means that,
being noiseless and sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha, they are unable to utter even a single word with their mouths raised, but remain brooding.
They sit as it were. "Tayidaṃ" means this very reason. The white side (the wholesome) should be understood by reversing what was stated [in the previous section]. 41.
In the ninth [section], "the cause for the basis of wrong practice" (*micchāpaṭipattādhikaraṇahetu*) means the cause for wrong practice; the meaning is the cause for engaging in [wrong practice].
"The method, the Dhamma, the wholesome" (*ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusalaṃ*) refers to the Path together with insight (*sahavipassanakaṃ maggaṃ*). For such a [Path] is indeed accompanied by insight.
He is unable to attain, accomplish, and fulfill the path. The white side (the wholesome sequence) should be understood by reversing what was stated above.
In this sutta, the path is taught together with insight (vipassanā).
42. In the tenth [case], "by those wrongly grasped" means by those grasped out of order. "By those that resemble the letter" means according to the phrasing.
"By means of counterfeit [teachings] obtained through the mere artistry of words": they reject both the meaning and the Dhamma;
that is, they reject the meaning and the text (*pāḷi*) of well-learned discourses (*sutta*), and instead present the meaning and the text of their own poorly learned discourses as being superior.
The "white side" (the virtuous alternative) should be understood by reversing what has been stated. In this discourse, there is growth for the Dispensation (*sāsana*).
And decline has also been explained. The fourth chapter, the Chapter on Even Mind, is concluded.
5. Explanation of the Chapter on the Assembly (Parisavagga).
43. Regarding the first [section] of the fifth [chapter]: "Superficial" means manifest and unhidden. "Profound" means secret and hidden.
"Agitated" means possessed of restlessness (*uddhacca*). "Arrogant" means with a stalk raised high; what is meant is one whose empty pride has arisen.
"Fickle" means endowed with fickleness through such things as the ornamenting of bowl and robes. "Garrulous" means harsh-mouthed, having harsh speech.
"Scattered in speech" means those whose words are unrestrained, who prattle away in meaningless talk even during the day. "Muddle-minded" means those whose mindfulness has been abandoned.
"Lacking clear comprehension" means those devoid of wisdom (*paññā*). "Unconcentrated" means those who do not possess even a modicum of one-pointedness of mind (*citt’ekaggatā*).

"With unguarded faculties" means those endowed with faculties that remain open and unprotected, left in their natural state. The "white side" (the virtuous counterpart) is to be understood by reversing what has been stated above.

44. Regarding the second [term], *bhaṇḍanajātā*: "quarrel" (*bhaṇḍana*) refers to the preliminary stage of a dispute; since that has arisen among them, they are called "those in whom a quarrel has arisen.
Likewise, they are those in whom a dispute has been produced by the occurrence of such statements as, "We shall have you fined, we shall have you bound," and so forth.
This, first of all, is the method regarding householders. As for those who have gone forth, however, they are those who speak words involving the transgression of an offense.

"Those who have given rise to quarrels" means those who have entered into disputes. "Piercing with the weapons of their mouths" means that ill-spoken words are called "weapons of the mouth" in the sense that they cut down virtues; piercing with these means striking or wounding with them.

"In concord" means being together through the performance of these acts: a common ritual, a common recitation, and a common training. "With eyes of affection" means with eyes of loving-kindness (*mettā*).

45. "Possessing the foremost" (aggavatī) means possessing the supreme person, or being endowed with the foremost, that is, the supreme practice. Conversely, those who lack this are "not possessing the foremost" (anaggavatī).
"Devoted to abundance" (bāhulikā) means practicing for the sake of an abundance of robes and so forth.

"Lax" (sāthalikā) means adopting the teaching in a slack manner. Regarding the phrase "pioneers in falling away" (okkamane pubbaṅgamā): here, "falling away" (okkamana) is spoken of in the sense of descending.

There are five hindrances; thus, it is said that they are the forerunners in the fulfillment of those five hindrances. "In seclusion" means in *nibbāna*, which is seclusion from the substrata (*upadhiviveka*).
"Having laid down the burden" means having set aside the burden in all three kinds of seclusion. "They do not arouse energy" means they do not perform either of the two kinds of energy.
"For the attainment of the unattained" refers to the specific excellence of the jhānas, insight, the path, and the fruit, which were previously unattained.
“For the sake of conviction. The other two phrases are synonyms for that same term. “The later generation” refers to the community of co-residents and pupils.
“Falls into conformity with what is seen” means that by imitating what has been done by the teacher and preceptor, one enters into conformity with their observed conduct.
The remainder should be understood according to the method of the opposites of what has already been stated.
46. In the fourth [verse], "noble ones" (ariya) refers to the assembly of noble disciples; "non-noble ones" (anariya) refers to the assembly of worldlings (puthujjana).

"They do not understand as it really is: 'This is suffering'" means that, setting aside craving, they do not understand according to its true nature that the five aggregates of the three planes are called the truth of suffering—that this alone is suffering and there is no suffering beyond this. This...
The method is the same everywhere. However, in the remaining sections of this sutta: the prior craving that gives rise to that suffering is called "origination" (samudaya);
the absolute destruction and non-arising of that very craving—or of both those truths—is called "the cessation of suffering" (dukkhanirodha);
and the Noble Eightfold Path is called "the way leading to the cessation of suffering" (dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā). Thus, in this sutta...
By means of the four truths, the four paths and the four fruits are explained.

47. In the fifth [verse], "the dregs of the assembly" (parisākasaṭa) means a dreg-like assembly, a refuse-like assembly, or a chaff-like assembly. "The cream of the assembly" (parisāmaṇḍa) means a faithful assembly or an essential assembly.
"They go by way of favoritism" (chandāgatiṃ gacchanti) means they go astray through favoritism.
The meaning is: "doing what should not be done. The same principle applies to the remaining terms as well.

These four ways of going on a wrong course (*agatigamana*) are found both in the context of the distribution of goods (*bhaṇḍabhājanīya*) and in the context of legal adjudication (*vinicchayaṭṭhāna*).

Regarding the distribution of goods, first, when a monk gives away an unpleasant article belonging to monks who have become his burden in exchange for one that is pleasant, he is acting out of favoritism (*chandāgati*).
One is said to go to a wrong course through greed when, after exchanging one's own unburdensome, pleasing articles for bowls, one gives away something unpleasant.

One is said to go to a wrong course through hatred when giving away something unpleasant after exchanging it for one's own pleasing articles. One is said to go to a wrong course through delusion when not knowing the rules regarding the distribution of articles and the established procedure.
Or, one goes to a wrong course through delusion when thinking of those who are talkative or those supported by kings and the like: "These [articles] are my unpleasant goods..."
Thinking, "If I give it, they might even do me harm," one turns back out of fear and gives what is pleasing;

this is called going by way of fear. However, he who does not act thus, but remains impartial as a balance and a standard for all, giving each person exactly what falls to them—this one is said to avoid all four kinds of wrong courses.
In a place of adjudication, however, one who describes a grave offense that is one’s own burden as a light offense is said to fall into partiality through desire (*chandāgati*).
One who describes another’s light offense as a grave offense is said to fall into partiality through hatred (*dosāgati*).
Furthermore, one who does not know the methods for emerging from offenses (*āpattivuṭṭhāna*) and the *Samuccayakkhandhaka* falls into partiality through delusion (*mohāgati*).

Regarding the name: if one who is talkative or honored by kings, thinking, "If I report this offense, he might cause me harm," or thinking that a grave offense is actually light, speaks accordingly, this is called "going by way of fear.
However, he who reports everything exactly as it is does not go by any of the four kinds of wrong ways.
48. In the sixth [lesson], "trained by being cajoled" means ill-trained. "Not trained by questioning" means not trained after having been questioned.
"Profound" means profound by way of the text (*pāḷi*), like the *Salla Sutta*. "Profound in meaning" means profound by way of the meaning (*attha*), like the *Mahāvedalla Sutta*.
"Supramundane" means illuminating supramundane meaning. "Connected with emptiness" refers to the emptiness of beings (*satta*).
They reveal only the mere phenomenon (*dhammamatta*), similar to those [discourses] connected with the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*).
"They do not apply their minds to anything else" means they do not apply their minds for the sake of discerning other things; they either sleep or are otherwise occupied.

"That which is to be learned and mastered" refers to both what is to be learned and what is to be mastered. "Poetry" (*kavitā*) means composed by poets. The other term is a synonym for that same thing.
"Cittakkharā" means variegated syllables; the other term is a synonym for that same thing. "Bāhirakā" means those who stand outside the teaching (sāsana).
"Sāvakabhāsitā" means spoken by their respective disciples. "Sussūsanti" means they listen with a delighted mind due to both the variety of the syllables and the excellence of the phrasing.
"Na ceva aññamaññaṃ paṭipucchanti" means [they do not ask one another... regarding each other.

They do not ask about the meaning, the connection, or the sequence of what precedes and follows. "They do not investigate" means they do not wander on tour for the purpose of questioning. [They do not ask:
"How is this?"—how should this phrasing be applied, and in what way should it be applied?
"What is the meaning of this?"—what is the meaning of this statement, what is its connection, and what is the sequence of what precedes and follows? "Unopened" means...
"Concealed" means they do not uncover it. "Not made plain" means made unmanifest.

"They do not make plain" means they do not make it manifest. "In matters that are grounds for doubt" means in those things that serve as causes for doubt. The white side (the virtuous alternative) is to be understood by reversing what has been stated [in the preceding black side].
49. “One who values material things” refers to an assembly that stands having regarded the four requisites as important and the supramundane Dhamma as inferior.
“One who values the true Dhamma” refers to an assembly that stands having regarded the nine supramundane states as important and the four requisites as inferior.
“One liberated in both ways” is one liberated by means of two factors. “One liberated by wisdom” is one liberated by means of wisdom.

The one whose taints are destroyed through dry insight (*sukkha-vipassaka-khīṇāsava*). The body-witness (*kāyasakkhī*) is one who, having touched the contact of jhāna with the body, subsequently realizes cessation, which is Nibbāna, and stands therein.
The one attained to vision (*diṭṭhippatto*) is one who has reached the end of vision. These two are found in six places.
The one liberated by faith (*saddhāvimutto*) is one who is liberated while possessing faith. This one is also found in six places. Regarding the Dhamma...
"One who recollects [the Dhamma]" is a follower by way of the Dhamma (*dhammānusārī*). "One who recollects faith" is a follower by way of faith (*saddhānusārī*).

Both of these possess the first path. "One of beautiful qualities" means one of excellent qualities. "One of evil character" means one devoid of virtue and of base qualities. Why are these two mentioned?
For when all those born are similar in every respect, there is no strong sense of reverence toward those who possess virtue; however, toward some...
However, thinking that when there are those who are immoral, the virtuous will be held in powerful respect, they accept [the gifts].
Thinking, "They will obtain gain through this," those monks receive the four requisites by speaking in praise of some and in dispraise of others.
"Gathitā" means bound by craving. "Mucchitā" means intoxicated by craving itself.
*Ajjhupanna* means having become attached, swallowed, and established through relishing.
*Anādīnavadassāvino* means those who do not see the danger in consumption that has not been reflected upon.

*Anissaraṇapaññā* means those devoid of the wisdom of renunciation—which draws one away from desire and lust for the four requisites—and thus they do not understand the purpose of these things. *Paribhuñjanti* means they consume while possessed by desire and lust.
In such passages as "in the bright fortnight, one liberated both ways," this is a brief exposition of all seven noble persons:
A certain bhikkhu, intent upon the primacy of wisdom, develops the eight attainments and reaches the path of stream-entry.
At that moment, he is called a "follower by Dhamma" (*dhammānusārī*) regarding the six stages beginning with the fruit of stream-entry.
One called a "body-witness" (kāyasakkhi) is one who is "liberated in both ways" (ubhatobhāgavimutta) at the moment of the fruit of arahantship.
The meaning is that he is liberated in two ways or by two parts: through suppression by means of meditative attainments (samāpatti), and through eradication by means of the path (magga).
Another person, being intent on the primacy of wisdom (paññādhura), being unable to produce the meditative attainments, remains merely a "dry-insight practitioner" (sukkha-vipassaka).

He attains the path of stream-entry. At that moment, he is called a "follower by Dhamma" (dhammānusārī); regarding the six stages beginning with the fruit of stream-entry, he is called one who has attained vision (diṭṭhippatto);
and at the moment of the fruit of arahantship, he is called one liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutto).
Another, established through the predominance of faith, develops the eight attainments and attains the path of stream-entry. At that moment, he...
He is called a "follower by faith" (saddhānusārī). Regarding the six stages beginning with the fruit of stream-entry, he is called a "body-witness" (kāyasakkhi);
at the moment of the fruit of arhatship, he is called one "liberated in both ways" (ubhatobhāgavimutto).

Another person, being intent on the side of faith but unable to produce meditative attainments (samāpatti), reaches the path of stream-entry while remaining merely a "dry-insight practitioner" (sukkha-vipassaka). At that moment, he is a follower by faith.

He is called "liberated by faith" (*saddhāvimutta*) in six instances, such as at the moment of the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*); he is called "liberated by wisdom" (*paññāvimutta*) at the moment of the fruit of arahantship.

50. In the eighth [section], "uneven" (*visama*) means uneven in the sense of stumbling. "Even" (*sama*) means even in the sense of not stumbling. "Acts contrary to the Dhamma" (*adhammakamma*) means acts that deviate from the Dhamma. "Acts contrary to the Vinaya" (*avinayakamma*) means acts that deviate from the Vinaya.
51. In the ninth [section], "unrighteous" (*adhammika*) means devoid of the Dhamma. "Righteous" (*dhammika*) means connected with the Dhamma.
52. *Adhikaraṇa* means the fourfold legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*), beginning with the legal issue of dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*).
"They take up" means they grasp [the matter]. "They inform" means they make it known. "And they do not come to an agreement" means they do not assemble for the purpose of reaching an agreement.
"And they do not cause reflection" means they do not cause [the other party] to consider. "And they do not come to a reconciliation" means for the purpose of mutual reconciliation.

They do not assemble. "Those whose strength is non-conciliation" means those for whom non-conciliation itself is their strength; thus they are "those whose strength is non-conciliation. "Those who speak of non-renunciation":
for those who think, "If the legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) taken up by us is lawful (*dhammika*), we shall uphold it;
if it is unlawful (*adhammika*), we shall relinquish it," they are called "those who speak of renunciation. But these [others] are not...

"Thus they maintain" means they maintain [their views] without relinquishing them. "With persistence and adherence, having become dogmatic" means having become dogmatic through the persistence of views and the adherence to views.
"This alone is the truth" means that this very statement of ours is the truth.
"All else is vain" means that the speech of the rest is vain and empty. The white side (the wholesome) is of plain meaning indeed.
The fifth chapter on Parisa is finished.
The first fifty-sections are completed.
2. The second fifty-sections.
(6) 1. Commentary on the Chapter on Persons (Puggalavagga): 53.

In the first [section] of the second fifty, because it is mentioned together with the universal monarch (cakkavattin), the phrase "out of compassion for the world" is not stated. Furthermore, through the arising of a universal monarch, two kinds of excellence are obtained; through the arising of Buddhas, all three are obtained. 54.
In the second [section], "wondrous persons" (acchariyamanussa) refers to those who are practiced persons (āciṇṇamanussa) and marvelous persons (abbhutamanussa).
55. "In the third [case], it causes remorse for many people" means that it causes remorse for the great multitude of people.

In this regard, the passing away of a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavattin) causes remorse among gods and humans within a single world-system (cakkavāḷa), whereas the passing away of a Tathāgata causes remorse throughout ten thousand world-systems.

56. "In the fourth [case], they are worthy of a stupa (thūpa)" means they are suitable or appropriate for a stupa. For by maintaining the shrine (cetiya) of a wheel-turning monarch, one obtains two types of success; but by maintaining the shrine of the Buddhas, one obtains all three.
57. In the fifth [verse], "awakened" (*buddha*) means they have awakened to the four truths through their own power.
58. In the sixth, "while crying out" (*phalantiyā*) means while making a sound. "Not trembling" (*na santasantī*) means they do not fear.

In that regard, one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*) does not fear because of the abandonment of their own view of a personal identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*); whereas a noble steed (*hatthājānīyo*) fears because of the strength of the view of a personal identity.
The same method applies to the seventh and eighth [chapters] as well.
61. Regarding the ninth: "Kimpurisā" refers to *kinnaras*. "They do not speak human speech" means they do not converse in the language of humans.
It is said that they once brought a *kinnara* to show it to King Dharmāsoka; he said, "Speak to me! The *kinnara*—
He did not wish to speak. A certain man, thinking, "I shall have him speak," descended to the lower terrace, split two wooden stakes, and placed a cooking pot upon them. It fell over on both sides.
Seeing this, the kinnara said only this: "Is it not possible to split another single stake? Later, at another time, two...
They brought the kinnaras and presented them. The king said, "Speak with them. They did not wish to speak.
One man, thinking, "I will make them speak," took them and went to the marketplace.
There, one saw mangoes and fish; another saw wood-apples (*kapiṭṭha*) and tamarind fruits (*ambilikā*). Thereupon, the first [thought], "This is a great poison..."
“People eat this; how is it that they do not become exhausted? he asked. The other replied, “How is it that these people, by depending on this, do not become afflicted with leprosy?
Thus, even though they are able to speak human speech, they do not speak because they perceive two purposes [in remaining silent].
62. In the tenth [case], "unopposed" means unobstructed and unretreated.
63. "In the eleventh [verse], 'association with the unpeaceful' means association with bad persons (*asappurisa*).

'One should not speak' means one should not speak by way of exhortation or instruction; the sense is: "let him not speak. 'I too would not speak to the elder' means that I too would not speak to an elder monk by way of exhortation or instruction.
'Compassionate toward what is harmful' means desiring what is harmful. 'Not compassionate toward what is beneficial' means..."
“Not desiring what is beneficial”: one would say to him, “I will not do your bidding. “One would vex him”:
by not doing his bidding, one would cause him distress. “Even seeing it, one would not act upon it”:
even though seeing and knowing it, I would not carry out his word. By this method, the meaning is to be understood in all instances.
"But in the bright fortnight, one should say 'Well done' to him" means that one should speak to him in approval of his words, saying, "Excellent! It is good; it has been well spoken by you.
64. In the twelfth [case], "verbal exchange on both sides" refers to the manner of mutual reviling and counter-reviling between the two parties.
The wandering of speech is *vācā-saṃsāra*. "Contempt for views" (*diṭṭhipaḷāsa*) means the contempt characterized by grasping at extremes that arises based on a view;
this is called "contempt for views. "Malice of mind" (*cetaso āghāto*) is anger, for it arises striking the mind.
"Discontent" (*appaccaya*) is a state of dissatisfaction; the meaning is "dejection. "Displeasure" (*anabhiraddhi*) is also anger itself, for it functions by way of non-delight.

"Discontent" is what is said. "It is unpeaceful within" means that all this is unpeaceful both in one's own mind—which is reckoned as the internal belonging to oneself—and in one's own retinue, which consists of co-residents and pupils.
"In that regard" means in that [context]. The remainder should be understood according to the method already stated.
The first chapter, on individuals, is concluded. (7) 2.
Explanation of the Chapter on Happiness (Sukhavagga): 65.

Regarding the first [sutta] of the second [chapter]: "Householder's happiness" is the happiness of householders rooted in the fulfillment of all desires. "Renunciant's happiness" is the happiness of renunciants rooted in renunciation.

66. In the second [tetrad], "pleasure of sensual desires" (*kāmasukha*) is the pleasure arising with reference to sensual desires. "Pleasure of renunciation" (*nekkhammasukha*)—renunciation (*nekkhamma*) refers to going forth (*pabbajjā*); it is the pleasure arising with reference to that. 67.

In the third [tetrad], "pleasure of acquisitions" (*upadhisukha*) is the pleasure of the three planes of existence. "Pleasure without acquisitions" (*nirupadhisukha*) is supramundane pleasure (*lokuttarasukha*). 68.

In the fourth [tetrad], "pleasure with taints" (*sāsavasukha*) is the pleasure of the round of existence (*vaṭṭasukha*), which serves as a condition for the taints (*āsava*). "Pleasure without taints" (*anāsavasukha*) is the pleasure of the cessation of the round (*vivaṭṭasukha*), which does not serve as a condition for them.

69. In the fifth [pair], "with material basis" (*sāmisam*) refers to the defiled happiness leading to the round of existence (*vaṭṭagāmi*); "without material basis" (*nirāmisam*) refers to the undefiled happiness leading to the cessation of the round (*vivaṭṭagāmi*).

70. In the sixth [pair], "noble happiness" (*ariyasukham*) is the happiness of those who are not worldlings (*aputhujjana*); "ignoble happiness" (*anariyasukham*) is the happiness of worldlings (*puthujjana*). 71.

In the seventh [pair], "bodily" (*kāyikam*) is that which arises simultaneously with body-consciousness; "mental" (*cetasikam*) is the happiness of the mind-door. This is explained as being a mixture of both mundane (*lokiya*) and supramundane (*lokuttara*).
72. In the eighth [case], "with rapture" refers to the bliss of the first and second jhānas; "without rapture" refers to the bliss of the third and fourth jhānas.
Therein, the mundane state without rapture is superior to the mundane state with rapture, and the supramundane state without rapture is superior to the supramundane state with rapture.
Thus, the status of being "foremost" should be understood as not transcending the respective planes.
73. In the ninth [section], "blissful happiness" refers to the happiness found in the first three jhānas. "Happiness of equanimity" refers to the happiness of the fourth jhāna. 74.

In the tenth, "happiness of concentration" refers to the happiness attained through either access (upacāra) or absorption (appanā). "Happiness not of concentration" refers to the happiness not attained through either of those two. 75.

In the eleventh, "an object accompanied by rapture" refers to the happiness arising in one who is reviewing the two jhānas accompanied by rapture. The same method applies to an object devoid of rapture. In the twelfth as well, the meaning should be understood by this very same principle.

77. In the thirteenth [section], "having a visible form as object" means having the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere as its object, or that which arises contingent upon any kind of visible form whatsoever.
"Having the immaterial as object" means having the immaterial-sphere jhānas as its object, or that which arises contingent upon any kind of immaterial phenomenon whatsoever.
The second chapter on happiness is concluded.
(8) 3. Explanation of the Chapter on Having Signs (*Sanimittavagga*) 78–79.

Regarding the first [sutta] of the third [chapter]: “Having signs” (*sanimittā*) means having a cause (*sakāraṇā*). The same method applies to the second and subsequent [suttas]. For *nidāna*, *hetu*, *saṅkhāra*, *paccaya*, and *rūpa*—all these are indeed synonyms for a cause. 84. Regarding the seventh [sutta]:

“Accompanied by feeling” (*savedanā*) means that they arise only when there is the associated feeling that serves as their condition, and not when it is absent. The same method applies to the eighth and ninth [suttas] as well.
87. "With conditioned objects" means they arise only by taking as their object a conditioned phenomenon produced by conditions.
"Not with unconditioned objects" means they do not arise by referring to the unconditioned, Nibbāna.

"They do not exist" means that at the moment of the Path (magga-khaṇa) they are said to "not exist," and when the Fruit (phala) is attained, they are said to "have not existed. Thus, in all these ten instances... up to [the end].
"From the state of Arahantship, the teaching was taught.
The third chapter, the Chapter on Signs, is concluded.
(9) 4. Commentary on the Chapter on Dhamma.

88. In the first [section] of the fourth [chapter], "liberation of mind" (cetovimutti) refers to the concentration of fruition (phalasamādhi); "liberation by wisdom" (paññāvimutti) refers to the wisdom of fruition (phalapaññā).
89. In the second [section], "exertion" (paggāha) refers to energy (vīriya); "non-distraction" (avikkhepa) refers to one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā). 90.

In the third [section], "name" (nāma) refers to the four formless aggregates (arūpakkhandhā); "form" (rūpa) refers to the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandho). Thus, in this discourse, what is called the knowledge of discerning the categories of phenomena (dhammakoṭṭhāsaparicchedañāṇa) has been explained.

91. In the fourth [section], "clear knowledge" (*vijjā*) refers to the knowledge of the fruit (*phala-ñāṇa*). "Liberation" (*vimutti*) refers to the remaining factors associated with that [knowledge]. 92.

In the fifth, "view of existence" (*bhava-diṭṭhi*) is the view of eternalism (*sassata-diṭṭhi*). "View of non-existence" (*vibhava-diṭṭhi*) is the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-diṭṭhi*). The sixth and seventh are of plain meaning. 95.

In the eighth, "difficult-to-admonishness" (*dovacassatā*) is the state of being difficult to speak to. "Association with evil friends" (*pāpa-mittatā*) is the state of associating with evil friends. The ninth should be understood by way of the opposite of what has been stated.

97. In the tenth [chapter], "skill in the elements" (*dhātukusalatā*) is the knowledge that the eighteen elements are "elements. "Skill in attention" (*manasikārakusalatā*) is the knowledge of those same elements by applying the three characteristics, such as impermanence, and so forth.

98. In the eleventh [chapter], "skill in offenses" (*āpattikusalatā*) is the knowledge of the five and seven classes of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*). "Skill in emerging from offenses" (*āpattivuṭṭhānakusalatā*) is the knowledge of emerging from offenses either through confession (*desanā*) or through the formal act (*kammavācā*).
The fourth section on phenomena (*dhammavagga*) is concluded.
(10) 5. Commentary on the Chapter on the Foolish (Bālavagga-vaṇṇanā) 99.
Regarding the first [sutta] of the fifth [chapter]: "He bears the future burden" refers to:
"The broom and the lamp, water and the seat, the proclamation of consent, purity, and the weather, the counting of monks, and the exhortation, the Pātimokkha, and the Elder’s burden."
"Thus it is said. Carrying this tenfold burden of an elder while being a novice, without having been requested by the elder, is called "carrying a future burden.

"One does not carry a present burden" means that although one is an elder, by neither performing that same tenfold burden oneself nor exhorting another to do so, one is said not to carry a present burden. This is also stated in the second sutta.
The meaning should be understood by this same method.
101. In the third case, "perceiving what is not allowable as allowable" means perceiving lion meat and so forth—which are not allowable—as "this is allowable.
"Perceiving what is allowable as not allowable" means perceiving the meat of hyenas, cats, and so forth—which are allowable—as "this is not allowable."
Perceiving it thus. The fourth [case] is to be understood in the same manner as already stated.

103. Regarding the fifth: "perceiving what is not an offense as an offense" refers to one who has asked for permission and then washes his belongings, cooks his bowl, cuts his hair, enters a village, and so forth—in these instances there is no offense; yet, in that regard, he perceives it thus: "This is an offense."
"Perceiving as non-offense what is an offense" means that there is an offense in performing those very same acts without having asked for permission; regarding this, one perceives it as "non-offense.
The meaning of the sixth [case] should also be understood by the method already stated. The seventh and subsequent cases are of obvious meaning. 109.
In the eleventh [case], "taints" (āsava) refers to the defilements (kilesa). "It should not be cause for remorse" refers to the failure to set aside property belonging to the Saṅgha.
That which is not to be scrutinized is called "not to be worried about," yet one worries about it.

That which is to be scrutinized is the application of thought and investigation toward that very thing, yet one does not worry about it. The twelve [factors] beginning with concentration are to be understood according to the method explained below.
This is the fifth chapter, the Chapter on the Fool.
The Second Fifty is finished.
3. The Third Fifty (11) 1.
Commentary on the Chapter on the Difficulties of Abandoning Hope (Āsāduppajahavagga).
119. In the first [chapter] of the third fiftieth section, "craving" (*taṇhā*) is "hope. It is difficult to abandon, difficult to give up, and difficult to remove.
