Because hope for gain is so difficult to abandon, beings serve kings for ten years, twenty years, or even sixty years, thinking, "Today we shall receive [something]," or "Tomorrow we shall receive [something]," and they perform agricultural labor and other such tasks, [even entering] a battle arrayed on both sides.
They leap forward; they set out upon goat paths, thorny tracks, and the like; they enter the great ocean by boat.
Because the hope for life is so difficult to abandon, even when the time of death has arrived, they imagine themselves to live for another hundred years.
Even while seeing the signs of karma and the signs of rebirth, they are addressed by compassionate ones: "Give a gift! Make an offering!"
“I shall not die; I shall live”—with such hope, one does not heed the words of anyone. 120.

Regarding the second [type], the *pubbakārī* (one who acts first) is one who performs a service at the outset. The *kataññū-katavedī* (one who knows and acknowledges what has been done) is one who, having recognized what was done by the other, performs a service in return.
Among them, the *pubbakārī* makes the thought, “I am giving a debt,” while the one who acts later [makes the thought], “I am paying a debt.”

He forms the perception: "I shall digest it. 121. Regarding the third [case], "one who is satisfied and one who satisfies": both the *paccekabuddha* and the disciple of the *Tathāgata* who has destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*) are called "satisfied. The *Tathāgata*, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One, is both satisfied and one who satisfies.

122. Regarding the fourth [case], "difficult to satisfy": they are difficult for a donor to satisfy; it is not easy to satisfy them. "Sets aside" means he stores it away and does not consume it. "Distributes" means he gives it to others.

123. "In the fifth [case], he does not relinquish" means that he does not give anything at all to others; rather, having taken for himself just enough for his own subsistence, he gives away the remainder.
124. In the sixth [case], "the sign of the beautiful" (subhanimitta) refers to a desirable object (iṭṭhārammaṇa).
125. In the seventh [case], "the sign of resistance" (paṭighanimitta) refers to an undesirable object.
126. In the eighth [fetter], "the voice of another" refers to hearing unwholesome teachings from another. 127.
In the ninth, "the voice of another" refers to hearing wholesome teachings from another. The remainder is clear in meaning throughout.
Thus ends the first chapter, "The Chapter on Hope and the Difficult-to-Abandon."
(12) 2. Commentary on the Chapter on Entreaties (Āyācanavagga) 131.
Regarding the first [sutta] of the second [chapter]: "One who entreats thus should entreat correctly"—this means that a faithful bhikkhu, having arisen, should entreat, saying:
"Just as the Elder Sāriputta is in wisdom, may I too become such. Just as the Elder Mahāmoggallāna..."

“By means of psychic power (*iddhi*), may I too become like that”—thus, one who prays, yearns, and aspires in this way is said to aspire rightly, because one aspires only for that which exists. To aspire beyond this would be to aspire wrongly.
For such an aspiration is called a wrong aspiration (*micchāpaṭṭhānā*) because it aspires for that which does not exist. Why is that? Because this...

“Monks, this is the balance, this is the measure. For just as a balance must be used by one weighing gold or silver, and a measure by one measuring grain—wherein the balance is for weighing and the measure is for measuring—so too, among my disciples, the monks Sāriputta and Moggallāna are the balance, they are the measure. Taking them [as the standard]...
“It is possible to weigh or measure oneself by thinking, ‘I too am equal in measure to him, whether by knowledge or by psychic power (iddhi),’ and not otherwise.
This same method applies to the second and subsequent verses as well. However, this is the specific distinction here:

regarding the bhikkhunīs Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā, Khemā was foremost in wisdom (paññā) and Uppalavaṇṇā was foremost in psychic power. Therefore, [the text says]: “Whether by wisdom or by psychic power...”

“May I become such as this,” thus one should pray with right aspiration. Likewise, the householder Citta was foremost in wisdom, and Prince Hatthaka was foremost in great psychic power (*mahiddhikatā*).
Therefore, one who prays with right aspiration should pray, thinking: “May I become such through wisdom or through psychic power.
Khujjuttarā was also foremost in great wisdom, and Nandamātā was foremost in great psychic power. Therefore, through wisdom...
"Or by means of psychic power, may I become such as this"—thus one should pray, making a proper supplication.
(135) "Wounded" (*khata*) is so called because of the wounding of virtues; "maimed" (*upahata*) is so called because of the maiming of virtues—the meaning is that its virtues are severed and lost.
"He preserves himself" means he tends to, guards, and protects his virtueless self.
“Blameworthy” means accompanied by fault. “Censurable” means subject to reproach. “Produces” means acquires. “Without having investigated” means without having known or determined.

“Without having scrutinized” means without having entered into [the matter]. “Of one who deserves dispraise” means of a sectarian (tīrthika) or a follower of a sectarian who is possessed of dispraise and has practiced wrongly.
“Speaks praise” means saying, “This person is well-practiced; this person is rightly practiced.”

He speaks of the virtues. "Of one worthy of praise" means of anyone among the Buddha and others who has practiced correctly. "He speaks dispraise" means he speaks of faults, saying, "This person has practiced poorly;

this person has practiced wrongly. "He speaks dispraise of one unworthy of dispraise" refers here to a certain individual who [speaks ill] of those who have practiced poorly or wrongly, such as the followers of other sects (*tīrthika*) and the disciples of those other sects.
“He speaks dispraise, saying: ‘In such a way they have practiced wrongly; in such a way they have practiced falsely. He speaks praise of those worthy of praise, saying:
‘In such a way they have practiced well; in such a way they have practiced rightly,’ referring to the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas who have practiced well and practiced rightly.”
136. In the sixth [section], "grounds for lack of confidence" (*appasādanīye ṭhāne*) means grounds for a lack of confidence.
"He displays a lack of confidence" means that regarding wrong practice and improper practice, he generates a lack of confidence by thinking, "This is right practice, this is proper practice.
Regarding grounds for confidence, he displays a lack of confidence by thinking, "This is wrong practice, this is improper practice," concerning right practice and proper practice.
"Janetī" (she gives birth). The rest here is self-evident. 137.
Regarding the seventh [case], "in two": this means in two locations or for two reasons. "Practicing wrongly" means practicing wrong conduct.
"Toward mother and father" refers to [the case of] Mittavindaka toward his mother, and Ajātasattu toward his father.
The bright fortnight (sukkapakkha) is to be understood in the same manner as previously stated. 138.
Regarding the eighth [case], "toward the Tathāgata and toward the Tathāgata’s disciples": Devadatta was like one toward the Tathāgata, and Kokālika was like one toward the Tathāgata’s disciples.
In the bright fortnight, Ānanda Thera was like one toward the Tathāgata, and Nanda, the son of the merchant Gopālaka, was like one toward the Tathāgata’s disciples.
And like a disciple of the Tathāgata.
139. "The purification of one's own mind" means the purification of one's own consciousness; this is the name for the eight attainments (*samāpatti*).
"And he does not cling to anything in the world" means that he does not grasp even a single phenomenon among the things in the world, such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
He does not grasp. Thus, herein, the second state is called non-clinging (*anupādāna*). The tenth and eleventh [sections] are of obvious meaning.
The second chapter, the Chapter on Entreaties (*Āyācanavagga*), is concluded. (13) 3. Commentary on the Chapter on Giving (*Dānavagga*)
142. Regarding the first [section] of the third [chapter]: "Gifts" (*dānāni*) refers to things given by way of being bestowed; this is a name for the object to be given (*deyyadhamma*).

Alternatively, the volition (*cetanā*) accompanied by its basis is "giving"; this is a name for the relinquishing of what has been acquired. "Material gift" (*āmisa-dāna*) refers to the four requisites by way of being bestowed; this is called a material gift.
"Dharma-gift" (*dhamma-dāna*) refers here to when someone, having explained the path leading to the attainment of the Deathless (*amata*), [bestows it].
This is what is called the gift of the Dhamma. 143.
In the second [case], the four requisites are called a sacrifice by way of being offered; it should be understood that the Dhamma is also a sacrifice by way of being offered. 144.

In the third, the relinquishing of material things is the relinquishment of material things (*āmisacāga*); the relinquishing of the Dhamma is the relinquishment of the Dhamma (*dhammacāga*). In the fourth, the difference is merely due to the prefix.

146. In the fifth [section], the enjoyment of the four requisites is the enjoyment of material things (*āmisa-bhoga*); the enjoyment of the Dhamma is the enjoyment of the Dhamma (*dhamma-bhoga*). In the sixth, the distinction is merely a prefix. 148.
In the seventh, the sharing of the four requisites is the sharing of material things (*āmisa-saṃvibhāga*); the sharing of the Dhamma is the sharing of the Dhamma (*dhamma-saṃvibhāga*). 149.
In the eighth, the gathering through the four requisites is the gathering of material things (*āmisa-saṅgaha*); the gathering through the Dhamma is the gathering of the Dhamma (*dhamma-saṅgaha*).

150. In the ninth [chapter], assistance by means of the four requisites is assistance with material things (*āmisa-anuggaha*); assistance by means of the Dhamma is assistance with the Dhamma (*dhamma-anuggaha*). 151.

In the tenth [chapter], compassion by means of the four requisites is compassion with material things (*āmisa-anukampā*); compassion by means of the Dhamma is compassion with the Dhamma (*dhamma-anukampā*).
This is the third chapter on Giving.
(14) 4. Commentary on the Chapter on Spreading (Santhāravagga) 152.
In the first [offense], "spreading" (*santhāra*) refers to the act of spreading out, by means of four conditions, for the purpose of concealing both oneself and another;

this is "spreading with material things" (*āmisa-santhāra*). "Spreading with the Dhamma" (*dhamma-santhāra*) refers to spreading out by means of the Dhamma. In the second [offense], the distinction is merely the prefix (*upasagga*).

154. In the third [section], the seeking (*esanā*) of material things (*āmisa*) of the kind already described is "seeking for material things" (*āmisesanā*); the seeking of the Dhamma is "seeking for the Dhamma" (*dhammesanā*). In the fourth, the distinction is merely the prefix (*upasagga*). 156.

In the fifth, the seeking for material things that has reached its culmination is called "craving for material things" (*āmisapariyeṭṭhi*); likewise, the seeking for the Dhamma that has reached its culmination is called "craving for the Dhamma" (*dhammapariyeṭṭhī*).
157. In the sixth, honoring with material things is "honor by means of material things" (*āmisapūjā*); honoring with the Dhamma is "honor by means of the Dhamma" (*dhammapūjā*).
158. In the seventh [chapter], "hospitalities" (*ātitheyyāni*) refers to gifts for guests; *atitheyyāni* is also a reading. 159.

In the eighth, "material success" (*āmisa-iddhi*) is so called by way of the attainment and accomplishment of material things; likewise, "Dhamma-success" (*dhamma-iddhi*) is so called by way of the attainment and accomplishment of the Dhamma.
160. In the ninth, "increase of material things" (*āmisa-vuddhi*) is increase by means of material things; "increase of Dhamma" (*dhamma-vuddhi*) is increase by means of the Dhamma.

161. In the tenth [chapter], in the sense of being a source of delight, material things are the treasure of material things (*āmisa-ratana*), and the Dhamma is the treasure of the Dhamma (*dhamma-ratana*).

162. In the eleventh [chapter], the gathering and increasing of material things is the accumulation of material things (*āmisa-sannicaya*); the gathering and increasing of the Dhamma is the accumulation of the Dhamma (*dhamma-sannicaya*). 163.
In the twelfth [chapter], the abundance of material things is the plenitude of material things (*āmisa-vepulla*); the abundance of the Dhamma is the plenitude of the Dhamma (*dhamma-vepulla*).
The Fourth Chapter on Reclining.
(15) 5. Explanation of the Chapter on Attainments. 164.
Regarding the first [sutta] of the fifth [chapter], "skill in attainments" means having discerned the suitability of nutriment and the suitability of the season.

Skill in attaining meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). Skill in emerging from meditative absorption means that just as one who emerges at the predetermined time is called "skilled in emerging" because he is proficient, so too is this proficiency.
165. In the second [set], *ajjava* is uprightness; *maddava* is softness.

166. In the third [tetrad], "patience" (*khanti*) refers to patience as endurance (*adhivāsanakhanti*). "Gentleness" (*soracca*) is the state of being well-disposed (*suratabhāva*) by virtue of good moral conduct (*susīlya*).

167. In the fourth [tetrad], "kindness" (*sākhalya*) is the state of being friendly through the use of gentle speech. "Hospitality" (*paṭisanthāra*) is the act of welcoming with either material gifts or the Dhamma. 168.

In the fifth [tetrad], "non-cruelty" (*avihiṃsā*) is the preliminary stage of compassion (*karuṇā*). "Purity" (*soceyya*) is the state of being pure by virtue of morality (*sīla*). The sixth and seventh tetrads have meanings that are self-evident.
171. In the eighth [chapter], "the power of reflection" (*paṭisaṅkhānabala*) means the power of reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇabala*). 172.

In the ninth, by being unshakable in regard to negligence (*muṭṭhassacca*), mindfulness itself is the power of mindfulness (*satibala*); by being unshakable in regard to restlessness (*uddhacca*), concentration itself is the power of concentration (*samādhibala*).
173. In the tenth, "serenity" (*samatha*) is one-pointedness of mind (*cittékaggatā*); "insight" (*vipassanā*) is the knowledge that discerns conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārapariggāhakaññāṇa*).
174. In the eleventh [section], "failure in virtue" (*sīlavipatti*) means immorality (*dussīlya*). "Failure in view" (*diṭṭhivipatti*) means wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*). 175.

In the twelfth [section], "perfection in virtue" (*sīlasampadā*) means the state of having complete virtue. "Perfection in view" (*diṭṭhisampadā*) means the state of possessing right view (*sammādiṭṭhikabhāva*).

By that, there is the right view of the ownership of action (*kammassakata-sammādiṭṭhi*), the right view of meditative absorption (*jhāna-sammādiṭṭhi*), the right view of insight (*vipassanā-sammādiṭṭhi*), and the right view of the path (*magga-sammādiṭṭhi*).
"Right view regarding the fruit" includes all five kinds of right view. 176.

In the thirteenth [chapter], "purification of virtue" refers to the virtue that brings about purification. "Purification of view" refers to the right view of the four paths that brings about purification, or alternatively, all five kinds of right view.
177. In the fourteenth [chapter], "purification of view" is precisely the right view that brings about purification. For one who possesses such a view...
"And striving" (*padhāna*) refers to the energy associated with the lower paths. For that [energy] is in accordance with that view;
thus it is said: "the striving of one who possesses such a view. 178.
Regarding the fifteenth, "non-contentment with wholesome states": this refers to the state of being unsatisfied with wholesome states, excluding the path of Arahantship.
179. In the sixteenth [chapter], "muddled mindfulness" (*muṭṭhassacca*) refers to the state of being forgetful. "Lack of clear comprehension" (*asampajañña*) refers to the state of ignorance. 180.
In the seventeenth [chapter], mindfulness has the characteristic of not forgetting. Clear comprehension has the characteristic of right understanding.
The fifth chapter on Attainments is finished. The third fiftieth section is completed.
1. The Catechism on Anger (Kodhapeyyāla) 181.

Among those that follow, anger (kodha) has the characteristic of being provoked to wrath. Resentment (upanāha) has the characteristic of persistent ill-will. Sycophancy (makkha) has the characteristic of smearing over one's own good deeds.

Hypocrisy (palāsa) has the characteristic of grasping at both ends [of a dispute]. Envy (issā) has the characteristic of envying. The state of the fifth kind of stinginess (macchariya) is avarice (macchariya).
All of these have the characteristic of being stingy. Deceit has the characteristic of concealing what has been done. Guile has the characteristic of crookedness.
Shamelessness (ahirika) is the mode of lacking moral dread. Fearlessness of blame (anottappa) is the mode of not fearing reproach.
Non-anger and the other [wholesome states] should be understood by way of their opposites.
185. Regarding "for a bhikkhu in training": it should be understood that for all seven types of those in training (*sekkha*), these [factors] lead to the decline of progressively higher qualities;
however, for an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), they lead to decline even more quickly.
"For the sake of non-decline" means for the purpose of not falling away from progressively higher qualities.
187. "As if placed there as a burden": it should be understood that he is established in hell just as he was brought and placed there.
190. "A certain person" (ekacca): he in whom these qualities such as anger exist is called a "certain person.
The series on anger is finished.

2. The Section on the Unwholesome (Akusala-peyyāla), §§ 191–200. "Blameworthy" means accompanied by hatred (*sadosa*). "Blameless" means free from hatred (*niddosa*). "Resulting in suffering" means increasing suffering. "Resulting in happiness" means increasing happiness.
"Afflictive" means accompanied by suffering. "Non-afflictive" means free from suffering. Up to this point, only the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*) have been explained.
The Section on the Unwholesome is finished.
3. The Vinaya Section. 201.
"Bhikkhus, depending upon these two purposes," means, bhikkhus, based on two aims and for two reasons.
"Having intended": the training rule was laid down; that is, a section of training was established.
"For the well-being of the Saṅgha" means for the state of the Saṅgha being well; the meaning is for the sake of receiving [the teaching] by saying, "Well, Bhante.

"For the comfort of the Saṅgha" means for the sake of the Saṅgha’s dwelling in ease. "The ill-behaved" refers to those of immoral conduct. "The well-behaved" refers to those of pleasant conduct. "Those pertaining to the present life" (diṭṭhadhammika).

"Of the taints (*āsava*)" refers to the taints characterized by suffering such as execution, imprisonment, and so forth, which are to be encountered in this very life, in this very selfhood, on account of transgression.

"For the sake of restraint" means for the purpose of closing them off. "Of those pertaining to the future" refers to similar taints arising in the future, characterized by the suffering of the states of deprivation (*apāya*).
"For the sake of warding off" means for the purpose of preventing them. "Of enmities" refers also to unwholesome enmities.
“Of persons”: of those who are hostile. “Faults” (*vajja*): of defects (*dosa*). Or rather, it is these very phenomena of suffering that are intended here as “faults” because they are to be avoided.
“Terrors” (*bhaya*): of both the fear consisting of mental trepidation and the causes of fear, which are likewise those same phenomena of suffering.
“Unwholesome” (*akusala*): of phenomena of suffering reckoned as unwholesome in the sense of being intolerable. “Out of compassion for householders.”

When householders were complaining, the training rule was laid down out of compassion for householders; it is said to have been "laid down" for that purpose. "For the sake of cutting off the faction of those with evil desires" means:
lest those with evil desires, relying upon a faction, should cause a schism in the Saṅgha—it was for the purpose of cutting off their faction.

"For the sake of inspiring confidence in those lacking confidence" means: even among wise people who previously lacked confidence, [it was for the sake of inspiring confidence] through the excellence of the laying down of the training rules.
"Having seen [this], for the purpose of inspiring confidence; for the increase of those who have confidence" means for the sake of producing further and further confidence in those already confident.
"For the stability of the true Dhamma" means for the sake of the long endurance of the true Dhamma.
"For the support of the Vinaya" means for the sake of supporting the fivefold Vinaya as well.
202–230. "The Pātimokkha has been laid down" means that two kinds of Pātimokkha have been laid down:

the Bhikkhu-pātimokkha and the Bhikkhunī-pātimokkha. "The recitation of the Pātimokkha" means that nine recitations of the Pātimokkha have been laid down: five for the bhikkhus and four for the bhikkhunīs.
"The suspension of the Pātimokkha" refers to the suspension of the Uposatha. [The same applies to] the Pavāraṇā.
"Proclaimed" means two types of invitation (*pavāraṇā*) have been proclaimed: that on the fourteenth day and that on the fifteenth day.
"The suspension of the invitation has been proclaimed" means that for a monk who has committed an offense, the suspension of the invitation is proclaimed while the invitation ceremony is underway.

Regarding the formal act of censure (*tajjanīyakamma*) and so forth, the formal act of censure was proclaimed for the monks Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka, who were piercing one another with the weapons of speech.
The act of demotion was prescribed for the foolish and incompetent monk Seyyasaka.

The act of banishment was prescribed concerning the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka, who were corrupters of families. The act of reconciliation was prescribed for the elder Sudhamma, who had reviled householders.
The act of suspension was prescribed for those who do not acknowledge an offense and so forth.
The granting of probation (*parivāsa*) was prescribed for one who has committed a grave offense (*garukāpatti*) that was concealed.

The sending back to the beginning (*mūlāya paṭikassana*) was prescribed for one who commits an intermediate offense (*antarāpatti*) during the period of probation. The granting of the trial period (*mānatta*) was prescribed for an offense, whether concealed or unconcealed.
The rehabilitation (*abbhāna*) was prescribed for one who has completed the trial period. Reinstatement (*osāraṇīya*) is for one who conducts himself properly.
It has been prescribed. Regarding improper conduct and so forth, that which entails expulsion has been prescribed.
There is ordination by the "Come, monk" formula; ordination by going for refuge; ordination by exhortation; ordination by answering questions;

ordination by a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatutthakamma*); ordination by the heavy rules (*garudhamma*); ordination before both Saṅghas; and ordination by messenger.
Eightfold ordination has been prescribed. "A formal act consisting of a motion goes to nine points"—thus a formal act consisting of a motion with nine points has been prescribed.

"A formal act consisting of a motion and a second [proclamation] goes to seven points"—thus a formal act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation has been prescribed as having exactly seven points.
"A formal act consisting of a motion and a fourth [proclamation] goes to seven points"—thus it has been prescribed as having exactly seven points.

The *ñatticatuttha-kamma* (formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) has been laid down. Regarding the first offenses such as the first *pārājika*, the "first laying down" (*paṭhamapaññatti*) refers to what was laid down when [the rule] was not yet laid down.
The "subsequent laying down" (*anupaññatti*) refers to what was laid down for those very same offenses once they had already been laid down.

*Sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of) has been laid down by way of these four kinds of presence: presence of the Dhamma, presence of the Vinaya, presence of the Saṅgha, and presence of the individual.
The verdict of mindfulness (*sativinaya*) was prescribed for the sake of not reproving one whose taints are destroyed and who has attained the fullness of mindfulness.

The verdict of past insanity (*amūḷhavinaya*) was prescribed for a monk who is insane. The verdict of acting according to what has been admitted (*paṭiññātakaraṇa*) was prescribed for the purpose of not clearing a charge against one who has been accused without his admission.
The majority decision (*yebhuyyasikā*) was prescribed for the purpose of settling a legal issue by adopting the view of the majority who speak in accordance with the Dhamma.
The *tassapāpiyasikā* (proceeding for further penalty) was prescribed for the purpose of restraining a person in whom evil has increased.

The *tiṇavatthāraka* (covering over as with grass) was prescribed for the purpose of settling the remaining offenses— excluding those that are grave (*thullavajja*) and those connected with householders— of monks who have committed many non-monastic acts through quarreling and the like.
The Vinayapeyyāla is finished.
4. The Rāgapeyyāla. 231.
"For the direct knowledge of lust, monks"—this is for the purpose of fully understanding and for the purpose of making manifest the lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure.

"For the sake of full understanding" means for the purpose of thorough comprehension. "For the sake of complete destruction" means for the purpose of reaching total exhaustion. "For the sake of abandoning" means for the purpose of relinquishing.
"For the sake of destruction and vanishing" means for the purpose of reaching destruction and vanishing. "For the sake of dispassion" means for the purpose of becoming dispassionate.
"For the sake of cessation" means for the purpose of ceasing. "For the sake of giving up" means for the purpose of relinquishing. "For the sake of relinquishment" means for the purpose of letting go.
232–246. *Thambhassa* means of stubbornness due to anger and conceit. *Sārabbhassa* means of contentiousness characterized by the desire for superiority in arguments.
*Mānassa* means of the ninefold conceit. *Atimānassa* means of the conceit that consists in overestimating oneself. *Madassa* means of intoxication in the form of exhilaration.
*Pamādassa* means of negligence, which is the absence of mindfulness and the relinquishing of the mind to the five strands of sensual pleasure.
The remainder is clear in meaning throughout.
The Section on Passion (*Rāgapeyyāla*) is finished.
From the *Manorathapūraṇī*, the commentary on the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Book of Twos is finished.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
[In the] Aṅguttara Nikāya.
The Commentary on the Book of Threes (Tikanipāta-aṭṭhakathā) 1.
The First Fifty (Paṭhamapaṇṇāsaka) 1.
The Chapter on Fools (Bālavagga)

1. Commentary on the Bhaya Sutta In the first sutta of the *Tikanipāta*, regarding the terms "fears" (*bhayāni*) and so forth: "fear" (*bhaya*) is mental terror. "Calamity" (*upaddava*) is the state of lack of one-pointedness of mind. "Misfortune" (*upasagga*) is the state of being afflicted, the state of being stuck here and there.
Their distinction should be understood as follows: thieves dwelling in mountainous wildernesses send word to the inhabitants of the countryside.
—“On such-and-such a day, we shall attack your village! From the moment they hear this news, they fall into fear and terror. This is what is called mental panic.
Thinking, “Lest those angry thieves bring us harm,” they take their valuables and, together with their bipeds and quadrupeds, enter the forest.
There, they lie down here and there on the ground, being bitten by gadflies, mosquitoes, and other insects;
entering into thickets, they trample over stumps and thorns. As they wander in this manner, their state of being distracted is called the mode of non-one-pointedness.
Then, when the thieves do not return on the aforementioned day, [the villagers] think, "The news must be false; we shall enter the village."

They enter the village with their full equipment. Then, having learned that they have entered, the thieves surround the village, set fire to the gates, kill the people, plunder all their wealth, and depart.
Those among them who survived the slaughter extinguish the fire and sit down here and there, clinging to the shadows of watchtowers, the shadows of trees, the shadows of walls, and so forth.
“Lamenting for what is lost. This is the mode of being beset;
it is called the mode of clinging. “Reed-houses” means houses thatched and covered with reeds; however, the other materials used here are made of wood.
The same principle applies to grass-houses as well. “Gabled houses” means houses constructed with gables. “Plastered inside and out” means [plastered] within...
"And plastered both inside and out. "Windless" means that the entry of wind has been prevented.
"With well-fitting bolts" means that because they were made by skilled carpenters, the doors fit perfectly within the wooden frames. "With windows closed" means that the windows are properly fitted.
By these two phrases, rather than stating the constant state of being shut for the doors and windows, their excellence alone is described.
However, at whatever moment one desires, those [gates] are closed and opened.
"They arise from a fool" means they arise depending solely upon a fool;
for a foolish, unwise person, when aspiring to sovereignty, viceroyalty, or some other great position, [employs] a few widows' sons who resemble himself...
Having seized a great bandit, he says, "Come, I shall make you lords," and while striking them in remote villages near mountain thickets and such places, he makes his status as a plunderer known;
gradually, he strikes even in market towns and the countryside.
People abandon their homes and depart, longing for a place of safety. Relying on them...
In the springtime, both monks and nuns depart, abandoning their respective places of residence.
In the places they have gone, almsfood and lodgings become difficult to obtain. Thus, fear has indeed come upon all four assemblies.
Even among those who have gone forth, two foolish monks, having initiated a dispute with one another, begin to accuse each other.
Thus, as in the case of the residents of Kosambī, a great quarrel arises.
Since fear has indeed come upon the four assemblies, he concluded the teaching by following the sequence: "Whatever fears arise, all of them arise from the fool.
2. Commentary on the *Lakkhaṇa Sutta* (The Discourse on Characteristics)

2. In the second [verse], it is "characterized by action" (*kammalakkhaṇo*) because its characteristic is action proceeding through the doors of the body and so forth, which is the cause for perceiving [the nature of things].
"Wisdom is adorned by its own manifestation" (*apadānasobhanī paññā*): the meaning is that wisdom which is called *paññā* is adorned by its own manifestation;
both fools and the wise become manifest through their own respective conduct. For the path traveled by a fool reveals trees, shrubs, villages, market towns, and so forth.
To one who has passed by after burning [something], it is like the path taken by the fire at the end of an aeon (*indaggi*);

only the site of the conflagration remains visible, filled with glowing embers and ashes. The path taken by a wise person is like the track of a cloud that covers the four continents, filling small ponds and other water sources and bringing about an abundance of various crops.
Just as on the path taken by that cloud, there are pools full of water and various kinds of grain, fruits, and produce.
And those various places become manifest; thus, on a path traveled by the wise, only success is seen, not failure.
The rest here is of plain meaning.
3. Commentary on the Cintī Sutta.

3. Regarding "the characteristics of a fool" (*bālalakkhaṇāni*) in the third [section]: they are called "characteristics of a fool" because by means of these he is characterized—that is, known—as "this one is a fool.

These very things are the causes for recognizing him, thus they are the "signs of a fool" (*bālanimittāni*). "The exploits of a fool" (*bālāpadānāni*) are the deeds of a fool. "One who thinks ill-thought thoughts" (*duccintitacintī*):
while thinking, he thinks only what is ill-thought by way of covetousness, ill-will, and wrong view. "One who speaks ill-spoken words" (*dubbhāsitabhāsī*):...
Even while speaking, he speaks only what is ill-spoken, such as the various forms of false speech and so forth.
"One who performs deeds of wrongdoing" means that even while acting, he performs only deeds of wrongdoing by way of killing living beings and so forth.

The "characteristics of a wise man," and so on, should be understood according to what has already been stated. Furthermore, the phrases "one who thinks well-thought thoughts" and so forth should be applied here by way of mental good conduct and the rest.
4. Commentary on the *Accayasutta* (Sutta 4).
In the fourth [verse], "he does not see a transgression as a transgression" means he does not see his own offense as an offense.
"Having seen it as a transgression, he does not make amends according to the Dhamma" means that even though he knows, "I have erred," whatever the Dhamma [requires]...
He does not do that; having brought forth a disciplinary act (*daṇḍakamma*), he does not confess his transgression nor ask for forgiveness.
When another, realizing "I have erred," brings forth a disciplinary act and asks for forgiveness, he does not accept the confession according to the Dhamma.
The "white side" (the virtuous counterpart) is to be understood as the opposite of what has been stated.
5. Commentary on the Ayoniso Sutta (The Discourse on Improper Attention) Regarding the fifth [sutta]:

"He asks questions improperly" means that when it was asked, "Udāyi, how many bases for recollection are there?", the Elder Lāḷudāyin, having thought, "Former abodes will be a basis for recollection," [acted] through improper reflection, just like the Elder Lāḷudāyin.
He makes what is not a question into a question; he is one who answers a question inappropriately.

Even when answering a question that has been thus formulated, he answers inappropriately—just like that same elder—by way of such statements as: "Here, Bhante, a bhikkhu recollects his manifold past abodes, that is to say, one birth," and so forth.
He speaks of what is not a question as if it were a question. Regarding the phrase "with well-rounded words and phrases" (*parimaṇḍalehi padabyañjanehi*):

here, "word-phrase" (*padabyañjana*) means that the word itself is the "phrase" because it expresses the meaning. That [word] is called "well-rounded" when it is spoken having fulfilled the phonemes (*akkhara*) and without omitting the tenfold analytical discernment of the phrasing (*byañjanabuddhi*). The meaning is: "with such words and phrases. "Cohesive" (*siliṭṭhehi*) refers to the cohesion of the words.
"By those who are proficient. "By those who have approached" means by those who have approached both the meaning and the reason.

"Does not express approval" means that even though one has thus properly prepared everything with the requisite reasons, one does not approve of or rejoice in another's answer to a question, as the Elder Lāḷudāyi did regarding the question of the Elder Sāriputta. As it is said: [the following passage].

“It is impossible, friend Sāriputta, it cannot happen, that one who has passed beyond the company of the devas who subsist on physical food and has been reborn in a certain mind-made body should enter and emerge from the cessation of perception and feeling;
such a thing is not possible.”
Regarding the phrases "one who asks a question methodically" and so forth: like the Elder Ānanda, one should reflect methodically upon the question and provide a methodical answer.
For when the Elder was asked, "Ānanda, how many bases for recollection are there?", he reflected methodically, thinking, "This will be the question," and then answered methodically, saying:
"In this case, venerable sir, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures... [and so on]."

“He enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna. Venerable sir, this basis for recollection, thus developed and thus cultivated, leads to a pleasant dwelling in this very life. [The Blessed One] gave his approval:
“It is well,” just as the Tathāgata gives wise approval when a question has been answered by the Elder Ānanda. For the Tathāgata... “Excellent!”... [and so on].
“Good, Ānanda! Therefore, Ānanda, you should also remember this sixth basis for recollection.
Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is mindful as he goes forward and mindful as he returns,” and so forth. The meaning of the sixth and subsequent [bases] is self-evident.
9. Commentary on the Khaṭa Sutta.

9. In the ninth [discourse], the bright fortnight (sukkapakkha) in its earlier stage is defined by the ten courses of wholesome action (dasakusala-kammapatha); subsequently, it extends as far as the path to Arhatship (arahattamagga). "And one generates much merit"—here, merit consisting of a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane is spoken of.

10. Commentary on the Mala Sutta: In the tenth [discourse], the state of being immoral is immorality (dussīlya); immorality itself is the stain, thus "the stain of immorality" (dussīlyamala). In what sense is it a stain?

It is [called] *mala* (stain) in the sense of burning along with it (*anudahanatthena*), in the sense of being foul-smelling (*duggandhatthena*), and in the sense of making things soiled (*kiliṭṭhakaraṇatthena*). For it burns along with one in the states of woe such as the hells;

thus, in the sense of burning along with it, it is a stain. A person possessed of this is loathsome even in the presence of his parents, in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks, and at the sites of Bodhi shrines; and in all directions, of him—
“Indeed, such evil karma has been committed by him”—thus, because the scent of disrepute spreads, it is *mala* (stain) in the sense of being foul-smelling.
Furthermore, a person possessed of that [stain] experiences distress wherever he goes, and his bodily actions and so forth become impure and lusterless;
thus, it is *mala* in the sense of making things defiled. Moreover, it [obstructs] the prosperity of gods and humans...

Furthermore, it should be understood as "stain" (*mala*) in the sense of causing both the attainment of Nibbāna and [the roots of merit] to wither; the same principle applies to the stains of envy, stinginess, and greed.
The first chapter, the Chapter on Fools, is concluded.
2. The Chapter on Cartwrights.

1. Commentary on the Ñātasutta 11. Regarding the first [verse] of the second [sutta]: "Known" (*ñāta*) means recognized or well-known. "Not in conformity" (*ananulomika*) means that which does not conform to the Teaching (*sāsana*);

thus it is "not in conformity," and [the phrase refers to] within that which is not in conformity. "Bodily action" (*kāyakamma*) refers to bodily misconduct such as the taking of life and so forth. "Coarse" (*oḷārika*).

Or, he is unable to encourage others in such [virtuous] ways. Instead, he encourages and causes others to adopt such things as saying, "It is proper to worship the directions," or "It is proper to offer sacrifices to spirits.

Regarding verbal action, although lying and so forth are gross, one who does not wish to give his own property to another thinks, "It is proper to say 'it is not there'"; this is called the lie of deception.

One encourages others in such a way. Even regarding mental action, covetousness and the like are coarse; however, one who speaks while deceiving the subject of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna) is said to encourage others in unwholesome states, like the Elder who dwelt in the Dakkhiṇavihāra.
It is said that a certain attendant, the son of a minister, approached that elder and asked: "When practicing loving-kindness (mettā), first toward what kind of person..."
"Should one practice loving-kindness? he asked. Without explaining whether the object was similar or dissimilar, the Elder replied, "Toward a beloved person.
Now, that man had a wife who was dear and pleasing to him; directing his loving-kindness toward her, he fell into madness.
But how did he come to act for the harm of many people? For those such as him—his fellow residents, his attendants, and others—[would likewise suffer].

And beginning with their own protective deities, all the other deities up to the Brahma-world who have become friends to them think, "This bhikkhu will not act without knowing," and they act accordingly; thus he has set out for the harm of many people.
In the case of the bright side (the wholesome), bodily and verbal actions are to be understood by way of the abstinence from killing living beings and so forth.

Furthermore, one who speaks on a meditation subject without deception is said to "encourage" others toward the conformable states (anulomika-dhamma), just like the Elder Tissa of the Four Nikāyas who resided at Koḷitavihāra.
It is said that his elder brother, the Elder Nandābhaya, while living at Potaliyavihāra, summoned his younger brother when a certain illness arose and said: "Friend, my [condition] is very light..."
“Having done so, explain one meditation subject. “What is the use of another meditation subject, venerable sir?
It is fitting to examine material food. “What is the purpose of this, friend? “Venerable sir, material food is derived form;
and when one derived form is seen, twenty-three derived forms become evident. He said, “It will suffice.”
Having dismissed him with the words, "Friend, that much is enough," and having grasped the nutriment of edible food,
observed derived form, and turned away from it, he attained Arahantship. Then, even before the Elder had stepped out of the monastery,
the younger brother summoned him and said, "Friend, you have become a great support for me," and he informed his younger brother of the qualities he had himself attained.
"For the welfare of many" means that even his co-residents and others, thinking "he will not act without knowing," perform exactly what he has done;
thus, he is said to be practicing for the welfare of many.
2. Commentary on the *Sāraṇīya-sutta* (The Discourse on Recollection)
12. Regarding the second [case], "of a khattiya" means of one who is a khattiya by birth.

"Of one whose head has been anointed" means of one who has been consecrated on the head with the royal inauguration ceremony (*rājābhiseka*). "They become memorable" means they are to be remembered and not forgotten. "Born" means produced. "Memorable for as long as life lasts":
even during childhood it is not possible to know [them]; however, later on, by means of parents and others...

Having heard relatives or slaves and others declare, "You were born in such-and-such a country, in such-and-such a city, on such-and-such a day, under such-and-such a constellation," one remembers this from that time forward for as long as life lasts and does not forget it. Therefore it is said:
"It is to be remembered for as long as life lasts."
“Monks, this is the second: a place where a king was consecrated brings great prosperity;
therefore, it remains memorable for him as long as he lives. The same principle applies to a place of victory in battle. Here, ‘battle’ means war.
‘Having completely conquered’ means having won and crushed the enemy. ‘That very head of the battlefield’ refers to that very spot.”
The place of battle. "He dwells having overcome" means he dwells having mastered [it].

Now, since there was no further duty to be performed for the King, the Perfectly Enlightened One, by way of his birthplace and so forth, this reason has been brought forward in order to show three types of persons who are his counterparts within this Teaching; therefore, showing them:

"Even so, monks," he said, beginning with those words. Therein, regarding the phrase "he has gone forth into homelessness," it should be understood that even the fourfold purification of virtue is dependent upon going forth.

Regarding the phrase "it is memorable": [one remembers], "I went forth in such-and-such a kingdom, in such-and-such a district, in such-and-such a monastery, in such-and-such a hall, in such-and-such a daytime resting place, in such-and-such a walking path, at the foot of such-and-such a tree."
Thus, for as long as life lasts, this must indeed be remembered and not forgotten.
"This is suffering": there is only this much suffering; there is no suffering beyond this. "This is the origin of suffering":
there is only this much origin of suffering; there is no origin of suffering beyond this. The same applies to the remaining two pairs of terms.
This is the method. Thus, herein the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga) is explained by means of the four truths.

Furthermore, the knowledge of the preliminary work for the kasiṇas and the knowledge of insight (vipassanāñāṇa) are indeed dependent upon that path. It is "to be remembered" (sāraṇīya) in the sense that for as long as life lasts, it is to be remembered and not forgotten, [thinking]:
"I was born as a stream-enterer in such-and-such a region... pe... at the foot of such-and-such a tree."
“The destruction of the taints” means by means of the destruction of the taints. “Liberation of mind” means the concentration of fruition.
“Liberation by wisdom” means the wisdom of fruition. “Having realized it for oneself with direct knowledge” means having made it manifest through one’s own preeminent wisdom.
“Entering upon and dwelling in” means having attained, one dwells. “Conducive to remembrance” [means]: “In such-and-such a place by me…” and so forth.
"The attainment of Arahantship at the foot of such-and-such a tree"—this name for the place where he attained Arahantship remained memorable and unforgettable for him throughout his life;
thus he concluded the teaching by following the natural sequence of the narrative.
3. Commentary on the Āsaṃsa Sutta (The Discourse on Hope)
13. "In the third [verse], *santa* means 'exist,' 'are found. *Saṃvijjamānā* is a synonym for that same word.

*Lokasmiṃ* means in the world of sentient beings (*sattaloka*). *Nirāsa* means without hope, without expectation, without longing. *Āsaṃsa* means one who hopes, one who longs. *Vigatāsa* means one from whom hope has departed.
*Caṇḍālakule* means in the family of outcasts (*caṇḍāla*). *Venakule* means in the family of bamboo-workers (*vilīvakāraka*). *Nesādakule* means..."
“In a family of deer-hunters”: in a family of leather-workers. “In a family of cartwrights”: in a family of tanners. “In a family of scavengers”: in a family of flower-scavengers.
Having thus far shown the failure of his lineage, he now says “poor,” etc., in order to show the failure of his wealth;
for although some who are born into a lowly family may be wealthy and possess great riches, this one was not such as that. Therein, “poor” means:
"Endowed with poverty": [meaning] having meager food, drink, and sustenance. "A life of hardship": a miserable livelihood;
the meaning is that it is such a state where they must achieve their means of living through strenuous effort and exertion.

"Where food and clothing are obtained with difficulty": in which family food—consisting of rice-gruel and boiled rice—is obtained with pain, and even a mere covering for the body is difficult to find.
And clothing is obtained. Now, because some person, even though born into a low family, is endowed with material requisites and stands possessed of a flourishing physical form,
whereas this one is not like that, [the Buddha] said "and he is ill-favored" and so forth, in order to show his bodily deficiency as well.
In this context, "ugly" means having the color of a burnt stump, like a dust-demon (*paṃsupisācaka*).
"Repulsive to look at" means unpleasant to behold even for one’s own mother who has given birth to him. "Dwarf" means a hunchback. "One-eyed" means blind in one eye or blind in both eyes.
"Lame" means lame in one hand or lame in both hands. "Lame" (in the sense of walking) means lame in one foot or lame in both feet.
Or: "Pakkhahato" means one whose wings are destroyed, that is, a cripple. "Of lighting materials" refers to the requisites for a lamp, such as a vessel for oil or a wick.
"It does not occur to him thus": why does it not occur? Because he was born into a low family. Regarding "the elder":
when there is another who is the elder, the younger brother does not harbor expectations [of succession]; therefore, he says "the elder. "The consecrated one" (ābhiseko).
Even the eldest, though worthy of consecration (*abhiseka*), does not entertain the hope for it; therefore, he is called "one who has not been consecrated" (*anabhisitta*).

"One who has not been consecrated" means that even one who is worthy of consecration—being free from defects such as being one-eyed or crippled—and having been consecrated once, does not again entertain the hope for consecration; therefore, he is called "one who has not been consecrated.
"One who has reached immovability" refers to the eldest, the one worthy of consecration, the one not yet consecrated, the dull-witted, or the one lying on his back; even he, regarding consecration...
He does not form [new] defilements. However, one who is sixteen years old, whose physical features are clearly manifest, is said to have "reached immovability" (acalappatta);
he is capable of governing even a great kingdom, which is why it is called "having reached immovability.
Why does this occur for him? Because of his noble birth.
“Immoral” means devoid of virtue. “Of evil nature” means having a base character. “Impure” means endowed with impure bodily actions and so forth.
“Of suspicious conduct” means one whose conduct is to be remembered with suspicion;

that is, one whose conduct is such that others suspect it upon seeing something inappropriate, thinking, “This must have been done by him,” or it is conduct that is to be remembered with suspicion even by oneself.

The meaning is "one whose conduct is attended by apprehension. For when he sees monks gathered together in places such as the daytime resting area and discussing something, he becomes apprehensive, thinking, "These are deliberating together;

could they be discussing whether they know of the action I have committed? Thus his conduct is attended by apprehension. "One whose actions are concealed" means one who possesses evil deeds that ought to be hidden.
Endowed [with these qualities]. "A non-recluse claiming to be a recluse" means that, being a non-recluse, he claims "I am a recluse" because of his resemblance to a recluse.

"One who does not live the holy life (abrahmacārī) claiming to live the holy life" refers to others who live the holy life—well-clad, well-dressed, carrying bright bowls—who sustain their livelihood by wandering for alms in villages, towns, and royal capitals.
Having seen this, because he himself practices in such a manner, it is as if he is giving the declaration, "I am a celibate practitioner" (*brahmacārī*).
Furthermore, when one says "I am a monk" (*bhikkhu*) and enters the Uposatha hall and other such places, one is indeed one who has given the declaration of being a celibate practitioner;
likewise when receiving gains belonging to the Saṅgha. "Rotten within" means having entered within by means of a rotten action.
"Corrupt" means steeped in lust and the other defilements. "Become like dregs" means one who has become a refuse-heap of lust and the rest.
Why does it not occur to him in this way? Because of the absence of the necessary condition (*upanissaya*) for supramundane states. Why does it occur to him in this way?
Because of his practice of fulfilling the great precepts (*mahāsīla*).
4. Commentary on the Cakkavatti Sutta 14.

In the fourth [sutta], one is called a *rājā* (king) because he delights the people by means of the four bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*). He is a *cakkavattī* (wheel-turning monarch) because he turns the wheel (*cakkaṃ vatteti*).
Or, he is a *cakkavattī* because the wheel has been turned by him. He is *dhammiko* (righteous) because he possesses the Dhamma; specifically, by means of the tenfold Dhamma.

A king is called a *dhammarāja* because he has arisen through the conduct of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*). The meaning is that even he cannot turn the wheel without a king; that is, without obtaining another king as his support, he is unable to turn it.
Thus the Teacher, having commenced the teaching, remained silent without bringing it to its natural conclusion.
Why? Because those skilled in the sequence of the discourse [would have] arisen and [completed] the connection.
“They will ask questions, for there are many such bhikkhus in this place; thus, when questioned by them, I shall expand upon the teaching.
Then a certain bhikkhu skilled in connecting the discourse asked the Blessed One, beginning with the words, “But who, venerable sir?
And as the Blessed One was answering him, he spoke, beginning with the words, “The Dhamma, bhikkhus.”
Therein, "Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma of the ten courses of wholesome action. "The Dhamma" refers to that very Dhamma described in the manner stated.
"Depending upon" means making that very thing the support with a mind that has that as its object.
"Honoring the Dhamma" means performing it in such a way that the Dhamma, once performed, becomes well-performed. "Revering the Dhamma" [refers] to that...
"Revering it by giving rise to respect": honoring it. "Honoring the Dhamma": acting with humility toward that very Dhamma through such acts as joining one's palms in reverence.

"Having the Dhamma as his banner and the Dhamma as his emblem": the meaning is that he proceeds having placed that Dhamma before him like a banner and raised it up like an emblem; thus, he becomes one who has the Dhamma as his banner and the Dhamma as his emblem. "Having the Dhamma as his authority."

Having become one who holds the Dhamma as supreme by virtue of having arrived at the state where the Dhamma is sovereign, and by performing all activities solely on the basis of the Dhamma, he becomes one for whom the Dhamma is paramount (*dhammādhipateyya*).
He provides righteous protection, defense, and security; thus, because he possesses this Dhamma, it is "righteous" (*dhammikā*).
Protection, defense, and security constitute "protection, defense, and security" (*rakkhāvaraṇagutti*). In this regard, it is said: "While protecting others, he protects himself."
According to the word of the Buddha, patience and so forth are protection (*rakkhā*). For it is said: "And how, monks, does one protecting another protect oneself?
By means of patience, non-violence, a mind of loving-kindness, and compassion. Clothing, upper garments, houses, and so forth are a shield (*āvaraṇa*).
Guarding (*gutti*) is the act of watching over for the purpose of warding off dangers such as thieves; all of that he arranges well.
The meaning is that he causes [them] to proceed and establishes [them].
Now, showing where she should be assigned, he said, "among the household folk," and so forth. Herein, this is the summarized meaning:
establishing his children and wife, who are designated as "household folk," in the restraint of virtue, and providing them with clothing, perfumes, garlands, and so on...
By giving and warding off all calamities for him, he provides lawful protection, defense, and security; this is what is meant by "establishing.
The same principle applies to the kṣatriyas and others as well. However, there is this distinction:

the anointed kṣatriyas should be won over even by the gift of precious things such as noble thoroughbred horses, while the subordinate kṣatriyas should be satisfied by the gift of suitable vehicles and mounts.
The army should be assisted by providing food and wages without letting the time pass; the brahmins by means of gifts such as food, drink, and clothing;
the householders by providing food, seed-corn, ploughs, and oxen; likewise the merchants living in the towns and the country-dwellers living in the countryside.
Furthermore, the recluses and brahmins who have stilled evil and cast out evil should be assisted by providing the requisites of a recluse.
They are to be honored; the birds and wild animals are to be reassured by the gift of fearlessness.
"He turns the wheel by means of the Dhamma alone" means that he sets the wheel in motion solely through the Dhamma of the ten courses of wholesome action.
"That wheel is irreversible" means that the wheel of authority thus set in motion by him is not to be turned back.

“By someone who was human”: deities are able to do exactly whatever they wish; therefore, excluding them, it is said “by someone who was human. “By an adversary” means by one who is hostile, that is, by an enemy.

“Righteous” (*dhammika*): a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*) is righteous by way of the ten courses of wholesome action, whereas the Tathāgata is so by way of the nine supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*).
"Dhammarāja" means a King of Dhamma because he gladdens the great multitude by means of the nine supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*).
"Dhammam eva" means relying solely upon the nine supramundane states—honoring them, respecting them, and revering them.

That Dhamma of his is a "banner" (*dhaja*) in the sense of being raised high; thus it is his "Dhamma-banner" (*dhammaddhaja*). It is his "crest" (*ketu*); thus it is his "Dhamma-crest" (*dhammaketu*).
"Having made that very thing his dominant influence and his chief," thus he is "one who has the Dhamma as his dominant influence.

"Protection, defense, and guard of what is righteous" refers to both protection, defense, and guard provided by one who bestows the mundane and supramundane Dhamma. "He arranges" means he establishes and ordains.
"Of such a kind" means: the threefold misconduct of body should not be practiced, while good conduct should be practiced; thus it is in all cases.

The meaning should be understood. "Having made an agreement" means having established and discussed. "He sets in motion the unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma by means of the Dhamma alone" means he sets in motion the incomparable Wheel of Dhamma by means of the nine supramundane states (navalokuttaradhamma) alone.
"That wheel is irreversible" means that the Wheel of Dhamma thus set in motion cannot be turned back by even one among these [groups], such as the recluses and others.
It is impossible to prevent it. The rest is clear everywhere. 5.
Commentary on the *Sacetana-sutta*. 15.
Regarding the fifth [sutta], "at Isipatana": this refers to the place where the *isīs*—namely, those designated as Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas—turned the Wheel of Dhamma.
"Having come for the purpose of performing the Uposatha, [he] fell"—the meaning is "at the place of assembly.
There is also a reading *padane*, which has the same meaning. "In the deer-park" (*migadāye*) means in a place given to the deer for their safety.
"In six months less six days"—it is said that on the very day he was commanded by the king, he prepared all the necessary requisites and went to the forest together with his disciples.
Having entered, he avoided trees standing at village gates, in the center of villages, in shrines, in cemeteries, and so forth, as well as trees that were withered, fallen, or dry;
instead, having selected trees standing in suitable locations, free from all defects, and appropriate for the nave and spokes, he fashioned that wheel.
While he was thus searching for and selecting the wood, and while he was fashioning it, this much—
The time has passed. Therefore it is said: “by six months less six days. *Nānākaraṇaṃ* means diversity (*nānattaṃ*).
*Nesaṃ* means not theirs. *Atthesaṃ* means there is this for them. *Abhisaṅkhārassa gati* means the movement of the application (*payoga*).
*Ciṅgulāyitvā* means having whirled around. *Akkhāhataṃ maññe* means as if placed after being inserted into a die.
“Full of sap” means possessed of swellings, being characterized by places that are elevated and depressed. “Full of resin” means possessed of both putrid heartwood and sapwood.
“Crooked in body,” and so forth, are names for bodily misconduct and the rest. “Fallen in this way” means fallen through the falling away from such qualities.
“Established in this way” means established by means of such qualities. In this context, worldly people are said to be “fallen,” while stream-enterers and the others are [established].

“Firmly established” means this. Among those [four types], the first three are said to have “fallen” at the moment when the defilements manifest; however, those whose taints are destroyed are exclusively “firmly established.
Therefore—because those who have not abandoned crookedness of body and so forth fall, while those who have abandoned crookedness of body and so forth are firmly established—therefore.
Furthermore, the abandonment of crookedness of body and so forth should be understood as follows: killing living beings, taking what is not given...
Sexual misconduct, false speech, malicious speech, and wrong view—these six are first abandoned by the path of stream-entry;
harsh speech and ill will—these two by the path of non-returning; and covetousness and idle chatter—these two by the path of arhatship.
6. Commentary on the Apaṇṇaka Sutta.

16. In the sixth [case], he has entered upon the "unerring way"—the unopposed way, the categorical way, the way leading to liberation, the causal way, the essential way, the refined way, the non-contradictory way, the conformable way, and the way that accords with the Dhamma—rather than by grasping through reasoning or grasping through method. Having grasped it thus...

For a bhikkhu, a bhikkhunī, a lay follower (upāsaka), or a lay follower (upāsikā) who has entered upon a wrong course of practice declines and falls away from the attainments of humans, devas, and nibbāna;
however, one who has entered upon the unerring course of practice does not fall away from those attainments.
In the past, among two caravan leaders traveling along a desert road, [one] having accepted the word of a yakkha...
It is like the foolish caravan leader who, together with his caravan, met with ruin and disaster;

whereas the wise caravan leader was like one who, refusing to accept the words of the yakkha, instructed the caravan members, saying, "We shall discard water at places where water is seen," and then set out on the path.
It is with reference to this that it was said:
“Some say there is one infallible position, others, the dialecticians, say there is a second;
having understood this, the wise man should take that which is infallible.
Herein, “source” (*yoni*) refers to a division of the aggregates, a cause, or the urinary passage.
It is a name. For in such passages as, “Sāriputta, there are these four modes of birth (*yoni*)”, *yoni* refers to a division of the aggregates (*khandha*).
In such passages as, “For this is the mode of birth for the attainment of the fruit, O Bhūmija”, it refers to a cause.

And in such passages as, “I do not call one a brahmin by birth, nor by being born from a mother,” and “Then the winds born of karma turn him back, with feet upwards and head downwards... [the term *yoni* is used].
In such passages as "having turned [the fetus] around, she delivers it into the mother's birth canal," it refers to the urinary passage.
But here, the intended meaning is the cause. "Aroused" means exerted and perfected.

Regarding the phrase "for the destruction of the taints" (*āsavānaṃ khayāya*): here, they are called "taints" (*āsava*) because they flow; they stream and proceed even from the eye... up to... the mind.

It has been said: they are called *āsava* (taints) because they flow (*savanti*) from the standpoint of the phenomena (*dhamma*) up to the stage of the lineage (*gotrabhū*), and from the standpoint of space (*okāsa*) up to the peak of existence (*bhavagga*).
The meaning is that they proceed by encompassing these phenomena and this space; for this prefix *ā-* has the sense of "encompassing.

In the sense of having been stored for a long time, wine and the like are *āsava*; they are also called *āsava* because they are like *āsava*. For even in the world, things that have been stored for a long time [are called *āsava*].
Wines and the like are called *āsava*. And if they are *āsava* in the sense of having been stored for a long time, then these alone ought to be so called.
For this has been said: "Bhikkhus, no prior limit of ignorance is known; before this, ignorance did not exist," and so forth.
Alternatively, they are called *āsava* because they flow (*savanti*) or pour out (*pasavanti*) the long-lasting suffering of *saṃsāra*. And among these, the former derivations [are intended].
Wherever defilements (kilesa) come as outflows (āsava), there they are applicable; this applies to future karma as well.
Furthermore, the outflows are not merely karma and defilements, but also various kinds of calamities. For in the Suttas, it is said:
"Cunda, I do not teach the Dhamma solely for the restraint of outflows pertaining to the present life," where [these outflows] consist of the roots of dispute.
The defilements are said to be the taints (*āsava*).
[It is asked: "By what would one be reborn among the gods, or become a Gandhabba or a bird;
by what would one go to the state of a *yakkha*, or attain human status?"
“Those taints of mine are exhausted, shattered, and rendered baseless.
Herein, this refers to karma pertaining to the three planes and all remaining unwholesome states.

Regarding the phrase, “for the restraint of taints pertaining to the present life and for the warding off of taints pertaining to future lives,” this refers to [the avoidance of] censure by others, remorse, execution, imprisonment, and so forth.
as well as various calamities consisting of the suffering of the states of deprivation.
These taints (āsava), moreover, should be understood according to the manner in which they are presented in each respective context. For in the Vinaya, they are presented in two ways:
"for the restraint of taints pertaining to the present life, and for the warding off of taints pertaining to future lives. In the Saḷāyatana-vagga...
“Friends, there are three taints for me: the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance”—thus they are presented in three ways.
In other discourses and in the Abhidhamma, those same three, together with the taint of views, are presented in four ways. According to the method of penetration:
“Monks, there are taints leading to hell; there are taints leading to the animal realm; there are taints...”

In the *Pettivisayagāmini* [Sutta], they appear in five ways: "There are taints leading to the realm of ghosts, there are taints leading to the human world, and there are taints leading to the world of the devas.
And here, it is specifically karma that is called "taints. In the *Chakkanipāta*, they appear in six ways according to the method beginning with:
"Bhikkhus, there are taints to be abandoned by restraint," and so forth. In the *Sabbāsavapariyāya*, those same [taints] are shown through vision...
It occurs in seven ways together with the things to be abandoned. However, it should be understood that here, according to the method of the Abhidhamma, the four taints (*āsava*) are intended.

Regarding the term "for the destruction" (*khayāya*): here, the intrinsic nature of the taints, their mode of exhaustion, and the path, fruit, and Nibbāna are all called "the destruction of the taints.
For in the passage, "That which is the destruction, passing away, breaking up, dissolution, impermanence, and disappearance of the taints," [it is used in this sense].

The destruction of the specific nature of the taints (*āsava*) is called "the destruction of the taints" (*āsavakkhaya*). In the passage, "Bhikkhus, I declare the destruction of the taints for one who knows and sees," the abandonment of the taints—
their absolute destruction, non-arising, the state of being exhausted, and their non-existence— is called "the destruction of the taints."
“For the trainee who is still in training, following the straight path, there is first the knowledge of destruction, and immediately after that, final knowledge.
Here, the path is called “the destruction of the taints. In the passage, “Through the destruction of the taints, one becomes a recluse,” it refers to the fruit.
“For one who observes the faults of others and is constantly inclined toward complaint, the taints increase; he is far from the destruction of the taints.
Here, *nibbāna* is meant. However, in this sutta, with reference to the fruit, it says “for the destruction of the taints,” meaning for the sake of the fruit of arahantship.
“Guarded in the doors of the sense faculties” means having the doors closed regarding the six sense faculties, with the mind as the sixth. “Moderate in eating” means knowing the measure in food;
the meaning is that one knows and understands the proper measure for receiving, consuming, and reflecting upon it.
“Devoted to wakefulness” means being devoted to the state of staying awake during five of the six divisions of the day and night.
The meaning is: "one who is truly devoted to wakefulness.

Having thus established the matrix (mātikā), he now speaks the passage beginning with "And how, bhikkhus, does a bhikkhu... while analyzing that very matrix according to the order in which it was set forth.
Therein, the meaning of "having seen a form with the eye," and so forth, has been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.
Likewise, he reflects wisely when taking food, [thinking], "I take food neither for amusement," and so forth.
"By obstructive states" means by the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). For these hindrances remain having obstructed the mind; therefore they are called "obstructive states.
"He lies down in the lion’s posture" means he lies down like a lion. "Placing one foot upon the other" means...
Having placed the left foot over the right foot. For if the feet were placed exactly level, the knee would strike the knee and the ankle the ankle, and from that pain would arise.
Therefore, in order to avoid that fault, he places this foot having moved it slightly forward.
Hence it is said: "having placed one foot over the other."
"Mindful and clearly comprehending" means being endowed with both mindfulness and clear comprehension.
But how is it that one who is sleeping is said to be mindful and clearly comprehending? It is by way of the previous activity.

For this person, while walking back and forth on the walkway, having recognized the state of falling asleep and having set aside the meditation subject currently being practiced, lies down on a bed or a bench.
When he falls asleep and wakes again, he wakes only while still grasping the meditation subject at the very place where it was established.
Therefore, even while sleeping, he is said to be mindful and clearly comprehending. This, first of all, is the method regarding the basic meditation subject.

Furthermore, he is also said to be mindful and clearly comprehending by way of the meditation subject for discernment. How so? For as he walks back and forth, he perceives the state of falling asleep.
Having understood this, he lies down on his right side on a stone slab or a couch and reflects:
"The insentient body is resting upon an insentient couch; the insentient couch is upon insentient earth;
the insentient earth is upon insentient water; the insentient water is upon insentient air; and the insentient air is resting upon insentient space."
In that regard, even the space does not know, “I am standing having lifted up the wind,” nor does the wind know, “I am established in space.
Likewise, the wind does not know, “I am standing having lifted up the water,” and so forth.
The bed does not know, “I am standing having lifted up the body,” nor does the body know, “I am established on the bed. For indeed... [no such knowing occurs].
"Among them, there is mutual attention, application of mind, mental engagement, volition, or aspiration.
As he reviews this, that reviewing-consciousness sinks into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
Thus, even while sleeping, one is said to be mindful and clearly comprehending.

"Having attended to the perception of rising" means having attended to the perception that delimits the time for rising, thinking, "I shall rise when the moon or a star has reached this point"; the meaning is that he has fixed it in his mind.
For one who lies down after doing so indeed rises at the very time delimited.

7. Commentary on the Discourse on One’s Own Harm (Attabyābādhasutta) In the seventh [discourse], "for one’s own harm" (*attabyābādhāya*) means for one’s own suffering (*attadukkha*). "For the harm of others" (*parabyābādhāya*) means for the suffering of others (*paradukkha*). "Bodily good conduct" (*kāyasucarita*) and so forth are presented here in terms of the ten courses of wholesome action (*dasakusalakammapatha*) belonging to the preliminary stage; however, above this, they remain unrestricted all the way up to Arahantship.
8. Commentary on the Discourse on the World of the Gods (Devalokasutta)
18. In the eighth [verse], *aṭṭīyeyyātha* means you would be distressed (*aṭṭā*) and oppressed (*pīḷitā*). *Harāyeyyātha* means you would feel ashamed (*lajjeyyātha*).

*Jiguccheyyātha* means you would feel disgust (*jigucchā*) toward that speech, as if toward excrement. Regarding the phrase *iti kira*: here, *iti* refers to the smoothness of the connection between words and syllables (*padasandhi-vyañjana-siliṭṭhatā*), while *kira* is a particle used in the sense of tradition (*anussava*).
The connection should be understood as: "Indeed, by means of divine life-span, you would be distressed."
"Pageva kho pana" means "even earlier.
9. Commentary on the First Merchant Sutta (Paṭhamapāpaṇikasutta). 19.
In the ninth [sutta], "pāpaṇika" means a shopkeeper; it refers to a merchant who has opened his shop and is selling goods.
This is a designation. "Incapable" means one who has become unfit as a vessel.
"He does not attend to his work with care" means he does not attend to it so that what was undertaken becomes well-undertaken, by personally verifying it for himself.
In this regard, rising at dawn at the sound of footsteps, lighting a lamp, and spreading out the merchandise, he does not remain seated during the morning time.
He applies himself diligently to his work. For instance, when thieves take goods at night and go to the market thinking, "We shall sell this from our hands," and offer it for a small price;
or when people with many enemies stay in the city at night and go to the market early in the morning to take their goods; or again—
People wishing to go to the countryside go to the market early in the morning and purchase goods; they do not become owners of the profit resulting from that.
However, when others arrive at mealtime to eat, [the owner] has already put away the goods early in the morning, gone home, eaten, and slept;
thus, returning to the market again in the evening, he does not attend to it properly during the midday period.

He resolves upon his business. For it was because he could not be reached by thieves even when they set out early in the morning, yet at midday—when others were not wandering about—he would go to the market and sell for a low price;

and because at mealtime, wealthy and influential people would send messengers saying, "It is right to obtain this and that from the market," and have things brought back for him—for the sake of these conditions...
He becomes a non-owner of his gains.
Furthermore, if he does not sit inside the shop with a lamp lit until the watch-drum sounds, it is said that he has not properly attended to his business in the evening.
For whatever thieves might release—whether at dawn or during the day—[he would lose].
They did not reach [the market]; however, having gone to the marketplace in the evening, they give for a low price, and the owner of the profit resulting from that becomes one who has no claim to it.
"He does not resolutely determine the sign of concentration" means he does not attain concentration through diligent practice.
And here, having performed the duties in the shrine courtyard and the Bodhi-tree courtyard early in the morning, and having entered his lodging until the time for the alms-round—

If one enters meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) and does not remain seated during the morning session, it is said that one has not properly resolved upon the sign of concentration (*samādhinimitta*).
Furthermore, if after the meal, having returned from almsround,

one enters the night-quarters or day-quarters and remains seated in attainment until the evening session, one has likewise not properly resolved upon the sign of concentration during the midday session.

This is what is called "resolving. However, if after paying homage at the shrine and attending upon the elder, one enters the lodging and attains a meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) during the first watch of the night, but does not sit [thereafter], then one has not properly resolved upon the sign of concentration (*samādhinimitta*) during the evening session.
The bright fortnight (the path of progress) should be understood by the method that is the opposite of what was stated above. Furthermore, in this context, regarding "attainment" (*samāpatti*):
In the passage where it says "having applied," if there is no attainment (*samāpatti*), insight (*vipassanā*) is also permissible;

and as for the phrase "the sign of concentration" (*samādhinimitta*), the object of concentration (*samādhi-ārammaṇa*) is also certainly permissible. For this has been said: "Concentration itself is the sign of concentration, and the object of concentration is also the sign of concentration.
10. Commentary on the Second *Pāpaṇika Sutta* (The Merchant’s Discourse)
20. "One who has eyes" means one who possesses the eye of wisdom (*paññā-cakkhu*).

"Vidhura" means one who bears a distinguished burden, an excellent burden, being endowed with energy associated with knowledge. "Endowed with support" means endowed with assistance, endowed with a foundation.
"Merchandise" refers to goods for sale. Regarding that [merchandise], he thinks: "There will be this much capital and this much profit. Thus...
Regarding the statement "this merchandise being sold thus," the meaning is: whatever price is paid for that which is sold, that price—designated as the "purchase"—will be this much;
and whatever profit arises from that sale, in that sale there will be this much gain, this much increase.
