"He is skilled in buying and selling": here, one is called "skilled" when, having gone to a place where goods are easily obtained, one buys them, and having gone to a place where they are scarce, one sells them;
thus one obtains a profit tenfold or even twentyfold. "Wealthy" (*aḍḍhā*) means those who are masters and possessed of much deposited wealth.

"Of great riches" (*mahaddhanā*) means those who possess great wealth by way of its circulation. "Of great enjoyments" (*mahābhogā*) means those who possess great goods for use and enjoyment. "Capable" (*paṭibalo*) [means capable] by way of physical strength.
And because he is endowed with both [skill] and the power of knowledge, he is capable.
"And to provide us from time to time" means to provide us from time to time with the interest based on the wealth we have lent him. "Nipatanti" means they invite;
there is also the reading "nipātenti," which has the same meaning.
"For the attainment of wholesome states" means for the purpose of accomplishing and acquiring wholesome states.
"Possessed of steadfastness" means endowed with the steadfastness of knowledge. "Of firm exertion" means endowed with firm exertion through knowledge.
"One who has not laid down the burden" means one who has not set aside the burden of effort, thinking: "I shall not lay this burden of energy down until I have reached the supreme path."
"Bahussutā" means those by whom much of the Buddha’s word has been heard, categorized according to the single Nikāyas and so forth; thus they are "bahussutā.
"Āgatāgamā" means that one Nikāya is called one Āgama, two Nikāyas are called two Āgamas, and five Nikāyas are called five Āgamas;
among these Āgamas, those by whom even a single Āgama has been mastered, made fluent, and put into practice are called "āgatāgamā. "Dhammadharā" means...
"Bearers of the Suttanta Piṭaka" means those who uphold the Suttanta Piṭaka. "Bearers of the Vinaya" means bearers of the Vinaya Piṭaka. "Bearers of the Mātikā" means bearers of the two Mātikās.
"He questions thoroughly" means he asks about what is the meaning and what is not the meaning, and what is the reason and what is not the reason.
"He reflects thoroughly" means he considers, weighs, and examines [the matter], thinking, "I shall ask this very question. The rest here is of plain meaning.
In this sutta, however, wisdom is mentioned first, followed by energy and the cultivation of good friends.
In this regard, one should not understand the meaning as implying that one must first attain Arahatship and only afterwards apply energy and cultivate good friends;
for in a teaching, there may be a sequence defined either by what precedes or by what follows, or even by both.

Or [it may be] by the millions. Here, however, the upper limit should be understood. Therefore, one who speaks should first show the necessary condition of a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitta-upanissaya*), then show diligence (*vīriya*) in the middle, and finally speak of *arahantship*.
This is the second chapter, the Chapter on the Cartwright.
3. Chapter on Persons (Puggalavagga) 1.
Commentary on the Samiddha Sutta 21.
Regarding the first [sutta] of the third [chapter]: "One first experiences the contact of the first jhāna, and afterwards realizes cessation, which is Nibbāna."
A body-witness (*kāyasakkhi*). One who has attained vision is one who has attained view (*diṭṭhippatto*). One who is liberated through faith is one liberated by faith (*saddhāvimutto*).
"Is agreeable" means it is pleasing. "More excellent" means more beautiful. "More sublime" means more refined. Regarding the statement that the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) is predominant:
it is said that at the moment of the path of arahantship for the Elder Samiddha, the faculty of faith was preeminent.
The remaining four co-nascent faculties were its attendants. Thus the Elder spoke while describing the path he himself had realized.
However, at the moment of the path of Arahatship for the Elder Mahākoṭṭhika, the faculty of concentration was predominant, and the remaining four faculties were its attendants.
Therefore, when he said that the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*) was predominant, he spoke only of the path he himself had realized.
However, at the moment of the arahant-path for the Elder Sāriputta, the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*) was primary; the other four faculties were merely its attendants.
Therefore, when he too said that the faculty of wisdom was predominant, [he spoke of the path he had realized].
He spoke only of the path realized by himself.
"Na khvettha" means "indeed not in this case. "Ekamsena byākātuṃ" means to answer categorically. "Arahattāya paṭipanno" indicates one who possesses the path to arahantship.
Thus, in this sutta, by all three elders, only the path realized by themselves was taught.
[The previous case] was spoken [by the Buddha] regarding the earth-plane; however, the Perfectly Enlightened One spoke this by means of the intermediate space itself.
2. Commentary on the Gilāna Sutta: 22.
In the second [verse], "suitable" (*sappāyāni*) means beneficial and conducive to growth. "Appropriate" (*patirūpaṃ*) means fitting. "Does not emerge" (*neva vuṭṭhāti*).
By the phrase "from that affliction," one who is afflicted with an incurable disease such as consumption (*vātāpamāra*) or the like, and whose illness has reached its terminal stage, is described.
By the phrase "he recovers from that affliction," minor ailments such as the various types of skin eruptions (*kacchu*), ringworm (*tiṇapupphaka*), and old age are described.
By the phrase "obtaining suitable foods, not failing to obtain them," [the text refers] to those whose care...

It becomes comfortable; all those ailments have been described. And here, a "suitable attendant" should be understood as one who possesses the qualities of a sick-nurse, being wise, skillful, and not lazy.
"An attendant is authorized" means he is authorized to be given by the Saṅgha of monks. For when that sick person is unable to maintain himself through his own nature, the Saṅgha of monks...
A single monk and a novice should be assigned to that monk with the instruction, "Look after him," after obtaining his permission.
Until they have looked after him, whatever is required for the sick person and for those two must be borne entirely by the Saṅgha of monks.
"Other sick persons should also be attended to" means that the other two types of sick persons should also be looked after. For what reason?
Even one who has reached the end of his life, if not attended to, might harbor mental resentment, thinking, "If they had looked after me, I might have been comfortable;
but they do not look after me," and thus be reborn in a state of misery. But for one who is being looked after...
It occurs to him: "Whatever ought to be done by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus has been done; however, such is the ripening of my own kamma.
Having established loving-kindness toward the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he will be reborn in heaven.
But as for one who, even when afflicted by a minor illness, recovers whether or not he receives medicine—for him, even without medicine—
When medicine is administered for a disease, it is more quickly pacified.
Consequently, he will be able to master the word of the Buddha or to practice the duty of a recluse.
For this reason it was said: "Other sick persons, too, should be attended."
"He does not enter" means he does not penetrate. "Rightness in the wholesome states, the certainty" refers to the rightness known as the certainty of the path regarding wholesome states.
By this, the person who is "merely a reciter of words" (*padaparama*) is described.

In the second section, the one who "understands through a condensed statement" (*ugghaṭitaññū*) is included, such as the Elder Nālaka in the Dispensation, or one who has received instruction once from the presence of Paccekabuddhas during the interval between Buddhas.
And having attained it, he has penetrated the knowledge of *paccekabodhi*. By the third turn, the person who gains knowledge through detailed exposition (*vipañcitaññū*) is described;
however, the person who is led to understanding (*neyya*) is dependent upon that very [turn].
"The teaching of the Dhamma was authorized" means that eight times during a month, discourse on the Dhamma was authorized. The Dhamma [was also taught] to others.
"It should be taught" means that the Dhamma should be expounded even to others. For what reason?
Because even for one who is unable to penetrate the Dhamma in this present life—being at most a "master of the words"—it will become a condition for the future.
Furthermore, whether one obtains a vision of the Tathāgata or not, and whether one obtains the opportunity to hear the Dhamma and Vinaya or not—

He penetrates the Dhamma; even if he does not yet attain it, he will penetrate it upon attaining it, and having attained it, he will penetrate it very quickly—for this reason, the Dhamma should be taught to them.
But for the third type, it must indeed be taught again and again.
3. Commentary on the Saṅkhāra Sutta.
23. In the third [verse], "with affliction" (*sabyābajjha*) means "accompanied by suffering. "Bodily formation" (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) refers to the heap of volition at the door of the body.
"One forms" (*abhisaṅkharoti*) means one accumulates, makes a heap, or makes a mass. The same method applies to the doors of speech and mind as well.

"The world with affliction" (*sabyābajjhaṃ lokaṃ*) means the world accompanied by suffering. "Afflictive contacts touch" (*sabyābajjhā phassā phusanti*) means contacts that result in suffering touch [the world]. "With affliction" (*sabyābajjhaṃ*).
"He experiences feeling" means he experiences a painful resultant feeling; the meaning is that it is accompanied by affliction and lacks gratification.
"Just as beings in hell" means that just as beings reborn in hell experience exclusively painful feeling, so too does he experience [feeling].
But is there no feeling of equanimity there? There is; however, it is [overwhelmed] by the painful feeling.
However, because of its powerful nature, it stands in a place that is beyond conventional usage (*abbhohārika*). Thus, hell itself has been brought forward as a simile for hell.
In this regard, it is said that this is a "counterpart simile" (*paṭibhāga-upamā*).
Just as with the phrase "the Subhakiṇha devas," here too, the heavenly world itself has been brought forward as a simile for the heavenly world. Because—

However, in the lower Brahma-worlds, the result of jhāna accompanied by rapture (sappītika-jhāna) prevails; in the Subhakiṇha realms, it is free from rapture (nippītiko) and consists of exclusive pleasure (ekantasukho).
Therefore, excluding those [lower realms], only the Subhakiṇhas are mentioned. Thus, this too should be understood as the "simile of the counterpart" (paṭibhāga-upamā) in that context.
"Mixed pleasure and pain" (vokiṇṇa-sukha-dukkha) means mixed pleasure and pain. "Just as among humans" (seyyathāpi manussā): for among humans, at times...
There is happiness at times, and suffering at times. "And some gods" refers to the sense-sphere gods (*kāmāvacara-deva*). For them too, there is happiness at times and suffering at times.

For when they see deities of greater power who are inferior to themselves, they must rise from their seats, move aside from the path, remove their wrapped garments, and perform the gesture of joining the palms in salutation; thus, for them...
All of it is indeed called suffering. And "some in the states of deprivation" refers to the *vemānika* ghosts;

for they experience prosperity at times and the results of their karma at other times, thus possessing a mixture of pleasure and pain. Therefore, it should be understood that in this sutta, the three types of good conduct are explained as being a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane.
4. Commentary on the Bahukāra Sutta 24.
In the fourth [sutta], "These three persons, monks," refers to three types of teacher-figures. "Of great benefit to the person" means they are of great assistance to the pupil-person.
"The Buddha" refers to the Omniscient Buddha. "Has gone for refuge" means he has gone to him as a protector.

"He has gone" (*gato hoti*). "The Dhamma" refers to the nine supramundane states (*navalokuttaradhamma*) which have the goal of liberation. "The Sangha" refers to the assembly of the eight noble persons (*aṭṭhaariyapuggala*).
Furthermore, this going for refuge is stated with reference to one who has not previously taken refuge and has not yet formed a firm resolve [to do so].
Thus, in this sutta, there are three [types of] givers of refuge: the giver of the stream-entry path, the giver of the once-return path, and the giver of the arahant path.

"The teachers are of great benefit" has been stated; however, those who have not been mentioned—the teacher who grants the going-forth (*pabbajjā*), the teacher who grants the word of the Buddha (*buddhavacana*), the teacher who recites the ritual formula (*kammavācācariya*), the teacher who brings one to the path of the once-returner (*sakadāgāmimagga*), and the teacher who brings one to the path of the non-returner (*anāgāmimagga*)—are these not of great benefit?

No, they are indeed of great benefit. Yet, this teaching is delimited by two types [of teachers]. Therefore, all of them are of great benefit. Among them, regarding the very act of going for refuge (*saraṇagamana*)...

It is permissible to have no fixed attachment; however, it should be understood that the fourfold purification, the preliminary work on the kasiṇas, and the knowledges of insight are dependent upon the first path, while the two higher paths and their fruits are dependent upon the path of arahantship.
"By this person" means by this person who is a resident pupil (*antevāsika*). "I say it is not easy to repay" means to perform a repayment.
I say it is not easy. For even if one were to prostrate five-fold hundreds or thousands of times in acts such as salutation,
rising from one's seat to go forward to meet him, raising one's joined palms at every moment of sight,
performing appropriate services of respect, and offering a hundred robes or a thousand robes, and a hundred portions of alms-food day after day— [it would still not be easy].

The meaning should be understood as follows: even one giving a thousand alms-meals, building a residence made of every kind of gem extending to the limits of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), and providing various kinds of medicine such as ghee and fresh butter, is still unable to make a repayment for what has been done by the Teacher.
5. Commentary on the Vajirūpama Sutta (The Diamond-like Simile)
25. "A mind like an old sore" means a mind resembling an ancient wound. "A mind like lightning" means a mind resembling lightning because of its illumination for only a brief moment.
"A mind like a thunderbolt" means a mind resembling a thunderbolt because of its capacity to strike at the very root of the defilements (*kilesa*).

"Becomes agitated" (*abhisajjati*) means it becomes attached. "Is provoked" (*kuppati*) means it is provoked by way of anger. "Becomes corrupted" (*byāpajjati*) means [it departs from] its natural state.
It decays; it becomes putrid. "It settles" means it falls into a state of stiffness and rigidity. "Anger" (kopa) is weak anger.
"Hatred" (dosa) is that which is stronger than the former due to its quality of malice. "Discontent" (appaccaya) is a state of dissatisfaction, namely mental distress.
"Putrid sore" (duṭṭhāruka) is an old wound. "With a stick" means with the tip of a staff. "With a potsherd" means with a fragment of a bowl.
"It exudes a secretion" means it flows again and again. For an old wound, by its very nature, exudes these three things—pus, blood, and lymph—and when struck, it exudes them even more abundantly.
"In the same way," here is the application of the simile: the angry person is like the malignant sore; his...
Just as hearing [an insult] is natural for oneself, so too is the walking about of one who is angry and puffed up with pride natural for himself;
a slight word is like being struck by a stick or a stone, while the state of becoming even more excessively puffed up—
thinking, "He speaks thus to someone like me"— is to be understood as like hearing it repeatedly.

"In the thick darkness of the night's gloom" means in the dense darkness that makes one blind by preventing the arising of visual consciousness during the night. "In the interval of lightning" means at the moment when lightning flashes.
Here too, this is the application of the simile: the practitioner (*yogāvacara*) is to be seen as like the man with keen vision;
the defilements to be abandoned by the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*) are like the darkness; and the movement of the lightning flash—

The moment of the arising of the knowledge of the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga-ñāṇa) is like the time when lightning flashes; the vision of Nibbāna at the moment of the path of stream-entry is like a man with sight seeing forms all around during that flash of lightning;

the subsequent envelopment in darkness is like the defilements to be abandoned by the path of once-returning (sakadāgāmi-magga); and the subsequent movement of another flash of lightning is like the knowledge of the path of once-returning.
Arising is like a sight-seer with clear vision seeing forms all around during a flash of lightning; the vision of Nibbāna at the moment of the once-return path is like that.

Then, the obscuration by darkness is like the defilements to be abandoned by the non-return path. Again, the movement of the lightning flash is like the arising of the knowledge of the non-return path;
it is like a sight-seer with clear vision seeing forms all around during a flash of lightning.
The vision of Nibbāna at the moment of the non-returner path (anāgāmimagga) should be understood in the same way.
There is also this application of the simile by way of the diamond-like mind: the knowledge of the path to Arahantship (arahattamaggañāṇa) is to be seen as like a diamond;
the defilements to be abandoned by the path to Arahantship are like a cluster of gems or a cluster of stones; and just as a diamond [penetrates] even a cluster of gems...
Just as there is no returning once one has passed through a stone wall or a cluster of rocks,
so too should the non-existence of the defilements severed by the knowledge of the path of Arahatship be understood; and just as a hole pierced by a thunderbolt cannot be filled again,
so too should the non-arising of the defilements cut off by the path of Arahatship be regarded.
6. Commentary on the *Sevitabba-sutta* (26).
In the sixth [verse], "to be served" (*sevitabbo*) means to be approached. "To be associated with" (*bhajitabbo*) means to be attached to.
"To be attended upon" (*payirupāsitabbo*) means to be waited upon repeatedly by sitting near [him]. "Having honored and having revered" (*sakkatvā garuṃ katvā*) refers to both honor and...
And having shown respect. Regarding the phrases "he is inferior in virtue" and so forth, inferiority should be understood in relation to each successive stage.
In this context, one who observes the five precepts should not associate with one who observes the ten precepts;
one who observes the ten precepts should not associate with one who observes the fourfold purification of virtue (*cātupārisuddhisīla*). Except out of compassion... [and so on].
"Compassion" (*anukampā*) excludes both mere sympathy (*anuddayā*) and compassion;
for such a person should not be associated with even for one's own sake, yet it is permissible to approach them by way of sympathy and compassion.

"Of those who have attained equality in virtue" (*sīlasāmaññagatānaṃ santānaṃ*): this refers to the continuity of those who have reached a state of equality through virtue. And let there be talk of virtue for us...
"It will come to pass" means that for us who share the same virtue, there will be conversation concerning our very virtue;
"and it will continue for us" means that this conversation of ours will proceed even if we speak for a whole day, and it will not be interrupted;
"and it will be comfortable for us" means that this discourse on virtue, even as it proceeds for a whole day, [will remain pleasant].
Our dwelling will be comfortable and our abiding will be happy. The same method applies to discourses on concentration and wisdom.
Regarding "the aggregate of virtue" (*sīlakkhandha*), it means the mass of virtue.

In the phrase "we shall assist with wisdom here and there," this refers to the aggregate of virtue at each respective stage, wherein one avoids those factors unsuitable or unhelpful to virtue and cultivates those factors suitable and helpful to it.
It is called "supporting with wisdom. The same method applies to the aggregates of concentration and wisdom as well.
"He is diminished" means that by associating with a person inferior to himself, he constantly and continuously declines and falls away, like water poured into a strainer of caustic ash.
"One who associates with equals" is one who associates with those equal to himself. "They incline toward the best" means they lean toward a superior person.
"One rises quickly, one grows quickly; therefore, one should associate with those who are superior to oneself.
Because one who approaches a person who is excellent rises quickly, for that reason one should associate with one who is more advanced and more distinguished than oneself.
7. Commentary on the Sutta on What is to be Loathed.
27. "He is to be loathed" means he is to be loathed like excrement. "Then indeed" (*atha kho nan ti*) means "then indeed for him.
"Fame" (*kittisaddo*) means the sound of report. "In this very way" (*evameva kho*): here, immorality is to be seen as a cesspool of excrement;
the immoral person is like one who has fallen into a cesspool and stands there; by one being pulled out from the cesspool...
Just as when a snake has climbed onto a person’s body, there is no possibility of being bitten, so too for one who associates with the immoral,

there is no possibility of performing [unwholesome] actions. The time when a bad reputation and sound of infamy arise for one associating with the immoral should be understood as being like the time when a snake has departed after smearing the body with excrement.

*Tindukālātaṃ* means a firebrand from a *tinduka* tree. "It crackles even more exceedingly" means that while burning, it naturally emits sparks and makes the sound "cicciṭā," or "ciṭiciṭā"; the meaning is that when struck, it produces this sound even more intensely.
"In just the same way" means that one who is prone to anger is agitated by his very own nature.

Having become fierce, he behaves [thus]; but when he hears even a slight word, thinking, "He speaks thus, he speaks thus to one like me," he becomes even more excessively arrogant and fierce in his behavior. "A cesspool" means a pit full of excrement, or simply a heap of excrement.
The application of the simile here should be understood in the same manner as before. Therefore, such a person...

"A person should be looked upon with equanimity and not associated with" means that because an angry person becomes angry even when treated with excessive kindness or approached too closely—even when one withdraws, thinking "What is the use of this?"—therefore, like a fire of chaff, he should be looked upon with equanimity;
he should not be associated with nor should he be cultivated. What is meant by this? For whoever approaches a fire of chaff too closely is burned.

His body burns. For one who withdraws too far back, his heat does not subside. But for one who, without approaching and without withdrawing, warms himself with a state of equanimity, the heat subsides.
Therefore, a person who is prone to anger is like a fire of chaff; he should be looked upon with equanimity, and should not be served, associated with, or attended upon.
A *kalyāṇamitta* is a virtuous friend (*sucimitta*). A *kalyāṇasahāya* is a virtuous companion (*sucisahāya*). "Companions" (*sahāyā*) means those who go along with one, those who walk together.
A *kalyāṇasampavaṅka* is one who is well-inclined toward the virtuous, toward pure persons; the meaning is that his mind is leaning toward them, sloping toward them, and tending toward them.
8. Commentary on the *Gūthabhāṇī-sutta* (The Sutta on the Excrement-Speaker)
28. In the eighth [verse], "one who speaks dung" refers to one who speaks foul-smelling talk like dung.
"One who speaks flowers" refers to one who speaks fragrant talk like flowers. "One who speaks honey" refers to one who speaks sweet talk like honey.
"Having gone to an assembly" means standing in an assembly. "Having gone to a gathering" means standing in a village gathering. "Having gone into the midst of kinsmen" means among kinsmen.
"Standing in the midst. "Having gone into the midst of a guild" means standing in the midst of a company.
"Having gone into the midst of the royal court" means standing in the midst of the royal court at a great judicial inquiry. "Summoned" means brought for the purpose of questioning.
"Questioned as a witness" means questioned after being made a witness. "Come here, O man!"—this is a form of address. "Either for his own sake or for the sake of another" means for himself or...
"Either for the sake of another's hand, foot, and so forth, or for the sake of wealth; or for the sake of some trifling material object.

Here, "material object" (*āmisa*) refers to a bribe (*lañja*). "Some trifling thing" (*kiñcikkha*) means any small thing whatsoever, even down to the mere amount of a quail’s egg, a ball of ghee, or a lump of butter;
the meaning is "for the sake of such a bribe. "One who speaks a deliberate lie" (*sampajānamusā bhāsita*) means one who intentionally commits false speech while being fully aware of it.
*Neḷa*: *Ela* is said to mean "fault" (*dosa*). That which has no *ela* is *neḷa*, meaning "faultless.
It is like the virtue described in the phrase, "With faultless limbs and a white canopy. *Kaṇṇasukhā*: Because of the sweetness of its phrasing, it is pleasant to the ears;
it does not produce earache, as if pierced by a needle. Because of the sweetness of its meaning, it generates affection rather than irritation throughout the entire body.
It is "pleasing" (*pemanīyā*). It is "heart-reaching" (*hadayaṅgamā*) because it reaches the heart without being obstructed and enters the mind with ease.
It is "urban" (*porī*) because it exists in the city due to its perfection in qualities; or, like a woman raised in the city, it is "refined" (*sukumārā*);
or, it belongs to the city (*purassa esā*), which means it is the speech of the city-dwellers. For the speech of city-dwellers is appropriate.
They say "father" for one who is merely a father, "mother" for one who is merely a mother, and "brother" for one who is merely a brother.

Such talk is "dear to many people" (*bahujanakantā*). Precisely because it is dear, it is "pleasing to many people" (*bahujanamanāpā*), meaning it is agreeable to many people and increases their mental well-being.
9. Commentary on the Andhasutta 29.
In the ninth [verse], "the eye does not exist" means the eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*) does not exist. "One should make it flourish" means one should make it prosperous and increased.
"Blameworthy and blameless" refers to that which is faulty and faultless. "Inferior and superior" refers to the low and the sublime. "Dark and bright with their counterparts" refers to...
The dark and bright states are called "with counterparts" because they oppose one another as contraries. This is the summary here:
one should know wholesome states as "wholesome states," and unwholesome states as "unwholesome states.
The same method applies to the blameworthy and so forth. However, regarding the dark, the bright, and those with counterparts:
He does not possess that kind of eye by which one would know dark qualities as "counterparts to the bright" and bright qualities as "counterparts to the dark.
The meaning should be understood in this same manner for the remaining sections as well.
"And his wealth is not of such a kind" means he does not possess wealth of that sort. "And he does not perform meritorious deeds" [is the rest].
"And he does not perform meritorious deeds. To this extent, the absence of both the eye for acquiring wealth and the eye for performing merit has been stated.
"A bad grasp in both cases" means that there is a grasping of failure, a grasping of defeat, in both—namely, in this world and in the next world.
Alternatively, "a bad grasp in both cases" refers to both those pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*) and those pertaining to the future life (*samparāyika*).

"An ill-chosen place" means a choice that leads to defeat. "By means of dhamma and adhamma" means by means of both the ten courses of wholesome action (dhamma) and the ten courses of unwholesome action (adhamma).
"A rogue" means a cheat. "He seeks wealth" means he searches for riches.
"By theft, by fraudulent work, and by falsehood—by both together" means he seeks it by means of both [the methods] among theft and the others.
How so? He seeks [wealth] by theft and by fraudulent practice; he seeks it by theft and by lying;

he seeks it by fraudulent practice and by lying. "To accumulate" means to pile up. "Acquired in accordance with the Dhamma" means acquired without violating the Dhamma of the ten courses of wholesome action.
"Attained through exertion" means attained through diligence. "With a mind free from fear" means with a mind devoid of doubt.
"A fortunate place" (*bhaddakaṃ ṭhānaṃ*) means the supreme state of the devas. "He does not grieve" (*na socati*) means that in that state he does not grieve with internal sorrow.
10. Commentary on the *Avakujja-sutta* (Sutta 30):

"One of downward-turned wisdom" (*avakujjapañño*) means one whose wisdom is turned downwards. "One of lap-like wisdom" (*ucchaṅgapañño*) means one whose wisdom is like a lap. "One of broad wisdom" (*puthupañño*)...

One of expansive wisdom. Regarding the phrase "good in the beginning" (*ādikalyāṇa*) and so forth: "beginning" (*ādi*) refers to the initial setting forth; "middle" (*majjha*) refers to the middle of the discourse;

"conclusion" (*pariyosāna*) refers to the final determination. Thus, when they teach him the Dhamma, they speak so as to make it good, auspicious, and blameless not only at the initial setting forth, but also in the middle and at the conclusion. And herein, there is [this] regarding the teaching...
There are beginning, middle, and end to the Teaching. Regarding that, first, in the case of a four-line stanza:
the first line is the beginning, the two middle lines are the middle, and the final line is the end. In the case of a sutta with a single sequence of meaning:

the introduction (*nidāna*) is the beginning, the sequence of meaning (*anusandhi*) is the middle, and "Thus he spoke" (*idamavoca*) is the conclusion. In the case of one with multiple sequences of meaning: the first...
The introduction and so forth; after that, one or several [sections] constitute the middle, and the last constitutes the conclusion.

This, first of all, is the method regarding the teaching (*desanā*). Regarding the Dispensation (*sāsana*), however, virtue (*sīla*) is the beginning, concentration (*samādhi*) is the middle, and insight (*vipassanā*) is the conclusion.
Or, concentration is the beginning, insight is the middle, and the Path (*magga*) is the conclusion. Or, insight is the beginning, the Path is the middle, and...
The fruit is the conclusion. Alternatively, the path is the beginning, the fruit is the middle, and Nibbāna is the conclusion.
Or, when treated in pairs: virtue and concentration are the beginning; insight and the path are the middle; and the fruit and Nibbāna are the conclusion.
"With meaning" means they teach having made it meaningful. "With phrasing" means they teach having ensured the completeness of the syllables.
"Entirely complete" means they teach having made it whole and complete, without deficiency. "Utterly pure" means they teach having made it utterly pure, free from tangles and free from knots.

"They proclaim the holy life" means that while teaching in this way, they proclaim the Noble Eightfold Path, which constitutes the supreme conduct and is comprised within the three trainings. "He does not attend to the beginning" means...
He does not even attend to what was previously set down.
"Kumbho" means a jar. "Nikujjo" means placed face-downward. "Even so" (evameva kho):
here, a person of downward-turned wisdom is to be seen as like a jar turned face-downward; the time of pouring water is like the time when the teaching of the Dhamma is received.
The time when one sitting on that seat is unable to grasp [the object] should be understood as being like the time when water is receding;
the time after having emerged and failing to observe it should be understood as being like the time when the water has ceased to hold its form.
"Scattered" means thrown in. "He would scatter through loss of mindfulness" means he would disperse them through forgetfulness. In the same way...
"Kha" means "lap. Here, a person of "lap-like wisdom" (ucchaṅgapañña) is to be understood as being like a lap;

the various kinds of food are like the diverse teachings of the Buddha; the time spent sitting while eating the various foods from the lap is like the time spent sitting on that seat learning [the Dhamma];
and the time when, upon rising, one scatters [the food] through loss of mindfulness is like [scattering it] from that seat.
The time when one who has risen and is walking is unaware [of the water] should be understood.
"Upside down" means placed with its opening facing upward. "It stands still" means it remains fixed.
"In the same way" refers here to the person of broad wisdom, who is to be seen like a jar placed with its opening facing upward; and the pouring of water is to be seen like the teaching.
The time [of the water] having been obtained is like the time when one sitting there perceives the stability of the water;
it should be understood as the time of grasping, not the time of discerning, which is like the time when one has risen and gone away.
"Dummedho" means devoid of wisdom (*nippanno*). "Avicakkhaṇo" means lacking the wisdom of circumspection (*saṃvidahana-paññā*). "Gantā" means one whose nature is to go (*gamana-sīlo*).
“Superior to him” means he is said to be more excellent than that person.

“Practicing in accordance with the Dhamma” means practicing the preliminary path together with virtue, which is the secondary practice (anudhamma) corresponding to the nine supramundane states (navalokuttaradhamma).

“Of suffering” means of the suffering of the round of existence (vaṭṭadukkha). “He would be one who makes an end” means he would be one who reaches the limit, one who effects a boundary, one who brings about a final enclosure.
The Third Chapter on Persons (Puggalavagga).
4. The Chapter on the Messengers of the Gods (Devadūtavagga). 1. Commentary on the Sutta with Brahmā (Sabrahmakasuttavaṇṇanā).
31. "In the first [verse] regarding the fourth [family], 'at home' means in their own house. 'They are honored' means they are looked after and protected with whatever is available in the house.

Having thus declared that families who honor their mother and father are 'families accompanied by Brahmā,' he now speaks the words beginning with 'families accompanied by their former teachers' in order to demonstrate their status as being accompanied by former teachers and so forth. In this regard:"
The terms "Brahmā" and so forth are stated for the purpose of establishing their status as Brahmā and the like. "Benefactors" (bahukārā) means those who are of great service to their children.
"Sustainers" (āpādakā) means those who provide life; for it is by their parents that the life of their children is provided, protected, maintained, and set in continuous motion.
"Nourishers" (posakā) means those who nourish them by developing their hands and feet and feeding them the blood of their own hearts.
"Showers of this world": for in this world, the seeing of desirable and undesirable objects by children arises depending upon their mother and father; thus, they are called "showers of this world.
"Brahmās" is a designation for the excellence of mother and father. Just as the four meditations (*bhāvanā*) are never abandoned by a Brahmā...
Just as loving-kindness, compassion, gladness, and equanimity exist, so too these four meditative developments (bhāvanā) are never abandoned by parents toward their children.
They are to be understood at their respective times: for when the child is still in the womb, the parents’ mind of loving-kindness is thus:
"When indeed shall we see our little son healthy, with all his limbs and members complete?"
When this child, being weak and lying on his back, is bitten by bedbugs, moths, or other such creatures, or is oppressed by the pain of a bad night's sleep, he cries out and wails;
hearing that sound, compassion arises in his parents, who run hither and thither.
But when he is at play, or has reached an age that is attractive [to others], they look upon the boy.
The minds of parents become as soft, gladdened, and delighted as a hundred-fold split cotton-wool pad placed in clarified butter;
at that time, sympathetic joy (muditā) is obtained by them.
But when this son, having provided for his wife, dwells in a separate household, then the parents think, "He is now able [to support us]..."
Thinking, "May my child be sustained by his own nature," a state of equanimity arises; at that time, *upekkhā* (equanimity) is obtained.
For this reason it is said: "Parents are Brahmās.
They are called "former teachers" because from the time of birth, parents [instruct]: "Sit thus, stand thus..."
"Go thus; lie down thus; eat thus; consume thus; this is for you, dear one," they say; "this is your brother," "this is your sister";

"it is proper to do this," "this is not proper"; "it is proper to approach such-and-such a person," "it is not proper to approach such-and-such a person"—thus they cause them to grasp and instruct them.
Then, at a later time, other teachers [teach] the arts of elephants, horses, chariots, archery, swordsmanship, finger-calculation, arithmetic, and so forth.

They train [others]: one gives the refuges, another establishes them in the precepts, another ordains them, another causes them to learn the Buddha’s word, another confers full ordination, and another leads them to the path of stream-entry and so forth.
Thus, all of these are called "subsequent teachers" (*pacchācariyā*); however, parents are the very first, which is why it says: "they are called 'original teachers' (*pubbācariyā*). In this regard:
“Are called” (vuccare) means they are spoken of or described. “And worthy of offerings from their children” (āhuneyyā ca puttānaṃ):

they are worthy of the food, drink, and so forth that has been offered, presented, and prepared by their children; they are fit to receive it. Therefore, it is said, “and worthy of offerings from their children.
“Compassionate toward their offspring” (pajāya anukampakā): even while depriving others of their lives, they look after their own offspring.
They protect [them]. Therefore it is said, "compassionate toward their offspring.
"One should honor" means one should pay homage. "One should revere" means one should receive them with respectful treatment. Now, demonstrating that reverence, he says, "with food," and so forth.
Therein, "with food" means with rice gruel, boiled rice, and hard foods. "With drink" means with the eight kinds of beverages.
"By means of clothing" means by means of a cloth for wearing as an undergarment and a cloth for wrapping as an upper garment. "By means of a bed" means by providing beds and chairs.

"By means of anointing" means by anointing that dispels foul odors and produces a pleasant fragrance. "By means of bathing" means by bathing after sprinkling the limbs with warm water when it is cold, and with cool water when it is hot. "By means of washing the feet" [means] by means of warm and cool water.
"By washing the feet and by anointing with oil. "Having passed away" means having gone to the other world. "Rejoices in heaven":
first, having seen here in this world the service rendered to mother and father, wise people praise that person for the sake of such service even here;
moreover, having gone to the other world and established in heaven, that attendant of mother and father rejoices and exults in celestial attainments.
2. Commentary on the Ānanda Sutta 32.
In the second [case], "of such a kind" means of such a nature. "Attainment of concentration" means the attainment of one-pointedness of mind.
And regarding the phrase "in this conscious [body]," here both one's own body and another's body are included by virtue of being "conscious."
"Having brought them together as one in this [state]" is what is said. "The underlying tendencies of the conceit of 'I-making' and 'mine-making'" refers to the defilements of both oneself and others:
namely, the view of "I-making," the craving of "mine-making," and the underlying tendency of conceit (*mānānusaya*). "May they not exist" means may they not come to be.
"And externally in all signs" refers to the sign of form, the sign of sound, the sign of odor, the sign of taste, and the sign of tangible objects.
Regarding such external signs as the sign of eternalism and so forth, the sign of a person, and the sign of phenomena—these being all external signs.
"Liberation of mind" and "liberation by wisdom" refer to both the concentration of fruition and the knowledge of fruition. "It might be" means it could come to pass.
"Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu" means, Ānanda, for a bhikkhu in this teaching. "This is peaceful, this is sublime."
He spoke thus while demonstrating Nibbāna. For Nibbāna is called "peaceful" (santa) because it is the peace resulting from the subsiding of the defilements;
furthermore, it is "peaceful" because even for one who has entered the attainment of Nibbāna and remains seated for a whole day, the arising of consciousness proceeds only in a state of peace.
It is "sublime" (paṇīta) because even for one seated after entering the attainment, the arising of consciousness proceeds only in a state of sublimity. Thus [he spoke of] Nibbāna.
“Exalted” (paṇīta) is its name. “The stilling of all formations” (sabbasaṅkhārasamatha), and so forth, are also synonyms for that very state.

For when one is seated having entered the attainment (samāpatti) called “the stilling of all formations,” even for a portion of a day, the arising of consciousness proceeds only as “the stilling of all formations”… and likewise, because of the absence of craving—which is termed “desire” (vāna)—within the three realms of existence, it has received the name “Nirvana.”
For one who has entered that attainment and is seated, the arising of consciousness occurs as Nibbāna alone, directed toward Nibbāna;

thus it receives such names as "the stilling of all formations" and so forth. Among these eight kinds of mental application (*ābhoga-samannāhāra*), at this point even one may be present, two may be present, or indeed all of them may be present.
"Having reckoned" means having known by means of wisdom (*ñāṇa*). "The higher and the lower" means both the higher (*parāni*) and the lower (*oparāni*).
For what is meant is that one’s own personal existence (*attabhāva*) and the personal existences of others are both the higher and the lower. "Of whom" means of which Arahant.
"Shaking" (*iñjita*) refers to these seven types of shaking, trembling, and quivering: the shaking of lust, the shaking of hatred, delusion, conceit, views, defilements, and misconduct.
"Is nowhere" (*natthi kuhinci*) means that he does not exist anywhere, even with respect to a single object.

"Peaceful" (*santo*) means peaceful due to the pacification of the opposing defilements (*kilesa*). "Smokeless" (*vidhūmo*) means free from the smoke of bodily misconduct and the like. "Untroubled" (*anīgho*) means free from the troubles (*īgha*) of passion and the rest. "Desireless" (*nirāso*) means free from craving.
"He has crossed over" (*atārī*) means he has crossed, has emerged, and has transcended. "He" (*so*) refers to that Arhat whose taints (*āsava*) are exhausted. "Birth and old age" (*jātijaraṃ*).
It should be understood that here, by the mention of birth and aging alone, sickness and death are also included.
Thus, both in the sutta and in the verse, only the attainment of the fruit of arahantship is spoken of.
3. Commentary on the Sāriputta-sutta.
33. "In brief" means by the laying down of the summary (mātikā). "In detail" means by the analysis of the summary already laid down.
"In both brief and detail" means at one time in brief and at another time in detail. "Those who understand are rare" means that persons capable of penetrating [the truth] are rare.
The Blessed One spoke this with the intention: "I shall stimulate the wisdom of the Elder Sāriputta."
Having heard this, although the Elder did not say, "Venerable sir, I shall understand," he nevertheless encouraged the Teacher to teach by saying, "Be confident, venerable sir, teach!
I shall penetrate the Dhamma taught by you through a hundred methods and a thousand methods;
let this be my task. Thus he spoke the words beginning with, "This is the time for it, Blessed One."
Then the Teacher began his teaching with the words, "Therefore, for this reason... In this context, the passage beginning with "In this conscious [body]... follows the same method already explained.
"He cut off craving" means he severed craving with the sword of path-knowledge (*magga-ñāṇa*).
"He shook off the fetters" means he uprooted and discarded all ten types of fetters (*saṃyojana*) together with their roots. "Through the perfect realization of conceit, he made an end of suffering."
"By means of right method and right practice, through the realization of the abandonment of the ninefold conceit, he brought an end to the suffering of saṃsāra.
And this, Sāriputta, was said by me with reference to this: in the *Pārāyana*, in the 'Udāyapañha', this was spoken by me with reference precisely to the attainment of the fruit."
Now, in order to show that which was spoken by the Blessed One, the passage beginning with "the abandoning of perceptions of sensual desire" (*pahānaṃ kāmasaññānaṃ*) is commenced.

In the *Udaya-pañha*, this phrase appears as "the abandoning of sensual desires" (*pahānaṃ kāmacchandānaṃ*); however, here it has been rendered as "perceptions of sensual desire" (*kāmasaññānaṃ*) by the reciters of the *Aṅguttara-nikāya*.
In this regard, there is only a difference in the phrasing (*byañjana*), but the meaning (*attha*) is one and the same. Regarding "perceptions of sensual desire":
[It refers to] the perceptions that have arisen with reference to sensual desires, or the perceptions co-nascent with the eight greed-accompanied consciousnesses.

Regarding "the abandoning of both sensual perceptions and mental distress": the meaning is that I declare the fruit of Arahantship—known as abandoning through subsiding and characterized as liberation through final knowledge—to be the abandoning of both these sensual perceptions and the mental distress that are mental factors.
In the *Niddesa*, however, [it says]: "of sensual desire and of mental distress..."
And when it is said, “the abandoning, the subsiding, the relinquishing, the calming, and the deathless Nibbāna of both,” that is stated by way of extracting the meanings.
For “abandoning” refers to the subsiding characterized by the state of being exhausted;
it refers to the Path which relinquishes the defilements; and it refers to the Fruit, which is the calming of the defilements, by resorting to which—
The defilements are abandoned; that is Nibbāna, the Deathless. Therefore, those terms are applied there.
However, because of the statement, “I declare the liberation through final knowledge,” it is specifically the fruit of Arhatship (arahattaphala) that is intended.
Furthermore, because it arises at the end of the removal of sloth (*thina*), it is specifically the fruit of Arhatship that is intended. [It is] the warding off of remorse (*kukkucca*).
Because it arises immediately after the path that wards off remorse, it is intended as the fruit itself.
"Purified by equanimity and mindfulness" means it is purified by the equanimity and mindfulness that have arisen in the fruit of the fourth jhāna.

"Preceded by reflection on the nature of things" (dhammatakkapurejava): "reflection on the nature of things" (dhammatakkā) refers to right intention; that [intention] comes first, it precedes [the fruit].

"He is the forerunner of the liberation through final knowledge" means he is preceded by the investigation of phenomena (*dhammatakkapurejava*). That which is preceded by the investigation of phenomena is *dhammatakkapurejava*.

"Liberation through final knowledge" (*aññāvimokkha*) refers to the liberation that arises at the conclusion of the faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*); or, it is the liberation *by means of* final knowledge, thus "liberation through final knowledge," meaning "liberation through wisdom.
"The shattering of ignorance" is said because [this liberation] arises at the point of the shattering of ignorance. Regarding ignorance...
Or, because it arises with reference to Nibbāna—which is known as the "destruction of distinctions"—it is given this name;
thus, it should be understood that by all these terms, beginning with "abandoning," it is precisely the fruit of Arahatship that is being manifested.
4. Commentary on the Nidāna Sutta.
34. "In the fourth [section], 'causes' (*nidānāni*) means reasons (*kāraṇāni*). 'Of karmas' (*kammānaṃ*) means of those karmas that lead to the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭagāmika*).

'Greed is the cause for the arising of karmas' (*lobho nidānaṃ kammānaṃ samudayāya*): greed, whose intrinsic nature is coveting and intense coveting, is the cause, the reason, the condition for the arising—that is, for the accumulation—of karmas leading to the cycle of existence;

this is the meaning. 'Hatred' (*doso*) is that which has the intrinsic nature of hating and being corrupt. 'Delusion' (*moho*) is that which has the intrinsic nature of being deluded and thoroughly deluded."
"Produced by greed" (*lobhapakata*) means performed by one who has been overcome by greed, having become greedy;
this is the meaning. "Born from greed" (*lobhaja*) means born from greed. "Greed is its source" (*lobhanidāna*) means that greed is its primary cause. "Greed is its origin" (*lobhasamudaya*);
"origin" (*samudaya*) means condition, so the meaning is "having greed as its condition. "Wherein its individual existence (*attabhāva*) is produced" means...
In whatever place the personal existence (*attabhāva*) of a person possessing karma born of greed arises, and the aggregates (*khandhā*) manifest—therein that karma ripens;

that is to say, that karma ripens within those very aggregates. Regarding the phrase "either in this very life" (*diṭṭhe vā dhamme*), etc., it is because that karma is either to be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*), or to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*), or to be experienced in some subsequent period (*aparapariyāyavedanīya*).
Therefore, this was said in order to demonstrate that classification. The same method applies to the other two pairs as well.
"Unbroken" means undivided. "Unrotted" means not having reached the state of being seedless through rotting. "Not damaged by wind or sun" means not harmed by the wind nor by the heat of the sun.
"Capable of holding the essence" means having grasped the core, possessing substance, and not being pithless.
"Sukhasayitāni" means they have lain comfortably due to being stored away. "Sukhette" means in a well-prepared field.
"Suparikammakatāya bhūmiyā" means on a field that has been thoroughly prepared by both plowing with the plow and by harrowing with the eight-toothed harrow.
"Nikkhittāni" means placed or sown. "Anuppaveccheyya" means he would cause them to enter [the soil]. Regarding "vuddhiṃ" and so forth:
By its upward growth it attains increase; by its downward rooting it attains growth; and by its spreading all around it attains abundance.
As for what is said here regarding "in this very life" (*diṭṭhe va dhamme*) and so forth, the analysis of action (*kamma-vibhatti*) should be explained in this place for the sake of non-confusion.
According to the method of the Suttantas, eleven types of action are analyzed, namely: [The list of eleven actions follows.]

— namely, karma to be experienced in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*), karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*), and karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparapariyāyavedanīya*);

furthermore, that which is weighty (*garuka*), that which is habitual (*bahula*), that which is proximate (*āsanna*), or karma performed by way of volitional formation (*kaṭattā kamma*); and finally, productive karma (*janaka*), supportive karma (*upatthambhaka*), obstructive karma (*upapīḷaka*), and destructive karma (*upaghātaka*).

In this context, within a single cognitive process (*javanavīthi*) consisting of seven moments of consciousness, the first impulsion volition (*paṭhamajavanacetanā*), whether wholesome or unwholesome, [is the most significant].
Kamma to be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīyakamma*) is that which yields its result in this very existence.

An example of wholesome (*kusala*) such kamma is that of the merchant Kākavaḷiya Puṇṇa; an example of unwholesome (*akusala*) is that of the yakkha Nanda, the youth Nanda-māṇavaka, the cow-slaughterer Nanda, Kokāliya, Suppabuddha, Devadatta, and the maiden Ciñcamāṇavikā.
However, when it is unable to do so, it is called "ineffective kamma" (*ahosikamma*) and remains without result.

This should be established by means of the simile of the deer-hunter. For just as when a deer-hunter, having seen a deer, draws his bow and shoots an arrow, if it does not miss, it fells that deer right there;
then the deer-hunter, having skinned it and cut it into pieces, takes the meat and goes away satisfying his wife and children. But if...
One becomes dispassionate; like a deer that has fled and no longer looks back toward that direction, so should this be understood.

For just as a deer being struck by an arrow is the obtaining of the opportunity for the ripening of karma to be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*), so too is the failure to strike it the occurrence of its remaining without ripening.

The seventh javana-consciousness, which accomplishes the purpose, is called "kamma to be experienced upon rebirth" (*upapajjavedanīya-kamma*). It yields its result in the immediately following existence. This should be understood as follows:

on the side of the wholesome, by way of the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*); and on the side of the unwholesome, by way of the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantariya-kamma*).
In that regard, one who has attained the eight meditative attainments is reborn in the Brahma-world through a single attainment. Of the five [deeds of immediate retribution] as well...

One who commits an *ānantariya* (immediate) offense is reborn in hell by that single kamma; the remaining attainments and other kamma-s enter the state of *ahosi-kamma* (kamma that has become past) and become non-resultant (*avipāka*). This matter also should be illustrated by the previous simile.
However, between those two, the five impulsion-consciousness volitions are called "kamma to be experienced in a subsequent life" (*aparapariyāya-vedanīya-kamma*). That [kamma] in the future...
When it finds an opportunity, then it yields its result. As long as the process of saṃsāra continues, there is no such thing as "lapsed karma" (*ahosikamma*).
All of this should be illustrated by the example of a hunter with his dog.
For just as when a hunter sees a deer and releases his dog, the dog pursues the deer and bites it at the very spot where it reaches; so too does karma.
In this very way, this kamma gives its result in the very place where it finds scope; there is no being liberated from that.
Among wholesome and unwholesome kamma, whether heavy or light, that which is heavy is called "the weightiest.

This should be understood as follows: on the side of the wholesome, it is exalted kamma; on the side of the unwholesome, it is the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantariya-kamma*). In that regard...
When other wholesome or unwholesome kamma exists, they are unable to ripen; rather, it is that [weighty kamma] alone—whether of either kind—that gives rebirth-linking.

For just as even a pebble the size of a mustard seed, or an iron ball, when thrown into a lake, cannot float on the surface of the water but sinks down, so too, whether it be wholesome or unwholesome, that which is weighty [determines rebirth].
Having grasped that very [object], it proceeds.
Among wholesome and unwholesome states, that which is predominant is called "the predominant" (*yabbahula*). This should be understood by way of long-term habitual practice.
Or else, it is that which produces joy among powerful wholesome kamma, and produces torment among unwholesome kamma.
This is what is called "preponderance. Just as when two Mallas have entered the field of battle,
the stronger one overthrows the other and proceeds, even so, having overwhelmed the other weak karma, that which is strong—
either by way of habitual practice (*āsevana*) or by way of proximity (*āsanna*)— gives its result, like the karma of King Abhaya, the wicked village headman.
It is said that after being defeated in the Battle of Cūḷaṅgaṇiya, he fled mounted on a thoroughbred mare.
His junior attendant, a minister named Tissa, was the only one following behind him. Having entered a certain forest and sat down, while he was being tormented by hunger, he said:
"Brother Tissa, we are exceedingly oppressed by hunger; what shall we do? "There is, Your Majesty."
“I have brought one measure of golden rice, having placed it inside my garment.
“Then bring it out,” he said. He brought it out and set it before the king. When the king saw it, he said, “Dear brother, divide it into four portions.
“We are three people; why does Your Majesty have it divided into four portions? “Brother Tissa, from this time forth—”
“I remember myself; there has never been a time when I have consumed food without first giving to my noble ladies.
Therefore, even today, I shall not consume it without having given. He divided [the food] into four portions. The king said, “Proclaim the time!
[The brahmin replied,] “O King, how could we obtain those who cast away [food] in the forest? Noble lady, if it is my faith...”
“There is, noble lady; we shall receive it. Call out the time with confidence,” he said. He then called out, “It is time, Bhante!
It is time, Bhante! three times.
Then the Elder Mahātissa, the Bodhi-mother, having heard that sound with his divine ear-element, [thought], “For what purpose is this...?”
Reflecting on that sound, he perceived: "Today, the Great King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi Abhaya, defeated in battle, has entered the forest and is staying there;
having had a single meal of rice-gruel divided into four portions, he has caused a proclamation to be made: 'I shall not consume it alone.
Realizing this, he thought, "Today it is fitting for me to show favor to the king," and arrived by means of his mental power.
He stood before the king. Upon seeing him, the king’s heart was filled with faith;
saying, "Behold, brother Tissa," he paid homage to the Elder and said, "Venerable sir, please accept my alms-bowl. The Elder brought forth his bowl.
The king, having placed his own portion together with the Elder's portion into the bowl, said, "Venerable sir, may there never be any danger regarding food for you."

Having paid homage with the words, "May it be so," he stood there. The minister Tissa also thought, "I shall not be able to eat while my noble sons are watching," and he poured his own portion into the Elder’s bowl.
The mare also thought, "It is right that I too give my portion to the Elder. The king looked at the mare and said, "She too [will give] her own portion to the Elder’s bowl."
Knowing that he was looking forward to having it thrown back in, the king threw that too right there, paid homage to the Elder, and sent him away.
The Elder took that food and went, giving it to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus in the form of mouthfuls starting from the beginning.
The king also thought: "We were exceedingly hungry; it would be well indeed if there were some leftover rice-grains."
“...should be sent. The Elder, knowing the king’s intention, set aside enough of the extra food for their sustenance and threw his bowl into the air;
the bowl returned and came to rest in the king’s hand. The food was sufficient for all three people to eat as much as they desired.
Then the king, having washed the bowl, thinking, “I will not send it back empty,” removed his upper garment.
Having wiped away the water and placed his upper garment in the bowl, he threw it into the air, saying, "May this bowl go and rest in the hand of my noble Lord.
The bowl went and rested in the hand of the Elder.
Later on, after the King had established an eighth portion of the Tathāgata’s bodily relics, [he erected] a stupa one hundred and twenty cubits high...
While he was having the Great Cetiya constructed, the time of his passing away arrived even before the Cetiya was finished.

Then, as he lay on his right side by the Great Cetiya while the Saṅgha of bhikkhus was reciting the scriptures according to the five Nikāyas, six chariots came from the six deva-worlds and stood in the air in front of him. The king [thought]: "This is the book of my merit..."
"Bring it," he said, and from the beginning he had the book of merit read aloud. When that did not satisfy him, he said, "Read further.

The reader began: "O King, when you were defeated in the Battle of Cūḷaṅgaṇiya and sat in the forest, you had a meal of rice and milk divided into four portions and gave one to the Great Elder Bodhimātu Tissa..."
“Alms have been given,” he said. The king, saying “Keep it,” asked the Saṅgha of monks, “Venerable sirs, which heavenly realm is the most delightful?
“The Tusita abode, O Great King, is the dwelling place of all Bodhisattvas.
Having passed away, the king was established on the very chariot that had come from the Tusita abode and went to the Tusita abode.
This is the basis for the giving of its result by a powerful kamma.
As for that which one is able to recollect among wholesome or unwholesome deeds when death is near, that is called "the proximate.
This is just as, for example, when the gate of a pen full of a herd of cattle is opened, [one would first see] those at the far end—such as the draft-oxen, the stallions, and the heifers.

Just as even among those present, whoever is closest to the gate—even if it be a weak old ox—goes out first, in the same way, although other wholesome or unwholesome kamma exists, it gives its result at the time of death because of its proximity to that moment. Here are some examples:
it is said that in the village of Madhu-aṅgaṇa, a certain Tamil doorkeeper, taking his snare early in the morning, [went forth].
Having gone and killed a fish, he divided it into three portions: with one he took rice, with another curd, and he cooked the third.
By this routine, having committed the kamma of taking life for fifty years, later on, when he had grown old, he lay down and ceased from his work.
At that moment, the Elder Cūḷapiṇḍapātika Tissa, who dwelt at Girivihāra, [arrived].
Thinking, "Let this being not perish while I am looking on," he went and stood at the door of his house.
Then his wife announced, "Master, the Elder has arrived. He replied, "I have never before gone to the presence of this Elder for fifty years;
by what merit of mine would the Elder have come? Go and tell him to leave. She said, "Please enter, Venerable Sir."
The Elder asked, "Lay follower, what is your physical condition? "I am weak, venerable sir," he replied.
The Elder entered the house, established mindfulness, and said, "Will you take the precepts? "Yes, venerable sir, please give them," he said.
Having administered the three refuges, the Elder began to give the five precepts. At the very moment he spoke the words for the five precepts, his tongue—
He fell down. The Elder, thinking, "It will suffice for this much," went out and departed.
He too, having passed away, was reborn in the realm of the Four Great Kings. At the very moment of his rebirth, reflecting, "What deed have I done to obtain this?
he realized it was through the Elder that he had gained it. Coming from the world of the gods, he paid homage to the Elder and stood to one side.
When asked, "Who is this? he replied, "Venerable sir, I am the Damila gatekeeper. "Where have you been reborn? "In the realm of the Four Great Kings, venerable sir;
had my master bestowed upon me the five precepts, I would have been reborn in a higher celestial world.
What could I do? You were unable to take them, my dear son. Having paid homage to the Elder, he departed for the celestial world itself.
This, first of all, is the basis for wholesome karma.
Now, during the time of the Great Teacher, there was a lay follower named Mahāvācaka.

For thirty years he recited the thirty-two aspects (dvattiṃsākāra) for the sake of the path of stream-entry, thinking: "While I am thus reciting the thirty-two aspects, even if I were to produce merely a flash of light..."
“I was unable [to do so]; the Buddha’s teaching will not lead to liberation.
Having fallen into this perversion of view, he died and was reborn as a *susumāra* (crocodile) spirit, the size of a young bull, in the Great Ganges.
On one occasion, sixty stone-pillar wagons passed by the Kacchaka ford; he devoured all those oxen and stones. This...
The basis for unwholesome karma consists of these three.
However, that which is performed apart from these three due to ignorance, or karma that has already been performed (*kaṭattā*), is called "karma.
Just as a stick thrown by a madman goes wherever it may, even in the absence of those [three conditions], it is exactly like that.
It gives its result anywhere.

That which is called "productive" (janaka) karma produces only one rebirth-linking and does not produce the course of existence; rather, it is another karma that produces the result during the course of existence.
For just as a mother only gives birth while a nursemaid only looks after [the child], even so is this like a mother.

Productive karma (*janaka-kamma*) is that which produces rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), like a nurse; whereas karma that provides for what is already attained during the course of existence (*pavatta-sampatta-kamma*) is like a wet-nurse.

Supporting karma (*upatthambhaka-kamma*) is found both in the wholesome (*kusala*) and the unwholesome (*akusala*). For instance, someone may perform a wholesome deed and be reborn in a happy destination (*sugati-bhava*).
Remaining there, they repeatedly perform wholesome deeds and, by strengthening that karma, [remain] for many hundreds of thousands of years.
One roams about within the state of a happy destination itself. Another, having committed unwholesome deeds, is reborn in a state of miserable destination.
Remaining there, he repeatedly commits unwholesome deeds and reinforces that karma, roaming about within the state of a miserable destination for many hundreds of thousands of years.
Another method: that which is called "productive" (janaka) is both wholesome and unwholesome.
It produces resultant aggregates, both material and immaterial, both at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence. However, it is not able to produce resultant [states] by way of support;
rather, it supports the pleasure or pain arising once the rebirth-linking has been produced by another kamma.

It causes the course [of existence] to proceed. That which is called "oppressive" (upapīḷaka) oppresses and hinders the pleasure and pain arising from the result produced by a rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) given by another karma;
it does not allow the course [of existence] to proceed. In this regard, the method is as follows:
when a wholesome karma is ripening, an unwholesome karma acts as an oppressor and does not allow it to ripen.
When unwholesome karma is ripening, wholesome karma acts as an obstructer and does not allow it to ripen.
It is just as if someone were to strike or cut with a stick or a sword a tree, a shrub, or a creeper that is growing; then that tree, shrub, or creeper would be unable to grow.
In the same way, wholesome karma that is about to ripen cannot ripen if it is suppressed by unwholesome karma,
nor can unwholesome karma that is about to ripen ripen if it is suppressed by wholesome karma. In this regard, Sunakkhatta’s unwholesome karma was suppressed by wholesome karma,
while the executioner’s wholesome karma was suppressed by unwholesome karma.
It is said that in Rājagaha, Vātakāḷaka performed the work of an executioner for fifty years. Then they reported to the king:
"Your Majesty, Vātakāḷaka has grown old and is no longer able to execute criminals. "Remove him from that office," [the king replied].
The ministers removed him and appointed another in his place. And Vātakāḷaka continued to perform that work until it was finished.
For so long he had not been able to clothe himself in new garments, nor adorn himself with fragrant flowers, nor eat milk-rice,
nor enjoy anointing and bathing. Thinking, "For a long time I have lived in soiled clothing," he commanded his wife,
"Cook some milk-rice," and having had the requisites for bathing brought, he went to the bathing place.
Having bathed his head, put on new clothes, anointed himself with perfumes, and adorned himself with flowers, he was returning home when he saw the Elder Sāriputta.
Thinking, "I have escaped from defiled karma, and I have seen my noble lord," he was filled with joy;
he led the Elder to his house and [prepared an offering] consisting of fresh ghee, sugar, and powdered rice.
He served him with milk-rice. The Elder offered a blessing of thanksgiving. Having heard the blessing, he attained the stage of conformity (anulomikakhanti).
Following the Elder as he was returning, he was crushed by a cow with a young calf on the path and died;
having passed away, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. The monks questioned the Tathāgata.
“Venerable sir, the executioner was removed from his defiled work this very day; he passed away this very day. Where has he been reborn?
“In the realm of the Thirty-three, monks. “Venerable sir, for a long time the executioner killed men, yet you say this:
‘There is no fruit of evil karma. Do not speak thus, monks!”

Thus you have spoken: having obtained the strong support of a virtuous friend, having given almsfood to the General of the Dhamma, having heard his expression of thanks, and having attained conformable patience (*anulomikakhanti*), he was reborn there.
"Having heard these well-spoken words, the noble elephant, the executioner of thieves..."
“Having attained conformity-patience (anulomakhanti), he rejoices, having gone to the triple heaven.

Furthermore, an obstructive [kamma], whether itself wholesome or unwholesome, destroys another weak kamma, wards off its result, and makes room for its own result. When this has been done by the kamma...
When that result has arisen in its opportunity, it is called "arisen. "Cutting-off" is also a name for this very thing.
Herein is the method: at the time when a wholesome kamma is about to ripen, a certain unwholesome kamma arises, cuts off that [wholesome] kamma, and causes it to fall away.
Likewise, at the time when an unwholesome kamma is about to ripen, a certain wholesome kamma arises, cuts off that [unwholesome] kamma, and...

It causes [the continuity] to fall away. This is called "cutting off. In this regard, the karma of Ajātasattu was a cutter-off of the wholesome, while that of the Elder Aṅgulimāla was a cutter-off of the unwholesome.
Thus, according to the method of the Suttantas, eleven types of karma have been analyzed.
However, according to the method of the Abhidhamma, sixteen types of karma are analyzed, as follows: "There are some..."
Certain undertakings of evil kamma do not ripen when obstructed by excellence of destination;
certain undertakings of evil kamma do not ripen when obstructed by excellence of physical basis;
certain undertakings of evil kamma do not ripen when obstructed by excellence of time; and certain undertakings of evil kamma do not ripen when obstructed by excellence of application.

They do not ripen. There are certain undertakings of unwholesome kamma that ripen by way of failure of destination, or they ripen by way of failure of the physical basis, failure of time, or failure of effort.

There are certain undertakings of wholesome kamma that do not ripen because they are obstructed by a failure of destination, or [by a failure of the physical basis, failure of time, or failure of effort].
"Those [karmas] obstructed by failure in application do not ripen. However, some undertakings of wholesome kamma ripen by way of success in destination;
they ripen by way of success in the physical basis, success in time, and success in application.
Therein, "evil" means inferior. "Undertakings of kamma" means the graspings of kamma. Of those that have been grasped and undertaken...

This is a designation for kamma. In such passages as "those [kammic forces] obstructed by the excellence of the destination do not ripen," even while a kamma capable of experiencing an undesirable object exists, it is said that for one reborn in a happy state of existence, that kamma does not ripen because it is obstructed by the excellence of the destination.
The meaning is that, having been obstructed by the excellence of the destination, it does not ripen. However, as for one who, by means of evil kamma—
Having been conceived in the womb of a female slave or a laborer, he is endowed with a physical basis and remains in the fullness of his personal existence.
Then, his masters, seeing the excellence of his appearance, think, "This is not suitable for one of defiled karma," and having formed this thought,
they place him in positions such as treasurer or storekeeper, just like their own biological son, and [provide him with] prosperity.
Having applied themselves, they maintain [the practice]. For such a person, karma obstructed by the excellence of material requisites (*upadhi-sampatti*) does not ripen.

Furthermore, for one who is born during a time of good harvest when food is easily obtained, rich in flavor, and similar to the era of the first cosmic age (*paṭhamakappika*), even existing evil karma that is obstructed by the excellence of the time (*kāla-sampatti*) does not ripen. However, for one who applies right effort...
One lives by depending [on others]; one approaches at the proper time for approaching; one withdraws at the proper time for withdrawing;
one flees at the proper time for fleeing. One gives a bribe at the proper time for giving a bribe; one commits theft at the proper time for committing theft.
For such a person, an evil deed—though it may be obstructed by the perfection of its execution—is said not to ripen.
Furthermore, for one reborn in a state of miserable existence, evil karma ripens by way of a failure of destiny (*gativipatti*).
One who is born from the womb of a female slave or a laborer may be ill-favored and misshapen, such that it arouses doubt as to whether he is a *yakkha* or a human being.
If he is a man, then others [think], "This is not anyone else's..."
"Suitable for such work," they have them guard elephants or horses or oxen,
or have them fetch grass, wood, and so forth, or have them carry spittoons. If she is a woman,
then they have her cook the food and fodder for the elephants, horses, and so on, or have her discard refuse, or perform some other loathsome task.
They cause [it] to be done. For one such as this, an evil deed ripens by way of the failure of the basis (*upadhivipatti*).

However, for one who is reborn during a time of famine, or at a time when prosperity has declined, or during an intermediate eon (*antarakappa*), his evil deed ripens by way of the failure of the time (*kālavipatti*).
Furthermore, for one who does not know how to prepare the necessary means, or at the appropriate time for approaching [the object],...
He does not know how to approach [the object], and so forth; at a time when it is appropriate for theft, he does not know how to commit the theft.
In such a case, his evil deed is said to "ripen" due to the failure of its application (*payoga-vipatti*).

However, when one is reborn in a state of miserable existence (*duggati-bhava*) despite the presence of a kamma capable of producing the experience of desirable objects, [this is due to the failure of the object].
For him, that karma—which is strongly obstructed by the failure of his destiny—is said not to ripen.

However, when someone, by the power of merit, is reborn in the household of a king, a royal minister, or the like, yet is one-eyed, has a withered arm, is lame, or has a paralyzed side, they do not grant him positions such as viceroy, general, or treasurer because he is unsuitable for them. Thus, for him—
That merit, being obstructed by a failure of the physical basis (*upadhivipatti*), is said not to ripen.

However, when one is reborn among humans during a time of famine, or at a time when prosperity has declined, or during an intermediate aeon (*antarakappa*), that wholesome deed is said not to ripen because it is obstructed by a failure of the time (*kālavipatti*).
As for one who, according to the method explained above, does not know how to carry out the practice, their wholesome deed—
An action that is obstructed by a failure in application is said not to ripen.
However, for one who has been reborn in a happy state of existence through a wholesome deed, that karma is said to ripen by virtue of the excellence of that destination.
This occurs within the prosperity of one’s personal being, having been born into a family of kings, royal ministers, and so forth, and having attained the excellence of material requisites.

When one sees their own physical form standing in the city of the gods like an erected jeweled archway, people say, "The positions of vice-regent, general, and treasurer are suitable for this person," and they grant those offices even while he is still young;

such is how wholesome karma ripens by means of the excellence of the physical basis (*upadhi*). This was the case for those among the first generation of world-creators (*paṭhamakappika*) during a time when food and drink were easily obtained.
Or it arises; for one who performs wholesome karma, that karma is said to ripen by way of the perfection of time.
For one who knows how to carry out the application in the manner already described, that karma is said to ripen by way of the perfection of application.
Thus, by way of the Abhidhamma method, sixteen types of karma have been analyzed.
Furthermore, another twelve types of kamma are analyzed according to the method of the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.
