They are as follows: "There was kamma, there was the result of that kamma; there was kamma, there was no result of that kamma; there was kamma, there is the result of that kamma;
there was kamma, there is no result of that kamma; there was kamma, there will be the result of that kamma; there was kamma..."
“There will be no ripening of karma; there is karma and there is ripening of karma; there is karma and there is no ripening of karma;
there is karma and there will be ripening of karma; there is karma and there will not be ripening of karma;
there will be karma and there will be ripening of karma; there will be karma and there will not be ripening of karma.”

In this context, that karma which was accumulated in the past and obtained its opportunity for fruition in the very same past— whether it produced rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) as a producer of rebirth-linking,
or produced material form (rūpa) as a producer of material form— is said to be "karma that has been, and the fruition of karma that has been. However,
that which did not obtain its opportunity for fruition, yet was capable of producing rebirth-linking as a producer of rebirth-linking, or material form as a producer of material form...
It is said: "That [kamma] was not able [to produce its result]; that kamma did not exist, nor did the ripening of that kamma exist.

However, regarding that which was accumulated in the past and has now reached the stage of having obtained its ripening—namely, that which produces rebirth-linking, and having produced rebirth-linking, remains having produced material form—it is said:
"That kamma existed; the ripening of that kamma exists. Regarding that which has not yet obtained the stage of ripening but is capable of producing rebirth-linking...
If it was unable to produce rebirth-linking or to produce matter that generates rebirth-linking, that is called "past karma" and "there is no fruition of that karma.
However, that which was accumulated in the past and will receive its opportunity for fruition in the future—
that which is capable of producing rebirth-linking or producing matter that generates rebirth-linking— is called "past karma" and "there will be fruition of that karma."

It has been said: that which will not obtain a stage of fruition in the future, and which will be unable to produce rebirth-linking, or to produce the matter associated with rebirth-linking, is called "past karma" and "karma whose fruition will not occur.
However, that which was accumulated right now and obtains a stage of fruition right now is "present karma" and "present fruition."
It is said: "There is action, there is the ripening of action. However, that which does not obtain the stage of ripening at present is described as:

"There is action, there is no ripening of action. But that which has been accumulated now and will obtain the stage of ripening in the future—that which can produce rebirth-linking, and can produce matter by generating rebirth-linking—is described as: "There is action, there will be the ripening of action."

It has been stated. However, that which will not obtain a stage of fruition (*vipākavāra*), yet is capable of producing rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) or producing matter that generates rebirth-linking—that is called "kamma that exists but whose fruition will not exist.
Furthermore, that which will be accumulated in the future and will obtain a stage of fruition only in the future—that is [the kamma] which generates rebirth-linking...
It is said: "That which will produce rebirth-linking, or will produce matter that generates rebirth-linking, will be karma; it will be the fruition of karma.

However, that which does not obtain the opportunity for fruition, and which is unable to produce rebirth-linking or produce matter that generates rebirth-linking, "will be karma; it will not be the fruition of karma."
Thus, by way of the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, twelve kamma-s have been analyzed.

Therefore, these same twelve and the sixteen kamma-s analyzed by way of the Abhidhamma method, when reduced to their own proper place, become only eleven kamma-s as stated by way of the Suttanta method. Those too, from there...

When excluded, there are only three types of kamma: that to be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*), that to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*), and that to be experienced in a subsequent life (*aparapariyāyavedanīya*).
There is no transference between them; they remain exactly as they are situated.
For if kamma to be experienced in the present life were to become kamma to be experienced upon rebirth or in a subsequent life, [the phrase] "in this very life" (*diṭṭhe vā dhamme*) would not apply.

The Teacher would not have said [that]. If it were to be experienced in the next life, or experienced in this very life, or experienced in a subsequent state, the Teacher would not have said, "or in the next life.
Furthermore, if it were to be experienced in a subsequent state, or experienced in this very life, or experienced in the next life, the Teacher would not have said, "or in another subsequent state."
The meaning should be understood by this same method for the bright fortnight as well. Here, however, "lust has departed" means that lust has gone away and ceased.
"Rendered like a palm stump" means made like the base of a palm tree; the sense is that it has been made of a nature that will not grow again, like a palm tree with its crown cut off.
"Brought to non-existence" means brought to a state of non-being, so that it does not arise again.
"Thus done" means in this way. "Let them be thus" means let them become so. In the phrase "even so," wholesome and unwholesome kamma should be regarded as seeds;
the practitioner is like the man burning those seeds with fire; path-knowledge is like the fire;

the time when the defilements are burnt by path-knowledge is like the time when the seeds are burnt after the fire has been applied; and the time when they have been reduced to ash is [the state of their destruction].

It is like the time when the five aggregates have been established with their roots cut; it is like the time when they have been winnowed in a great wind or swept away by a river so that they no longer function.

Through the cessation of the continuum of what is clung to (*upādinnaka-santāna*), the five aggregates—whose roots have been severed—cease without further rebirth-linking (*appaṭisandhika*) and do not undergo rebirth-linking again in a future existence.
The time of its non-grasping is to be understood.
"Born of delusion and ignorant" means born of delusion and also ignorant. This is what is meant:
whatever action that foolish, blind person performs—born of greed, born of hatred, and born of delusion—by performing it in this way, the action that has been done by him...
"Whether little or much": that karma must be experienced right here by that fool;
it means that very karma ripens within his own personal existence (*attabhāva*) here. "No other basis exists" means there is no other basis for the ripening of that karma;
for karma performed by one person does not ripen in the personal existence of another.
It ripens. Therefore, "the wise one [abandons] greed, hatred, and that which is born of delusion":

thus, the wise, intelligent, and learned person does not perform such karma distinguished by its origin in greed and the rest. That bhikkhu, generating true knowledge (*vijjā*), shall abandon all miserable destinies;
or rather, while generating that very knowledge by means of producing the knowledge of the path to Arahantship, he abandons all miserable destinies.
“They abandon it. This is merely a conventional expression for teaching; however, even in the happy destinies, one whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava) indeed abandons it.

Furthermore, regarding what was said, “Therefore, both greed and hatred,” it should be understood that here too, by way of the headings “greed” and “hatred,” it is actually the karma born of greed and born of hatred that is being pointed out.
Thus, even in the Suttantas and in this verse, only the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) and its cessation (vivaṭṭa) are explained.
5. Commentary on the Hatthaka Sutta 35.
In the fifth [verse], "at Āḷavī" means in the province of Āḷavī. "On a cow-path" means on a path used by cattle for traveling.
"On a bed of leaves" means on a bed of leaves that have fallen of their own accord. "Then" (atha) means: thus, having [sat] by a straight great road serving as a path for cattle...
When the Tathāgata had sat down, having spread out a seat made by gathering together fallen leaves in a *siṃsapā* grove and spreading the Great Robe of the Sugata,
and had folded his legs crosswise in the *pallaṅka* posture— [then] Hatthaka Āḷavaka,
the prince of Āḷavaka who had received that name because he passed from hand to hand, spoke these words: "Venerable sir, I hope the Blessed One is well," and so forth.
He said: "But why did the Perfectly Enlightened One go to that place and sit there, and why did the prince go there?
The Perfectly Enlightened One sat there because he saw it as the occasion for a teaching on the Dhamma arising from a specific incident;
the prince also rose early in the morning and went to attend upon the Buddha, surrounded by five hundred lay followers.
While traveling along the great road, he left it, took a bypath, and set out thinking, "I shall gather a mixed garland for the purpose of honoring the Buddhas.
On his way, having seen the Teacher, he approached him, paid homage, and sat down to one side;
thus it was that he went there. "He slept happily" means he slept in comfort.
*Antaraṭṭhaka*: A period of eight days between the months of Māgha and Phagguṇa.
For four days at the end of Māgha and four days at the beginning of Phagguṇa constitute what is called the "antaraṭṭhaka.
*Himapātasamaya*: The season of the falling of snow. *Khara*: Harsh, rough, or hard. *Gokaṇṭakahatā*: [Ground] trampled by oxen when it has rained for the first time.
In places where cows have repeatedly trodden, mud rises up between their hooves and remains there;
dried by the wind and sun, it becomes like the teeth of a saw and is painful to the touch. With reference to this, it is said: "The ground is struck by cow-hooves.
The meaning is also that it is torn up by the spaces between the hooves of cattle. "The Verambha wind blows" means it blows from all four directions.
The wind blows. A wind blowing from one direction, or two directions, or three directions is not called a "Veramba wind.
Therefore, O Prince, the Teacher said this while expanding upon the subsequent teaching, thinking: "This prince does not know whether those in the world dwell in happiness or dwell in suffering;
I shall cause him to know. In that context, "so that it may be acceptable to you" means:
"Whatever may please you. "Idhassa" means "in this world" (*imasmiṃ loke assa*).
"Covered with *gonaka* wool" means covered with black wool that is more than four finger-breadths thick. "Covered with *paṭika*" means covered with a white woolen spread (*uṇṇāmaya-attharaṇa*).
"Covered with *paṭalika*" means covered with a woolen spread made of dense flowers. "With a choice coverlet of *kadalimiga* deer-skin" means made from the skin of the *kadalimiga* deer.

"By means of a superior spread" refers to its purpose. It is said that they make that spread by sewing a deer-skin from a kadali antelope over a white cloth. "With an upper canopy" means together with an upper canopy;
the meaning is together with a red awning fastened above. "With red pillows on both sides" refers to both a head-pillow and a foot-pillow.
With red pillows placed on both sides of the couch. "Wives" means consorts.
"They would attend with what is pleasing" means they would attend by means of a pleasing mode of service.
"Bodily" means agitating the body of the five sense-doors. "Mental" means agitating the mind-door. That lust...

"Such lust has been abandoned by the Tathāgata" means that such lust as that has been abandoned by the Tathāgata; however, whatever lust he may have [in other contexts], that is not said to be "abandoned" by the Tathāgata.
This same method applies to hatred and delusion as well.
"Brahmin" refers to a brahmin whose taints are exhausted, having warded off evil. "Parinibbūta" means one who has attained final nibbāna through the nibbāna of the defilements.
"He is not smeared by sensual pleasures" means he is not smeared by the stains of craving and views regarding both material objects (*vatthukāma*) and defilements (*kilesakāma*).
"Become cool" means he has become cool due to the absence of the defilements that burn within.
"Without substrate" means without substrate because of the absence of the substrate of defilements (*kilesūpadhi*). "Having cut all attachments": attachments are called cravings; all of those—

Having severed attachments—that is, having cut through the clinging and the entanglement regarding objects such as visible forms; having removed the distress residing in the heart—that is, having disciplined and pacified the agitation dependent upon the heart;

and having attained peace of mind—that is, having reached the extinction of defilements (nibbāna) for the consciousness—or alternatively, this is an instrumental expression, as in phrases such as "having applied the whole mind" (*sabbacetaso samannāharitvā*), [meaning] by means of the mind.
The meaning is: "having attained Nibbāna. 6.
Commentary on the *Devadūta Sutta* (Discourse on the Divine Messengers). 36.
Regarding the sixth [verse], *devadūtāni* means "divine messengers. Herein, this is the etymological analysis: *deva* refers to Death (*maccu*). His...

“Messengers” means messengers of the gods. For the aged, the sick, and the dying act like goads, urging one on in the sense of generating spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) by saying, as it were, “Now you must go into the presence of Death”;
therefore they are called messengers of the gods. Alternatively, they are called messengers of the gods because they are messengers like the gods.
For just as when a goddess, adorned and prepared, stands in the sky and says, “On such-and-such a day you will die,” her word is to be believed.
In the same way, even when seeing those who are old, sick, and afflicted, they seem to reproach one, saying, "You too are subject to this same nature.
And because that speech of theirs is not otherwise than what has been realized, it is like the declaration of a deity; thus they are called *devadūtā* (divine messengers).

Alternatively, they are called *devadūtā* because they are messengers of the pure deities (*visuddhideva*). For all Bodhisattvas, upon seeing those who are old, sick, afflicted, and those who have gone forth...

Having seen this, they were moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and, having gone forth, they renounced the world. Thus, they are called "messengers of the gods" (*devadūtā*) because they are messengers from the pure devas.
However, here the term is stated as "devadūtāni" (the messengers of the gods) due to a grammatical shift in gender.

Why was the passage beginning with "bodily misconduct" (*kāyena duccaritaṃ*) introduced? It is for the purpose of showing the preliminary actions that lead to being pursued by the messengers of the gods.
For by this karma this being is reborn in hell; then King Yama interrogates him there before the divine messengers.
In that context, "he practices misconduct with the body" means he practices the threefold misconduct through the door of the body.
"With speech" means he practices the fourfold misconduct through the door of speech. "With the mind" means through the door of the mind.
He practices the threefold misconduct.
Regarding this, monks, as for the statement "the wardens of hell," some elders say: "There are no such things as wardens of hell;
rather, it is karma itself that acts as the cause, like a mechanical puppet. To that [objection], [the reply is]: "There are wardens of hell in hell; yes, there are."
This has indeed been refuted in the Abhidhamma by such methods as "There are judges," and so forth.

For just as there are those who carry out judicial punishments in the human world, even so there are wardens of hell in hell. Regarding the phrase "of King Yama," King Yama is the king of the *vemānika* (disembodied) *petas*.
At one time, in a celestial mansion (*vimāna*), he possessed every excellence, including divine wishing-trees (*kapparukkha*), divine parks, divine dancers, and so on.
He experiences the ripening of kamma at one time; he is a righteous king, and he is not alone—rather, there are four persons at the four gates.
*Matteyyo* means "one who is beneficial to his mother"; the meaning is "one who behaves rightly toward his mother.
*Amatteyyo* means "one who is not beneficial to his mother"; the meaning is "one who behaves wrongly toward his mother. The same applies to the remaining terms as well.
This is the method. Regarding the term "non-Brahmin" (*abrahmañña*): here, those whose taints are destroyed are called Brahmins; one who practices wrongly among them is called a non-Brahmin.

"He cross-examines" means he questions while imposing a formal line of inquiry; however, when establishing a particular tenet, it is called "interrogating," and when asking for the underlying reason, it is called "reproving. [They] do not see anyone sent into their presence.
He spoke thus with reference to the absence of a divine messenger.
Then Yama, knowing that the man did not perceive the meaning of what was said and wishing to make him perceive it, spoke the words beginning with "Ambho! (O man!).
Therein, *jiṇṇaṃ* means decayed by old age; *gopānasivaṅkaṃ* means crooked like a rafter.
"Bhogganti bhaggaṃ" means it is broken; by this, he also illustrates its state of being crooked.
"Daṇḍaparāyaṇaṃ" means having a staff as one's resort, having a staff as one's companion. "Pavedhamānaṃ" means trembling. "Āturaṃ" means afflicted by old age.
"Khaṇḍadantaṃ" means having teeth broken due to the power of old age. "Palitakesaṃ" means having white hair. "Vilūnaṃ" means bald, like one whose hair has been plucked out.
*Khālitasīran ti* means a head with a large bald patch. *Valitan ti* means having wrinkles that have formed. *Tilakāhatagattan ti* means a body covered with white and black moles.
*Jarādhammo* means subject to aging; one is not yet liberated from aging, thinking, "Aging indeed occurs within me.
The same method applies to the subsequent two phrases: "subject to illness" and "subject to death."
"Having first interrogated the divine messenger": here, the being aged by old age speaks thus in terms of the actual meaning:
"Behold, sirs, I too was once young like you—possessed of strength in the thighs, strength in the arms, and endowed with speed;
those perfections of strength and speed have now vanished from me. Although my hands and feet still exist, they no longer perform the functions of hands and feet."

“They do not act [rightly], because they are not yet freed from old age; thus one is born in such a state. But it is not only I who am not freed from old age—you too are indeed not freed from old age.
For just as it will come upon me, so too will old age come upon you. Therefore, before it arrives, perform what is wholesome.
For this very reason, he became known as the “Divine Messenger” (*devadūta*). “Afflicted” (*ābādhika*) means that which causes affliction (*bādhika*).
“Afflicted” means one who has reached suffering. “Severely ill” means one who is extremely sick.
Regarding the second divine messenger, here too the afflicted being speaks thus in substance: “See, sirs!
I too was once free from disease like you; but now I am struck down by illness, amidst my own urine and excrement.”
"I am fallen into distress; I cannot even rise up. Although my hands and feet exist, they do not perform the functions of hands and feet.
I have become like this because I am not free from illness. It is not only I who am thus; you too are certainly not free from illness.
For just as it has happened to me, so will illness come to you as well. Therefore, while it has not yet arrived, it is good [to prepare]."
"Make [it so]," he said. For that very reason, he became known as "Devadūta" (the Messenger of the Gods).
Regarding the terms beginning with *ekāhamata*: one who has been dead for one day is *ekāhamata*; that state is *ekāhamata*.
The same method applies to the two subsequent terms as well. Like a bellows filled with air, after the cessation of life, it gradually becomes bloated by the process of putrefaction.
Because it is bloated, it is "the bloated" (*uddhumātaka*). "Discolored" (*vinīla*) refers to that which has changed its natural color;
being discolored, it is "the discolored" (*vinīlaka*). Alternatively, because it is repulsive, it is loathsome and discolored, thus "the discolored.
"Festering" (*vipubbaka*) means having pus oozing out; the meaning is that it is smeared with pus that has flowed out from the ruptured places.
Regarding the third divine messenger, the deceased being speaks thus in terms of the actual meaning:
"Behold, sirs, me cast away in the raw charnel ground, having reached the state of a bloated corpse and so forth;
I have become such because I was not liberated from death. It is not only I who am not liberated from death; for just as it is with me, so it is with you."
"Death will come; therefore, before it arrives, perform what is wholesome. For this very reason, he became known as his "messenger from the gods" (*devadūta*).
Now, who receives this application of the divine messengers, and who does not? First, one by whom much evil has been committed goes and is reborn in hell itself.
However, one by whom only a small amount of evil has been committed receives [this warning]. Just as...
For when they catch a thief with the stolen goods, they do exactly what must be done and do not pass judgment;
however, once he has been investigated and apprehended, they bring him before the court of justice, and there he receives his judgment. This is just like that case.
For those who have committed only minor evil deeds remember [their transgression] by their own nature, and they also remember it when being interrogated.
Therein, one named Dīghajayantadamiḷa remembered by his own natural disposition. It is said that this Damiḷa had worshipped the Ākāsacetiya at the Sumanagiri Mahāvihāra with a red cloth;

then, having been reborn in the vicinity of the Ussada hell, upon merely hearing the sound of the flames of fire, he recollected the cloth he himself had worshipped, and having gone there, he was reborn in heaven. Furthermore, another [son], while his young bhikkhu son...
While giving a plain cotton cloth, he placed it at the Buddha’s feet; at the time of death, he took as a sign the sound "paṭapaṭā.
He was reborn in the Ussada hell, but by means of the sound of the cloth, he recollected that garment and was reborn in heaven.
Thus, indeed, by recollecting one's own wholesome kamma through its own nature, one is reborn in heaven.

But when they do not remember by their own nature, he questions them regarding the three divine messengers. In this regard, one remembers by means of the first divine messenger, another by the second or third, and another does not remember even by all three. When King Yama sees this, he himself causes him to remember. It is said that a certain minister, having worshipped the Great Cetiya with a jar of jasmine flowers, gave the merit thereof to Yama. Upon seeing him, [Yama asks: "Did you give the merit? He replies: "Yes, sire. "To whom did you give it? "To you, sire. "What did you see of me? [He replies: "Sire, I saw you sitting on a throne made of gold and silver, wearing a crown and earrings, adorned with necklaces and bracelets, and surrounded by ministers. "Was there anyone else besides me? "Sire, I saw a man with a black head, covered in sores, with a body like a heap of bruises, and with hands and feet bound in iron chains. "Who was that? "That, sire, was the first divine messenger. "Did you see a second? "Yes, sire, I saw one who was blind from birth, with no eyes at all. "Who was that? "That, sire, was the second divine messenger. "Did you see a third? "Yes, sire, I saw one who was very old, bent over, leaning on a staff, trembling, with grey hair, and broken teeth. "Who was that? "That, sire, was the third divine messenger. "Did you see a fourth? "No, sire, I did not see a fourth. "Well then, you have seen the three divine messengers; why do you not remember? You must remember! Thus, King Yama himself causes him to remember. It is said that one minister, having worshipped the Great Cetiya with a jar of *sumana* flowers, gave the merit thereof to Yama. Having been reborn in hell due to unwholesome karma, they were led into the presence of Yama.
While he was not being reminded of his wholesome deed by the three divine messengers, Yama himself looked and saw him;
he then reminded him, saying, "Did you not honor the Great Cetiya with a bowl of jasmine flowers and give me the merit? At that moment, he remembered it and went to the world of the gods. Yama...
But even though he looked for himself and still did not see it, he remained silent, thinking: "This being will experience what is called great suffering.

Regarding the "red-hot iron pillar": having laid the being prone upon a blazing iron ground with his body measuring three *gāvutas*, they drive an iron spike the size of a palm tree into his right hand; likewise into his left hand and so forth. And as that—
Having laid them on their backs, and likewise having laid them on their chests, on their left sides, and on their right sides, they continue to inflict that punishment upon them.
"Having made them lie down" means having made their bodies, three *gāvutas* in length, lie down upon the blazing iron ground.
"With axes" means they plane [the flesh] with great axes as large as the roof-covering of a single wing of a house.
It flows as a river of blood; flames rising from the iron ground seize the place where they are being planed, and great suffering arises.
Yet those who plane them fashion the wood into eight-sided or six-sided shapes, even though it has been struck by saws.
"With axes" means with axes the size of large winnowing-fans. "Having yoked to a chariot" means together with the yoke, the shafts, the side-boards, the wheels, and the pole.
Having yoked the chariot that was blazing on all sides. "Great" means the size of a large gabled house (*kūṭāgāra*).
"They cause to be mounted" means they force them onto it while striking them with glowing iron hammers.
"It goes up and down" means it moves upward and downward like rice grains placed in a pot that has been thoroughly boiled. "In the Great Hell" refers to the Avīci Great Hell.
"Divided into portions" means having been set aside and apportioned into shares. "Enclosed" means surrounded. "Covered above with iron plates" means it is covered from above by a sheet of iron.
"Standing pervading a hundred leagues all around" means it stands having pervaded in this way;
such that for one standing at a hundred leagues all around and looking [at it], the eyes almost pop out like twin marbles.
"Having approached an inferior body" means having entered upon an inferior existence. "In clinging" (*upādāne*) refers to the grasping of craving and views.
"In the origin of birth and death" means in that which serves as the cause for both birth and death. "Without clinging" (*anupādā*) means without grasping by means of the four kinds of clinging.

"In the destruction of birth and death" means they are liberated in *nibbāna*, which is designated as the destruction of birth and death. "Extinguished in this very life" (*diṭṭhadhammābhinibbutā*) means in this present world...

In this very existence, they have attained extinction (*nibbāna*) through the extinguishing of all defilements (*kilesa*). "They have transcended all suffering" means they have passed beyond the entire suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
7. Commentary on the *Catumahārājasutta* 37.
In the seventh [verse], "ministers and courtiers" refers to the attendant deities. "Wandering through this world" refers to the eighth day.
It is said that Sakka, the king of the gods, commanded the four Great Kings:
“Sirs, today, on the eighth day, go through the world of men, observe those performing meritorious deeds, and having learned their names and clans, return.
Having gone there, they dispatched their own attendants: “Go, sirs, travel through the world of men and [learn] the names and clans of those who perform meritorious deeds.”
“Write this down on golden plates and bring them here. They did so. Therefore it was said: “Wandering through this world. The phrase beginning with “Are there many?
is stated for the purpose of showing the manner of their investigation; for it is while investigating in this way that they wander.
In that context, “observing the Uposatha” means they undertake the Uposatha factors eight times during the month.
“They keep watch” means they perform the Uposatha observance known as “keeping watch.
While performing it, they do so by way of approaching and following the four Uposatha days within a half-month.
Those who approach the fifth-day Uposatha observe it on the fourth day; those who follow it observe it on the sixth day. Regarding the eighth-day Uposatha...
Going forward on the seventh day, they go back on the ninth; going forward on the fourteenth, they go back on the thirteenth;

and going forward on the fifteenth Uposatha day, they observe the Uposatha on the first of the month (pāṭipada). "Performing meritorious deeds" means they perform various kinds of merit, such as taking refuge, observing the regular precepts, making offerings of flowers, listening to the Dhamma, lighting thousands of lamps, building monasteries, and so forth.
Having thus wandered about, they [record] the names and clans of those who have performed such meritorious deeds.
Having written [the message] on a golden plate and brought it, they give it to the Four Great Kings.
"The sons wander through this world" means that they wander, dispatched by the Four Great Kings in the same manner as before.
"On that day" (tadahū) means on that very day. "On the Uposatha" means on the Uposatha day.

“Bhikkhus, if there are few [of them], then when the ministers and counselors of the Four Great Kings approach various villages, market towns, and royal capitals, the deities dwelling in dependence upon those places, thinking, ‘The ministers of the Great Kings have arrived,’ take gifts and go into their presence.
Having taken the gifts, they ask: ‘Is all well?”’
Having asked about the meritorious conduct of humans in the manner of saying, "Venerable sirs, many people are filial toward their mothers," and being told,
"Yes, venerable sir, such-and-such a person and such-and-such a person in this village are performing meritorious deeds," they record their names and clans and depart elsewhere.
Then, on the fourteenth day, even the sons of the Four Great Kings [do the same].
Taking a golden plate and following that same method, they record names and clans.
On the fifteenth day of the month, the Uposatha, the four Great Kings likewise record their names and clans upon that very golden plate.
According to the dimensions of that golden plate, they write: "At this time humans were few; at this time..."
They know [them] as "many. With reference to this, it was said: "If, monks, humans are few," and so forth.
"Of the Tāvatiṃsa devas" refers to those who have acquired that name starting from the thirty-three sons of the gods first reborn there.
The account of their origin has been explained in detail in the commentary on the Sakkapañha Sutta of the Dīgha Nikāya. "By that" means by that.
Either because of this announcement, or because those who perform meritorious deeds are few in number:

"Alas, sirs, the divine hosts will decline!"—because new sons of the gods do not appear, the divine hosts will diminish, and the delightful city of the gods, ten thousand yojanas in extent, will become empty.
"The asura hosts will swell"—the four states of misery (apāya) will become full.
Because of this, they were displeased, thinking, "We shall not be able to enjoy the festival in the midst of the assembly of gods in the perfect city of the devas.
The same purpose should be understood by this very means regarding the bright fortnight as well.
"Once upon a time, monks, Sakka, the lord of the devas..."—this he says referring to his own time as the king of the devas.
It is said that he spoke either by taking into account the inclination of a single Sakka. "Anunayamāno" means "making [him] understand.
"Tāyaṃ velāyaṃ" means "at that time.
Regarding the phrase "pāṭihāriyapakkhañca," here "pāṭihāriyapakkha" refers to the three months of the rainy season during which the Uposatha is held regularly.
For one unable to do that, there is a fixed *uposatha* for one month between two *pavāraṇās*.
For one unable even to do that, starting from the first *pavāraṇā*, there is a period of half a month known as the "miracle fortnight" (*pāṭihāriyapakkho*).
"Well-endowed with the eight factors" means possessed of the eight qualities as factors. "Whatever being like me" means whatever sentient being might be similar to me.

It is said that even Sakka, having understood the virtue of the Uposatha observance practiced in the manner described, abandoned the prosperity of two celestial realms and observed the Uposatha eight times a month; therefore, he spoke thus. According to another interpretation:
"Whatever being might be like me" means that whatever being, similar to myself, might wish to attain the prosperity reached by me.

The meaning is as follows: for it is possible to attain the state of Sakka through such an observance of the Uposatha; this is the intended sense here. "One who has lived" (*vusitavā*) means one who has completed the residence [in the training].
"One who has done what was to be done" (*katākaraṇīyo*) means one who stands having performed the duties to be accomplished by means of the four paths.

"One who has laid down the burden" (*ohitabhāro*) means one who stands having set down the burden of the aggregates, the burden of the defilements, and the burden of volitional formations. "One who has attained his own goal" (*anuppattasadattho*).
The "highest good" (sadattha) is said to be Arahantship; he has attained that. "One whose fetters of existence are completely destroyed":

because that fetter by which one bound is dragged through various states of existence has been exhausted, he is one whose fetters of existence are completely destroyed. "Liberated through perfect knowledge":
liberated having known [the truth] by means of the cause, the method, and the reason. "It is fitting to speak": it is appropriate to say.
"Any man who is like me"—that is, even one who is like me, having exhausted the taints (*khīṇāsava*), would observe such a Uposatha;
this is what one who knows the virtue of the Uposatha rite would say. Another interpretation is:
"Any being who is like me"—the meaning is that such a being would wish to attain the prosperity attained by me. For it is indeed possible for one of such a kind...
The intention here is that one attains the perfection of one whose taints are exhausted through the Uposatha ritual. The eighth [sutta] has a meaning that is already evident.
9. Commentary on the *Sukhumāla-sutta*: 39.
In the ninth, "delicate" (*sukhumāla*) means free from suffering; "extremely delicate" (*paramasukhumāla*) means extremely free from suffering; "absolutely delicate" (*accantasukhumāla*)...
"Always free from suffering. The Blessed One said this, taking into account his state of being free from suffering starting from the time of his birth in Kapilavatthu;
however, during the period of his spiritual practice, there was no end to the suffering he experienced. "In one place" means in a single lotus pond.
"A blue lotus is planted" means he plants a blue lotus. That [pond] becomes covered with groves of blue lotuses. "Paduma" (the red lotus)...
*Paṇḍarapadumaṃ* means the white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*). *Puṇḍarīka* refers to the red lotus. In this way, the other two [lakes] were also covered with groves of lotuses and white lotuses.
It is said that when the Bodhisatta was seven or eight years old, the king asked his ministers:
"What kind of play do young children delight in? "Water-sports, Your Majesty," they replied. Thereupon, the king assembled the laborers who used spades.
He had lotus ponds constructed. Then Sakka, the king of the gods, perceiving that event through his supernormal knowledge, thought:
"Human enjoyment is not fitting for the Great Being; divine enjoyment is what is fitting. He addressed Vissakamma, saying:
"Go, dear one, and construct lotus ponds in the Great Being’s pleasure grounds. "Of what kind should they be? [he asked].
"O gods! May they be free from the mire of the *kalala* stage; may they be strewn with scattered gems, pearls, and corals;
may they be surrounded by walls made of the seven precious substances; may they be provided with stairs whose handrails are made of gems and whose steps are made of coral, gold, silver, and jewels.
And let there be boats here made of gold, silver, gems, and coral; and in a golden boat, let there be a silver couch."
“Let there be a golden couch for the silver ship, a coral couch for the jewel ship, and a gem-studded couch for the coral ship;
let the water-dripping conduits be made of gold, silver, jewels, and coral, and let them be covered with lotuses of five colors.
“Very well, Your Majesty,” replied Vissakamma, the son of the gods, and having assented to Sakka, he descended during the night.
He had lotus ponds constructed in the very same places where the king had previously had them dug, following that same method.
[The question arises: "Are these not devoid of mud and mire; how then did the lotuses bloom there?
It is said that he had small boats made of gold, silver, gems, and coral placed here and there in those ponds, thinking, "These are filled with mud and mire."
"And let five-colored lotuses bloom here," he resolved. Thus, five-colored lotuses bloomed;
columns of pollen rose up, overspreading the surface of the water and drifting about. Five kinds of swarms of bees wandered about, humming.
Having thus fashioned those [lotuses], Vissakamma returned to the city of the gods. Then—

When the night had turned to dawn, the great multitude, seeing [the lotus ponds], thought, "These must have been laid out by the Great Man," and having gone [to inform him], they reported it to the king.
The king, accompanied by a great retinue, went and saw the lotus ponds;
thinking, "These must have been laid out by the deities through the power of my son's merit," he was filled with joy. From that time forth, the Great Man went to enjoy himself in the water.
"Only for my own benefit": here, "only" (*yāvadeva*) is a term that defines the limit of purpose;
the meaning is: "only for my own sake, there is no other reason here. "But I did not do it for him" means: "but I did not do it for his sake.
"Kāsika sandalwood" means coarse sandalwood. "But that head-wrap of mine was from Kāsī, monks," [he said]. Monks...
"My turban is also of Kāsī cloth. Here, *su* and *iti* are merely particles; *me* is the genitive case.
This shows that even my turban is indeed soft. "Kāsī jackets" refers to both the outer jacket worn as a cloak and the soft inner jacket.
"A white parasol is held over [me]" means that either a human white parasol or a divine white parasol is indeed held above.
"May cold not touch him" means: "May this Bodhisatta not be touched by cold, heat, or any other such condition.

There were three palaces; it is said that when the Bodhisatta had reached the age of sixteen years, King Suddhodana, thinking, "I shall have palaces built for my son to dwell in," summoned carpenters and, under an auspicious constellation and moment, [ordered them to begin].
Having performed the preparatory work for nine months, he had three palaces built; it is with reference to these that this was said. Regarding the terms "hemantika" and so forth:
that which is suitable for dwelling comfortably during the winter is "hemantika. The same method applies to the others as well.
Here, however, is the etymological meaning: dwelling in winter is "hemanta"; that which is fit for winter is "hemantika. The same method applies to the others as well.
There, the winter palace had nine stories, and its floors were low for the purpose of retaining heat.
There, the doors and windows had well-fitted panels and were without lattices.
Furthermore, those performing the decorative paintings there depicted masses of blazing fire in various places. As for the floor-covering there—
There were also canopies made of wool, as well as coverings and wraps for the ceiling and for wrapping the body.
The windows were open by day and closed at night in order to ward off the heat.
However, the summer palace had five stories; here, the floors were high and spacious in order to ward off the cold.

The doors and windows were not too tightly closed, being provided with lattices and screens. For the decorative paintings, they depicted nothing but blue lotuses (*utpala*), red lotuses (*paduma*), and white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*).
The floor-coverings there were made of fine linen (*dukūla*), as were the canopies, undergarments, outer robes, and head-wraps.
Furthermore, having placed nine water-jars near the windows and filled them with water, they covered them with blue lotuses and other flowers.
In various places they created water-channels from which streams of water gushed forth as if the devas were raining.
Inside the palace, they placed troughs filled with mud here and there and planted five-colored lotuses.
On the roof of the palace, having bound a dried antelope skin and turned the mechanism, [they caused it to reach] as far as the surface of the thatched roof.
Having placed them upon the stone, they let them fall; as they rolled across its surface, the sound was like the thundering of clouds.
Here, however, the doors and windows were closed during the day and opened at night.
It was seven stories high for the rainy season. Furthermore, the floors here were not too high, so that one could grasp both seasons.
They did not make them too low. Some doors and windows were well-fitted, while others had openings.
There, the decorative paintings in some places were executed in the form of blazing masses of fire, and in others, in the form of still waters.
As for the floor coverings and such, they were made of both woolen blankets (*kambala*) and fine silk (*dukūla*). Some doors and windows...
One palace was open at night and closed by day; some were open by day and closed at night.
All three palaces were equal in height, though there was a difference in their floor levels.
When the palaces were thus completed, the king thought: "My son has reached maturity; I shall raise the royal parasol over him."
“I shall see the glory of sovereignty. He sent a message to the Sakyans: “My son has reached maturity;
I shall establish him in the kingdom. All those who have reached maturity in their respective homes, let your daughters send them to this house.
Having heard the message, they thought: “The prince is merely fit for looking upon, endowed with beauty, but he knows no craft whatsoever.”
"He will not be able to support a wife; we shall not give our daughters [in marriage]," they said.
When the king heard this report, he went to his son and informed him of it. The Bodhisatta asked, "Father, what craft should I demonstrate?
"It is fitting to string the bow of a thousand-fold strength, father," he replied. "Then have it brought here," the king said. The king—
Having had it brought, he gave it [to him]. He had a thousand men string the bow and a thousand men unstring it.
The Great Man, having had the bow brought, while sitting cross-legged, wound the bowstring around his big toe;
pulling with that very big toe, he strung the bow, took the handle with his left hand, and pulled the string with his right hand.
The bowstring snapped. The entire city was thrown into a state of agitation. When they asked, "What is that sound?
they replied, "It is the thundering of the rain god. Then others said, "You do not know; it is not the thundering of the rain god.
This is the sound of the bowstring as Prince Aṅgīrasa, having strung his thousand-fold-strength bow, strikes it. The Śākyas...
With that much alone, they became intent on their task.
The Great Man asked, "What else should be done? "It is fitting to pierce through with an arrow an iron plate eight finger-breadths thick," they replied.
Having pierced that, he asked, "What else should be done? "An iron plate four finger-breadths thick."
"It is permissible to pierce through the seat-board. Having pierced it, he asked, "What else is permissible to do?
"It is permissible to pierce through a fig-wood board one span thick. Having pierced that, [he asked], "What else is permissible to do?
"It is permissible to pierce through a hundred boards fastened to a mechanical device."
Having pierced through that, he asked, "What else should be done? [They replied,] "It is necessary to pierce through the sixty-layered hide of a dried-up buffalo.
Having pierced through that as well, he asked, "What else should be done? Then they pointed out the sand-carts and so forth.
The Great Being, having pierced through both the sand-cart and the straw-cart, [continued].
He sent a shaft measuring one ox-length into the water, and eight ox-lengths onto dry land.
Then they said, "Now it is time to shoot a hair with the aim of a vātingaṇa fruit. "In that case, have it tied," he said.
"Let it be tied at intervals, dear father. "Let them go forward and tie it at intervals of a gavuta. "Let them go forward; [tie it] at half a yojana."
"Let them bind [the hair]! "Let them go forward and bind it at the distance of one *yojana*! "Have it bound, dear father," he said;

and having had the hair bound at the distance of a *yojana* by means of a *vātingaṇa* (a type of plant), he shot an arrow while it was night, in the darkness, and when the quarters were covered by a mass of clouds.
That arrow went and, having split the hair at the distance of a *yojana*, entered the earth. And not only this much—
On that day, however, the Great Being demonstrated every craft currently practiced in the world.
The Śākya kings sent their respective daughters after having adorned them; there were forty thousand dancing women.
In the three palaces, the Great Man enjoyed great prosperity, as if he were a god sporting [there].
"Devoid of men" means without men. Here, not only were the musical instruments devoid of men, but all the places were likewise devoid of men.
Even the gatekeepers were women, and even those who performed services such as bathing were women. It is said that the king thought:
"If I see a man while experiencing such an abundance of sovereignty and pleasure, suspicion will arise."
“Let her not be for my son,” thinking thus, he appointed her alone to all duties. “While enjoying himself” means while delighting.
“I will not descend from the upper palace” means I do not go down from the palace.
Thus, for four months, no other man with hair-knots (a layman) was able to see me. “In such a manner” means by whatever method. “Of the slaves, laborers, and servants.”
[It refers to] those living by depending on the daily food and wages provided for slaves and laborers.
"Kanājaka" means rice mixed with broken grains. "Bilaṅgadutiya" means accompanied by sour gruel.
"Possessed of such psychic power" means endowed with such a kind of merit-based psychic power (*puññiddhi*). And "by one so delicately nurtured" [means...].
And by such a state of being free from suffering—*sokhumālena* is also a reading. Thus, in this manner, the Tathāgata described his own glorious attainment through these points.
And in describing it, he did not speak for the sake of becoming elated;
rather, he spoke specifically to characterize his heedfulness, thinking: "Even while established in such an attainment, he remained vigilant and did not fall into negligence."
He spoke for the purpose of illumination. For that very reason, he said, "The uninstructed worldling," and so forth. Therein, *paraṃ* means another person. *Jiṇṇaṃ* means aged by old age.
*Aṭṭīyati* means he is distressed (*aṭṭo*), being oppressed. *Harāyati* means he feels shame; he becomes modest and feels abashed.
*Jigucchati* means that upon seeing [the state], like something impure, he gives rise to disgust. *Attānaṃ yeva atisitvā* means even having surpassed himself, though he too is subject to aging...
The meaning is that, having surpassed one’s own equal, one feels distressed and ashamed. "Subject to aging" means having the nature of aging.
"Not transcending aging" means not having gone beyond aging; I am subject to aging within the realm of aging. "Reflecting thus" means for one who is contemplating in this way.
"The intoxication of youth" is the pride and intoxication arising in dependence upon youth. "It was entirely abandoned" means...
It has been abandoned in every way. It is shown as if it were abandoned by the Path, but it should be understood that this was not abandoned by the Path;

rather, it is said to have been abandoned through reflective contemplation (*paṭisaṅkhāna*). For when the deities showed the Bodhisatta one who had reached old age, from that moment until his attainment of Arahantship, no conceit of youth ever arose in the Great Being in the interim. This applies to the other two phrases as well.
The same method applies here. In this context, however, "the intoxication of health" (*ārogyamada*) is the pride and intoxication arising based on health, thinking, "I am free from illness.
"The intoxication of life" (*jīvitamada*) is the pride and intoxication arising based on that [health], thinking, "I shall live long.

"Having renounced the training" (*sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya*) means having rejected the training. "He returns to the lower state" (*hīnāyāvattati*) means he returns to the inferior and base state of a householder.

"According to their nature" (*yathādhamma*) means according to their true essence (*yathāsabhāva*), such as that of disease and so forth. "As they actually are" (*tathāsanta*) means being exactly as they are;
the sense is that they remain precisely as the unerring nature of disease and so on. "Disgusted" means they feel disgust toward another person.
"For me, who dwells thus" means for me, who dwells in this manner of dwelling characterized by disgust, such a state of disgust would not be fitting, nor would it be appropriate.
"Thus dwelling"—meaning, thus dwelling while feeling disgust for others, or dwelling in this manner by means of this abiding in reflective discernment.
"Having known the Dhamma that is without substrate"—having known the Dhamma of Nibbāna, which is devoid of all substrates.
"I have overcome all intoxications"—I have overcome and transcended all three types of intoxication. "Seeing safety in renunciation."
"Having seen the state of security in Nibbāna. There is also a reading, "Seeing renunciation as secure," which means having seen Nibbāna as secure.
"In that, there arose in me an effort": for me, who was beholding that Nibbāna known as renunciation, an effort arose;
the meaning is that exertion occurred. "I am not capable now of indulging in sensual pleasures."
"Now I am incapable of indulging in either of the two kinds of sensual pleasure.
'I shall not turn back' means that I shall not retreat from my renunciation nor from omniscience; I shall be one who does not turn back.

'Devoted to the holy life' (brahmacariyaparāyaṇa) means that I have become one whose goal is the holy life of the Path. Thus, with these verses, [he declared] his own [resolve] upon the seat of Great Enlightenment.
He spoke on the energy that leads to arrival.
10. Commentary on the Ādhipateyya Sutta:
In the tenth [sutta], "dominants" (*ādhipateyya*) means those produced from being the primary cause. Regarding "having oneself as the dominant," etc., "self" (*atta*)...

That which is produced by making the self the foremost is "having the self as its overlord" (*attādhipateyya*). That which is produced by making the world the foremost is "having the world as its overlord" (*lokādhipateyya*).
That which is produced by making the ninefold supramundane Dhamma the foremost is "having the Dhamma as its overlord" (*dhammādhipateyya*).
"Thus-becoming-and-non-becoming" refers to "thus-becoming"; that is, thus [in the future], not for the sake of this or that state of becoming (*sampattibhava*).
*Hetu*: "Immersed" (*otiṇṇa*) means entered. For one into whom birth has entered is said to be "immersed in birth.
The same principle applies to aging and the rest. "Of the entire mass of suffering" (*kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa*) means of the whole heap of suffering within the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).

"The making of an end would be discerned" (*antakiriyā paññāyetha*) means that the making of an end—the effecting of a limit or a boundary—would be discerned. "Having abandoned" (*ohāya*) means having relinquished.
*Pāpiṭṭhatara* means more inferior or base. *Āraddha* means exerted and fulfilled; precisely because it is exerted, it is not slack.
*Upaṭṭhitā* means established by way of the four foundations of mindfulness; precisely because it is established, it is not muddled.

"The body is tranquil" refers to both the mental body (nāmakāya) and the physical body (karajakāya) being tranquil and with their agitation stilled. Precisely because it is tranquil, it is not agitated.
"Concentrated mind" means the mind is properly placed and well-established upon the object. Because it is properly established, it is one-pointed.
"Making it predominant" means making it the chief. "He maintains himself pure" means he maintains himself by making him stainless;
he looks after and protects him—this is the meaning. And this [practice] continues up to the path of arahantship.

One is said to maintain a self that is pure only in a figurative sense (*pariyāyena*); however, only one who has attained the fruit maintains a self that is pure in the literal sense (*nippariyāyena*).
The terms "well-expounded" (*svākkhāto*) and so forth have been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"Dwelling knowing and seeing": they dwell knowing and seeing that Dhamma. "These, monks, are the three authorities": up to this point, the three [authorities] are established.
The sovereignties have been explained as being a mixture of mundane and supramundane.
"Pakubvato" means of one who is acting. "Your own self knows you, O man, whether it be truth or falsehood":
whatever you do—whether it be according to its true nature or not according to its true nature—your own self alone knows that.
And for this reason it should be understood: "In this world, there is no place where one who commits an evil deed can remain concealed.
*Kalyāṇa* means beautiful or excellent. *Atimaññasi* means you think beyond [the bounds of propriety].
*Attānaṃ parigūhasi* means you strive to conceal yourself so that even your own self does not know [your deeds]. *Attādhipateyyo* means having oneself as the chief, or having oneself as the foremost.
"Lokādhipo" means the foremost in the world. "Nipako" means possessed of wisdom (*paññavā*). "Jhāyī" means one who meditates (*jhāyanto*). "Dhammādhipo" means the foremost in the Dhamma.
"Saccaparakkamo" means one of firm exertion, one of true exertion. "Pasayha māraṃ" means having overcome Māra.
"Abhibhuyya antakaṃ" is a synonym for that very same thing. And "yo ca phusi jātikkhayaṃ padhānavā" refers to one who has touched the destruction of birth through striving.
He who, meditative and resolute, having overcome Māra, touched the destruction of birth—Arahatta—is "of such a kind" (*tādiso*);
that is, he is of such a nature, established in such a state. "Knower of the worlds" (*lokavidū*) means one who stands having made the three worlds known and manifest.

"Sumedha" means one of excellent wisdom. "The Sage who is not 'made of that' regarding all phenomena" (*atammayo muni*) refers to one who, regarding all phenomena of the three planes, is free from the state of being "made of that" (*tammayatā*), which is synonymous with craving.
It is said that because of this absence of "mine-ness," the sage whose taints are exhausted never declines nor falls away, anywhere or at any time.
The Fourth Chapter, the Devadūta-vagga.
5. The Cūḷa-vagga.
1. Commentary on the *Sammukhībhāva-sutta* 41.
In the first [sutta] of the fifth [chapter], *sammukhībhāvā* means "by way of presence," that is, by way of existing. *Pasavati* means "obtains.
Regarding *saddhāya sammukhībhāvā*: for if faith (*saddhā*) were not present, the object to be given (*deyyadhamma*) would not...
If there were no individuals reckoned as worthy of offerings to serve as recipients, how could one perform meritorious deeds?
However, since it is possible to do so through their presence, he said, "through the presence of faith," and so forth.
In this context, two things are easy to find—the objects to be given and those worthy of offerings—but faith is difficult to find.
For the faith of an ordinary person is unstable and varies from one occasion to another;
for this very reason, even a chief disciple such as Mahāmoggallāna, being unable to act as a guarantor, said:
"Friend, I can be a guarantor for two things for you—your wealth and your life—but as for your faith, you alone must be the guarantor."
2. Commentary on the *Tiṭṭhāna Sutta* 42.
In the second [verse], "with the stain of stinginess gone" means with the stain of avarice removed. "Liberally giving" means one who has relinquished their possessions.
"With hands cleansed" means with washed hands; for one who lacks faith remains with stained hands even if they wash them a hundred times.

He is [so called] because he delights in giving; for one who delights in giving, even if his hands are soiled, they are as if washed. "Delighting in relinquishment" means delighting in giving, which is synonymous with relinquishment.
"Devoted to begging" means fit for begging, or alternatively, one who has a connection (*yoga*) with beggars is "devoted to begging.
"Delighting in giving and sharing" means that while giving a gift and making a distribution, one is said to be "delighting in giving and sharing."
"One who desires to see one possessed of virtue" means that, desiring to see one perfected in virtue, one would travel ten, twenty, thirty, or even a hundred *yojanas*,
like the brāhmaṇa of Pāṭaliputta and like King Saddhātissa the Great.
It is said that two brāhmaṇas, sitting in a hall at the city gate of Pāṭaliputta, [heard] of the Elder Mahānāga, a resident of the Kāḷavalli pavilion...
Having heard the account of his virtues, both men thought, "It is fitting for us to see that bhikkhu," and set out.

One of them died along the way. The other, having reached the shore of the ocean, disembarked at the port of Mahātittha by boat, arrived at Anurādhapura, and asked, "Where is the Kāḷavallimaṇḍapa? [The reply was: "In the Rohaṇa province. He then proceeded by stages...
Having reached the elder’s dwelling place, he took up residence in the main house in the village of Cūḷanagaragāma;
having prepared food for the elder, he rose early in the morning, inquired after the elder’s dwelling place, and went there.
Standing at the edge of the crowd, he saw the elder approaching from afar; standing right there for a moment, he paid homage and then approached him again.
Grasping firmly at his ankles and paying homage, he said, "Venerable sir, you are very tall.
But the Elder was neither too tall nor too short, being of perfectly proportioned stature; therefore, the boy spoke to him again:
"You are not too tall, but your virtues have gone over the crest of the deep-blue ocean and have overspread the entire surface of Jambudīpa."
"I too, sitting at the gate of the city of Pāṭaliputta, heard the talk concerning your virtues.
Having given the elder his alms-food and having prepared his own triple robe, he went forth in the presence of the elder;
by abiding in his instruction, after only a few days, he attained Arahantship.
King Saddhātissa also asked, “Venerable sirs, please point out to me one noble monk worthy of my veneration.
The monks replied, “The Elder Kuṭṭatissa, who dwells at Maṅgala. The king, accompanied by a great retinue, traveled five yojanas along the road.
The elder asked the Saṅgha of monks, “Friends, what is that noise? “It is the king, Venerable sir, coming for you,” they said.
“I have come to see him. The Elder thought, “What business do I have with the royal palace in my old age?
So he lay down on his bed in the daytime quarters and remained there drawing figures on the ground. When the king asked, “Where is the Elder?
and was told, “In the daytime quarters,” he went there and saw the Elder drawing figures on the ground.

Seeing him, [the king] thought, "One who has destroyed the taints (khīṇāsava) has no remorse regarding his hands; this man is not one who has destroyed the taints," and so he did not pay homage but turned back.
The community of monks said to the Elder, "Venerable sir, why did you cause such regret in the king, who was so full of faith and confidence?
[The Elder replied,] "Friends, protecting the king's confidence is not your responsibility; it is the responsibility of an elder of long standing."
Having said, "The burden," later on, while passing away into the Nibbāna-element without residue, he addressed the Saṅgha of bhikkhus:
"Spread another couch in my gabled chamber. When it had been spread, the Elder thought:
"May this gabled chamber, without coming to rest in the interim, land upon the ground at the very moment the King sees it."
Having made his resolve, he attained final Nibbāna. The gabled chamber traveled through the air along a path five *yojanas* long.

Along that five-*yojana* path, the trees were capable of supporting the banner, and they remained as if their banners were already raised. All the paths and groves stood facing toward the gabled chamber.
They sent a message to the king, saying: "The Elder has attained final Nibbāna; the gabled chamber is coming through the air. The king—
He did not believe it. Having traveled through the air to the Kūṭāgāra, he circumambulated the Thūpārāma and went to the site of the Silācetiya.
The Cetiya, together with its base, rose up and stood upon the roof of the Kūṭāgāra, and thousands of shouts of "Sādhu!
arose. At that moment, the Elder Mahābyaggha was seated in the seventh upper chamber of the Lohapāsāda.
While the monks were performing a formal disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*), he heard that sound and asked, "What is this sound?
"Venerable sir, the Elder Kuṭṭatissa of Maṅgalavāsi has attained final Nibbāna; his gabled chamber has come through the air across a path of five *yojanas*, and that is the sound of his applause.
"Friends, by relying on those possessed of merit, we shall receive honor," [he said to] his pupils.
Having asked for forgiveness, he returned through the air, entered that gabled chamber, sat upon the second couch, and attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue.
The king, taking perfumes, flowers, and powders, went there and saw the gabled chamber standing in the sky;
he made offerings to the chamber. At that moment, the gabled chamber descended and settled upon the earth. The king—
Having performed the funeral rites for the body with great honor and having taken the relics, he erected a stupa.
Such is the longing people have to see those possessed of virtue.
"Desiring to hear the true Dhamma" means that one wishes to hear the true Dhamma proclaimed by the Tathāgata, such as from the Elder Piṇḍapātika and others.
It is said that thirty bhikkhus entered the rains retreat in the courtyard of the Gaṅgāvana-vālika monastery.

Every half-month on the Uposatha day, they would discourse upon the four requisites, contentment, the delight in meditation, and the Great Noble Lineage (mahāariyavaṃsa). One elder who was an alms-food eater (piṇḍapātika) arrived from the rear and sat down in a concealed spot.
Then, a certain bull, with its snout... [the text continues with the bull attempting to take a piece of meat from the elder's leg].
As if seizing it, it bit him. The Elder, looking down and seeing the snake, thought, "Today I shall not cause an obstacle to the hearing of the Dhamma.
He took the snake, placed it in his bag, tied the mouth of the bag, set it aside at a short distance, and sat down listening to the Dhamma. At dawn, the poison was neutralized for the Elder.

The attainment of the three fruits, the descent of the poison into the earth at the very spot where it was applied, and the conclusion of the elder monk’s discourse on the Dhamma all occurred at one and the same moment.
Then the elder said, "Friend, I have caught one thief," and releasing the snake from his bag, he let it go. When the monks saw this, they said:
“At what time were you bitten, venerable sir? they asked. “Yesterday, at the time of evening, friends.
“Why, venerable sir, did you perform such a grave deed? “Friends, had I said that I was bitten by Dīghajāti, I would not have obtained this much benefit.
This, first of all, is the story of the Elder Piṇḍapātika.
In Dīghavāpi as well, a young monk residing at the Tissamahāvihāra in Tissamahāgāma heard that the Elder Mahājātaka-bhāṇaka would recite the Mahāvessantara Jātaka in a thousand verses.
Upon hearing this, he departed from there and arrived after traveling nine yojanas in a single day.
At that very moment, the Elder began his discourse on the Dhamma. Because the young monk had become physically exhausted from the long journey, he—
He established the concluding verse together with the *Paṭṭhāna-gāthā*.
Then, as the Elder was rising to depart after saying, "This is what I have said," he stood weeping, thinking, "My mission to come here has become fruitless.
A certain man, having heard this conversation, went and reported it to the Elder: "Venerable sir, regarding your discourse on the Dhamma..."
"A young bhikkhu named Sossāmi has come from the Tissa Mahāvihāra;
he stands weeping, thinking, 'My journey here has become fruitless because of my physical exhaustion. Go and persuade him, saying, 'We shall speak further tomorrow.
On the following day, having heard the Elder’s discourse on the Dhamma, he attained the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala).

Furthermore, another woman living in Ullakolikaṇṇi, while nursing her young son, heard that the Elder Mahā-Abhaya, a reciter of the Dīgha Nikāya, was preaching on the practice of the Noble Lineage (ariyavaṃsa).
Having traveled five yojanas, she entered the monastery at the very moment the Elder Divākathika was seated; she laid her son down on the ground and [approached] the Elder Divākathika.

She listened to the Dhamma while standing. When the Elder Sarabhāṇaka rose, the Elder Mahā-Abhaya, a reciter of the Dīgha Nikāya, began the discourse on the Great Noble Lineage concerning contentment with the four requisites and delight in meditation. While she was still standing, she grasped the teaching.
After the Elder had explained only the three requisites, he made a gesture to rise. That laywoman said: "Venerable sir, the 'Noble Lineage'..."

“I shall speak,” he thought; thus, having eaten wholesome food and drunk sweet beverages, and having prepared medicine with *yaṭṭhimadhuka* oil and other ingredients, he rose up at the very spot suitable for speaking.

The Elder said, “Excellent, sister,” and established her in the delight of higher cultivation (*bhāvanārāma*). And at the rising of the dawn, the Elder [recited] the words, “This he said. The laywoman—
And the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry occurred at that very same moment.
Furthermore, another woman living in Kaḷampara, taking her son on her hip, went to Cittala Mountain thinking, "I shall hear the Dhamma.
Having laid the boy down leaning against a tree, she herself listened to the Dhamma while remaining standing.
Immediately after the first watch of the night had passed, a certain long-tusked snake bit the child who was lying near her while she was looking on, and then departed. She thought:
"If I say, 'My son has been bitten by a snake,' it will be an obstacle to the Dhamma. For many times already have I wandered through this cycle of existence."
She was the daughter of Vaṭṭanī and thought, “I shall practice only the Dhamma. Thus, throughout the three watches of the night, she remained standing, exerting herself in the Dhamma.
Once established in the fruit of stream-entry, as the dawn rose, she neutralized her son’s poison through an act of truth (*saccakiriya*).
Taking her son with her, she departed. Such individuals are truly those who desire to hear the Dhamma.
3. Commentary on the *Atthavasa Sutta* 43.
Regarding the third [sutta], "seeing three purposes, monks": this means seeing three benefits or three reasons.

"It is indeed sufficient" (*alam eva*) means it is indeed appropriate. "One who teaches the Dhamma" refers to that person who proclaims the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. "Experiencing the benefit" (*atthapaṭisaṃvedī*)...
He experiences the commentary through knowledge. "Experiencing the Dhamma" means experiencing the canonical Dhamma (pāḷidhamma).
4. Commentary on the Discourse on the Occurrence of Discussion (Kathāpavatti-sutta):
44. "By four grounds" means by four reasons. "Occurring" means unimpeded and leading to liberation (niyyānika).
5. Commentary on the Paṇḍita Sutta 45.
In the fifth [verse], "proclaimed by the wise" means proclaimed, spoken, and praised by the wise.

"Proclaimed by true persons" means proclaimed, spoken, and praised by true persons, that is, great beings (*mahāpuruṣa*). "Non-violence" refers to both compassion (*karuṇā*) and the preliminary stage to compassion.
*Saṃyama* means restraint through virtue (*sīla*). *Dama* means restraint of the sense faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*), or the taming of oneself by way of the Uposatha;
patience, which was spoken of in the *Puṇṇovāda*, and wisdom, as spoken of in the case of Āḷavaka, are also applicable here in this sutta.
*Upaṭṭhāna* toward mother and father means protecting, guarding, and attending to them. *Santāna* elsewhere...
The Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and noble disciples (ariyasāvakas) are called "the good" (santa); however, in this context, those who attend upon their mothers and fathers are intended.

Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as follows: "of the good" (santānaṃ) in the sense of being supreme, and "of those living the holy life" (brahmacārīnaṃ) in the sense of excellent conduct.
"This service to mother and father is proclaimed by the good"—thus is the meaning to be seen here. "These are the stations of the good" (santānaṃ) means of the supreme persons.

These are the bases and the reasons. "The noble one endowed with vision" should be understood here as being both noble and endowed with vision by virtue of these very three bases; it does not refer to the Buddhas and others, nor to stream-enterers.
Alternatively, "these are the bases for the good" means that serving the mother and serving the father—these are the bases for the virtuous, the supreme persons.
"Causes": thus, the meaning of this verse should be understood by way of one who attends upon his mother and father.

For it is precisely such a person who attends upon his mother and father who is described here as "the noble one, possessed of vision. "He resorts to the auspicious world" means that he goes to the secure world of the devas.
6. Commentary on the Sīlavanta Sutta (The Discourse on the Virtuous)
46. Regarding the sixth [section], "by three grounds" means by three causes.

In the phrases beginning with "by body," monks generate merit by body when they go out to meet incoming monks upon seeing them, follow after departing monks, sweep and smear the assembly hall, arrange seats, and provide drinking water.
Seeing the community of bhikkhus wandering for alms, those who generate merit by means of speech say such things as: “Give rice gruel! Give solid food! Give ghee, fresh butter, and so forth!
Worship with perfumes, flowers, and the like! Observe the Uposatha! Listen to the Dhamma! Pay homage to the cetiya!
Seeing the bhikkhus wandering for alms, they say, “May they receive [offerings]!”
"Thinking with the mind, they produce merit. "Produce" means they acquire. Here, however, merit is spoken of as a mixture of both mundane and supramundane.
7. Commentary on the Discourse on the Characteristics of the Conditioned (Saṅkhatalakkhaṇasutta)

47. Regarding "of the conditioned" (*saṅkhata*) in the seventh [verse]: it refers to that which has been produced by the coming together of conditions. "Characteristics of the conditioned" (*saṅkhatalakkhaṇa*) are the signs (*nimitta*) that serve as the causes for perceiving something as "conditioned.
"Arising" (*uppāda*) is birth (*jāti*). "Passing away" (*vaya*) is dissolution (*bhedo*). "Alteration of what is present" (*ṭhitassa aññathattaṃ*) is called aging (*jarā*).

In this context, "the conditioned" refers to phenomena belonging to the three planes of existence (*tebhūmaka-dhammā*). However, the Path and its Fruits (*magga-phala*) are not included because they do not fall within the scope of such contemplation (*asammasanūpaga*).

These are not discussed here. Arising and so forth are called the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṅkhatalakkhaṇa*). Among them, arising occurs at the moment of arising, decay at the moment of duration, and passing away at the moment of dissolution. The characteristic itself is not conditioned, nor is the conditioned the characteristic;
rather, the conditioned is delimited by the characteristic. Just as spears, spikes, and so forth are the characteristics for identifying elephants, horses, cows, buffaloes, and the like.
It is not the elephants and so forth themselves, nor are the elephants and so forth merely the characteristics;

rather, it is by means of the characteristics that they are known as "the elephant of so-and-so," "the horse of so-and-so," "so-and-so's elephant," or "so-and-so's horse. This should be understood in the same way.
8. Commentary on the Discourse on the Characteristics of the Unconditioned.
48. Regarding the eighth [section], "of the unconditioned" (*asaṅkhata*) means that which is not made by coming together through conditions.

"Characteristics of the unconditioned" (*asaṅkhatalakkhaṇāni*) refers to the signs (*nimittāni*) that serve as the grounds for the recognition: "This is the unconditioned. By the phrases beginning with "arising is not discerned," the absence of arising, aging, and dissolution is stated. For it is through the absence of arising and the other [characteristics] that it is discerned as "unconditioned."
9. Commentary on the Pabbatarāja Sutta 49.

In the ninth [verse], "great sāl trees" (*mahāsālā*) refers to large trees. "Head of the clan" (*kulapati*) means the eldest member of the family. "Rock" (*sela*) means made of stone. "In the forest" (*araññasmiṃ*) means in a place devoid of villages.
"Brahmā" means great. "In the woods" (*vane*) means in the wilderness (*aṭavī*). "Forest-lords" (*vanappati*) means the preeminent trees of the forest. Here...
"Having practiced the Dhamma, the path leading to a happy destination": having practiced the Dhamma known as the path leading to a happy destination.
10. Commentary on the *Ātappakaraṇīya-sutta* 50.
In the tenth [verse], "ardor should be made" means it is fitting to exert energy. "For the sake of non-arising" means for the purpose of non-arising.
The meaning is: "It must be done for this reason, namely, 'I shall bring about non-arising. The same method applies to what follows as well.
"Of bodily" means arising from the body. "Pains" means painful things.
"Intense" means thick, or intense in the sense of burning. "Harsh" means rough. "Bitter" means sharp. "Unpleasant" means not sweet.
"Unpleasant things" (*amanāpānaṃ*) means those that are incapable of increasing one's mental well-being. "Life-taking" (*pāṇaharānaṃ*) means those that take away life.
"For the sake of endurance" (*adhivāsanāya*) means for the purpose of enduring, bearing, and forbearing.
Having thus commanded and issued this instruction regarding these points, the Teacher now, in order to exhort them, said: "But when, monks... and so forth.

In this context, "when" (*yata*) means at which time. "Ardent" (*ātāpī*) means possessing energy. "Circumspect" (*nipaka*) means possessed of wisdom. "Mindful" (*sata*) means endowed with mindfulness.
"For the making of an end to suffering" (*dukkhassa antakiriyāya*) means for the act of delimiting and terminating the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
Furthermore, these three qualities—ardor and so forth—are explained as being a mixture of both mundane and supramundane.
11. Commentary on the Mahācorasutta 51.
In the eleventh [sutta], "a great thief" (*mahācoro*) means a powerful thief. "A breach" (*sandhiṃ*) means a breach in a house. "Plunder" (*nillopaṃ*) means a great looting.
"Robbing a single house" (*ekāgārikaṃ*) means plundering after surrounding a single dwelling. "He stands by the wayside" (*paripanthepi tiṭṭhati*) refers to the act of waylaying travelers.
He does so. "A river-difficulty" (*nadīvidugga*) is a difficult place among rivers, such as an island in the middle where one can hide together with two or three thousand infantrymen.
"A mountain-unevenness" (*pabbatavisaṃ*) is a rugged place among mountains, such as a mountain cleft where one can hide together with seven or eight thousand infantrymen.
"Thicket of grass" (*tiṇagahana*) means a place two or three *yojanas* in extent that is overgrown and covered with grass.

"Grove" (*rodha*) means a dense, great forest thicket where the branches are intermingled and joined together. "Having cleared up, they will explain the meaning" (*pariyodhāya atthaṃ bhaṇissantīti*) means that having cleared it up and included the respective reasons, they will speak the meaning.
"To them" (*tyāssa*) means "to those [who have explained] of him. "Having cleared up the meaning" (*pariyodhāya atthaṃ*).

“They speak”: even when someone has begun to say something about another, they speak for the sake of the matter, concealing even a great fault by adding various reasons such as, “Do not speak thus; we know this from our family lineage;
he will not do such a thing. Alternatively, *pariyodhāya* also means “having concealed. For they [conceal] even that...
They speak of the meaning while concealing their fault. "Wounded and mangled" means wounded by the digging out of virtues and mangled by the striking down of virtues.
"By uneven bodily action" means by action performed through the door of the body that is "uneven" in the sense of being unsteady or deviating from the right path.
The same method applies to verbal and mental actions as well. "Of those who hold to extremes" refers to the view that stands by grasping at one extreme or the other, which has ten bases.
The remainder is clear in meaning throughout.
The Fifth Minor Chapter is finished. The First Fifty is completed.
2. The Second Fifty (6) 1.
The Chapter on Brahmins 1.
Commentary on the First Discourse on Two Brahmins (*Paṭhamadvebrāhmaṇasutta-vaṇṇanā*)
52. In the first [discourse] of the Brāhmaṇa-vagga: "Worn out" (*jiṇṇā*) means worn out by old age. "Aged" (*vuddhā*) means advanced in years. "Elderly" (*mahallakā*) means advanced in birth.
