*Kho* is a particle used for emphasis or merely to fill out the meter. Therein, in the sense of emphasis, [it means] "they indeed heard."
The meaning should be understood as follows: "There was no obstacle whatsoever to their hearing. The phrase [“samaṇo khalu... serves merely to fill out the meter and provide elegance of expression.
Now, in order to reveal the matter they heard, the passage beginning with “samaṇo khalu, bho, Gotamo” was spoken.
Therein, he is to be known as a *samaṇa* because he has stilled (*samita*) evil. *Khalu* is a particle used in the sense of tradition. *Bho* is [a term of address] among themselves.
"Ālapanamattaṃ" means merely a form of address. "Gotama" is an indication of the Blessed One’s clan;
therefore, in the phrase "the ascetic Gotama, sir," the meaning should be understood as: "The ascetic, sir, belongs to the Gotama clan.

"Sakyaputta" (Son of the Sakyas), however, is an indication of the Blessed One’s noble birth. "One who has gone forth from the Sakya clan" is an indication of his state of having gone forth out of faith.
It is said that he went forth out of faith, having abandoned that very family which was not overcome by any misfortune and was indeed undecayed.
As for the phrase "Taṃ kho pana" (But as for him), it is used in the sense of describing one who has become such;
the meaning is "of that venerable Gotama. "Kalyāṇo" means endowed with excellent qualities; it is said to mean "supreme."
“Kittisaddo” means fame itself, or the sound of praise. “Abbhuggato” means risen up, having overspread the world together with its devas.
How so? “Itipi so bhagavā... pe... buddho bhagavā. Herein, this is the connection between the words:
“That Blessed One is indeed an Arahant, he is indeed a Fully Enlightened One... pe... he is indeed the Blessed One. And by this and by that [he is so called].
It is said "by way of reason.

Having set forth the matrix (mātikā) in such a manner as: "In this regard, that Blessed One is to be understood as 'Arahant' for these reasons: because of being remote (āraka), because of having slain enemies (arī) and spokes (ara), because of being worthy of requisites (paccaya) and so forth, and because of the absence of secrecy (raha) in doing evil," [the author] explains all of them...
These terms have been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga* in the section on the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*); therefore, their detailed exposition should be taken from there.
"He [knows] this world" (*so imaṃ lokaṃ*): the venerable Gotama knows this world; he now points out what is to be said.
"Together with the devas" (*sadevakaṃ*): together with the devas, thus *sadevakaṃ*. Likewise, together with Māra, thus *samārakaṃ*. Together with Brahmā, thus *sabrahmakaṃ*. Together with...
Together with recluses and brahmins, it is *sasamaṇabrāhmaṇi*. It is called *pajā* because it has been born; that is the "generation" (*paja*). Together with gods and humans, it is *sadevamanussaṃ*.
In this context, by the term "together with gods" (*sadevaka*), the inclusion of the five classes of sense-sphere gods (*kāmāvacara*) should be understood;

by the term "together with Māra" (*samāraka*), the inclusion of the sixth class of sense-sphere gods; by the term "together with Brahmā" (*sabrahmaka*), the inclusion of the Brahmā-world deities such as the *Brahmakāyika*s; and by the term "together with recluses and brahmins"...

The inclusion of "ascetics and brahmins who are adversaries and enemies of the Dispensation" and the inclusion of "ascetics and brahmins who have stilled evil and cast out evil," as well as the inclusion of the "world of beings" by means of the word *pajā* (people),
and the inclusion of "conventional gods and the rest of humanity" by means of the phrase "together with gods and humans"—

thus it should be understood that here, by three terms, the world of beings is taken along with the physical world (*okāsaloka*), while by two terms, only the world of beings is taken according to the category of *pajā*.
Another method: by the inclusion of "together with devas," the immaterial-sphere world (arūpāvacara-loka) is included;
by the inclusion of "together with Māras," the six sense-sphere deva worlds (chakāmāvacara-devaloka); by the inclusion of "together with Brahmās," the material Brahma-world (rūpī-brahmaloka);

and by the inclusion of "with recluses and brahmins, etc.," it refers to the world of human beings together with the four assemblies, or else the world of all remaining sentient beings including conventional deities (sammutideva). However, the Ancients said: "Together with devas... [and so forth].
"Together with the devas" means the rest of the world together with the devas. "Together with Māra" means the rest of the world together with Māra.

"Together with Brahmā" means the rest of the world together with the Brahmas. Thus, having included all beings subject to the three states of existence within these three categories in three ways, he then exhausts the meaning with two further terms:
"the generation with its recluses and brahmins, with its devas and humans."
Thus it is said. In this way, by means of these five terms, the entire threefold world (*tedhātuka*) is encompassed in its various modes.

"Having realized it for himself through direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), he declares it": *sayaṃ* means "by oneself," that is, having become independent of others. *Abhiññā* means "through direct knowledge";

the meaning is "having known by means of superior knowledge (*adhika-ñāṇa*). *Sacchikatvā* means "having made manifest" (*paccakkhaṃ katvā*); by this, inference (*anumāna*) and other such means of cognition are excluded.
He has done it. "He proclaims" means he awakens, makes known, and reveals.
He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning... [as above] ...and good in the end;
that Blessed One, out of compassion for beings, even having abandoned the unsurpassed bliss of seclusion, teaches the Dhamma. And that indeed, whether little or much—
When teaching, he teaches precisely that which is good in the beginning and so forth;
it is said that he teaches having made it good, auspicious, and blameless in the beginning, and likewise having made it good, auspicious, and blameless in the middle and in the conclusion.
In this regard, there is the beginning, middle, and conclusion of the teaching, and there is that of the Dispensation. First, concerning the teaching, even in the case of a four-line verse:
In a verse, the first quarter is called the beginning (*ādi*); the next two are called the middle (*majjha*); and the last one is called the end (*pariyosāna*).
In a sutta with a single sequence of meaning, the introduction (*nidāna*) is the beginning; the words "Thus he spoke" (*idam avoca*) are the end; and everything between these two is the middle.

In a sutta with multiple sequences of meaning, the first sequence is the beginning; the final sequence is the end; and whether there is one, two, or many [sequences] in between, they constitute the middle.
In the Dispensation, virtue, concentration, and insight are called the beginning. For it is said: "And what is the beginning of wholesome states?
Virtue that is well-purified and a view that is straight. Furthermore, the Noble Path—spoken of thus:
"There is, monks, a middle way discovered by the Tathāgata"—is called the middle. The fruit and Nibbāna are the end.
[The word] "name. Regarding the statement, "Therefore, brahmin, this holy life has this as its further shore, this as its consummation," here it is said that the fruit is the consummation.

Regarding the statement, "For, friend Visākha, the holy life is lived with Nibbāna as its abyss, Nibbāna as its goal, Nibbāna as its consummation," here it is said that Nibbāna is the consummation. Here [in the present context]...
However, what is intended here is the beginning, middle, and end of the teaching itself.
For when the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma, he shows virtue at the beginning, the path in the middle, and Nibbāna at the end. Thus it is said:
"He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end. Therefore, another teacher of the Dhamma, when speaking the Dhamma—
“At the beginning one should show virtue; in the middle, one should clarify the path;
at the conclusion, Nibbāna—this is the established method for a speaker.
Regarding the phrase “with meaning and with phrasing”: this refers to a teaching that relies on descriptions such as rice-gruel, food, women, men, and so forth.
He does not teach with a meaningful purpose. But the Blessed One, having set aside such a teaching, teaches a discourse based on the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth;
therefore, he is said to "teach with a meaningful purpose.
However, his teaching may consist of words joined by a single consonant, or it may consist entirely of retroflex consonants, or entirely of open consonants, or entirely of nasalized consonants.

Because it lacks the fullness of phonetic expression, like the languages of the non-Aryan peoples such as the Damilas, Kirātas, and Yavanas, this teaching is called "without phonetic expression" (*abyañjana*).
However, the Blessed One [taught]:
"The lax and the emphatic, the long and the short, the light and the heavy, and the nasalized (*niggahīta*);..."
“Having established the connection and being liberated, there is a tenfold distinction through the intelligence regarding the phrasing.
Having spoken thus, he teaches the Dhamma by making the phrasing complete, without omitting any of the ten kinds of phrasing mentioned.
Therefore, it is said: “He teaches having made it with its phrasing. Regarding the term *kevalaparipuṇṇa*: here, *kevala* is a designation for the whole.
"Complete" means that the words are neither deficient nor redundant. This is what is meant: he teaches only that which is entirely complete;
there is not even a single portion of teaching that is incomplete. "Pure" means free from defilement.
For if one teaches with the thought, "By means of this Dhamma-teaching, I shall obtain gain or honor," his teaching is called impure. The Blessed One...

However, being indifferent to worldly gain and possessing a heart softened by the cultivation of loving-kindness that radiates benefit, he teaches with a mind established in the nature of uplifting others.
Therefore, it is said that "he teaches purely. Regarding the phrase "he proclaims the holy life" (*brahmacariya*):
here, "the holy life" refers to the entire Dispensation (*sāsana*) comprised within the three trainings. Thus, "he proclaims the holy life" means...
He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning... [and so on] ...perfectly pure.
And while teaching thus, he reveals the entire holy life (*brahmacariya*) of the Dispensation, which is comprised within the three trainings; such is the meaning to be understood here.

"Holy life" (*brahmacariya*) means a conduct that has become sublime (*brahma*) in the sense of being excellent, or it is said to be the conduct of those who have become sublime, namely the Buddhas and others.
“Sādhu kho panā” means “it is indeed excellent,” which is to say it brings about welfare and brings about happiness.
“Of such Arahants” means of those such as the venerable Gotama, whose sight is difficult to obtain even in many hundreds of thousands of millions of aeons,
and who are encircled by a fathom-wide radiance, adorned with the eighty minor marks, and endowed with the supreme thirty-two marks of a Great Man.

Of the Arahants—whose bodies are beautiful and well-proportioned, whose appearance is not slight, whose utterances of the Dhamma are exceedingly sweet, and who have acquired the title "Arahant" in the world through the realization of qualities as they truly are—the sight is attained.
"The sight is attained" means that even the mere act of seeing is excellent when one opens eyes that are serene and gentle with faith;
especially so if [one hears] the Dhamma with the Brahma-voice endowed with the eight factors.
Having formed the aspiration, "If we can hear even a single word as he descends, it will be even better," they approached the Blessed One with joyful minds, having abandoned all their duties.
Having extended their hands in reverential salutation (*añjali*), those who belonged to both sides thought thus: "If we are holders of wrong view..."
If those of wrong view should reprove us, saying, “Why did you pay homage to the ascetic Gotama?,” we shall say to them, “Is it not enough to have paid homage by the mere act of joining one’s palms?

If those of right view should reprove us, saying, “Why did you not pay homage to the Blessed One?,” we shall say, “Is it only by striking the ground with one’s head that homage is paid? Is not the joining of the palms also [an act of homage]?”
“We shall say that it is indeed for the sake of paying homage.
Regarding “name and clan”: when people say, “Sir Gotama, I am the son of so-and-so, named Datta, named Mitta, and have come here,” they are announcing their name.
Or when they say, “Sir Gotama, I am named Vāseṭṭha, named Kaccāna, and have come here.”

Those who speak are said to "proclaim their lineage. It is said that these poor sons of noble families, thinking, "We shall become well-known in the midst of the assembly by means of our names and clans," acted in this way. But those who sat in silence were both fickle and blind fools.
In this regard, a fickle person becomes trusted when he engages in one or two exchanges of conversation; then—
Thinking, "When there is such trust, it is not right not to give even one or two alms," they sit in silence, seeking to protect themselves.
Like lumps of clay thrown away by the ignorant due to their lack of wisdom, these blind fools sit in silence wherever they are.
"Venāgapurika" means a resident of Venāgapura. "He said this" refers to [the description] of the Tathāgata from the tips of his feet up to the crown of his head.
Beholding the body of the Tathāgata— adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, radiant with the eighty minor characteristics,
and surrounded by dense, six-colored Buddha-rays that issued forth from his body and pervaded an area of eighty cubits on all sides— he was filled with wonder and praised its beauty.
Speaking thus, he uttered these words beginning with, "It is wonderful, Master Gotama!
In this context, the phrase *yāvañcidaṃ* is an expression delimiting an extreme measure.
Its connection is with the word *vippasannāni*. The meaning is: "to such an extent they are clear" or "extremely clear. *Indriyāni* means...
The six faculties, beginning with the eye. For, having seen the clarity of the physical bases for those five faculties, their clarity became manifest to him.

Since that clarity exists only when the mind is clear—because there is no such thing as clarity of the faculties in those whose minds are unclear—the clarity of his mind-faculty (*manindriya*) also became manifest. He [perceived] that clarity...
Having taken them up, he said, "The faculties are serene. "Pure" means stainless. "Bright" means radiant.
"An autumn jujube cluster" refers to a jujube fruit grown in the autumn season that is not yet fully ripe; for it is both pure and bright.
"A palm fruit that has fallen" refers to a palm fruit that is fully ripe. "Just now released from its bond."

At that very moment, it was released from its bonds. For when its binding roots had been removed and it was placed face-up upon a wooden plank, to those looking at even a space of only four finger-breadths, it appeared perfectly pure and radiant.
It was with reference to this that he spoke thus. "A *nekkha* of Jambū-river gold" refers to the deep red color of Jambū-river gold.
Ghaṭikā. "Well-wrought by the son of a skilled smith" means it has been thoroughly prepared by the son of a skillful goldsmith.

"Well-beaten by one highly skilled at the mouth of the furnace" means that after being heated in the goldsmith’s oven, it was well-beaten, rubbed, and polished by a highly skilled goldsmith; this is the meaning.
"Placed upon a pale-red cloth" means that after being cooked by fire, polished with a leopard’s fang, and treated with red ochre, it was set down on a crimson blanket.
"It shines" (bhāsate) means it shines because radiance has arisen. "It glows" (tapate) means it glows because it dispels darkness.
"It blazes" (virocati) means it blazes while emitting light; the meaning is that it is beautiful.
Regarding the phrase "high and luxurious beds": here, a "high bed" (*uccāsayana*) is one that exceeds the prescribed measure;
a "luxurious bed" (*mahāsayana*) is one that is long and wide and made of unsuitable materials. Now, to illustrate these, he said, "such as, for example, a chair," and so forth.
Therein, a "chair" (*āsandī*) is a seat that exceeds the prescribed measure. A "couch" (*pallaṅka*) is one made by placing animal figures on its legs.
*Gonaka*: A long-haired great woolen rug; it is said that its hairs are more than four finger-breadths in length.
*Cittakoti*: A woolen covering with woven patterns. *Paṭika*: A white woolen rug made of wool. *Paṭalika*:
A thick, flowered woolen rug, which is also called an *āmalaka-paṭṭa*. *Tūlika*: Filled with one of three types of cotton down.
*Tūlikā*. *Vikatikā* is a woolen bedspread (*uṇṇāmayatthara*) variegated with the forms of lions, tigers, and so forth.
*Uddalomī* is a woolen bedspread with the nap on both sides; some say it has flowers raised on one side. *Ekantalomī* is a woolen bedspread with the nap on one side;
some say it has flowers raised on both sides. *Kaṭṭissa* is a silk bedspread (*koseyyakaṭṭissamaya*) inlaid with jewels.
*Paccattharaṇaṃ*: "Silken" (*koseyya*) refers specifically to a spread made of silk thread that is sewn with jewels.
*Kuttaka* is a woolen spread suitable for sixteen dancing girls to stand upon and perform a dance.
"Elephant-spreads" (*hatthatthara*) and so forth refer both to spreads used for covering the backs of elephants and to those made by depicting the forms of elephants and other such figures.
*Ajina-paveṇī*: a rug made by sewing together pieces of antelope skin to the size of a bed. The rest has already been explained above. *Nikāmalābhi*: one who obtains things according to his wish;
one who obtains whatever he desires. *Akicchalābhi*: one who obtains things without difficulty. *Akasiralābhi*: one who obtains things abundantly; one who obtains them in great measure.
He says this with the thought, "He surely obtains only things that are most excellent. This, it is said, is...
The brahmin was heavy with sleep; seeing the Blessed One’s serene faculties and so forth, he thought, “Surely this man sits and lies down upon such high and grand beds.
That is why his faculties are so serene, and his complexion is so pure and radiant,” and thus he spoke this praise of lodgings.
Regarding the phrase "but having obtained them, they are not allowable," here some things are indeed allowable. For pure silk (*suddhakoseyya*) is permitted even to spread upon a bed;
likewise, elephant-hides (*gonaka*) and so forth are allowable by way of using them as floor coverings. As for the high chair (*āsandi*), one may use it after cutting off its legs;
and as for the couch (*pallaṅka*), one may use it after tearing out the hair and disentangling the cotton stuffing, because of the statement: "and one may make a bolster. These [other items] also...
They are allowable by one method; however, with reference to what is unallowable, it is said that all of them are not allowable.

"I shall enter only the edge of the forest" means I enter the forest itself. "Whatever they may be" means whichever ones they are. "Having folded the legs crosswise" means having bound the posture with the thighs crossed on all sides.
"Holding the body erect" means [aligning] the eighteen vertebrae.

"Placing the body straight" means moving from one end to the other. "Establishing mindfulness facing the object" (*parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā*) means establishing mindfulness directed toward the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*);
the meaning is that one has made the way of deliverance clearly defined. For it has been said: "‘Facing’ (*pari*) has the sense of encompassing;
‘mouth’ (*mukha*) has the sense of deliverance; ‘mindfulness’ (*sati*) has the sense of establishment. Therefore it is said: ‘establishing mindfulness facing the object.’"
"I dwell having attained" means that having acquired [it] and made it manifest, I dwell. "Being thus" means being one who possesses any one of the first jhāna and so forth.
"At that time my walking is divine" means that for one who walks after having entered the four fine-material jhānas, the walk is called a "divine walk";
this is also the case for one who walks after emerging from the attainment.
The walking path was indeed a divine walking path. The same method applies to standing and the other postures as well, and likewise to the other two monasteries.

When he said, "I understand thus: 'Lust has been abandoned by me,'" he spoke thus while demonstrating that lust had indeed been abandoned by him through the path of Arahantship at the Great Enlightenment Seat (Mahābodhipallaṅka). The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well. By this—
But what has been stated? Reviewing has been stated; by means of reviewing, the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) has been stated.
For even for one who has entered the attainment of fruition, and even for one who has emerged from that attainment, walking and so forth are noble walkings and so forth.
The rest here is of obvious meaning.
4. Commentary on the Sarabha Sutta. 65.
In the fourth [sutta], "at Rājagaha" means in the city of that name. "On Vulture Peak Mountain":
its peaks resemble vultures, or vultures dwell upon its peaks; thus it is called Gijjhakūṭa. On that Vulture Peak Mountain—by this [it is described].
Having made Rājagaha his alms-resort village, the place where he dwelt was shown.
For a monastery had been built there for the Tathāgata on the Vulture Peak (Gijjhakūṭa), and its name was simply the Gijjhakūṭa Monastery;
it was there that he was dwelling at that time. "The wanderer named Sarabha had recently departed"—"Sarabha" means one who has such a name.
The wanderer, having gone forth in this dispensation, departed before long; the meaning is that he has recently fallen away.
For when the Perfectly Enlightened One appeared in the world, the sectarian teachers lost their gains and honor, while great gain and honor arose for the Three Jewels. As it is said:
Now at that time, the Blessed One was honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated,
and he received robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. But the wanderers of other sects were not honored,
not revered, not esteemed, not worshipped, and they did not receive robes, almsfood, lodgings, or medicinal requisites for the sick.
(Udāna 14; Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.2.70) Having thus lost their gains and honor, those five hundred [monks] gathered together in a certain park for wandering ascetics and deliberated:
"Sirs, from the time the ascetic Gotama appeared, we have been deprived of gains and honor."
“Once born, you should find some fault in the ascetic Gotama and his disciples;
by spreading that blame and reviling his teaching, we shall increase our own gain and honor.
As they looked for a flaw, they found none—neither in the three doors of action nor in livelihood; in all four respects, they could see no fault in the ascetic Gotama.
"It is possible; leaving these four places, look elsewhere," they said.
Then, one among them spoke thus: "I see nothing else; every half-month these men assemble, close the doors and windows, and do not even allow the novices to enter.
Even their attendants, who are as dear to them as their own lives, are not permitted to see them."
"By repeatedly casting out their magical illusions and repeatedly ensnaring people, they devour them.
If we are able to bring that [man] here, then great gain and honor will be ours. Another also stood up speaking in the same way.
They all became of one mind. Then they said: "Whoever is able to bring him here, we..."
“We shall make you our leader.
Then, starting from Koṭi, they asked each one, “Can you do it? Can you do it?
When many replied, “I cannot; I cannot,” they asked Sarabha, “Teacher, can you do it?”
He said: "It is no trouble to bring this, provided that you stand by your own word and make me the eldest.
They replied: "Teacher, it is no trouble to bring this; you have already been made the eldest by us. He said:
"One who brings this cannot do so by deceiving or plundering; rather, one must act like a disciple of the ascetic Gotama."
"Having made the offering, having paid homage to his disciples, and having performed the duties of service, it is possible to bring back food after eating from their bowls.
Does this much activity suit you? "Whatever must be done, bring it back and give it to us.
Then, giving a sign to the wanderers, saying, "Upon seeing me, you should act as if you did not see me," on the following day—
Rising early in the morning, he went to the Gijjhakūṭa Great Monastery and paid homage at the feet of every monk he saw with the fivefold prostration.
The monks said, "Other wanderers are fierce and harsh, but this one must be faithful and devout.
"Venerable sirs, you have gone forth only after knowing yourselves to be fit for the place; we, however, did so without prior reflection."
"We have set out on a wrong path; we are wandering on a trackless road.

Having said this, he repeatedly paid homage to whichever monks he saw, prepared bathing water and such, made tooth-sticks allowable, washed and anointed their feet, and ate whatever extra food he obtained.
While he was living there in this manner, a certain great elder saw him and said, "Paribbājaka, you are faithful and full of confidence;
why do you not go forth? [The other replied,] "Venerable sir, who would ordain me?
For we have wandered about for a long time as adversaries to the venerable ones. The elder said, "If you desire to go forth, I shall ordain you."
Having said this, he ordained him. From the time of his ordination, he performed his duties and services without interruption.
Then, the Elder, being pleased with his conduct, conferred full ordination upon him before long.
On the Uposatha day, having entered the Uposatha hall together with the monks, he saw the monks reciting the Pātimokkha with great enthusiasm and thought: "By this..."
"Having concealed it again and again with mist, they devour the world; I shall take it away within a few days," he thought.
He went to the courtyard, paid homage to his preceptor, and asked, "Venerable sir, what is the name of this teaching? "It is called the Pātimokkha, friend.
"This must be the supreme teaching, venerable sir. "Yes, friend; it is the upholder of the entire Dispensation."
“This is the training. “Venerable sir, if this rule of training is supreme, I shall take up this very one first.
“Take it, friend,” the elder accepted. While he was taking it up, he saw some wanderers and was asked, “What kind of teacher is yours?
He replied, “Friends, do not worry; we shall master it in a few days,” and before long he had mastered it.
He said to his preceptor, "Is it only this much, venerable sir, or is there more? "It is only this much, friend," he replied.
On the following day, dressed exactly as he had been before and with the same manner of carrying his bowl, he departed from Vulture Peak and went to the park of the wanderers.
When the wanderers saw him, they said, "Teacher, what has happened? We thought you had failed."
“Let us bring the art of the whirlpool,” they said, and they surrounded him. “Do not worry, friends; I have brought the art of the whirlpool.
From now on, our gain and honor will be great. You must remain in harmony with one another; do not engage in disputes.
“If you have mastered it well, Master, please teach it to us as well. He [then began] from the beginning...

Having begun, he recited the Pātimokkha. Then all of them, thinking, "Come, sirs, as we wander about the city, we shall speak dispraise of the ascetic Gotama," went to the vicinity of the city gates while the gates were still unopened;
through the open gate, they were the very first to enter. Thus did that wanderer depart, still wearing his own sectarian marks.
With this in mind, it was said: "The wanderer named Sarabha has not long since departed.
On that day, however, as the Blessed One surveyed the world at the time of dawn, he saw this:
"Today the wanderer Sarabha, having wandered through the city, will perform a work of disparagement, slandering the Three Jewels."
“While he is speaking, having poured poison [over the ground], he will go to the wanderers’ park;
I too shall go right there, and all four assemblies will likewise gather there. In that assembly, eighty-four thousand beings will drink the drink of the Deathless.
Then, thinking, “Let him have his opportunity; let him spread his criticism as he pleases,” [he remained silent].
He addressed the Elder Ānanda: “Ānanda, announce to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus that they are to go for alms together with me at the eighteen great monasteries. The Elder did so.
Taking their bowls and robes, the bhikkhus surrounded the Teacher. Taking the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with him, the Teacher went for alms right near the gateway village.
Cari. Sarabha also entered the city together with the wanderers;

having gone here and there among the assemblies and to the king’s gate, the streets, the crossroads, and other such places, he spoke such words as, "I have understood the Dhamma of the recluses, the sons of the Sakyans," and so forth.
With reference to him, it was said: "He speaks these words thus in the assembly at Rājagaha," and so on. In that context:

"Known" (*aññāta*) means recognized and understood; it indicates that [the teaching] was mastered by making it manifest. "Having known" (*aññāya*) means having understood. "Departed" (*apakkanta*) means departed while still wearing the very same robes.
For if there were any essence in the teaching of the ascetic Gotama, I would not have departed.
But his teaching is without essence, devoid of substance; having reduced it to mere deception and trickery, the ascetics [deceive] the world.
He spoke thus, illuminating the meaning that "they eat. Then,
while that wanderer was speaking in this way, five hundred forest-dwelling bhikkhus—
unaware that "the Teacher has gone to such-and-such a place for alms"— [approached] at the time for the alms-round.
They entered Rājagaha for alms; it was with reference to them that this was said. "They heard" means they listened.
"They approached the Blessed One" means they approached thinking, "We shall report this matter to the One of Ten Powers.
"The bank of the Sippinikā River" refers to the bank of the river named Sippinikā. "The Blessed One consented by remaining silent" means he gave his assent through silence.
The meaning is that, without moving his limbs of body or speech, he endured it with his mind alone, maintaining patience within.
Having thus endured it, he thought again: "Should I go today to crush Sarabha’s argument all by myself, or surrounded by the community of monks? Then this occurred to him: "If I..."
“Surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, I shall go; the great multitude will think thus:
‘The ascetic Gotama, when going to the place where the debate arises, goes having raised his own side and crushes the debate that has arisen through the power of his assembly;
he does not allow the opponents to raise their heads. Yet for me, there is no need to take hold of another and crush him when a debate has arisen.”
"There is; I myself shall go and crush him. And this is no marvel that I, having now become a Buddha, should crush the argument that has arisen against me;

for even when I was practicing the perfections and was reborn with a non-causal rebirth-linking (*ahetuka-paṭisandhi*), there was no one capable of bearing the burden that I had to bear. To accomplish this matter—"
“Whenever a heavy burden is to be borne, whenever there is a path that leads deep, then they yoke the black ox;
he indeed carries that burden.”—This *Kaṇha Jātaka* should be cited.
It is said that in the past, a certain caravan leader [was staying] in the house of a certain elderly woman.
She took up residence there. Then, shortly after the first watch of the night, one of her cows gave birth;
she brought forth a calf. From the moment the old woman saw the calf, maternal affection arose within her.
On the following day, the merchant’s son said, “Take your wages for your work. The old woman—
“I have no other business; give me this very calf,” she said. “Take it, mother,” he replied.
She took him, gave him milk to drink, and raised him by providing rice gruel, food, grass, and so forth.
As he grew up, he became fully developed in form, endowed with strength and vigor, and possessed of excellent conduct; his name was Kāḷaka. Then, for one...
As the caravan leader was approaching with five hundred carts, one of the wheels became stuck in a place where the water had receded.
Unable to have it pulled out even after yoking ten, twenty, or thirty oxen, he approached Kāḷaka and said, "Dear son, I will give you wages; lift this cart up for me. Having spoken thus, he—
Taking [the bull], and thinking, "There is no one else capable of bearing the burden with him," he tied a yoke to the load-cart and yoked him alone.
He lifted that cart, set it down on dry land, and in this very manner hauled out five hundred carts. When he had hauled out the very last cart and was being unyoked—
Saying, “I will,” he lifted up his head.
The caravan leader thought, “This man has never done such a thing while lifting so many wagons; I suppose he does it for the sake of a wage.
He took coins according to the count of the wagons and had five hundred bundles tied around the man’s neck. As for the others—
Not allowing him to come near her, she went straight home. Seeing him, the old woman released him;
having realized he was a kahāpaṇa coin, she said, "Why did you do this, my son? Do not entertain the thought that 'this man will live on what I have earned by working.
She then bathed the ox with warm water, rubbed it with oil, and...

"From now on, do not act in this way again," he advised. Thus the Teacher, thinking, "Even when I was wandering as a bodhisatta, there was no one else capable of bearing the burden that had to be borne by me, even though I was reborn with a non-causative rebirth-linking (ahetuka-paṭisandhi)," went forth all alone.
To demonstrate this, it is said: "Then the Blessed One, having emerged from seclusion in the evening time," and so forth.
In this context, "seclusion" (*paṭisallāna*) means withdrawing the mind from various objects; the meaning is "the attainment of fruition" (*phalasamāpatti*).

"He approached him" (*tenupasaṅkami*): having performed his duty of making himself known among the wanderers throughout the entire city, he departed from the city, gathered at the wanderers' monastery, and [said]:
"Friend Sarabha, if the ascetic Gotama should come, what..."
“Will you do it? “When the ascetic Gotama does one, I will do two; when he does two, four; when he does four, five;
when he does five, ten; when he does ten, twenty; when he does twenty, thirty;
when he does thirty, forty; when he does forty, fifty; when he does fifty, a hundred; when he does a hundred...”
While they sat there, having raised a mutual lion’s roar, saying, "I shall do a thousandfold; I shall do it," he approached them.

As he approached, since the path to the wanderers' park lay right through the middle of the city, he put on his bright red lower garment and donned the Great Robe of the Sugata, and like a king with full vigor, he went alone through the center of the city.
He departed. Those of wrong view, seeing him, thought, "The wanderers were spreading disrepute while performing a public display for the ascetic Gotama;
he is surely going now to follow them and persuade them. Thus they followed after him.
Those of right view also thought, "The Perfectly Enlightened One has set out alone, taking only his bowl and robe; today, by means of the Sarabha..."
"A great Dhamma-council will take place; we too shall become witnesses with our own eyes at that assembly," they said, and followed after him.
Even as the great multitude looked on, the Teacher approached the wanderers' park.
From between the trunks, branches, and twigs of the trees, the wanderers emerged, [beholding] the six-colored, dense rays of the Buddha's light.
Seeing it, they thought, "Never before has there been such a radiance; what indeed is this?
and looking up, they said, "The ascetic Gotama is coming. Upon hearing this, Sarabha placed his head between his knees and sat with his face turned downward.
At that moment, the Blessed One approached that monastery and sat upon the prepared seat. Thus did the Tathāgata...
Indeed, because he was born into a preeminent family on the surface of Jambudīpa, he was worthy of the foremost seat;
thus, a seat was prepared for him everywhere. He sat upon that magnificent, prepared seat of the Buddha.
Those wanderers said this to the wanderer Sarabha: "It is said that the Perfectly Enlightened One [will sit] together with Sarabha..."
Even as he was speaking thus much, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, following step by step behind the Teacher, reached the wanderers’ park;
all four assemblies likewise entered the wanderers’ park. Then those wanderers said, “It is a marvelous feat of the ascetic Gotama!
Having wandered through the entire city and spread his disrepute about, he has performed this act of self-proclamation.”
"Having approached those who had come as enemies, adversaries, and opponents, he did not engage in even the slightest contentious speech;
rather, from the moment they arrived, he spoke sweet words to them as if anointing them with hundredfold-refined oil or as if pouring the drink of immortality into their mouths.
Thus all of them, following the Perfectly Enlightened One, spoke these words.
"You should entreat" means you should pray for, yearn for, and long for [it]. "Becoming silent" means having entered into a state of silence.
"Becoming abashed" means having fallen into a state of dejection. "With shoulders drooping" means with the neck bent down. "With face cast downward" means with the face turned downwards.
"Of you who claim to be a Perfectly Enlightened One" means of one who claims: "I am a Perfectly Enlightened One; all phenomena have been fully realized by me."
"Of you": "These things indeed have not been fully awakened to by you. "Therein": "In regard to those things shown as 'not fully awakened to'.
"He will evade with one thing another": he will conceal one statement with another statement;
the intention is that when asked about one thing, he will speak of another. "He will divert the conversation to external matters."

By bringing up some other external, irrelevant talk, he will cause the previous conversation to be set aside. "Appaccaya" means he will manifest dissatisfaction (*anabhiraddhi*) and a state of discontent;
he will make it evident. And here, by "appaccaya," mental grief (*domanassa*) is expressed;
whereas by the preceding two terms, anger (*kodha*) itself is meant, distinguished by its weak and strong degrees.
Thus, having roared the lion’s roar with the first ground of self-confidence (*vesārajja*), the Blessed One, roaring again with the second and subsequent grounds, said:

"Whosoever, O wanderers... and so forth. Therein, "for the sake of which purpose the Dhamma has been taught by you" means for the sake of whichever path or fruit the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths was taught by you. "That does not lead out" means that Dhamma...
It does not lead out, it does not go forth; that is to say, it does not accomplish that goal.
"Of the doer" means of the person who performs it, the individual who fulfills the practice—that is the meaning.
"Rightly for the destruction of suffering" means for the destruction of the entire suffering of saṃsāra by way of cause, method, and reason. Alternatively, "for whatever purpose yours [is]..."
"The Dhamma has been taught": for whose sake the Dhamma was taught by you. That is to say:

the meditation subject on the foul for the purpose of overcoming lust; the development of loving-kindness for the purpose of overcoming hatred; the five qualities for the purpose of overcoming delusion;
and mindfulness of breathing for the purpose of cutting off discursive thought. "It does not lead the practitioner to the complete destruction of suffering": that...

The meaning here is this: for one who practices the Dhamma as it has been taught, that [Dhamma] does not lead out, does not go forth, and does not accomplish the goal for the sake of the destruction of the suffering of saṃsāra by means of the correct cause, method, and reason.
"Just like the wanderer Sarabha" means just as this wanderer Sarabha was brooding.
"he sits speechless; thus he will sit.

Having thus let out a lion’s roar with these three statements, even as the Tathāgata was withdrawing from his teaching, the assembly gathered at that place—numbering eighty-four thousand beings—drank the drink of the Deathless. The Teacher [bestowed it] upon the assembly.
Having recognized that the nectar had been drunk, he rose up into the air and departed.

To illustrate this matter, the passage beginning with "Then the Blessed One" was spoken. In that context, "lion's roar" means the best of roars, the roar of fearlessness, the roar that cannot be countered.
"He departed through the air" means that having attained the fourth jhāna as a basis for the higher knowledges (abhiññā), and having emerged from it, he made a resolution.
Together with the community of bhikkhus, he leapt into the air. Having thus leapt, at that very moment he alighted at the Gijjhakūṭa Mahāvihāra.
"With the goad of speech" means by the spur of words. "They made it a continuous roar" (sañjambharimakaṃsu) means they made it compact and closely packed;
it is said that they pierced it from above. "In the great forest" (brahāraññe) means in the vast wilderness. "I shall roar the lion's roar."
Seeing the lion’s manner of roaring, he thought, "He too is an animal, and I am also one; he has four feet, and I have them too; I shall likewise let out a lion's roar.
Unable to roar in the presence of the lion, when the lion had departed for his prey, he began to roar all alone. Then, it was merely the sound of a jackal.
"Nicchari. By this it is said: "He roars like a jackal. "Bheraṇḍaka" is a synonym for that very same thing.
Furthermore, it means he roars with a broken voice, an unpleasant sound.
"In just the same way, you"—by this simile, the wanderers have compared the Tathāgata to a lion and made Sarabha like a jackal. "Ambukasañcarī" (the water-walker).
The little hen. Seeing a large cock crowing with the thought, "I shall crow like a male," she thought, "He has two feet and two wings; I have those too. I too shall crow such a cry.
Being unable to crow in his presence, she, when he had departed, let out only a hen's cry while crowing. Because of that—
It is said: “He roars only with the sound of one moving through water. *Usabho* means a bull. *Suññāya* means empty, devoid of the leading bulls.
*Gambhīraṃ naditabbaṃ maññatī* means he thinks he should roar a deep roar like the bellowing of a leading bull. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
5. Commentary on the Kesamutti Sutta 66.
Regarding the fifth discourse: "The town of the Kālāmas" refers to the town belonging to those of the Kālāma clan, who were kṣatriyas.
"The Kesamuttis" are the inhabitants of the town of Kesamutta. "They approached" means they came bringing medicinal substances such as ghee and fresh butter, as well as the eight kinds of drinks.
And having caused them to enter [the water], they approached. "Expounding their own doctrine" means they state their own views.
"Illuminating" means making clear. "Humiliating" means striking down. "Contemptuously treating" means despising. "Despising" means making something lowly.
"Making an object of mockery" means making it something suspended; having suspended it, they cast it away. Others also—
"Bhante" refers to a village at the entrance of the forest; therefore, those who have already passed through the forest and those wishing to pass through it stay there.
Among them, those who arrived first departed after proclaiming their own doctrine.
Those who arrived later said, "What do they know? They are our pupils; they have learned some small craft or other from us."
Having declared their own view with the words, “We have grasped it,” they departed. The Kālāmas were unable even to settle upon a single view.
Having explained this matter and reported it to the Blessed One, they said, “Venerable sir, for us...
and so forth. In that context, *hoteva kaṅkhā* means there is indeed doubt; *vicikicchā* is a synonym for that very same thing. *Alaṃ* means it is appropriate.

"Do not [accept] out of oral tradition" means: do not accept even on account of hearsay. "Do not [accept] out of lineage" means: do not accept even on account of traditional lore. "Do not [accept] out of speculation" means:
do not accept thinking, "It is said that this is so. "Do not [accept] out of agreement with a scriptural collection" means:
do not accept thinking, "This accords with our own scriptural tradition. "Do not [accept] out of logical reasoning" means: do not accept even by grasping at logic.
"Do not grasp it. Do not grasp it even by way of "reasoning" (*nayaggāha*). Do not grasp it even by way of "reflection on modes" (*ākāraparivitakka*), thinking, "This is a beautiful reason.
Do not grasp it even by way of "acceptance after reflection on views" (*diṭṭhinijjhānakkhanti*), thinking, "It accords with the view we have accepted after reflecting upon it.
Do not grasp it by way of "the appearance of possibility" (*bhabbarūpatā*).
"Do not think, 'This monk is of a suitable appearance; it is fitting to accept his word.
Do not think, 'This ascetic is our teacher; it is fitting to accept his word. *Samatta* means fulfilled.
*Samādinnā* means taken up and adhered to. *Yamassa hoti* means whatever reason he has."
it occurs to the person. Non-greed and the others are to be understood by way of being the opposites of greed and the others.

By means of the phrases "free from covetousness" and so forth, the preliminary stage of loving-kindness (*mettā*) has been explained. Now, while explaining the meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*) beginning with loving-kindness, he says: "accompanied by loving-kindness," and so on. Regarding that, in the discourse on the meditation subject:
Whatever needs to be said regarding the method of meditation or the commentary on the text has all been stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
Thus, "with a mind free from enmity" means having a mind free from enmity due to the absence of both unwholesome enmity and persons who are enemies.
"With a mind free from ill will" means having a mind free from suffering due to the absence of a mind of anger. "With a mind free from defilement" means [due to the absence] of the defilements...
"Because of non-existence, his mind is undefiled. "Pure-minded" means that his mind is pure by virtue of being free from the stains of the defilements (*kilesa*).
"Of him" refers to such a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*). "Consolations" means supports or foundations.
"If indeed there is another world" means if there is a so-called "other world" beyond this world. Then, as for my body...
"Upon the breakup of the body, after death... 'I shall be reborn,' there is a reason for this, by which I think:
'Upon the breakup of the body, after death, I shall be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. In this way, the method is to be understood in all instances.
'Free from distress' means without suffering. 'Happy' means possessing happiness. 'By both of these I behold myself as purified' refers to the fact that I do not commit evil."
And that which one does, yet is not done—by both of these I regard myself as purified.
The rest is clear in meaning everywhere.
6. Commentary on the Sāḷha Sutta.
67. "Migāra’s grandsons" means the grandsons of the merchant Migāra. "Sekhuniya’s grandsons" means the grandsons of the merchant Sekhuniya.
"They approached" means that, having finished their morning meal, they approached accompanied by their slaves and laborers.
It is said that before breakfast, at the very time of the morning watch, a certain question had arisen in their house, but there was no opportunity to discuss it.
There was none. Thinking, "We shall hear that question," they went to the Elder, paid homage, and sat down in silence.
The Elder, perceiving their intention and thinking, "They must have come to hear the question that arose in the village," began with that very question, saying, "Come, Sāḷha...
and so forth. In this context, *lobho* means the nature of being greedy.
"He asks, 'Does that which is called greed exist? [The Buddha replies: 'Sāḷha, I call this state known as greed "covetousness" (abhijjhā);
I call it "craving" (taṇhā). Thus he spoke, illuminating the meaning of the question raised.
In this manner, the method should be applied to all sections.

"He understands thus" means that the noble disciple, having established himself by developing the four divine abodes (brahmavihāras) and emerging from meditative attainment, begins insight (vipassanā) and understands as follows:

"This exists"—understanding by way of delimiting the five aggregates, which are comprised of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and designated as the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca), he understands thus: "This exists."
When it is said, "This," [it refers to the truth of suffering]. "Inferior" is the truth of the origin. "Superior" is the truth of the path.
"The further escape from this state of perception" means that the further escape from this state of perception—consisting of insight-perception—is called Nibbāna;
by saying "that exists," he shows the truth of cessation. "In liberation, the knowledge 'it is liberated'"...
The nineteenfold knowledge of reviewing is thus explained: "There was greed before" means that greed existed for me previously;
"that was unwholesome" means that it was indeed called unwholesome, or that at that time it was called unwholesome.
"And this is wholesome" means that this is wholesome; he says this with reference to the absence of that very unwholesomeness, [considering] the wholesome as security.
"Free from craving" (*nicchāto*) means devoid of thirst. "Extinguished" (*nibbuto*) means extinguished by the absence of the defilements that cause internal burning.
"Become cool" (*sītibhūto*) means having become cool. "Experiencing happiness" (*sukhappaṭisaṃvedī*) means one who experiences physical and mental bliss.
"Having become sublime" (*brahmabhūtena*) means having become supreme. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
7. Commentary on the *Kathāvatthu-sutta* 68.
Regarding the seventh [section], "bases for discussion" (*kathāvatthu*) means the causes for discussion; the meaning is that they are the grounds or foundations for discussion.
In the passage, "The past time, monks," the term "past time" (*atītamaddhāna*) refers both to time and to the aggregates (*khandha*). This applies likewise to the future and the present.
The same method applies here. In that regard, when one speaks concerning the past by saying, "In the past there was a Perfectly Enlightened One named Kassapa;
his chief patron was the King of Kāsi named Kikī, and his lifespan was twenty thousand years," this is what is meant by speaking about the past.
When one says, "In the future there will be a Buddha named Metteyya; his [patron] will be Saṅkha..."
By saying, "A king named so-and-so will be the foremost supporter, and his lifespan will be eighty thousand years," one speaks concerning the future in this manner.
By saying, "At present, a king named so-and-so is righteous," one speaks concerning the present in this manner.
"By means of discourse" (*kathāsampayogena*) means through the meeting of conversation. "Fit to speak" (*kaccho*) means suitable to speak; "unfit to speak" (*akaccho*) means unsuitable to speak.
Regarding the questions that are to be answered categorically (*ekaṃsabyākaraṇīya*) and so forth: when asked, "Is the eye impermanent? one must answer categorically, "Yes, it is impermanent.
This same method applies to the ear and the other sense bases. This is the question to be answered categorically. "Impermanent..."

When asked, "Is the eye the eye?", one must answer by analyzing it thus: "It is not only the eye; the ear is also impermanent, and the nose is also impermanent. This is a question to be answered by analysis (*vibhajjabyākaraṇīyo pañho*).
When asked, "As the eye is, so is the ear; as the ear is, so is the eye," one should first counter-question: "In what sense do you ask?"
When it is asked, "I ask in the sense of seeing," one should answer, "No. When it is asked, "I ask in the sense of impermanence," one should answer, "Yes.
This is a question to be answered by counter-questioning. However, when asked such things as "Is that which is the soul the same as the body?
one should set it aside, saying, "This was left undeclared by the Blessed One. This question is not to be answered; this is a question to be set aside.
“He does not stand firm in what is possible and impossible” means he does not stand firm in what is a valid reason and what is not. Herein, this is the method:
the eternalist is able to refute the annihilationist with a logical reason; being thus refuted, the annihilationist thinks, “But why do I advocate annihilation?
and instead demonstrates his own position as being that of an eternalist, unable to establish himself in his own doctrine.

Thus, when an annihilationist is refuted by an eternalist, a personalist is refuted by an advocate of emptiness, and an advocate of emptiness is refuted by a personalist—in this way, one is said not to be established in what is possible and what is impossible.
"Not being established in conventional designation" applies both to the asking of a question and to the answering of a question. How so? Someone...
For indeed, one who thinks, "I shall ask a question," clears his throat;
when addressed by the other, "This is exactly what you will ask," he recognizes the state of being known and says, "Not this, I shall ask something else.

Likewise, even when a question has been asked, one who thinks, "I shall answer the question," clears his jaw; when addressed by the other, "This is exactly what you will say," he recognizes the state of being known...
Having understood this, he thinks, “This is not [the right time]; I shall speak of something else,” and so says. In such a preparation, one is said to “not stand firm.
Regarding “one does not stand firm in speaking what is unknown”: one does not stand firm in speaking what is unknown—that is, in speaking what ought to be known.
How so? Someone asks a question, and the other says to him, “A pleasing question you have asked; where did you learn this?”
Even when one asks a question according to the proper method of inquiry, another may harbor doubt regarding that person's discourse, wondering, "Was this not asked as a question?
Another, having been asked a question, explains it; yet someone else says to him, "You have explained the question well!
Where did you learn this? One who explains a question ought to speak in such a manner. Another, however, [speaks] according to the very method of exposition.
Even after explaining a question, he harbors doubt regarding that discourse, thinking, "Was this not actually a non-question that I have explained?

He does not stand firm in the practice (*paṭipadā*); that is to say, he does not abide in the course of conduct (*paṭipatti*), for he asks questions in places where he should not ask them, being ignorant of the proper procedure (*vatta*).
This so-called "question" must not be explained when asked on the courtyard of a shrine (*cetiyāṅgaṇa*), nor likewise on the path of alms-round.
When walking for alms in the village; when sitting in the assembly hall; when sitting after having received rice gruel or a meal;
when sitting while eating; and also when going to the place for the midday rest—on these occasions [it may be told].

However, when sitting at the day-resting place, it should be told only to one who asks after first making an opportunity (by clearing the space), but it should not be told to one who asks without having made an opportunity. This is...
One who asks without knowing the proper procedure (*vatta*) is said not to be established in the path of practice.
"In this way, monks, such a person is unfit," means that because of this reason, such a person is indeed unfit to be spoken with.
"He is established in what is possible and impossible" means that an eternalist (*sassatavādin*), by means of a valid reason, is able to refute an annihilationist (*ucchedavādin*).
Even when being refuted by him, the proponent of annihilationism says, “Though I am being refuted by you a hundred times, I am still a proponent of annihilationism.

In this same manner, the method should be applied to the doctrines of eternalism, the person (pudgala), emptiness, and so forth. Thus it is said that one is "established in what is possible and impossible" (*ṭhānāṭhāne saṇṭhāti*).
To be "established in the formulation" (*parikappe saṇṭhāti*) means: [thinking] “I shall ask a question,” while clearing one’s throat, one says, “You—”
When it is said, "You will ask this question," he says, "Yes, I shall ask that very one.
When it is said, "You will explain this answer," even while rubbing his jaw in preparation, he says, "Yes, I shall explain that very one.
In this way, one is said to be "established in the preliminary arrangement" (*parikappa*).
When he asks the question, "He stands firm in the declaration of what is known," and is told, "The question you have asked is excellent;
indeed, one who asks a question should ask in this way," he accepts it and does not give rise to doubt.
Likewise, even after the question has been answered, when he is told, "The answer you have given is excellent; indeed, one who answers a question should answer in this way," he accepts it.

He does not give rise to doubt. "He stands firm in the practice" means that after having him sit in his own house and being given rice gruel, solid food, and so forth, he remains seated until the meal is finished and asks a question.
Or, taking the eight kinds of medicinal requisites such as ghee, or drinks, or robes, coverings, garlands, perfumes, and so on, he goes to the monastery, gives them, and [asks a question].

Having entered the daytime dwelling and requested permission, he asks a question. For one who asks in this way, having understood the proper conduct (*vatta*), it is said that he is "established in the practice" (*paṭipadā*). It is appropriate to explain his question.
"He evades with one thing" means he conceals one matter with another word, or when asked about one thing, he speaks of another.
He speaks. How does he divert the conversation to something external? By introducing an irrelevant topic, he diverts the previous conversation to something external. Here is an illustration:
it is said that some monks, having assembled, said to a certain young monk, "Friend, you have fallen into this and this offense.
He replied, "Venerable sirs, we have gone to Nāgadīpa. "Friend," [they said].
“We do not need you to go to Nāgadīpa; rather, we ask because you have fallen into an offense.
“Venerable sir, they eat fish on Nāgadīpa. “Friend, you have no business eating fish; it is because you have fallen into an offense that we ask.
He said, “Venerable sir, the fish was not well-cooked enough, and it caused me discomfort. “Friend,” [he replied].
"You have no concern whether you are comfortable or uncomfortable; you have fallen into an offense. "Venerable sir, for as long as I lived there, I experienced nothing but discomfort.
In this way, it should be understood that one diverts the conversation to external matters by means of talk concerning newcomers.
"He brings forth" means that he draws out and spreads forth the Sutta from here and there, like the Elder Tipiṭaka Tissa. It is said that formerly,
when the bhikkhus had assembled in the courtyard of the Great Cetiya, performed their communal duties, given the exhortation to the bhikkhus,
and engaged in mutual discussion of questions, this elder would [draw] the Sutta from here and there by means of the three Piṭakas.
Having brought forward [an example], he does not allow even a single question to be concluded during the course of the day. "He tramples" means that having brought forward a reason, he crushes it.

"He mocks" means that even when another asks a question or speaks, he claps his hands and laughs a great laugh, by which the other thinks, "Did I ask what should not be asked? Did I say what should not be said?"
Doubt arises. "He seizes upon a slip" means he seizes upon even a slight fault of speech;
or, when a syllable, word, or phoneme is poorly uttered, he wanders about complaining, "This indeed should have been said thus.
"With a proximate cause" means having a supporting condition, having a causal basis.
"One with attentive ear" means one who has set up the ear. "He directly knows one thing" means he directly knows one wholesome state, the Noble Path.
"He fully understands one thing" means he fully understands one thing, the truth of suffering, through the full understanding of scrutiny (*tīraṇapariññā*).
"He abandons one thing" means he abandons, dispels, and brings to an end one thing, all unwholesome states. He realizes...
"One dhamma" means he makes manifest either the single dhamma of the fruit of arahantship or cessation itself.
"He touches right liberation" means that by means of the correct cause, method, and reason, he touches the liberation of the fruit of arahantship through the contact of knowledge.
"This is the purpose of the talk, monks"—that is, monks, this talk which has been shown in connection with discourse.

That has this as its purpose; this is the ground, the foundation for that discourse. This is the basis, namely, "the liberation of the mind through non-clinging"—in this way, the application should be understood for all instances.

"Counsel has this as its purpose" means that whatever counsel there is among individuals who are close to one another, that too has precisely this as its purpose. "The proximate cause has this as its purpose" refers to one who has lent an ear.

"Along with its underlying cause (*sopanisa*)"—the underlying causes mentioned in this way are for this very purpose. "Attentive listening to that" means attentive listening to those underlying causes;
that too is for this very purpose. "Without clinging" means not grasping by means of the four types of clinging.
"Liberation of the mind" refers to the liberation of the fruit of Arhatship. For it is for the sake of the fruit of Arhatship that all this discourse on the Suttanta is set forth.
Summing up with verses, he says, "Those who are hostile," and so forth.
Therein, "hostile" (*viruddhā*) means those who are opposed by anger, which is termed "enmity. "Conversing" (*sallapanti*) means they engage in talk.

"Settled" (*viniviṭṭhā*) means having become firmly attached. "Exalted" (*samussitā*) means well-raised up by the arrogance of pride (*mānussaya*). "Having resorted to ignoble qualities" (*anariyaguṇamāsajja*)...

They speak by attaching themselves to the qualities of ignoble persons. For speech that strikes at the virtues of others is indeed called "ignoble speech" (*anariyakathā*), not "noble speech" (*ariyakathā*);
the meaning is that they speak such things. "Seeking each other's openings" means searching for one another's flaws or faults.
"Ill-spoken" means poorly delivered. "Slipped" refers to a slight verbal error or lapse.
They overcome mutual confusion and defeat through carefulness regarding each other’s faults.
"They rejoice" means they are satisfied. "One should not practice" means one does not act or speak.

"Connected with what is established in the Dhamma" refers to that speech which is uttered by one who stands firm in the Dhamma; it is both established in the Dhamma and connected with that very Dhamma.
Connected with the established Dhamma. With an unarrogant mind means with a mind that is not puffed up. Without disparagement means being free from disparagement through the disparagement of rivalry.
Without violence means being free from violence through the violence of lust, hatred, and delusion. Not being envious means not being jealous.
"One should not disparage what is poorly spoken" means one should not find fault with what has been badly said.
"One should not train in finding fault" means one should not train in finding fault characterized by seeking out reasons for superiority.
"And one should not cause another to be seized for their lapse" means one should not seize upon even a slight verbal slip and say, "This is your fault.

"One should not bring it forward" means one should not lay it out. "One should not crush it" means that having brought forward a single reason, one should not crush [the other person] with it. "One should not speak mixed words."
One should not speak words associated with lying. "For the sake of knowing" means for the purpose of understanding.
"For the sake of confidence" means for the purpose of generating trust. "One should not speak with pride" means one should not be uplifted by the arrogance of conceit.
For the wise do not speak while being puffed up with conceit; rather, it is one who is not supported by pride who should deliberate, speak, and discourse.
8. Commentary on the Aññatitthiyasutta 69.
Regarding the eighth [sutta], "rooted in the Blessed One" (*bhagavaṃmūlakā*): those for whom the Blessed One is the root are "rooted in the Blessed One. This is what is meant:
"Venerable sir, these teachings of ours were previously originated by the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa; when he had attained final Nibbāna..."
"For one entire interval between Buddhas, there was no other ascetic or brahmin capable of giving rise to these teachings;
yet it is by the Blessed One that these teachings have been brought forth. Indeed, it is by depending on the Blessed One that we understand and penetrate these teachings.
"Thus, Venerable Sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One; the Blessed One is their guide," they said. "The Blessed One is the guide," [the Buddha replied].

The Dhammas are called "having the Blessed One as their guide" (bhagavā-nettikā) because he is the leader, the trainer, and the instructor who demonstrates them by taking up each one individually according to its true nature.

They are called "having the Blessed One as their refuge" (bhagavā-paṭisaraṇā) because when the phenomena of the four planes come within the range of the knowledge of omniscience, they are, as it were, reflected back upon the Blessed One.

“They come back” means they descend and gather together. Furthermore, when the Blessed One was seated at the Great Seat of Enlightenment (Mahābodhimaṇḍa), contact (phassa) approached by way of his personal realization, asking:
“Blessed One, what is my name? “In the sense of touching, you are called ‘contact.

Feeling (vedanā), perception (saññā), formations (saṅkhārā), and consciousness (viññāṇa) approached, asking: “Blessed One, what is my name? “In the sense of cognizing, you are called ‘consciousness.’”
"Consciousness is called 'name'. Thus, by grasping the individual names of the phenomena belonging to the four planes according to their specific nature, the Blessed One "takes refuge in the Dhamma";
this is "having the Blessed One as one's refuge. "May the Blessed One himself be the one to explain it" means:
may the meaning of this spoken word be made manifest by the Blessed One alone; the sense is, "You yourself must speak and give it to us."

"Lust" (*rāga*) refers to the lust that arises by way of being attached. "Slight fault" (*appasāvaja*) means it is slightly blameworthy both in terms of worldly blame and in terms of the blameworthiness of its result;
thus, it is "slightly blameworthy" by way of both types of blame. How so?
For parents, brothers, sisters, and others perform what is called the auspicious ceremony of marriage for their sons and brothers. Thus, they [commit this act] by way of worldly blame.

It is "less blameworthy" (appasāvajja) in the sense that there is no rebirth-linking in the states of misery rooted in contentment with one's own wife; thus it is less blameworthy by way of its result.
It is "slowly fading away" (dandhavirāgī) in that, while fading away, it fades away gradually and is not released quickly.
Like the color of oil or lac, it persists for a long time; even after going through two or three other existences, it does not depart—thus it is slowly fading away.
In this regard, there is this story: It is said that a certain man committed adultery with his brother’s wife.
That woman, moreover, loved him even more than her own husband. She said to him, "When this matter becomes public, there will be great infamy;
therefore, kill your brother. He replied, "Begone, you vile woman! Do not speak thus again."
She dismissed him. Remaining silent for a few days, she spoke again; his mind became inclined toward her.
When he spoke to her a third time, she said, "What must I do to obtain your favor?
Then, explaining a stratagem to him, she said, "Do exactly what I tell you: at such-and-such a place, near the Mahākakudha tree, there is a bathing spot..."
“There is; go there and stand holding a sharp stick. He did so. His eldest brother also returned home from working in the forest.

She, as if her heart were softened toward him, said, “Come, husband, I will comb your hair,” and while combing it, she gave him a cluster of *āmalaka* fruits, saying, “Your head is very dirty; go [and wash it].”
"Go wash your head at such-and-such a place and then return," he sent her.
She went to the very bathing place she had been told of, smeared her head with *āmalaka* paste, and descending into the water, she bent down and washed her head.
Then the other man emerged from among the trees, struck her on the neck bone, took her life, and went home.
Unable to renounce his affection for his wife, he was reborn in that very same house as a large lizard (*mahādhammani*).
He would go and fall upon her body whether she was standing or sitting. Then, thinking, "This must be that very same man," she had him killed.
Out of lingering affection for her, he was reborn again in that same house as a dog.
He was reborn. From the moment he began walking on foot, he followed right behind her.
Even when she went into the forest, he went along with her. Seeing him, people mocked them, saying, "A dog-catcher has come out;
where will he go? She had him killed once again.
He was reborn again in that very same house as a calf. He followed right behind her in the same manner.
Even then, when people saw him, they mocked them, saying, "The cowherd has gone out; where will the cows graze?
She had him killed in that place as well. Even then, he was unable to sever his affection for her.
Unable [to escape], he was reborn in her very womb for the fourth time, possessing the memory of his former births (*jātissara*).

Seeing that he had been killed by her in each of those four successive existences, he thought, "I have been born in the womb of such an enemy," and from then on, he would not allow her to touch him with her hand. If she...
She touches herself, weeps, and cries out. Then her grandfather looks after her. Later, when she had grown up, the grandfather said to her:
"My dear, why do you not allow yourself to be touched by your mother's hand?
Even if she touches you, you cry out and wail with a great sound. When questioned thus by his grandfather, she replied: "This is not my mother; she is an enemy."
He related the entire account, saying, "It is thus. He embraced him and wept, saying, "Come, dear one, what need have we to dwell in such a place?
Taking him with him, he departed, went to a certain monastery, and both of them, having gone forth there, attained arahantship while living together.
"Highly blameworthy" means it is highly blameworthy for two reasons: by way of being blameworthy in the world and by way of being blameworthy in its result.
How so? For one who has become corrupted by hatred offends even his mother, even his father, even his brothers and sisters and so forth, and even those who have gone forth.
Wherever he goes, [people say]: "This person offends even his mother and father, even his brothers and sisters..."
He incurs great censure even among those who have gone forth. Thus, first of all, it is a grave offense by way of worldly blame.

Furthermore, by way of its fault, one who has committed an act of immediate retribution (ānantariya-kamma) is tormented in hell for an eon; thus, it is a grave offense by way of its karmic result (vipāka).
"Quickly dispassionate" means that he quickly becomes free from passion; for one who is corrupted by hatred [feels it] even toward his mother and father, or even toward a shrine (cetiya).
Having committed an offense even against those who have gone forth for enlightenment, one confesses the transgression, saying, "Forgive me.
Through that very act of seeking forgiveness, the deed becomes as it was before.
Delusion (*moha*) is also greatly blameworthy for two reasons; for when one is deluded by delusion, [one commits offenses] even toward mother and father, or even toward a shrine (*cetiyā*).

Even if one does not offend against those who have gone forth for enlightenment, one receives censure wherever one goes. Thus, first of all, it is a grave offense by way of worldly transgression (*lokavajja*).

Furthermore, by performing an act of immediate retribution (*ānantariya-kamma*) through delusion (*moha*), one is cooked in hell for an eon (*kappa*); thus, it is also a grave offense by way of the ripening of its result (*vipākavajja*).
"Slowly fading away" (*dandhavirāgī*) means it fades away gradually. [This refers to what was done] by one deluded by ignorance.
For an action performed while deluded by ignorance is not released quickly; it is released only slowly.

Just as a piece of clear hide does not become white even when washed a hundred times, so too an action performed by one who is deluded by ignorance is not released swiftly; it is released only gradually.
The rest here is self-evident.
9. Commentary on the Discourse on the Roots of the Unwholesome (Akusalamūlasutta) 70.

Regarding the ninth [discourse]: "Roots of the unwholesome" (*akusalamūlāni*) means the roots of what is unwholesome; or, they are called "roots of the unwholesome" because they are both unwholesome and roots.

"Whatever greed there is, monks" (*yadapi, bhikkhave, lobho*) means: whatever greed there is, monks—that too is a root of the unwholesome (*tadapi akusalamūlaṃ*). That too is a root of the unwholesome.
Or, with reference to the unwholesome roots (*akusala-mūla*), the meaning "even that here" is indeed appropriate. By this method, the principle should be applied everywhere.
"He conditions" (*abhisaṅkharoti*) means he exerts himself, collects, and makes a heap.
"He produces suffering by means of what is non-existent" (*asatā*) means that by speaking of some unreal fault of his—something untrue and non-existent—he produces suffering. By killing...
This was said in order to show the manner in which wind and other such factors produce suffering. In that context, "loss" (*jāni*) refers to the loss of wealth.
"Banishment" (*pabbājanā*) refers to being banished from a village or a kingdom by means of a formal act of banishment (*pabbājanīyakamma*).
"I am strong" (*balavāmhi*) means "I possess strength. "And 'I have need of strength'" (*balattho itipi*) means he says, "I have a purpose for strength," or "I am established in strength."
"One who speaks at the wrong time" means he does not speak at the proper time; it is called speaking at the wrong time.

"One who speaks what is untrue" means he does not speak what is true; it is called speaking what is untrue. "One who speaks what is unbeneficial" means he does not speak what is beneficial; it is called speaking what is unbeneficial.

"One who speaks what is contrary to the Dhamma" means he does not speak the Dhamma; it is called speaking what is contrary to the Dhamma. "One who speaks what is contrary to the Vinaya" means he does not speak the Vinaya; it is called speaking what is contrary to the Vinaya.

"In such a way they diminish, for in such a way this [person] does not exert ardor for the unraveling of that"—this means he does not apply energy for the purpose of unraveling that which has arisen. "Thus this is untrue"—for this reason also, this is untrue.
The other [term] is a synonym for that very same thing.
"Anticipating an unhappy destination" means that an unhappy destination such as hell is to be expected;
it will inevitably happen to him, the sense being that he must be reborn there. "Overturned" means turned upside down. "Enveloped" means covered all over.
"He meets with misfortune" means he meets with lack of progress. "He meets with calamity" means he meets with ruin. For in the summer season...
When the *māluvā* creeper has borne fruit, the seeds fly off and fall at the roots of trees such as the banyan.

If three seeds have fallen at the root of a tree from three different directions, and that tree is rained upon by a rain-cloud, three sprouts will emerge from those three seeds and cling to that tree. Then...
From that time on, the tree deities were unable to maintain their own forms. Those sprouts, as they grew, took the form of creepers;
having climbed that tree, they entwined it with all its branches and sub-branches, completely enveloping the tree from above.
Thus entwined by the *māluvā* creepers, it was covered with thick, large *māluvā* leaves.
When it is covered by rain or when the wind blows, it will fall apart here and there until only a mere stump remains.
It was with reference to this that it was said.
As for the phrase "even so," the application of the simile here is as follows: just like a certain tree among the *sāla* trees and others...
This being is to be seen: the three unwholesome roots are like the three *māluvā* creepers.
Just as those creepers climb straight up the tree as long as they have not yet reached the branches, so too is the time when greed and the other [roots] have not yet reached their gateway.

The time of traveling along the branches is like the time of proceeding by way of the gateway; and the state of being completely enveloped is like [the state of being covered] by greed and the others.

The time of being overwhelmed is like the time when small branches are falling away; it is the time of having incurred minor and secondary offenses (āpatti) due to defilements (kilesa) that have reached the door.
The time of having incurred a grave offense is like the time when large branches are falling away.
It is like the time when a tree falls to the ground once its roots have become saturated by water descending along the creepers.
The time for being reborn in the four states of misery should be understood as occurring after one has gradually committed the four *pārājika* offenses.
The "white side" (the virtuous course) is to be understood by reversing what was stated above. Regarding the phrase "even so," here is the application of the simile:
