this sentient being is to be seen as like any one of the trees among the *sāla* trees and others; the three roots of unwholesomeness are like the three *māluva* creepers.
The practitioner of yoga is like the man who has come to bring about their non-occurrence; wisdom is like the hoe; the basket of faith is like the basket for the hoe;
insight-wisdom is like the digging spade; the time of cutting the root of ignorance with the knowledge of insight is like the cutting of the root with the spade;
and the time of cutting it into small pieces is like [the breaking up of the soil].
The time when [the aggregates] are seen by way of the aggregates is like the time of splitting [wood]. The time when defilements are eradicated by path-knowledge is like the time of making ink.
The time of the currently existing five aggregates is like the time of turning [the wood] into ink.

The time of not taking rebirth-linking in a future existence after the aggregates subject to clinging have ceased through non-relinking is like the time when [the wood] has been winnowed in a great wind and no longer functions.
"It should be seen": in this sutta, the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) and its cessation (vivaṭṭa) are explained.
10. Commentary on the Uposatha Sutta: 71.
Regarding "on that very day of the Uposatha," it means on that day which was the Uposatha; that is, on the day of the full-moon Uposatha.
This is what is said. "She approached" means that, having resolved upon the factors of the Uposatha, she approached with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings in her hands.
"Handa" is a particle used in the sense of an exhortation. "Divā divassā" means "in the middle of the day";
the meaning is "while standing in this midday time. "From where have you come?"—he asks this, [implying], "What are you doing as you wander about?"
The *gopālakuposatha* is the observance-day fast (upavasana-uposatha) together with cowherds. The *nigaṇṭhuposatha* is the observance-day fast of the Nigaṇṭhas.
The *ariyuposatha* is the observance-day fast of the Noble Ones (*ariya*).
"Just as, Visākhā" means, for example, Visākhā. Having returned the cows to their owners in the evening time—for cowherds [receive] daily wages—
Or they take and guard cows for a period of five days, ten days, half a month, a month, six months, or a year.
But here, this is said with reference to one who guards them for a daily wage—having "caused them to be led away" means having had them accepted and given [to him], saying, "These cows are yours.
Thus he reflects: having gone to his own home, having eaten, on his bed...
Lying down, he reflects thus: "With a mind accompanied by covetousness" means associated with craving.
"In this way, Visākhā, there is the cowherd’s uposatha"—this is indeed the noble uposatha, but because of its impure thoughts, it stands in the place of the cowherd’s uposatha.
"It is not of great fruit" means it is not of great fruit by way of its resultant fruit. "It is not of great benefit" means...

It is not of great benefit by way of the advantage of its kamma-result (*vipākānisamsa*). It is not of great radiance; that is, it does not possess a great effulgence by way of the light of its kamma-result.
It is not of great expansion; that is, it is not of great expansion because the expansion of its kamma-result is not great.
"Of the same class as recluses" means they are indeed recluses. "Beyond a hundred leagues" means having passed beyond a hundred leagues, further than that.
"Among them, lay down the rod": among those beings situated beyond a hundred leagues, lay down the rod;
be one who has laid down the rod. "I am not anything belonging to anyone anywhere": I do not exist as anything belonging to another anywhere.
"Belonging" (kiñcana) is said to mean an impediment (palibodha); it means "I am not an impediment," so it is said.

"Nothing exists anywhere for me": this means that for me, too, there is no possessiveness (*kiñcanatā*)—no impediment (*palibodha*)—regarding any single requisite, whether internally or externally; the meaning is: "I am one whose impediments have been severed.
"Possessions" (*bhoja*) refers to beds, chairs, rice-gruel, food, and so forth. "He uses them as if they were not given" means on the following day...
Whether lying on a couch, sitting on a chair, drinking rice-gruel, or eating a meal, he enjoys those riches without ever giving them away.
"Not of great fruit" means it is fruitless. For here, only the phrasing (*byañjana*) is incomplete, but the meaning (*attha*) is complete.
Indeed, even a very slight result of the maturation of an observance-day (*uposatha*) thus observed—

There is nothing called "desirable," "attractive," or "pleasing. Therefore, it should be understood that [the observance] is indeed fruitless. The same principle applies to the remaining phrases as well.
Why did he say, "of a defiled mind"? Because it was shown that an observance (uposatha) observed with a defiled mind does not bear great fruit;
thus, by implication, the fact that an observance observed with a purified mind bears great fruit is authorized.
Therefore, he said this in order to show that meditation subject which purifies the mind—that meditation subject by which the mind becomes purified.
In this context, "by means of an effort" means by one's own personal exertion or by a skillful method.
"He recollects the Tathāgata" means he recollects the qualities of the Tathāgata by way of eight reasons. For herein, [the first reason is]: "Indeed, he is the Blessed One."
Thus, by the phrases "endowed with such virtue" and "endowed with such concentration," all the mundane and supramundane qualities of a Buddha are included.

The terms "Arahant" and so forth merely indicate individual qualities. "The mind of one who recollects the Tathāgata becomes serene" means that the arising of consciousness in one who recollects the mundane and supramundane qualities of the Tathāgata becomes clear and confident.
The defilements of the mind are the five hindrances. *Kakka* refers to an ointment made from *āmalaka* fruit.

"Appropriate effort" means the effort consisting of smearing, rubbing, washing, and cleansing with such an ointment as is suitable and appropriate for that purpose. "Purification" means the making of a state of purity.
For indeed, one who is sporting at a festival does not shine if he applies ornaments while his head is soiled.
But when that [body] is purified, one shines while sporting at the festival after having adorned oneself with ornaments;

even so, the Uposatha observed by one who has resolved upon the Uposatha factors with a defiled mind is not of great fruit, whereas the Uposatha observed by one who has resolved upon the Uposatha factors with a completely pure mind is of great fruit— this is the intended meaning.
Thus it was said: "He observes the Brahma-uposatha. The Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) is called "Brahmā";
by way of recollecting His qualities, this Uposatha is named the "Brahma-uposatha," and he observes it.
"He dwells together with Brahmā" means he dwells together with the Perfectly Enlightened One. "And having taken Brahmā as his object" means having taken the Perfectly Enlightened One as his object.
"He recollects the Dhamma" means he recollects the supramundane Dhamma together with its constituent factors (*sahantika*).

"A thread" refers to a *kuruvindaka* thread. For, having mixed lac with *kuruvindaka* stone powder, having made beads, pierced them, and strung them on a thread, they take hold of both ends of that stringed cluster of beads and rub them against their backs; it is with reference to this that it was said.
“‘And depending on soap’: ‘Powder’ means bath-powder. ‘The appropriate effort’ refers to the effort corresponding to that, such as rubbing, scrubbing, and washing.
‘The Dhamma Uposatha’: because this Uposatha is observed by taking as its object the nine supramundane states together with their concomitants, it is called the ‘Dhamma Uposatha.
Here too, the construction should be made by standing upon the word ‘cleansing’ (*pariyodapanā*) in the same manner as before.”
"He recollects the Saṅgha" means he recollects the qualities of the eight noble persons (*ariyapuggala*).
"And depending on heat" means depending on the warmth that has been applied two or three times. There is also a reading *usaṃ*, which has the same meaning. "Ashes" refers to lime-dust.
"Cow dung" refers either to cow urine or to dried cow dung. "Purification" is to be construed here also according to the previous method.

It should be performed. Regarding the phrase "the Saṅgha Uposatha": this Uposatha is called the "Saṅgha Uposatha" because it is observed by taking as its object the virtues of the eight types of noble persons (ariyapuggala). Regarding the "precepts" (sīla):

a layperson [observes] the precepts of a layperson, and one who has gone forth [observes] the precepts of one who has gone forth. The meaning of the terms "unbroken" (akhaṇḍa) and so forth is as follows: [text continues].
This has indeed been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*. "Vālaṇḍupaka" refers to a scrubber made from horse-hair or from materials such as the fibers of a *makaci* tree.
"Appropriate effort" (*tajja-vāyāma*) means the effort of scrubbing with the hair-scrubber after moistening it with oil, knowing that the dirt has become saturated, and then adding ash.
This construction should be applied by standing upon the word "cleansing" (*pariyodapana*) here.
For when a mirror is soiled, even if one’s own person is adorned and beautified, it does not shine when looked upon; when it is pure, it shines.
In the same way, the *uposatha* observed with a defiled mind is not of great fruit, but when observed with a pure mind, it is of great fruit.
"The *uposatha* of virtue" refers to the *uposatha* observed by means of recollecting one's own virtues.
This is called the Uposatha of virtue (*sīluposatha*). "Together with virtue" means together with one's own fivefold or tenfold virtue.
"Taking virtue as his basis" means taking the fivefold and tenfold virtue as his basis.
"He recollects the deities" means that, having placed the deities in the position of witnesses, he recollects his own qualities such as faith.
*Ukkanti* means a furnace. *Loṇaṃ* means salt-clay. *Gerukaṃ* means red-ochre powder. *Nāḷikasaṇḍāsaṃ* means both the blow-pipe and the tongs for turning.
*Tajjaṃ vāyāmaṃ* means the appropriate effort such as placing [the metal] in the furnace, blowing, and turning it.
Here, standing upon the word *pariyodapanaṃ*, the construction should be understood thus: by means of a vessel made of purified gold...
For women adorned with ornaments made of ordinary metal do not shine while sporting at a festival; they shine when adorned with ornaments made of pure gold.
In the same way, the Uposatha of one with a defiled mind is not of great fruit, whereas that of one with a pure mind is of great fruit.
"The Uposatha of the deities" means: by placing the deities in the position of witnesses and recollecting one's own virtues.

The observance of the Uposatha is called the "Deva-Uposatha. Regarding the rest of what ought to be said concerning these meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) such as the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati) and so forth, all of that has already been stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.

"Killing living beings" (pāṇātipāta) means the slaughter of living beings. "Having abandoned" (pahāya) means having relinquished that misconduct (dussīlya) consisting of the volition (cetanā) of killing living beings.
"Abstaining" means that from the moment [the unwholesome state] has been abandoned, one has indeed desisted and refrained from that misconduct.
"With staff laid aside, with weapon laid aside" means that because they do not take up a staff or a weapon for the purpose of harming others, they have set aside the staff and set aside the weapon;
this is the meaning. And here, with the exception of the staff, all remaining implements are included because they possess the nature of harming living beings.

It should be understood that this refers to a weapon (*sattha*). However, when monks wander about carrying walking sticks, tooth-stick scrapers, or small knives, they do not do so for the purpose of harming others.
Therefore, they are reckoned as those who have laid aside the weapon because they have laid aside the stick (*daṇḍa*).
"Conscientious" (*lajjī*) means endowed with a sense of shame characterized by a loathing for evil. "Compassionate" (*dayāpanna*)...
They have attained compassion and a mind of loving-kindness (*mettā*). "Compassionate toward the welfare of all breathing beings" means they are sympathetic toward the welfare of all living beings;
the meaning is that by virtue of having attained that very compassion, they possess a heart of benevolence toward all living beings. "I too today" means "I also today.
"By this factor as well" means by this quality-factor (*guṇa-aṅga*) as well. "I emulate the Arahants" means just as [they did] when walking in front...
"One who follows behind is said to 'follow after'; likewise, by performing later this same quality that was first performed by the Arahants, I am emulating those Arahants.
By doing so, thinking, 'The Uposatha will have been observed by me,' I shall both have emulated the Arahants and the Uposatha will have been observed."
*Adinnādānaṃ* means the taking of what is not given, that which is owned by another; the meaning is theft or robbery. *Dinnādāyī* means those who take only what is given.
*Dinnapāṭikaṅkhī* means those who expect only what has been given, even in their thoughts.
*Theno* means one who steals; *athena* means one who does not steal. Precisely because of this non-stealing, it is "pure. *Attanā* means by way of one's own person (*attabhāvena*); [he is] pure.
It is said that they dwell having made their own person pure. "Unholy life" (*abrahmacariya*) means a non-noble way of life.
One who practices the noble (*brahma*), supreme conduct is a "practitioner of the holy life" (*brahmacārī*). An "ārācārī" is one who lives far removed from unholy life.
Regarding "sexual intercourse": because they are alike in being overwhelmed by lust, they are called "those engaged in sexual union" (*methunaka*).

"Unrighteous practices" (*asaddhamma*) are so designated because they are practiced by those who have entered into worldly conventions as "sexual intercourse. "Village-dharma" (*gāmadhamma*) refers to the practices of village dwellers.

"False speech" (*musāvāda*) means untrue or empty words. "Truth-tellers" (*saccavādī*) are those who speak the truth. "Those who bind themselves with truth" (*saccasandha*) are those who touch upon or confirm the truth with truth;
the meaning is that they do not speak falsely from time to time. For a man who...
He speaks falsehood, though occasionally he speaks truth. Because his speech is obstructed by falsehood, his truth does not cohere with truth.
Therefore, he is not one whose bond is truth. But these [others] are not like that; even for the sake of their lives, they do not speak falsehood, but rather join truth with truth.
Thus, they are "those whose bond is truth" (*saccasaṃdhā*). "Firm" (*theta*) means stable; the meaning is that their speech is steadfast. One person is like the dye of turmeric.
Like a pillar sunk in a heap of chaff, or like a gourd placed on the back of a horse, he does not maintain his speech.

One who maintains his speech like a line carved in stone or like a city-gate post—such that even when his head is being severed with a sword, he does not utter two words—is called *theto* (steadfast).
*Paccayikā* means those who are to be trusted; *saddhāyikā* means those who are to be believed.
The meaning is as follows. For one kind of person is not trustworthy; when it is said, "This was spoken by whom?
By such-and-such a person," he becomes subject to being told, "Do not believe his word. Another is trustworthy; when it is said, "This was spoken by whom?
By such-and-such a person," [he thinks], "If it was spoken by him, this alone is the authority; it should not now be rejected."
"...there is not; it is exactly so," thus he becomes one who speaks in such a way. This is called "one who possesses the conditions" (*paccayika*).
"Not deceiving the world" means that by virtue of his truthful speech, he does not deceive the world.
"The basis for negligence consisting of fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants" refers to the cause of negligence known as the volition of drinking fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants.
“Eating one meal a day” (*ekabhattika*) means there are two meals: the morning meal (*pātarāsa-bhatta*) and the evening meal (*sāyamāsa-bhatta*).
Of these, the morning meal is delimited by the end of midday, while the other is from after midday until before dawn.
Therefore, even if one eats ten times within the period of midday, one is still considered an “eater of one meal a day. It is with reference to this that it is said: “eaters of one meal a day.”
"Eating at night" is *ratti*; one who has desisted from that is "one who has desisted from eating at night" (*rattūparatā*).
Eating after midday until the setting of the sun is called "eating at the improper time" (*vikālabhojana*); because of abstaining from that, one is "abstinent from eating at the improper time.

Because it is contrary to the Teaching, seeing what is unsuitable—that is, that which acts as an obstacle—is "seeing unsuitable sights" (*visūkadassana*); [this refers to] by means of dancing oneself or causing others to dance, and so forth.
"Dancing, singing, and instrumental music," as well as the viewing of spectacles—
even those consisting of things like peacock dances— is what is meant by "dancing, singing, instrumental music, and witnessing spectacles. Indeed,
for neither monks nor nuns is it permissible to personally engage in dancing and so forth, to cause others to engage in them, or even to watch them when they have been performed.
Regarding "garlands" and so forth: "garland" refers to any kind of flower; "scent" refers to any kind of fragrant substance; "unguent" refers to that which colors the skin.
In this context, one who wears them is said to "wear"; one who fills out deficient parts is said to "adorn";
and one who relishes them by way of scent and by way of coloring the skin is said to "beautify. "Place" (ṭhāna) means cause; therefore, by whatever unvirtuous volition—
The meaning is that he abstains from those things such as wearing garlands and so forth, which the great multitude of people practices.
"High bed" refers to one exceeding the prescribed measure; "luxurious bed" refers to an unworthy covering; the meaning is that he abstains from these.
"How great is the fruit? means to what extent is the fruit great. This same method applies to the remaining phrases as well. "Abounding in various red jewels..."

The meaning is: for those endowed with abundant wealth reckoned as "red" (ratta), which is to say jewels (ratana), having made the entire surface of Jambudīpa like the surface of a drum, it was filled with seven kinds of jewels reaching up to the waist.
*Issariyādhipaccaṃ* means sovereignty (*issariya*) by way of lordship (*issara*), or lordship itself as sovereignty; here, sovereignty does not refer even to a tyrannical act. *Rajjaṃ*.
"Should exercise" means he should exercise such sovereignty as that of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*). "Limbs," etc., are the names of those constituent parts of his realm.
"It is not worth a sixteenth part" means that if the merit of having observed the *uposatha* for a single day and night were divided into sixteen portions, it would not even equal one portion.
This refers to the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) resulting from a sixteenth part of a single night’s *uposatha*.
The meaning is that it becomes much greater than that. "Kapaṇaṃ" means meager. "Abrahmacariyā" means from the conduct of one who is not noble.
"Rattiṃ na bhuñjeyya vikālabhojanaṃ" means that while observing the Uposatha, one should not eat at night nor eat at an improper time during the day.
"Mañce chamāyaṃ va sayetha santhate" means one should lie down either on a bed or on the ground spread with a mat.

The meaning is that one should lie down on a bed made of hands, feet, or fists— whether it be a permissible bed (*kappiya-mañca*) or a surface prepared with plaster and the like, or a spread made by laying down grass, leaves, straw, and so forth.
For this is called the "eight-factored Uposatha" because the Uposatha observed by one who refrains from taking life and the other [unwholesome deeds] is endowed with eight factors.

They say it is "eightfold. Furthermore, by one who is observing the fast, on the very day [prior], thinking, "Tomorrow I shall observe the Uposatha," the arrangements for food and so forth must be considered, saying, "You should do this and that.
On the Uposatha day, early in the morning, in the presence of a bhikkhu, a bhikkhunī, or a lay follower (upāsaka) or lay follower (upāsikā) who knows the characteristics of the ten precepts—
Having broken one’s speech [of silence], the factors of the Uposatha should be undertaken. However, by one who does not know the Pāḷi, it should be resolved thus:
"I resolve upon the Uposatha prescribed by the Buddha. If no other person is available, one may resolve it oneself;
nevertheless, a verbal expression must indeed be made. By one observing the Uposatha, occupations connected with the obstruction of others [should be avoided].
One should not engage in investigation; one should not spend time calculating income and expenditure.

However, having obtained food at home and consumed it like a bhikkhu who eats a regular meal, one should go to the monastery and either listen to the Dhamma or attend to one of the thirty-eight meditation objects.
"Sudassanā" means beautiful to behold. "Obhāsayanti" means illuminating. "Anupariyanti" means they move about.
"Yāvatā" means as much space as there is. "Antalikkhagā" means those who travel through the sky. "Pabhāsanti" means they shine, emitting radiance.
"Disāvirocanā" means shining in all directions; or alternatively, "pabhāsanti" means they illuminate direction after direction.
“Virocanā” means shining. Although he says “veḷuriya-maṇi,” by this he shows that it is a natural gem (*jātimaṇi*).
For a veḷuriya the color of a one-year-old bamboo is called a natural gem; it is with reference to this that he spoke thus. “Bhaddaka” means obtained.
“Siṅgīsuvaṇṇa” is gold so named because it arises resembling the *siṅgisu* (the horn of a cow). “Kañcana” refers to mountain-gold found on a mountain.
*Jātasuvaṇṇaṃ*: "Born-gold" refers to gold of natural color. *Haṭakaṃ*: "Extracted gold" refers to gold extracted by ants. *Nānubhavanti*:
"They do not experience" means they do not attain. *Candappabhā*: The nominative case is used in the sense of the genitive; the meaning is "of the moon's radiance. *Upavassuposathaṃ*:
Having observed the fast, [they observe] the Uposatha. *Sukhudrayāni*: "Having happy results" means having pleasant fruits, to be experienced as pleasure.
“They go to the heavenly state” means they approach the place designated as heaven; the sense is that, being beyond reproach by anyone, they arise in the world of the devas.
Whatever else has not been stated here in between should be understood according to what has already been said.
The second Great Chapter.
(8) 3. The Chapter on Ānanda. 1.
Commentary on the Channa Sutta. 72.
Regarding the first [sutta] of the third [chapter]: *Channo* refers to the wanderer named Channa. *Tumhepi, āvuso* means "you too, friend."
He asks: "Just as we teach the abandoning of lust and the other defilements, do you also teach it in this way?

Then the Elder, rejecting that by saying, "This wanderer says, 'Teach us the abandoning of lust and the other defilements,' but this does not exist in the external systems," spoke the words beginning with "We indeed, friends... Therein, *kho* is used in the sense of emphasis.
The meaning is: "This is a mere conventional expression; we ourselves shall define it. Then the wanderer thought:
"This elder, while plucking away the doctrines of outsiders, says 'we ourselves. What disadvantage must they have seen that they prescribe the abandoning of these things?
Then, questioning the elder, he said: "But what, venerable sir... and so forth. The elder, answering him, said: "One who is lustful... and so forth.

In this context, "one's own welfare" (*attattha*) refers to one’s own benefit pertaining to both the present life and future lives, as well as to the mundane and supramundane. The same principle applies to "the welfare of others" (*parattha*) and "the welfare of both" (*ubhayattha*).

Regarding the terms "causing blindness" (*andhakaraṇo*) and so forth: it is called "causing blindness" because when lust arises in someone, it makes them blind by obstructing their vision of things as they truly are (*yathābhūta-dassana*).

It is called "causing sightlessness" (*acakkhukaraṇo*) because it does not produce the eye of wisdom (*paññā-cakkhu*). It is called "causing ignorance" (*aññāṇakaraṇo*) because it does not produce knowledge (*ñāṇa*).

It is "one that causes the cessation of wisdom" because it brings about the cessation—by way of non-arising—of these three types of wisdom: the wisdom of self-agency (*kammassakata-paññā*), the wisdom of meditative absorption (*jhāna-paññā*), and the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*).
It is "on the side of affliction" because, by yielding undesirable fruits, it falls on the side of affliction (*vighāta*) which is synonymous with suffering.
It is "not conducive to Nibbāna" because it does not lead to the extinction of the defilements (*kilesa-nibbāna*). And yet, friend, it is sufficient...
"Ānanda, 'through diligence,' friend Ānanda—if such a practice exists, it is sufficient for you;
it is fitting and appropriate for you to be diligent. Be diligent, friends! Having thus expressed his appreciation for the elder’s words, he departed.
In this sutta, the Noble Path is taught as mixed with the supramundane. The rest here is of plain meaning.
2. Commentary on the Ājīvaka Sutta (73).
Regarding the second [discourse], "In that case, householder," it is said that the Elder thought: "This man did not come here desiring merely to gain knowledge;
rather, he has come for the sake of testing me. I shall answer the question asked by him with that very same [teaching]."
Thus, wishing to have him explain that very same point, he said, "Therefore, etc. Therein, "therefore" (*tena hi*) is a statement of reason:
"Since you ask thus, therefore I shall question you on that very matter here. "Of whom? (*kesaṃ nu*) means "of which ones?

"Exalting one's own doctrine" (*sadhammukkaṃsanā*) is the act of setting forth one's own view by way of exaltation. "Disparaging the doctrines of others" (*paradhammāpasādanā*) refers to [the disparagement] of others'...
"By their tenets" means by their contact, their disparagement, and their rejection. "Teaching the Dhamma only in accordance with the occasion" means teaching the Dhamma only for a specific reason.

"And the meaning has been stated" means that the meaning of the question asked by me has been clarified. "And the self has not been introduced" means that we have not been presented as being of such a nature;
thus the self has not been introduced. There is also a reading: *nupanīto* (not introduced).
3. Commentary on the Mahānāma Sutta of the Sakyans 74.
In the third [sutta], "recovered from illness" means having recovered after being ill. "From illness" means from the state of being ill.
"Approached" means that, having eaten his morning meal and taken flowers, perfumes, and so forth, he approached surrounded by a large retinue. "Taking him by the arm" means...
It should be understood that he did not pull him by the arm; rather, rising from his seat, he went to him, signaled with his right thumb on the [other's] right arm, and led him aside.

Then, having explained to him—in the manner beginning with "Mahānāma, there is indeed the virtue of one in training"—the virtue, concentration, and wisdom of the seven types of trainees, [he spoke] further...

Explaining the virtues, concentration, and wisdom of one beyond training (asekha) by way of the fruit of arahantship, he demonstrated: “After the concentration of one in training (sekha), the insight-knowledge of one in training and the fruition-knowledge of one beyond training arise later; and after the insight-knowledge of one in training, the concentration of the fruition of one beyond training arises later.
However, it should be understood that for those associated [mental states] consisting of concentration and knowledge, their arising is neither successive nor simultaneous.
4. Commentary on the Nigaṇṭha Sutta 75.
In the fourth [discourse], "in the hall with the peaked roof" refers to the fragrant chamber (*gandhakuṭi*) constructed with two corner-arches and covered with a *haṃsavaṭṭaka* roof.
"He claims to possess knowledge and vision without remainder" means that he claims to possess all knowledge and vision, leaving nothing even the slightest behind.
He declares: "Constantly and continuously" means at all times, without interruption.
"Knowledge and vision are established" shows that omniscient knowledge is indeed present before me. "Of past karmas" refers to karmas already accumulated.
"By means of asceticism, their exhaustion" means the bringing about of their disappearance through difficult austerities. "Of new karmas" refers to karmas being accumulated now.
"Non-doing" means by way of non-accumulation. "The destruction of the bridge" refers to the destruction of the path and the destruction of the condition.

"With the destruction of karma, there is the destruction of suffering" means that with the destruction of the cycle of karma, there is the destruction of suffering. "With the destruction of suffering, there is the destruction of feeling" means that with the destruction of the cycle of suffering, there is the destruction of feeling;
for when the cycle of suffering is exhausted, the cycle of feeling is likewise exhausted. With the destruction of feeling...
"All suffering will be worn away" means that through the destruction of feeling (*vedanā-kkhaya*), the entire suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa-dukkha*) will indeed be worn away.
"Visible here and now" (*saṃdiṭṭhikāya*) means it is to be seen by oneself, directly perceived. "Through wearing away for the sake of purification" (*nijjarāya visuddhiyā*) means:

through the practice that wears away the defilements (*kilesa*), or because of the wearing away of defilements, there is the purification of beings through wearing away (*nijjarā*). This is the transcendence (*samatikkama*).
"It occurs" means that there is a transcendence of the entire suffering of saṃsāra. "In this regard, Bhante, what does the Blessed One say?"—Bhante, he asks:
regarding this practice, what does the Blessed One say? Does he prescribe this very path for the wearing away of the defilements, or is it something else?
"Knowing" means by one who knows with unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*). "Seeing" means by one who sees with the universal eye (*samantacakkhu*).

"For the sake of purification" means for the purpose of attaining purification. "For the sake of transcending" means for the purpose of transcending. "For the sake of the setting [of the sun]" means for the purpose of going to its setting.
"For the sake of the attainment of the method" means for the purpose of attaining the path together with insight (*vipassanā*). [And] for the sake of *Nibbāna*...
"For the sake of realization" means for the purpose of realizing *nibbāna*, which is free from conditions.
"And he does not perform new karma" means he does not accumulate new karma. "And old karma" refers to karma accumulated in the past.
"He makes it vanish as he contacts it, contact after contact" means that having contacted it, contact after contact—having contacted the contact of ripening—he brings it to its end.
The meaning is that it exhausts karma. "Visible here and now" (sanditthika) means it is to be seen by oneself. "Timeless" (akālika) means it does not perform its function at some other time.

"Inviting one to come and see" (ehipassika) means it is suitable to be shown by saying, "Come and see. "Leading onward" (opanayika) means it is suitable for leading forward, suitable for being relied upon.
"To be personally realized by the wise" (paccattaṃ veditabbo viññūhi) means it is to be known within their own individual mental continua by the wise, but not by fools.

But they are difficult to discern. Thus, by way of virtue (*sīla*), two paths and two fruits have been explained; for the stream-enterer and the once-returner are those who fulfill their practice in virtue.

Furthermore, by way of the perfection of concentration (*samādhi*)—beginning with "quite secluded from sensual pleasures"—three paths and three fruits have been explained; for the noble disciple who is a non-returner is one who fulfills his practice in concentration.

It has been stated. By the words "the destruction of the taints" (*āsavānaṃ khaya*) and so forth, the fruit of arahantship is described. However, some maintain that virtue (*sīla*) and concentration (*samādhi*) are also intended here as being associated with the fruit of arahantship;
yet, they are presented separately in the discourse (*tanti*) for the purpose of showing the practice according to each one individually.
5. Commentary on the *Nivesaka Sutta* (The Discourse on the Settlers)

76. "Ministers" (amaccā) means close friends. "Relatives" (ñātī) means those on the side of one's father-in-law and mother-in-law. "Kinsmen" (sālohitā) means those of the same blood, such as brothers, sisters, and so forth.
"Unshakable confidence" (aveccappasāda) refers to the immovable confidence that has arisen through having understood the qualities [of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Sangha] by penetrating them.
"Alteration" (aññathatta) means a change in state. Regarding the twenty parts beginning with "the earth element" (pathavīdhātu), it refers to the earth element which consists of the mode of hardness.

There might be a change in the water element, which acts as a binding agent present in the twelve portions; there might be a change in the fire element, which acts as a digestive agent present in the four portions;
and there might be a change in the air element, which acts as a distending agent present in the six portions.
But "not even thus" means that there could not be a change in these four great elements by way of their mutual transformation into one another.

But it shows that for the noble disciple (ariyasāvaka), it is not so. And here, "alteration" (aññathatta) refers both to the alteration of confidence (pasāda) and the alteration of destination (gati).
For that [alteration] does not occur for him; rather, there is an alteration of state (bhāva).
For the noble disciple, having been a human, may also become a deva or even a Brahmā. However, his confidence does not vanish even in another existence. It does not...
And he reaches a change of state in his destiny, known as a destination of woe. The Teacher, demonstrating that very point, said:
"In this regard, this is the change of state," and so forth. The rest here is of plain meaning.
6. Commentary on the First Bhavasutta.

77. In the sixth [verse], "ripening in the sense-sphere realm" (*kāmadhātuvepakkam*) means that which ripens within the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*). "Sense-sphere existence" (*kāmabhava*) refers to the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*) within the sense-sphere realm.
"Karma is the field" (*kammaṃ khettam*): wholesome and unwholesome karma is the field in the sense of being the place where [results] grow.

"Consciousness is the seed" (*viññāṇaṃ bījam*): the co-nascent consciousness of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇa*) is the seed in the sense of growing. "Craving is the moisture" (*taṇhā sneho*)...
Craving is called "water" by way of its grasping and swelling. "Obscured by ignorance" means obscured by ignorance.
"Bound by the fetter of craving" means bound by the bond of craving. "In the inferior element" means in the sense-sphere element (kāmadhātu).
"Consciousness has become established" means the consciousness of volitional formations has become established. "In the middling element" means in the fine-material element (rūpadhātu).
"By means of a sublime element" refers to the formless element (*arūpadhātu*). The rest here is of plain meaning. 7.
Commentary on the Second Discourse on Existence (Bhava-sutta) 78.
In the seventh [discourse], "volition" (*cetanā*) is volitional action (*kamma-cetanā*). "Aspiration" (*patthanā*) is likewise aspiration for action (*kamma-patthanā*). The rest is exactly as before.
8. Commentary on the Sīlabbata Sutta (79).
In the eighth [sutta], *sīlabbata* means both virtue (*sīla*) and observance (*vata*). *Jīvita* refers to the pursuit of the practice of austerities.
*Brahmacariya* refers to the life of holy living. *Upaṭṭhānasāra* means having service as its essence, thinking: "This is the best; this is the ultimate goal."
"Established in this way" is the meaning. "With fruit" means it becomes accompanied by benefit and increase; thus he asks.
"But not categorically here, venerable sir"—the meaning is that this should not be explained categorically here. "One who cultivates what has attendance as its essence":
for one who cultivates what is established in this way, this is the essence, the excellence, and the culmination. "Without fruit" means without the desired fruit.

"Without fruit": by this much, all other non-Buddhist systems (bāhiraka-samaya) are included, with the exception of the renunciations of those who maintain the doctrine of karma and the doctrine of action.
"With fruit": it is fruitful because it possesses desirable fruits; it is accompanied by excellence.

By this much, starting from this very teaching (sāsana), all the renunciations of those who maintain the doctrine of karma and the doctrine of action are included. And yet, it is not easily found as being exactly equal to that.
"By wisdom": this shows that it would not be easy to find anyone equal to Ānanda in wisdom when he speaks on a question while standing upon the plane of one in training (*sekkhabhūmi*).
In this sutta, what is called "the plane of one in training" is thus explained.
9. Commentary on the Gandhajāta Sutta.

80. In the ninth [chapter], with the words "he said this," it means that after returning from his alms-round following the meal, having performed the duties for the One of Ten Powers, he went to his own place for the midday rest and thought:

"In this world there is such a thing as the scent of roots, there is the scent of heartwood, and there is the scent of flowers. Yet these three kinds of scents travel only with the wind; they do not [travel against it]."
"Is there anything whose fragrance travels even against the wind?

Having thought this, because he had chosen the privilege of approaching at the very moment his doubt arose—precisely when he was choosing the eight boons—he immediately rose from his daytime resting place, went into the presence of the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down to one side. With the doubt that had arisen...
In order to dispel his doubt, he spoke these words beginning with, "Venerable sir, there are these three...
In this context, *gandhajātāni* means types of fragrance. *Mūlagandha* is a fragrance based on roots, or rather, the root itself when it is endowed with fragrance;
for its scent travels with the wind. However, there is no such thing as the "scent of a scent. This applies to fragrances of heartwood and fragrances of flowers as well.

The same method applies here. Regarding the phrase "There is, Ānanda, a certain kind of fragrance": herein, the taking of refuge and so forth are called "fragrances" because they resemble fragrances in their quality of spreading in all directions by way of proclaiming one's virtues.
The person who is the basis for these is called a "source of fragrance.
It is said that "the fragrance goes" because it goes by way of proclaiming one's virtues. "Virtuous" means either by way of the five precepts or the ten precepts.
Or he is virtuous. "Of lovely nature" means that by virtue of that very quality of virtue, he is of lovely nature, of beautiful nature.

The meaning of "with the stain of stinginess removed," and so forth, has already been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*. "In the directions" means in the four cardinal directions and the four intermediate directions.
"Ascetics and brahmins" refers to those who have stilled evil and cast out evil; these are the ascetics and brahmins.
"The fragrance of flowers does not go against the wind" means that the scent of jasmine and other such flowers does not travel against the wind.
"Neither sandalwood, nor tagara, nor mallikā wafts [against the wind]" means that even the fragrance of sandalwood, tagara, and mallikā does not go against the wind.
In the world of the devas, there is a flower called *phuṭasumana*; on the day it blooms, its fragrance extends for a hundred *yojanas*.
It overspreads. They say that even such a scent cannot travel against the wind for even a span’s length or the distance of a jewel’s throw.

"The scent of the good goes against the wind" means that the fragrance of the virtues—such as moral discipline—of the wise, namely Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the sons of the Buddha, travels against the wind.
"A true person wafts in all directions" means that a true person is a wise one.
The meaning is: by the fragrance of qualities such as virtue, he wafts through all directions; he pervades all directions with that fragrance. 10. Commentary on the Cūḷanikāsutta. 81.
There are two ways of introducing the tenth [sutta]: arising from a specific occasion (*atthuppatti*) or prompted by a question (*pucchāvasika*). In which specific occasion does it arise?

If it is asked, "In response to whose question was this spoken?"—it was spoken in response to the question of the Elder Ānanda during the introductory narrative (*atthuppatti*) of the *Aruṇavati-sutta*.
If it is asked, "By whom was the *Aruṇavati-sutta* spoken?"—it was spoken by two Buddhas:
by the Blessed One Sikhī and by our own Teacher. For thirty-one eons ago from this present eon, in the city of Aruṇavatī, [there lived] Aruṇavata...
Having been born from the womb of the King’s chief queen named Pabhāvati, and having gone forth on the Great Renunciation once his knowledge had matured,
the Blessed One Sikhī— having penetrated the knowledge of omniscience at the seat of enlightenment and set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma—
was dwelling near Aruṇavatī. One day, early in the morning, after tending to his body, he was surrounded by a great community of monks.
Thinking, “I shall enter Aruṇavatī for alms,” he went out and stood near the gatehouse of the monastery.
There he addressed his chief disciple named Abhibhū: “It is still too early, monk, to enter Aruṇavatī for alms;
let us go to a certain Brahmā-world. As it is said:
“Then, monks, the Blessed One Sikhi, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, addressed the monk Abhibhū:
‘Come, brahmin, let us go to a certain Brahmā world; it will not yet be time for the meal.
‘Very well, Bhante,’ the monk Abhibhū replied to the Blessed One Sikhi.”
He replied to the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Then, monks, the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, and the bhikkhu Abhibhū approached a certain Brahma-world.
There, having seen the Perfectly Enlightened One, Mahābrahmā was delighted; he went out to meet him and offered him a Brahma-throne.
Having prepared it, he gave it to him; they also prepared a seat suitable for the Elder.
The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat, and the Elder also sat down on his own prepared seat. Mahābrahmā too, having paid homage to the One of Ten Powers, sat down to one side.
Then, monks, the Blessed One Sikhī addressed the bhikkhu Abhibhū: “May it occur to you, brahmin.”
“A Dhamma talk for Brahmā, for the assembly of Brahmā, and for the retinue of Brahmā.

“So be it, Bhante,” the bhikkhu Abhibhū replied to the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, and he delivered a Dhamma talk for Brahmā, for the assembly of Brahmā, and for the retinue of Brahmā. There...
While he was preaching the Dhamma, the hosts of Brahmās complained: "It has been a long time since we have had the opportunity to see the Teacher come to the Brahma-world;
yet this bhikkhu, setting aside the Teacher, has himself begun a discourse on the Dhamma.
The Teacher, perceiving their displeasure, said this to the bhikkhu Abhibhū: "They are indeed complaining..."
“Those, brahmin, are Brahmā, the assembly of Brahmā, and the retinue of Brahmā. Therefore, brahmin, you should be even more deeply stirred.
The Elder, having accepted the Teacher’s words, performed various kinds of supernatural transformations and, making his voice heard throughout a thousandfold world-system, recited these two verses:
“Exert yourselves! Strive on! Apply yourselves with diligence to the Buddha’s teaching. Soon you shall make an end of suffering— For those who are heedful, there is no sorrow.”
But what did the Elder do to make himself known throughout the thousandfold world-system? First, having attained the blue kasiṇa, he enveloped everything in darkness.
Then, when beings wondered, "What is this darkness? and their attention was aroused, he showed them light.
To those who were investigating, "What is this light?", he revealed himself; thus the gods and humans within the thousandfold world-system [perceived him].
Raising their joined palms again and again, they stood there paying homage to the Elder alone.
The Elder, thinking, "Let the great multitude hear my voice as I teach the Dhamma," recited these verses.
All of them, having sat down in the midst of the assembled crowd, heard his voice as if he were teaching the Dhamma from right in their presence; the meaning also became clear to them.
Then the Blessed One, having returned with the Elder to Aruṇavatī and walked for alms, after his meal, upon returning from his alms round, asked the Saṅgha of bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, did you hear the verses being spoken by the bhikkhu Abhibhū while he was standing in the Brahmā world? They replied, “Yes, venerable sir.”
Manifesting the nature of what had been heard, they recited those same two verses. The Teacher, giving his approval by saying, "Excellent, excellent," brought the teaching to its conclusion.
Thus, this sutta was first spoken by the Blessed One Sikhī about thirty-one eons ago.
However, our own Blessed One, having attained omniscience and set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma, [spoke it] while residing near Sāvatthī.
While dwelling in Jeta’s Grove, on the full-moon day of the month of Jeṭṭhamūla, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus and began this Aruṇavatīsutta.

The Elder Ānanda, standing while fanning him with a fan, mastered the entire sutta from beginning to end without missing even a single syllable. On the following day, having returned from his almsround...
Having performed the duties toward the One Possessing the Ten Powers, he went to his own place for the midday rest;

then, after performing the duties toward his co-residents and pupils, they departed. He sat down reflecting upon the *Aruṇavati-sutta* spoken the previous day, and the entire discourse appeared clearly before him.
He thought: "The chief disciple of the Blessed One Sikhi was in the Brahma-world..."
"Standing within a thousand world-systems, dispelling the darkness, displaying the radiance of his body,
and making his own voice heard, he preached a discourse on the Dhamma"— this was what the Teacher spoke of yesterday. "If such is the range of a disciple,
how much further afield can the voice of a Perfectly Enlightened One reach, who has attained omniscience by fulfilling the ten perfections?"
“...should inform [the Saṅgha]. In order to dispel the doubt that had arisen in this way, he approached the Blessed One at that very moment and asked about the matter.
To show this point, it is said: “Then the Venerable Ānanda. In that context, “in my presence” means:
“This was heard by me while I was face-to-face [with the Buddha], not through hearsay, nor through a succession of messengers.”
It was with this intention that he spoke thus. "How much can he make known by his voice? means:
how far a distance is he able to make known by his voice, having dispelled the darkness with the radiance of his body? "He is a disciple, Ānanda;
the Tathāgatas are immeasurable"—the Blessed One said this with this intention: "Ānanda, what do you say? He is a disciple established in limited knowledge."
But the Tathāgatas, having fulfilled the ten perfections and attained omniscience, are immeasurable.
Like one who takes a speck of dust from the tip of a fingernail and compares it with the dust of the great earth, what is this that you say?
For the domain of the disciples is one thing, and the domain of the Buddhas is another; the range of the disciples is one thing, and the range of the Buddhas is another. It is different...
“The power belongs to the disciples; it is different for the Buddhas. Thus, with this intention, the Blessed One spoke of their immeasurability and became silent.
The Elder asked a second time. The Teacher said, “Ānanda, you are like one who, having taken hold of a keyhole, attempts to measure the infinite sky;
you are like one who, having taken hold of a cātaka bird, attempts to measure it with a garuḷa king of one hundred and fifty leagues; [you are like one who] with the trunk of an elephant...”
It was like one approaching the Great Gaṅgā after taking up water; like one approaching with seven verses after taking up water in a pit four spans deep;
like a Universal Monarch approaching a person who has received only a measure of boiled rice from a hollow stalk;
like Sakka, the King of the Devas, approaching a dust-demon; [and like the light of] a firefly.

Taking [the bowl] as if warming it with the radiance of the sun, he asked, "What is this you say? and after pointing this out, he remained silent, having stated once more that [the Buddha's power] was immeasurable.
Then the Elder thought: "The Teacher, though questioned by me, has not yet spoken;
well then, I shall entreat him a third time and cause him to let loose the lion’s roar of a Buddha. He made his request for the third time. To show that:
The passage beginning with "A third time... was spoken. Then the Blessed One, providing an explanation to him, said, "Have you heard them, Ānanda? and so forth. The Elder thought:
"The Teacher has remained silent after saying to me only this much, 'Ānanda, have you heard of the thousandfold minor world-system?
Now he will let out the lion's roar of a Buddha. Thus, entreating the Teacher, he said, "Now is the time for this, Blessed One," and so forth.
The Blessed One spoke the words beginning with "Therefore, Ānanda," in order to give a detailed explanation for him as well. Therein, "as far as" (*yāvatā*) means to whatever extent of space.
"The moon and the sun" (*candimasūriyā*) refers to both the moon and the sun. "They revolve" (*pariharanti*) means they move about.

"Illuminating all quarters" (*disā bhanti*) means they shine upon all directions. "Radiating" (*virocanā*) means shining brightly. By this much, he has defined the limits of a single world-system (*ekacakkavāḷa*).
This has been shown. Now, demonstrating that same [world-system] multiplied a thousandfold, he said:
"a thousandfold world. In that "thousandfold world" means in that thousandfold great chiliocosm (*sahassacakkavāḷa*).
"A thousand Cātumahārājika [heavens]" means a thousand divine worlds of the Four Great Kings. For in each individual great chiliocosm, there are four Great Kings.
Therefore, it is said, "four thousand Great Kings. By this same method, the meaning is to be understood in all instances.
"Cūḷanikā" means small. This is the domain of the disciples. But why was this brought up? It is for the purpose of showing the boundaries of the medium-sized world-system (lokadhātu).
"Yāvatā" means as many as there are. "Tāva sahassadhā" means by that same thousandfold division. "The two-thousandfold middle world-system":

having counted a thousand sets of a thousand world-spheres (cakkavāḷa), this world-system consisting of one hundred thousand world-spheres is called the two-thousandfold middle world-system. This is beyond the range of disciples; it is the range of Buddhas alone. Even in such a vast extent...
For it is shown that in such a place, the Tathāgatas, having dispelled the darkness and displayed the radiance of their bodies, are able to make themselves known by their voice.
By this much, what is called the "birth-field" (*jātikkhetta*) of the Buddhas is demonstrated.
For on the day when Bodhisattas, descending from the world of the gods in their final existence, take rebirth in the mother’s womb, [the earth trembles] from the womb...

On the day of the Great Departure, on the day of the Great Renunciation, and on the days of the attainment of full enlightenment, the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, the relinquishing of the life-force, and the final passing away (parinibbāna), this much of the world-system shakes.

Regarding the term *tisahassī mahāsahassī*: starting from the thousandfold system, it is the third, thus it is "three-thousandfold" (*tisahassī*); [the phrase] *sahassaṃ sahassadhā* means a thousandfold thousand.
Having calculated it as "middling," and having calculated it by multiplying it a thousandfold, it is called "great-thousandfold" (*mahāsahassī*) because it is calculated by great thousands.
At this point, the world-system measuring one hundred thousand million *cakkavāḷas* has been shown.
The Blessed One, if he so desired, could dispel the darkness over such an extent of space, display the radiance of his body, and make himself known by his voice.
But the Elder Tissa, son of the accountant, spoke thus: "The measure of the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system is not such as this.

For this is merely the teachers' mnemonic device for recitation—a point lost from oral tradition. Rather, the extent of one hundred thousand times ten million world-spheres is what is called the 'three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system.
For up to this point, the domain of the Blessed One’s authority was [described].

The name has been shown. For within this interval, the command of the Āṭānāṭiya Paritta, the Esigili Paritta, the Dhajagga Paritta, the Bojjhaṅga Paritta, the Khandha Paritta, the Mora Paritta, the Mettā Paritta, and the Ratana Paritta pervades.
As for the phrase "as far as one might wish," it indicates the extent of the field of influence; for there is no limit or boundary to the field of influence of the Buddhas.
There is no such thing; and regarding this state of non-existence, they bring forward this simile:
suppose someone were to fill as many world-systems as there are in a hundred thousand million world-systems, up to the Brahma-world, with mustard seeds;
and if someone were to come from the eastern direction, dropping a single mustard seed in each world-system, all those mustard seeds would eventually be exhausted, but not so [the number of beings].
The world-systems in the eastern direction; the same method applies to the southern and other directions as well. In this regard, there is nothing that is beyond the range of the Buddhas.
When this was said, the Elder reflected: "The Teacher has spoken thus:

'Ānanda, if he so desired, the Tathāgata could make himself heard by his voice throughout a triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system, or even as far as he might wish. Yet this world is uneven, and the world-systems are infinite."
In one place the sun has risen; in another place it is at midday; in another place it has set.
In one place it is the first watch of the night; in another place it is the middle watch; in another place it is the last watch.
Likewise, beings are intent on karma, intent on play, or intent on food; thus they are distracted by various such causes.
"And they are negligent. How indeed might the Teacher make them understand by means of a parable?
Having reflected thus, and desiring to cut through their doubt, he asked the Tathāgata, beginning with "But how, sir...
Then the Teacher, giving him an answer, said: "In this case, Ānanda, the Tathāgata... and so forth. Therein, "he should pervade with radiance" means:
He would pervade it with the radiance of his body. But what would he do while pervading it?
In whatever place the sun is visible, he would cause it to set by means of his own power;
but where it is not visible, he would raise it up and place it in the center. Then, wherever the sun is visible, the people there [would say]: "Just now—"

"The sun was seen [before], yet it has just now set; could this be a serpent-possession, or a possession by a spirit, a yakṣa, or a deity?"—such a thought they might conceive. But where it is not seen, there people think:
"The sun has just now set, yet it has just now risen again; what indeed is this—a serpent-possession, a spirit-possession, a yakṣa-possession, or a deity-possession?"

...some might give rise to the thought, "What is this? Then, as those people, having directed their attention toward both light and darkness, were searching, "By what condition does this arise?", the Teacher would enter the attainment of the blue kasiṇa and spread forth a vast darkness. Why?
For the purpose of generating terror in those beings who are preoccupied with karma and the like. Then, for them—
Knowing that [the world] had fallen into a state of terror, he would enter the attainment of the white kasiṇa and emit a thick, pale radiance of the Buddha’s rays;

as if at the moment when a thousand moons and a thousand suns rose simultaneously, he would instantly make the whole world one mass of light, even while emitting that illumination from an area of his body no larger than a sesame seed. For he [could illuminate] the earth of the world-system...

If one were to make a lamp-vessel from the great ocean, use the water as oil, and make Mount Sineru the wick, placing it upon another Mount Sineru and lighting it, it would illuminate only a single world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).
Beyond that, it would not be able to shed light even for the distance of a cubit.
But the Tathāgata, by means of a portion of his body the size of a sesame seed, sheds radiance.
Having released it, he would make the three thousandfold great thousandfold world-system one mass of light, or even more than that.
For so great indeed are the qualities of a Buddha.
"They would recognize that light" means that upon seeing that light, they would think: "By him the sun, which had both set and been made to rise..."
And seeing that the thick darkness had been dispelled, they would sit with palms joined in reverence, saying, "This is that man who has now brought light; oh, what a marvelous person!
"He should cause the sound to resound" means he should cause the sound of the Dhamma discourse to resound.
For suppose one were to make a single world-system mountain into a drum, the great earth into the drumhead, and Mount Sineru—
If one were to strike a staff after placing it upon another Mount Sineru, it would cause that sound to be heard only within a single world-system (*cakkavāḷa*),
and it would not be possible for it to extend even a single span (*vidatthi*) beyond that. But the Tathāgata, sitting cross-legged on a couch or a seat,
makes himself known by his voice throughout the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system (*tisahassimahāsahassilokadhātu*), or even beyond that.
"Furthermore, the Tathāgatas are thus of such great power. In this way, the Blessed One shows the field of his domain by means of this much alone.
And having heard this lion’s roar of the Buddha, strong rapture arose within the Elder;

through that rapture, uttering an inspired utterance (*udāna*), he said, "It is a gain for me," and so forth. Therein, "for whom the Teacher is thus of such great psychic power" refers to one for whom...
"My Teacher is so powerful; for me, having obtained such a powerful Teacher, it is a gain and a great blessing"—this is the meaning.

Or else: that I, having taken up the bowl and robe of such a Teacher, am able to wander about, to perform services for his feet and his back, and to provide him with water for washing his face and water for bathing—[this is a gain].
He spoke thus with the intention that, "I am able to sweep the Gandhakuṭi courtyard, to ask questions regarding arisen doubts, and to hear sweet discourses on the Dhamma;
all these are my gains and what I have well-obtained.

And herein, the Blessed One’s status as one of great psychic power (*mahiddhika*) is due to the greatness of his supernormal powers (*iddhi*), specifically those consisting of the hearing of sounds in darkness and light.

Their great majesty is to be understood through the very persistence of that [power]. "Udāyī" refers to the Elder Lāḷudāyī. It is said that in the past he lived harboring resentment toward his attendant elders.

Therefore, having now found the opportunity at the conclusion of this "Lion’s Roar of the Buddha," as if extinguishing a burning lamp-flame or striking a bull on the muzzle as it was walking along, [he acted].
As if overturning a bowl filled with food, he spoke thus, causing a breach in the Elder’s confidence.

When this had been said by the Venerable Udāyin, the Blessed One—just as a well-wishing person standing to one side might repeatedly call out "Come this way! Come this way! to a man who is trembling while standing on the edge of a precipice—said: *Evaṃ vutte bhagavā...* (When this had been said, the Blessed One... [and so forth].
Just as one would stop someone from saying such a thing, so too, in order to prevent the Elder Udāyin from speaking those words, [the Buddha] said: "Not so, Udāyin; not so, Udāyin!
In this context, *hi* is a mere particle; the meaning is "do not speak thus. "Great sovereignty" (*mahārajja*) refers to the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*).
Now, is it not the case that the Teacher has declared the great benefit of a single teaching of the Dhamma given to a disciple who has conceived faith to be immeasurable?
Why did he define the benefit of the faith that arose in him concerning this "Lion's Roar" of the Buddha?
Because the measure of the personal existence (*attabhāva*) of a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*) is limited to such an extent.
For even a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) of dull wisdom obtains personal existence among gods and humans for seven more times; thus, defining his destiny, he spoke in this way.
"In this very life" means while remaining in this very personal existence (*attabhāva*).

"He will attain final Nibbāna" means he will attain final Nibbāna by means of the unconditioned Nibbāna (*appaccaya-parinibbāna*). Thus, grasping the pinnacle by means of Nibbāna, [the Blessed One] brought this *Sīhanāda Sutta* to its conclusion.
The third chapter, the Ānanda-vagga.
(9) 4. The Chapter on Ascetics (Samaṇavagga). 1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Ascetic (Samaṇasutta). 82.

In the first [discourse] of the fourth [chapter], "belonging to an ascetic" (*samaṇiyāni*) means things belonging to an ascetic. "To be done by an ascetic" (*samaṇakaraṇīyāni*) means [to be done] by an ascetic.
The duties to be performed. Regarding the phrase “the undertaking of the training in higher virtue” and so forth: *samādāna* means taking up;
the undertaking, the taking up, the fulfilling of the training in higher virtue is “the undertaking of the training in higher virtue. The same method applies to the other two phrases as well.
Furthermore, in this context, the distinction should be understood as follows: virtue is “higher virtue,” mind is “higher mind,” and wisdom is “higher wisdom.”
In this context, the five precepts are called "virtue" (sīla); based upon that, the ten precepts are called "higher virtue" (adhisīla);
and based upon those, the fourfold purification of virtue is called "higher virtue. Furthermore, all mundane virtue is called "virtue," while supramundane virtue is "higher virtue";
because it is to be trained in, it is also called "training" (sikkhā). Sensual-sphere consciousness, however, is called "consciousness" (citta).

Based on that, there is what is called the higher mind (*adhicitta*) pertaining to the fine-material sphere; based on that, too, there is what is called the higher mind pertaining to the immaterial sphere.
Furthermore, all mundane consciousness is simply "consciousness," whereas supramundane consciousness is "higher mind. The same principle applies to wisdom (*paññā*).

Therefore—because these three are the duties of a recluse (*samaṇa*)—therefore. "Intense" (*tibba*) means thick or abundant. "Zeal" (*chanda*) is the wholesome desire characterized by the wish to act.
Thus, in this sutta, the three trainings—both mundane and supramundane—are explained.
2. Commentary on the Gadrabha Sutta: 83.
"From behind, from behind" means following after, following after. "I too am to be tamed, I too am to be tamed" means that I too...
One who says, "I am giving, I am giving," is speaking of a cow. "Just as with cows" means as it is with cows. For cows may be black, red, or white in color, but a donkey does not have such a color.
And just as the color is different, so too are the voice and the word different. The rest is self-evident. In this sutta as well, there are three...
"The training is said to be mixed.
3. Commentary on the Khettasutta: 84.
In the third [verse], "right from the start" means first of all. "He makes it well-plowed" means he makes it well-plowed with the plow.
"Sumatikataṃ" means well-straightened by means of wisdom (*mati*). "At the proper time" means at the time suitable for sowing. The rest is self-evident.
Here too, the three trainings (*sikkhā*) are explained as being intermingled.
4. Commentary on the Vajjiputta Sutta.
85. "The son of the Vajjiputtas" means a son of the Vajji royal family.

"One hundred and fifty training rules" (diyaḍḍhasikkhāpadasataṃ) refers to one hundred and fifty training rules; this was said with reference specifically to those training rules established at that time.
It is said that the monk was endowed with integrity, upright by nature, not crooked or devious; therefore, [he thought], "I [shall observe] these many training rules..."
Having reflected, "Am I able to guard them or not? he reported this to the Teacher. "Sakkomahan" means "I am able.
It is said that he spoke thus because he thought, "It is not difficult for one training in these many rules of training to train in the three [higher] trainings.
Then the Blessed One, just as one who is unable to lift fifty bundles of grass might [be asked to lift] a hundred bundles—

“Having bound it, one would place it upon the head. In the very same way, for one who is unable to train in even a single training rule, [the Buddha] spoke the words beginning with “Therefore, monk,” while placing two other training rules on top of him.
It is said that a delicate man from the countryside named Uttara was living in the Lohapāsāda Monastery. Then the young monks said to him: “Uttara,…”
“The fire-hall is leaking; having made some grass allowable, give it to us.
Taking that [grass], they went into the forest, tied the grass he had gathered into bundles of fifty, and said, “Uttarā, will you be able to carry fifty bundles?
He replied, “I shall not be able. “But will you be able to carry eighty? “I shall not be able, venerable sirs. “Then one—”
“Will you be able to carry a hundred skull-bowls? “Yes, venerable sir, I will take them. The young bhikkhus tied a hundred skull-bowls together and placed them upon his head.
He lifted them up and, groaning as he went, set them down near the fire-hall.
Then the bhikkhus said to him, “You look quite exhausted, Uttarā. “Yes, venerable sirs; the young bhikkhus [burdened] me.”
They deceived me; though I was unable to lift even this single hundred karahas, they said to me, "Lift fifty karahas.
"Yes, Uttara, they deceived me"—this is how it should be understood. Here too, the three trainings are spoken of in a mixed manner.

5. Commentary on the Sekkha Sutta 86. Regarding the fifth [verse], "those who follow the straight path" (*ujumaggānusārino*): the "straight path" (*ujumagga*) refers to the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*). The meaning is: for one who recollects that and has entered upon it.

"First knowledge regarding destruction" (*khayasmiṃ paṭhamaṃ ñāṇaṃ*): first of all, the knowledge of the Path (*maggañāṇa*) arises. For the Path [is the means] for the destruction of the defilements (*kilesānaṃ*).
"Exhaustion" (khaya) means the act of exhausting; the knowledge associated with that is called "knowledge of exhaustion.
"Subsequent to that is final knowledge" (tato aññā anantarā) means that immediately after that fourth-path knowledge, final knowledge arises; the meaning is that the fruit of arahantship arises.

"Of one liberated by final knowledge" (aññāvimuttassa) means of one liberated by the liberation of the fruit of arahantship. "Knowledge indeed exists" (ñāṇaṃ ve hoti) refers to the knowledge of review.
Thus, both in the discourses and in the verses, the seven trainees (*sekha*) are mentioned; however, at the conclusion, the one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) is shown.
6. Commentary on the First Sikkhā Sutta:

In the sixth [verse], "those desiring their own welfare" (*attakāmā*) means those desiring their own benefit. "Where all this comes together" (*yatthetaṃ sabbaṃ samodhānaṃ gacchati*) refers to those [trainings] in which...
All of this—one hundred and fifty training rules—is included within the trainings. "One who fulfills them" means one who completes them.
"One who practices partially" means one who acts according to a measure; the meaning is that he is unable to perform them in their entirety.
"Minor and lesser rules" refers to the remaining training rules, excluding the four *pārājika* offenses. Among those as well—
A *saṅghādisesa* offense is called minor; a *thullaccaya* is called non-minor. A *thullaccaya* is also minor;
a *pācittiya* is called non-minor. A *pācittiya* is also minor; *pāṭidesanīya*, *dukkaṭa*, and *dubbhāsita* offenses are called non-minors.
However, these teachers who employ the *Aṅguttara Mahānikāya* [state]: "The four *pārājika*s..."
"Excluding those [two], all the rest are minor and lesser rules," they say. Regarding the statement "one both incurs and emerges from them":
first, one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) does not incur an offense that is a transgression by nature (lokavajja), but only an offense that is a transgression by formal rule (paṇṇattivajja).
And when he incurs such an offense, he incurs it by way of body, speech, and mind. Incurring it by way of the body, he incurs offenses such as building a hut or sleeping on the same bed with another.
One who commits [an offense] by means of speech incurs [offenses] such as acting as a go-between (*sañcaritta*) or suborning a monk (*padasoḍhamma*);
one who commits [an offense] by means of the mind incurs [the offense of] accepting gold or silver (*rūpiyapaṭiggahaṇa*). The same principle applies to those in training (*sekkha*).
For it was not said here, monks, that there is incapacity; that is to say, monks, I have not stated that an Ariyan person is incapable of either committing such an offense or of emerging from it.
"Expounded" means taught. "Pertaining to the beginning of the holy life" refers to the four great training precepts of virtue (*sīla*) which constitute the beginning of the holy life of the Path.
"Conducive to the holy life" means that those very same [precepts] are suitable and appropriate for the holy life of the four paths.
"In that regard" means among those training precepts. "One of constant virtue" means one whose virtue is steadfast. "One of established virtue" means one whose virtue is firmly grounded.
"Sotāpanna" means one who has attained the fruit by means of the path known as the stream. "Avinipātadhamma" means one whose nature is not to fall into the four states of misery.
"Niyata" means fixed by the certainty of the stream-entry path. "Sambodhiparāyaṇa" means destined for the full enlightenment of the three higher paths. "Tanuttā" means the state of being attenuated;
for in a once-returner, lust and the other defilements are like a film of cloud or like the wing of a gnat.

And they become thin, not thick. "Lower-fettering" (orambhāgiyānaṃ) means belonging to the lower part. "Fetters" (saṃyojanānaṃ) means bonds. "By the total destruction" (parikkhayā) means by way of complete exhaustion.

"He becomes one of spontaneous birth" (opapātiko hoti) means he is one who has arisen [in a higher realm]. "There he attains final Nibbāna" (tattha parinibbāyī) means that, without descending further, he is of a nature to attain final Nibbāna right there above.
"One of a nature not to return" (anāvattidhammo) means one of a nature not to come back again by way of the various wombs or destinations.

Regarding the passage beginning with "one who practices partially" (*padesakārī*), a person who practices partially refers to the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), the once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*), and the non-returner (*anāgāmī*);
such a person accomplishes only a portion [of the training]. One who practices in full (*paripūrakārī*) refers to the arahant; such a person accomplishes the training in its entirety.
"Not barren" (*avañjhāni*) means they are not empty, but fruitful and productive. Here too, the three trainings (*tisso sikkhā*) are spoken of as being mixed together.
7. Commentary on the Second Training Sutta (Sattama-sikkhāsutta-vaṇṇanā) 88.
Regarding the seventh [sutta], *kolaṃkolo* means one who goes from family to family (*kulā kulaṃ gamanako*). Here, "family" (*kula*) is intended to mean "existence" (*bhava*).

Therefore, even in the phrase "two or three families," the meaning should be understood as "two or three existences. For this [person]— [The text continues: ...is indeed... [the remainder of the commentary follows].
He runs through two or three existences, or at the very most, six. Therefore, the alternative here should be understood as "two, or three, or four, or five, or six.

One who has a single seed (*ekabījī*) is so called because he possesses the seed for only one further existence. Regarding the terms "one who flows upwards" (*uddhaṃsota*) and so forth: there is one who flows upwards and goes to the Akaniṭṭha heaven; there is one who flows upwards... [and so on].
There is one who goes to Akaniṭṭha, there is one who is an upstreamer going to Akaniṭṭha, and there is one who is an upstreamer but not going to Akaniṭṭha.

In this context, one who has attained the fruit of non-returning here, is reborn in the Aviha realm or others, and after remaining there for the full lifespan, is reborn successively higher until reaching Akaniṭṭha—this is called an upstreamer going to Akaniṭṭha. However, one who [is reborn] in the Aviha realms...
One who is reborn right there, without attaining final nibbāna, and without reaching the Akaniṭṭha realm, attains final nibbāna in the higher Brahma-worlds;

this one is called an "upstreamer" (uddhaṃsota) who does not go to Akaniṭṭha. One who, having passed away from here, is reborn in Akaniṭṭha itself is called an "Akaniṭṭha-goer" who is not an upstreamer.
However, one who is reborn in any one of the four [realms] beginning with the Aviha...
One who attains final nibbāna right there is called "one who does not go upstream nor go to the Akaniṭṭha realm.
However, one who has been reborn anywhere and attains arahantship with effort and exertion is called "one who attains final nibbāna with effort" (sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī).
One who attains it without effort or exertion is called "one who attains final nibbāna without effort" (asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī). Furthermore, regarding those whose lifespan is a thousand eons...

Having been reborn in the Aviha realm and having passed five hundred kappas, he attains arahantship; this one is called an *upahaccaparinibbāyī* (one who attains parinibbāna after the passing of half the lifespan).

The same method applies to the Atappa and other realms as well. As for the *antarāparinibbāyī* (one who attains parinibbāna in the interval), he is one who attains parinibbāna without having passed the midpoint of his lifespan;
he is of three types. First, having been reborn in the Aviha realm among those with a lifespan of a thousand kappas, one [attains it] on the very day of rebirth.
He attains arahantship. If he does not attain it on the very day of his rebirth, he attains it at the conclusion of the first hundred aeons;
this is the first type of *antarāparinibbāyin*. Another, being unable to do so, attains it at the conclusion of two hundred aeons;
this is the second. Another, being unable even to that, [attains it] at the conclusion of four hundred aeons.
He attains [Nibbāna]; this is the third type of one who attains Nibbāna in the interval (*antarāparinibbāyī*). The rest is exactly as previously stated.
However, standing at this point, twenty-four stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), twelve once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*), forty-eight non-returners (*anāgāmin*), and twelve arahants should be described.
For in this Dispensation, there are the burden of faith (*saddhādhura*) and the burden of wisdom (*paññādhura*).
There are two burdens and four modes of practice: the difficult mode of practice with sluggish direct knowledge, and so forth.
Among these, one who applies himself to the burden of faith, having attained the fruit of stream-entry, produces only one more existence and makes an end of suffering;
this is the "single-seeder" (*ekabījī*). He is of four kinds according to his mode of practice. Just as he is, so too is the one who applies himself to the burden of wisdom.

"Even those who are still attached" refers to the eight types of *ekabījins*. Likewise, there are twenty-four types of stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), namely the *kolaṃkola* and the *sattakkhattuparama*.

Furthermore, among the three liberations, there are four types of once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*) who have attained the stage of a once-returner by means of the liberation of emptiness (*suññatavimokkha*) according to the four modes of practice (*paṭipadā*); likewise, there are four who have attained it by means of the signless liberation (*animittavimokkha*).
There are twelve once-returners who have attained [the fruit] by means of the wishless liberation. Furthermore, among those in the Aviha heaven, there are five non-returners:
three who attain final nibbāna in the interval, one who attains final nibbāna upon landing, and one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm;
these consist of five who attain final nibbāna without exertion and five who attain final nibbāna with exertion, making ten.
It is the same with the Atappa and other Pure Abodes. However, in the Akaniṭṭha realm there is no one who goes upstream;
therefore, there are eight there—four who attain final nibbāna with exertion and four who attain final nibbāna without exertion. These are the forty-eight non-returners.
Just as it is with the once-returners, so too should the arahants be understood to be twelve. Here also, the three trainings are spoken of as being mixed together.
8. Commentary on the Third Training Sutta (Tatiyasikkhāsutta) 89.
