In the eighth [sutta], "but not attaining or penetrating that" means not reaching or not penetrating that state of *arahantship*.
In this manner, the meaning is to be understood in all instances. Here too, there are three trainings (*sikkhā*).
The trainings are spoken of as mixed. The ninth [sutta] has its meaning already explained. Here too, the three trainings are spoken of as mixed. 10.
Commentary on the Second Sutta on the Three Trainings: 91.

Regarding the tenth [sutta], "the destruction of the taints" (*āsavānaṃ khayo*): here, the path to arahantship is called the training in higher wisdom (*adhipaññāsikkhā*). However, the fruit (*phala*) should not be called a "training," because it arises for one who has already completed the training.
"As before, so after" means that just as one trains in the three trainings first, one trains in exactly the same way afterwards.

The same method applies to the second phrase. "As below, so above" means that just as one contemplates the lower part of the body in terms of its foulness, one pervades the upper part of the body in exactly the same way. The same method applies to the second phrase. "As by day, so..."
"Night as by day": the meaning is that he trains in the three trainings just as he does by day, training in the same way even at night.
"Having overcome all directions" means having overcome all directions by way of their objects. "By means of immeasurable concentration" means by means of the concentration of the path to Arahatship.

"The learner" (*sekha*) refers to one who is still training and has duties yet to be performed. "One on the way" (*paṭipada*) refers to one who is practicing the path. "Of pure conduct" (*saṃsuddhacārin*) refers to one whose conduct is completely purified.

Of one whose virtue is perfectly pure. "The Fully Awakened One" (Sambuddha) means one awakened to the Four Noble Truths. "The Wise One who has reached the end of the path" (Dhīraṃ paṭipadantagaṃ) means wise by way of being wise regarding the aggregates and wise regarding the sense bases;
thus he is endowed with steadfastness and has reached the culmination of practice. "Of consciousness" (viññāṇassa) refers to the final consciousness.

"Of one liberated through the destruction of craving" (taṇhākkhayavimuttino) refers to one possessed of the liberation of the fruit of Arhatship, which is designated as liberation through the destruction of craving. "Just as of a lamp" (pajjotasseva)...
"Nirvana" is like the nirvana of a lamp. "There is liberation of the mind" means there is the liberation, the releasing, and the state of non-occurrence of the consciousness.
For one whose taints are destroyed and who is liberated through the destruction of craving, there is liberation of the mind through the cessation of the final consciousness, just as in parinibbāna;
no place gone to is discerned, for it is simply the attainment of the state of being unmanifest—this is the meaning.
11. Commentary on the Saṅkavā Sutta 92. Regarding the eleventh [case]:
"Saṅkavā" refers to a market town (*nigama*) of the Kosalans; thus, it is a market town in the kingdom of Kosala by that very name.

"A resident" (*āvāsika*) is one who carries the burden [of maintenance]; he establishes new dwellings and looks after those that are old. "Connected with the training rules" (*sikkhāpada-paṭisaṃyuttāya*)...
The meaning is: "connected with words designated as training" and "endowed with the three trainings.
*Sandasseti* means he shows it as if it were right before his eyes. *Samādapeti* means he causes [others] to take it up. *Samuttejeti* means he inspires them.
*Sampahaṃseti* means, by speaking in praise of the qualities already acquired, he purifies them. *Adhisallikhatī* means he sharpens [them] exceedingly; exceedingly...
The meaning is that, having smoothed it over, he speaks very gently. *Accaya* means an offense.
*Maṃ accagamā* means it occurred having passed me by or overcome me. *Ahu deva akkhandī* means there was indeed non-endurance.
*Ahu appaccayo* means there was a state of dissatisfaction. *Paṭiggaṇhātu* means may he accept [it], i.e., may he forgive it.
"Āyatiṃ saṃvarāya" means for the sake of restraint in the future; the meaning is: for the purpose of not committing such an offense, fault, or transgression again.
"Taggha" means certainly. "Yathādhammaṃ paṭikarosi" means you act according to how the Dhamma stands;
it is said that you make amends. "Taṃ te mayaṃ paṭiggaṇhāma" means we accept that from you.
“We forgive this offense. This, Kassapa, is growth in the Noble One’s Discipline; this, Kassapa, is what is called ‘growth’ in the teaching of the Buddha, the Blessed One.

What is it? It is that, having seen a transgression as a transgression and having made amends according to the Dhamma, one undertakes restraint for the future. Now, speaking with reference to the individual, he said: “He who, having seen a transgression as a transgression...”
"Having seen [the fault], he makes amends in accordance with the Dhamma and undertakes restraint for the future," he said.
"One who does not desire the training" means one who does not desire, aspire to, or yearn for the three trainings. "Of the undertaking of the training" means of the fulfillment of the training.
"One who does not speak in praise" means one who does not proclaim its virtues. "At the proper time" means at the time when it is appropriately applied. The rest here is of plain meaning.
The fourth chapter on the Ascetics is finished.
(10) 5. The Chapter on the Lump of Salt. 1.
Commentary on the Sutta on Urgent Matters.
93. Regarding the first [section] of the fifth [chapter]: "Urgent matters" (*accāyikāni*) means those that are very pressing. "Duties" (*karaṇīyāni*) means necessary tasks.
For that which does not need to be done necessarily is called a "task" (*kicca*); that which must necessarily be done is called a "duty" (*karaṇīya*). "Quickly, quickly" means with great speed.
In the phrase "of that indeed" (*tassa kho taṃ*), the word *taṃ* here is merely a particle. There is no such psychic power (*iddhi*) there.
There is no such power, or majesty, or psychic potency. "On the following day" means on the third day. "Subject to seasonal change" means having undergone the transformation of the seasons.
"They even grow" means that on the third day white sprouts emerge, and when seven days have passed, they become green sprouts.
"They even become pregnant" means that after reaching one and a half months, they have conceived a fetus.
"Boiling in the border regions" means they boil for three months.
Now, since Buddhas have no need for householders or crops, they nevertheless bring forth various similes to illustrate a person or a matter corresponding to those things within the Teaching.
Therefore, showing what purpose he intended to illustrate when he brought this [simile], [the Buddha said]: "In just this way..."
He said "what" and so forth. That is clear in meaning. However, here too, the training is explained as being mixed.
2. Commentary on the Paviveka Sutta (94).
In the second [sutta], "seclusion from robes" means the state of being secluded from the defilements that arise dependent upon robes. In the other two cases as well...
The same method applies here. *Sāṇāni* means garments made of hemp (*sāṇa-vāka*). *Masāṇāni* means mixed garments.
*Chavadussāni* means cloths discarded from a dead body, or robes made by sewing together *eraka* grass and the like. *Paṃsukūlāni* means rags cast away upon the earth.
*Tirīṭāni* means garments made from tree bark. *Ajināni* means the skins of the *ajina* deer. *Ajinakkhipaṃ*...
That very same [garment] split in the middle is also called the *sahakhurakaṇṭhī*. A *kusacīra* is a garment made by weaving together blades of *kusa* grass.
The same principle applies to garments made of bark (*vākacīra*) and wooden splinters (*phalakacīra*). A *kesakambala* is a blanket made from human hair.
A *vālakambala* is a blanket made from horsehair and the like. An *ulūkapakkhika* is a lower garment made by stitching together owl feathers.
"Eaters of greens" means those who eat fresh greens. "Eaters of millet" means those who eat the grains of millet. Regarding *nīvāra* and the others:
*nīvāra* refers to a species of wild rice that grows spontaneously in the forest. *Daddula* is the husk discarded by leather-workers after they have scraped the hide.
*Haṭa* refers to slime, moss, or the resin of trees such as the *kaṇikāra*. *Kaṇa* refers to broken rice. *Ācāma* refers to...
*Jhāma-odana* is rice stuck to the bottom of a cooking pot. They take it from where it has been discarded and eat it;

some also call it "rice gruel" (*odanakañjiya*). *Piññāka* and so forth are well known. "One who eats fallen fruit" means one who eats fruit that has dropped. A "threshing floor" (*bhusāgāra*) is a barn for threshed grain.
"Virtuous" (*sīlavā*) means endowed with the fourfold purity of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*). "And his immorality is abandoned" refers to the five types of immoral conduct (*pañca dussīlyāni*).
They have been abandoned. "One of right view" means one who sees things as they truly are. "Wrong view" means seeing things not as they truly are.
"Taints" refers to the four taints. "Reached the summit" means reached the summit of virtue. "Reached the core" means reached the core of virtue. "Pure" means completely purified.
"Established in the core" means established in the core of virtue, concentration, and wisdom.
“Seyyathāpi” means “just as if. “Sampannaṃ” means full, filled with ripened rice. “Saṅgharāpeyya” means would have it gathered together.
“Ubbahāpeyya” means would have it brought to the threshing floor. “Bhusikaṃ” means chaff.
“Koṭṭāpeyya” means would have it placed in a mortar and pounded with pestles. “Aggappattāni” means those that have reached the tip [of the grain].
The same method applies to the sections beginning with "Sārappatta" (Attained to the Essence). The remainder is self-evident.

Furthermore, as for what is stated here—"His immorality has been abandoned and his wrong view has been abandoned"—it should be understood that this was said with reference to the state of having abandoned them by means of the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*).
3. Commentary on the *Sarada-sutta* (The Autumn Discourse)

95. "In the third [verse], 'when' (*viddhe*) means when [the clouds] have moved far away due to their disappearance. 'Deva' means in the sky. 'Abhivihacca' means having struck down. 'Yato' means at which time.
'Dustless' (*virajaṃ*) means free from the dust of passion and so forth. 'Stainless' (*vītamalaṃ*) is because those very stains have departed.

'The eye of Dhamma' (*dhammacakkhu*) is the eye of the path of stream-entry that grasps the Dhamma of the Four Truths. 'There is no fetter for it'—[this refers to the fact that] there is no fetter [remaining]."
He has no twofold fetter; furthermore, it is said that he has none other because they are incapable of bringing him back again to this world.
In this sutta, one who is a non-returner by means of meditative absorption (jhāna-anāgāmī) is described.
4. Commentary on the *Parisā Sutta* (The Discourse on the Assembly)
96. In the fourth [chapter], "they do not become luxurious" means they do not indulge excessively in requisites.

"They do not become lax" means they do not undertake the three trainings in a slack manner. "They have abandoned the task of falling away"—here, "falling away" (okkamana) refers to the five hindrances in the sense of descending;
they have abandoned the task regarding them. "They are pioneers in solitude" means in that which is comprised of the solitude of body, mind, and material possessions.
In all three kinds of seclusion, they are the forerunners. "Exerting energy" means they apply themselves to both types of energy.
"Of what has not been attained" refers to the specific distinctions not yet reached, namely jhāna, insight, the path, and the fruit. The same method applies to the other two phrases as well.
"The later generation" refers to co-residents, pupils, and so forth. "They fall into following one's example" means...
She imitates what has been done by her teachers and preceptors. She is said to follow the example of whatever she has seen among those people regarding her teachers and preceptors.
This, monks, is called an assembly that has a leader; this assembly, monks, is called one that possesses the foremost person.
“Engaged in brawling” means they have become brawling. “Engaged in quarreling” means they have become quarreling. Herein, “brawling” (*bhaṇḍana*) refers to the preliminary stage of quarreling;
transgression by way of seizing each other by the hands and so forth is called “quarreling” (*kalaha*). “Fallen into dispute” means they have entered into opposing arguments.
“With the weapons of the mouth” means harsh speech is called “weapons of the mouth” in the sense that it pierces one’s virtues.
"By those weapons of the mouth": they dwell piercing one another;
that is, they wander about stabbing each other. "In harmony": being together. "Rejoicing": their joy proceeding equally. "Become like milk and water":
having become as one with milk and water. "With loving eyes": with peaceful, eyes of loving-kindness (*mettā*). "Joy arises": five-colored joy (*pañcavaṇṇā pīti*) arises.
“The body becomes tranquil” means that both the mental body (nāmakāya) and the physical body (rūpakāya) are free from distress. “With tranquil body” means with a body that is not agitated.
“He experiences pleasure” means he experiences bodily and mental pleasure. “He becomes concentrated” means he is properly established upon the object of focus.
“In large raindrops” means in heavy raindrops. Regarding the phrase “mountain clefts, ravines, and creeks,” here a “cleft” (kandara) is [derived from] “ka”—
A mountain region split by water that has obtained its name from that water is called "water-divided" (*udakabhinnā*); it is what is also termed a "slope" (*nitamba*) or a "river-bend" (*nadikuñja*).
A "cracked place" (*padara*) is a section of ground that has split open when it has not rained for eight months.

"Branches" (*sākhā*) refers to small irrigation channels leading to small reservoirs (*kusobbha*). "Small reservoirs" (*kusobbha*) are small ponds. "Large reservoirs" (*mahāsobbha*) are large ponds. "Little rivers" (*kunnadī*) are small streams.
"Great rivers" refers to the great streams such as the Ganges, the Yamunā, and so forth.
5–7. Commentary on the First Discourse on the Breeding Elephant, etc., §§97–99.
Regarding "by five factors" in the fifth [discourse], it means by the factors of quality (*guṇa-aṅga*). "Worthy of a king" means suitable for a king; "fit for a king's use" means...
He has become an object of enjoyment for the king. He is called a "limb of the king" because, by virtue of being equal to the king's own limbs such as hands and feet, he is reckoned simply as a limb.
"Endowed with beauty" means endowed with the beauty of the body. "Endowed with strength" means endowed with physical strength.
"Worthy of offerings" (āhuneyya) means fit to receive alms-food, which is designated as an *āhuti*. "Worthy of hospitality" (pāhuneyya) [means fit to receive] the meal of a guest...
"Anucchaviko" (fitting): He is fitting for the sacrificial gift (*dakkiṇā*), which consists of the offering of faith, by virtue of relinquishing the ten bases of giving (*dānavatthu*).
"Añjalikaraṇīyo" (worthy of reverential salutation): He is fitting for the raising of the hands in salutation.
"Anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ lokassa" (the unsurpassed field of merit for the world): He is the peerless place for the growth of merit for the entire world.
"Endowed with beauty" means endowed with the beauty of virtues. "Endowed with strength" means endowed with the strength of energy (*vīriya*).

"Endowed with speed" means endowed with the speed of knowledge (*ñāṇa*). "Possessing fortitude" means possessed of the fortitude of knowledge. "Firm in exertion" means one whose exertion is steadfast.

"One who has not laid down the burden" means one who has not set aside the burden, but has taken up the burden; until reaching the supreme fruit, *arahantship*, he does not relinquish the burden of energy.

"One who has practiced thus [thinking], 'I shall not lay [the burden] down'—in this sutta, the path of stream-entry is explained by way of the Four Noble Truths, and the possession of the speed of knowledge (*ñāṇajava*) is explained by means of that path of stream-entry.

In the sixth [sutta], the three paths and the three fruits are mentioned, and the possession of the speed of knowledge is explained by means of those three paths and fruits. In the seventh, the fruit of arhatship [is mentioned]."

And by the fruit of arahantship itself, the function of the path is explained. Furthermore, because it arises with a swiftness that has already surged forward, it is appropriate to call the fruit "speed" (*java*).
8. Commentary on the Potthaka Sutta (Sutta 100) In the eighth [sutta], "nine" is stated with reference to the act of making. "Potthaka" refers to cloth made of wool. "Majjhima" means...
"Middle-aged" refers to one who is middle-aged in terms of usage. "Worn out" means worn out by usage. "Rubbing the mortar" means wiping the mortar clean.
"Immoral" means lacking virtue (*nissīla*). "By way of ugliness" means by way of being ugly due to the absence of the beauty of virtues. "Following his example" means imitating what was done by him.
"It is not of great fruit" means it is not of great fruit in terms of its resultant fruit (*vipākaphala*). Not...
"It is of great benefit" means it is of great benefit by way of the benefit of its result (*vipākānisamsa*), not [merely] by way of the benefit of the action itself.

"By way of its low value" means by way of the low value of its result. "Kāsika cloth" refers to cloth made from thread spun by three cotton fibers; furthermore, that [cloth] originated specifically in the kingdom of Kāsi.
The rest is self-evident. However, in this context, virtue (*sīla*) is explained as being mixed.
9. Commentary on the Loṇakapalla Sutta 101.
Regarding the ninth [verse], "In whatever way...": "In whatever way" means *yathā yathā*. "So too" means *tathā tathā*.
"That action" refers to that very deed. This is what is meant: one might say, "In whatever way a person performs an action, so too will it be for him..."
"One simply experiences the result; for it is not possible to ward off the ripening of a deed that has been done.
Therefore, whatever karma one performs, one must experience the ripening of exactly that much. "This being so" means this being the case.
"There is no living of the holy life" refers to that karma which, prior to the cultivation of the path, is to be experienced upon rebirth.
Because that [kamma] must inevitably be experienced, even though one has lived the holy life (*brahmacariya*), it is as if one has not lived it at all.
"No opportunity is seen for the complete making of an end to suffering" means that since this is so, there occurs both the accumulation of that kamma and the experiencing of its result;
therefore, by that cause and method, no opportunity indeed appears for the making of an end to the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*).
"In whatever way it is to be experienced" means in whichever manner it is to be felt. "In that very way one experiences its result" means one undergoes its result in that very manner.

This is what is meant: among the seven impulsion moments, that first impulsion-kamma which, when conditions are present, receives a result-phase, is *diṭṭhadhammavedanīya* (to be experienced in the present life).

When it does not exist, it is called "non-existent karma" (*ahosikamma*). Furthermore, that seventh impulsion-karma which becomes "to-be-experienced-in-the-next-birth" (*upapajjavedanīya*) when conditions are present is also called "non-existent karma" when they are absent.

And that middle five-impulsion-karma is called "to-be-experienced-in-a-subsequent-life" (*aparapariyāyavedanīya*) for as long as the round of existence continues. Among these modes, karma is to be understood according to whichever mode is appropriate.
"This person performs [an action], and by that very same [action] he experiences its result"—this is what is meant.
For it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary) that "kamma which has obtained the occasion for its result" is called "kamma to be experienced as such.
This being so, monks, there is the living of the holy life (*brahmacariyavāsa*), because the holy life that brings about the destruction of kamma arises from the very kamma that is to be destroyed.
"Garment" means it becomes worn; the meaning is that it is indeed well-worn. "An opportunity is seen for the right making of an end of suffering":

because this being so, through the cessation of volitional consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa*) by means of this or that path, the round of suffering (*vaṭṭa-dukkha*) does not arise in those various states of existence in the future; therefore, an opportunity is seen for the right making of an end of suffering.
Now, showing the nature of that karma according to how it is experienced, he said: "In this case, monks, for a certain person," and so forth.
Therein, *appamattakaṃ* means limited, slight, weak, or inferior. *Tādisaṃyeva* means exactly similar to that.
*Diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṃ* means that which must ripen in that very same present life, obtaining the opportunity for its result within that very karma.
"It is to be experienced in this very life" (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*). "Not even an atom is seen" (*nāṇupi khāyati*) means that not even an atom is seen in a second existence;
the meaning is that it does not yield even the slightest result in a second existence. "Much more so for many gods" (*bahudeva*) implies: how much more will it give abundant results?

By the terms "one who has not developed the body" (*abhāvitakāya*) and so forth, the worldling (*puthujjana*) who goes toward the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭagāmī*) and is devoid of the development of the body is shown.
"Paritta" means having limited qualities. "Appātuma": *ātuma* refers to one's own person (*attabhāva*); even though that person is large, because his qualities are limited, he is indeed "appātuma.
"Appadukkhavihārī" means one who dwells in suffering even on account of a small evil deed. By the phrases beginning with "bhāvitakāyo," the one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) is indicated;
for he is called "one who has cultivated the body" (*bhāvitakāyo*) by virtue of the cultivation of the body known as the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*).

Or, he is "one whose body is developed" because his body has been developed. "One whose virtue is developed" means one whose virtue has been developed. The same method applies to the other two phrases as well.

Alternatively, he is "one whose body is developed" through the development of the five sense doors; by this, the virtue of restraint of the faculties is expressed, while by the phrase "one whose virtue is developed," the remaining three types of virtue are meant.
"Not limited" means not having limited qualities. "Greatness" [is so called] even when the personal existence (*attabhāva*) is limited.
He is "great" because of the greatness of his qualities. "One who dwells in the immeasurable" is simply a name for one whose taints are destroyed;
for he is called "one who dwells in the immeasurable" due to the absence of lust and other defilements that create limits.
"Paritta" means small. "Udakamallaka" means a water-cup. "Orabbhika" is the owner of sheep. "Urabbhaghātaka" is the slaughterer of sheep.
The butcher. “To cause to recite” means to cause [the debtor] to recite for the loss of his wealth. *Jhāpetuṃ* is also a reading, with the same meaning.
“Or to do as required” means to act according to his wish. “The price of the sheep” refers to the cost of a goat. If he wishes, he gives it;
if he does not wish, he has him dragged away by the neck. The rest is in the manner already stated.
This should be understood. However, in this sutta, the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*) are explained.
10. Commentary on the *Paṃsudhovaka Sutta* (The Dust-Washer Sutta) 102.
"Washes" (*dhovati*) means he cleanses. "Washes thoroughly" (*sandhovati*) means he washes well; he washes again and again.
*Niddhovati* means having rinsed it out, one washes it. *Aniddhantakasāvaṃ* means having its impurities not yet scraped away, with the dross not yet removed.
*Pabhaṅguṃ* means having the nature of breaking; apart from a mortar, it breaks as soon as it is merely struck with the fist.
*Paṭṭikāya* means with a gold band. *Gīveyyake* means on a neck ornament.

"Higher mind" (*adhicitta*) refers to the mind of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*). "Of one who is devoted" (*anuyuttassa*) means of one who is cultivating it. "Possessed of a good heart" (*sacetaso*) means endowed with a noble mind. "Of a steadfast nature" (*dabbajātikassa*) means of a wise nature.
Among the thoughts of sensual desire and so forth, a thought arisen concerning sensual pleasures is called a "thought of sensual desire" (*kāmavitakka*).

Thoughts associated with ill will and cruelty are called "thoughts of ill will and cruelty" (*byāpādavihiṃsavitakka*). Among the thoughts of relatives and so forth, [the thought] "our... [is a thought of relatives].
Thought arisen with reference to relatives in the manner beginning, “My relatives are many and meritorious,” is thought concerning relatives (*ñātivitakka*).
Thought arisen with reference to a country in the manner beginning, “Such-and-such a country is peaceful and has abundant food,” is thought concerning a country (*janapadavitakka*).
Thought arisen in the form, “Oh, may others not despise me! is that associated with non-disparagement (*anavaññattipaṭisaṃyutta*).
"Applied thought" (vitakka) means: "There will remain thoughts of phenomena" refers to the ten types of applied thought that are defilements of insight (vipassanupakkilesa).
"That concentration is not peaceful" means that because the remaining thoughts of phenomena have not calmed the defilements, the concentration of insight is not peaceful.
"Not sublime" means it is not refreshing. "Not attained to tranquility" means it has not attained the tranquility of the defilements.
"Attained": not "attained to a state of oneness," meaning not having reached one-pointedness (*ekaggabhāva*).
"Gone by restraining with effort" means that by restraining and warding off defilements through effort—that is, through application—it has been warded off;
it has not arisen at the very moment the defilements were severed, but rather it has arisen after the defilements had been warded off.

“There is that time, monks”: here, “time” (*samaya*) refers to the occasion of obtaining these five favorable conditions—favorable weather, favorable food, favorable lodging, favorable persons, and favorable hearing of the Dhamma.
“That mind” refers to that moment when the insight-mind (*vipassanā-citta*). “It settles within itself alone” means within one’s own self.
It remains. For here, "internal" (ajjhatta) refers to one's own internal domain (niyakajjhatta); it is also appropriate as the internal domain of its object (gocarajjhatta).

What is meant is that, having abandoned various objects, it remains fixed upon the single object of Nibbāna alone. "Sits down" (sannisīdati) means it sits down well. "Becomes unified" (ekodi hoti) means it becomes one-pointed.
"Is concentrated" (samādhiyati) means it is properly centered. In the passage beginning with "peaceful" (santa), [it is peaceful] by the subsiding of the adverse defilements.
It is peaceful. It is sublime in the sense of being untroubled. It is "attained through subsiding" because it is obtained by the subsiding of the defilements.

It is "reached by singleness" because it has attained a state of one-pointedness. It is "not reached by suppression with exertion" because it arises when the defilements have been severed at the root;
it is not something that has been suppressed or restrained by forcibly holding back the defilements through effort. Up to this point, this...
Having turned away from the round of existence, the bhikkhu is said to have attained arahantship.
Now, showing the path to direct knowledge for one whose taints are exhausted, he says: "Of whatever...," and so forth.
In this context, "direct knowledge" (*abhiññā*) refers to that which is to be realized by knowing directly and making manifest. "In each respective base" (*sati sati-āyatane*) means...

When there exist both the previously accumulated causes and the presently acquired conditions—namely, the various types of jhānas that serve as the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā)—this is the cause for mindfulness.
Furthermore, this detailed exposition on direct knowledge should be understood according to the method set forth in the *Visuddhimagga*.
And here, the passage beginning with "the destruction of the taints" (āsavānaṃ khaya) should be understood as referring to the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti).
11. Commentary on the Nimittasutta (Sutta 103).
In the eleventh [sutta] as well, "higher mind" (*adhicitta*) refers precisely to the mind of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*). "Three signs" (*tīṇi nimittāni*) means three causes.

"From time to time" (*kālena kālam*) means at the proper times; the meaning is "at the appropriate occasion. This is seen in such passages as: "From time to time, the sign of concentration (*samādhinimitta*) should be attended to," and so forth.
Having observed the appropriate time for each, at the moment one is fit for unification, unification should be brought to mind.
For here, unification is called the "sign of concentration" (*samādhinimitta*). Regarding the meaning of the words: concentration itself is the sign, thus it is the "sign of concentration.

The same method applies to the other two terms as well. Furthermore, "exertion" (*paggaha*) is a name for energy (*vīriya*), while "equanimity" (*upekkhā*) refers to the state of neutrality (*majjhattabhāva*).
Therefore, energy should be brought to mind at the time when energy is appropriate, and one should abide in equanimity at the time when equanimity is appropriate.
There exists a reason why that mind might lead to indolence, by which it would remain in a state of indolence.
The same principle applies to the others as well. One should attend only to the sign of equanimity.
And here, "one should remain equanimous with the speed of knowledge" is the meaning. "For the destruction of the taints" means for the sake of the fruit of arahantship.

"One should prepare a crucible" means one should ready a charcoal pan. "One should kindle it" means having placed coals therein and applied fire, one should blow with a bellows and cause the fire to catch.
"One should cast [the gold] into the mouth of the crucible" means after the coals have been leveled out...
He might place it on a heap of embers or throw it into a crucible. "He looks on" means he observes whether it is cooked or uncooked.
"He is rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints" means he is correctly established for the sake of the fruit of arahantship.
For up to this point, the bhikkhu who has reached arahantship by increasing insight has been shown. Now, regarding that one whose taints are destroyed:
Demonstrating the path of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), he said, "Of whatever... and so forth. This should be understood according to the method already explained below.
The fifth chapter, the *Loṇakapalla-vagga*, is concluded.
The second fiftieth section (*paññāsaka*) is finished.
3. The Third Fifty (11) 1.
The Chapter on Awakening (Sambodhavagga) 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on Prior to Awakening (Pubbeva-sambodha-sutta-vaṇṇanā)
104. Regarding the first part of the third [statement]: "Even before enlightenment" means even prior to enlightenment;
it is said that this occurs only at a time subsequent to the attainment of the Noble Path. "Of one who has not yet fully awakened" means of one who has not yet penetrated the Four Truths.
"While being still a bodhisatta" means while being a being capable of awakening, while being one who has merely begun to attain full perfect enlightenment.
Or rather, it is because he was attached and intent upon full enlightenment (sambodhi).

For from the moment the aspiration was fulfilled at the feet of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara through the convergence of the eight factors, the Tathāgata remained attached and intent upon perfect self-enlightenment (sammāsambodhi), thinking, "This must be attained by me," and never relinquishing his exertion toward its realization; therefore, he is called a Bodhisatta.

"Who indeed? means "Which one indeed? "The world" refers to the world of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra-loka*). "The gratification" is its sweet aspect. "The danger" is its aspect as something not to be delighted in.
"To me, who am such"—that is, to me while being a Bodhisatta in this way. "The removal of desire and lust" means the abandoning of desire and lust;
by resorting to, aiming at, and depending upon Nibbāna, desire and lust undergo removal and are abandoned; therefore, [it is] Nibbāna.
“The subduing of desire-and-lust, the abandoning of desire-and-lust”—this is what is said. "This is the escape from the world": this is Nibbāna;
because it has escaped from the world, it is called the escape from the world. "As long as": for whatever measure of time. "I directly knew":
I knew by means of the distinguished knowledge of the Noble Path (ariyamagga-ñāṇa). "And the knowledge and vision arose in me": by both these phrases...
The knowledge of reviewing has been explained. The rest here is self-evident. 2.
Commentary on the First Discourse on Gratification (Assādasutta). 105.
In the second [verse], "I wandered in search of gratification" means I wandered for the purpose of seeking gratification. From what point [did this begin]?
From the time of Sumedha onwards. "By wisdom" means by the path-wisdom accompanied by insight (*vipassanā*). "Well-seen" means well-penetrated.
By this method, the meaning is to be understood in all instances. The third [section] is clear throughout. 4.
Commentary on the *Samaṇabrāhmaṇa-sutta*.
107. In the fourth [discourse], “the goal of recluseship” (*sāmaññattha*) refers to the fourfold noble fruit (*ariyaphala*). The other term is a synonym for that very same thing.

Alternatively, by the sense of “recluseship,” the four paths are meant; by the sense of “brahminhood” (*brahmaññattha*), the four fruits are meant. Furthermore, in all these four suttas, only the world of the aggregates (*khandhaloka*) is discussed.
5. Commentary on the *Ruṇṇasutta* (The Discourse on Weeping)
108. The fifth [case] is set forth by way of an occasion for a rule. On what occasion? On account of the improper conduct of the group of six.
It is said that they wandered about singing, dancing, and laughing. The monks reported this to the One of Ten Powers.
The Teacher, having summoned them, began this discourse for the purpose of instructing them. In that context, *ruṇṇaṃ* means weeping. *Ummattakaṃ* means...
The actions of the insane. "Childish" means what ought to be done by children. "Laughing with bared teeth" refers to the loud laughter of those who strike their hands while showing their teeth.
"The destruction of the bridge regarding song" means: "May there be for you the destruction of the conditions for song;
abandon song that is accompanied by worldly motives"—this is what it indicates. The same principle applies to dancing as well. "Enough" means it is appropriate. For those who delight in the Dhamma...
Here, "cause" (*satam*) refers to a reason; it is the continuum of those who are gladdened by some particular cause.

"A smile, merely for the sake of smiling" means that when that cause for smiling exists, whatever smile you make is appropriate only for the sake of smiling—that is, merely for showing the tips of the upper teeth and displaying the mere appearance of being delighted. This is what is meant.
6. Commentary on the *Atitti-sutta* (109).
Regarding the sixth [verse], "of sleep": *soppassa* means of sleep (*niddā*). "There is no satiety in indulgence" means that however much one indulges, it remains pleasing;
thus, there is no such thing as satiety. The same principle applies to the other two phrases as well. For if...
If the water in the great ocean were to become liquor, and one were reborn as a fish intoxicated by liquor, there would be no satiety for it even while wandering or sleeping there.
In this sutta, only the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is discussed. 7. Commentary on the *Arakkhitasutta* (The Discourse on the Unprotected).

110. "In the seventh [case], it is 'corrupted' (*avassuta*) means it is stained. 'An auspicious death does not occur' means it is not obtained because it serves as the condition for rebirth in the states of misery (*apāya*).
'The passing away' (*kālakiriyā*) is a synonym for that very thing. In the bright side (*sukkapakkha*), it is auspicious and obtained because it serves as the condition for rebirth in heaven.
That, moreover, belongs exclusively to the three types of noble disciples, beginning with the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*)."
It is permissible. The rest here is self-evident.
8. Commentary on the Sutta on the Corrupt (Byāpanna-sutta) 111.
In the eighth [sutta], "corrupt" (*byāpanna*) means remaining after having abandoned its natural state. The rest is exactly according to the method explained in the preceding sutta.
9. Commentary on the First Discourse on the Origin (Paṭhamanidānasutta) 112.

In the ninth [section], "origins" (*nidānāni*) means causes (*kāraṇāni*). "For the arising of kamma" means for the purpose of aggregating the kamma that leads to the round of existence (*vaṭṭagāmika-kamma*).
"Produced by greed" means fashioned by greed. "Blameworthy" means accompanied by hatred. That kamma conduces to the arising of further kamma.
That karma leads to the arising and accumulation of other karmas that lead to the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
"That karma does not lead to the cessation of karma" means that such karma does not lead to the cessation of those karmas leading to the cycle of existence.
In the bright side (*sukkapakkha*), "for the arising of karmas" means for the sake of the arising of karmas leading to the turning away from the cycle (*vivaṭṭa*). By this method...
All of this should be understood according to its meaning.
10. Commentary on the Second Nidāna Sutta. 113.

In the tenth [sutta], "of kamma" refers specifically to the kamma that leads to the round of existence (*saṃsāra*). "In the place of desire and lust" means in that which serves as the cause for desire and lust.

"Ārabbhā" means having come to, having referred to, or depending upon. "Chanda" means the desire of craving (*taṇhā-chanda*). "Whatever lust of the mind" means whatever lust, passioning, or state of being impassioned of the consciousness;
the meaning is: "I call this a fetter (*saṃyojana*); I call it a bond (*bandhana*).

In the bright side (*sukkapakkha*), "of actions" refers to actions leading to the turning away from the round of existence (*vivaṭṭagāmika-kamma*). "He turns that back" means he causes that to turn back. Or, when by that...
When the result (vipāka) is known and understood, one then turns away from both those phenomena and that result.
By this phrase, insight (vipassanā) is spoken of; by "having turned away from that," the path (magga) is meant. And by "having penetrated with the mind," it is the path itself.
"Having pierced through with wisdom, he sees" means having pierced through with the wisdom of the path together with insight.
He sees. In this way, the meaning is to be understood in all instances. However, in this sutta, the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*) are explained.
The first chapter, the Sambodha-vagga, is concluded.
(12) 2. The Āpāyika-vagga.
1. Commentary on the Āpāyikasutta 114.
Regarding the first [verse] of the second [stanza]: they will go to an *apāya* (state of loss), thus they are *āpāyika*; they will go to hell (*niraya*), thus they are *nerayika*.

"Without abandoning this" means without having relinquished these three unwholesome qualities, beginning with the claim of being a practitioner of the holy life (*brahmacāripaṭiññatā*). "One who claims to be a practitioner of the holy life" (*brahmacāripaṭiñño*)...
One who merely resembles a celibate student (*brahmacāripaṭirūpaka*), or one who makes such a claim by not abandoning their outward appearance, thinking "I too am a celibate student.

"He reviles" means he abuses, scolds, or reproaches. "There is no fault in sensual pleasures" means there is no fault for one who indulges in sense-objects (*vatthukāma*) with the defilement of craving (*kilesakāma*).
"That which is to be drunk" means that which is to be consumed or enjoyed without hesitation.
It is like drinking water for one who is thirsty with the mind; it is the state of being enjoyed [by the mind]. In this sutta, only the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is discussed.
2. Commentary on the *Dullabha-sutta* (The Rare One): 115.

In the second [sutta], "grateful and thankful" (*kataññū katavedī*) refers to a person who, having recognized and understood—"This was done for me by him"—makes known and manifests that deed performed by the other, and thus repays them.
3. Commentary on the Appameyya Sutta 116. In the third [verse]:
"Easily measured" means easily fathomed (*suppameyya*). "Hard to measure" means difficult to fathom (*duppameyya*).
"One who cannot be measured" means immeasurable (*appameyya*). "Arrogant" (*unnaḷa*) means one whose *naḷa* (reed) has risen up; the meaning is that he stands having raised up an empty pride.
*Capala* means one who possesses fickleness through such things as the ornamenting of robes. *Mukhara* means one whose mouth is harsh.

*Vikiṇṇavāca* means one whose speech is unrestrained. *Asamāhita* means devoid of one-pointedness of mind. *Vibbhantacitta* means one with a wandering mind, resembling a wandering ox or a wandering deer.
*Pākatindriya* means one with unrestrained faculties. The rest here is self-evident.
4. Commentary on the Āneñjasutta 117.
In the fourth [verse], "he relishes that" means he relishes that jhāna. "He desires that" means he aspires for that very same thing.
"And he finds satisfaction through it" means he attains contentment through that jhāna. "Established therein" means established in that jhāna.
"Established" (*ṭhito*). "Devoted to that" (*tadadhimutto*) means devoted to that very thing. "Dwelling frequently therein" (*tabbahulavihārī*) means dwelling extensively by means of that.
"He is reborn into companionship" (*sahabyataṃ upapajjati*) means he is reborn into a state of association; the meaning is that he is produced in that world of the devas.
"He goes even to hell," and so forth, refers to his going there by way of subsequent rebirth (*aparapariyāya*), because he is not yet liberated from hell and the other realms.

This was said with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). For there is no unwholesome state more powerful than access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*) by which one would be reborn in a state of misery immediately thereafter.
"A disciple of the Blessed One," however, refers to any one among the stream-enterers, once-returners, or non-returners.

"In that very existence" means in that very same immaterial realm (*arūpa-bhava*). "Attains final Nibbāna" means he attains final Nibbāna through the Nibbāna without remainder (*appaccaya-parinibbāna*).
"Adhippāyāso" means excessive application (*adhika-payoga*). The rest here should be understood according to the method already stated.

In this sutta, however, the jhāna of rebirth for an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) is explained; for a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*), that same jhāna of rebirth as well as the jhāna that serves as a basis for insight (*vipassanā-pādaka-jhāna*) are explained.
5. Commentary on the *Vipattisampadā-sutta* (The Discourse on Failure and Success)
118. In the fifth [view], "failure in virtue" (*sīlavipatti*) refers to the manner in which virtue has failed. The same method applies to the other two as well.

"There is no gift" (*natthi dinnaṃ*) is said with reference to the absence of fruit for what has been given. "Sacrifice" (*yiṭṭhaṃ*) refers to a great ritual sacrifice (*mahāyoga*). "Offering" (*hutaṃ*) is intended to mean hospitality consisting of food parcels.
Both of these he rejects with reference precisely to the absence of fruit. "Of the well-done and the ill-done" (*sukatadukkaṭānaṃ*)...
"Of good and bad deeds" means of wholesome and unwholesome [actions]. "There is no fruit, no result" means he asserts that whatever is called "fruit" or "result" does not exist.
"This world does not exist" means that for one situated in the next world, this world does not exist;
"there is no other world" means that even for one situated here in this world, the next world does not exist; [he holds that] all things are annihilated right there and then.
He shows this. "There is no mother, there is no father": he says this by way of the absence of fruit for right conduct and wrong conduct toward them.
"There are no spontaneously born beings (*opapātika*)": he says that there are no beings who arise after having passed away from one state. "Accomplishments" (*sampadā*) means fulfillments.
"Accomplishment in virtue" (*sīlasampadā*) is the state of virtue being complete and without deficiency. The same method applies to the other two as well.
"‘There is what is given,’ etc., should be understood by way of the opposite of what was stated [in the previous sutta].
6. Commentary on the Apaṇṇaka Sutta: 119.
‘An apaṇṇaka gem’ means a die possessed of six faces. ‘A happy destination, a heavenly realm’ refers to the realms of the Four Great Kings and so forth."
[He is reborn] in a certain heavenly world. In this sutta, both virtue and right view are spoken of as mixed together.
The seventh [sutta] is self-evident. 8.
Commentary on the First Purity Sutta (Paṭhama-soceyya-sutta).
121. In the eighth [sutta], "purities" (*soceyyāni*) means states of purity. "Purity of body" (*kāyasoceyya*) is the state of purity at the door of the body.

The same method applies to the other two as well. In these four suttas in sequence, the practice of the householder is taught; this is also appropriate for stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) and once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*).
9. Commentary on the Second Sutta on Purity (*Dutiyasoceyyasuttavaṇṇanā*)
122. In the ninth [verse], "internal" (*ajjhatta*) refers to one's own internal state. "Sensual desire" (*kāmacchanda*) refers to the hindrance of sensual desire.

The same method applies to ill will (*byāpāda*) and the others as well. The rest here follows the same method explained below. In the verse, however, "purity of body" (*kāyasuci*) means purity at the door of the body, or purity by means of the body.
The same method applies to the other two [doors] as well. "One who has washed away evil" (*ninhātapāpa*) means having caused all evils to be washed away and cleansed.
It is established. By this sutta as well as by the verse, it is the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) who is spoken of.
10. Commentary on the Moneyya Sutta 123.
In the tenth [verse], "moneyyāni" means states of being a sage (munibhāva). "Kāyamoneyya" is the state of being a sage, the state of being excellent, at the door of the body.
The state of being wise. This same method applies to the other two as well.

"This, monks, is called bodily modesty (*kāyamoneyya*)"—this refers to the abandoning of the threefold misconduct of body, which is what is meant by bodily modesty. Furthermore, the threefold good conduct of body is also bodily modesty;

likewise, knowledge having the body as its object is bodily modesty; the full understanding (*pariññā*) of the body is bodily modesty; and that which is accompanied by full understanding [is also bodily modesty].
The path is bodily purity; the abandoning of desire and lust for the body is bodily purity;
the cessation of bodily formations and the attainment of the fourth jhāna is bodily purity. The same method applies to verbal purity as well.
However, this is the distinction here: just as there is the attainment of the fourth jhāna here, there [in the case of verbal purity] is the cessation of verbal formations.

The attainment of the second jhāna should be understood as verbal *moneyya*. Having understood the meaning by this same method, the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saññā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*), which is the cessation of mental formations (*citta-saṅkhāra-nirodha*), should be understood as mental *moneyya*.
Regarding "the sage in the body-door" (*kāya-muni*): it means the supreme, perfectly pure sage in the door of the body, or the sage by means of the body. The same applies to the other two [doors].
This is the method. "The one who abandons everything" refers to the one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*). For indeed, the one whose taints are destroyed is called "the abandoner of all.
The second chapter, on those bound for states of misery, is concluded. (13) 3. The Chapter on Kusinārā.
1. Commentary on the Kusināra Sutta 124.
Regarding the first [section] of the third [chapter]: "In Kusinārā" refers to the city of that name.
"In the Baliharaṇa grove" refers to the grove of that name. It is said that they bring offerings there for the purpose of making offerings to spirits; therefore, it is called Baliharaṇa.
"Desiring" means wishing. "With his own hand" means with his own hand. "Invites [him] to eat" means he causes him to refuse by means of both speech and gestures, saying, "Enough, enough.
"May this be good for me" means "May this be good for me.
"Attached" means attached by the greed of craving (*taṇhā*). "Infatuated" means infatuated by the very delusion of craving. "Adhering" means by craving.
It is that which proceeds after having swallowed and finished [the food].

"One of no wisdom regarding escape" means that one who eats by gathering it together while abandoning desire and lust is called "one of wisdom regarding escape"; this person is not such, for he eats with desire and lust, thus he is "one of no wisdom regarding escape.
The bright side (sukkapakkha) should be understood by reversing what has been stated. Furthermore, here there are thoughts of renunciation (*nekkhamma-vitakka*) and so forth.
It should be understood that these have been spoken of as mixed.
2. Commentary on the Bhaṇḍana Sutta (Discourse on Quarreling) 125.
In the second [verse], "they abandoned" means they are abandoning; "they practiced extensively" means they do so repeatedly. Here too, the three types of thoughts are spoken of as being mixed.
3. Commentary on the Gotamakacetiyasutta 126.
Regarding "at the Gotamaka Shrine" in the third [sutta]: it was in the abode of the yakkha Gotamaka.
For during the first twenty years after his enlightenment, the Tathāgata stayed sometimes at the Cāpāla Shrine, sometimes at Sārandada, sometimes at Bahuputta, and sometimes at Gotamaka.
Thus, for the most part, he dwelt among the shrines of the gods. But at this time, he dwelt near Vesālī, in the abode of the yakkha Gotamaka.
Therefore it is said: "at the Gotamaka Shrine. He spoke this: he spoke this sutta beginning with "Having directly known... and so forth.
And it should be understood that this sutta was spoken by the Blessed One on account of a specific occasion.

What occasion? The occasion of the *Mūlapariyāya*. It is said that a number of brahmin renunciants, relying on the Buddha’s word they themselves had mastered, developed a conceit of knowledge and did not go to the assembly for hearing the Dhamma, thinking: "The Fully Enlightened One, when speaking..."
"He will speak only of what we already know, not of what we do not know. The monks reported this to the Tathāgata.
The Teacher summoned those monks, took their word, and taught the *Mūlapariyāya*. Those monks did not see, in that teaching, either a point they had reached or a point they had not reached.
Not seeing it, they said, "The Perfectly Enlightened One [is speaking] 'my discourse'..."
They thought, "By saying 'it leads out,' he is speaking only of the excellence of the mouth. The Teacher, knowing their thoughts, began this sutta.

Therein, "having directly known" means: "These five aggregates, twelve bases, eighteen elements, twenty-two faculties, four truths, nine causes, seven contacts, seven feelings, seven volitions, and seven perceptions..."

The meaning is: having known, penetrated, and made manifest "the seven consciousnesses," and likewise, having known, penetrated, and made manifest each respective state according to the method beginning with "these four foundations of mindfulness.
"With its cause" means I speak having established it as possessing conditions, not as being without conditions. "With its demonstration" means by way of refuting opposition.

"I speak only what is authoritative (sappāṭihāriya), not what is unauthoritative (appāṭihāriya). And it is sufficient for you (alañca pana vo) means: it is indeed appropriate for you. Regarding 'contentment' (tuṭṭhiyā):

the meaning is that it is fitting to produce contentment in you who recollect the three jewels by way of their qualities—thinking, 'The Blessed One is the Perfectly Enlightened One; the Dhamma is well-expounded; the Saṅgha is practicing rightly. The same method applies to the remaining two phrases as well."
"It shook" means it shook in six ways. For such an earthquake occurred even at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).

It is said that when the Bodhisatta ascended the seat of enlightenment from the southern direction, the southern quarter seemed to descend as far as the Avīci hell, while the northern quarter rose up as if striking the peak of existence (bhavagga). The western direction...
When it moved toward the west, its western side seemed as if it were reaching down to the Avīci hell, while its eastern side rose up as if striking against the peak of existence (*bhavagga*).

When it moved toward the north, its northern side seemed as if it were reaching down to the Avīci hell, while its southern side rose up as if striking against the peak of existence. When it moved toward the east, its eastern side...
It was as if reaching down to the Avīci hell, and its western side, having risen up, was as if striking against the peak of existence (bhavagga).
The Bodhi tree likewise was as if once reaching down to the Avīci hell, and once, having risen up, it was as if striking against the peak of existence.
On that very day, the great earth of a thousand world-systems (cakkavāḷa) trembled in these six ways.
4. Commentary on the Bharaṇḍukālāma Sutta 127.
In the fourth [sutta], *kevalakappaṃ* means the entire region (*sakalakappaṃ*). *Anvāhiṇḍanto* means wandering about.
"He did not see him"—for what reason did he not see him? It is said that this Bharaṇḍu Kālāma was wandering about eating the choice alms-food (*aggapiṇḍa*) of the Sakyans.
Knowing that when he arrived at his dwelling place, a discourse on the Dhamma would arise, the Blessed One made such a resolution that no other lodging appeared there; therefore, he did not see it.
"Former fellow-celibate" means an old fellow-celibate. It is said that he had been in that very hermitage during the time of Āḷāra Kālāma; it was with reference to him that he spoke thus.
"Spread out a rug" means "spread out what ought to be spread. "Having spread out a rug" means having spread out a covering on a permissible couch (*kappiyamañcaka*).
"He makes known the full understanding of sensual pleasures": here, "full understanding" (*pariññā*) means transcendence;
therefore, he makes known the first jhāna as the transcendence of sensual pleasures. "Not the full understanding of forms": [of] forms...

He does not designate the formless-sphere attainment as something that has transcended [the lower realms]. "Full understanding of feelings" means he does not designate Nibbāna—the transcendence of feelings—as such.
"Terminus" (*niṭṭhā*) means destination or accomplishment. "Or manifold" (*udāhu puthū*) means or diverse.
5. Commentary on the Hatthaka Sutta.

128. Regarding the phrase *pañcame abhikkantāya rattiyā* (“in the fifth watch of the night”), the word *abhikkanta* is seen used in the senses of destruction (*khaya*), beautiful (*sundara*), handsome (*abhirūpa*), and rejoicing (*abbhanumodana*).
Among these, in such passages as, “Venerable sir, the night has passed; the first watch has ended; the community of monks has been sitting for a long time;
let the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha to the monks,” it is seen in the sense of destruction. This...
In such passages as, “The most excellent and the most sublime among these four persons,” it means beautiful.
And: “Who is saluting my feet, shining with supernatural power and glory, illuminating all directions with a most excellent complexion?”—here too it means beautiful.
In such contexts as these, it means "beautiful. In expressions such as "Excellent, Master Gotama," it means "rejoicing.
But here, it means "lovely. Therefore, "at the lovely night" means at a night that is desirable, pleasing, and agreeable.

As for the phrase "of lovely complexion," here the word *abhikkanta* refers to being beautiful, while the word *vaṇṇa* refers to skin, praise, lineage, class, cause, shape, measure, the sense-sphere of form, and so forth.
It is seen. In that regard, in such passages as “The Blessed One is golden-colored,” it refers to the skin.

In such passages as “But when, householder, were the praises of the ascetic Gotama first uttered? it refers to praise. In such passages as “There are these four castes, Master Gotama,” it refers to the class of families.
In such passages as “Now by what characteristic is one called a ‘seeker of fragrance’? it refers to...

[The word *vaṇṇa*] is used in the sense of cause in such passages as “having manifested the form of a great king of elephants”; in the sense of shape in such passages as “[the three shapes] of the bowl”;
in the sense of measure in such passages as “the three sizes of the bowl”; and in the sense of the sense-sphere of visible form in such passages as “color, odor, taste, and nutritive essence.
Here, however, it should be understood as the skin. Thus, by the phrase “of surpassing beauty,” what is meant is a beautiful skin, a desirable color, or a pleasing color.
Regarding the term *kevalakappa*: here the word *kevala* has many meanings, such as "without remainder," "for the most part," "unmixed," "excessive," "firm," "disjoined," and so forth.
For instance, in passages such as "the holy life (*brahmacariya*) that is complete (*kevala*), perfect, and pure," its meaning is "without remainder.
Likewise, in the passage, "And they from the entire region of Aṅga-Magadha will approach, bringing abundant solid food and soft food," [it means "entire"].
In such cases as these, it refers to a majority. In such cases as “There is the origin of this entire mass of suffering,” it refers to unmixedness.
In such cases as “Surely this venerable one has only mere faith,” it refers to non-excess.
In such cases as “Venerable sir, the venerable Anuruddha’s co-resident named Bāhiya has stood for the schism of the entire Saṅgha,” [it refers to totality].
“Firmness of purpose” (*daḷhatthatā*). In such passages as, “He who is solitary, who has lived the holy life, he is called the Supreme Person,” it refers to dissociation (*visaṃyoga*).
But here, what is intended by the meaning is the state of being without remainder (*anavasesatā*). Furthermore, this word *kappa* has many meanings, such as:

conviction (*abhisaddahana*), conventional usage (*vohāra*), time (*kāla*), designation (*paññatti*), cutting off (*chedana*), alternative (*vikappa*), a trace (*leśa*), and all-inclusiveness (*samantabhāva*).
For instance, in such passages as, “This is truly credible of Master Gotama, as it is for an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha,” its meaning is *abhisaddahana* (firm conviction).
In such passages as, “I allow you, monks, to consume fruit according to the five conventions of the recluses,” its meaning is *vohāra* (convention).
And in such passages as, “By means of which indeed I dwell constantly throughout my life,” its meaning is *kappa* (time/life-span).
Time. In such passages as “Thus the venerable Kappa,” it is a designation (*paññatti*). In such passages as “adorned, with hair and beard trimmed,” it is cutting (*chedana*).

In such passages as “the two-finger-breadth allowance is permitted” (*kappati dvaṅgulakappo*), it is an arrangement (*vikappa*). In such passages as “there is the opportunity to lie down,” it is a slight amount (*leso*).
In such passages as “having illuminated the entire Veḷuvana grove,” it is the state of being all around (*samantabhāvo*). Here [it means]...
The meaning intended here is its state of being all-around. Therefore, regarding the phrase "the entire Jeta’s Grove," the meaning is "the Jeta’s Grove on every side without exception.
"Having illuminated" means having pervaded with light. "With sand" means with fine sand. "Does not settle" means it does not remain fixed.
"Coarse" (*oḷārika*): For when the Brahmā deity established himself upon the earth, his personal existence (*attabhāva*) had become coarse;
or rather, it was appropriate for him to manifest [the earth] as coarse. Therefore, he spoke thus. "The teachings" (*dhammā*):

By this, he shows the Buddha-word (*buddhavacana*) previously learned by heart. "They did not proceed": they became forgotten through lack of recitation, and were indeed lost. "Irresistible" (*appaṭivāna*): meaning without turning back, without weariness.
"Of seeing" means by means of visual consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*). "Of manifestation" means by means of the four conditions.
"Higher virtue" (*adhisīla*) refers to the tenfold virtue; for that is called "higher virtue" in relation to the five precepts.
"Gone to the Aviha realm" indicates that he has been reborn in the Aviha Brahma-world.
6. Commentary on the Kaṭuviya Sutta 129.
Regarding the sixth [verse], "near the Pilakkha tree at Goyoga": this means near a Pilakkha tree that had grown at the place where cows were sold.

"Empty enjoyment" (rittassāda) refers to the absence of the bliss of meditative absorption (jhāna). "External enjoyment" (bāhirassāda) refers to the pleasure derived from the strands of sensual desire (kāmaguṇa).
"Bitter" means defiled. "By a raw stench" means by the foul odor known as anger. "Lustful" means tainted.
"Flies" refers to the flies of the defilements (*kilesa*). "They shall not swarm upon it" means that having risen up, they will not follow after it.
"They shall not settle upon it" means that having followed after it, they will not consume it. "He attained a sense of spiritual urgency" means he became a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*).
"From what is bitter" means from what is vomited up. "He remains far away" means he is distant. "A partaker only of distress" means a partaker only of suffering.
"He wanders" means he moves about or goes. "Dull-witted" means lacking wisdom. In this sutta, only the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is discussed;
in the verses, both the cycle of existence and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*) are discussed. In the seventh [verse], only the cycle of existence is spoken of.
8. Commentary on the Second Anuruddha Sutta 131.
In the eighth [sutta], "This is your conceit" means this is your conceit increased in nine ways.
"This is your restlessness" means this is your restlessness, the state of agitation of the mind. "This is your worry" means...
This is your remorse.
9. Commentary on the Paṭicchanna-sutta (9):
"Brings along" means leads away. "The concealed one brings along" means that, being indeed concealed, it leads away.

Regarding the phrase "it shines forth, being open," the fourfold nature of openness should be understood here as: openness on one side, openness on both sides, openness within oneself, and openness everywhere.
Among these, "openness on one side" refers to the training rules (sikkhāpada) that are not shared [with other sects]. "Openness on both sides" refers to the training rules that are shared.
"Openness within oneself" refers to the qualities of the Dhamma attained by oneself. "Openness everywhere" refers to the word of the Buddha contained in the Three Baskets (Tipiṭaka).
10. Commentary on the Lekhasutta 133.
In the tenth [verse], *abhiṇhaṃ* means constantly and without interval. *Āgāḷhena* means with what is intense or harsh.
*Pharusena* means with harsh speech; the meaning is: even when being spoken to after having been made intense and harsh. *Amanāpena* means [that which is] not pleasing to the mind.
"By not clinging and by not increasing. "It is joined together" means it is indeed brought into connection.
"It is blended together" means it becomes continuous. "It is harmonized" means it attains a state of unity. The rest is clear in every respect.
The third chapter, the Kusinārā Chapter.
(14) 4. The Chapter on Warriors (Yodhājīvavagga). 1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Warrior (Yodhājīvasuttavaṇṇanā). 134.
In the first [discourse] of the fourth [chapter], one who lives by war is a warrior (*yodhājīva*). One who is worthy of a king is suitable for a king.

"Royal enjoyment" (*rājabhoga*) means the king’s use and consumption. "It is reckoned as a limb" means that because it must necessarily be desired—just like the hand or the foot—it is reckoned as a limb.
"He shoots far" means he discharges an arrow such that it falls a distance of one *usabha* in water, eight *usabhas* on land, or even further than that. [This was said] of Duṭṭhagāmaṇi Abhaya.
For while a professional warrior might shoot an arrow the length of a young bull, in his final birth the Bodhisatta [shot one] measuring a *yojana*.

"One who shoots through the joint" (*akkhaṇavedhī*) means one whose shooting is never missed; the meaning is that he is capable of piercing the joint of lightning—that is, the space between flashes of lightning.
"One who splits a great body" refers to being able to split even a hundred shields bound together on one side or a hundred buffalo hides.
The meaning is that it is capable of piercing even an iron plate as thick as a thumb, a wooden board four fingers thick, a plank of *udumbara* wood a span thick, or even a cartload of sand.
"Whatever form," and so forth, has already been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"This is not mine," and so forth, is stated by way of the rejection of craving, conceit, and views.
It has been said: "He sees with right wisdom" means he sees with the path-wisdom accompanied by insight, by means of the correct cause and reason.
"He shatters" means he shatters it by means of the path of Arahatship.
2. Commentary on the *Parisā Sutta* (The Discourse on the Assembly)
135. In the second [verse], "trained by suppression" (*ukkācita-vinītā*) refers to a poorly trained assembly that has been disciplined without being questioned.

"Trained by questioning" (*paṭipucchā-vinītā*) refers to a well-trained assembly that has been disciplined after being questioned. "Trained to such an extent" (*yāvatā-vinītā*) means trained according to measure;

the meaning is an assembly disciplined having recognized the proper measure. However, regarding the Pāḷi reading *yāvatajjhā*, the meaning is "to the extent of their intention" (*ajjhāsaya*); [the phrase] *ajjhāsayaṃ*...
"Having known, the assembly was disciplined"—this is what is meant. The third [sutta] is self-evident.
4. Commentary on the Uppāda Sutta (Sutta 137).

In the fourth, "the stability of phenomena" (*dhammaṭṭhitatā*) means the stability of their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). "The fixed course of phenomena" (*dhammaniyāmatā*) means the fixedness of their intrinsic nature.
"All formations" refers to the formations of the four planes. "Impermanent" means impermanent in the sense of having ceased after having come to be.
"Suffering" means suffering in the sense of being oppressed. "Non-self" means non-self in the sense of being devoid of mastery.
Thus, in this sutta, the three characteristics are taught in combination.
5. Commentary on the Kesakambala Sutta 138.
Regarding the phrase "of garments woven from threads" (*tantāvutānaṃ vatthānaṃ*), this is a genitive used in the sense of the nominative;

the meaning is "garments woven by means of threads. "Hair-cloth" (*kesakambalo*) is a blanket woven from human hair. Regarding the phrase "the various doctrines of recluses and brahmins" (*puthusamaṇabrāhmaṇavādānaṃ*), this also...
The genitive case is used in the sense of the individual. "Paṭikiṭṭho" means the lowest, the most wretched. "Moghapuriso" means a hollow man. "Paṭibāhati" means he prevents.
"Khippaṃ uḍḍeyya" means he would cast down a fish-net. The sixth and seventh [sections] have meanings that are already clear.
8. Commentary on the Assakhaḷuṅkasutta (The Discourse on the Wild Colt)
141. In the eighth [simile], "a wild colt" means a young horse. "I say this refers to its speed" means I say this refers to its speed of knowledge (*ñāṇajava*).
"I say this refers to its beauty" means I say this refers to its beauty of qualities (*guṇavaṇṇa*).
"This refers to its height and girth" means I say this refers to its tallness and well-proportioned form.
9. Commentary on the *Assaparassa Sutta* (Sutta 142).

Regarding the ninth [sutta], "among horses" (*assesu parasse*) means among those who are superior among horses. "Among men" (*purisesu parasse*) means among those who are superior among men; the sense is "among the best of men.
In this sutta, the three paths and fruits are explained. Therein, he should be understood as one endowed with the speed of knowledge through these three paths.
10. Commentary on the *Assājānīyasutta* 143.
In the tenth [verse], "bhadre" means in the excellent one. "Assājānīye" refers to a horse that knows what is possible and what is impossible.

The same method applies to "purisājānīye" (noble persons). In this sutta, the fruit of arahantship is discussed. Therein, he should be understood as being endowed with the speed of knowledge by means of the path to arahantship.
11. Commentary on the First Peacock Feeding Ground Sutta (Paṭhamamoranivāpasutta) 144.

Regarding the eleventh [sutta], "one who has reached the ultimate goal" (*accantaniṭṭha*) means one whose goal has transcended the end; the meaning is that his goal is unshakable and permanent. The rest is exactly the same. 12.
Commentary on the Second Peacock Feeding Ground Sutta (Dutiyamoranivāpasutta)

145. Regarding the twelfth [section], "by the miracle of psychic power" (*iddhipāṭihāriya*) means by the miracle of success. "By the miracle of mind-reading" (*ādesanāpāṭihāriya*) means by the miracle of discourse consisting of speaking and counter-discourse after having indicated and pointed out [the thoughts].
13. Commentary on the Third Sutta on the Pea-Hopper (*Moranivāpa-sutta*) 146.

Regarding the thirteenth [section], "by right view" (*sammādiṭṭhi*) means by right view for the sake of attaining the fruition-attainment (*phalasamāpatti*). "By right knowledge" (*sammāñāṇa*) means by the knowledge of fruition (*phalañāṇa*).

"By right liberation" means by the remaining phenomena of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*). In these three suttas as well, it is only the one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*) who is spoken of.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Chapter on the Warrior.
(15) 5. The Chapter on Auspiciousness (*Maṅgalavagga*).
1–9. Commentary on the Akusala-sutta and others, 147–155.
In the first [sutta] of the fifth [chapter], "laid down as it was brought" means as it was placed after being carried there.

In the second, "by what is blameworthy" means by that which is accompanied by hatred (*sadosena*). In the third, "by the uneven" means by that which is accompanied by stumbling; "by the even" means by that which is free from stumbling. In the fourth...
"Unclean" means impure, filthy, and like excrement. "Clean" means pure and stainless.
The fifth and subsequent [terms] are self-evident.
10. Commentary on the Pubbaṇha Sutta.

156. Regarding the passage beginning with “On the tenth day, Sunakkhatta,” that day on which the three factors of good conduct are fulfilled is called “having obtained an auspicious conjunction of stars” (*laddhanakkhattayoga*);
therefore, it is said that for him there is always “good star-time” (*sunakkhatta*). That very same day is called “having performed an auspicious rite” (*katamaṅgala*);
therefore, it is said that for him there is always “good auspiciousness” (*sumaṅgala*). For him, even the break of dawn is always [auspicious].
The dawn has truly broken; rising from bed is truly well-timed; the moment is indeed a good moment; even the brief interval is a fine interval.
Herein, a period of time measuring ten finger-snapshots is called a *khaṇa* (moment);
ten such *khaṇas* is a period called a *laya* (instant); ten such *layas* is a period called a *khaṇalaya*; and ten times that is called a *muhutta* (hour).
By that [unit], a *khaṇa* (moment) and a *muhutta* (hour) are each tenfold; this distinction should be understood.

"Well-given among those who lead the holy life" (*suyiṭṭhaṃ brahmacārisu*) means that on whichever day the three types of good conduct are fulfilled, a gift given by him to those of excellent conduct is called "well-given.
"Wholesome bodily action" (*padakkhiṇaṃ kāyakammaṃ*) refers to the bodily action performed by him on that day, which is an increasing bodily action.

This is the name [of the section]. The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well. "Having performed auspicious acts" (*padakkhiṇāni katvāna*) means having performed bodily actions and so forth that are conducive to growth.
Regarding the term *padakkhiṇa* in the sense of "obtaining," one obtains only that which has the meaning of growth. The rest is self-evident.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the Chapter on Auspiciousness (*Maṅgalavagga*).
The Third Fifty is finished.
(16) 6. Explanation of the Chapter on the Naked Ascetics (Acelakavagga), §§ 157–163.
Regarding the subsequent sections: "Arduous practice" (*āgāḷhā paṭipadā*) means that which is strict, harsh, and characterized by a firm grasping due to greed. "Emaciated" (*nijjhāmā*)...
"By means of devotion to self-mortification," he is well-burnt, heated, and consumed. "Moderate" means neither harsh nor burnt, being situated in the middle.
"Naked" means unclothed, bare. "One of loose conduct" means one of abandoned behavior;
devoid of the conduct of worldly sons of good family regarding the acts of defecation and so forth, he voids excrement, urinates, and eats while remaining standing.
He eats. "Licking the hands" means that when the morsel in the hand has been finished, he licks the hand with the tongue;
or, having even defecated, perceiving it as a mere stick, he licks it off with his hand.
He is not one who says "Come, Venerable Sir" because, when told "Come, Venerable Sir" for the purpose of receiving alms, he does not come. [When told] "In that case, stay, Venerable Sir,"...
"Even when told [to accept], he does not stay," thus he is called *na-tiṭṭha-bhadantika*.
It is said that he does not do either of those two things, thinking, "His word will have been carried out. *Abhihaṭa* refers to alms-food brought and received beforehand.
*Uddissakata* refers to alms-food announced as, "This was prepared specifically for you. *Nimantana* refers to [an invitation from] a specific family...
“...or enter a street or a village,” he does not consent to or accept even a monk so invited.
“Not from the mouth of a jar”: he does not accept alms-food being given after it has been taken out from a jar.
“Not from the mouth of a vessel”: *kaḷopī* means either a cooking pot or a basket; he does not accept from that either. Why? [Because] “the jars and baskets, depending on me...”
“...receiving a blow with a ladle. *Na eḷakamantaraṃ*: he does not accept food being given while placing a threshold-block (*ummāra*) in between.
Why? [He thinks: “Because of this, he receives an intervention (*antarakaraṇa*) on my account. The same principle applies to sticks and pestles as well. *Dvinnaṃ*:
when two people are eating and one rises up to give [food], he does not accept it. Why? Because it would cause an obstruction to his mouthful (*kabaḷantarāyo*).
Regarding the phrases "not from a pregnant woman" and so forth: one does not accept [food] from a pregnant woman because the child in her womb suffers;
from a nursing woman because it causes an interruption of milk for the child; and from a woman who has gone to another man because it causes an interruption of sexual pleasure.

"Not from those where food is being collected" means from meals prepared by collecting [various items). It is said that during a time of famine, disciples of the Acelakas, for the sake of the Acelakas, [prepared food by]...
Having had rice and other grains collected from here and there, they cook the meal; however, the strict naked ascetic does not accept it from there.

"Where there is no *sā*": where a dog is waiting, thinking, "I will get a morsel," he does not take what has been brought there without first giving to the dog. Why? Because that would be an obstacle to the dog's alms-food. "Moving in groups" means moving in large crowds.

For if people, upon seeing a naked ascetic, enter a meal-house thinking, "We shall give alms to him," and while they are entering, flies that were hidden in baskets, pots, and so forth fly up and swarm in thick clusters, he does not accept the alms brought from there. Why?
Because [he thinks]: "On account of me, an obstacle to the foraging of the flies has arisen."
*Thusodaka* means sour gruel (*soviraka*) made from all kinds of grain ingredients. In this context, the drinking of *surā* (fermented liquor) alone is blameworthy;
however, this person perceives everything as blameworthy. An *ekāgārika* is one who returns after receiving alms at only a single house.
An *ekālopika* is one who sustains himself with only a single mouthful (*ālopa*). The same principle applies to those who go to two houses (*dvāgārika*), and so forth. Even for a single...
"By means of a *datti*": by means of a single *datti*. A *datti* is a small bowl in which the first alms-food is placed and set aside.
"Daily" (*ekāhika*) means occurring with an interval of one day. "Fortnightly" (*addhamāsika*) means occurring with an interval of half a month.
"Taking meals by turn" (*pariyāyabhattabhojana*) means taking meals according to a rotation—by a turn of one day, two days, seven days, or half a month, and so forth.
"Eating the meal brought on a daily basis. "Eating only vegetables," and so forth, have already been explained in their respective contexts.
"One who stands upright" means one who remains standing. "Devoted to the exertion of squatting" means devoted to the energy of squatting;
even when walking, he does so by repeatedly springing up while remaining in a squatting posture. "One who uses a bed of thorns" [means one who uses] iron thorns...
Or, having pounded natural thorns into the ground and spread his hide over them, he performs standing, walking meditation, and so forth.
As for "lying down," even while sleeping, he makes his bed right there. "Sāyatatiyakaṃ" means three times every day:
in the morning, at midday, and in the evening, he dwells devoted to the practice of descending into water, thinking, "I shall wash away evil."
