"Contemplating the body in the body," and so forth, are to be understood according to the method already explained in the commentary on the section of single items below.
"This, monks, is called the Middle Way"— this, monks, is the middle way that does not approach the two extremes of devotion to sensual pleasure and devotion to self-mortification,
or rather, it is the middle way liberated from the extremes of eternalism and annihilationism.
The practice is to be understood.
The sixth chapter, the Chapter on the Naked Ascetics (Acelakavagga), is concluded.
17–18. Commentary on the Shorter Chapters (Peyyālavagga), etc.

164–184. *Samanuñño* means having a similar inclination. *Rāgassa* refers to the lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇika-rāga*). *Abhiññāya* means for the purpose of direct knowledge.
By the three types of concentration beginning with "emptiness" (*suññato samādhi*), it is precisely insight (*vipassanā*) that is being described.
For insight receives these names because of the absence of adherence to permanence, signs of permanence, and aspirations for permanence, and so forth. *Pariññāya* means...
For the purpose of full comprehension. This same method applies to the remaining sections as well.
The section beginning with the *Peyyālavagga* is concluded.
From the *Manorathapūraṇī*, the commentary on the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Tika-nipāta is completed.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
In the Aṅguttara Nikāya.
Commentary on the Book of Fours (Catukkanipāta-aṭṭhakathā) 1.
The First Fifty (Paṭhamapaṇṇāsaka) 1.
The Chapter on the Village of Bhaṇḍa (Bhaṇḍagāmavagga)
1. Commentary on the *Anubuddhasutta*.

In the first [sutta] of the Catukka-nipāta: "Through non-awakening" (*ananubodhā*) means by way of not awakening, that is, by way of not knowing. "Through non-penetration" (*appaṭivedhā*) means by way of not penetrating, that is, by way of not making it manifest to direct experience.
"For a long stretch of time" (*dīgham addhānaṃ*) means for a long duration. "Run through" (*sandhāvitaṃ*) means by way of going from one existence to another existence.
"Run about" (*sandhāvitaṃ*). "Wandered on" (*saṃsaritaṃ*) means wandered on by way of repeated going and coming.

"Both mine and yours" (*mamañceva tumhākañca*) means both by me and by you. Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood as: "The running about and the wandering on—both mine and yours—have taken place.
"Of the Noble One" (*ariyassa*) means of the faultless one. Virtue and concentration...
As for these three states—wisdom (*paññā*), liberation (*vimutti*), and craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*)—they should be understood as being associated with the paths and fruits (*maggaphala*).

Liberation is specifically designated here by the name of the fruit itself. Craving for existence is craving for the various realms of becoming. The "rope of existence" (*bhavanetti*) is the tether of becoming; this is simply another name for craving.
For it is by means of this that beings are led from one state of existence to another, bound by the neck like oxen; therefore, it is called the "rope of existence."
"Anuttara" means supramundane (*lokuttara*). "One who makes an end of suffering" means one who brings an end to the suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*).

"Possessing eyes" means possessing eyes by way of the five kinds of eyes. "Parinibbūta" means parinibbūta through the parinibbāna of the defilements (*kilesa*). This was his first parinibbāna at the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*);
later, however, between the twin *sāla* trees, [he attained parinibbāna] through the element of nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*).
"He has attained final Nibbāna" (*parinibbuto*): thus he brought the teaching to its conclusion by following the sequence of the connection.
2. Commentary on the *Papatita Sutta*. 2.
In the second [sutta], "fallen" (*papatito*) means fallen away or deceased. "Not fallen" (*appapatito*) means not fallen, but established. In this regard, the worldling (*lokīya-mahājana*)...
"Fallen" (patita) indeed means: stream-enterers and the others are called "fallen" at the moment a defilement arises; one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) is called "absolutely established.

"The fallen fall" means those who have passed away (cuta) are said to fall. "The fallen" means those who have fallen are said to have passed away. The meaning is: because they have passed away, they are fallen;
because they are fallen, they have passed away. "Greedily" means colored by passion (rāga). "Returning again" means again to birth, again...

They are said to have "come upon" old age, sickness, and death once again. "What was to be done has been done" means that what ought to be accomplished by means of the four paths has been accomplished.
"Delighted in what is delightful" means delighted in the various qualities worthy of delighting in.

"Attained happiness through happiness" means that happiness has followed upon, or reached, happiness—namely, divine happiness following upon human happiness, and the happiness of insight following upon the happiness of meditative absorption (jhāna).

The meaning is that through the happiness of insight (vipassanā-sukha), the happiness of the path (magga-sukha) is attained; through the happiness of the path, the happiness of the fruit (phala-sukha);
and through the happiness of the fruit, the happiness of Nibbāna is reached and realized.
3. Commentary on the First Khatasutta.
3. This has already been stated in the commentary on the Third Pair (Tatiyaṃ Dukanipāta). Regarding the verses: "blameworthy" (nindiya) means that which is worthy of blame.
"He blames" (nindati) means he censures. "Praiseworthy" (pasaṃsiya) means worthy of praise. "He gathers misfortune with his mouth" (vicināti mukhena so kalin):
one who acts in this manner is said to gather misfortune (kali) with that mouth. "By that misfortune he finds no happiness" (kalinā tena sukhaṃ na vindati): by that [misfortune]...
And one does not obtain happiness through that [ordinary] misfortune (*kalī*).
"Even with all, even with oneself" means that whatever defeat occurs, whether by all of one's own wealth or even together with oneself, that is but a trifling misfortune—this is the meaning.
"He who [harbors malice] toward the Sugatas" refers to one who would corrupt the mind toward persons who have attained the right path; this corruption of mind is a misfortune greater than that.
The *kali* age is even greater. Now, in order to show its state of being even greater, he said:
"A hundred thousand," and so forth. Therein, "a hundred thousand" means one hundred thousand by the calculation of *nirabbudas*.
"Thirty-six" means another thirty-six *nirabbudas*. "And five" means five *abbudas* by the calculation of *abbudas*. "He who reviles the Noble Ones."
Regarding the statement, "He who reviles the Noble Ones is reborn in hell; such is the measure of his lifespan there":
this is the commentary on the second *Khaṭa Sutta*.
In the fourth [sutta], concerning the words "toward mother, toward father," and so forth, *Mittavindaka* is one who practiced wrongly toward his mother, while *Ajātasattu*...

One who behaves wrongly toward his father is called "one who practices wrongly"; Devadatta is called "one who practices wrongly" toward the Tathāgata; Kokālika is called "one who practices wrongly" toward the disciples of the Tathāgata.
*Bahuñca* means "much indeed. *Pasavati* means "he acquires. *Tāya* means "by that," namely, by that unrighteous conduct characterized as wrong practice. *Pecca* means "having gone from here.
*Apāyaṃ gacchati* means "he goes to a state of deprivation," i.e., he is reborn in one of the hells or other such realms.
The same method applies to the bright fortnight as well.
5. Commentary on the *Anusotasutta*:

In the fifth [sutta], one who goes with the stream is called "one who goes with the stream" (*anusotagāmī*). One who proceeds against the stream by way of a practice that is contrary to the stream of defilements is [called] "one who goes against the stream" (*paṭisotagāmī*).

"He goes against the stream" means he moves upstream. "Established" means having a stable nature. "Crossed over" means having stood after crossing the flood. "Gone to the further shore" means having reached the opposite bank.
"He stands on dry land" means he stands on the dry land of Nibbāna. "A brahmin" means one who is supreme and faultless. "In this world" means in this very world.
"And indulges in sensual pleasures" means he indulges in objective sensual pleasures by means of defilement-sensualities. And evil...
"He performs karma" means he performs evil karma such as the taking of life and so forth. "He does not perform evil karma" means he does not perform the fivefold karma of enmity.
"This, monks, is called one whose mind is steadied": this person, a non-returner (anāgāmī), is called "steadied" because he does not return again from that world by way of rebirth-linking.

"Overcome by craving" means overcome or overwhelmed by craving; or, having entered into craving, they have plunged deeply into it. "Perfect in training" means established in the fulfillment of the training.
"One whose nature is not subject to decline" means one whose essential character has not fallen away. "Attained to mastery over the mind" means one who has reached the state of mastery over the mind.
Such a person is an arahant with taints destroyed, but here an non-returner is intended. "With faculties composed" means one whose six sense-faculties are composed.

*Paroparā* means "superior and inferior," that is, the excellent and the low; the meaning is "the wholesome and the unwholesome. *Samecca* means having approached through knowledge. *Vidhūpitā* means destroyed or consumed by fire.
*Vusitabrahmacariyo* means one who has dwelt and stands firm in the holy life of the Path.
*Lokantagū* means one who has gone to the end of the threefold world. *Pāragato* means one who has reached the further shore in six ways.

Here, it is the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) who is described. Thus, both in the discourses and in the verses, only the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) and its cessation (vivaṭṭa) are discussed.
6. Commentary on the Appassuta Sutta:

In the sixth [verse], "not arrived" (anupapanno) means not having reached [the goal]. Regarding the terms "discourse" (sutta) and so forth, there are the two Vibhaṅgas, the Niddesa, the Khandhaka, the Parivāra, the Suttanipāta, the Maṅgalasutta, the Ratanasutta, and so on.
The *Nāḷaka-sutta* and the *Tuvaṭaka-sutta*, as well as any other word of the Tathāgata bearing the name "sutta," should be understood as *sutta*.
Every discourse (*sutta*) that contains verses should be understood as *geyya*, especially the entire Sagāthāvagga within the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*.

Furthermore, the entire *Abhidhamma Piṭaka*, discourses (*sutta*) that are devoid of verses, and whatever else is not included among the eight factors (*aṅga*) [of the Dharma] should be understood accordingly.

The word of the Buddha (*buddhavacana*) should be understood as *veyyākaraṇa*. The *Dhammapada*, the *Theragāthā*, the *Therīgāthā*, those verses in the *Suttanipāta* that do not bear the name of a specific sutta, and pure verses (*suddhikagāthā*) should be understood as *gāthā*.
The eighty-two discourses connected with verses consisting of joy and knowledge should be understood as *udāna*.
The one hundred and ten discourses occurring in the manner beginning with "This was said by the Blessed One" (*vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā*) [should be understood as *itivuttaka*].
They should be understood as the *Itivuttaka*. The more than five hundred and fifty Jātakas, beginning with the *Apaṇṇaka-jātaka*, should be understood as the *Jātaka*.

All discourses (*suttanta*) connected with wonderful and marvelous qualities that proceed according to the method beginning with, “Bhikkhus, there are these four wonderful and marvelous qualities in Ānanda,” should be understood as the *Abbhutadhamma*.
[These include] the *Cūḷavedalla*, *Mahāvedalla*, *Sammādiṭṭhi*, *Sakkapañha*, *Saṅkhārabhājaniya*, *Mahāpuṇṇama-sutta*, and others.
All those discourses that have been asked about, having repeatedly received both knowledge (*veda*) and satisfaction (*tuṭṭhi*), should be understood as *vedalla*.
"Without knowing the meaning and without knowing the Dhamma" means without knowing both the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) and the canonical text (*pāḷi*).

"One who practices in accordance with the Dhamma" means one who does not practice the preliminary path consisting of the ninefold supramundane Dhamma together with its corresponding Dhamma, which is the virtue of the trainee (*sāvakasīla*).
...it exists. By this method, the meaning should be understood in all sections. Here, however, in the first section, one who is of little learning and immoral is described;

in the second, one who is of little learning and has destroyed the taints (khīṇāsava); in the third, one who is of much learning and immoral; and in the fourth, one who is of much learning and has destroyed the taints.
"Not concentrated in virtue" means one who does not fulfill virtue. "In virtue and in learning" means by way of the factor of virtue and the factor of learning.
And the meaning is that they revile him, thinking, "This person is immoral and of little learning.
"His learning succeeds" means that because that person has performed the function of learning through that which was learned, his learning is said to succeed.
"It does not succeed for him" means it does not succeed because the function of learning has not been performed. "One who upholds the Dhamma" refers to those teachings heard.
"Being the foundation. "Possessing wisdom" (*sappañña*) means having good wisdom (*supañña*). "Like a pendant of Jambūnada gold": *jambūnada* refers to gold produced from the Jambu river;
it is like a pendant (*nekkha*) of that Jambūnada gold, meaning like a golden coin (*suvaṇṇaghaṭikā*) measuring five [units] of gold.
7. Commentary on the *Sobhana-sutta*.

7. In the seventh [verse], "learned" (*viyatta*) means endowed with the clarity of wisdom (*paññāveyyattiya*). "Disciplined" (*vinīta*) means well-disciplined, having approached the discipline (*vinaya*).

"Confident" (*visārada*) means endowed with self-confidence (*vesārajja*), which is knowledge accompanied by joy. "Upholders of the Dhamma" (*dhammadhara*) means those who have become the repositories of the Dhamma as it was heard.
And in the verse beginning with "a bhikkhu perfected in virtue," although each quality is mentioned for each individual, [the meaning remains the same].
However, all [of these] are indeed possible for everyone.
8. Commentary on the Discourse on the Grounds of Self-Confidence (Vesārajja-sutta).
Regarding the term *vesārajjāni* in the eighth [discourse]: here, *vesārajja* is the opposite of *sārajja* (timidity/fear); it refers to the absence of fear (*sārajjābhāva*) regarding four points.
This is the name for the knowledge consisting of joy that arises in one who is reflecting. "The place of the bull" (*āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ*) means the best place, the supreme place.
Alternatively, the "bulls" (*āsabhā*) are the previous Buddhas; the meaning is "the place of them.
Furthermore, a *usabha* is the leader of a hundred cows, while a *vasabha* is the leader of a thousand cows. Or, a *usabha* is the leader of a hundred bulls, while a [leader of] a thousand bulls...
The bull (*vasabha*)—the best of all cattle, the endurer of all perils, white, beautiful, the bearer of great burdens, and unshakable even by the sound of a hundred thunderbolts—is called *nisabha*.
Here, it is this *usabha* that is intended. For this too is a synonym for it.
"Belonging to the bull" (*usabhassa idaṃ*) is *āsabhaṃ*. "Station" (*ṭhānaṃ*) means the firm establishment [of the body] by pressing down upon the earth with all four feet.
But this is "bull-like" (*āsabhaṃ*) because it is like a bull (*usabha*), known as a leader (*nisabha*). For just as a bull called a leader stands immovably,
having pressed down upon the earth with all four feet, so too the Tathāgata stands, having pressed down upon the earth of the eight assemblies with the four feet of self-confidence (*vesārajja*),
unshakable by any adversary or enemy in the world including the devas.
He stands by means of an immovable position. Standing thus, he claims, approaches, and does not renounce that bull-like position;
he ascribes it to himself. Therefore it is said: “He claims the bull-like position.
“In assemblies” means in the eight kinds of assemblies. “He roars the lion’s roar” means he roars the best roar, the fearless roar, which is like the roar of a lion.
Or he roars a roar. This meaning should be shown by means of the *Sīhanāda Sutta*.

Just as a lion is called "sīha" because of his endurance (*sahana*) and his slaying (*hana*), so too the Tathāgata is called "sīha" because of his endurance of worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*) and his slaying of the doctrines of others.
The roar of such a lion is the "lion's roar" (*sīhanāda*). In that regard, just as a lion—
Just as one endowed with the strength of a lion roars the lion’s roar, confident in every respect and free from horripilation,
so too the Tathāgata-lion, endowed with the powers of a Tathāgata, is confident in the eight assemblies and, free from horripilation, roars the lion’s roar—
endowed with the various graces of teaching in the manner beginning with "Such is form"— by way of the phrase "iti rūpaṃ. Therefore it was said:
“He roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies.
Regarding the phrase “He sets in motion the Brahma-wheel”: here, *brahma* means supreme, most excellent, and pure.
As for this word *cakra* (wheel), it is used in the sense of prosperity, a characteristic mark, a chariot part, and deportment: “In prosperity, a characteristic mark, a chariot part, and deportment;”

The term *cakra* (wheel) is seen in reference to the wheel of giving (*dāna-cakra*), the wheel of the supreme Dharma (*dhamma-cakra*), the wheel of sovereignty (*issariya-cakra*), and so forth. Here, however, it is intended as the Wheel of the Dharma (*dhammacakka*).
One should analyze that in two ways. For it is said: "Bhikkhus, there are these four wheels, possessed of which gods and humans... and so on. In such passages, this [term]...
It is seen in the sense of prosperity: “Wheels have appeared on the soles of his feet”—here it refers to a mark (lakkhaṇa).
“Like the wheel of one who drives”—here it refers to a part of a chariot (rathaṅga). “The four-wheeled, nine-gated [city]”—here it refers to the modes of deportment (iriyāpatha).

“Give, enjoy, and do not be negligent; set the wheel in motion for all living beings”—here it refers to giving (dāna). “The divine wheel-treasure appeared”—here it refers to the Wheel-turning Monarch’s wheel.
In this context, it refers to the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakka*). In the phrase "the wheel set in motion by me," it refers to the Wheel of Dhamma.

In the phrase "the wheel whirls upon the head of the man struck by desire," it refers to the chest-wheel (*uracakka*). In the phrase "even with a wheel whose edge is like a razor," it refers to a weapon-wheel (*paharaṇacakka*).
In the phrase "a thunderbolt-wheel," it refers to a circle of lightning (*asanimaṇḍala*). But here, it is understood as the Wheel of Dhamma.

Furthermore, this Wheel of Dhamma is twofold: the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of teaching (*desanā-ñāṇa*). Therein, the knowledge of penetration is that which is developed through wisdom and brings about the noble fruit for oneself;
the knowledge of teaching is that which is developed through compassion and brings about the noble fruit for disciples.
Therein, the knowledge of penetration is twofold: that which is arising and that which has arisen. For, from the time of the Great Departure...
From the moment the path of arahantship arises until the moment of its fruition, it is called "arisen.
Or, from the Tusita heaven until the moment the path of arahantship arises on the Great Enlightenment Seat, it is called "arisen" at the moment of fruition.
Or, from the time of Dīpaṅkara Buddha until the moment the path of arahantship arises on the Enlightenment Seat, it is called "arisen" at the moment of fruition.

Knowledge of teaching, when it occurs, occurs in two ways. That which occurs up until the moment of the stream-entry path of Aññā Koṇḍañña is called "occurring at the moment of the fruit. Among these, penetrative knowledge is supramundane, while knowledge of teaching is mundane.
Yet both of these are not shared by others; they are the unique, direct knowledge of the Buddhas alone.

"Of you who claim to be a Perfectly Enlightened One" means: of you who claim, "I am a Perfectly Enlightened One; all phenomena have been fully realized by me. "Not fully realized" means: these specific phenomena have not been fully realized by you.
"In that regard" means: regarding those phenomena shown as "not fully realized. "With reason" means: with cause and with motive.
"By word. Regarding "this is a sign" (*nimitta*): here, both a person (*puggala*) and a phenomenon (*dhamma*) are intended by the term "sign.

"I do not see that person who would reproach me; I do not see that phenomenon which, having been pointed out, would reproach me by saying, 'This very phenomenon has not been fully realized by you'"—this is the meaning here. "One who has attained security" (*khemappatta*).
He has attained security. The remaining two phrases are synonyms for this very [attainment]. All of this is stated with reference specifically to the knowledge of fearlessness (*vesārajja-ñāṇa*).

For when the One Possessed of the Ten Powers (*dasabala*) does not perceive—whether it be a person who challenges him by saying, "This particular Dhamma has not been fully awakened to by you," or the reason for the challenge, namely, the Dhamma that has not been fully awakened to—he thinks: "Indeed, while being one who has truly awakened to the true nature of things..."
When one reflects, "I am a Buddha," a more powerful joy arises;

the knowledge associated with that is called *vesārajja* (fearlessness). It is with reference to this that he said, "He has attained security," and so forth. In this way, the meaning is to be understood in all instances. Regarding the phrase "obstructive states" (*antarāyikā dhammā*):
here, they are called "obstructive" because they create an obstruction (*antarāyaṃ karonti*). In terms of their actual nature, they are intentional...
The seven classes of offenses have been transgressed. For even a deliberate transgression, down to a *dukkaṭa* or a *dubbhāsita*, creates an obstacle to the paths and fruits.
However, what is intended here is sexual intercourse (*methunadhamma*).
For anyone who indulges in sexual intercourse, there is undoubtedly an obstacle to the paths and fruits.

"But for whatever purpose you [taught] the Dhamma"—that is, for whatever purpose among the destruction of lust and so forth. "The Dhamma was taught" means the Dhamma such as the meditation on foulness (*asubha-bhāvanā*) was explained.
"In that, alas, me [in] this Dhamma which does not lead out"—in that Dhamma which does not lead to liberation, [he says] "me. The rest should be understood according to the method already stated.
"Paths of speech" means merely discourses. "Diverse" means many. "Set down" means bound together or constructed. Alternatively, "diverse set-downs" (*puthussitā*).
"Attached to diversity" (*puthussitā*) means either those who have come to be attached to a state of multiplicity, or those who are attached to many things; thus they are "attached to diversity.
"Whatever they rely upon" refers to whatever path of discourse they rely upon even now. "They do not exist" means those paths of discourse no longer exist; they break apart and perish.

"The Wheel of Dhamma" (*dhammacakka*) is a name for both the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of teaching (*desanā-ñāṇa*). Among these, the knowledge of teaching is mundane (*lokiya*).
Penetrative knowledge (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*) is supramundane (*lokuttara*). "The Perfect One" (*kevalī*) means one endowed with all virtues. "Such as that" (*tādisaṃ*) means of that same kind. 9.

Commentary on the *Taṇhuppāda-sutta* (Discourse on the Arising of Craving). In the ninth [verse], they are called "arisings" (*uppādā*) because craving arises within them. What arises? Craving. The "arisings of craving" (*taṇhuppādā*) are the arisings of that craving.

The meaning is: "bases for craving" (taṇhāvatthūni) refers to the causes of craving (taṇhākāraṇāni). "For the sake of robes" (cīvarahetu) means that [craving] arises for the purpose of robes, thinking, "Where shall I obtain pleasing robes?
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of this or that state of existence" (itibhavābhavahetu): here, *iti* is a particle used in the sense of illustration. The meaning is:

just as there is [craving] for the sake of robes and so forth, so too is there [craving] for the sake of this or that state of existence (*bhavābhava*). And here, "this or that state of existence" (*bhavābhava*) refers to more refined things such as ghee, fresh butter, and so on.
These are what is intended. They also say that among states of prosperity, it refers to existences that are increasingly more excellent.
"With craving as his companion" (taṇhādutiyo): for this being, while wandering through the beginningless cycle of existence (saṃsāra), does not wander alone;
rather, he wanders only by obtaining craving as his companion. Therefore it is said, "with craving as his companion. "This state and another state" (itthabhāvaññathābhāvaṃ)...
Herein, "this state" (*itthabhāva*) refers to this present personal existence (*attabhāva*); "otherwise-ness" (*aññathābhāva*) refers to future personal existence.
Or, a personal existence of such a kind is called "this state," while one that is not of such a kind is called "otherwise-ness. That is "this state and otherwise-ness.
"Samsara" refers to the succession of the aggregates (*khandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*). "Does not transcend" means does not go beyond. [He sees] such danger (*ādīnava*).
"Having known" means having thus understood the danger (*ādīnava*) in the aggregates (*khandha*) of the past, future, and present.
"Craving as the origin of suffering" means having understood craving as well, thinking: "This is the inherent nature and cause from which the suffering of saṃsāra arises.
Up to this point, the state of this bhikkhu having attained *arahantship* by increasing his insight (*vipassanā*) has been shown. Now...
Praising that one whose taints are destroyed, he said, "Free from craving," and so forth. In this context, "without grasping" means without seizing.

"A mindful bhikkhu goes forth" means that a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, having attained abundance in mindfulness and clear comprehension, should move about and dwell mindful and clearly comprehending.
Thus, having explained the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) in the prose sutta, the round and its cessation (*vaṭṭa-vivaṭṭa*) are explained in the verses.
10. Commentary on the Discourse on the Bonds (Yogasutta) 10.

In the tenth [discourse], they are called "bonds" (*yoga*) because they yoke one to the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*). Among the "bond of sensual desire" (*kāmayoga*) and so forth: the passion consisting of the five strands of sensual pleasure is the bond of sensual desire.

The will and passion for existence within the realms of form and formlessness is the bond of existence (*bhavayoga*), as is attachment to meditative absorption (*jhāna*). And that which is accompanied by the view of eternalism...
Lust and the sixty-two views constitute the yoke of views (*diṭṭhi-yoga*). Ignorance regarding the four truths is the yoke of ignorance (*avijjā-yoga*).

It is called the yoke of sensual desire (*kāma-yoga*) because it yokes one to sensual pleasures; the yoke of existence (*bhava-yoga*) because it yokes one to states of existence; the yoke of views (*diṭṭhi-yoga*) because it yokes one to views;
and the yoke of ignorance (*avijjā-yoga*) because it yokes one to ignorance. These are synonyms for the very same phenomena mentioned above.
Now, showing this in detail, he said, "And what, monks," and so forth. Therein, *samudaya* means arising; *atthaṅgama* means dissolution; *assāda* means the state of sweetness;
*ādīnava* means the state of lack of sweetness, that is, the fault; *nissaraṇa* means the state of escape. Regarding *kāmesu*, it refers to sense-objects (*vatthukāma*).
*Kāmarāga* is the lust that has arisen with reference to sense-pleasures. The same applies to the remaining terms.
The same method applies. "Underlies" (*anuseti*) means it is produced. "This, monks, is called the yoke of sensual desire" (*kāmayoga*);
this, monks, is said to be the cause for joining and the cause for binding to sensual pleasures—thus the meaning should be understood in all instances.

"Of the bases of contact" (*phassāyatanānaṃ*) refers to the eyes and so forth, which are the causes of eye-contact and the rest. "Ignorance is non-knowing" (*avijjā aññāṇaṃ*) by way of being the opposite of knowledge.
Ignorance is what is designated as *avijjā*. In the phrase "thus the bond of sensual desire" (*iti kāmayogo*), the word "thus" (*iti*) should be connected with all four bonds, [meaning]:
"such is the bond of sensual desire; such is the bond of existence. "Entangled" (*saṃyutto*) means surrounded. "By evil things" (*pāpakehi*) means by base things.

"By unwholesome things" (*akusalehi*) means by those produced through lack of skill. "By defiling things" (*saṃkilesikehi*) means by those which cause defilement; that is, by those which corrupt the clarity of a clear mind.
The meaning is as follows: "By those leading to renewed existence" means by those that produce renewed existence. "Accompanied by craving" means accompanied by the chariot of craving.

"Resulting in suffering" means those that produce suffering at the time of their ripening. "Leading to future birth, aging, and death" means those that repeatedly produce birth, aging, and death in the future.
Therefore, one is called "one who has not attained security from bondage" because a person whose bonds have not been abandoned is associated with these states.
Because it has not attained the security that is Nibbāna through the four bonds, it is not called "one who has attained security from bonds" (*yogakkhemi*).
"Disjunction" (*visaṃyoga*) refers to the causes for disjoining. "Disjunction from the bond of sensual desire" (*kāmayoga-visaṃyoga*) means the cause for disjoining from the bond of sensual desire.
The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. In this context, the meditation on the foul (*asubha-jjhāna*) is the disjunction from the bond of sensual desire; taking that as a basis...
The attainment of the path of non-returning is exclusively called "disjunction from the yoke of sensual desire. The path of arahantship is called "disjunction from the yoke of existence";
the path of stream-entry is called "disjunction from the yoke of views"; and the path of arahantship is called "disjunction from the yoke of ignorance.
Now, showing these in detail, he said, "And which, monks," and so forth. Its meaning should be understood in the same manner as previously explained.

"By means of both bonds of existence" (*bhavayogena cobhayaṃ*) means they are conjoined with both bonds of existence; "and somewhat more connected by both" means they are endowed with whichever bond [is applicable].
"Placed before" (*purakkhatā*) means made to precede, or surrounded.

"Having fully understood the two kinds of sense-desires" (*kāme parijñāya*) means having thoroughly known both types of sense-desire. "And the bond of existence in its entirety" (*bhavayogañca sabbaso*) refers to the bond of existence in its totality.
“Having fully understood all” means having completely eradicated it. “They cause it to fade away” (virājayanti) means they are causing it to fade away, or having caused it to fade away.
For when “causing to fade away” is said, the Path is indicated; when “having caused to fade away” is said, the Fruit is indicated.
“The Sage” (muni) refers to the Sage whose taints are exhausted. Thus, in this Sutta as well as in these verses, only the cycle of existence and its cessation (vaṭṭa-vivaṭṭa) has been explained.
The First Chapter: The Chapter on Bhaṇḍagāma.
2. The Chapter on Wandering. 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on Wandering.

11. Regarding the second [case], "he abides with the first": having directed the mind toward it, he causes it to abide. "He does not abandon" means he does not relinquish it. "He does not dispel" means he does not remove it.
"He does not bring it to an end" means he does not make it reach its limit—that is, he does not make it delimited and circumscribed.
"He does not cause it to come to non-existence" means he does not cause it to go to non-existence, decay, or destruction. "Even while walking" means even while moving about.
"Without ardor" means lacking energy. "Without a sense of shame" means being devoid of fear regarding censure. "Constantly" means always. "Continually" means without interruption.
Thus, having understood the meaning in all instances, the sense should be understood by way of the opposite of what was stated for the bright fortnight (the wholesome side).

Regarding the verses: "dependent on the household" means dependent on the defilements. "In things that lead to delusion" means in objects that produce delusion. "Unable" means not being a fit vessel. "To touch the supreme enlightenment" means to touch the supreme knowledge known as the path of Arahantship.
2. Commentary on the Sīla Sutta 12.
In the second [verse], "endowed with virtue" (*sampannasīlā*) means possessing complete virtue. "Endowed with the Pātimokkha" (*sampannapātimokkhā*) means possessing the complete Pātimokkha.

"Restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha" (*pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutā*) means that you should dwell having become restrained, closed off, and endowed with the virtue of the restraint of the Pātimokkha.
"Endowed with proper conduct and resort": be fully possessed of and established in both proper conduct (*ācāra*) and proper resort (*gocara*).
"Regarding even minor faults": regarding defects of even minute measure. "Seeing them as fearful": having the habit of viewing those minor faults as a source of fear.
"Training yourselves by undertaking the rules of training": having undertaken—that is, having accepted—all the points of training that ought to be undertaken.
“Train yourselves. Having encouraged them to undertake the three trainings with this brief exposition of the Dhamma—beginning with “For those of perfected virtue... [and so on]...

in the rules of training”—and having spoken in praise of the qualities already attained, he now spoke the words beginning with “What would there be for him? in order to show what further must be done.
In that context, “What would there be for him? means: what would it be?
"One should walk with restraint" means that one should walk in such a way that while walking, one is restrained. This same method applies everywhere.

"One should sit" means one should sit. "One should extend this with restraint" means that whatever limb or member one should extend, one should extend it only after making it restrained and well-controlled.
"Upward" means above. "Sideways" means across the middle. "Downward" means below. By this much, the past [is explained].
The five aggregates of the present and the future have been described. The word *yāvatā* is a term denoting limitation.

"The course of the world" means the manifestation of the world. "And the one who has scrutinized the arising and passing away of the aggregates" means that he has scrutinized both the arising and the passing away of these five aggregate-phenomena—which are divided into past, future, and so forth—within the entire world. [Regarding] "the five aggregates..."

"When it is said, 'Seeing arising, one sees twenty-five characteristics; seeing passing away, one sees twenty-five characteristics,' one has correctly scrutinized by means of these fifty characteristics.
'The proper way of mental serenity' (cetosamathasāmīci) refers to the practice suitable for mental serenity. 'One who is training' (sikkhamānaṃ) means one who is practicing, one who is fulfilling."
The meaning is as follows: *pahitatta* means one whose self is sent forth (*pesitatta*). *Āhu* means they say. The rest here is self-evident.
However, in this sutta, virtue (*sīla*) is explained in a mixed manner, whereas in the verses, the one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*) is described.
3. Commentary on the *Padhāna-sutta* (The Discourse on Striving)
13. "The three right efforts" (*sammappadhāna*) means beautiful efforts, supreme energies. "Right efforts" (*sammappadhāna*) means perfected energies.

"Having overcome the realm of Māra" means having overcome and transcended the realm of Māra, which is comprised of the cycle of existence in the three planes of being, and thus remaining [in victory].
"They are unattached" (*asita*) means those whose taints are destroyed are called "unattached. "Of the fear of birth and death" means of both birth and death.
Of the fear arising through dependence, or specifically of the fear consisting of birth and death. *Pāragū* means those who have gone to the further shore (*pāraṅgatā*).
*Te tusitā* means those whose taints are destroyed are called "the contented. *Jetvā māraṃ savāhiniṃ* means they stand having conquered Māra together with his army (*sasenakaṃ*).
*Te anejā* means those whose taints are destroyed are called "unshaken" (*anejā*), immovable because of the lack of the "urge" (*ejā*) known as craving (*taṇhā*). *Namucibalaṃ*...

"Mārabala" means the power of Māra. "Upātivatta" means having transcended it. "Te sukhitā" means those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) are called "happy" by virtue of supramundane happiness (lokuttara-sukha).
Therefore he said: "Happy indeed are the Arahants;
craving does not exist in them. The conceit 'I am' is utterly cut off; the net of delusion is shattered."
4. Commentary on the Saṃvara Sutta 14.

In the fourth [verse], "strivings" (*padhānāni*) refers to energies (*vīriyāni*). The "striving for restraint" (*saṃvarappadhāna*) is the energy that arises in one who restrains the eye and the other sense faculties.
The "striving for abandonment" (*pahānappadhāna*) is the energy that arises in one who abandons sensual thoughts and so forth. The "striving for development" (*bhāvanāppadhāna*) is...

The energy that arises in one developing the factors of enlightenment (*sambojjhaṅga*). "The effort of preservation" is the energy that arises in one preserving the sign of concentration (*samādhinimitta*). Regarding "dependent on seclusion," etc.:
seclusion (*viveka*), fading away (*virāga*), and cessation (*nirodha*)—these three are all names for Nibbāna.

For Nibbāna is "seclusion" because it is secluded from the bases of existence (*upadhi*); it is "fading away" because by resorting to it, lust and the other defilements fade away; and it is "cessation" because they cease there.
Cessation. Therefore, in such passages as "dependent on seclusion," etc., the meaning is that it is "dependent on Nibbāna" either by way of its object or by way of what is to be attained.
Regarding the phrase "ending in relinquishment," there are two kinds of relinquishment: relinquishment as giving up (*pariccāgavossagga*) and relinquishment as entering into (*pakkhandanavossagga*).
Therein, insight relinquishes both the defilements and the aggregates through the function of "overcoming" (*tadaṅgavasena*), thus it is relinquishment as giving up.

The path plunges into Nibbāna by way of its object; thus, it is the "launching-off relinquishment" (*pakkhandana-vossagga*). Therefore, regarding the phrase "turning towards relinquishment" (*vossagga-pariṇāmim*):

the meaning here is that he develops mindfulness-enlightenment-factor in such a way that, as it is being cultivated, it turns toward relinquishment and reaches the state of insight and the state of the path. The same method applies to the remaining terms. "Auspicious" (*bhaddakam*)...
"Attained" means that very concentration which has been achieved by way of the perception of a skeleton and so forth; this is what is called the "sign of concentration.
"He guards it" means he protects it while purifying it of lust, hatred, and delusion, which are the states that obstruct concentration.
Here, only five perceptions beginning with the perception of a skeleton were mentioned, but at this point, all ten kinds of foulness (*asubha*) should be explained in detail.
The detailed explanation of these has already been stated in the *Visuddhimagga*. In this verse, it is specifically energy (*vīriya*) that is said to accomplish restraint and the other [foundations].
"He reaches the destruction of suffering" means he should reach Arahantship, which is designated as the destruction of suffering.
5. Commentary on the Paññatti Sutta (The Discourse on Designation)

15. "In the fifth [section], 'the designations of the foremost' means the supreme designations. 'Of those possessing a personal existence' (*attabhāvīnaṃ*) means of those who have a personal existence (*attabhāvavantaṃ*).
'Namely, Rāhu, the lord of the asuras' means that this very Rāhu, the lord of the asuras, is the foremost.
Here, it is said that Rāhu, the lord of the asuras, is four thousand eight hundred *yojanas* in height, and his arm-span is twelve hundred *yojanas*."
The breadth of the palms of his hands and the soles of his feet was three hundred *yojanas*.
His finger-joints were fifty *yojanas*, the space between his eyebrows was fifty *yojanas*, his forehead was three hundred *yojanas*, and his head was nine hundred *yojanas*.
Among those who enjoy sensual pleasures, this one named King Mandhātā is the foremost—this King Mandhātā, who enjoys both divine and human sensual pleasures.

He is called the foremost among beings. For, having been reborn among humans with an incalculable lifespan, he rained down showers of gold at every desired moment and enjoyed human pleasures for a long time.
Furthermore, in the world of the devas, he enjoyed exquisite pleasures for as long as the lifespan of thirty-six Indras; thus, he is the foremost among those who enjoy sensual pleasures.
“...named [so-and-so]. “Of those exercising sovereignty” means of those who exercise the position of lordship, the position of the eldest.
“The Tathāgata is declared the foremost” means that by way of mundane and supramundane qualities, the Tathāgata is declared the foremost, the best, the most excellent.
“Blazing with psychic power and glory” means blazing with the perfection of divine attainments and with glory in the sense of a retinue.
"Upward, across, and downward" means above, in the middle, and below. "As far as the range of the world" means as much as the manifestation of the world.

**Commentary on the Sūkṣma-sūtra (The Discourse on Subtlety), Chapter 6, Section 16:** "In the sixth [section], 'subtle' (*sokhumma*) refers to those knowledges that penetrate subtle characteristics. One who is endowed with subtlety of form..."
"He possesses" means he is endowed with the knowledge that discerns the subtle and delicate characteristics within form.
"Supreme" means the highest. "And by that subtlety of form" means by that knowledge discerning subtle characteristics which has reached the state of conformity (*anuloma*).
"He does not perceive" means he does not see precisely because of its non-existence. "He does not aspire" means he does not aspire precisely because of its non-existence.
The same method applies to feelings, perceptions, and so forth.
"Having known the subtlety of form" means having known the subtlety by means of the knowledge that discerns the subtle and refined characteristics of the aggregate of form.
"And the origin of feelings" means having known the source of the aggregate of feeling.
"From whatever perception arises": having known that cause from which the aggregate of perception arises and is produced;
"and where it goes to its end": having known the place where it ceases; "having known formations as other":
having known the aggregate of formations as other by way of their nature of breaking up through impermanence. For by this phrase...

The contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) has been explained. By the phrase "as suffering and not as self," the contemplations of suffering (*dukkha*) and non-self (*anattā*) are indicated.

"Peaceful" means peaceful due to the pacification of the defilements (*kilesa*). "Delighting in the state of peace" means delighting in Nibbāna. Thus, in the Sutta, insight (*vipassanā*) alone is taught in four places;
however, in the verses, supramundane states (*lokuttaradhamma*) are also mentioned.
7. Commentary on the First Discourse on Wrong Courses (Paṭhama-agatisutta-vaṇṇanā) 17–19.

Regarding the seventh [verse], "wrong courses" (*agatigamanāni*) means non-courses (*nagatigamanāni*). "He goes by way of desire" (*chandāgatiṃ gacchati*) means he goes by way of desire to what is not a course;

he does what ought not to be done. The same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well. "By way of desire, hatred, fear, and delusion" (*chandā dosā bhayā mohā*) means by way of desire... [and so forth].
[It is] by way of hatred, fear, and delusion. "Transgresses" means oversteps. The eighth [sutta] is self-evident.
In the ninth, it is explained by two methods according to those who awaken in that manner.
10. Commentary on the Bhattuddesakasutta.

20. "The assigner of meals on the tenth day" (*dasame bhattuddesako*) means one who assigns *salākabhatta* (lottery meals) and so forth. "Unrestrained in sensual pleasures" (*kāmesu asaṃyatā*) means unrestrained by the defilements of sensual desire (*kilesakāma*) regarding the objects of sensual pleasure (*vatthukāma*).
"And he is called the dregs of the assembly" (*parisākasaṭo ca panesa vuccati*): the meaning is that such a person is called a "scum of the assembly" (*parisākacavara*).
"By a recluse" (*samaṇena*) means by a recluse who is a Buddha. "And he is called the cream of the assembly" (*parisāya maṇḍo ca panesa vuccati*): [this refers to the opposite].
Such an assembly as this is called a "pure core of the assembly.
The second chapter, the Chapter on Wanderers (Caravagga).
3. The Chapter on Uruvelā (Uruvelavagga).
1. Commentary on the First Uruvelā Sutta 21.
Regarding the phrase “at Uruvelā” in the first [sutta] of the third [vagga]: here, *uruvelā* means a great bank (*mahāvelā*), that is, a great heap of sand.
Alternatively, *uru* refers to sand, and *velā* refers to a boundary. It is called *uruvelā* because the sand was brought there by reason of overstepping the boundary (*velātikkamana*).

The meaning here should be understood in this way: It is said that in the past, before a Buddha had arisen, ten thousand sons of good family went forth as ascetic recluses and, while dwelling in that region, gathered together one day and made a formal agreement:
"Bodily and verbal actions are indeed evident even to others, but mental action is not evident. Therefore—"
"Whoever thinks thoughts of sensual desire, or thoughts of ill will, or thoughts of cruelty, has no other accuser;
he should accuse himself. Let him bring sand in a leaf-bag and scatter it in this place—this shall be his disciplinary act.
From that time forth, whoever thought such a thought, he...
There, he poured sand from the fold of his robe; thus, by degrees, a great heap of sand was formed there.
Then, later people surrounded it and made it a site for a shrine (*cetiya*). With reference to that, it is said: "Uruvelā means 'the great bank' (*mahāvelā*);
the meaning is 'a great heap of sand' (*mahāvālikarāsi*). With reference to that very thing, it is further said: "Or else, *uru* means sand."

It is said that *velā* means a boundary (*mariyādā*). Because it was brought [to this place] due to the transgression of that boundary, it is called *Uruvelā*; thus the meaning should be understood here.
By saying, "On the bank of the river Nerañjarā," he shows that he was dwelling on the bank of the river Nerañjarā, dependent upon the village of Uruvelā.
Regarding "at the Goatherds' Banyan Tree" (*ajapālanigrodhe*): goatherds would sit and stand in the shade of that banyan tree; therefore—
"Under the Goatherd’s Banyan Tree" means beneath that very tree. "First after attaining full enlightenment" means immediately after becoming a Sambuddha.
"Arisen" means this reflection arose during the fifth week. Why did it arise?
Because it is the custom of all Buddhas and due to previous habituation. Regarding that, as for the previous habituation:

To clarify this point, the Tittira Jātaka should be cited. It is said that while the elephant, the jackal, and the partridge were dwelling in one place, they thought, "We shall dwell with respect toward whoever among us is the eldest.
Having pointed to the banyan tree [to test their age], and while investigating, "Who indeed is the eldest among us?", they recognized the partridge's seniority and [honored him].
Having performed the duty of honoring their elders, they lived together in harmony and mutual affection, destined for heaven.
Knowing this reason, the deity dwelling in the tree spoke this verse:
“Those men skilled in the Dhamma who honor the aged, ... [the rest of the verse follows]”
"Praised in this very life, and a happy destination in the world to come.
Thus, even though he was reborn in the womb of an animal without a cause [for such status], the Tathāgata commended living with reverence; why then would he not commend it now?
"Without reverence" means devoid of respect for others; the meaning is that he does not place anyone in a position of venerability.
"Without deference" (*appatissa*) means devoid of deference; the meaning is that he does not place anyone in the position of seniority.
"Whether a recluse (*samaṇa*) or a brahmin (*brāhmaṇa*)"—here, only those who have stilled evil and cast out evil are intended by the terms "recluse" and "brahmin.
"Having honored and revered" means having both performed honor and established reverence.
In the phrase "in the world with its devas" (*sadevake loke*) and so forth, *sadevake* means "together with the devas.
Although both Māra and Brahmā are included here by the mention of "devas," Māra—known as Vasavatti—is one who exercises power over all;
and Brahmā is one of great majesty, who can radiate light throughout a thousand world-systems with a single finger, two thousand with two fingers, and ten thousand world-systems with ten fingers.
He radiates light. He spoke separately, saying "together with Māras and Brahmās," so that they might not be allowed to say, "He is more accomplished in virtue than this [person].
Likewise, those called *samaṇas* are those who are learned, virtuous, and wise by way of belonging to a single school (*nikāya*) and so forth;

and *brāhmaṇas* are also those who are learned and wise by way of the science of omens (*vatthuvijjā*) and so forth. He said this so that they might not be allowed to say, "He is more accomplished than these."

It is said, "together with the generation of recluses and brahmins. However, the phrase "together with devas and humans" is stated by taking what was already mentioned as a complete enumeration for the sake of showing [the full extent].
Furthermore, here the first three terms are spoken in terms of the world (*loka*), while the latter two are spoken in terms of the generation (*pajā*).
"More endowed with virtue" means more endowed with virtue; the sense is "more excellent. Here...

Furthermore, the four qualities beginning with virtue (*sīla*) have been described as both mundane and supramundane, whereas the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuttiñāṇadassana*) is exclusively mundane; for this is merely the knowledge of review (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*). Regarding the phrase "he appeared": [the Buddha] saw no one from the Avīci hell up to the peak of existence who was superior to himself in virtue and the other qualities, and thus, honoring and relying solely upon the nine supramundane states he had himself realized— [The text continues: ...he appeared. He appeared to the world including its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, to the generation of beings, including ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans, by means of his own super-knowledge (*abhiññā*), having fully awakened to it through direct realization (*sacchikārapaññā*); therefore, he is called the Tathāgata. Because he has reached the ultimate goal, because he has attained the ultimate security from bondage, because he has reached the ultimate perfection of the holy life, because he is the ultimate teacher of the Dhamma, because he is the ultimate knower of the world, because he is the ultimate trainer of those to be tamed, because he is the ultimate bull among men, because he is the ultimate caravan leader who has safely crossed over and brought his company across, because he is the ultimate enlightened one, and because he is the ultimate bringer of peace, he is called the Arahat. He thought, "I shall dwell," and the Blessed One thought of the reason; he thought of the purpose, the growth, and the distinction [of the teaching], thinking, "I will go and inspire him.
Having thus reflected, he became manifest before him; the meaning is that he stood facing him.

Regarding the phrase "they have dwelt and they dwell": if someone were to say, "From the word 'they dwell,' there must be many Buddhas even in the present," he should be refuted by this statement: "The Blessed One, venerable sir, is now an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One."
“‘I have no teacher; there is none equal to me;
in this world with its devas, there is no rival to me’”—by such suttas as these, the non-existence of other Buddhas should be illustrated. Therefore, because all Buddhas...
Because he is one who honors the true Dhamma; therefore, "desiring greatness" means by one aspiring to a state of greatness.
"Remembering the teaching of the Buddhas" means by one recollecting the instruction of the Buddhas.
"When" means at which time. "Endowed with greatness" refers to the greatness of long-standing seniority, the greatness of abundance, and the greatness of the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
"Endowed with the greatness of gain and greatness" means he was possessed of these four kinds of greatness.
"Then I have reverence for the Saṅgha too" means that at that time, reverence for the Saṅgha arose in me. At what time, however, did the Blessed One show reverence for the Saṅgha?
At the time of giving the pair of cloths to Mahāpajāpatī. For then the Blessed One [addressed] the pair of cloths offered to him, saying: "In the Saṅgha..."
"Gotamī, give it; when it is given to the Saṅgha, both I and the Saṅgha will be honored"—by saying this, he indeed showed reverence for the Saṅgha.
2. Commentary on the Second Uruvela Sutta:
22. "Many" (sambahula) means numerous. "Brahmins" (brāhmaṇa) refers to those who had come together with a brahmin of the Huhukka caste.
"Brahmins. "Aged" means aged by old age. "Elderly" means advanced in years. "Venerable" means venerable by birth.
"Advanced in life" means those who have passed through the three stages of life. "We have heard this" means we have heard this from others.
"And that, Master Gotama, is exactly so" means, Master Gotama, the reason we have heard is indeed just so. "And that, Master Gotama, is not at all fitting" [is the conclusion].
Therefore, this failure to perform salutations and so forth is indeed improper. Regarding the terms "one who speaks at the wrong time" and so on:

one who speaks at an improper time is "one who speaks at the wrong time" (*akālavādī*). One who speaks what is not factual is "one who speaks what is untrue" (*abhūtavādī*). One who speaks what is harmful, rather than what is beneficial, is "one who speaks what is unbeneficial" (*anatthavādī*).

One who speaks what is contrary to the Dhamma, rather than the Dhamma, is "one who speaks what is contrary to the Dhamma" (*adhammavādī*). One who speaks what is contrary to the Vinaya... [is "one who speaks what is contrary to the Vinaya" (*avinayavādī*)].

He speaks, but he does not discipline; thus he is one who speaks without discipline. "He has spoken words that are not to be laid up" means he has spoken words that are not fit to be stored in the heart.
"At an improper time" means at a time unfit for speaking. "Without foundation" means devoid of a foundation;
he does not speak by making it well-founded or providing a reason. "Without limit" means devoid of a limit; he does not speak by showing a boundary.
He speaks. "Not connected with the goal" means he does not speak by making it dependent on mundane or supramundane goals.
"The fool is reckoned as an elder" means the blind fool is reckoned as an elder.

"One who speaks at the right time," and so forth, should be understood by way of the opposites of what has been stated. "The wise man is reckoned as an elder" means that because he is endowed with wisdom, he is wise; and because he has attained a state of stability, he is reckoned as an elder.

"Learned" means that much has been heard by him; the meaning is that the Teacher’s dispensation in its ninefold form has been mastered according to the sequence of the text, the connections, and the preceding and following passages.
"A bearer of what is heard" means one who is a receptacle for what has been heard.
For one from whom what was learned here escapes elsewhere—like water in a cracked jar—it does not remain; [such a person cannot recite] even a single sutta or a Jātaka in the midst of an assembly.
Or if one is unable to explain or recite it, this person is called "one who does not retain what has been heard" (*asutadhara*).
However, for one whose learned Buddha-word remains exactly as it was at the time of learning—even after twenty or thirty years of not reciting it—it does not perish;

such a person is called "one who retains what has been heard" (*sutadhara*). "Accumulation of what has been heard" (*sutasannicaya*) means that which constitutes an accumulation of what has been heard. For one who...
For what has been heard remains stored in the casket of the heart like an inscription on stone, or like lion’s fat placed upon a golden plate;
this is called the "accumulation of what has been heard. "Dhātā" means one who has mastered [the teachings].
For some, the Buddha-word they have learned is not mastered, not proficient, and not fixed; when told, "Recite such-and-such a sutta or Jātaka," [they are unable].
He says, "Having recited, compared, and investigated it, I shall know it. For some, what has been mastered becomes as fluent as the flow of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga-sota*);
when told, "Recite such-and-such a sutta or Jātaka," they retrieve it and recite that very one.

It is with reference to this that it is said, "one who has mastered it" (*dhātā*). "Familiarized by speech" means by way of the ten-fold groups of suttas, the ten-fold chapters, and the ten-fold fifties.
"Recited by way of speech": recited with the voice. "Examined by way of mind": examined with the consciousness (*citta*).
For one who has recited the Buddha’s word by way of speech and reflects upon it with the mind, it becomes clear in various respects;
it appears like visible forms to one standing by a lit great lamp. It is with reference to this that it was said. "Thoroughly penetrated by view": [in terms of] meaning.
And they have been well-penetrated through reasoning and through wisdom.
Regarding the phrase "pertaining to higher consciousness" (*ābhicetasika*): "higher consciousness" (*abhiceto*) refers to an excellent, purified mind, or to "higher mind" (*adhicitta*).

Those things born in the higher consciousness, or those dependent upon the higher consciousness, are "pertaining to higher consciousness. Regarding the phrase "pleasant dwellings in this very life" (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*):...
“Of those who dwell in happiness in this very life. “This very life” (*diṭṭhadhamma*) refers to the directly perceived personal existence;
the meaning is “of those who have become dwellers in happiness therein. This is a designation for the fine-material-sphere jhānas.

For when meditators have entered these and are seated, they experience the undefiled happiness of renunciation in this very personal existence; therefore, they are called “dwellings in happiness in this very life.”
It is said: "One who obtains at will" means one who obtains according to his wish; that is to say, one who is able to attain [jhāna] at any desired moment by the power of his own desire.
"One who obtains without difficulty" means one who is able to attain it easily by suppressing contrary states.
"One who obtains without trouble" means one who obtains what is not difficult—that is, what is abundant—according to his specific determination.
This means he is capable of emerging [from attainment]. For some indeed obtain [the attainment], yet they are not able to enter it at any desired moment.
Another is able to enter it in that way, but suppresses obstructive states only with difficulty.
Still another enters it in that way and suppresses obstructive states without any difficulty whatsoever.

He is unable to emerge exactly according to his limit, like a water-clock mechanism. However, he who possesses this threefold perfection is called "one who gains without difficulty, one who gains without trouble.
The phrases beginning with "the destruction of the taints" have already been explained in their proper places.
Thus, in this context, both virtue and learning belong only to one whose taints are destroyed; likewise, the meditative absorptions belong only to one whose taints are destroyed.
The jhānas for practice have been explained. By the words "through the destruction of the taints" (āsavānaṃ khayā) and so forth, however, arahantship is explained.
And it should be understood that here the function of the path is manifested by means of its fruit.
"By one who is agitated" means by one accompanied by restlessness. "Frivolous talk" means idle chatter. "With unconcentrated intention" means with unsettled intention.
*Maga* means like a deer. *Āra* means far away. *Thāvareyyamhā* means from the state of stability. *Pāpaditthi* means a base view. *Anādara* means devoid of respect.
*Sutavā* means one who has approached through learning. *Paṭibhānavā* means endowed with two kinds of inspired eloquence.
*Paññāyatthaṃ vipassati* means one sees the meaning of wisdom through the path-wisdom accompanied by insight regarding the four truths.
Having pierced through the meaning, he sees. "One who has gone beyond all phenomena" means one who has reached the further shore of all phenomena such as the aggregates;

that is, one who has gone beyond by way of these six kinds of transcendence: transcendence through direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), transcendence through full understanding (*pariññā*), transcendence through abandoning (*pahāna*), transcendence through development (*bhāvanā*), transcendence through realization (*sacchikiriyā*), and transcendence through attainment (*samāpatti*).
Thus, he has reached the further shore, the ultimate limit, of all phenomena.
Gato. *Akhilo* means one who is free from the barrenness of passion (*rāga*) and other such defilements. *Paṭibhānavā* means endowed with both types of inspired eloquence (*paṭibhāna*).
*Brahmacariyassa kevalī* means one who possesses the entirety of the holy life (*brahmacariya*). The rest here is self-evident.
3. Commentary on the Lokasutta.

23. "In the third [verse], 'the world' (loka) refers to the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca). 'Fully awakened' (abhisambuddha) means it has been known and made directly manifest. 'In the world' (lokasmiṃ) means from the perspective of the truth of suffering.

'Abandoned' (pahīna) means abandoned at the Great Seat of Awakening (mahābodhimaṇḍa) by the knowledge of the path of Arhatship. 'Cultivated by the Tathāgata' (tathāgatassa bhāvitā) means cultivated by the Tathāgata.
Thus, having declared his own state of Buddhahood by way of these four truths through this much, he now [declares] his state of being a Tathāgata."

He said, “Monks, that which is to be told,” and so forth. Therein, “seen” (*diṭṭha*) refers to the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*). “HearD” (*suta*) refers to the sense-sphere of sound (*saddāyatana*).
“Sensed” (*muta*)—so called because it is to be grasped by reaching it—refers to the sense-spheres of odor (*gandhāyatana*), flavor (*rasāyatana*), and the tangible (*phoṭṭhabbāyatana*).

“Cognized” (*viññāta*) refers to mental objects (*dhammārammaṇa*) such as pleasure, pain, and so on. “Obtained” (*patta*) means obtained either through seeking or without seeking. “Sought after” (*pariyesita*)...
"Whether already reached or not yet reached, it has been sought. "Mentally traversed" means it has been mentally roamed over.
By the phrase "fully awakened to by the Tathāgata," this is what is shown:
whatever objective form—blue, yellow, and so forth—arises within the range of the eye-door in these immeasurable world-systems of this world with its devas.
“The Tathāgata has thus fully awakened to everything, such as: ‘At this very moment, having seen this particular visible object, this being has become glad, dejected, or neutral.

Likewise, he has fully awakened to the sound-object—such as the sound of drums or the sound of tabors—which enters the range of the ear-door throughout the immeasurable world-systems of this world with its devas.”
When the object of smell—such as the scent of roots or the scent of bark—comes into the range of the nose-door;
when the object of taste—such as the taste of roots or the taste of stalks—comes into the range of the tongue-door;
and when the object of touch, consisting of the divisions of the earth-element, fire-element, and air-element—such as hardness or softness—comes into the range of the body-door.
“This being, at this very moment, having touched such-and-such a tangible object as an objective condition, has become glad, dejected, or neutral”—
all this is thus fully awakened to by the Tathāgata. Likewise, regarding the mental door,
he knows the objective conditions consisting of phenomena— such as pleasure, pain, and so forth— within this world with its devas across immeasurable world-systems.

When it comes within range [of his knowledge], the Tathāgata has thus fully awakened to everything: "At this moment, having cognized such an object of consciousness, this being has become glad, or dejected, or neutral.
For, monks, whatever is seen, heard, sensed, or cognized by all these beings, therein the Tathāgata [has full knowledge].

There is nothing unseen, unheard, unperceived, or unknown; yet for this great multitude of people, there are things that exist which they have not attained even after searching, and things that exist which they have not attained without searching, and things that exist which they have attained after searching, and things that exist which they have attained without searching.
But for the Tathāgata, there is nothing whatsoever that is called "unattained" or not realized through his knowledge.
"Therefore he is called the Tathāgata": because he has gone (*gata*) exactly as the world has gone (*yathā lokena gataṃ*), he is called the Tathāgata.
In the Pāḷi, however, it is said "fully awakened" (*abhisambuddha*); that is synonymous with the word *gata*.
By this method, the meaning of the conclusion "Tathāgata" should be understood in all sections. Its logical justification is found in the "Description of the One Person" (*Ekapuggalavaṇṇanā*).

This has already been explained in the *Tathāgatasaddavitthāra*. Furthermore, in this context, *aññadatthu* is a particle used in the sense of emphasis (*ekamsatthe*). *Dakkhati* means "he sees"; thus he is a *dasa* (a seer).
*Vasavattī* means "one who exercises mastery.
"Having directly known the entire world" means having understood the world-dwelling within the three realms (*tedhātuka*). "The whole world as it truly is" means...
Having known, exactly as it is and without error, whatever is to be known within that dwelling of the world of the three realms;
"detached" (visaṃyutta) means detached through the abandoning of the four bonds (yoga); "unattached" (anūpaya) means devoid of attachment through craving and views;
"all-conquering" (sabbābhibhū) means established having overcome all objects such as form and so forth; "wise" (dhīra) means endowed with steadfastness (dhiti).
"Released from all bonds" means he stands having liberated himself from all four types of bonds (*gantha*). "Of one who has touched" (*phuṭṭhassa*) means "one who has touched" (*phuṭṭho assa*);
here the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental. "Supreme peace" (*paramā santi*) refers to Nibbāna; for that was touched by him through the touching of knowledge.
Thus it is said: "Nibbāna is fearless from every quarter. Alternatively, "supreme peace" means the highest tranquility.
What is that? It is Nibbāna. Because there is no fear in Nibbāna from any quarter, it is called "fearless from all sides" (*akutobhaya*).

"Liberated through the destruction of the substrata" (*upadhisaṅkhaye*) means liberated by the liberation of fruition which has that [Nibbāna] as its object, within what is termed the destruction of the substrata.
"The Lion, the Unsurpassed" refers to the Tathāgata in the sense of enduring dangers and in the sense of destroying the defilements.
"Anuttaro" means the peerless. "Brahmā" means the supreme. "Iti" means having thus known the qualities of the Tathāgata.
"Saṅgamma" means having come together. "Taṃ namassanti" means that those who have gone for refuge to that Tathāgata pay him homage.
Now, in order to show what they say as they pay him homage, the words beginning with "danto" (the Tamed One) are spoken. That [passage] has its meaning already explained.
4. Commentary on the Kāḷakārāma Sutta. 24.
This was placed [in the collection] by way of a specific occasion (atthuppatti). By what occasion? By way of a discourse on the qualities of the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala).
It is said that Anāthapiṇḍika’s daughter, Cūḷasubhaddā, [was married] to the son of the merchant Kāḷaka in the city of Sāketa. At his house...
“I shall go,” he said, and having approached the Teacher, he made this request: “Venerable Sir, I am going to a family of wrong views.
If I receive hospitality there, there may be delay while a messenger is sent; therefore, may the Blessed One attend to me.
Having thus obtained his consent, he departed. The merchant, thinking, “My daughter-in-law has arrived,” performed an auspicious ceremony.
While preparing a great quantity of hard and soft food, he invited five hundred naked ascetics (acelakas).
When they were seated, he sent Cūḷasubhaddā with the message: "Let my daughter come and pay homage to the Arahants.

Having attained the fruit [of stream-entry], she was a noble female disciple; as soon as the word "Arahant" was uttered, she thought, "What a gain for me! and rising up, she went to those who were devoid of splendor.
Upon seeing the naked ascetics, he said, "Dear father, those who possess neither internal shame nor external dread of blame cannot truly be called 'ascetics (samaṇā)';
these are no ascetics! Having uttered "Shame on them! Shame on them!", he spat out phlegm, turned back, and went straight to his own dwelling place.
Then the naked ascetics (acelakas) reviled the great merchant, saying, "Great merchant, where did you get such an ill-omened girl?

Is there no other maiden in all of Jambudīpa? He replied, "Whether the teachers acted with knowledge or without it, I shall find out about this," and having dismissed the naked ascetics, he went to Subhaddā and said, "My dear, why..."
“You have done such a thing; why did you cause the Arahants shame? he asked. “Father, those called Arahants are not like that. Then he said to him:
“What kind of recluses are they to whom you praise them so greatly?
What is their virtue and what is their conduct? Tell me when you are questioned.”
She said:
“With senses calmed, with minds calmed, with radiant energy calmed, established on the path of virtue;
with downcast eyes and measured speech—such are the recluses for me.”
“Having severed their bonds, the elephant dwells having entered the forest;
solitary and without a second—such are the recluses for me.
Having spoken thus, he stood before the merchant and spoke of the virtues of the Three Jewels. The merchant, hearing her...
Having heard these words, he said, "If it is so, let us bring your ascetics here and perform the auspicious ceremony.
She asked, "When will you do it, dear father? The merchant thought, "If I say 'in a few days,' she might send someone to summon them.
So he told her, "Tomorrow, mother. In the evening, she ascended to the upper terrace of the palace with a large casket of flowers.
Having taken them and recollected the virtues of the Teacher, she scattered eight handfuls of flowers over the One Possessing Ten Powers;
then, raising her joined palms in reverence, she stood there paying homage and spoke thus: "May the Blessed One, together with five hundred bhikkhus, accept my alms tomorrow.
Those flowers went and formed a canopy above the head of the One Possessing Ten Powers.
They stood there. The Teacher, reflecting, saw the reason for this.

At the conclusion of the teaching of the Dhamma, the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika paid homage to the One of Ten Powers and said, "Venerable Sir, please accept alms at my house tomorrow with five hundred bhikkhus.
"Merchant, we have been invited by Cūḷasubhaddā. "Venerable Sir, I do not see anyone who has come [to invite us]."
"Yes, householder, but a faithful female lay follower, even if she stands a hundred yojanas or a thousand yojanas away, appears as clearly as the Himalayas. Having said this, he continued:
"The virtuous shine from afar, like the Himalayan mountain."
“Those who are not virtuous are not seen here, like arrows shot at night.
Having spoken this verse, Anāthapiṇḍika paid homage, saying, “Venerable Sir, please accept my daughter,” and departed.
The Teacher addressed the Elder Ānanda: “Ānanda, I shall go to Sāketa with five hundred bhikkhus.”
“Give me a voting tally. And as you give it, you should give it only to those possessing the six supernormal powers.
The Elder did exactly so. At that moment, when the night was half spent, Cūḷasubhaddā thought: “The Buddhas have many duties and much to do;
whether he notices me or not, what indeed shall I do? At that very instant, the Great King Vessavaṇa [appeared] to Cūḷasubhaddā.
He said, “Bhadde, do not be despondent; do not be dejected.
The Blessed One has accepted your invitation for tomorrow’s meal together with the community of bhikkhus. She, thrilled and overjoyed, made the necessary preparations for the gift.
Sakka, the king of the gods, also addressed Vissakamma: “Dear son, the One of Ten Powers is at Cūḷasubhaddā’s side...”
“He will go to the city of Sāketa; build five hundred gabled houses.
He did so. Surrounded by five hundred monks possessing the six supernormal powers, the Teacher traveled to the city of Sāketa by means of a gabled carriage, as if scraping the sapphire-colored sky.

Having given alms to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, Subhaddā paid homage to the Teacher and said, "Venerable Sir, my father-in-law’s family holds wrong views; please teach them the Dhamma appropriate for them.
The Teacher taught the Dhamma. Having become a stream-enterer, the merchant Kāḷaka gave his own park to the One of Ten Powers.
The naked ascetics (acelakas), thinking, "It was given to us first," did not wish to leave. [The king] said, "Go; expel them according to the rule for those who must be expelled.
Having had them all expelled, he had a monastery built right there for the Teacher, established it as a royal gift (brahmadeyya), and poured water upon it.
Because it was caused to be built by Kāḷaka, it became known as the Kāḷakārāma. At that time, the Blessed One—
He dwelt there. Therefore it is said: “He dwelt at Sāketa in the Kāḷaka Grove.

He addressed the bhikkhus; that is, he addressed five hundred bhikkhus. It is said that these were sons of good family residing in the city of Sāketa who, having heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, went forth in the presence of the Teacher and were seated in the assembly hall, saying: “Oh!...”

"The qualities of the Buddha are indeed great; for having liberated from wrong view such a person as the merchant Kāḷaka who held such views, and having led him to the fruit of stream-entry, the Teacher has made the entire city like the world of the gods. Thus they spoke of the virtues of the One Possessed of the Ten Powers.
The Teacher, examining their minds as they were speaking of his virtues, thought: "When I have gone..."
"A great teaching will arise; at the conclusion of that teaching, these five hundred bhikkhus will be established in arahantship, and the great earth, bounded by the waters, will tremble.

Having said this, he went to the Dhamma Hall, sat upon the excellent Buddha-seat that had been prepared, and beginning with those bhikkhus, delivered this teaching: "Bhikkhus, whatever in this world with its devas... and so forth.
It was begun. Thus it should be understood that this sutta was introduced by way of a discourse on qualities.
Therein, at the conclusion of the phrase "I know that," the great earth, bounded by the waters, trembled.
*Abbaññāsiṃ* means "I directly knew" (*abhiaññāsiṃ*), the sense being "I knew. *Viditaṃ* means known by making it manifest. By this, this...
He shows this: "Others indeed know [these things], but I have made them manifest and known. By these three phrases, what is called the "ground of omniscience" is described.

"The Tathāgata did not stand by that" means that the Tathāgata did not stand by—that is, he did not approach—that object pertaining to the six sense-doors through either craving or views. For the Blessed One sees thus:
The Blessed One has no desire or lust for a form seen with the eye; that Blessed One is well-liberated in mind. The Blessed One hears a sound with the ear.
The Blessed One smells an odor with the nose. The Blessed One tastes a flavor with the tongue.
The Blessed One touches a tangible object with the body. The Blessed One cognizes a mental phenomenon with the mind; the Blessed One has no desire or lust [for it].
The Blessed One is not [subject to such things]; he is perfectly liberated in mind. Therefore it was said: "The Tathāgata does not attend to that.
By this phrase, it should be understood that the stage of one whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava) is being described.
"That would be a lie for me" means that such a statement of mine would indeed constitute false speech. "Behold him as being exactly like that."
That too would be false speech. "That would be a misfortune for me" means that such a statement would be a fault on my part.
Up to this point, it should be understood that what is called the "ground of truth" has been explained.
"Seen, seen" means having seen what is to be seen. "He does not conceive of what is seen" refers to that seen object-base (rūpāyatana).
“I see only what has been seen by the multitude”—thus he does not conceive through craving, conceit, or views. “He does not conceive what has not been seen”:
