“I see this very thing which has not been seen by the multitude”—even thus he does not conceive through such conceivings as craving and the rest.
“He does not conceive what is to be seen”: “I see what has been seen by the multitude”—even thus [he does not conceive] through those conceivings.
He does not conceive. For even that which is yet to be seen is indeed "to be seen. Such statements are found in all three times;
therefore, their meaning has been explained. "He does not conceive of the seer" means that he does not conceive of a single being called "the viewer" by means of those conceivings.
In the remaining instances as well, the meaning should be understood according to this same method.
By this much, the stage called emptiness (*suññatābhūmi*) has been explained.
"Thus indeed, monks" means: in this way, monks. "Suchness indeed is suchness" (*tādīyeva tādī*): "suchness" (*tāditā*) refers to being exactly the same.
And just as the Tathāgata is toward gain and so forth, he is exactly the same toward loss and so forth. Therefore it was said: "He is such even in gain..."
“Likewise in loss; likewise in fame, likewise in disrepute; likewise in blame, likewise in praise; likewise in pleasure, likewise in pain.

Because of this state of being “such,” he is *tādī*. And from that state of being *tādī*—that is, other than the Tathāgata who is *tādī*, there is no one else more excellent or more sublime who is *tādī*.
To this extent, what is called the “ground of the *tādī*” has been described. By these [verses]...
As he brought his teaching to a conclusion through five stages, the great earth trembled as a witness at each of those five points.
At the end of the discourse, eighty-four thousand beings— including those five hundred newly ordained sons of noble family who were the first to reach that state— drank the drink of the Deathless.
The Blessed One, having concluded the prose discourse (*sutta*), spoke the passage beginning with "Whatever" (*yaṃ kiñci*) and so forth, taking up the summary in verse (*gāthā*).
Therein, "clung to" (*ajjhositaṃ*) means that which has been swallowed, finalized, and grasped after being imagined as "true and real" through the faith of others—that is, through reliance on others.
"In those who are self-restrained" (*sayasaṃvutesu*) refers to those who have grasped what they have grasped by restraining themselves and cherishing it.
The meaning is "among those who hold to views. For those who hold to views are said to be "self-restrained" [in their own way].

Regarding those who hold to views, who are reckoned as self-restrained, and who might burn others with either truth or falsehood—the Tathāgata, being such (tādī), does not regard even a single word of theirs as "this alone is the truth, all else is vain," nor does he consider truth or falsehood to be supreme for another.
Having done so, one would not kindle [the fire], would not believe, and would not trust. "This is the dart" means this is the dart of views (*diṭṭhisalla*).
"Having seen it beforehand" means having seen it even earlier, while still at the foot of the Bodhi tree. "Entangled" means stuck, clung to, and obstructed.
"I know and see it to be exactly thus" means that just as these people are obsessed with it, having swallowed it and finalized it, they are entangled.
"Attached, clinging"—thus I too know and see. "In such a way that there is nothing clung to by this generation, even so there is nothing clung to by the Tathāgatas"—this is the meaning.
5. Commentary on the *Brahmacariya Sutta* (The Discourse on the Holy Life)

25. “For the sake of deceiving people” means for the sake of deceiving people by means of the three bases of deception. “Not for the sake of pleasing people” means not for the sake of winning over people.
“Not for the sake of the benefits of gain, honor, and renown” means not for the sake of robes and so forth, nor for the sake of words of praise.
“Not for the sake of the benefits of escaping from such-and-such talk” means not for the sake of the benefits of making statements based on various reasons. Not...
For the purpose of the benefit and advantage of debate; not for the sake of people knowing me, thinking, "It is said that this monk is such-and-such, this monk is such-and-such";
for the purpose of restraint, meaning for the sake of restraining by means of the five restraints;

for the purpose of abandoning, meaning for the sake of relinquishing by means of the three abandonings; for the purpose of dispassion, meaning for the sake of becoming free from passion and the other defilements.
"For the purpose of cessation" means for the sake of the very cessation of those [defilements]. "Free from reliance" (*anītihā*) means devoid of reliance on tradition;
the meaning is that it is not dependent on others. "Leading to the depth of Nibbāna" means entering into the interior of Nibbāna.
For the holy life of the Path (*maggabrahmacariya*), having made Nibbāna its object, exists and proceeds only within the interior of Nibbāna. "They practice" refers to both kinds [of practice].
They practice [the path]. In this sutta, having explained the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*), only the cessation is explained in the verses.
6. Commentary on the *Kuha Sutta*: 26.
In the sixth [verse], "deceitful" (*kuha*) means those who are deceitful. "Stubborn" (*thaddha*) means stubborn due to anger and pride. "Chatterers" (*lapa*) means those who engage in idle chatter.

“Siṅgīti”: they are possessed of manifest defilements similar to a horn, as described by the passage: “In this context, what is a ‘horn’? That which is a horn, being ornamental, playful, cleverness, shrewdness, and craftiness.
*Unnaḷā* means those with upraised reeds; they stand having raised up empty pride. *Asamāhitā* means those who do not obtain even a mere one-pointedness of mind.
“Those monks, bhikkhus, are not ‘mine’; those monks do not belong to me.
But when it was said, ‘They are mine,’ this was said because they went forth under the Teacher.
And here too, when it is said, ‘Those monks, bhikkhus, are mine,’ he says ‘mine’ because they went forth under himself and because they have practiced rightly.”
But he said, "They are mine. They attain growth, increase, and abundance because they reach growth through the expansion of qualities such as virtue (*sīla*);
they reach increase by being unshakable; and they reach abundance by being spread everywhere.
These, moreover, grow up to the path of arahantship; once the fruit of arahantship is attained, they are said to have reached full maturity. Thus, in this...
In both the discourses (*sutta*) and the verses (*gāthā*), only the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*) have been explained.
7. Commentary on the *Santuṭṭhisutta* 27.
In the seventh [verse], "few" (*appāni*) means limited. "Easy to obtain" (*sulabhāni*) means they can be acquired with ease anywhere at all.

"They are possible to obtain. "Blameless" means faultless. "Food consisting of scraps from alms" refers to food obtained in the measure of a mouthful after wandering by the strength of one's leg-scraping power. "Putrid urine" means any kind of urine.
For just as even a body that is golden-colored is called a "putrid body," so too even fresh urine is indeed "putrid urine."
"Vighāta" means the absence of affliction; the meaning is that there is no mental suffering. "He is not repelled by the directions":
for one whose thought arises, "I shall obtain robes and so forth when I have gone to such-and-such a place," his mind is indeed repelled by those directions.
For one in whom such a thought does not arise, he is not repelled. "Dhammas" refers to the dhammas of practice.
"Conducive to the state of a recluse" means they are in accordance with the qualities of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*).
"Attained" means that all these are attained by a bhikkhu of contented mind; they are included within him and not outside of him.
8. Commentary on the *Ariyavaṃsa Sutta* (The Discourse on the Noble Lineages)
28. The eighth: the placement [of the discourse] according to intention (*ajjhāsayika*).

It is said that the Blessed One, while seated upon the excellent Buddha-throne prepared in the Dhamma Hall at the Great Monastery of Jetavana, surrounded by forty thousand bhikkhus who were seated there both out of their own inclination and that of other individuals, addressed them, saying, "Bhikkhus," and spoke these four: [The text continues with the four noble lineages.]
"Monks, the noble lineages," he began. Therein, "noble lineages" (*ariyavaṃsa*) means the lineages of the noble ones (*ariya*).

For just as there are the kṣatriya lineage, the brahmin lineage, the vaiśya lineage, the śūdra lineage, the ascetic lineage, the family lineage, and the royal lineage, so too this eighth noble lineage is called a noble stream, a noble tradition, and a noble succession. Furthermore, this noble lineage [consists] of these...
Just as the fragrance of black sandalwood (*kāḷānusāri*) and so forth is declared to be the foremost among the fragrances of bamboo roots and the like, so too is this [practice] considered supreme.
But who are those Noble Ones (*ariya*) of whom these are the "bamboos" (*vaṃsa*)? The Noble Ones are said to be the Buddhas, the Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Tathāgata;
these are the "bamboos" of those Noble Ones, thus they are called the "Noble Bamboos" (*ariyavaṃsa*). For prior to this, during the four [aeons] exceeding one hundred thousand *kappas*...
At the end of incalculable eons, four Buddhas appeared: Taṇhaṅkara, Medhaṅkara, Saraṇaṅkara, and Dīpaṅkara.
They were noble ones (ariya), and the lineages of those noble ones are thus called "noble lineages" (ariyavaṃsa).
After the final nirvana of those Buddhas, once an incalculable eon had passed, a Buddha named Koṇḍañña appeared... [and so on] ...in this present eon.
The four Buddhas who have appeared—Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, Kassapa, and our Blessed One Gotama—the lineages of those Noble Ones are thus called the "Noble Lineages" (ariyavaṃsa).

Furthermore, they are called the "Noble Lineages" because they are the lineages of all the Noble Ones of the past, future, and present: the Buddhas, the Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Buddhas.
Furthermore, these should be known as "foremost" because they are supreme; they should be known as "ancient" because they have existed for a long time;

they should be known as "of lineage" because they are of a continuous line. They are ancient, not newly arisen. They are unmixed, unconfused, and unabandoned. They were never mixed even by past Buddhas;
they were never previously confused, nor were they ever abandoned with the thought, "What is the use of these? They are not...
"They are being recited" means they are not removed even now. "They will not be recited" means they will not be removed by future Buddhas as well.
"Not censured by those in the world who are wise ascetics and brahmins" means they are not reviled, not blamed, and not disparaged by wise ascetics, brahmins, and the learned.

"He is content" means he is content by way of contentment with the basic requisites. "With whatever [is available]" means not [discriminating] between coarse and fine, rough and refined, or worn-out and new.
"By whatever means" means that one is content with whatever is obtained by this or that method, such as what has been acquired.

For regarding robes, there are three kinds of contentment: contentment with what is obtained (*yathālābha-santosā*), contentment with what is suitable to one's strength (*yathābala-santosā*), and contentment with what is appropriate (*yathāsāruppa-santosā*).
The same principle applies to alms-food and the other requisites. Regarding these, the detailed explanation is: "Bhikkhus, for one who is content, unarisen [defilements do not arise]..."
And wholesome states arise—this is to be understood according to the method stated in this very sutta.
Thus, with reference to these three kinds of contentment, it is said: "He is content with any kind of robe whatsoever; he is content with whatever robe he has obtained."
And here, the robe must be understood; the field for robes must be understood; the rag-robe must be understood;
contentment with robes must be understood; and the ascetic practices connected with robes must be understood.
Therein, "the robe must be understood" means that the six types of robes beginning with linen and the six types of secondary robes beginning with *dukūla* must be understood. These make twelve.

Permissible robes (*kappiyacīvara*) are as follows: a robe made of *kuśa* grass, a robe made of flax, a robe made of bark, a blanket of human hair, a blanket of animal fur, a coarse cloth (*potthaka*), hide, an owl’s wing, tree-bark, vine-cloth, *eraka*-grass cloth, plantain-bark cloth, and bamboo-cloth;
however, such items as these are impermissible robes (*akappiyacīvara*).

Regarding "the field for robes" (*cīvarakkhetta*): six fields should be understood as those from which [robes] arise—namely, from the Saṅgha, from a group, from relatives, from friends, from one’s own wealth, or as a rag from a dust heap (*paṃsukūla*)—and eight fields should be understood by way of the eight headings (*mātikā*). As for the rag from a dust heap (*paṃsukūla*), it consists of:
that from a charnel ground, that from a shop, that from a street, that from a rubbish heap, that from a weaver’s workshop, that from a bathhouse, and so forth.

The twenty-three kinds of refuse rags (*paṃsukūla*) should be understood as follows: one from a bathing place, one returned after being taken away, one burnt by fire, one gnawed by cattle, one gnawed by termites, one gnawed by rats,
one cut at the edge, one torn by mice, one carried off by a flag, one from a stupa, one from a monk’s robe, one from the ocean, one used for consecration,
one from a traveler, one blown by the wind, one produced by supernormal power, and one given by a deity.

And here, "midwifery" refers to that which removes the impurities of the womb. "That which has been gone to and returned from" refers to a robe brought back after having clothed a corpse and carried it to the cemetery.
"Brought by a flag" refers to what is brought after raising a flag. "From a stupa" refers to a robe worshipped at an anthill.
"Ocean-borne" refers to what has been washed onto dry land by the waves of the sea. "Of travelers" refers to [what is obtained] by those going along a road.
Having been pounded with stones out of fear of thieves, his robe was worn away. "Produced by psychic power" refers to the robe of one who has come as a bhikkhu (*ehibhikkhu-cīvara*).
The rest is self-evident. Regarding contentment with robes, there are twenty forms of contentment with robes: contentment with thoughts regarding robes; contentment with going [for alms];
contentment with seeking; contentment with acquisition; contentment with accepting a moderate amount; contentment with avoiding greediness; contentment with whatever is obtained;...
Contentment according to one's strength; contentment according to what is appropriate; contentment with water; contentment with washing; contentment with making [robes]; contentment with measurement;
contentment with thread; contentment with sewing; contentment with dyeing; contentment with allowable [robes]; contentment with use;
contentment through avoiding hoarding; and contentment through relinquishing.
In this regard, after a bhikkhu seeking [a robe] has stayed in a fixed residence for three months, it is permissible for him to engage in reflection for about one month.
For one who has performed the *pavāraṇā* ceremony makes his robe during the robe-month, whereas a wearer of rag-robes (*paṃsukūlika*) makes it in just half a month.
This reflection for about a month and a half is called "contentment with reflection. And by one who is satisfied with contentment through reflection...
A monk should be like the Elder Paṃsukūlika who lived at Pācīnakhaṇḍarāji.
It is said that the Elder, having come thinking, "I shall worship the shrine at the Cetiyapabbata monastery," worshipped the shrine and thought:
"My robe is worn out; I shall obtain one where many people dwell. He then went to the Mahāvihāra.
Having seen the Elder of the Saṅgha, he asked for a place to stay and resided there. On the following day, taking his robe, he returned and paid homage to the Elder.
The Elder said, "What is it, friend? "Venerable sir, I am going to the village gate.
"I too shall go, friend. "Very well, venerable sir," he replied. As they were departing, he stood at the gateway of the Great Bodhi tree.
Thinking, "I shall obtain a pleasant dwelling place in the abode of those possessed of merit," he turned back from that very spot, reflecting, "My thought is not pure.
On the following day he turned back from near the mango courtyard; on the next day, from the northern gate of the Great Cetiya;
and having turned back at each of those places, on the fourth day he went into the presence of the Elder. The Elder said, "For this bhikkhu..."
“His thought will not be purified,” he thought; so, taking his robe and asking him questions along the way, he entered the village.
That same night, a certain man, obstructed by the urge to defecate, voided his excrement right onto his own garment and discarded it in a rubbish heap.
When the Elder Paṃsukūlika saw that it was swarming with blue flies, he [reflected].
He raised his hands in salutation. The Great Elder asked, "Friend, why do you raise your hands in salutation to a rubbish heap? [The boy replied:
"Venerable sir, I am not raising my hands in salutation to a rubbish heap; I am raising them to my father, the One of Ten Powers.
Having shaken off the insects from a rag as large as a water-pot that had been discarded after wrapping it around the body of the maidservant Puṇṇā, I have taken it from the cemetery..."
"Venerable sir, he who took it has done what is most difficult," [the monk said]. The Great Elder thought, "The intention of this wearer of rag-robes is pure.
Standing right there, the Elder Paṃsukūlika developed insight and attained the three fruits;
then, taking that cloth, making it into a robe, and putting it on, he went to Pācīnakhaṇḍarājī and attained the supreme fruit of Arahantship.
Furthermore, for one going for the sake of a robe, not thinking "Where shall I get it?
but going with the meditation subject as the primary aim, is called "contentment in going.
For one searching, however, not searching with just anyone, but taking a modest and virtuous bhikkhu along to do the searching, is called "contentment in searching. While searching in this way—
Seeing a robe being brought from afar, one does not reflect, "This will be pleasing; this will be unpleasing.
Rather, contentment with whatever is obtained—whether coarse or fine—is called "contentment with acquisition" (*paṭilābhasantosa*).
Even when receiving what has been thus obtained, one does not think, "This much will be for a double-layered robe; this much will be for a single-layered robe," nor for oneself...
Contentment with receiving only what is sufficient is called "contentment in accepting a moderate amount. Furthermore, for one seeking robes,
walking from door to door without thinking, "I will obtain something pleasing at such-and-such a house," is called "contentment in avoiding greediness."
For one who is able to subsist on any kind of coarse or refined food, subsisting with whatever is obtained is called "contentment with what is received" (*yathālābha-santosa*).
For one who, knowing his own strength, subsists with whatever he is able to sustain himself with, it is called "contentment according to one's capacity" (*yathābala-santosa*).
For one who gives what is pleasing to another and sustains himself with whatever [else] he has, it is called "contentment with what is suitable" (*yathāsāruppa-santosa*).
“Contentment with water” means washing with whatever water is available for washing, without discriminating as to whether the water is pleasant or unpleasant.
However, it is permissible to avoid water that is turbid with yellow clay, red ochre, or the juice of rotting leaves.
Furthermore, when washing, one should not strike with clubs or other such implements, but wash by rubbing with the hands.
“Contentment with washing” means this: likewise, if it does not become clean, it is permissible to wash it by adding leaves and using boiled water.

For one who makes [the robe] after washing it in this way, making it according to the available amount without being bothered by whether “this part is coarse” or “that part is fine,” is called contentment with making. Making it merely to cover the three circles is contentment with measure.
This is called "contentment with thread. However, one should not seek out beautiful thread for the purpose of making robes;

rather, without deliberation, having brought whatever thread is found on the streets or in shrines for deities, or even that which has been placed at the feet [of a donor], one takes it and makes [the robe]. This is what is meant by contentment with thread.
Furthermore, when sewing the cloth, one must not pierce [the needle] more than seven times within the space of a finger's breadth. For if one acts in this way—
If a monk does not have a companion, there is no breach of the rule for him. However, [the cloth] must be pierced seven times with a needle three finger-breadths in length.
One who acts in this manner must also have a companion who has set out on the path; if he does not, there is a breach of the rule.
This is called "satisfaction with sewing. But when dyeing, one should seek out black antelope skins and the like.
One should not go about [wearing robes of any color]. One should dye them with whatever is obtained from *soma*, bark, and so forth.
However, if these are not available, one should take grass discarded by people in the forest, or dye with the dye-ashes discarded by monks after boiling, or take the dregs discarded by monks;
this is called "contentment regarding dye. Having taken any of the blue, mud-color, black, or dark-grey [dyes], upon the back of an elephant...
Making an allowable alteration for one who is sitting [to wear the robe] is called "satisfaction with what is allowable.
Using it merely to cover the private parts out of a sense of shame is called "satisfaction in use.
However, having obtained cloth, if one does not obtain thread, needle, or a maker, it is permissible to set it aside; if one does obtain them, it is not.
It is permissible. Even if one wishes to give it to a resident pupil (*antevāsika*) or others, but they are not present, it is permissible to set it aside until their arrival.
As soon as they have arrived, it must be given. If one is unable to give it, one should make a formal determination (*adhiṭṭhātabba*).
When another robe-cloth is available, it is also permissible to determine even a rug (*paccattharaṇa*). For indeed, that which has not been determined constitutes "storing" (*sannidhi*).
"It is not determined," said the Elder Mahāsīva. This is called contentment in the avoidance of hoarding.

Furthermore, when distributing [robes], one should not give by looking at the faces [of others]; rather, one should distribute while standing in the *sāraṇīya-dhamma* (the qualities conducive to harmony).

This is called contentment in distribution. The ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) connected with robes are the refuse-rag-wearer's practice (*paṃsukūlikaṅga*) and the three-robe-wearer's practice (*tecīvarikaṅga*). Of these two...
The detailed exposition should be understood from the *Visuddhimagga*.

Thus, a bhikkhu fulfilling the noble lineage of contentment with robes guards these two ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*). By guarding these, he is content by way of the noble lineage of contentment with robes.
Regarding "one who speaks in praise": one person is content but does not speak in praise of contentment; another is not content...
He speaks in praise of contentment. One person is neither contented nor speaks in praise of contentment;
another is both contented and speaks in praise of contentment. To demonstrate this, it is said: "and one who speaks in praise of contentment with whatever robe is available."
“Improper search” (*anesanā*) refers to various kinds of improper seeking, such as acting as a messenger, being sent on errands, or engaging in such pursuits.
“Unbecoming” (*appatirūpa*) means unsuitable. “And not having obtained” (*aladdhā ca*) means without having acquired [robes].
For example, someone might associate with meritorious monks, thinking, “How indeed shall I obtain a robe? and while doing so, he acts with hypocrisy, becoming anxious and agitated.
A contented bhikkhu, having not obtained a robe in this way, does not become agitated. "Having obtained" means having acquired it righteously and fairly.
"Unattached" means free from greed and longing. "Uninfatuated" means not having fallen into a swoon of excessive craving.
"Unswallowed up" means not submerged or enveloped by craving. "Seeing the danger" refers to the peril in improper search and in the commission of offenses.

Seeing the danger in the enjoyment of what is acquired through craving; being "one who understands the escape" means understanding precisely that escape which has been stated as "only for the warding off of cold.
"Contentment with whatever robe" means contentment with any kind of robe whatsoever. "He does not exalt himself" means...
“I am a rag-robe wearer; I took up the practice of wearing rag-robes right at the time of my full ordination;
who is there equal to me?”—thus he does not engage in self-exaltation. “He does not disparage others” means:
he does not disparage others by saying, “But these other monks are not rag-robe wearers,” or “They do not possess even the mere practice of wearing rag-robes. For whoever therein...
“Skilled” means one who is clever, dexterous, and competent in that contentment with robes or in speaking in praise thereof and so forth.
“Diligent” means free from laziness through constant application. “Possessed of clear comprehension and mindfulness” means endowed with both the wisdom of clear comprehension and mindfulness.
“Established in the noble lineage” means firmly grounded in the noble lineage.

“With whatever almsfood” means with any kind of almsfood whatsoever. Here too, the almsfood must be understood, the field for almsfood must be understood, contentment with almsfood must be understood, and the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) connected with almsfood must be understood.
Therein, “almsfood” refers to boiled rice, sour gruel, flour, fish, meat, milk, curds, ghee, and fresh butter.
Oil, honey, molasses, rice gruel, solid food, soft food, and syrups—these are the sixteen types of alms-food (*piṇḍapāta*). The field for alms-food consists of:

a meal provided for the Saṅgha, a designated meal, an invitation, a meal by ticket, a fortnightly meal, a meal on the Uposatha day, a meal on the first of the month, a meal for newcomers, a meal for those departing, a meal for the sick, and a meal for those attending to the sick.
The fifteen fields for alms-food are: food provided by rotation, food from a fixed house, food on alternate days, and food at a monastery.

Contentment with alms-food consists of contentment with thoughts regarding alms-food, contentment with the journey, contentment with the search, contentment with the acquisition, contentment with the receiving, contentment with receiving a moderate amount, contentment with avoiding greediness, and contentment with whatever is obtained.

There are fifteen kinds of contentment: contentment with what one’s strength permits, contentment with what is appropriate, contentment with what is helpful, contentment with moderation, contentment with the use [of requisites], contentment with avoiding hoarding, and contentment with relinquishing.
In this regard, a monk who is seeking [requisites] reflects after having washed his face. However, [this is not the case for one] together with a group of alms-collectors...
While wandering for alms in the evening at the time of attending upon the elders, one may think only this much: "Where shall we wander for alms tomorrow?"—"In such-and-such a village, venerable sirs.
From that point on, one must not engage in discursive thought. One who wanders alone should stand in the "pavilion of thought" and engage in reflection.
If from that point on one continues to indulge in discursive thought, one has fallen away from and is excluded from the Noble Lineage. This is called "contentment with thought."
When entering for alms, one should go with the meditation subject as one's primary focus, without thinking, "Where shall I get [something]?
This is called contentment in going. When seeking, one should not take just anything, but should seek only from those who are modest and virtuous.
This is called contentment in seeking. Seeing food being brought even from a distance, one should think, "This is pleasing..."
One should not give rise to the thought, "This is unpleasant. This is called contentment with what is obtained (*paṭilābha-santosa*).
Without thinking, "I will take this pleasant thing, I will not take that unpleasant thing," one should simply accept whatever is sufficient for subsistence.
This is called contentment in receiving (*paṭiggahaṇa-santosa*).
In this case, however, when the object to be given is abundant but the donor wishes to give little, one should accept only a small amount.
When the object to be given is abundant and the donor also wishes to give much, one should accept only a moderate amount.

When the object to be given is not abundant and the donor wishes to give little, one should accept only a small amount. But when the object to be given is not abundant, yet the donor wishes to give much—

It should be accepted with moderation. For one who does not know the proper measure in receiving defiles the confidence of people, squanders what is given in faith, fails to carry out the Teaching, and is unable to win over even the mind of his own mother.
Thus, it should be accepted only after knowing the proper measure; this is called "contentment in receiving with moderation. Only families of means...

One should proceed by visiting the doors in regular succession. This is called contentment through the avoidance of greed. Contentment with whatever is obtained and the other types of contentment regarding robes are to be understood in the same manner as explained for robes.
Consuming almsfood after recognizing its benefit by thinking, "I shall maintain the duty of a recluse," is [contentment].

This is called contentment with assistance. One should not accept what has been brought after filling a bowl. If there is one who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna), it should be made to be received by them;
if there is none, one should have it carried away and then accept only the mere act of receiving.
This is called contentment with measure. "The dispelling of hunger—this is the escape here"—thus using [the food] is contentment in enjoyment.

This is called "avoidance of hoarding contentment. One should distribute [the alms] without looking at the face, remaining established in the qualities conducive to harmony (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*). This is called "contentment in distribution.

Furthermore, there are five ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) connected with almsfood: the practice of eating only almsfood (*piṇḍapātika-aṅga*) and the practice of wandering for alms from house to house in regular order (*sapadānacārika-aṅga*).
The single-session practice, the bowl-food practice, and the later-food-refuser practice. A detailed exposition of these is given in the *Visuddhimagga*.
Thus, a bhikkhu fulfilling the great noble lineage of contentment with almsfood observes these five ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*).
By observing these, he is satisfied by the great noble lineage of contentment with almsfood. [The terms] "one who speaks in praise," etc., [follow].
These should be understood in the manner already stated.
Regarding "lodging" (*senāsana*): here, the lodging itself must be known; the field for lodging must be known; contentment with lodging must be known;
and the ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*) connected with lodging must be known. In this context, "lodging" refers to a bed (*mañca*).

A seat, a mattress, a pillow, a dwelling, a gabled house, a mansion, a stilt house, a cave, a grotto, a watchtower, a storied building, a bamboo thicket, the foot of a tree, or wherever else monks stay—these are the fifteen types of lodgings (*senāsana*).
"The field of lodgings" refers to six fields: from the Saṅgha, from a group, from relatives, from friends, from one's own wealth, or as a rag-robe (*paṃsukūla*).

Contentment with resting places (*senāsanasantosa*) refers to the fifteen kinds of contentment, beginning with contentment regarding thoughts concerning resting places. These are to be understood in the same manner as those explained in the section on almsfood (*piṇḍapāta*).
Furthermore, there are five ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) connected with resting places:

the practice of dwelling in the forest (*āraññikaṅga*), the practice of dwelling at the foot of a tree (*rukkhamūlikaṅga*), the practice of dwelling in the open air (*abbhokāsikaṅga*), the practice of dwelling in a charnel ground (*sosānikaṅga*), and the practice of accepting whatever seat is provided (*yathāsanthatikaṅga*). An extensive explanation of these is found in the *Visuddhimagga*.
Thus it is said. A bhikkhu who fulfills this Great Noble Lineage of Contentment with Lodgings guards these five ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas).
By guarding them, he becomes content through the Great Noble Lineage of Contentment with Lodgings.

As for the requisite of medicine, it is already included within almsfood; therein, one should be satisfied simply by whatever is obtained, whatever strength one has, and whatever is suitable. The practice of sitting (nesajjikaṅga) belongs to the Noble Lineage of Delight in Meditation. And this has been said:
“Five are spoken of in relation to lodgings, five are dependent on food;
one is associated with energy, and two are dependent on robes.
Thus the Blessed One spoke, as if spreading out the earth, as if filling the belly of the ocean, and as if expanding the sky.
Just as one who, having first explained the noble lineage of contentment with robes, now raises up the moon or surpasses the sun, so too,
having explained the second noble lineage of contentment with almsfood, and having explained the third noble lineage of contentment with lodgings—
like one lifting up Mount Sineru— he now explains the fourth, which is delighting in meditation, adorned with a thousand methods.

Furthermore, in order to explain the Noble Lineage (*ariyavaṃsa*), the Blessed One began the teaching, saying: "Moreover, monks, a monk delights in development (*bhāvanārāmo*). In this context, *āramaṇa* means delight; the meaning is "delight.
One for whom there is delight in development is "one who delights in development" (*bhāvanārāmo*). One who finds pleasure in development is "one who delights in development" (*bhāvanārato*).
One for whom there is delight in the fivefold abandoning is "one who delights in abandoning" (*pahānārāmo*). Moreover, he develops and thus finds delight.
"Delighting in development" (*bhāvanārāma*). "One who delights while abandoning" is "delighting in abandonment" (*pahānārāma*); this is how the meaning should be understood here.
For he delights while developing the four foundations of mindfulness; the meaning is that he finds pleasure therein.
Likewise with the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the seven contemplations.
He delights in and finds joy in cultivating the eighteen great insights, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the thirty-eight classifications of objects.
Furthermore, he delights in and finds joy in abandoning the defilements such as sensual desire.
Now, among these four noble lineages, by means of the first three, [one fulfills] the thirteen ascetic practices and contentment with the four requisites.
By way of delight in study, the entire Vinaya Piṭaka has been explained; by way of delight in meditation, the remaining two Piṭakas [have been explained].

Furthermore, this Noble Lineage of delight in meditation should be explained by a bhikkhu according to the passage on renunciation in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, according to the method of the *Dasuttara-sutta* in the *Dīghanikāya*, and according to the method of the *Satipaṭṭhāna-sutta* in the *Majjhimanikāya*.
It should be explained; it should be explained according to the method of exposition in the Abhidhamma.
Therein, in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, in the "Discourse on Renunciation" (*Nekkhammapāḷi*), it is said:
"One who cultivates renunciation finds delight; one who abandons sensual desire finds delight. One who cultivates non-ill will [finds delight]; one who abandons ill will..."
the perception of light... sloth and torpor... non-distraction... restlessness... the definition of phenomena... doubt... knowledge...
ignorance... joy... discontent... the first jhāna, the five hindrances...
the second jhāna, applied and sustained thought... the third jhāna, rapture... the fourth jhāna, pleasure and pain... the attainment of the base of infinite space.
He delights in developing; he delights in abandoning the perception of form, the perception of resistance, and the perception of diversity.

He delights in developing the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness… [and so on] …he delights in developing the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; he delights in abandoning the perception of the base of nothingness.
“He delights in developing the contemplation of impermanence; he delights in abandoning the perception of permanence. He delights in developing the contemplation of suffering…
Contemplation of suffering in what is pleasant; contemplation of non-self in what is self; contemplation of disenchantment in delight;
contemplation of dispassion in passion; contemplation of cessation in arising; contemplation of relinquishment in grasping;
contemplation of destruction in the perception of compactness; contemplation of vanishing in accumulation; contemplation of change in the perception of permanence; and contemplation of the signless.

… the sign … the contemplation of the wishless … wishing … the contemplation of emptiness … misinterpretation … insight into phenomena through higher wisdom … misinterpretation as grasping at a core … knowledge and vision in accordance with reality … misinterpretation as delusion … the contemplation of danger … misinterpretation as attachment … the contemplation of reflection … non-reflection … the contemplation of turning away … misinterpretation as bondage …

“He delights in developing the path of stream-entry... [abandoning] the defilements associated with views; he delights in developing the path of once-returning... [abandoning] the gross defilements; he delights in developing the path of non-returning... [abandoning] the residual defilements; he delights in developing the path of arahantship, abandoning all defilements.
Thus it should be recited in the *Nekkhamma-pāḷi* of the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.
According to the method of the *Dasuttara-sutta* in the *Dīgha Nikāya*:
“One delights in developing one quality, one delights in abandoning one quality...

[and so on] ...one delights in developing ten qualities, one delights in abandoning ten qualities. What is the one quality that one delights in developing? Mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*).”
He delights in developing this one quality accompanied by pleasure. What one quality does he delight in abandoning?
He delights in abandoning the conceit "I am. What two qualities...
[and so on] ...what ten qualities does he delight in developing? The ten bases of totality (*kasiṇāyatana*); he delights in developing these ten qualities.
“Which ten things does he delight in abandoning? The ten forms of wrongness; it is by abandoning these ten things that he delights.
In this way, monks, a monk is one who delights in development.
Thus it should be explained according to the method of the *Dasuttara-sutta* in the *Dīgha Nikāya*.
According to the method of the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta in the Majjhima Nikāya:
"Monks, this is the one-way path... [as it is said] ...merely for the sake of knowledge and mindfulness.
And he dwells independent, not clinging to anything in the world. In this way too, monks, a monk delights in development."
He delights in development; he finds joy in abandoning and delights in abandoning. Furthermore, monks, when a monk is walking, he understands:
"I am walking"... and so on... Furthermore, monks, suppose a monk were to see a body discarded in a charnel ground...
rotting and reduced to powder. He compares this very body [to that]: "This, too, is of the same nature..."
‘This body has such a nature, such a character, and does not transcend this. Thus, he dwells contemplating the body in the body internally...
[as before] ...In this way too, monks, a monk is one who delights in development.
This should be explained according to the method of the *Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta* in the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
"In the Abhidhamma, by way of exposition" means: "He delights in contemplating all conditioned things as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a tumor...
[and so on] ...as phenomena subject to defilement; in this way, bhikkhu, one is 'delighting in development'.
Thus it should be explained by way of exposition.

“He does not exalt himself” means that he does not engage in self-exaltation by thinking, “Today I have been practicing the work of insight into impermanence, suffering, and non-self for sixty or seventy years; who is there equal to me?

“He does not disparage others” means that he does not think, “These people do not even possess a mere measure of insight into impermanence and suffering; what is the use of these who have abandoned their meditation subjects?”
"Thus he does not engage in disparaging others. The rest is exactly as previously stated.

"Monks, these are the four noble lineages (ariyavaṃsa). Monks, having thus turned back from the Sutta on the four noble lineages—which are the noble streams, the noble traditions, the noble straight paths, and the noble tracks—[the Buddha now speaks] concerning one who fulfills the Great Noble Lineage.
Showing the directions in which a bhikkhu should dwell, he said, "And by these, monks," and so forth.
Therein, "he alone endures discontent" means that he alone endures, overcomes, and masters discontent, lack of delight, and weariness.
"Discontent does not endure him" refers to that very discontent which arises toward the cultivation of wholesome states in remote lodgings.

There is one so named who is unable to endure or overcome it. "One who endures discontent and delight" (*aratiratisaho*) means he endures both mental aversion and the delight in the five strands of sensual pleasure;
he is able to overcome them.

Now, summarizing the point by means of verses, the Blessed One said, beginning with "Not discontent," and so forth. In that context, "the steadfast" (*dhīra*) refers to one possessed of energy. Not discontent...
"He endures the steadfast" is a statement of the very same reason as before.
Because she does not endure the steadfast, is not able [to do so], and cannot overcome the steadfast, therefore "discontent does not endure the steadfast. For the steadfast one endures discontent;
indeed, it is because he endures discontent that he is called "steadfast. Therefore, the meaning is: "he endures discontent. Regarding the phrase "one who has abandoned all karma":
Having abandoned all karma of the three planes and having made it delimited and circumscribed, it stands firm.
"Who could obstruct that which has dispelled [defilements]?"—having dispelled the defilements, what indeed, whether greed or hatred, could obstruct it?
"Like a gem of Jambūnada gold—who would be worthy to censure it?"—like a gem of naturally red gold known as Jambūnada, it is free from the faults that should be condemned.
Who is worthy to censure that person? "Even by Brahmā praised" means that this person has indeed been praised even by Mahābrahmā.
At the conclusion of the teaching, forty thousand bhikkhus were established in Arahatship.
9. Commentary on the Dhammapada Sutta.
29. “In the ninth [chapter], ‘Dhamma-padas’ means sections of the Dhamma. Regarding ‘non-covetousness’ and so forth:

non-covetousness (*anabhijjhā*) should be understood as the opposite of covetousness (*abhijjhā*); non-ill-will (*abyāpāda*) as the opposite of ill-will (*byāpāda*); right mindfulness (*sammāsati*) as the opposite of wrong mindfulness (*micchāsati*); and right concentration (*sammāsamādhi*) as the opposite of wrong concentration (*micchāsamādhi*).”
"Free from covetousness" means having become free from craving. "With a mind devoid of ill will" means with a mind that at all times does not abandon its natural state.

"Mindful and with one-pointed mind" means he should be endowed with mindfulness and have a one-pointed mind regarding the object. "Well concentrated within" means having his mind well-established within his own internal self.
In this sutta, as well as in the verse, the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*) are explained.
10. Commentary on the Paribbājakasutta 30.
In the tenth [sutta], "renowned" (*abhiññāta*) means known and well-known. *Annabhāra* and so forth are their names.

"Emerging from seclusion" (*paṭisallānā vuṭṭhita*) means emerging from the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*). For that [attainment] is what is intended here by the term "seclusion. "Having rejected" (*paccakkhāya*) means having refused.
"Covetous" means having craving. "Intense passion for sensual pleasures" means having thick attachment toward the objects of sensual pleasure (*vatthukāmā*).

"I would say this to him regarding that" means I would speak thus to him on that account. "He would consider it to be censurable" means he would consider it to be something to be condemned or rejected.
"In accordance with the Dhamma" means having a valid reason. "Adherence to their own views" [is so called].
"Striking at the discourse on the Dhamma while following discourses that are not in accordance with the Dhamma" means the occurrence of such debates.
"Grounds for censure" refers to conditions that are worthy of being censured. "They come" means they approach.
"Ukkalas" refers to those dwelling in the country of Ukkala. "Vassabhañña" refers to two people: Vassa and Bhañña. "Proponents of the doctrine of no-cause" (ahetukavāda).
They were proponents of such views as: “There is no cause, there is no condition for the purification of beings.

They were proponents of non-action (*akiriyavāda*), meaning they spoke in opposition to action, saying: “No evil is done by the one who acts. They were proponents of nihilism (*natthikavāda*), meaning they spoke such things as:

“There is nothing given,” and so forth. They had entered into the fixed course (*niyāma*) regarding these three views. But how did the fixed course come to be among them? It was [as follows]: whoever...

For one who, having adopted such a view, sits in places for night-watching or day-watching and recites and investigates it, his wrong mindfulness becomes established upon that object—"There is no cause, there is no condition; no evil is done by the doer... [and so on]... there is no gift...
[and so on]... with the breakup of the body, one is annihilated"—and his mind becomes one-pointed.
[The citta] becomes [defiled], and the impulsions (javana) impel. In the first impulsion, it is curable; likewise in the second and so on.
In the seventh, even for Buddhas, it is incurable and irreversible, like the thorn of Ariṭṭha. In that regard, one person falls into one wrong view, another into two, and another into all three.
He becomes one whose wrong view is fixed, having reached the obstruction to the path to heaven.
And because it is an obstruction to the path of liberation, such a being is incapable of going even to heaven immediately after that existence, let alone to liberation.
This being is indeed a "stump in the cycle of existence" (vaṭṭakhāṇuka), a guardian of the earth; for the most part, there is no emergence from such a state of existence.
Even the Vassabhaññas were like this. Out of fear of censure, reproach, and attack—that is, out of fear of being censured by others—...

The meaning is: "out of fear of collision" and "out of fear of reproach. Regarding the training in the restraint of covetousness (*abhijjhāvinaya*), "restraint of covetousness" refers to *arahantship*.
One who trains in *arahantship* with diligence is called "heedful" (*appamatta*).
Thus, having explained the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*viṭṭha*) in the Sutta, the verse explains the attainment of the fruit (*phalasamāpatti*).
The Third Chapter: Uruvelā.
4. The Chapter on the Wheel (Cakkavagga). 1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Wheel (Cakkasuttavaṇṇanā).

31. Regarding the first [section] of the fourth [chapter]: "Wheels" (*cakkāni*) refers to excellences (*sampatti*). "The fourfold wheel turns" means that the four wheels of excellence turn and function together;
this is the sense. "Dwelling in a suitable locality" (*patirūpadesavāsa*) means dwelling in a fitting place where the four assemblies (*parisā*) are seen.
"Reliance on true persons" (*sappurisāvassaya*) means depending upon true persons such as the Buddha and others.
"Attendance" means cultivation, not [mere] service to a king. "Right disposition of oneself" means establishing oneself rightly;

if one was previously possessed of lack of faith and so forth, it is the abandoning of those and the establishment of oneself in faith and so forth. "Merit performed in the past" means wholesome states accumulated previously.
And this alone is the criterion here: by whichever consciousness associated with knowledge the wholesome kamma [is performed].
When it has been done, that very wholesome deed leads that person to a suitable place, causes them to associate with true persons, and that individual likewise establishes themselves rightly.
"One who has made merit" means one who has performed meritorious deeds.
"And this happiness turns toward him" means that this happiness approaches that person; the meaning is that it settles upon them.
2. Commentary on the Saṅgaha Sutta 32.
In the second [sutta], "bases of sympathy" (*saṅgahavatthūni*) means the causes for gathering [people]. Regarding the phrase "generosity, and so forth":
some indeed must be gathered by generosity alone; for such a person, only generosity should be given. "Pleasant speech" (*peyyavajja*) means endearing words. For some indeed...
One person says: "This man gives what is called a gift, but having smeared everything with every single word, he destroys it;
what is the value of his giving? Another person says: "Although this man does not actually give a gift, he smears everything as if with oil while speaking.
Whether he gives or not, his mere words are worth a thousand. Such a person...
A person does not expect a gift; he expects only kind words. To such a person, only kind words should be spoken.
"Beneficial conduct" refers to discourse that increases one's welfare. For some do not expect either a gift or kind words, but expect only discourse on their own benefit and on progress.
To such a person, [one should say]: "This is what you ought to do..."
"This should not be done; such a person should be associated with, and such a person should not be associated with"—thus should one speak only on the matter of beneficial conduct (*atthacariyā*).
"Sharing in the same state" (*samānattatā*) means having the same experience of pleasure and pain. For some person does not expect even a single [return] for acts such as giving;
rather, they share in the same pleasure and pain by sitting on the same seat, lying on the same bed, or eating together. Thus is the state of sharing in the same pleasure and pain.
He expects [reciprocity]. If he is equal to a householder in birth or to one who has gone forth in virtue, this equality should be practiced toward him.
"In each case as is appropriate" means equality that is fitting for those respective qualities.
"Like the linchpin of a moving chariot" means just as the linchpin is the support for a moving chariot.
It exists; it holds together the chariot. In the same way, these means of integration hold the world together.
“Not for the sake of the son” means that if a mother were not to perform these acts of integration for her son, she would not receive honor or worship on account of him.
*Saṅgahā ete* is the nominative case used in the sense of the accusative. Alternatively, the reading is *saṅgahe ete*. *Samavekkhanti* means “they look upon correctly.”
They look upon [them]. And they become praiseworthy means that they become worthy of praise.
3. Commentary on the Sīha Sutta 33.
In the third [verse], "lion" refers to four types of lions: the grass lion, the black lion, the pale lion, and the maned lion. Among these—
The grass-lion resembles a pigeon-colored goat and feeds on grass; the black lion resembles a black goat and likewise feeds on grass;
the pale lion resembles a goat the color of a withered leaf and feeds on meat.
The maned lion is endowed with a mouth as if treated with lac, with a fore-toe and four extremities of the feet; from the top of his head, moreover—
Three lines, like those made by a lac-dyed brush, run along the middle of his back and terminate in a rightward curl at the base of his spine.
On his shoulders, he has a mane like a cloak worth a hundred thousand pieces;
the rest of his body is the color of a pure heap of rice or a mass of powdered conch-shell. Among these four...
Among lions, this refers specifically to the maned lion.

"King of beasts" means the king of the entire host of wild animals. "From his lair" means from his dwelling place, or rather, it is said that he emerges from a golden cave, or from a cave of silver, gems, crystal, or emerald.
Furthermore, as he emerges, he does so for four reasons: being oppressed by darkness...
Or for the sake of light; or for the sake of discharging feces and urine when oppressed by them; or for the sake of seeking food when oppressed by hunger;
or for the sake of indulging in unrighteousness when oppressed by lust. But here, it is intended as one who goes out for the sake of seeking food.
"She stretches" means that on a golden floor, or on one of the surfaces of silver,
gems, crystal, or emerald, she places both hind feet evenly, extends her forefeet forward, draws back the rear part of her body,
brings the front part forward, arches her back, raises her neck, and [utters] a sound like a thunderclap.
As if making sounds, he beats his nostrils together and stretches while shaking off the dust clinging to his body.
On the ground where he stretches, he runs back and forth like a young calf; as he runs, his body appears like a firebrand whirling in the darkness.

"He surveys": why does he survey? Out of compassion for others. For it is said that when he roars his lion’s roar, elephants, cattle, antelopes, and other creatures wandering in uneven places such as precipices and pits fall into those very precipices and pits;
he surveys out of compassion for them. But one might ask: "How can there be such a thing as compassion in a hunter who eats the flesh of others?"
“Yes, there is. For instance, thinking ‘What is the use of many being killed by me,’ he does not even take small living beings for his own sustenance.
Thus he exercises compassion; and this has also been said: ‘May I not bring about the destruction of small living beings who have come into my path.’”
"He roars the lion’s roar" means that he first roars a fearless roar three times.
And as he stands on his stretching-ground and roars, his sound makes a single resonance throughout an area of three *yojanas*.
Upon hearing that resonance of his, the multitudes of bipeds and quadrupeds within the three *yojana* radius are unable to remain in their respective places. For the sake of his range...
"He goes forth" means he goes for the sake of food. How so?
For standing on the ground where he stretches himself, leaping either to the right or to the left, he covers a space of one *usabha*; leaping upwards, he leaps four or even eight *usabhas* high;
and leaping straight forward on level ground, he covers a distance of sixteen or even twenty *usabhas*.
He leaps into a place; leaping from dry land or from a mountain, he leaps across a distance of sixty usabhas or even eighty usabhas.
Seeing a tree or a mountain on the path, he avoids it by moving six usabhas to the left, to the right, or upward. Then, having let out his third lion’s roar:
He is perceived at a distance of three *yojanas* from that very place; having gone three *yojanas*, he turns back and hears the echo of his own roar.
Thus he sets out with such swift speed.
"For the most part" means generally. "Fear, terror, and agitation"—all these are merely names for mental trepidation. Of the lion...
Indeed, upon hearing a sound, many are afraid, while few are not afraid. Who, then, are those who are not afraid?
They are the lion among equals, the noble elephant, the noble horse, the noble bull, the noble man, and the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava).

But why do these not fear? First, the lion among equals does not fear because he thinks, "I am equal [to others] in birth, lineage, family, and courage. As for the noble elephant and the others, it is because of the strength of their own view of self-existence (sakkāyadiṭṭhi).
They do not fear; one whose taints are exhausted does not fear because the view of a personal identity has been abandoned.
"Hole-dwellers" refers to those who live in holes, such as snakes, mongooses, lizards, and so forth. "Water-dwellers" refers to those who live in water, such as fish, turtles, and so forth.
"Forest-dwellers" refers to those who live in the forest, such as elephants, horses, gavaya-deer, and so forth. "Enter" means [thinking], "Now he will come and seize me."
They enter after looking for the path. "With strong" means with firm ones. "With leather thongs" means with leather ropes. Regarding "of great psychic power" and so forth:
standing on a ground for leaping, his state of being "of great psychic power" (*mahiddhika*) consists in his ability to leap a distance of about twenty *usabhas* straight ahead, or even more;
his state of being "of great influence" (*mahesakkha*) consists in his sovereignty over other animals; and his voice [reaches] within an area of three *yojanas* all around.
The greatness of his majesty is to be understood by the way those who heard [him] fled.
"In this very way," the Blessed One spoke of himself in various ways in various discourses.
First, in this passage: "Monks, 'Lion' is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One."
In the *Sutta*, he describes himself as being like a lion. In the passage, “‘Physician, surgeon’ is, Sunakkhatta, a designation for the Tathāgata,” he is like a physician.
In the passage, “‘Brāhmaṇa,’ monks, is a designation for the Tathāgata,” he is like a brāhmaṇa.
In the passage, “‘A man skilled in the path,’ Tissa, is a designation for the Tathāgata... [he is like a guide].
The term "designation" (*adhivacana*) refers here to one who resembles a man showing the way; the phrase "I am a king, Sela" refers here to one who resembles a king.
However, in this sutta, speaking of himself by making himself resemble a lion, he said thus.
This is the similarity: just as for a lion there is a time of dwelling in golden caves and so forth, so too for the Tathāgata at the feet of Dīpaṅkara.

The period to be understood is that following his making of the resolution, after fulfilling the perfections for an immeasurable time, when—by both taking rebirth in his final existence and by emerging from his mother’s womb—he caused the ten-thousandfold world system to tremble;
and as he grew up, experiencing a splendor like that of divine majesty while dwelling in the three palaces. [This begins] from Sīha’s Golden Cave...
Just as at the time of the Tathāgata’s Great Departure, having mounted Kaṇḍaka through the open gate at the age of twenty-nine,
he went forth accompanied by Channa; after crossing three kingdoms and donning the saffron robes given by Brahmā on the bank of the Anomā River,
on the seventh day he went to Rājagaha and there [sought] almsfood.

Having practiced his conduct in the cave of Paṇḍava Hill and finished his meal, from the time he attained supreme enlightenment until the moment he gave his promise to the King to first go to the kingdom of Magadha—
just as a lion stretches its limbs after waking— the Tathāgata’s visit to Āḷāra Kālāma occurred once he had given that promise.
Starting from that point, one should understand the period up until the time he partook of forty-nine mouthfuls of milk-rice given by Sujātā.
Then, like the shaking of Siṃha’s body, at the time of evening, having taken the eight handfuls of grass given by the grass-cutter,
while being praised by the deities of ten thousand world-systems and worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, [he circumambulated] the Bodhi tree three times.
Having performed a circumambulation and ascended the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), he spread a layer of grass upon a spot fourteen cubits high;
then, having resolved upon the fourfold energy (caturaṅgavīriya) and sat down, he instantly shattered the host of Māra.

Having purified the three knowledges (tisso vijjā) throughout the three watches of the night, he churned the great ocean of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) with the double-knowledge (yamakañāṇa) in both forward and reverse order.

When he was churning [the waters] and omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) was penetrated, it should be understood that by its power the ten-thousandfold world-system (*dasasahassilokadhātu*) trembled.
Just as a lion surveys the four quarters, so too, having spent seven days at the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) after penetrating omniscient knowledge and consuming his meal of honey-clots,
he received the request for a teaching on the Dhamma from Mahābrahmā at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree.
Having accepted [the alms-food] and dwelling there, on the eleventh day,
at the time of dawn, thinking, "Tomorrow will be the full moon of Āsāḷha," and perceiving that Āḷāra and Uddaka had passed away,
he looked toward the group of five monks for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma— just as a lion surveys his range for prey.

Just as the time for traveling three *yojanas* [is long], so too was the time for the Tathāgata to travel the eighteen-*yojana* road after rising from beneath the Goatherd’s Banyan tree following his meal, taking his bowl and robe with the thought, "I shall set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion for the group of five.
It was like the time of a lion’s roar; having traveled that eighteen-*yojana* road, the Tathāgata [reached] the group of five.

Having thus instructed him, while the Tathāgata was seated on the immovable throne surrounded by a host of devas assembled from ten thousand world-systems, the time for setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion should be understood as occurring through the method beginning with: "Bhikkhus, these two extremes are not to be pursued by one who has gone forth.
And while this passage was being taught, the lion-like roar of the Tathāgata’s Dhamma reached down to the Avīci hell.
Reaching as far as the peak of existence above, he covered the ten-thousandfold world system. Just as small creatures fall into a state of terror at the sound of a lion,
so too, when the Tathāgata— having revealed his three marks—
expounded the Dhamma by analyzing the Four Truths in sixteen aspects and sixty thousand methods, there arose a trembling of the consciousness of the long-lived devas.
The time of his arising should be understood.
According to another method: the Tathāgata, having attained omniscience like a lion, [his] departure from the fragrant chamber is like the lion’s emergence from its den, the golden cave;
and his approach to the Dhamma Assembly is like the lion’s stretching.
The surveying of the assembly is like the surveying of the quarters; the time for preaching the Dhamma is like the roaring of the lion’s roar;
the departure for his range is like the going forth for the purpose of crushing the arguments of opponents.
According to another method: the Tathāgata is like a lion, and his emergence from the golden cave situated in the Himālayas is like [the lion’s own emergence].
The emergence from the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) which is supported by Nibbāna by way of its object should be understood as follows: reviewing-knowledge is like stretching;
surveying those to be trained is like looking around the quarters; teaching the Dhamma to the assembled company is like the lion’s roar;
and approaching the presence of those to be trained who have not yet arrived is like setting out for one's range.
*Yadā* means at which time. *Tathāgata*: he is called a *tathāgata* for the eight reasons explained below. *Loke*: in the world of beings (*sattaloka*). *Uppajjati*:
from the moment of the initial aspiration (*abhinīhāra*) until reaching the seat of enlightenment (*bodhipallaṅka*), or until the knowledge of the path of *arahantship*, one is said to be "arising";
however, once the fruit of *arahantship* is attained, one is said to be "arisen. *Arahaṃ sammāsambuddho*, etc.
These have been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga* in the description of the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*).
Thus, "this is personality" (*sakkāyo*); this is personality, this much is personality, there is no personality beyond this.
To this extent, all five aggregates of clinging (*pañcupādānakkhandhā*) are [defined] by way of their individual nature, their essence, their limit, their delimitation, and their circumscription.
Thus they are shown. "The origin of identity" (*sakkāyasamudaya*) means this is called the origin of identity.

To this extent, everything beginning with "from the arising of nutriment comes the arising of form" has been shown. "The passing away of identity" (*sakkāyassa atthaṅgama*) means this is the passing away of identity.
By this as well, everything beginning with "from the cessation of nutriment comes the cessation of form" has been shown.

“Possessed of beauty” means possessed of beauty by way of the color of the body. “Having heard the teaching of the Dhamma” means having heard the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma, which is adorned with the fifty characteristics within the five aggregates.
“For the most part”—whom does this exclude here? Noble disciples and devas.
For because their taints are exhausted, even fear of mental trepidation does not arise in them; and for one who is stirred with urgency, through wise exertion—
For one who has attained what is to be attained, there arises even a sense of spiritual urgency through knowledge (*ñāṇasaṃvega*).

But for the other deities, as they reflect, "This, monks, is impermanent and fearful," there arises both a trembling of the mind out of fear and a dread born of knowledge at the time of powerful insight (*vipassanā*).
The address "Sir" is merely a form of polite address. "Included within personality" (*sakkāyapariyāpannā*) means included within the five aggregates.

Thus, while the Fully Enlightened One was teaching the Dhamma—having shown the fault of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) to them and having struck it with the three characteristics—the so-called "fear of knowledge" (*ñāṇabhaya*) assailed them.
"Having known" (*abhiññāya*) means having understood.
"The Wheel of Dhamma" (*dhammacakka*) refers both to the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of teaching (*desanā-ñāṇa*). As for the knowledge of penetration:
The knowledge called *nāma* is that wisdom by which, while seated at the seat of enlightenment (*bodhipallaṅka*), he penetrated the Four Truths in sixteen aspects and sixty thousand methods.
The knowledge called *desanāñāṇa* is that wisdom by which he set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma with its three revolutions and twelve aspects.
Both of these are indeed the "wisdom born on the breast" of the One Possessed of Ten Powers (*dasabala*). Among them, the knowledge of teaching the Dhamma—

It should be understood that this [turning of the wheel] is said to be "set in motion" only so long as the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) has not yet arisen for the Elder Aññā Koṇḍañña together with eighteen koṭis of Brahmās;
once that has arisen, it is then truly "set in motion. "Peerless" (appaṭipuggalo) means devoid of any person equal to him.
"Glorious" (yasassino) means endowed with a retinue. "Imperturbable" (tādino) means remaining the same regardless of gain, loss, and so forth.
4. Commentary on the Pasāda Sutta 34.
In the fourth [verse], *aggappasādā* means "confidence in the foremost" or "foremost confidence. *Yāvatā* means "as many as there are.

*Apadā* refers to those without feet, such as snakes and fish. *Dvipadā* refers to those with two feet, such as humans and birds. *Catuppadā* refers to those with four feet, such as elephants and horses.
"Many-footed" refers to those with a hundred feet and so forth. "Neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient" refers to beings reborn in the peak of existence (*bhavagga*).
"It is declared the highest" means it is declared to be the foremost, supreme, and best by virtue of its qualities. "Unconditioned" is said specifically with reference to Nibbāna.

"Dispassion" and the other terms are names for Nibbāna itself; for it is by coming to that [Nibbāna] that all defilements become dispassionate, and all intoxications such as lust and pride are abandoned.
They become free from pride; they go to non-existence; all thirst comes to cessation; all attachments are eradicated;
the rounds of existence are cut off; craving is exhausted; the suffering of the rounds ceases;
and all fevers are extinguished. Therefore, these names are obtained. The rest here is clear in meaning.
5. Commentary on the Vassakāra Sutta 35.
In the fifth [verse], *anussarito* means having followed and remembered; the meaning is one capable of remembering again and again.
*Dakkho* means skillful. *Tatrupāyāya* means by way of the appropriate means for each respective occasion, such as "at this time, this very thing must be done."
"Endowed with wisdom. "Should be rejoiced in" means it should be welcomed. "Should be rejected" means it should be refused.
"Neither indeed do I [say] to you" means "neither indeed do I [say] to you. But why does the Blessed One neither rejoice in this nor reject it?
He does not rejoice because it is worldly; he does not reject it because he stands having grasped a worldly matter. "Of the great multitude..."
"Much of the populace" (*bahu assa janatā*): here, the genitive case (*sāmivacana*) should be understood in the sense of the instrumental (*karaṇatthe*).

"In the noble knowledge" (*ariye ñāye*) refers to the path together with insight (*vipassanā*). "The state of having wholesome qualities" (*kalyāṇadhammatā*) and "the state of having skillful qualities" (*kusaladhammatā*) are also synonyms for that same thing. "Whatever thought" (*yaṃ vitakkaṃ*) refers to any one among thoughts of renunciation (*nekkhamma-vitakka*) and so forth.
"He does not think that thought" (*na taṃ vitakkaṃ vitakketi*) means he does not think even one among sensual thoughts (*kāma-vitakka*) and so forth. The other...
This is a synonym for that very same thing. Regarding the phrase "the path of thought" (*vitakkapatha*): here, thought itself is the path of thought.

In the passages beginning with "I am a brahmin," it should be understood that by the first method the virtue and great learning of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) are described; by the second and third, the functional thoughts and functional jhānas of one whose taints are destroyed; and by the fourth, the state of having destroyed the taints is described.

"Deliverance from the snare of death" means the path that brings deliverance from the snare of death. "The methodical Dhamma" refers to the path accompanied by insight (*vipassanā*). "Having seen and heard" means having seen and heard by means of knowledge itself.
The rest here is self-evident. 6. Commentary on the *Doṇa Sutta* (36).
Regarding the phrase "between Ukkaṭṭhā and Setavyā": here, "Ukkaṭṭhā" is so called because it was maintained by torches (*ukkāhi dhārīyamānāhi*).
A city that has received such a designation because it was measured out. *Setavya* refers to the birthplace of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa in the past.

The word *antara*, however, is used in the senses of cause, moment, the middle of the mind, opening, and so forth—as in the phrases, “Who could know that interval except for the Tathāgata? and “People gather and deliberate; what is the difference between me and them? and others.
In the sense of a cause: as in “Venerable sir, a certain woman saw me while she was washing a vessel between [the flashes of] lightning,” and so on;

in the sense of a moment: as in “He in whom there are no internal corruptions,” and so on; in the sense of the middle: as in “He reached the intermediate cessation,” and so on; in the sense of an interval or gap:
as in “Moreover, this Tapodā flows through the interval between two great hells,” and so on. Now, here [it is used in the sense of]...
It occurs in the sense of "between. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as "between Ukkaṭṭhā and Setavyā.
However, because it is joined with the word *antarā*, the accusative case is employed. In such instances, grammarians employ the word *antarā* only once, as in the example:
"He goes between the village and the river," and that [single word] is used even with the second member [of the compound].
It ought to have been joined [to the verb]; had it not been joined, the accusative case would not have been reached. But here it is stated having already been joined.
"He was traveling on a long journey" means he was traveling on a path reckoned as a journey; that is to say, a long road. Why was he traveling?
It is said that on that very day the Blessed One saw this: "While I am traveling on that path..."

The brahmin Doṇa, having seen the footprints that serve as my shrines, will follow along those footprints and come to the place where I am seated to ask a question. Then I shall teach him one truth-dharma.
Having realized the three fruits of recluseship, the brahmin will deliver a discourse known as "Doṇa’s Roar," measuring twelve thousand words, after I have attained final Nibbāna.
"Having pacified the great strife that has arisen throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, he will distribute the relics. For this reason, he set out.

As for the brahmin Doṇa: the brahmin Doṇa, having mastered the three Vedas and teaching the craft to five hundred young students, rose early on that very day, attended to his personal grooming, and [prepared] a hundred pieces of gold...

Having dressed himself, putting on one shoulder his excellent robe worth five hundred [pieces], wearing sandals with leather straps and red soles upon which were fastened golden cords, and accompanied by a retinue of five hundred young men, he set out along that very same path. It was with reference to this that it was said.
"On the feet" means in the places trodden by the feet. "Wheels" refers to the wheels of the marks (*lakkhaṇa-cakkāni*). But as the Blessed One was walking...
Is a footprint seen in the place where [a Buddha] has stepped? It is not seen. Why? Because of its subtlety, because of his great power, and because of the assistance rendered by the great multitude.
Indeed, due to the exquisite smoothness of the Buddhas' skin, the place where they have stepped is like a spot where cotton-wool has been placed;
no trace of a footprint is seen. And just as for a powerful horse, swift as the wind, even on a lotus leaf—

It becomes as if only just stepped upon; because of the Great Power of the Tathāgata, the place where he has stepped becomes as if only just stepped upon, and no trace of a footprint is perceived there. Furthermore, a great multitude of people follows in the footsteps of the Buddhas;
if they were to see the Teacher’s footprints and were unable to tread over them, their progress would be interrupted. Therefore...
Even where there might have been footprints in the places he stepped upon, they simply vanished. However, the brahmin Doṇa saw them by virtue of the Tathāgata’s resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*).

For when the Blessed One wishes to show a footprint shrine (*padacetiya*) to someone, he makes a resolve concerning that person, saying, "Let such-and-such a one see it. Therefore, like the brahmin Māgaṇḍiya, this man too—
The brahmin saw this through the power of the Tathāgata’s resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*).

"Pleasing" (*pāsādika*) means that which produces confidence; the other term is a synonym for that very same quality. Regarding the phrase "having attained the highest self-subduing and tranquility" (*uttamadamathasamathamanuppatta*):

here, "highest self-subduing" (*uttamadamatha*) refers to the path of Arhatship (*arahattamagga*), and "highest tranquility" (*uttamasamatha*) refers to the concentration of the path of Arhatship (*arahattamaggasamādhi*).

The meaning is that they both attain it. "Tamed" (danta) means free from the goad. "Guarded" (gutta) means protected. "With senses restrained" (saṃyatindriya) means with senses guarded. It is called a "nāga" for four reasons:
because it does not go (na-āgacchati) by way of desire and so forth; because it does not return again to abandoned defilements;
because it does not commit harm (āguṃ); and because of its strength. Thus, it is a nāga for these four reasons.
Regarding the phrase "Devo no bhavaṃ bhavissati," the question would have been concluded even with the words "Devo no bhavaṃ.

However, this brahmin spoke thus because he was speaking in accordance with the nature of his question regarding the future, namely: "In the future, you will become a certain deity-king of great power.
The Blessed One, likewise speaking in accordance with the nature of his question, said: "No, brahmin, I..."
"I shall become a deva," he said. This same method applies everywhere. "Of the taints" (āsavānaṃ) means of the four, beginning with the taint of sensual desire.

"Abandoned" (pahīnā) means abandoned precisely through the attainment of omniscient knowledge at the seat of enlightenment. "Unstained by the world" (anupalitto lokena) means unstained by the world of conditioned phenomena because of the abandonment of the stains of craving and views.
"Buddha"—because of having awakened to the Four Truths—bear me in mind as "the Buddha."
"By which" means by which taint (*āsava*). "May there be rebirth as a deva for me" means that my rebirth as a deva might come to pass.

"A bird" (*vihaṅgama*) refers to a deva belonging to the host of *gandhabbas* who moves through the sky. "Scattered" (*viddhasta*) means dispersed. "Rendered free from reeds" (*vinaḷīkata*) means made devoid of reeds, made free from bonds. "Charming" (*vaggū*) means beautiful.
"It is not smeared by water" means it stands having risen up a cubit (*ratana*) above the water.
"Adorning the lake and making the swarm of bees laugh, it is not defiled by the water. Therefore, O Brahmin, I am a Buddha.
