At the conclusion of this teaching, [the listener] attained the three paths and fruits; he then recited the praise known as the *Doṇagajjita* in twelve thousand verses.
Furthermore, after the Tathāgata had attained Parinibbāna, there arose a great conflict upon the surface of Jambudīpa.
"Having pacified [the conflict], he divided the relics.
7. Commentary on the *Aparihāniya-sutta* (37).
In the seventh [verse], "in the very presence of Nibbāna" means that he moves within the peace of Nibbāna itself. "Established in virtue" refers to the *pātimokkha* virtue.
"Established. "Dwelling thus" means dwelling in this manner. "Ardent" means endowed with ardor, that is, energy.
"Of security from bondage" means of Nibbāna, which is secure from the four bonds. "Seeing danger in negligence" means perceiving negligence as a source of fear.
8. Commentary on the *Patilīna Sutta* (The Discourse on Withdrawal)

38. "One who has shaken off individual truths" (*panuṇṇapaccekasacca*) means one by whom the "individual truths"—that is, views regarded as individual because they were grasped separately in the form "only this is truth, only this is truth"—have been shaken off, removed, and abandoned.
Regarding the term "one who has completely given up quests" (*samavayasaṭṭhesano*): here, *avaya* means "not deficient," and *saṭṭha* means "abandoned."
"Samavayasaṭṭhesano" means one whose seeking has been rightly relinquished; the meaning is that all forms of seeking have been completely cast aside.
"Patilīno" means withdrawn, having attained a state of solitude. "Puthusamaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ" refers to many recluses and brahmins.
Here, "samaṇā" refers to those who have gone forth into homelessness, while "brāhmaṇā" refers to those who address others as "bho. "Puthupaccekasaccāni" means many individual truths.
The individual truths. "Expelled" (*nuṇṇāni*) means removed. "Completely expelled" (*panuṇṇāni*) means thoroughly removed.
"Abandoned" (*cattāni*) means let go. "Vomited out" (*vantāni*) means vomited forth. "Released" (*muttāni*) means made free from their bonds. "Relinquished" (*pahīnāni*) means cast off.
"Renounced" (*paṭinissaṭṭhāni*) means relinquished in such a way that they do not rise up in the mind again. All of these refer to what has been grasped.
These are synonyms for the state of being abandoned.

"The search for sensual pleasures (*kāmesanā*) has been abandoned" means it has been abandoned by the path of the non-returner (*anāgāmimagga*). However, the search for existence (*bhavesanā*) is abandoned by the path of arhatship.

Furthermore, the search for the holy life (*brahmacariyesanā*), which consists of the underlying tendency (*ajjhāsaya*) occurring in the thought, "I shall seek, I shall search for the holy life," is also [abandoned].
It reaches subsiding and pacification through the path of arahantship alone.
However, it should be understood that the search for views and the search for the holy life are extinguished by the path of stream-entry itself.

"In this way, monks" means that in this manner, one whose bodily formations have been stilled by the fourth jhāna is said to have "pacified inhalation and exhalation. "The conceit 'I am'" refers to the ninefold conceit that arises as "I am."

In the verses, "the search for sensual pleasures" (*kāmesanā*) and "the search for existence" (*bhavesanā*)—these are two searches—and "together with the search for the holy life" (*brahmacariyesanā sahā*);
thus, including those very two, there are these three. Here, one should make the construction together with the phrase "the search has been relinquished.
Thus, "clinging to [wrong] truths" (*saccaparāmāso*) and "the towering mass of standpoints of views" (*diṭṭhiṭṭhānā samussayā*) refers to "this is the truth, this is the truth."

Both the grasping and the misapprehension, as well as all those bases for views (diṭṭhiṭṭhāna) which consist of views themselves and are called "elevations" because they stand having risen up and become prominent—all these are included here.
This should be construed with the phrase: "Having stood here, the bases for views have been eradicated.
But for whom have these searches been relinquished, and by whom have these bases for views been eradicated?
For one who is detached from all lust, liberated through the destruction of craving:

he who is indeed detached from all forms of lust and endowed with the liberation of the fruit of Arhatship that occurs through the exhaustion of craving and Nibbāna—for him, seeking has been relinquished and the bases for views have been uprooted.
He is truly "peaceful" (santo) because of the pacification of his defilements; he is "calmed" (passaddho).
He is "tranquil" by means of the two types of tranquility: of body and mind. He is "unconquered" because, having conquered all defilements, he stands unvanquished by anyone.

He is "one who has attained the realization of conceit" through the realization that consists in the abandoning of conceit. He is "awakened" (Buddha) because he stands having awakened to the Four Truths.
Thus, in this sutta as well as in the verses, it is one whose taints are exhausted who is described.
9. Commentary on the Ujjayasutta 39.
In the ninth [verse], "they meet with slaughter" means they meet with execution or death. "Constant alms" refers to *salākabhatta* (tickets for daily meals).
"Family sacrifice" means that because it was given by our fathers and grandfathers, it is to be offered in this manner from generation to generation within the family line.
The meaning is "should be given. Regarding the term *assamedha* and others: it is called *assamedha* because horses (*assa*) are sacrificed (*medhanti*) therein;

this is a designation for that sacrifice which is to be performed with two *pariyañña* rites, consists of twenty-one sacrificial stakes (*yūpa*), and has all remaining possessions as its fee (*dakṣiṇā*), with the exception of the earth and human beings.
It is called *purisamedha* because men (*purisa*) are sacrificed (*medhanti*) therein; [this is performed] with four *pariyañña* rites...
This is a designation for the sacrifice that is to be performed together with the ground, where the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of the wealth described in the *Aśvamedha*.

"Sammāpāsa" means those who throw correctly (*sammā*) here; having thrown [the stone] correctly day after day, one constructs an altar (*vedi*) at the place where it falls, and then proceeds upstream from the point where the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) and other items, which are to be collected, were submerged in the river Sarassatī.
This is a designation for every sacrifice that is to be offered. "Vājapeyya" means "drinking the strength (vāja)" here;

it is a designation for the sacrifice consisting of a single *pariyāga* with seventeen animals, featuring a sacrificial post made of *beluva* wood and having seventeen-fold sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
"Niraggaḷa" means there is no bolt (*aggaḷa*) here; it refers to that which is to be sacrificed with nine *pariyāgas*.

This is a designation for a variant of the Aśvamedha sacrifice, which—along with the earth and men—is called by the name "All-Sacrifice" (*sabbamedha*) and involves the distribution of wealth as a sacrificial fee as described in the Aśvamedha.

"Great undertakings" (*mahārambhā*) means great tasks or great duties. Furthermore, they are indeed "great undertakings" because of the vastness of the commencement of the taking of life (*pāṇātipāta*).
Regarding the phrase "they do not yield great fruit," the term with a remainder (*sāvasesa-rūpa*) is used here to express the sense of "without remainder" (*niravasesattha*).
It is said. Therefore, the meaning is that they become fruitless indeed because of their desirable result.

And this was stated specifically with reference to the undertaking of the destruction of living beings. As for the gift that is given here and there within that [sacrifice], because it is impaired by this undertaking, it does not have great fruit;
the meaning is that it has meager fruit. "Haññare" means they are killed. "Yajanti" [means they sacrifice].

"Those who always sacrifice in accordance with what is favorable, and others who sacrifice in accordance with what is favorable"—the meaning is that because their ancestors sacrificed, the descendants also sacrifice.
"It becomes better" means there is indeed an improvement. "Not worse" means nothing evil occurs.
10. Udāyisuttavaṇṇanā (Commentary on the Udāyi Sutta)
40. "Prepared" (*abhisaṅkhataṃ*) means made into a heap. "Without exertion" (*nirārambhaṃ*) means free from the harming of living beings.

"Sacrifice" (*yaññaṃ*) refers to the object to be given; for it is called a sacrifice because it is to be offered. "At the proper time" (*kālena*) means at the appropriate and fitting time. "They approach" (*upasaṃyanti*) means they go near.

"Having passed beyond the family and the destination" (*kulaṃ gatiṃ atikkantā*) means having transcended both the cycle of families and the cycle of destinations. "Skilled in sacrifice" (*yaññassa kovidā*) means...
The sacrifices belonging to the four planes are wholesome. "Sacrifice" (*yañña*) refers to an ordinary gift. "With faith" (*saddhā*) refers to a gift given for the deceased.
"Having prepared the offering" (*habyaṃ katvā*) means having made ready the material object to be offered and given. "In a good field, among those living the holy life" (*sukhettaṃ brahmacārisu*):

the meaning is "in a good field known as those who practice the holy life. "Well-bestowed" (*supattaṃ*) means well-received. "Whatever is done toward those worthy of offerings" (*dakkhiṇeyyesu yaṃ kataṃ*) refers to whatever is performed toward those who are suitable recipients of offerings.
"Prepared" means it is well-offered, well-sacrificed, and well-presented. "Faithful" means one who has faith through conviction in the qualities of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha.
"With a liberated mind" means with a mind that is released; by this, his practice of open-handed generosity is illuminated.
This is the fourth chapter, the Chapter on the Wheel.
5. The Chapter on Rohitassa.
1. Explanation of the Discourse on the Development of Concentration. 41.
In the first [discourse] of the fifth [chapter], "for the attainment of knowledge and vision" means for the attainment of the knowledge and vision of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).
"He resolves upon the perception of day" means he resolves upon the perception thus: "It is day.
"As by day, so by night" means that just as the perception of light was attended to during the day, he attends to it in exactly the same way during the night.
The same method applies to the second phrase as well. "Luminous" means accompanied by the radiance of the knowledge of the divine eye. Although it is similar to light...
This has been said; however, the meaning here should not be understood in that way. For what is intended here is the light of the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*).
"Known" means having become manifest. But how are feelings known as they arise, and known as they pass away?
Here, a bhikkhu grasps the physical basis and grasps the object. By virtue of his grasping of the basis and the object, [the feelings are known].
Those feelings arise known as "having arisen thus, having stood thus, they cease thus";
they abide known, and they pass away known. The same method applies to perceptions and thoughts.
"Contemplating rise and fall" means seeing both arising and passing away. "Thus is form" means such is form, this much is form.
"There is no form beyond this. Thus, "the arising of form" refers to the origination of form.
"Cessation," however, is intended to mean its dissolution. This same method applies to feeling and the other aggregates as well.

And when it was said, "Bhikkhus, it was with reference to this that I spoke," this refers to what I spoke in the *Puṇṇaka* discourse, beginning with the words, "Having reckoned in the world... and so forth.
The meaning is that this was said with reference to the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).

Therein, "having reckoned" (*saṅkhāya*) means having known by means of wisdom (*ñāṇa*). "In the world" (*loke*) means in the world of sentient beings (*sattaloka*). "High and low" (*paroparāni*) means superior and inferior, or excellent and base.
"Shaken" (*iñjita*) means moved. "Nowhere in the world" (*natthi kuhiñci loke*) means nowhere at all in the world, not even in a single aggregate (*khandha*) or a single sense-base (*āyatana*).

There is no [distraction] even with respect to a single element or a single object. It is "peaceful" (santo) because of the subsiding of opposing defilements. It is "smokeless" (vidhūmo) because it is free from the smoke of anger.
Thus, although one-pointedness of mind (magge-ekaggatā) is mentioned here in the prose of the sutta, it is the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) alone that is spoken of in the verse.
2. Commentary on the Pañhabyākaraṇa Sutta.
42. In the second verse, "he who knows their respective *anudhamma*" means he who knows the explanation of these questions in each of their respective places.

"Skilled in the four questions, they call such a one a monk"—they speak thus of a monk of such a kind as being skilled in those four questions. "Hard to assail, hard to overcome" means difficult for others to provoke.
It is impossible to overcome it. "Profound" means as profound as the great ocean extending seven hundred yojanas.
"Hard to shake" means difficult to cause to release its hold; the meaning is that one cannot make it relinquish what it has grasped.
"In gain and loss" means in prosperity and adversity. "Through the realization of the goal" means by the attainment of the goal. "The wise one, the learned one."
"He is called thus" means that a person endowed with steadfastness is called "wise.
3–4. Commentary on the Two Suttas on Reverence for Anger (Kodhagaru).

43–44. In the third [sutta], "one who reveres anger, not the true Dhamma": because of his reverence, he holds and grasps anger as something weighty, but not the true Dhamma; rather, out of a lack of reverence, he treats the true Dhamma as something base and grasps it [negatively]. The same principle applies to the remaining phrases as well.

"Virūhanti" means they grow; or, having established roots through faith, they become firmly grounded and immovable. In the fourth [case], "kodhagarutā" means reverence toward anger. This same method applies everywhere. 5. Commentary on the Rohitassa Sutta (45).
In the fifth [verse], "yattha" is the locative case referring to a single location within the world-system of the Cakkavāḷa. "Na cavati na upapajjati" means he does not pass away nor is he reborn.
This has been taken in terms of successive deaths and rebirths (*cuti-patisandhi*). "By going" means by the movement of the feet.

"The end of the world," the Teacher says, refers to the end of the world of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra-loka*). Regarding "to be known" (*ñāteyya*) and so forth, the meaning is that which is to be known, seen, and attained.
Thus, while the son of the gods asked about the end of the world-system of the world-spheres (*cakkavāḷa-loka*), the Teacher [replied] regarding the world of conditioned phenomena.
It was explained. However, perceiving that "the Teacher’s answer accords with his own question," he spoke the words beginning with "How wonderful!
in order to express his joy.
"Daḷhadhamma" means one who possesses a firm bow, a bow endowed with the highest standard of excellence. "Dhanuggaha" means a master archer.
"Trained" means he has practiced the art of archery for twelve years. "Skilled of hand" means he is capable of piercing even a hair-tip the size of a bull.
"One who has performed the practice" means one who has executed the throw and demonstrated his skill. "With an arrow" means with a shaft.
"Should overpass" means should go beyond. In the time it would take him to overpass the shade of a palmyra tree, [the arrow would reach the mark].
"I am traversing one world-system" shows his own perfection of speed.
"From the eastern ocean to the western" means he says: "Just as the western ocean is distant from the eastern ocean, so too was my stride [distant].
It is said that while standing on the eastern rim of the world-system, he placed his foot...
Having extended [his foot], he passes beyond the western rim of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*); then, extending his second foot, he passes beyond the eastern rim of the world-system.
"As desired" means simply according to his wish. "Except elsewhere" indicates the state free from conceptual proliferation (*nippapañca*).
It is said that during the time for alms-round, after chewing a tooth-stick of *nāgalatā* and rinsing his mouth in Lake Anotatta, when the proper time arrived, he went to Uttarakuru.
Having wandered for alms, he sits upon the rim of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa-mukhavaṭṭi*) and performs his meal;

having rested there for a moment, he runs back again. "One with a lifespan of a hundred years" means that at that time it was an era of long life, yet he began his journey when only a hundred years remained of his lifespan.
"Living for a hundred years" means living through those hundred years without any obstacles. [The phrase] "in the midst" (*antarā eva*)...
"Passed away" means he died in the interval before reaching the end of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).
Even though he passed away there, having returned, he was reborn in this very world-system.

"Without reaching" means without reaching the end of the conditioned world (*saṅkhāra-loka*). "Of suffering" refers to the suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa-dukkha*). "The making of an end."
The making of a boundary. "In the body" means in the personal existence (*attabhāva*). "In one possessing perception, in one who is conscious" means in one endowed with perception and mind.

"The world" refers to the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*). "The origin of the world" refers to the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*). "The cessation of the world" refers to the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*).
"The way leading [to its cessation]" refers to the truth of the path (*maggasacca*). Thus: "Friend, I do not [see] these four truths among grass, wood, and so forth..."
"I do prescribe [a destination], but I prescribe it only with reference to this very body composed of the four great elements"—thus he shows.
"Samitāvī" means one who has stilled evil. "Nāsīsati" means he does not long for. The sixth sutta is of plain meaning.
7. Commentary on the Suvidūra Sutta.
47. Regarding the phrase *suvidūravidūrāni*: by whatever method they are not near, they are indeed very far away;
thus they are "very far away. As for the phrase *nabhañca bhikkhave pathavī ca*: this refers to space and the great earth.
Although space is not far from the earth—indeed, it exists even at a distance of two finger-breadths—nevertheless, in the sense of not being attached to one another, they are called "very far away."

It has been said. "Virocana" means the sun. "The Dhamma of the good," monks, refers to the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment, classified as the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth.
"The Dhamma of the bad" refers to the sixty-two types of speculative views, which constitute the false Dhamma.
"Light-maker" means one who produces illumination. "He is imperishable" means his essential nature does not pass away. "The meeting of the good" means...
The meeting of the wise occurs through friendship and intimacy. "As long as he remains" means for however long a duration he might stay.
"He remains just so" means he remains exactly as he was; he does not abandon his natural character. "For he quickly departs" means he swiftly vanishes.
8. Commentary on the Visākha Sutta:
48. In the eighth [sutta], "Pañcālaputta" means the son of a Pañcāla brahmin woman. "With full speech" means with complete speech. "With clear speech" means with unobstructed speech.

"With flawless speech" means speech that is faultless, not faltering, and where the words and phrases do not fall away. "Included in the roundabout" means included in the turning away from saṃsāra (*vivaṭṭa*).
"Independent" means independent of the roundabout (*vaṭṭa*); it is indeed dependent on the turning away from saṃsāra.
The intention here is this: he speaks having made it relevant to the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), but he does not speak having made it irrelevant to the cycle of existence.

"Not failing to manifest" means not failing to speak. "The deathless state" (*amataṃ padaṃ*) refers to the state of *nibbāna*. "He would manifest" (*bhāsaye*) means he would illuminate. "He would illumine" (*jotaye*) is a synonym for that same term.
"He would raise the banner of the seers" (*paggaṇhe isinaṃ dhajaṃ*): the nine supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*) are so called because they have risen up.
"Isi-dhaja" (the sage’s banner) is said to mean that very thing one should grasp, raise up, and speak after having made it high—this is the meaning.
Those for whom well-spoken words are their banner, illuminating the nine supramundane states, are "those whose banner is well-spoken words" (*subhāsitadhajā*).

"Sages" (*isayo*) refers to the Noble Ones, such as the Buddhas and others. For it was stated previously according to the same method: "The Dhamma is indeed the banner of the sages," meaning that the supramundane Dhamma is called the banner of the sages.
9. Commentary on the *Vipallāsa Sutta* 49.
In the ninth [sutta], "perverisions of perception" (*saññā-vipallāsa*) means the state of being perverted by perception; the sense is that there are four types of distorted perception.

The same method applies to the other two pairs of terms as well. Regarding the phrase, "Bhikkhus, the perversion of perception that takes what is impermanent to be permanent": this refers to a basis that is actually impermanent.

The meaning is: perception that arises by grasping [something] as "this is permanent"; it is a perversion of perception (*saññā-vipallāsa*). In this same manner, the meaning should be understood for all the following phrases.
Regarding "in what is not-self, [perceiving] self": the meaning is those who possess such a perception as "self" in regard to what is not-self. "Struck down by wrong view" means not only...
They are "as if possessed of perception," for they are destroyed by wrong view even as it arises, just as they are by perception.

They are "of distracted mind" because they are endowed with a mind that has become distracted, just as those [who possess] perception and view [are]. "Of perverted perception" is merely a designation; the meaning is that they possess perverted perception, mind, and view.
"Yoked to Māra's yoke" means that they are indeed yoked to Māra's yoke. "Not finding security from the yoke" refers to the four...
"Without having attained the secure Nibbāna through the yogas. "Beings" (satta) refers to persons (puggala). "Buddhas" refers to those awakened to the Four Noble Truths.
"This Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. "Having regained their own minds" means having recovered their respective consciousness.
"Seeing it as impermanent" means they saw it by way of its impermanent nature. "They saw it as foul" means they saw the foul precisely as foul. "By undertaking right view" means...
"Having grasped right vision": they have transcended all suffering, meaning they have completely passed beyond the suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*).
10. Commentary on the *Upakkilesa Sutta* 50.
In the tenth [verse], "defilements" (*upakkilesa*) refers to those things which, by causing a state of being defiled, do not allow one to shine forth. "Mist" (*mahikā*)...

“Hima” means frost. “Dhūmo rajo” means smoke and dust. Regarding “Rāhu,” it should be understood that while the previous three are defilements that have not yet arrived, Rāhu is spoken of by way of defilements that have already arrived.

“The recluses and brahmins do not glow, do not shine, and do not radiate” means they do not glow with the heat of their virtues, they do not shine with the luster of their virtues, and they do not radiate with the brilliance of their virtues.

They do not shine. "Not abstaining from the drinking of fermented and distilled liquors" means they have not desisted from drinking the five kinds of fermented liquor (*surā*) and the four kinds of distilled liquor (*meraya*).
"Enveloped by ignorance" means obstructed and covered by ignorance. "Delighting in pleasant forms" means rejoicing in and being satisfied with what is agreeable and pleasurable.
"Accepting" means grasping [them]. "Ignorant" means blind fools. "Together with their kinsmen" means...
"Bound by the very cord of craving. "The heap of straw" refers to the individual existence (*attabhāva*). "Terrible" means harsh.
In this sutta as well as in the verses, only the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is discussed.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the Rohitassa-vagga.
The First Fifty [Discourses] is concluded.
2. The Second Fifty [Discourses] (6) 1.
The Chapter on the Floods of Merit.
1. Commentary on the First Discourse on the Overflow of Merit (Paṭhamapuññābhisandasutta-vaṇṇanā) 51.
In the first [discourse] of the second [chapter], "overflow of merit" (*puññābhisanda*) means the overflowing of merit; the sense is "attainments of merit.
"Overflow of the wholesome" (*kusalābhisanda*) is a synonym for that same term. Furthermore, because these bring about happiness, they are "nutriments of happiness" (*sukhassāhārā*). Well...
They are "leading to heaven" (*sovaggika*) because they give the foremost things, such as robes and so forth. They are "having a pleasant result" (*sukhavipāka*) because their ripening is pleasant.
They are "conducive to heaven" (*saggasaṃvattanika*) because rebirth in heaven is "heaven," and they lead toward that heaven. "While using a robe" means:
having obtained cloth for the purpose of a robe, even when setting it aside, making it, or wearing it due to the absence of needles, thread, and so forth.
Even when making a spread for a bed that is worn out, though it may be impossible to spread it properly;
or even when making a floor-covering, though it may be unsuitable for a floor-covering and thus cut up to make a foot-wiper—even in these cases, one is said to be "using" it.
However, when one thinks, "This is not even fit to be a foot-wiper," and after sweeping it away, it has been discarded, [then one is no longer using it].
At that time, it is said that he is not "consuming" [the gift]. "The immeasurable concentration of mind" refers to the concentration of the fruit of Arhatship.
By the phrase "his outflow of merit is immeasurable," he explains the immeasurability of the donor's volition of merit.
For that [volition] proceeds by way of repeated recollection: "An arahant whose taints are destroyed is consuming my robe."

The volition of merit is immeasurable; it is with reference to this that it was said. However, among those who give alms-food and so forth, one who, having consumed a portion of alms-food, sustains himself on that alone for seven days and consumes nothing else, is indeed said to be consuming that very same alms-food for seven days.
But in the case of a single dwelling place, whether at night or during the day, in the standing or sitting areas, etc., [the situation is different].
Even while walking up and down, as long as one has not abandoned that lodging and taken up another, one is said to be "using" it. Furthermore,
when an illness has been cured by a single medicine, as long as one does not consume another medicine,
for that duration alone one is said to be "using" it.
"Bahubheravanti" means possessed of many terrifying objects. "Ratanavarānaṃ" refers to the seven excellent treasures.
"Ālayaṃ" means a place of dwelling. "Puthū savantīti" means flowing forth in great numbers. The rest here is self-evident. 2.
Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Overflowing of Merit.

52. In the second [verse], "by those dear to the Noble Ones" means by those associated with the paths and fruits (*maggaphala*). For these are indeed dear, beloved, and pleasing to the Noble Ones (*ariya*). As for the rest that might need to be said regarding the sutta, it has already been stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
Regarding the verses, however, "faith" (*saddhā*) is intended as the faith of a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*). "Virtue" (*sīla*) is likewise the virtue of a stream-enterer.
And "upright vision" (*ujubhūta-dassana*) refers to the vision of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), owing to the absence of crookedness of body and so forth.
This is the name. They speak of the *āhuti* (offering). They clarify faith—that is, they clarify confidence in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha.
"Vision of the Dhamma" means the vision of the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. 3. Commentary on the First Discourse on Dwelling Together (*Paṭhamasaṃvāsasutta-vaṇṇanā*).
53. In the third case, many householders and housewives—many men and women of the household—set out upon that very same road while traveling for the purpose of arranging marriages.
"Living together" means dwelling together, residing in one place.
"A corpse with a corpse" refers to one who is a corpse because of the death of their virtues, [approaching] another who is a corpse because of the death of her virtues.
"Together with. "Together with the queen" means together with her who has become like a goddess (*devī*) by virtue of her qualities. "Immoral" means devoid of virtue.
"Of evil nature" means of base character. "Abusive and reviling" means one who abuses by means of the ten grounds for abuse, and one who reviles by means of intimidation and threats.
In this way, the meaning is to be understood in all instances.
"Kadariyā" means those who are stubbornly stingy. "Jānipatayo" means husband and wife. "Vadaññū" means they understand the purpose of the requests of supplicants.
"Saññatā" means endowed with restraint through virtue (*sīla*). "Dhammajīvino" means those who maintain their livelihood by abiding in the Dhamma;
thus they are "dhammajīvino. "Atthāsaṃ pacurā hontī" means that for them, the goals known as prosperity (*vaḍḍhi*) abound.

"They become many" means they increase in number. "A comfortable state arises" means that a state of mutual comfort and well-being arises among them. "Those who desire sensual pleasures" means those who long for sense-objects.
4. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Living Together (Dutiyasaṃvāsasutta):

In the fourth [discourse], the teaching proceeds by way of the courses of kamma. The rest is exactly the same. In these two suttas, however, the practice of the householder is described; it is also suitable for stream-enterers and once-returners.
5–6. Commentary on the Two *Samajīvī* Suttas (55–56).
Regarding the fifth [sutta], as for the phrase "he approached him," for what purpose did he approach? It was for the sake of favoring him.
For when the Tathāgata reached that kingdom, he arrived specifically for the purpose of gathering these two together. [This refers to] Nakulapitā.
It is said that for five hundred births the Tathāgata’s father was his father, for five hundred births his paternal grandfather, and for five hundred births his paternal great-grandfather.
Nakulamātā also was the Tathāgata’s mother for five hundred births, his maternal grandmother for five hundred births, and his maternal great-grandmother for five hundred births.
From the moment they saw the Teacher, they felt the affection of a son toward him.
Having regained consciousness and seeing her calf, she cried out "Alas, my child! Alas, my child! like a cow greedy for her calf.
As she approached, at the very first sight of him, she became a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*).
In her residence, seats for five hundred monks were always prepared; thus, the Blessed One approached in order to favor them.
*Aticaritā* means transgressed. *Abhisamparāyañca* means in the future world (the next life). *Samasaddhā* means equal in faith, identical and alike.
The same method applies to virtue (*sīla*) and the other [perfections]. The sixth [discourse] was taught specifically for the bhikkhus.
The rest here is exactly the same. 7. Commentary on the Suppavāsā Sutta.
57. *Sattame* is the name of that town. *Koliyānaṃ* means of those belonging to the royal clan of Kola.
“Having given life” (*āyuṃ kho pana datvā*) means having given the gift of life. “She becomes a partaker of life” (*āyussa bhāginī hoti*) means she is one who receives a share of life;
or she is one who possesses life; the meaning is that she is a recipient of life. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
"Endowed with flavor" means endowed with taste, possessed of flavor.

"In those who have gone straight" means in those whose taints are exhausted, who have indeed gone straight because they are free from crookedness of body and so forth. "Possessed of conduct" means endowed with the fifteen factors of conduct.
"Of great attainment" means having attained greatness; this is a name specifically for those whose taints are exhausted. "Mingling merit with merit" means by means of merit...
Accumulating merit together. "Highly fruitful and praised by those who know the world":
such an offering, known as giving (*dāna*), is praised by the Buddhas—those who know the world—because they abide having made the threefold world known;
the meaning is that it is extolled by the Buddhas. "Recalling the sacrifice" means recalling the gift of alms. "Born of wisdom" means born of satisfaction.
8. Commentary on the Sudatta Sutta 58.

In the eighth [verse], "of those who are restrained" means of those restrained in body and speech. "Those who eat what is given by others" means those who maintain themselves by eating only what has been given by others.
"At the proper time" means at the appropriate and timely moment. "He gives respectfully" means with his own hands and with honor.
Having performed [these], he gives. "He bestows four grounds" means he introduces and gives four reasons.
"He becomes possessed of fame" means he has a large retinue. The ninth [sutta] is spoken solely for the sake of the bhikkhus; the rest here is exactly the same. 10.
Commentary on the Gihisāmīci Sutta.

60. "The way of practice for a householder's duty" (*gihisāmīcipaṭipadā*) means the conduct appropriate for householders. "He stands ready" (*paccupaṭṭhito hoti*) means he stands near or has approached with the desire to give after having brought [the requisites]; the meaning is that he gives robes to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

"One who stands ready" (*upaṭṭhita*) is an attendant. "Of those, by day and by night" means that for those who thus attend with the four requisites, their merit always increases by way of relinquishment and by way of recollection, both by day and by night.
"And he goes to the heavenly realm": having performed such auspicious karma, he approaches the heavenly state.
In these four suttas, the practice of the householder is explained. This is also appropriate for stream-enterers and once-returners.
The first chapter: The Section on the Overflow of Merit.
(7) 2. The Chapter on Deserving the Act (*Pattakamma-vagga*). 1. Commentary on the Sutta on Deserving the Act (*Pattakamma-sutta-vaṇṇanā*). 61.

In the first [sutta] of the second [chapter], they are "desirable" (*iṭṭhā*) by way of the negation of what is undesirable. They are "attractive" (*kantā*) because they move toward and enter the mind (*mane kamanti pavisanti*).
They are called "agreeable" (*manāpā*) because they nourish and increase the mind. "Hard to obtain" means extremely rare.

"Wealth" (*bhoga*) refers to the objects of the senses, such as forms and so forth, which are to be enjoyed. "In accordance with the Dhamma" (*sahadhammena*) means: may they arise together with the Dhamma alone, and not through unrighteousness (*adhamma*) by causing harm to the Dhamma.
Alternatively, "in accordance with the Dhamma" means "with its cause," that is, by means of various causes such as the positions of general or treasurer.
The meaning is: "May they arise together. *Yaso* refers to the excellence of one's retinue. *Saha ñātīhi* means "together with kinsmen.

*Saha upajjhāyehi* means "together with those known as preceptors (*upajjhāya*), who are those with whom one has seen and associated because they are to be looked upon in times of happiness and suffering."

"He does what should not be done" means he performs that which ought not to be performed. "He offends against what should be done" means that by failing to perform the appropriate duty, he is said to offend against it.
"He falls away" means he descends or declines. "Covetousness and improper greed" refers to improper greed characterized as covetousness.
"He abandons" means he pushes away or expels. "Of great wisdom" means one of vast wisdom. "Of broad wisdom" means...
"Puthulapañño" means one of broad wisdom. "Āpātadassī" means he sees each respective matter as it comes into his range of vision;

the meaning is that even a subtle category of matter comes into his range of vision. "Uṭṭhānavīriyādhigatehi" means acquired through the energy known as exertion. "Bāhābalaparicitehi" means accumulated by the strength of the arms.
“By means of strength acquired through exercise” means by means of strength increased through practice. “Drenched with sweat” means with sweat shed;
the meaning is that they were attained through exertion and effort involving the shedding of sweat. “Righteous” means consistent with the Dhamma.
“Acquired righteously” means acquired without violating the Dhamma of the ten courses of wholesome action. “Appropriate deeds” means suitable deeds, deeds that are fitting.
"Sukheti" means he makes happy. "Pīṇeti" means he makes nourished, that is, endowed with strength. "Ṭhānagataṃ hoti" means it has reached its proper cause. What, then, is that?
Among the four types of meritorious deeds (*pattakamma*), the deed to be performed with wealth is "reached its proper place" (*ṭhānagata*) precisely because it consists of wealth itself.
"Reached its proper attainment" (*pattagata*) means it has reached the appropriate and fitting state. "Enjoyed according to its source" (*āyatanaso paribhutta*)...
The mass of wealth becomes as if enjoyed for a specific purpose.
"It leads to purification" means it functions by being covered over.

Just as when calamities arise from fire and so forth, one closes off the path to those calamities by making a sacrifice of wealth for the sake of extinguishing the burning house and similar emergencies.
He wards off [evil]. "He makes himself safe" means he makes himself free from calamity and secure.

"The offering to kinsmen" (ñātibalim) is the offering for relatives. "The offering to guests" (atithibalim) is the offering for visitors. "The offering to the departed ancestors" (pubbapetabalim) is the offering for relatives who have gone to the other world.
"The offering to the king" (rājabalim) is the offering appropriate to be performed for the king. "The offering to the deities" (devatābalim) is for the deities.
"Offering the sacrifice that ought to be offered": all this is a designation for the giving of gifts appropriate to each respective occasion.
"Established in patience and gentleness" means established in both the patience of endurance and in virtuous conduct.
"Taming themselves alone" means they tame their own single individuality through the restraint of the sense faculties. "Pacifying" means [they pacify] their own minds.

They bring about peace by means of the subsiding of the defilements (*kilesa*). "They cause [beings] to attain final nibbāna" means they cause them to attain final nibbāna precisely through the nibbāna of the defilements.
Regarding the terms beginning with *uddhaggikā*: it is called *uddhaggikā* because its path ascends higher and higher toward the upper planes by way of yielding fruit.
It is called *sovaggikā* because it is beneficial for heaven, as it produces rebirth there. Its result is exclusively happiness in whatever place it is produced.
"Assā" means having a pleasant result. Because it produces the ten distinctions such as divine beauty and so forth, which are most excellent, it leads to heaven (*saggasaṃvattanikā*);
the meaning is that it establishes such a sacrificial gift (*dakkhiṇa*).
"Standing in the noble Dhamma" means established in the Dhamma of the five precepts. "Rejoicing in heaven after passing away" refers to the next world.
Having gone there, one rejoices wherever one takes rebirth in heaven.
Whether they be stream-enterers, once-returners, or non-returners, this path of practice is indeed attainable for all of them.
2. Commentary on the Ānaṇya Sutta (The Debtless Discourse)

62. "In the second [verse], 'to be attained' (*adhigamanīyāni*) means those things to be reached. 'By one enjoying sensual pleasures' (*kāmabhoginā*) means by one who partakes of both objective sensual pleasures (*vatthukāma*) and defilement-sensual pleasures (*kilesakāma*).
Among 'the happiness of having,' etc.: 'having' (*atthi*) refers to the happiness that arises when one has [possessions]; this is called the 'happiness of having.

The happiness that arises for one who is enjoying wealth is called the 'happiness of enjoyment. The happiness that arises from the thought 'I am free from debt' is the 'happiness of freedom from debt.'"
The happiness called "freedom from debt" (*ānaṇyasukha*). The happiness that arises from the thought "I am faultless and blameless" is called the happiness of blamelessness (*anavajjasukha*).
"They eat" means while eating. "Wisdom sees" means one sees with wisdom. "Both parts" refers to two sections:
the preceding three constitute one section, and the happiness of blamelessness constitutes the other section; thus one sees with wisdom.
The meaning is that he knows two portions. Regarding the phrase "of blameless happiness," these three kinds of happiness do not equal even a sixteenth part of blameless happiness.
3. Commentary on the Brahma Sutta.

63. The third [sutta] has already been explained in the *Tikanipāta*. The only distinction here is the single word "with the former deity" (*sapubbadevatā*). In the fourth, everything is of plain meaning.
5. Commentary on the *Rūpasutta* (Sutta 65):

In the fifth, one who has gained confidence by grasping the measure of form is called "one who has confidence in form" (*rūpappamāṇo*). "Confident in form" (*rūpappasanno*) refers to that same person.
This is the explanation of the terms. One who gains confidence by taking the voice as the criterion is called "one whose measure is the voice" (*ghosappamāṇa*).

One who gains confidence by taking the coarseness of robes and bowls as the criterion is called "one whose measure is the coarse" (*lūkhappamāṇa*). One who gains confidence by taking the Dhamma as the criterion is called "one whose measure is the Dhamma" (*dhammappamāṇa*).
The other [terms] are merely synonyms for these. Furthermore, having divided all sentient beings into three groups, two groups...

In terms of the measure of form (*rūpappamāṇa*), one [unit] is not the measure of form. Dividing it into five parts, four parts are the measure of sound (*ghosappamāṇa*), while one is not the measure of sound.
Dividing it into ten parts, nine parts are the measure of the coarse (*lūkhappamāṇa*), while one is not the measure of the coarse.
However, when dividing it into one hundred thousand parts, only one part is the measure of the phenomenon (*dhammappamāṇa*); the rest should be understood as not being the measure of the phenomenon.
"They measured out forms" means that those who, having seen a form, were inspired with confidence, they are said to have "measured out" the form; the meaning is that they became confident.
"They followed after the sound" means they were pursued by the sound; the meaning is that they became confident by taking the sound as their measure.
"Possessed by the power of desire and lust" means fallen under the sway of both desire (*chanda*) and lust (*rāga*). "And does not know within" refers to his own internal self.
He does not know the quality (*guṇa*). "And he does not see externally" means that he does not see his own practice externally either.

"Enveloped on all sides" (*samantāvaraṇo*) means obstructed on all sides; or, it is "enveloped on all sides" because it has an obstruction on all sides. "Carried away by sound" means led by sound, not by quality.
"He does not know internally and sees externally" means [he does not know] the quality within his own self.
He does not know [the truth], yet he perceives the practice of others. "One who sees the fruit externally" means one who perceives the fruit of honor bestowed by others.
"One who sees with unobstructed vision" means one whose vision is open. "He is not carried away by sound" means he is not led astray by mere report.
6. Commentary on the Sarāga Sutta (66). "In the sixth [verse]:
*mohajaṃ cāpaviddasū* means those born of delusion and devoid of knowledge, the unwise. *Savighātaṃ* means accompanied by suffering.
*Dukhudrayaṃ* means that which brings about an increase in suffering in the future. *Acakkhukā* means those lacking the eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*). Just as..."
"Dhammas as they truly are" means that just as the dhammas such as lust and so forth exist, they remain with that very same intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
"They do not conceive 'this is mine'" means that, being thus situated and possessing such an intrinsic nature, they do not conceive of it as "mine"; the meaning is that they do not imagine it.
In this sutta, as well as in the verses, only the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is discussed.
7. Commentary on the *Ahirājasutta* (Discourse on the Snake Kings). 67.
Regarding the seventh [discourse], the phrase "these four families of snake kings" is stated with reference specifically to those whose venom is in their bite.
For whatever beings have venom in their bite, they are all included within these four families of snake kings.

"For one's own protection" means for the sake of guarding oneself. "For one's own defense" means for the sake of protecting oneself. "For one's own preservation" means for the sake of securing oneself. The meaning is: "I authorize this as a protective chant (*paritta*).
Now, showing how that protective chant is to be performed, he said: "From the Virūpakkhas, may I... and so forth. Therein:
"By the Virūpakkhas" means by the clans of the Virūpakkha nāgas. The same method applies to the others as well. "By the footless" means by footless beings;

the same method applies to the others as well. "All beings": having thus far explained directed loving-kindness (*odissaka-metta*) up to this point, this [verse] is now commenced in order to explain undirected loving-kindness (*anodissaka-metta*).
In that context, "beings," "living creatures," and "born beings"—all these [terms refer to the same].
These are merely synonyms for the person (*puggala*). "May they see auspicious things" means may they see auspicious objects (*ārammaṇa*).
"May no evil come to anyone" means may no evil or base thing come to any being. Regarding the phrase "The Buddha is immeasurable," here "Buddha" should be understood as the qualities of a Buddha;
for these are indeed called "immeasurable. The same method applies to the other two phrases as well. "Those possessing measure" refers to the measure of their qualities.
"Yuttāni. "Uṇṇanābhi" refers to a spider with hairy legs. "Sarabū" refers to a house-lizard.
"Protection has been made for me, a safeguard has been made for me": by me, protection and a safeguard have been established for so many people.
"Let the spirits depart": let all beings for whom a safeguard has been made by me go away; the meaning is, "let them not harass me."
8. Commentary on the Devadatta Sutta 68.
In the eighth [verse], "not long after Devadatta had departed" means not long after he had departed having split the Saṅgha.
"For ruin" means for decline or destruction. "A mule" is one born to a mare from a donkey. "For his own destruction."
"She takes conception" means they mate her with a horse;
having conceived, when the time for birth arrives, she is unable to give birth and stands striking the ground with her feet.
Then, having bound her four feet to four stakes and ripped open her belly, they pull out the foal. She dies right there. That is why this was said.
9. Commentary on the *Padhānasutta* (69).
In the ninth [verse], "striving for the purpose of restraint" (*saṃvarappadhāna*) is striving for the sake of restraining the defilements and closing the doors of entry;

"striving for the purpose of abandoning" (*pahānappadhāna*) is striving for the sake of relinquishing them; and [striving] for the purpose of increasing and expanding wholesome states (*kusalā dhammā*).
The striving for development is the striving for cultivation; the striving for their very preservation is the striving for protection.
10. Commentary on the *Adhammika Sutta*:
"They act unrighteously" means they do not observe the one-tenth tax established by former kings, nor do they act in accordance with offenses.
They are unrighteous because they seize both excessive force and an excessive staff without having taken up [the proper] staff themselves.

"Royal officials" (*rājāyutta*) refers to the appointed men who manage affairs in the king’s territories. "Brahmins and householders" (*brāhmaṇagahapatika*) refers to the Brahmins and householders residing within the city.
"Townsmen and countryfolk" (*negamajānapada*) refers to those residing in market towns (*nigama*) as well as those residing in the countryside (*janapada*). They act unjustly...
"Being uneven" means blowing at improper times. "Uneven" means not level; the meaning is that they are either too stiff or too soft.
"Irregular" means having departed from the path; the meaning is that they blow as if following a wrong course.
"The deities become enraged" means that when winds blow unevenly and irregularly, trees are broken and celestial palaces [are destroyed].
They break apart. Therefore, the deities become incensed; those deities do not allow the rain to fall properly for the king.
Hence it is said: "The rain does not pour down its stream properly.
"The crops ripen unevenly" means that in one place they are deep, in another they have produced sap, and in one place they are parched; thus [it is].
Crops ripen out of season.
The constellations and star-forms revolve regularly;

thus, just as the full moon of Kattika coincides with the Kattika constellation alone, and the full moon of Migasira coincides with the Migasira constellation alone, so too does each respective full moon fall within its corresponding month.
They obtain each respective constellation, and thus they revolve correctly. "The winds blow evenly" means that, being without irregularity, they blow only at the proper time;
for six months the winds blow from the north, and for six months from the south—thus they blow at the appropriate time corresponding to the various regions.
"Even" means they proceed in balance, being neither too rigid nor too weak.
"Five hundred [go] set out upon the path": the meaning is that they proceed by way of the path itself, not by a non-path.
"It goes crookedly" means it goes in a curved manner; it takes hold of a place that is not a proper ford (*atittha*).

"When the leader has gone crookedly": one leads, thus he is a "leader" (*nettā*). When that leader has gone crookedly—having gone in a curved manner and taken hold of a place that is not a proper ford—the others likewise take hold of a place that is not a proper ford.
The meaning is "they seize. There is also a reading "they lead. "He lies in suffering" means he lies in pain; the meaning is that he becomes afflicted.
The second chapter, on Appropriate Karma, is concluded.
(8) 3. The Chapter on the Inevitable (Apaṇṇaka-vagga).
1. Commentary on the *Padhānasutta* (71).

In the first sutta of the third chapter, "the way that is unfailing" (*apaṇṇakappaṭipadā*) means the way that is not deviant. "The basis for it has been undertaken" means the cause for it is complete. "For the destruction of the taints" means for the sake of Arahantship.
The second [sutta] is self-evident. 3. Commentary on the *Sappurisasutta*.
73. In the third [verse], "dispraise" (*avaṇṇa*) means lack of virtue (*aguṇa*). "Makes manifest" (*pātu karoti*) means he speaks; he makes it evident.
"Led by a question" (*pañhābhinīta*) means led for the sake of a question. "Without letting go, without clinging" (*ahāpetvā alambitvā*) means having made it clung to without being abandoned.

And here, the person of bad character (*asappurisa*) conceals his own dispraise due to evil desire (*pāpicchatā*), while the person of good character (*sappurisa*) conceals his own praise due to modesty (*lajjitā*). Now, since—

For an untrue person, lacking a sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing, despises others through living together; but a true person, endowed with a sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing, does not despise others even through living together.
Therefore, in order to show the simile of the newly arrived bride which illustrates the nature of an untrue person, the Blessed One said:
"Just as if, monks, a bride... and so forth. In that context, "bride" (*vadhukā*) means a daughter-in-law. "Thick" (*tibba*) means dense.
The meaning here is entirely obvious. 4–5.
Commentary on the Two Suttas on the Foremost. 74–75.
In the fourth [sutta], "the foremost virtue" (*aggappattaṃ uttamasīlaṃ*) means the highest, most excellent virtue. This same method applies everywhere. In the fifth...
"The peak of form" (*rūpagga*) refers to that form by means of which, having comprehended it, one attains *arahantship*; this is called the "peak of form.

The same principle applies to the remaining [aggregates] as well. Regarding the "peak of existence" (*bhavagga*): here, the particular personal existence (*attabhāva*) in which one remains while attaining *arahantship* is called the "peak of existence.
6. Commentary on the Kusināra Sutta.
76. In the sixth [case], "in the vicinity" (*upavattanā*) means in the middle of the row of *sāla* trees situated to the north of the eastern row of *sāla* trees which turns back.
"Between the twin *sāla* trees" (*antarena yamakasālānaṃ*) means between two *sāla* trees. "Doubt" (*kaṅkhā*) is perplexity (*dveḷhaka*).
"Uncertainty" (*vimati*) is the inability to reach a definitive decision. "Is he a Buddha or not a Buddha? Is it the Dhamma or not the Dhamma? [and so forth].

“Monks, if doubt should arise in you as to whether it is indeed the Saṅgha or not the Saṅgha, whether it is indeed the Path or not the Path, or whether it is indeed the Practice or not the Practice—I tell you: ask about that.
This is the summary of the meaning here. [The phrase] “you might not ask out of reverence for the Teacher” means: “In the presence of the Teacher, we...”
"We have gone forth; even the four requisites belong to our Teacher alone.

Having spent all this time without raising doubts, we ought not today, at this final hour, to harbor doubt"—if you do not ask thus out of reverence for the Teacher, then let each friend, monks, inform his friend: "Whichever monk among you..."
"Seen and trusted"—this shows that he should inform him: "I shall speak to one bhikkhu;
having heard his account, may you all become free from doubt. "Thus confident" means "thus do I have faith, saying 'I am [so-and-so]'";
"knowledge itself" means that here it is the knowledge that makes the state of being free from doubt manifest for the Tathāgata, not mere faith.
The meaning is as follows: "Of these, Ānanda," refers to these five hundred bhikkhus sitting within the enclosure.
"Whoever is the last" refers to one who is last by way of spiritual qualities; this is said with reference specifically to the Elder Ānanda.
7. Commentary on the Acinteyya Sutta (The Discourse on the Inconceivable)
77. "Inconceivable" (*acinteyya*) means those things which are unfit to be thought about.
"They should not be thought about" means that precisely because they are inconceivable, they are not to be reflected upon. "While thinking about them" means while reflecting on those causes.

"Of madness" means of the state of insanity. "Of distress" means of suffering. "The domain of the Buddhas" means the sphere of the Buddhas, consisting of the Buddha-qualities such as omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).

"Occurrence and power": "The object of jhāna" means the object of the jhānas of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*). "Kamma-result" means the result of kamma such as that to be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*), etc.
"Worldly speculation" refers to such worldly speculation as: "By whom were the moon and sun made? By whom was the great earth made?
By whom was the great ocean made? By whom were beings produced? By whom were the mountains, mangoes, palm trees, coconut trees, and so forth, created?"
8. Commentary on the Dakkhiṇa Sutta 78.
In the eighth [sutta], "purification of the offering" (*dakkhiṇāvisuddhi*) refers to the causes for the purification of the offering (*dakkhiṇā*), which is to say, the act of giving.
"It is purified by way of the donor" means it is purified by way of its great fruitfulness; the meaning is that it becomes of great fruit. "One of beautiful qualities" (*kalyāṇadhamma*)...
"Of pure nature. "Of evil nature" means of base nature. Regarding "one is purified by the giver," the story of the Great King Vessantara should be told here;
for it was he who, having given his children to the Brahmin Jūjaka, caused the great earth to tremble.
Regarding "one is purified by the recipient," the story of the fisherman living at the mouth of the Kalyāṇī River should be told here; it is said that he [gave] to the Elder Dīghasumana...
Having given alms-food three times, while lying on his deathbed, he said, "May the alms-food I have given to the venerable Elder Dīghasumana rescue me.
Regarding the phrase "not even by the giver," the hunter who lived in Vaḍḍhamāna should be told here.

It is said that when he was giving an offering to a departed spirit (peta), he gave it three times to one who was immoral. On the third occasion, [he thought], "It is a non-human being who is immoral..."
“...she is plundering me! he cried out. When it was given to a single virtuous bhikkhu and brought back, it reached him at that very moment.
Here, the gift of the peerless one (*asaddhadāna*) should be discussed, for it is purified both from the giver and from the recipient.
9. Commentary on the Sutta on Trade (*Vaṇijjasutta*).
79. "In the ninth [case], it blows 'of that kind' means exactly like that, similar to that. 'It goes to destruction' means it undergoes cutting off;
the meaning is that everything which was desired perishes. 'It does not accord with one's intention' means it does not accord with one's aspiration (*ajjhāsaya*).
'It exceeds the intention of another' means that, compared to the aspiration of another, it yields a fruit greater than the aspiration itself. [Regarding] the ascetic...
Or a brahmin—here, the state of being a *samaṇa* and a *brāhmaṇa* should be understood through the qualities of having stilled evil and having cast out evil.
"Let him speak, venerable sir, regarding the requisite": "Venerable sir, you may speak regarding the fourfold requisite consisting of robes and so forth"—thus one invites or entreats.
"Regarding which he invites": having delimited it, by whatever amount he invites. "He does not give that": he does not give that at all.
"He does not give" means he does not give according to his intention; that is, he is unable to give in accordance with his own desire, and having diminished it, he gives only a little.
"He gives according to his intention" means he gives exactly as much as he wishes.
"He gives according to another's intention" means that after inviting [the recipient] to accept a small amount, he gives a large amount by overstepping that limit.
10. Commentary on the Kambhojasutta 80.
Regarding the tenth [verse]: "He does not sit in the assembly" means he does not sit in the judicial assembly for the purpose of making legal determinations.
"He does not engage in business" means he does not engage in great enterprises such as agriculture, trade, and so forth. "He does not [go to] Kambhoja... [The text continues: ...Kambhoja.
"He goes" means he does not go to the kingdom of Kamboja for the sake of amassing wealth.

This is merely a figurative expression; the meaning is that he does not go to any foreign land whatsoever. Regarding the terms "angry" and so forth: through anger, being overwhelmed by wrath, one does not discern what is beneficial and what is harmful;
through envy, one cannot endure the prosperity of others; and through stinginess, even after giving wealth...
He is unable to perform his duties; due to a lack of wisdom, he is unable to arrange what needs to be done.
Therefore, he does not perform these tasks, such as sitting in the assembly hall and so forth.
The third chapter, the *Apaṇṇaka-vagga*.
(9) 4. The Chapter on the Fickle (Macalavagga). 1–5. Commentary on the Five Discourses on Killing Living Beings, etc. (81–85).
The first [discourse] of the fourth [chapter] and those following have their meanings already explained. In the fifth, by means of the passage beginning with “reborn in a low family,” etc.,...
It is "darkness" (*tama*) because it is joined with darkness. Furthermore, because one goes from bodily misconduct and so forth to the darkness of hell, it is "destined for darkness.
Thus, by both [terms], the darkness of the aggregates (*khandha-tama*) alone is described. Because he is joined with light—by such phrases as "born into a wealthy family"—he is "light";

what is meant is that he has become like illumination. Furthermore, because one attains the state of light through rebirth in heaven by means of bodily good conduct and so forth, [he is called "light"].
Jotiparāyaṇa. By this same method, the other two [stories] are also to be understood.

"In a family of bamboo-workers" means in a family of reed-weavers. "In a family of hunters" means in a family of deer-trappers and the like. "In a family of cartwrights" means in a family of leather-workers.
"In a family of scavengers" means in a family of flower-throwers. "With a difficult livelihood" means with a painful livelihood. "Ugly" means like a dust-demon.
"Like a charred stump" means having the color of a burnt log. "Hard to look upon" means unpleasant to behold even for one's own mother who has given birth to him.
"A cripple" (*okoṭimaka*) means a hunchback. "One-eyed" (*kāṇa*) means blind in one eye or blind in both eyes. "Lame" (*kuṇī*) means lame in one hand or lame in both hands.
"Lame" (*khañja*) means lame in one leg or lame in both legs. "Palsy-stricken" (*pakkhahata*) means one whose limbs are paralyzed, such as a person who crawls on a wooden board (*pīṭhasappī*).
"Of lighting materials" means of lamp equipment such as oil-lamps and bowls.
"In this way, monks," here refers to a certain person who, not seeing light outside, passes away right within his mother’s womb and, being reborn in the states of misery, wanders for an entire aeon.
He too is one whose destination is from darkness to darkness; he would be a person who is a hypocrite.
For it is said that such is the accomplishment of a charlatan.
Herein, by the phrases "in a low family" and so forth, both the failure of lineage and the failure of present conditions are shown;
by "poor" and so forth, the failure of existing conditions is shown; and by "a life of hardship" and so forth, the failure of the means of livelihood is shown.

By the terms "ugly" and so forth, there is the failure of one's personal existence (*attabhāva-vipatti*); by "afflicted with many diseases" and so forth, there is the conjunction with causes of suffering;

by "not obtaining" and so forth, there is both the failure of the causes of happiness and the failure of enjoyment; by "bodily misconduct" and so forth, there is the conjunction with the causes for having the dark realm as one's destination;
and by "with the breakup of the body" and so forth, there is the arrival at the dark realm in the future life (*samparāyika-tamūpagama*).
The bright fortnight (sukkapakkha) is to be understood by way of the method opposite to what has been stated.
6. Commentary on the Oṇatoṇata Sutta: 86.
In the sixth [verse], "Oṇatoṇato" means that one who is low now will also be low in the future. "Oṇatuṇṇato" means that now...
"One who is low will become high in the future. "One who is high will become low" means that one who is currently high will become low in the future.

"One who is high will become high" means that one who is currently high will also be high in the future. The detailed explanation for these, however, should be understood according to the method of the preceding sutta.
7. Commentary on the Sutta of Sons.
87. In the seventh [verse], *samaṇamacalo* means "the ascetic who is immovable"; the letter *m* is used for euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*).
The meaning is "an immovable ascetic. By this, he shows the sevenfold trainee (*sekha*). For he is called "immovable" because he is established in faith that has taken root in the Teaching.
*Samaṇapuṇḍarīko* means an ascetic who resembles a white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*). A "white lotus" is one that has fewer than a hundred petals.
“*Saroruhaṃ*. By this, he shows the one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) through dry insight (*sukkha-vipassaka*).

For, because his qualities are incomplete due to the absence of meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), he is called a “white-lotus ascetic” (*samaṇa-puṇḍarīka*). A “lotus-like ascetic” (*samaṇa-paduma*) is an ascetic who resembles a lotus.
A “lotus” (*paduma*) is a water-born flower with a full hundred petals. By this, [he shows] the one whose taints are destroyed who is liberated in both ways (*ubhatobhāga-vimutta*).

He shows this. For, because his qualities are perfected through the cultivation of the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), he is called a "lotus among recluses" (*samaṇapaduma*).

Regarding the phrase "the most delicate of recluses among recluses": among all these recluses, he is the most delicate recluse, possessing a supple mind and body, free from physical and mental suffering, and exclusively happy.
By this, he shows himself as well as those similar to himself.
Having thus laid down the matrix (mātikā), he now speaks the passage beginning with "And how, bhikkhus," while analyzing it in sequential order.
Therein, "one in training" (sekha) refers to all seven types of trainees. "One who has entered upon the way" (paṭipada) means one who is practicing.
"He dwells aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage" means he dwells aspiring for arahantship. "Of one anointed on the head" (muddhāvasitta) means on the head...
"Of one who has sat down," means "of one for whom the consecration has been performed. "One fit for consecration" (*ābhiseko*) means one who is suitable to undergo the consecration.

"Not yet consecrated" (*anabhisitto*) means not yet having received the consecration. "Having reached the state of *macala*" means that, by virtue of being the son of a consecrated Kṣatriya king and by virtue of being the eldest among the sons, he has reached the stage for the purpose of attaining the consecration, even though he has not yet been consecrated.

He has attained immovability; he has attained the state of being unshakable. The letter *m* is merely a grammatical particle (*nipātamatta*). "Having touched with the body" means having touched with the mental body (*nāmakāya*).

"He mostly uses robes only when asked" means that he uses much of the robe-cloth brought forward by donors who have themselves requested, saying, "Venerable sir, please use this," while only a very little is used without being asked—such as the Elder Bākula.
...as if. Regarding almsfood: like the Elder Sīvali on the path through the Khadiravana forest.
Regarding lodgings: like the Elder Ānanda in the Aṭṭhakanāgara Sutta. Regarding medicinal requisites: like the Elder Pilindavaccha. *Tyassa* means "for him.
*Manāpen' eva* means "with that which is pleasing to the mind. *Samudācaranti* means they perform the duties to be done, or they proceed [in service]. *Upahāraṃ*.
"Bringing forth" means they bring forth or present bodily and mental offerings. "Congenital" means produced by the combination of all three [humors].
"Produced by change of season" means born from seasonal changes such as excessive cold or excessive heat.
"Produced by irregular conduct" means born from irregular habits such as sitting or standing for too long. "Produced by external injury" means...

These are produced through such means as killing, binding, and so forth. "Born of the ripening of kamma" means they are born solely by the power of the ripening of kamma performed in the past, even without these aforementioned causes.

Regarding the phrase "of the four jhānas," here it is intended that for both those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) and for Buddhas, only functional jhānas (kiriyajjhāna) are meant. The rest is of plain meaning.
8. Commentary on the Saṃyojana Sutta (88).
In the eighth [sutta], one who has attained a firm footing in the Dispensation is called a "Samaṇa-macala" (the immovable ascetic) because he is a stream-enterer;

a Sakadāgāmī is called a "Samaṇapuṇḍarīka" (the white-lotus ascetic) because his virtues are not yet very numerous, like a lotus with few petals; and one with even more abundant virtues is called a "Samaṇasatapaṭṭa" (the hundred-petaled ascetic).

The non-returner is called a "lotus-like ascetic" because he resembles a lotus; and the one whose taints are destroyed is called a "delicate ascetic" because he has attained a state of extreme softness through the total eradication of those defilements that cause rigidity.
9. Commentary on the Discourse on Right View.
89. In the ninth [section], by means of the eightfold path beginning with "right view" and so forth, the seven trainees (*sekha*) are included as in the first sutta.

In the second turn, either by means of the tenfold path together with the knowledge of the fruit of arahantship and the liberation of the fruit of arahantship, or by means of the eightfold path, the dry-insight practitioner (*sukkha-vipassaka*) whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) is described; in the third turn, the one liberated in both ways (*ubhatobhāga-vimutta*).

In the fourth section, it says: "the Tathāgata and one who is like a Tathāgata, having exhausted the outflows. Thus, this sutta is spoken solely by way of the individuals mentioned in the first sutta;
however, the difference here is merely in the teaching itself.
10. Commentary on the Khandha Sutta.
90. In the first instance of the tenth [section], the person in training (sekha-puggala) who dwells in negligence, having not yet applied himself toward the attainment of Arahatship, is described.
In the second instance, the person in training who dwells in diligence, having not yet produced jhāna but having commenced insight (vipassanā), is described.
In the third instance, the person in training who dwells in diligence, has commenced insight, and has attained the eight liberations (aṭṭha-vimokkha), is described.
Thus it was spoken; on the fourth occasion, "one who has utterly exhausted the taints and is most delicate.
The Fourth Chapter on the Unsteady is concluded.
(10) 5. The Chapter on Asuras.
1. Commentary on the *Asurasutta* (91).
In the first [sutta] of the fifth [chapter], "asura" means one who is like an asura, hideous; "deva" means one who is like a deva, beautiful and pleasing by virtue of his qualities.
2. Commentary on the *Paṭhamasamādhisutta* (First Discourse on Concentration)
92. In the second [case], "internal mental serenity" (*ajjhattaṃ cetosamatha*) refers to the concentration of the mind in absorption (*appanācittasamādhi*) within one's own internal domain.
"Higher wisdom and insight into phenomena" (*adhipaññādhammavipassanā*) refers to the knowledge of insight (*vipassanāñāṇa*) that discerns formations (*saṅkhāra*).

For that [knowledge] is both designated as "higher wisdom" (*adhipaññā*) and constitutes insight into phenomena (*dhamma*) consisting of the five aggregates; therefore, it is called "higher wisdom and insight into phenomena."
3. Commentary on the Second Samādhi Sutta 93.
In the third [sutta], "exertion (*yoga*) is to be practiced" means that being properly engaged and applied must be performed. "Zeal" (*chanda*) is the desire to act.
"Effort" (*vāyāma*) is the application. "Arousal" (*ussāha*) is energy (*vīriya*) even more intense than that. "Exertion" (*ussoḷhi*) is like pulling a cart stuck in the mud.
Great energy. "Irreversible" means the state of not turning back.
4. Commentary on the Third Samādhi Sutta: 94.
Regarding the passage in the fourth [sutta], "In this way, friends, formations are to be seen," and so forth—"friends, formations" refers to [those things] from the perspective of impermanence...
It should be seen, comprehended as impermanent, and viewed as impermanent. Likewise, it should be seen as suffering and as non-self;

such is the meaning to be understood. Thus, in the passages beginning with "In this way, friend, the mind should be steadied," [it means] that by means of the first jhāna, friend, the mind should be steadied, by means of the first jhāna it should be composed, by means of the first jhāna...
It should be made one-pointed; it should be concentrated by means of the first jhāna.
Likewise by means of the second jhāna and so forth—thus the meaning should be understood. In these three suttas, both mundane and supramundane serenity and insight are discussed.
5. Commentary on the Charcoal-Ember Sutta.
95. "In the fifth [case], 'a charcoal from a charnel ground' means a charcoal found in a cemetery. 'Smeared with dung in the middle' means smeared with dung in its central portion.

'It does not serve the purpose of wood in the village' means that it is not suitable for use as wood in the village because it cannot be brought in for purposes such as rafters, roof-ribs, pillars, or steps;
nor can it be brought in to make a leg for a field-hut or a bed-leg."
One does not obtain firewood from the forest. If one grasps it at either of the two ends, the hand is burned;
if one grasps it in the middle, it is smeared with dung. "Like that" means similar to that. "More excellent" means more beautiful.
"More refined" means more supreme. "Milk from a cow" means milk from a cow. In the sequence beginning with "from milk, curd," each subsequent item is superior to the preceding one.
Among these, the cream of ghee is the very pinnacle; indeed, it is the foremost among them all.
Regarding terms such as "foremost" (*agga*), one should understand that it is preeminent, best, chief, supreme, and excellent by virtue of its qualities.

By the simile of the cow-hair torch, it should be understood that the person of immoral conduct is not what is being described here; rather, the person who is of little learning and neglects his duties is described as being like an ox.
In the sixth [sutta], everything is already clear in meaning.
7. Commentary on the Khippanisanti-sutta (Sutta 97):
"Quickly understanding" (*khippanisanti*) means one who understands quickly, capable of knowing swiftly. And of the teachings heard...
Of the qualities of the Sutta and the principles of the Thread (*tantidhamma*). "One who examines the meaning" (*atthūpaparikkhī*) means one who investigates the meaning.
"Having understood the meaning and understood the teaching" (*atthamaññāya dhammamaññāya*) means having known both the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) and the canonical text (*pāḷi*).

"One who practices in accordance with the Dhamma" (*dhammānudhammappaṭipanno*) means one who practices the preliminary path together with its moral discipline, which is the teaching corresponding to the nine supramundane states (*navalokuttaradhamma*). "But not one of beautiful speech" (*no ca kalyāṇavāco*)...
"Not of beautiful speech" means he does not have a beautiful sound of voice.
The negative particle (*no*) should be construed with "poriya" and the following terms.

The meaning is that he is not endowed with speech that is complete in its qualities, unobstructed, faultless, with well-articulated words and phonemes, and capable of making the meaning understood. The meaning is to be understood in this same manner for all [the subsequent terms].
8. Commentary on the Attahita Sutta (98–99):
The eighth discourse was spoken both in accordance with the inclinations of individuals and as a display of the Buddha’s knowledge of teaching; the ninth was spoken by way of the five offenses.
10. Commentary on the Potaliya Sutta.
100. "At the proper time" means at the appropriate and opportune time. "Is agreeable" means it is pleasing.
Regarding the phrase "that which is the knowledge of the proper time in each respective instance": this refers to the understanding of the proper time in each particular case.
For it shows that speaking dispraise of one who deserves dispraise, and speaking praise of one who deserves praise, once that respective time has been known, is the natural disposition of the wise.
The fifth chapter, the Asura Chapter, is finished.
The second fiftieth section is completed.

(11) 1. The Chapter on Clouds (Valāhakavagga) 1–2.

“I shall do it”—thus one speaks only but does not act. “One who acts but does not speak”: without having spoken, one acts with the thought, “This and that ought to be done by me.
In this way, the meaning is to be understood in all instances. The second [verse] has a plain meaning. 3.
Commentary on the Kumbha Sutta (The Pot Sutta)

103. In the third [simile], "jars" (*kumbha*) means pots. "Empty and covered" means void and with its mouth closed. "Full and uncovered" means filled with water and with its mouth open. The same method applies to the other two as well. 104.

5–6. Commentary on the Amba Sutta (The Mango Sutta) 105–6.

Regarding the fifth [verse]: "Raw, yet appearing ripe" means that to those looking at it while it is still raw, it appears as if it were ripe. All the other phrases should be understood in this same way. The sixth is of plain meaning. 7.
Commentary on the Mūsika Sutta (The Mouse Sutta)

107. Regarding the seventh [simile]: he who digs a pit but does not dwell therein is called "one who makes a footing, but not one who dwells. *Khantā* is also a reading. All the following phrases should be understood according to this method.
8. Commentary on the Discourse on the Bull (Balībaddasutta) 108. Regarding the eighth:

he who tramples his own herd of cattle, but not another's herd of cattle, is "fierce toward his own cattle, but not fierce toward another's cattle. All the phrases should be understood in this way. "He causes agitation" means that by striking and piercing, he brings about a state of agitation.

Regarding the ninth [simile]: "Pithless, surrounded by pithless trees" means a tree without core (nissāra), a pithless tree, surrounded by pithless trees. "Surrounded by heartwood" means surrounded by heartwood trees such as the *khadira* and others. This same method applies everywhere. 10.
Commentary on the Venomous Snake Discourse (Āsīvisasutta)

110. In the tenth [verse], "one whose poison has arrived is not one of terrible poison" means that although his poison arrives, it is not terrible; it does not afflict for a long time. This same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.
The first chapter, the *Valāhaka-vagga*, is concluded.
