(12) 2. The *Kesiva-vagga*.
1. Commentary on the Kesī Sutta 111.
Regarding the first [verse] of the second [sutta]: "Kesī" is his name. "One who trains horses" (*assadammasārathi*) means one who disciplines horse-animals.
In the phrases "he guides even with gentleness," etc., it refers to providing him with appropriate honor, feeding him excellent food, and giving him sweet drink.
Having given drink and treated [the animal] with gentle speech, one who tames it by means of mildness is said to tame it "gently.
One who tames it by means of knee-straps, nose-rods, and so forth, as well as by prodding with goads, striking with whips, and harsh words, is said to tame it "harshly.
One who performs both of these from time to time is said to tame it "both gently and harshly."

2. Explanation of the *Javasutta* 112. In the second [verse], "by straightforwardness" (*ajjava*) means by way of uprightness. "By speed" (*java*) means by the momentum of the footstep. "By patience" (*khanti*) means by the patience of endurance (*adhivāsanakkhanti*).

"By gentleness" (*soracca*) means by a virtuous nature that is pure. Among the qualities and factors of a person, "by speed" means by the speed of knowledge (*ñāṇajava*). The rest here is of obvious meaning.
3. Commentary on the *Patodasutta* 113.
In the third [verse], "the shadow of the goad" (*patodacchāya*) refers to the shadow of the goad raised for the purpose of piercing.
"He is stirred" (*saṃvijjati*) means he is stirred by way of reflecting, "I must acquire speed. "He attains a sense of urgency" (*saṃvegaṃ āpajjati*) means he attains a sense of spiritual urgency.
"Practicing as one pierced by the piercing of the hair" means merely pierced by the piercing of a goad into the pores of the skin.

"Pierced by the piercing of the skin" means pierced by the piercing of a goad that cuts through the outer skin. "Pierced by the piercing of the bone" means pierced by a piercing that breaks through the bone.
"With the body" means with the mental body (*nāmakāya*). "The supreme truth" refers to *nibbāna*. "Realizes" means sees.
"By wisdom" means by the path-wisdom accompanied by insight (*vipassanā*).
4. Commentary on the *Nāga-sutta* 114.
"Making it a bone" means becoming a skeleton. Regarding the phrase "the sounds of grass, forests, and reeds," here "grass" (*tiṇa*) refers to—

*Ḍiṇḍima*: a great sound produced by all [instruments] mixed together, a resounding noise. Regarding *ḍaṃsa* and the others: *ḍaṃsa* refers to the brown fly (*piṅgalamakkhikā*), and *makasa* refers simply to mosquitoes.
"One who goes quickly" means that having fulfilled virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, one becomes a swift goer.
5. Commentary on the *Ṭhānasutta* 115.
In the fifth [sutta], "grounds" (*ṭhānāni*) means causes. "Leads to harm" (*anatthāya saṃvattati*) means it leads to disadvantage and to lack of growth.
And here, the first [ground] consists of various types such as digging pits, fishing, and housebreaking; it is accompanied by suffering and accompanied by affliction.

The first type of evil deed is to be understood [as such]; the second is to be understood as the work of householders living in common, such as throwing away flowers and so forth, as well as plastering with lime, roofing houses, sweeping places of filth, and so forth;

the third is to be understood as the drinking of liquor, the use of perfumes, ointments, garlands, and ornaments, as well as deeds such as the taking of life that proceed from a sense of gratification;
and the fourth is at the time of going for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma.

Taking clean garments, garlands, perfumes, and so forth, going [to a shrine], worshipping the *cetiya*, worshipping the Bodhi tree, listening to sweet Dhamma discourses, and undertaking the five precepts—in such cases as these, wholesome karma associated with joy (*somanassa*) is to be understood.
"In the strength of a man" (*purisathāme*) means in the strength of a man’s knowledge (*ñāṇa*); the same method applies to the other two as well.
6. Commentary on the *Appamāda-sutta* 116.
In the sixth [verse], "yato kho" means "when indeed. "Of the future life" (*samparāyikassa*) is merely a way of teaching;

however, one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*) fears neither death pertaining to the future life nor that pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*). It is precisely such a person who is intended here.
However, some say: "Because of the statement 'right view is developed,' all noble ones (ariya) are intended here, beginning with the stream-enterer (sotāpanna).
7. Commentary on the Ārakkha Sutta 117.
In the seventh [verse], *attarūpena* means "in accordance with oneself," that is, suitable or fitting for oneself; the meaning is "one who desires one's own welfare. *Rajanīyesu* means...
"In phenomena that have become conditions for lust" means in intrinsic natures; the meaning is "in desirable objects.
This method should be understood in all instances. "He does not lust" means he does not lust by way of views. The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.
"Nor does he go even because of the words of ascetics" means that even because of the words of other teachers who are ascetics, he does not [abandon] his own view.
The meaning is that, having abandoned them, one does not proceed by way of those views. Here too, only one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) is intended.
8–10. Commentary on the Triad of Suttas beginning with "Arousing Dread" (Saṃvejanīya), §§118–120.
In the eighth [sutta], "worth seeing" (dassanīya) means fit to be seen; "arousing dread" (saṃvejanīya) means producing a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega).
In the ninth [verse], "fear of birth" (*jātibhaya*) means the fear that arises with reference to birth. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
In the tenth, "fear of fire" (*aggibhaya*) means the fear that arises in dependence upon fire. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
This is the second chapter, the Chapter on Hair (*Kesivagga*).
(13) 3. The Chapter on Fear (Bhayavagga). 1. Commentary on the Discourse on Self-Repentance (Attānuvādasutta). 121.
Regarding the first [sutta] of the third [chapter], "fear of self-reproach" (*attānuvādabhaya*) refers to the fear that arises in one who reproaches oneself.
"Fear of reproach by others" is the fear arising from being reproached by another. "Fear of punishment" is the fear arising in dependence upon the thirty-two types of penal servitude.
"Fear of an unhappy destination" is the fear arising in dependence upon the four states of deprivation.
Regarding the passage beginning with, "This, monks, is called the fear of self-reproach," and so forth: first, for one who reflects upon the fear of self-reproach—
Internally, a sense of shame (*hirī*) arises; it produces restraint at the three doors, and restraint at the three doors constitutes the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*).
Established in that virtue and having developed insight (*vipassanā*), he becomes established in the supreme fruit.
Furthermore, for one who reflects upon the fear of being censured by others, a sense of dread (*ottappa*) arises externally.
Thus he generates restraint at the three doors; restraint at the three doors is the virtue of the fourfold purification.
Established in that virtue, he develops insight and becomes established in the supreme fruit.
When one reflects upon the fear of the miserable destinies, internal moral shame (*hirī*) arises within him; it generates restraint at the three doors for him.
Restraint at the three doors constitutes the virtue of the fourfold purification. Established in that virtue, one develops insight and becomes established in the supreme fruit.
2. Commentary on the Sutta on the Fear of Waves.
122. “In the second [case], for one descending into water” means for one entering the water.
“To be expected” means to be desired. “Fear of sharks” means fear of fierce fish. “They seem to make a covering for the mouth” means they act as if closing the mouth.
“Of gluttony” means of having a large belly, of a nature that eats excessively. Regarding the phrases beginning with “with an unguarded body,” etc.:
Because of the absence of the threefold restraint regarding the door of the body, it is by means of an unguarded body;
because of the absence of the fourfold restraint regarding the door of speech, it is by means of unguarded speech.
3. Commentary on the First Discourse on Diversity.
123. In the third [case], "he relishes that" means he relishes that jhāna by way of the relishing of pleasure (*sukha-assāda*).
"He desires it" means he yearns for it. "He attains zest" means he attains satisfaction (*tuṭṭhi*). "Intent upon that" means intent on that, or devoted to that.
"Dwelling frequently therein" means dwelling extensively by means of that jhāna. "He is reborn into companionship" means into a state of coexistence (*sahabhāva*).
"He goes" means that he is reborn there. Regarding the phrase "an aeon is the measure of his lifespan":
here, the first jhāna is of three kinds—inferior, middling, and superior. Among these, for those born with the inferior [jhāna], the measure of their lifespan is one-third of an aeon;
for those with the middling, it is half an aeon; and for those with the superior, it is a full aeon. It is with reference to this that this was said. [And] even hell...
"He goes" means that because the karma leading to rebirth in hell has not been abandoned, he goes from one state to another, and not immediately.

"He attains final nibbāna in that very same existence" means that he attains final nibbāna while remaining in that very same fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*), and does not descend to a lower realm.
"This being so, with respect to destination and rebirth" refers to this situation where, for a trainee (*sekha*), there exists both a destination (*gati*) and a rebirth (*upapatti*).

The distinction is this: for the noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*), without descending further by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), there is final Nibbāna (*parinibbāna*) right there in that same fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*) in one of the higher Brahma-worlds, such as the second or third; whereas for the worldling (*puthujjana*), there is a descent into the hells and so forth.
"Two aeons" (*dve kappā*): here too, the second jhāna is of three kinds according to the method already stated. Among these, by means of sublime cultivation...
The lifespan of those reborn there is eight *kappas* by the highest measure, four by the middling, and two by the lowest;
it is with reference to this that it was said. Regarding the phrase "four *kappas*," the meaning should be understood by bringing in what was stated previously: "a *kappa*, two *kappas*.
Furthermore, *kappa* is also a name for a quality (*guṇa*); therefore, [the sequence] is: one *kappa*, two *kappas*, four *kappas*.

This is how the meaning here should be understood. This is what is meant: the aeon (kappa) mentioned first is counted twice, and when multiplied by one [factor], it becomes two aeons; by a second [factor], four;
then those four aeons, multiplied by these four factors, become eight by one factor, sixteen by a second, and thirty-two by a third.
"By the fourth, sixty-four": thus it should be understood that in this context, sixty-four eons are taken by way of the sublime jhānas.
"Five hundred eons": this is stated by way of the jhāna of rebirth for those very same sublime [beings].

Or rather, because there is an absence of three Brahma-worlds—as there are in the Vehapphala realms and in the planes of the first jhāna and so forth—the lifespan measure is only this much; therefore, it is stated thus.
4. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Differentiation (Dutiya-nānākaraṇa-sutta-vaṇṇanā) 124.

In the fourth [section], "form itself" (*rūpam eva*) is "that which has become form" (*rūpagataṃ*). The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. Regarding the phrases "as impermanent," etc.:

it is "as impermanent" (*aniccato*) in the sense of non-existence after having existed; "as a disease" (*rogato*) in the sense of being an affliction; "as a boil" (*gaṇḍato*) in the sense of internal corruption; and "as an arrow" (*sallato*) in the sense of having entered within.
As a dart, in the sense of being painful; as a calamity, in the sense of oppression; as an affliction, in the sense of being incurable;

as an enemy, in the sense of being hostile; as disintegration, in the sense of falling apart; as empty, in the sense of being devoid of a sentient being; and as non-self, in the sense of being beyond one's control.

And here, the characteristic of impermanence is explained by the two terms "impermanence" and "disintegration," while "emptiness" and "non-self" [explain the characteristics of emptiness and non-self].
It should be understood that the characteristic of non-self (*anattalakkhaṇa*) is taught by two [of these], while the characteristic of suffering (*dukkhalakkhaṇa*) is taught by the remainder.
"He contemplates" means he sees with wisdom (*ñāṇa*). Thus, seeing by applying the three characteristics to the five aggregates, he realizes the three paths and the three fruits.
"He is reborn into the company of the Suddhāvāsa deities" means he stands there [in that realm].
Having developed the fourth jhāna, one is reborn [therein].
5–6. Commentary on the Two Mettā Suttas (125–126):

In the fifth sutta, loving-kindness (*mettā*) is shown by way of the first jhāna, while compassion (*karuṇā*) and the others are shown by way of the second and subsequent jhānas. The sixth sutta is to be understood according to the same method as that stated for the fourth.
7. Commentary on the First Discourse on the Marvels of the Tathāgata (Paṭhamatathāgataacchariyasuttavaṇṇanā) 127.
In the seventh [verse], "by manifestation" (*pātubhāva*) means by way of appearing. "Enters the womb" (*kucchiṃ okkamati*): here the meaning is that he has entered the womb;
for it is when he has already entered that this occurs, not while he is in the process of entering. "Immeasurable" (*appamāṇa*) means immeasurable in terms of growth; "vast" (*vipula*).
This is the meaning. "Exalted" (*uḷāra*) is a synonym for that very same thing. Regarding the phrase "the divine power of the devas":
this is the power of the devas—namely, the radiance of their garments pervades twelve *yojanas*, as does that of their bodies and their celestial mansions (*vimāna*);
the meaning is "having transcended that. "The world-intervals" (*lokantarika*): between every three world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), there is one world-interval.
It is like the space between three chariot wheels or the feet of three [wheels] placed so that they touch one another.
Furthermore, that Lokantarika Niraya is eight thousand yojanas in extent. It is "aghā" (unobstructed), meaning it is perpetually open.
It is "asaṃvutā" (uncovered), meaning there is no support even below. It is "andhakāra" (darkness), meaning it has become gloom. It is "andhakāratimisa" (pitch-black darkness).
They are possessed of a gloom that causes blindness because it obstructs the arising of eye-consciousness; for it is said that in such a place, eye-consciousness does not arise.
"Of such great power" means that the moon and sun appear simultaneously over the three continents;
they are of such great power that, having dispelled the darkness for nine hundred thousand yojanas in each direction, [they illuminate the world].
They display light; they are of such great power that their radiance does not reach [there], meaning their effulgence does not extend.
It is said that they move through the middle of the Cakkavāḷa mountain range and even beyond it to the Lokantara hells. Therefore, their radiance does not reach there.
"And those beings who are there" refers to those beings who have been reborn in that Great Lokantara Hell. But what is the karma?
Having committed grave and cruel offenses against their parents and against righteous recluses and brahmins,
and having performed other acts of violence such as the killing of living beings day after day, they are reborn there— just like the Abhaya-cora, Nāga-cora,
and others on the island of Tambapaṇṇi. Their physical form measures three gavutas in height, like that of the Vagguli spirits.
They have long nails like those of a bat. Like bats on a tree, they cling with their nails to the base of the Cakkavāḷa mountains.

When, while crawling about, they come within arm’s reach of one another, they think, "We have found food," and becoming intent upon it, they turn over and fall into the water that sustains the world; even when struck by the wind, they are like madhuka fruits.
They fall into the water as if they were cut into pieces; as soon as they have fallen, they dissolve like a lump of dough in extremely caustic water.

On that very day, they see others as well, thinking, "Friends, there are indeed other beings; just as we experience great suffering, so too have other beings been reborn here for the sake of experiencing this same suffering. This is...
However, the radiance does not remain for even the duration of a single spoonful of rice-gruel.
It lasts only as long as it takes for one who has slept and awakened to discern the object. But the Dīgha reciters say:
"Like a flash of lightning, it flashes forth for only the duration of a finger-snap and vanishes even while people are saying, 'What was that?'"
8. Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Marvels of the Tathāgata 128.

In the eighth [discourse], "attachment" (*ālaya*) refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) in the sense of being clung to by craving and views, or it refers to the entire cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).

It is called a "pleasure grove" (*ārāma*) because they delight therein; thus, one for whom the attachment is the pleasure grove is "one who delights in attachment" (*ālayārāmā*). One who finds joy in attachment is "one who rejoices in attachment" (*ālayaratā*).

"Delighting in attachment" (*ālayasammuditā*) means one who delights in attachment. "In the phenomena that are non-attachment" (*anālaye dhamme*) refers to the noble phenomena (*ariyadhamma*) which are the opposite of attachment and are the necessary conditions for turning away from the round of existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissita*).
"Desires to hear" (*sussūsati*) means he becomes desirous of hearing. "Lends an ear" (*sotaṃ odahati*) means he fixes his ear.

"Establishes a mind intent on understanding" (*aññā cittaṃ upaṭṭhapeti*) means he applies his mind for the purpose of thorough comprehension. "Conceit" (*māna*) is the act of conceiving; it is so called in the sense of being something to be conceived.

Or it is the entire cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) itself. "In the Dhamma of the discipline for human beings" means in the Dhamma of the discipline for human beings. Non-quiescence (*anupasama*) is the opposite of quiescence;

or rather, the cycle of existence itself is called non-quiescence in the sense of being unpacified. "Leading to quiescence" means leading to the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭa*), which produces quiescence.
"Enveloped by ignorance" means possessed of or gone into ignorance. Because they are wrapped in the shell of the egg of ignorance, they are like an egg.
"Become" means become like an egg. "Enveloped on all sides" means completely covered. "In the removal of ignorance":
the removal of ignorance is said to be Arahantship; the meaning is that when the states dependent upon that are being taught.
Thus, in this sutta, the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is explained in four places, and the turning away from the round (*vivaṭṭa*) is explained in four places.
9. Commentary on the Ānanda-acchariya Sutta 129.
Regarding the ninth [sutta], "The assembly of monks approached Ānanda for a visit": this refers to those who, desiring to see the Blessed One, approach the Elder;
or those who think, "Venerable Ānanda is indeed all-encompassing in his grace, handsome, beautiful to behold, learned, and an ornament to the Saṅgha."
Having heard of the Elder’s virtues, they come; it is with reference to them that it is said, “The assembly of bhikkhus approaches Ānanda for the sake of seeing him.

This same method applies everywhere. “Satisfied” (attamanā) means having their own desire fulfilled and their minds gladdened by the thought, “Our seeing [of him] coincides with our hearing [of his teachings].
Regarding the word “Dhamma”: “Friend, we hope you are bearing up, we hope you are getting along; we hope your work of wise attention is proceeding?”
"Perform it; fulfill the duties toward your teachers and preceptors"—such is the nature of this hospitable greeting. In that regard, concerning the bhikkhunīs, there is this distinction:
"Sisters, do you conduct yourselves having undertaken the eight *garudhammas*?
Concerning the laymen (*upāsakas*), [he says]: "Welcome, layman; is nothing wrong with your head or any limb? Are your sons and brothers free from illness?"
He does not offer hospitality in that way; rather, he does it thus: "How, lay followers, do you maintain the three refuges and the five precepts?
Do you observe the eight Uposatha days of the month? Do you fulfill the duty of service toward your mother and father?
Do you support righteous recluses and brahmins? The same method applies to the female lay followers as well.
10. Commentary on the Discourse on the Marvels of the Wheel-Turning Monarch (Cakkavatti-acchariya-sutta) 130.
In the tenth [discourse], "The Assembly of Khattiyas" refers to both consecrated and unconsecrated khattiyas.
For it is said that the so-called Wheel-Turning Monarch (cakkavatti-rāja) is handsome and pleasing, who, traveling through the sky, rules his kingdom; he is righteous...
Having heard this account of his virtues, they become delighted, as hearing brings them close to seeing him.
He speaks thus, offering a greeting: "How, dear ones, do you fulfill the duties of a king? Do you protect the ancestral tradition? But toward the brahmins, he says:
"And how, teachers, do you recite the mantras? Are the students mastering the mantras?"
He extends such hospitality as this: "May you receive alms, or clothing, or [instruction on] virtue. Toward householders he extends such hospitality as this:
"How is it, dear sirs, that you have no affliction from the royal family through punishment or imprisonment?
Does the rain fall properly from the sky? Are the crops successful? Toward ascetics he extends such hospitality as this: "How is it..."
“Venerable sir, are the requisites for one gone forth easy to obtain? Do you not neglect the duty of a recluse?”—in this way he offers such greetings.
Thus ends the third chapter, the Chapter on Fear.
(14) 4. The Chapter on Persons.
1. Commentary on the *Saṃyojana-sutta* 131.
Regarding the first [fetter] of the fourth [chapter]: "Those conducive to rebirth" (*upapattipaṭilābhiniyo*) refers to those by means of which one obtains rebirth immediately after death.
"Those conducive to obtaining existence" (*bhavapaṭilābhiniyo*) refers to the conditions for obtaining the existence of rebirth (*upapattibhava*). "For a once-returner" (*sakadāgāmissa*)—this...
This is taken as the ultimate limit among noble ones who have not yet abandoned the fetters.

However, since there is no "arising" for one who attains parinibbāna in the interval, the jhāna that he enters into there is reckoned as a "condition for rebirth-existence" (upapattibhava) precisely because it is wholesome.
Therefore, for him, the fetters pertaining to the acquisition of rebirth have been abandoned.
It is said: "The fetters pertaining to existence have not been abandoned.

And with reference to those lower-tier fetters that have not been abandoned, it is stated without distinction regarding the once-returner: "The lower-tier fetters have not been abandoned. The rest here is self-evident. 2.
Commentary on the *Paṭibhāna-sutta* (The Discourse on Ingenuity)

132. Regarding the second [type], "one who has a reasoned response but not a spontaneous response": when speaking on a question, he speaks only what is reasoned, but he does not speak quickly; the meaning is that he speaks only slowly. All the phrases are to be understood according to this method.
3. Commentary on the *Ugghaṭitaññū-sutta* (133).
In the third [sutta], the distinction between all four types of persons is to be understood by means of this sutta.
“And what kind of person is one who gains knowledge by a condensed statement? It is that person for whom there is a breakthrough to the Dhamma at the very moment it is uttered;
this is called a person who gains knowledge by a condensed statement. And what kind of person is one who gains knowledge by detailed exposition?
It is that person for whom there is a breakthrough to the Dhamma when the meaning is being analyzed in detail; this is called a person who gains knowledge by detailed exposition.”

And what kind of person is one who is to be guided (neyya)? That person for whom, through brief instruction, through questioning, through wise attention, and by serving, associating with, and attending upon spiritual friends, there comes about the gradual realization of the Dhamma—this is called a person who is to be guided.
And what kind of person is one for whom the words are the limit (padaparama)? That person for whom, even though they have heard much...
“Even though one speaks much, retains much, and recites much, there is no realization of the Dhamma through that birth;
this person is called ‘one for whom the words are the limit.
4. Commentary on the Uṭṭhānaphala Sutta.
134. In the fourth case, one spends the day solely through the energy of exertion;
having obtained some mere trifling result as the outcome of that, one maintains one's livelihood. Yet, by virtue of that exertion, one does not obtain any fruit of merit.
This person is called one who lives on the fruit of exertion, not one who lives on the fruit of kamma. Starting from the gods of the Four Great Kings...

All the devas, because they subsist solely on the fruit of merit without the effort of exertion, are called "those who subsist on the fruit of karma," not "those who subsist on the fruit of exertion. Kings, royal ministers, and others are both those who subsist on the fruit of exertion and those who subsist on the fruit of karma.
Beings in the niraya hells are neither those who subsist on the fruit of exertion nor those who subsist on the fruit of karma. In this sutta...
"Only the fruit of merit" is intended here as "the fruit of kamma," and that does not exist for them.
5. Commentary on the Sāvajja Sutta (The Blameworthy Discourse). 135.

In the fifth [discourse], the first is the blind, foolish worldling (*andhabālaputhujjana*); the second is the worldly worldling who occasionally performs wholesome deeds (*antarantarā kusalakārako lokiyaputhujjana*).
The third is the stream-enterer; the once-returner and non-returner are also included by this very term. The fourth is the one whose taints are destroyed, for he is exclusively blameless.
6–7. Commentary on the Sīla-sutta and others.
136–137. In the sixth [category], the first is the ordinary worldling; the second consists of the dry-insight practitioner, the stream-enterer, and the once-returner;
the third is the non-returner. For since he indeed attains even for a moment the jhāna associated with the sign of rebirth, the dry-insight practitioner is likewise one who fulfills concentration.
The fourth is exclusively the one whose taints are destroyed. He...
Indeed, because all adversaries to virtue and the other [perfections] have been abandoned, he is called "one who fulfills them in every respect.
In the seventh [chapter] as well, the classification of individuals should be understood according to the same method stated in the sixth.
8. Commentary on the *Nikaṭṭha-sutta*.
138. In the eighth [verse], "with body withdrawn" (*nikaṭṭhakāya*) means with the body gone forth. "With mind not entered" (*anikaṭṭhacitta*) means with the mind not having entered.
What is meant is that although he has physically departed from the village, even while dwelling in the forest, his mind has entered the village.
The meaning is to be understood in this same manner in all instances.
9. Commentary on the Dhammakathikasutta 139.

In the ninth [verse], "unconnected" (*asahita*) means not joined with the meaning. "He is not skillful" means he is not clever. "Of what is connected and unconnected" refers to that which is based on the meaning or that which is not so based. In this way, the meaning is to be understood in all instances.
10. Commentary on the Vādīsutta.
140. "In the tenth [case], it reaches exhaustion in meaning" means that when questioned regarding the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), it reaches exhaustion—that is, depletion—and he is unable to speak.
"But not in phrasing" means that his phrasing (*byañjana*) proceeds and is not exhausted.
This same method applies in all instances.
The Fourth Chapter on Persons (Puggalavagga).
(15) 5. The Chapter on Radiance (Ābhāvagga) 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on Radiance (Ābhāsutta-vaṇṇanā)

141. In the first [verse] of the fifth [chapter], it is like the moon because of its appearance (*ābhāsa*); thus it is "moon-light" (*candābhā*). The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
2–5. Commentary on the *Pabhā-sutta* and others: 142–145.

In the second and subsequent [verses] as well, it is like the moon because of its radiance (*pabhāsa*); thus it is "moon-radiance" (*candappabhā*). It is like the moon because of its illumination (*āloka*).
“Moonlight”: it is like the moon by way of its illuminating; it is like the moon by way of its shining—thus it is “moonlight.
In this manner, the meaning should be understood for all the terms as well.
6. Commentary on the First Sutta on Time.

146. In the sixth [sutta], "at the proper time" (*kālāti*) means at the appropriate and suitable time. "Listening to the Dhamma at the proper time" (*kālena dhammassavanaṃ*) means listening to the Dhamma at the appropriate and suitable time. "Discussion of the Dhamma" (*dhammasākacchā*) refers to a conversational discourse proceeding by way of asking and answering questions.
7. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Time (Kālasutta) 147.
In the seventh [sutta], "at the proper time" (*kālāti*) refers to wholesome states (*kusaladhammā*) that proceed at their respective times by way of listening to the Dhamma and so forth.
This is the designation. They are both cultivated and repeatedly turned over. "The destruction of the taints" refers to Arhatship.
The eighth [sutta] is clear in meaning. 9–10.
Commentary on the *Sucarita-sutta* and others.

149–150. In the ninth [chapter], "smooth speech" means soft speech. "Measured speech" refers to discourse spoken after having discerned it with wisdom (paññā), which is so designated. In the tenth, "the essence of virtue" (sīlasāra) refers to virtue that brings about the attainment of the essence. The same principle applies to the remaining [terms].
The fifth chapter on Radiance is concluded.
The third fiftieth section is finished.
4. The Fourth Fifty (16) 1.
The Chapter on Faculties (Indriyavagga) 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Faculties, etc. (Indriyasuttādivaṇṇanā)
151. In the first [section] of the fourth [chapter], it is called the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) because it exercises lordship through the burden of faith.
The same method applies to the remaining [faculties]. In the second [section], it is the power of faith (*saddhābala*) in the sense of being unshakable by lack of faith;

the same method applies to the remaining [powers]. In the third [section], "the power of blamelessness" means the power that is free from fault. "The power of gathering" means the power of gathering those who are worthy of being gathered.
The fourth and fifth [suttas] are indeed self-evident.
6. Commentary on the Kappa Sutta: 156.
Regarding the sixth [sutta], concerning the phrase "it contracts" (*saṃvaṭṭati*), there are three types of contraction: contraction by water, contraction by fire, and contraction by wind.
There are three limits of dissolution: the Ābhassara, the Subhakiṇha, and the Vehapphala realms.
When the world-system dissolves by fire, everything below the Ābhassara realm is consumed by flames. When it dissolves by water, everything below the Subhakiṇha realm is dissolved away by water.
When it dissolves by wind, everything below the Vehapphala realm is scattered away by the wind. As for its extent:
However, at all times, one Buddha-field perishes. This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
7. Commentary on the Discourse on Disease (*Rogasutta*).
157. "Afflicted" (*vighātavatī*) means being possessed of the suffering of affliction due to the condition of great desire.
"Dissatisfied" (*asantuṭṭha*) means being dissatisfied with regard to the four requisites by means of the three forms of contentment.

"For the sake of obtaining non-contempt" (*anavaññappaṭilābhāya*) means for the purpose of obtaining not being despised by others. "For the sake of obtaining gain, honor, and fame" (*lābhasakkārasilokappaṭilābhāya*) refers to that which consists of the four requisites well-prepared.
For the sake of obtaining gain and honor, as well as renown, which is to say, praise.
"He approaches families with calculation" means he approaches families for the purpose of being known, thinking, "In this way they will know me.
The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.
8. Commentary on the Parihānisutta 158.
In the eighth [verse], "in the deep" means in those things that are profound in meaning. "In the possible and the impossible" means in causes and non-causes.

"It does not penetrate" means it does not plunge into or proceed therein. Regarding "the eye of wisdom," both the wisdom of learning and inquiry (*uggahaparipucchā-paññā*) is applicable here, as is the wisdom of comprehension and penetration (*sammasanappaṭivedha-paññā*).
9. Commentary on the Bhikkhunīsutta 159.
In the ninth [sutta], she spoke thus in order to send the Elder, her heart being bound to him, saying, "Come, sir.
"Having covered herself including the head" means having covered the body together with the head. "She lay down on the couch" means having quickly prepared a small couch and [lying] upon it.

He lay down. "He said this" means that, having observed his disposition, [the Blessed One] spoke these words in order to teach a discourse on the foul (*asubha*) in a gentle manner for the sake of abandoning greed.
"Produced by nutriment" means produced by nutriment, grown depending upon nutriment.
"Depending on nutriment, one abandons nutriment" means that, depending on the present edible nutriment (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*), one who practices it wisely in this way...
One abandons the nutriment known as past karma. Furthermore, even regarding present edible nutriment, the craving for it must be abandoned.
"He abandons craving" means that by means of abandoning the craving currently occurring in this way, one abandons the past craving rooted in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
Is this present craving wholesome or unwholesome? It is unwholesome. Is it to be cultivated or not to be cultivated? It is not to be cultivated.
"It should be cultivated. Does it draw on rebirth-linking or not? It does not draw on it. Furthermore, even for this present craving that is to be cultivated, attachment must indeed be abandoned.
"That venerable one will dwell having attained the destruction of the taints—how much more so, then, am I!"—here, "how much more so, then? is a reflection upon the reason. This...
The meaning is this: "That venerable one will dwell having realized the fruit of arahantship; for what reason should I not dwell having realized it?
For that venerable one is indeed the Son of the Perfectly Enlightened One, and I too am the Son of the Perfectly Enlightened One;
this [fruit] shall arise for me as well. "On account of conceit" refers to the conceit that has arisen in this way and is being cultivated.
"Depending on": one abandons conceit; that is, one abandons the prior conceit rooted in the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
That upon which he depends in order to abandon it is likewise unwholesome and should be cultivated, yet it does not draw along rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
However, even attachment to that [state] must be abandoned.
"‘The destruction of the bridge was spoken by the Blessed One’ means that the destruction of the words and the destruction of the conditions were taught by the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Thus, as the Elder turned back his teaching through these four factors, the desire and lust that had arisen in that bhikkhunī toward the Elder subsided.
She too, in order to ask the Elder for forgiveness, confessed her transgression, and the Elder accepted it from her.
To demonstrate this, the passage beginning with "Then that bhikkhunī" was spoken.
10. Commentary on the Sugatavinaya Sutta: 160.
In the tenth [sutta], "misapprehended" means grasped out of sequence. "Mastering" means practicing and discussing.
Regarding the phrase "by means of words and syllables" (*padabyañjanehi*): here, the word itself is called "syllable" (*byañjana*) because it expresses the meaning.

"Ill-placed" (*dunnikkhitta*) means poorly placed, set down in the wrong order. "The meaning also becomes difficult to lead" (*atthopi dunnayo hoti*) means that one is unable to extract and explain the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
"With its root cut" (*chinnamūlaka*) means that its root—the monks who constitute the foundation—has been severed.
"Without a refuge" means without a support. "Luxurious" means those who have entered upon a practice characterized by an abundance of requisites.
"Negligent" means those who grasp the three trainings with laxity. "Pioneers in falling away": the five hindrances are called "falling away" because they cause one to fall away from progress;
in this context, it means being pioneers therein. "In seclusion" refers to the three kinds of seclusion. "Those who have laid down their burden" means...
Lacking energy. In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all instances.
The first chapter, on the Faculties, is concluded.
(17) 2. The Chapter on the Way of Practice.
1. Commentary on the *Saṃkhittasutta* 161.
In the first [classification] of the second [sutta], it is called "the painful way of practice" (*dukkhāpaṭipadā*) because it is to be practiced as painful by way of the rejection of pleasure.
It is called "slow direct knowledge" (*dandhābhiññā*) because its direct knowledge is sluggish due to its heavy nature and lack of rapid occurrence.
In this same manner, the meaning should be understood in all instances.
2. Commentary on the Detailed Discourse (Vitthārasutta). 162.
In the second [discourse], "frequently" (*abhikkhaṇaṃ*) means constantly. "Immediate" (*ānantariya*) refers to the concentration of the path that yields immediate fruition.
"Through the destruction of the taints" means for the sake of the fruit of Arahantship. "The five faculties" refers to the five faculties with insight as the fifth.
For here, by "the faculty of wisdom," it is specifically the wisdom of insight that is intended. The rest here is clear according to the text.
Now, this is the exposition of these modes of practice: here, a bhikkhu who has not previously formed a fixed inclination, in the prior stage...

One exerts oneself in grasping at form, one exerts oneself in grasping at the formless, one exerts oneself in grasping at conditions, one exerts oneself regarding the three periods of time, and one exerts oneself regarding what is the path and what is not the path.
Thus, exerting oneself in these five places, one attains insight (vipassanā).
Having attained insight, [one proceeds] through the contemplation of rise and fall, the contemplation of dissolution, and the appearance as terror.
Having exerted himself even in these nine insights-knowledges— namely, the contemplation of danger, the contemplation of disenchantment,
the knowledge of the desire for liberation, the knowledge of equanimity toward formations, the knowledge of conformity, and the knowledge of change-of-lineage— he reaches the supramundane path.
Because that supramundane path is realized through such difficulty and heaviness, it is "difficult to practice" and possesses "slow direct knowledge."
However, for one who, having exerted effort during the preliminary stage in the five knowledges, realizes the path later on without wearying oneself in the nine insight-knowledges,

that path is called "difficult practice with quick direct knowledge" because it is realized through such difficulty and lack of ease. By this same method, the other two [paths] are also to be understood.
These points should be clarified by means of the Simile of the Search for the Oxen: Suppose a man had four oxen that, having escaped, entered a forest.
While searching for them in that thorny and dense jungle, he traveled with difficulty and toil along a path through the thickets;
and there, in that very place of density, he saw the oxen hidden away, having found them only with difficulty and toil. One [ox] was found with difficulty...
One who went and saw [the ox] standing in the open space saw it very quickly. Another, having gone easily by way of the open space, saw it hidden in a thicket with difficulty and great effort.
Yet another, having gone easily by way of the open space itself, saw it immediately as it was standing in the open space.
In this context, the four noble paths are to be understood as being like the four oxen.
The practitioner of yoga (*yogāvacara*) is like a man searching for a cow;

the painful practice (*dukkhāpaṭipadā*) is like traveling with difficulty and toil through a dense forest on the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*) while struggling through the five knowledges (*pañca-ñāṇa*).

The vision of the Noble Paths (*ariyamagga*) while struggling through the nine knowledges on the subsequent stage (*aparabhāga*) is like seeing those hidden in a thicket only with great difficulty. By this—
By means of this method, the remaining similes should also be applied.
3. Commentary on the *Asubha-sutta* 163.
Regarding the third [sutta]: "He dwells contemplating the foulness in the body," he [contemplates] his own physical body, thinking, "As this is, so is that."
In this manner, by way of applying the ten external foul objects, one dwells contemplating foulness;
the meaning is that one sees one’s own body with knowledge as foul and repulsive.
“Perceiving repulsiveness in nutriment” means perceiving repulsiveness in edible food by way of the nine kinds of repulsiveness. “Perceiving non-delight in the entire world” means...
He is endowed with a sense of disenchantment, being dissatisfied with the entire dwelling of the world within the three realms.
"Contemplating the impermanence of all formations" means contemplating all formations of the three planes as impermanent.
"The perception of death" is the perception arisen concerning death. "Well-established internally" means well-established within one's own internal self.

...there is. Up to this point, powerful insight (*balavavipassanā*) has been explained. "The powers of the trainee" (*sekhabalāni*) means the powers of those who are training. The rest here is clear from the text (*pāḷi*).

However, the phrases beginning with "contemplating the foul" (*asubhānupassī*) are stated for the purpose of showing the painful way of practice (*dukkhāya paṭipadāya*), whereas the first jhāna and so on belong to the pleasant way of practice (*sukhāya*).
For the foul and so forth have repulsive objects; yet among them, by their very nature, ...
A mind that is fondly attached clings. Therefore, one who develops those [lower stages] is said to have entered upon a practice that is painful.
Since the first jhāna and the others possess sublime bliss, one who enters upon them is said to have entered upon a practice that is pleasant.
Here, however, this is the simile common to all: suppose a man engaged in battle has constructed a defensive breastwork...

Having equipped himself with the five weapons, he enters the battle; wishing to rest midway, he enters a sheltered enclosure (*phalakakoṭṭhaka*) where he rests and partakes of food, drink, and so forth. Then, having entered the battle again, he performs his duty.
In this context, the battle should be understood as the battle of the defilements (*kilesasaṅgāma*), and the sheltered enclosure as—

The five powers of reliance are like a man entering a battle; the five faculties, with insight as the fifth, are like the equipment of the five weapons; the time of performing the work of insight is like the time of entering the battle;
and the time of entering the gatehouse and partaking of rest, drink, and food by one desiring to rest is [like the time of attaining fruition].
When the arising of consciousness in one performing the work of insight (vipassanā) becomes devoid of zest, it is the time to gladden the mind by relying on the five powers;
this is like the time of entering battle again after resting, eating, and drinking.
Having gladdened the mind with the five powers and then performed the work of insight once more, one turns away [from the defilements].
The time for attaining *arahantship* is to be understood. However, in this sutta, the powers (*bala*) and the faculties (*indriya*) are taught as being mixed together.

4. Commentary on the First Akkhamā Sutta (Sutta 164) In the fourth [verse], "intolerant" (*akkhamā*) refers to the practice of non-endurance; "tolerant" (*khamā*) refers to the practice of endurance; and "tamed" (*damā*)...
The "way of taming the faculties" (*indriyadamana-paṭipadā*) is the method for subduing the senses. "Composure" (*samā*) is the way of pacifying unwholesome thoughts (*akusala-vitakka*).

"He resists him who resists" means he strikes back at one who strikes. "He quarrels with him who quarrels" means he returns a blow to one who attacks. The fifth and sixth [terms] have their meanings obvious.
7. Commentary on the Mahāmoggallāna Sutta.

167. For the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, the first three paths were of pleasant progress and slow direct knowledge, while the path of Arahantship was of painful progress and quick direct knowledge. Therefore, he spoke thus:
“By means of this practice which is painful with quick direct knowledge, my mind was liberated from the taints through non-clinging.”
8. Commentary on the Sāriputta Sutta 168.

In the eighth [sutta], for the Elder Dhammasenāpati, the three lower paths are of pleasant progress and slow direct knowledge, while the path of Arahantship is of pleasant progress and quick direct knowledge. Therefore, it is said: "This practice which is pleasant and of quick direct knowledge."
He said: "In these two suttas, however, it should be understood that the practice described is indeed mixed.
9. Commentary on the *Sasaṅkhāra-sutta* (9.169):

In the ninth [sutta], the first and second types of persons are dry-insight practitioners (*sukkha-vipassaka*) who, with exertion and application, [overcome] the sign of formations (*saṅkhāra-nimitta*).
They establish [the meditation object]. Among them, one, due to the strength of his insight-faculties, attains final nibbāna right here through the extinction of the defilements;

another, being unable to do so here due to the weakness of his faculties, obtains that same original meditation subject in the next existence and, with effort and application, having established the sign of formations, attains final nibbāna through the extinction of the defilements.
He attains final Nibbāna; these are the third and fourth types who take serenity as their vehicle.
Of these, one, due to the strength of his faculties, exhausts the defilements right here without exertion or effort;

the other, being unable to do so here due to the weakness of his faculties, obtains that same original meditation subject in his next existence and exhausts the defilements there without exertion or effort—this is how it should be understood.
10. Commentary on the Yuganaddha Sutta 170.
In the tenth [sutta], "preceded by serenity" (*samathapubbaṅgama*) means having made serenity the precursor or forerunner.
"The path arises" means that the first supramundane path is produced. "He cultivates that path" refers to the repetition and so forth of that path which lasts for a single moment of consciousness.
It is not that there is no second path and so forth; rather, when one causes them to arise, it is said that one "cultivates," "develops," and "repeatedly practices" that very same [first] path.
Regarding the phrase "preceded by insight" (*vipassanāpubbaṅgama*): having made insight the precursor and the forerunner, one develops serenity (*samatha*).
The meaning is that one who naturally possesses insight stands upon that insight and gives rise to concentration (*samādhi*).
“He develops the coupled pair” means he develops it having made them a couple.

In that regard, it is not possible to enter attainment with that very same mind and then comprehend formations with that very same [mind]. However, to whatever extent he enters attainments, to that extent he comprehends formations; and to whatever extent he comprehends formations, to that extent he enters attainments.
How? He enters the first jhāna; emerging from that, he contemplates formations. Having contemplated formations, he enters the second jhāna.
Emerging from that, he again contemplates formations. Having contemplated formations, he enters the third jhāna...
[and so on] ...he enters the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Emerging from that, he contemplates formations.
He reflects. Thus, this is called developing serenity and insight in conjunction.
"Grasped by agitation regarding phenomena" means grasped by agitation—known as the ten imperfections of insight—regarding the phenomena of serenity and insight;
the meaning is that it is well-grasped. "That, friend, is the occasion" refers to the seven suitable [conditions].
The time of acquisition has been explained. "That mind" refers to the mind that has arisen at the moment it has entered the path of insight (*vipassanā-vīthi*).

"It settles within itself" means that, having emerged from the path of insight, it settles upon that very object designated as the internal range of its own domain (*gocarajjhatta*). "It becomes composed" means it sits rightly by way of the object.
“Becomes one-pointed” means it becomes concentrated on a single object. “Is concentrated” means it is properly fixed; it is well-established. The rest here is of plain meaning.
The second chapter, on the Way, is finished. (18) 3.
The Chapter on Volitional Intentions (Sañcetaniya-vagga)
1. Commentary on the *Cetanā-sutta* 171.
Regarding the first [sutta] of the third [chapter]: "In the body" (*kāye*) means in the door of the body (*kāyadvāre*), that is, when there is bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*).

In the phrases "caused by bodily volition" (*kāyasañcetanāhetu*) and so forth, "bodily volition" (*kāyasañcetanā*) refers to volition (*cetanā*) or mental formation (*pakappanā*) in the door of the body. That is eightfold, according to the eight types of wholesome states of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara-kusala*).
By way of the unwholesome, there are twelve kinds; thus, there are twenty kinds [of volition]. Likewise for verbal volition, and likewise for mental volition.
Furthermore, nine sublime (mahaggata) volitions are also found here. "With bodily volition as cause" means with bodily volition as condition.
"Pleasure and pain arise internally" means that pleasure arises within one's own internal continuum due to the eight wholesome kamma-conditions.
Suffering arises with the twelve unwholesome courses of action as its condition. This same method applies to the other doors as well.

"With ignorance as condition" means precisely by way of ignorance as the cause. For if ignorance, while concealing, acts as a condition, then in that case volition—which has become the condition for pleasure and pain—arises through the three doors.
Thus, this was stated by way of ignorance, which serves as the root.

Regarding the phrases "by oneself" (*sāmaṃ*) and so forth: when one performs a bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) spontaneously, without being commanded by others, it is said that "one performs that bodily formation by oneself.
However, when others cause someone to act by inciting or commanding them, it is said that "others perform that bodily formation for him.
Furthermore, when one perceives the wholesome as "wholesome," the unwholesome as "unwholesome," and the result of the wholesome as "the result of the wholesome"—
One who knows an unwholesome result as an unwholesome result and performs the twentyfold bodily formation at the door of the body is said to perform it with full awareness (*sampajañña*).
One who performs it without knowing this is said to perform it without full awareness.
The same method applies to the remaining doors as well.
In this regard, action performed without clear comprehension should be understood as follows:
young children pay homage to a shrine, offer flowers, and pay homage to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, thinking, "We are doing what has been done by our parents.
Even though they do not know that this is wholesome, it is indeed wholesome for them. Likewise, animals such as deer and birds listen to the Dhamma and pay homage to the Saṅgha.
When they pay homage to a cetiya, that is wholesome for them, whether they know it or not.
But young children strike their parents with their hands and feet;
they brandish clods of earth at monks, throw sticks, and abuse them. Cows follow the Saṅgha of monks, and dogs follow them as well, biting them.
Lions, tigers, and other such creatures pursue [them] and deprive them of life.
It should be understood that unwholesome kamma occurs for them whether they are aware of it or not.
Now, the volition of exertion (*āyūhana-cetanā*) must be combined across all three doors as follows: in the door of the body, it is based on what one has done oneself.
There are twenty volitions rooted in an order, twenty rooted in clear comprehension, and twenty rooted in lack of clear comprehension;
thus there are eighty volitions. The same applies to the door of speech. However, in the door of mind, by calculating twenty-nine for each single permutation, there are one hundred and sixteen.
Thus, in all three doors, there are two hundred and seventy-six.
Volition—all these are designated as the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha).

The aspect of feeling associated with that is the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha); the aspect of perceiving is the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha); the mind is the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha);
and the body is derived form (upādārūpa), whose conditions are the four elements (dhātu) or the four great primaries (bhūta). These five aggregates are called the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca).

“Bhikkhus, ignorance has descended upon these phenomena”: this means that ignorance has descended upon these aforementioned types of volitional phenomena by way of co-nascence and by way of decisive support.
In this way, both the round of existence itself and the ignorance rooted in the round are shown.

Having thus increased insight and attained arahantship, the Blessed One now speaks the praise of the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) with the words beginning, "With the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance...
In this context, "with the remainderless fading away and cessation" means by both the remainderless fading away and the remainderless cessation.
"That body does not exist" refers to the fact that for one whose taints are destroyed, no karmic activity is perceived through the body.
Sweeping the courtyard of the shrine, sweeping the courtyard of the Bodhi tree, approaching, returning, performing duties and secondary duties, and so forth.
However, twenty volitions (cetanā) pertaining to his bodily door fall into the state of being non-resultant (avipākadhamma). Therefore it was said:
"That body does not exist such that, conditioned by it, pleasure or pain arises within him. [This refers to] those proceeding via the bodily door.

For here, it is volition that is intended by the term "body. The same principle applies to the other two [bases] as well. Terms such as "field" (*khetta*) and so forth are also names for wholesome and unwholesome kamma itself.

For that [kamma] is called a "field" in the sense of being the place where the result grows; a "base" (*vatthu*) in the sense of being a foundation; a "sphere" (*āyatana*) in the sense of being a cause;
and a "legal case" (*adhikaraṇa*) in the sense of being the locus of the matter.

Thus the Teacher, having shown by this much how karma is accumulated through the three doors, now spoke the words beginning with “Bhikkhus, these four” in order to show the place where that karma ripens.
Therein, "acquisition of a personal existence" (*attabhāvappaṭilābha*) means those who have acquired a personal existence.
"Self-intention carries on" (*attasañcetanā kamati*) means that the intention fashioned by oneself proceeds and continues.

In such passages as, "By reason of their own volition, those beings pass away from that body," it is said that the *khiḍḍāpadosika* (those corrupted by play) gods pass away because of their own volition.
For when they are sporting, fully absorbed in divine pleasures in the Nandana Grove, the Cittalatā Grove, the Phārusaka Grove, and so forth, they forget to take food and drink;
through the cessation of nutriment, they wither like garlands cast into the sun.
They meet together. The gods corrupted by mind fall away due to the volition of others; these are the gods of the Four Great Kings.
It is said that among them, one son of the gods, thinking, "I shall play at the festival," sets out upon the street in his chariot with his retinue.
Then another, coming out and seeing him going before him, says, "What is this, sir? This wretch has never been seen before!"
Seeing him thus, he becomes angry, thinking: "He goes along puffing with joy as if intoxicated and as if roaring.
Even one who was walking ahead turns back; seeing that he is angry, and realizing that those who are angry are easy to recognize, he understands his state of mind and says:
"What will you do to me while you are angry? This prosperity [was acquired] by me through the power of generosity, virtue, and so forth..."
“Having obtained [this], it shall not be under your control,” he retorts. For when one is angry and the other is not, the one who is not angry protects himself;

but when both are angry, the anger of one becomes a condition for the other’s, and the anger of that one also becomes a condition for the other’s—thus both pass away while their harem women are still weeping. This is due to one’s own volition and the volition of others.
"And by reason" means they pass away because of their own volition and the volition of others acting as causes.
For humans, having become angry, strike themselves with their own hands or with sticks; they bind themselves with ropes and the like;
they cut off their own heads with swords; they consume poison; they fall from precipices; and they [drown] in water.
They enter [fire], they even enter fire, and they kill others by striking them with sticks or weapons.
Thus, in their case, both self-intention and the intention of others operate.
"Which gods are to be seen by him? means which gods indeed are to be seen by him. Or, by that personal existence (attabhāva).
The meaning is also: "Which gods are to be seen? But why did the Elder ask this question?

Is it because he was not capable of explaining it himself? He was indeed capable; however, the Elder did not explain it because this term refers to a subject within the domain of the Buddha by its very nature.
Therefore, "to be seen" means to be seen by that [specific] personal existence (attabhāva). Furthermore, this question [is related to what follows] below.

It is obtainable both in the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) and in the form-sphere (rūpāvacara); however, having been defined by the limit of existence (bhavagga), it is spoken of exhaustively—thus it was spoken by the Blessed One.
"Comers to this state" means comers to this very condition, namely, the state of the five aggregates of the sense-sphere; they do not [come] to anything else.
They are those who arise there, not those who arise above. "Non-returners to this state" means they do not return to this pentad of aggregates;

they are not those who arise in lower realms, but rather those who arise there, or arise above, or attain final Nibbāna right there—this is the meaning. And here, "those who arise above" refers to those reborn in a lower existence.
[These] are to be understood. However, this [distinction] does not exist in the Peak of Existence (*bhavagga*). The remainder is clear everywhere. 2.
Commentary on the Vibhattisutta 172.

In the second [sutta], "analytical knowledge of meaning" (*atthapaṭisambhidā*) is knowledge that has reached differentiation regarding the five kinds of meanings. "Respectively" (*odhiso*) means by way of cause.
"Phrasing" (*byañjana*) means the flavor of the syllables. "In many ways" (*anekapariyāyena*) means by means of many reasons.

"I declare" (*ācikkhāmi*) means I speak. "I teach" (*desemi*) means I speak having made it manifest. "I make known" (*paññāpemi*) means I cause [others] to know. "I establish" (*paṭṭhapemi*) means I speak having established and set it forth.
"I reveal" (*vivarāmi*) means I speak having opened it up. "I analyze" (*vibhajāmi*) means I speak having analyzed. "I make plain" (*uttānīkaromi*) means...
"I shall explain what is profound by making it shallow. "He approaches me with a question" means: let him come to me with a question.
"I [shall respond] with an explanation" means: I shall satisfy his mind by answering his question. "He who is most skilled in our teachings" means:
that Teacher who is most skilled in the teachings we have attained is present here before us. If, by me, the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*)...
Thinking, "He has not yet realized it; if I say, 'Sāriputta, realize it first,' he will prevent me," he lets out a lion's roar while sitting right in front of the Teacher.
By this method, the meaning is to be understood in all instances.
Furthermore, among these analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), three are mundane, while the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*) is both mundane and supramundane.
3. Commentary on the Mahākoṭṭhika Sutta 173.
In the third [verse], "bases of contact" (*phassāyatana*) means those things that produce contact; the meaning is the places where contact arises.
"There is nothing else whatsoever" means that when these have ceased without remainder, there is not even the slightest defilement remaining thereafter.
He asks: "Is there nothing else? Here too, he asks whether "there is not even the slightest defilement.

The same method applies to the other two [questions] as well. However, these four questions he asks by way of eternalism (sassata), annihilationism (uccheda), partial-eternalism (ekaccasassata), and the evasionist (amarāvikkhepa).
Therefore, warding off each question as it was asked, the Elder said, "Do not say so" (mā hevaṃ). For herein...
The particle *evaṃ* is used merely as a filler; the meaning is "do not speak thus.

By way of his adherence to a self-grasping, he asks in the manner of an eternalist and so forth, thinking, "Is there some other thing called a self? But is he one who has actually grasped a self? No, he is not one who has grasped a self.
Rather, a certain monk sitting there held such a view, and being unable to ask [the question himself], he [asked on his behalf]. His view...

He asks in this way for the purpose of eliciting an answer. Furthermore, he asks specifically so as to cut off any ground for the claim that those who might arise in the future with such views could say, "Even during the time of a Buddha, this question was answered by the Great Disciples.

He "proliferates what is not to be proliferated" means that he creates conceptual proliferation (*papañca*) regarding a matter where no proliferation should be made, following a path that ought not to be practiced.

It proceeds. To that extent is the range of *papañca*: as far as is the range of the six bases of contact (*phassāyatana*), so far is the range of *papañca*—which is divided into craving, views, and conceit.

"Friends, with the remainderless fading away and cessation of the six bases of contact, there is the cessation of *papañca*, the stilling of *papañca*"—when these six bases have ceased entirely, *papañca* also ceases.

The meaning is that they have ceased and are stilled. In the case of the deities who are worldlings (*puthujjana*) in the formless realm (*ārūpa*), although the five bases of contact (*phassāyatana*) have indeed ceased, because the sixth has not ceased, the three kinds of proliferation (*papañca*) remain unabandoned.

Moreover, the question was stated specifically with reference to existence in the five-aggregate realm (*pañcavokārabhava*). In the fourth [case], the meaning should be understood by this same method.
5. Commentary on the Upavāṇa Sutta (175–176).
Regarding the fifth [verse], "one who makes an end through clear knowledge" (*vijjāyantakaro hoti*): by means of clear knowledge, one makes an end of the suffering of the round of existence;
having delimited and enclosed the entire suffering of the round, one stands [beyond it]. The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.
"With clinging" means being still possessed of grasping. "One who makes an end" means one who stands having made an end to the suffering of the round of existence (*saṃsāra*).
"Endowed with conduct" means being possessed of conduct consisting of fifteen types of qualities.

"Knowing and seeing according to reality, one makes an end" means that by knowing and seeing the true nature [of things] through the wisdom of the Path, one makes an end to the suffering of the round of existence.
"He is said to be 'standing having made an end'": thus he concluded the question with the pinnacle of *arahatta*.
The sixth [section] is to be understood in the same manner as explained in the commentary on the preceding *ekakanipāta* (Single Chapter).
7. Commentary on the Rāhula Sutta.
177. Regarding the seventh [meditation subject], "internal" refers to the earth element characterized by the quality of hardness among the twenty parts, beginning with head hair.
"External" refers to the earth element characterized by the quality of hardness in external objects not bound to sense faculties, such as stones and mountains.
In this same manner, the remaining elements are also to be understood. "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self."
This was stated by way of rejecting the grasping at craving, conceit, and views.

"To be seen with right wisdom" means it should be seen by means of the wisdom of the path (*maggapaññā*) through its cause and reason. "Having seen" means having seen with the wisdom of the path together with insight (*vipassanā*).
"He cut off craving" means he severed the craving to be abandoned by the path along with its root. "He shook off the fetters" refers to the tenfold [fetters].
Having turned back and uprooted the fetter, he abandoned it. "Through the perfect realization of conceit" means by way of the cause or reason of the realization that abandons the ninefold conceit.
"He made an end of suffering" means he made the suffering of the cycle of existence (vaṭṭadukkha) limited and circumscribed;
the meaning is that he remained having done so. Thus ends the section on insight in the *Rāhulovāda* of the *Saṃyutta Nikāya* as taught by the Teacher.
In the *Cūḷarāhulovāda*, insight (*vipassanā*) was taught;
in the *Ambaṭṭhikarāhulovāda*, the abstention from false speech was taught even while he was still a youth; and in the *Mahārāhulovāda*, insight was taught.
In this *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, this is what is called the "fourfold emptiness" (*catukoṭika-suññatā*).
8. Commentary on the Jambālīsutta 178.
Regarding the eighth [sutta], "the peaceful liberation of mind" (*santaṃ cetovimuttiṃ*): this refers to any one of the eight attainments (*samāpatti*).

"The cessation of identity" (*sakkāyanirodhaṃ*) means the cessation of identity (*sakkāya*), which is comprised of the cycle of existence in the three realms; the meaning is *nibbāna*. "Does not leap forward" (*na pakkhandati*)...
One does not leap forward by way of the object. The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well. "Not to be expected" means it is not to be anticipated.
"Smeared with plaster" means covered with plaster.
And regarding this matter, the simile of the man wishing to go to the far bank of a river should be cited: it is said that there was once a certain man...
Desiring to cross to the far shore of a river with a fierce current, teeming with predatory fish, he thought: "The near shore is dangerous and fearful;
the far shore is safe and free from fear. What indeed must I do to go to the far shore?
Seeing eight *kakudha* trees standing in a row, he reflected: "It is possible to go by means of this succession of trees."
“Kakudha trees have smooth branches; one’s hands would not find a foothold on the branches.
Having smeared his hands and feet with lac from one of the *nigrodha*, *pilakkha*, or other such trees, he grasped a branch with his right hand.
His hand stuck right there. Then, with his left hand, then his right foot, then his left foot—he tried all four hands and feet.
They clung right there. Hanging with his head downward, when it rained above and the river became full, he was submerged in the current and became food for crocodiles and other creatures.
In this context, the river current should be understood as the stream of saṃsāra, and the man desiring to go to the further shore of the stream as [the seeker].
The practitioner of yoga regards self-identity (sakkāya) as the near shore and Nibbāna as the far shore;
the eight meditative attainments (samāpatti) are like eight *kakudha* trees standing in a row;
entering the attainments without first clearing away the obstacles to meditation and insight is like grasping at branches with a hand smeared with plaster; [and] with the four hands and feet...
The time of clinging due to attachment to the first jhāna should be understood as being like the hanging down of one bound to a branch;
the time when defilements arise at the six sense doors as like rain falling upon an upper stream;

and the time of experiencing suffering in the four states of misery while submerged in the stream of saṃsāra as like crocodiles and other predators preying upon one who has sunk into the current of a river filled with water.
"With a clean hand" means with a well-washed, thoroughly purified hand. Regarding this matter as well, a similar simile should be made:
for instance, a man wishing to go to the other shore, thinking, "The *kakudha* trees have smooth branches;
if I grasp them with a soiled hand, my hand might slip," washes his hands and feet thoroughly, takes hold of a branch, and first—
He climbed the first tree. Then, having descended from that, he [climbed] the second... and so on... then, having descended from that, he climbed the eighth.
Having descended from the eighth tree, he reached the land of safety on the opposite shore.
Therein, it was as if that man had spent the time thinking, "I shall go to the opposite shore by means of these trees."
For the yogi, the time of thinking, "Having attained the eight attainments and emerged from them, I shall reach Arahantship," is like grasping a branch with a clean hand;
the attainment of the meditative absorptions after having cleared away the obstructive states (pāripanthika-dhamma) from both jhāna and vipassanā is like that.
Therein, the time of attaining the first jhāna is like the time of first climbing the tree.

Just as when one has descended from the first tree and ascended the second, so it is with one who is unattached to the inclination for the first jhāna: having emerged from that, he attains the second jhāna...
[and so on] ...just as when one has descended from the seventh tree and ascended the eighth, so it is with one who is unattached to the inclination for the attainment of the base of nothingness:
having emerged from that, he attains the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Just as one who has descended from the eighth tree reaches the further shore, the land of safety, so too should the time of attaining Arahatship be understood: it occurs when one, having emerged from the attainment without being bound by attachment to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, contemplates conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra).
"He brings to mind the breaking up of ignorance" means that he attends to the destruction of the dense, great mass of ignorance consisting of non-knowing regarding the eight bases.
He brings to mind arahantship as characterized by its various distinctions. "He does not leap forward" means that he does not leap forward solely by way of the object.
"A swamp" (jambālī) is a great pit where the great waters collect once they have flowed out from a village.
"Arising for many groups of years" means arising for many groups of years because it arose at the very time the village or city itself arose.
"Of these" refers to a courtesan who has been so for many years. "Inlets" refers to the four openings through which water enters.
"Outflows" refers to the apertures through which it is carried away. "A breach of the embankment is not to be expected" means that a breaking of the bank is not to be anticipated;
for the water does not rise from there, break through the bank, carry off the debris, and reach the great ocean.
To illustrate this matter, the simile of the park-seeker should be cited.
It is said that a certain son of a good family living in a city, while searching for a park, saw a large swamp not too far from the city and not too near.
Observing that "a delightful park will be located in this spot," he took up a spade and [set about clearing] all four...
Having closed the ravines and opened the drainage holes, he stood there. The rain did not fall properly;
the remaining water flowed out through the drainage holes and was gone.
The pieces of hide, rags, and so forth became putrid right there, and insects settled in them, making the area around it unfit to approach. Even those who did approach had to close their nostrils.
He had to depart. After returning for a few days, he stood back, looked, and thinking, "It is not possible to approach," he went away.

In this context, the city-dwelling son of good family should be seen as the practitioner (*yogāvacara*); the time when the mango grove was seen at the village gate by one searching for a garden is like the body composed of the four great elements;
and the time when the openings of the streams were closed is like [the closing of the gates] to the water of hearing the Dhamma.

It is like the time when [the water] has not been obtained; it is like the time when the gates of the six doors of ruin are wide open, or like the time when the restraint of the six doors has been abandoned;
it is like the time when there is no rain for a king, or like the time when a suitable meditation subject has not been obtained;
it is like the time when the remaining water has flowed out through the outlets of ruin, or like the time when the internal virtues have declined; it is like the water rising up against the bank...

The time when one is unable to reach the great ocean after breaking through the refuse and taking hold [of it] is like the time when one is unable to realize Nibbāna after breaking through the wall of ignorance with the path of Arahatship and dispersing the heap of defilements;
it is like the rotting of leather scraps, rags, and so forth right there on the spot— the time when the interior is completely filled with defilements such as lust.

The time when a person participating in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭasamaṅgipuggala*) delights in that cycle should be understood as being like the time after [the man] has returned, seen [the water], and become remorseful.

"The breaking of the embankment is to be expected" means that the breaking of the text (*pāḷippabheda*) is to be expected; for from there, the water, having risen up and broken through the embankment, will be able to take the refuse and reach the great ocean—this is the meaning.
Here too, this same simile should be brought forward. In that context, the time when the openings of the inflow are opened is like the hearing of the Dhamma that is conducive [to progress].
It is the time when [the defilements] have been obtained; it is the time when restraint is established at the six sense-doors, like the closing of the gates of ruin;
it is the time when a suitable meditation subject has been obtained, like the proper raining of a deity;
and it is the time when ignorance is [overcome] by the path of Arahatship, like water rising up, breaking through the embankment, taking the refuse, and reaching the great ocean.
It was the time when he had shattered the mass of unwholesome states and realized Arahatship;
it was like the time when a lake is filled by water entering through its inlets, for he was now filled within with supramundane qualities.
It was as if, having constructed a fence all around and planted trees, one were to build a palace in the middle of a garden and provide performances there.

The time spent sitting after having eaten a fine meal should be understood as being like the time spent sitting after ascending the Palace of Dhamma and entering the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) with Nibbāna as its object.
The rest here is of plain meaning. However, the teaching given is a discourse mixed with both mundane and supramundane matters.
9. Commentary on the Nibbāna Sutta.

179. Regarding the phrases "perception partaking of decline" and so forth in the ninth [chapter], the meaning should be understood according to the method stated in the Abhidhamma: "For one who has attained the first jhāna, perceptions and mental applications accompanied by sensual desire still occur; thus, wisdom is partaking of decline.
"Not knowing things as they truly are" means they do not know them according to their actual nature by means of path-knowledge (*magga-ñāṇa*).
10. Commentary on the Mahāpadesa Sutta 180.
"He was dwelling at Bhoganagara" means that while wandering on his final journey at the time of his Parinibbāna, he reached that city and dwelt there.
"At the Ānanda Cetiya" refers to the monastery established at the site of the residence of the yakkha Ānanda.
*Mahāpadesa* means a great occasion or a great reference; the meaning is that these are great authorities spoken by referring to the Buddha and others who are truly great.
*Neva abhinanditabbaṃ* means that one should not, with a joyful and delighted heart, give a cry of "well done" and listen [to it] beforehand.
For if this is done, then later when it is said, "This does not agree," even if one is told so, [one will say], "What was this before?"...
Having said, "Previously it was Dhamma, now it is not Dhamma," he does not relinquish his tenet.
"It should not be censured" means that one should not say beforehand, "What is this fool saying? For if one says this, he will not speak even what is appropriate to say.
