Therefore he said: “‘Recluse’s lodging’—a couch is a recluse’s lodging, a chair, a mattress, a pillow, a monastery, a gabled house, a mansion, a pavilion, a cave, a watchtower, an upper story, a rock shelter, a bamboo thicket, the foot of a tree, a tent, or wherever else monks resort—all this is a recluse’s lodging.”

“Requisites for the dwelling” (*senāsana*). Furthermore, a monastery (*vihāra*), a gabled house (*aḍḍhayoga*), a mansion (*pāsāda*), a tower (*hammiya*), and a cave (*guhā*)—this is called the “dwelling-requisite of the monastery.
A bed (*mañca*), a bench (*pīṭha*), a mattress (*bhisi*), and a pillow (*bimbohana*)—this is called the “dwelling-requisite of beds and benches.
A rug (*cimilika*), a piece of leather (*cammakhaṇḍa*), a grass mat (*tiṇasanthāra*), and a leaf mat (*paṇṇasanthāra*)—this is called the “dwelling-requisite of mats. Or wherever...
"But the monks retreat"—this is what is called a lodging that provides space. Thus, there are four kinds of lodgings, and all of them are indeed included by the term "lodging.
Now, showing what is suitable for this bird-like bhikkhu who dwells in the four directions, [the text speaks of] the forest...

He spoke the passage beginning with "at the foot of a tree. Therein, regarding "the forest": "Having gone out beyond the threshold post, all this is the forest"—this is the definition of "forest" as it applies to bhikkhunīs.
However, "A forest dwelling (āraññaka) is a resting place that is at least five hundred bow-lengths distant"—this is what is appropriate for this bhikkhu.
Its characteristic is described in the *Visuddhimagga* in the section on the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*).
It has been said: "At the foot of a tree" means any secluded spot at the foot of a tree that provides cool shade. "A mountain" means a rocky peak;

for there, having performed one's water-related duties by the mountain springs, the mind of one sitting in the cool shade of a tree while the various directions are visible and being fanned by a cool breeze becomes one-pointed. "A glen" (*kandara*): "kaṃ" is said to mean...
Water; a mountain region split by that water, which they call a "slope" (*nitamba*) or a "river-grove" (*nadīnikuñja*).
For there, the sand is like silver plates, the dense forest above is like a canopy of jewels, and water flows like a mass of gems.
Having descended into such a ravine and drunk the water, [he washed] his limbs...
Having smoothed out the sand, raised it up, and spread out a rag-robe, the mind becomes one-pointed for one who sits performing the duty of a recluse.
A mountain cave (*giriguhā*) is the space between two mountains, or a single great hollow resembling a subterranean chamber.
The characteristics of a charnel ground (*susāna*) are described in the *Visuddhimagga*. A forest retreat (*vanapattha*) is [beyond] the village boundary...
Having passed beyond the vicinity of human habitation, it is a place where they neither plough nor sow. For this very reason, it is said:
“‘Forest-thicket’ (vanapattha) is a designation for remote lodgings,” and so forth. “Open space” (abbhokāsa) means uncovered.
However, if one so desires, one may dwell there having constructed a robe-tent. “Heap of straw” (palālapuñja) means a pile of straw. From a large heap of straw...
For indeed, having cleared away the straw, they make dwellings resembling mountain caves or rock shelters;
or, having thrown straw over bushes, thickets, and the like, they sit beneath them and practice the duty of a recluse. It is with reference to this that it was said.
"After the meal" means after the meal. "Returned from the alms-round" means returned from the seeking of alms-food.
*Pallaṅkaṃ*: a cross-legged posture with the thighs bound all around. *Ābhujitvā*: having folded [the legs]. *Ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya*:
having set the upper body straight, having aligned the tips of the eighteen vertebrae one against the other.
For when one is seated in this way, the skin, flesh, and sinews do not bend. Then, for him, that which arises due to their bending...
Feelings might arise moment by moment, but they do not arise [in this case]. While those feelings do not arise, the mind becomes one-pointed;
the meditation subject does not fall away, and it attains growth and expansion.

"Having established mindfulness facing the front" means having placed mindfulness directed toward the meditation subject, or having brought it near to the face; such is the meaning. For that very reason, in the Vibhaṅga:
It is said: “This mindfulness is established, well-established, at the tip of the nose or on the sign of the mouth.
Therefore it is called ‘having established mindfulness facing the opening. Alternatively, in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*: “*Parī* has the sense of encompassing;
*mukhaṃ* has the sense of an outlet; *sati* has the sense of establishing. Therefore it is called ‘mindfulness facing the opening (*parimukhaṃ sati*)’. Thus [it is explained] in the *Paṭisambhidā*.
The meaning here should be understood according to the method already stated. To summarize it: "having established mindfulness directed toward the outlet.
Regarding the phrase "free from covetousness for the world" (*abhijjhāṃ loke*): here, the "world" (*loka*) is the five aggregates of clinging in the sense of breaking up and disintegrating.
Therefore, the meaning here is: having abandoned lust for the five aggregates of clinging and having suppressed sensual desire. "By one free from covetousness" (*vigatābhijjhena*).
"By means of having abandoned covetousness through suppression" means that it is free from covetousness, not in the same manner as eye-consciousness; this is the meaning.
"He purifies the mind of covetousness" means he completely liberates the mind from covetousness;

the meaning is that he acts in such a way that the mind both releases itself from it and, having released it, does not take hold of it again. This same method applies to the phrases "having abandoned ill will and hatred," and so forth.
It is called *byāpāda* because by means of it the mind becomes corrupted, abandoning its former natural state, like rotten rice;
it is called *padosa* because, having reached a state of change, it becomes defiled, or it defiles and destroys another. Both of these are synonyms for anger (*kodha*).
*Thina* is a sickness of the mind, while *middha* is a sickness of the mental factors. *Thinamiddha* is both *thina* and *middha*.
"Perceiving light" means being endowed with a perception that is pure and free from hindrances, capable of cognizing the light seen both by night and by day.
"Mindful and clearly comprehending" means being endowed with mindfulness and knowledge.
These two are mentioned because they are conducive to the perception of light. "Restlessness and worry" refers to *uddhacca-kukkucca*. "One who has crossed beyond doubt" means...
Having crossed over and transcended doubt, he stands firm. Because [the thought] "How is this? How is this?
does not occur in him, he is one who is free from perplexity (*akathaṃkathī*). Regarding "wholesome states" (*kusalesu dhammesu*), it means regarding blameless states.
The meaning is that he does not doubt or hesitate thus: "Are these indeed wholesome? How are these wholesome? This is the summary here. Now, in these...
Whatever needs to be said regarding the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) by way of their etymology, characteristics, and so forth, has been stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.

Regarding "weakening wisdom" (*paññāya dubbalīkaraṇe*): because these five hindrances, when they arise, do not allow unarisen mundane or supramundane wisdom to arise, and even when [wisdom] has arisen, they cut off the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) or the five direct knowledges (*abhiññā*).
They cause one to fall. Therefore, they are called "the weakening of wisdom. "Quite secluded from sensual pleasures," and so forth, have been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"These are the taints," and so forth, has been stated by another method for the purpose of revealing the Four Noble Truths.

"He understands: 'There is nothing further beyond this state'"—up to this point, having shown by means of the first three factors the fruitlessness of the external systems, [he shows it] by the fourth.
Having demonstrated the profound nature of his own teaching through this limb, he reached the pinnacle of the instruction with the attainment of *arahantship*.
Now, introducing the teaching, he said: "In this way, monks," and so forth.
9. Commentary on the *Taṇhā-sutta* (Discourse on Craving).
199. In the ninth [verse], *jālinī* means "net-like. For just as a net is woven all around in a tangled and confused mass, so too craving (*taṇhā*) is called *jālinī* because it resembles a net.

Alternatively, she is called *jālinī* because she stands pervading the three realms of existence (*bhava*), possessing a net consisting of her own portions here and there. *Saritaṃ* refers to that therein...
Therein, "having wandered about" means having transmigrated and remained [in various states]. "Spread out" (*visaṭa*) means expanded and scattered.

"Clinging" (*visattikā*) means stuck, adhered, and attached here and there. Furthermore, the meaning here should also be understood according to such methods as: "Clinging has poison as its root; clinging has poison as its fruit," and so forth.
"Tossed upward" (*uddhasta*) means blown upwards. "Completely enveloped" (*pariyonaddha*) means wrapped all around.
"Tantākulakajāto" means born as tangled like a thread. Just as a weaver’s thread that has been poorly laid out and gnawed by mice becomes entangled here and there,
making it difficult to coordinate the end with the end or the beginning with the beginning—
saying "this is the end" or "this is the beginning"— so too, beings who are enveloped by this craving become confused and utterly bewildered.

They are unable to make straight the path of their own deliverance. "Become like a ball of *gulāguṇṭhika*": *gulāguṇṭhika* refers to the sizing thread used by weavers. Some say that *gulā* is a type of bird, and its nest is what is meant.
Just as it is difficult to bring either of those two together—end with end or root with root—this should be applied according to the previous method.
"Muñjapabbajabhūto" means he has become like muñja grass and like pabbaja grass; he has become just like that.

Just as when a rope made from those grasses has worn out and fallen somewhere, it is difficult to take hold of it and match end to end or root to root, thinking, "This is the tip, this is the root. That too—
And while it might be possible to make it straight by relying on one's own individual personal effort, there is no other being— apart from a Bodhisatta— who,
by his own inherent nature, is capable of tearing through the net of craving and making straight for himself the path to liberation.
Thus, this world, enveloped by the net of craving, [falls] into the states of loss, miserable destinies, and the abyss.
One does not transcend saṃsāra. In this context, "state of loss" (apāya) refers to the realms of hell, the animal womb, the sphere of hungry ghosts, and the host of asuras.
Indeed, all of these are called "states of loss" because of the absence of any gain (āya) characterized by prosperity.

Likewise, they are called "bad destinations" (duggati) because they are the destination of suffering, and "ruin" (vinipāta) because one has fallen away from the heights of happiness. As for the other—
“The succession of the aggregates, and of the elements and sense-bases, occurring without interruption, is called ‘saṃsāra.
One does not transcend, nor does one go beyond, all that; rather, from death there is rebirth-linking, and from rebirth-linking there is death.”
Thus, undergoing death and rebirth again and again within the three realms of existence, the four modes of birth, the five destinations,
the seven stations of consciousness, and the nine abodes of beings, one merely wanders about like a ship tossed by the winds upon the great ocean,
or like an ox yoked to a waterwheel.
"Depending on the internal" means depending on the fivefold aggregate of the internal. For this is a genitive case used in the sense of the accusative.
"Depending on the external" means depending on the fivefold aggregate of the external; this too is a genitive case used in the sense of the accusative.
"In the thought 'I am,' monks"—that is, monks, when there is this [thought] based on the fivefold internal aggregate by way of craving, conceit, and views...
From grasping the aggregate as a whole, the thought "I am" arises; the meaning is: "when that [aggregate] exists.

In the cases of "I am thus" and so forth, however, when there is such grasping of the self from the aggregate, there is a twofold grasping: namely, grasping without comparison and grasping with comparison.
Therein, "without comparison" means: without approaching another mode, taking the object as its own nature alone, one thinks "I am thus."
The meaning is that it exists by way of craving, conceit, and views, such as "I am of this kind among the kṣatriyas and so forth.
This, first of all, is grasping without comparison (*anupanidhāya*). Grasping with comparison (*upanidhāya*), however, is twofold:

by way of similarity (*sama*) and by way of dissimilarity (*asama*). To show that, it is said: "I am thus" (*evam-asmi*) and "I am otherwise" (*aññathā-asmi*). Therein, "I am thus" refers to grasping by way of similarity.
"Grasping" means: "Just as this kshatriya is, just as this brahmin is, so am I"—this is the meaning.
"I am otherwise," however, is grasping by way of dissimilarity; the meaning is: "Just as this kshatriya is, just as this brahmin is, I am otherwise than that—either inferior or superior.
These, first of all, are the four modes of craving's wandering with reference to the present.
However, as for these two—“I am” (*asasmī*) and “I exist” (*satasmī*)—since "it exists" (*atthi*) is *asaṃ*, this is a designation for the permanent (*nicca*).

"It perishes" (*sīdati*) is *sataṃ*, which is a designation for the impermanent (*anicca*). Therefore, they should be understood as stated by way of eternalism (*sassata*) and annihilationism (*uccheda*).
Those following this, beginning with "there are" (*santi*), are four [terms] stated by way of skeptical reflection (*saṃsayaparivitakka*). "There are, there is" (*santi hoti*)...

In such passages as these, the meaning should be understood as "I might be" or "I might exist. However, the underlying intention here should be grasped in the same manner as that stated for the preceding tetrad.
Furthermore, the four terms beginning with "I might not be" (*apihaṃ santi*) are stated by way of aspiration and conceptualization, thinking, "May I indeed not be.
These too should be understood in the same manner as that stated for the preceding tetrad.

The four beginning with "will be" (bhavissanti), however, are stated with reference to the future. Their meaning should also be understood in the same manner as that explained for the preceding tetrad. Thus these are:
"Two are called 'heads' because they are heads; four are rooted in the head."
One should discern these eighteen [conceits]: "Tayo tayo" (three by three).

For among these, "I am" (*asmi*) and "I exist" (*santamhi*) are called the two heads of views (*diṭṭhisīsa*). "I shall be" (*bhavissam*), "I will exist" (*bhavissanti*), "I might be" (*apiham santim*), and "I will exist" (*bhavissanti*)—these four are merely heads of pure conceit (*suddhasīsa*).
"I am thus" (*ittham-asmi*) and so forth—the three groups of three, totaling twelve—are called the heads based on the roots (*sīsamūlaka*).
Thus, these two types of views, four types of pure heads, and twelve types of head-based [views]—these eighteen phenomena of the wanderings of craving (taṇhāvicarita) are to be understood.
These, first of all, are the eighteen wanderings of craving based on the internal [self].
The same method applies to the wanderings of craving based on the external [world]. "By this" means: "by this form... pe ... or by consciousness."
This distinction is to be understood. The remainder is exactly as before.
Thus, thirty-six such [instances] in the past mean thirty-six for each individual person in the past period;
thirty-six in the future mean thirty-six for each and every individual person in the future period; and [thirty-six] in the present...
"Thirty-six" means that for either a single individual or for many individuals, according to what is possible, there are exactly thirty-six in the present course.
However, for all beings, there are necessarily thirty-six in the past course, thirty-six in the future, and thirty-six in the present.

For beings are infinite, distinguished by the various types of craving, conceit, and views, numbering one hundred and eight. There are one hundred and eight modes of the movement of craving (*taṇhāvicarita*).
Regarding the phrase "they exist" (*honti*), the meaning here should be understood as: "the eighty types of craving-proliferations (*taṇhāvicarita*) exist.
10. Commentary on the *Pema Sutta* (Sutta 200):

In the tenth [verse], "he does not exalt" (*na usseneti*) means he does not elevate [his view] by way of dogmatic views (*diṭṭhi*). "He does not disparage" (*na paṭiseneti*) means he is not opposed [to others].

Having offered [the sacrifice], he does not cast it out by way of quarreling and contention. "It does not smolder" means that, with respect to the internal, it does not smolder by way of the wandering of craving (*taṇhāvicarita*).
"It does not blaze up" means that, with respect to the external, it does not blaze up by way of the wandering of craving.
"It does not burn intensely" means that, by way of the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*), it does not burn intensely. The remainder should be understood according to the method of the text (*pāḷinaya*).
In this sutta, the cycle of existence and its cessation (vaṭṭa-vivaṭṭa) are explained.
The Fifth Great Chapter (Mahāvagga) is finished.
The Fourth Fifty (Catuttha-pannāsaka) is completed.
5. The Fifth Fifty (21) 1.
The Chapter on True Persons (Sappurisavagga) 1–6.
Commentary on the Discourses on the Training Rules (Sikkhāpadasuttavaṇṇanā)
201. In the first [section] of the fifth [chapter], "an untrue person" (*asappurisa*) refers to a base person, a hollow person, a deluded person, a fool blinded by ignorance.
"An even more untrue person" (*asappurisatara*) means one who is excessively an untrue person. The other two [terms] should be understood by way of their opposites to what has been stated.
The rest here is of plain meaning. And as it is here, so it is in the five [sections] following this. Among these—

For indeed, the first was taught by way of the five enmities (*pañcavera*), the second by way of the qualities contrary to the true Dhamma (*assaddhamma*), the third by way of the doors of body and speech, the fourth by way of the door of mind, the fifth by way of the eight wrongnesses (*micchatta*), and the sixth by way of the ten wrongnesses. 7–10.
Commentary on the Tetrad of Discourses on Evil Qualities (*Pāpadhammasutta-catuṣka*).
207–210. In the seventh [verse], "evil" (*pāpa*) refers to a base, defiled person; "good" (*kalyāṇa*) refers to an auspicious, blameless person.
The rest here is of plain meaning. The same method applies to the eighth as well. In the ninth, "of evil nature" (*pāpadhamma*) means a base nature;
"of good nature" (*kalyāṇadhamma*) means a blameless nature. The rest here is of plain meaning. The same method applies to the tenth as well.
In this chapter, the practice of the householder is explained in all ten suttas. Even if they are stream-enterers or once-returners, it is indeed appropriate [for them to follow this practice].
Thus ends the first chapter, "On True Persons."
(22) 2. The Chapter on the Assembly (Parisāvagga). 1. Explanation of the Discourse on the Assembly (Parisāsutta). 211.
In the first [sutta] of the second [chapter], "corrupting the assembly" means those who defile the assembly; "beautifying the assembly" means those who adorn the assembly.
2. Commentary on the Discourse on Views (Diṭṭhisutta-vaṇṇanā) 212.
In the second [discourse], wrong view—even though it is included within mental misconduct—is mentioned separately because of its great blameworthiness; and right view is mentioned as its opposite.
3. Commentary on the Discourse on Ungratefulness (Akataññutāsutta-vaṇṇanā)

213. In the third [sutta], *akatattā* means "unknowing" and *akatavedittā* means "not acknowledging what has been done. Both of these are identical in meaning. The same method applies to the bright side (*sukkapakkha*) as well.
4–7. Commentary on the *Pāṇātipātī-sutta* and others. 214–217.
The fourth [sutta] is stated by way of the four defilements of action (*kamma-kilesa*) and their respective opposites; the fifth...
The first four [factors] of the bright side (sukkapakkha) are by way of the four wrong states (micchatta); the sixth is by way of the remaining four;

and the seventh is by way of ignoble and noble modes of speech (anariya-ariya-vohāra). Likewise, the eighth, ninth, and tenth are stated by way of the unwholesome qualities (assaddhamma) together with their opposites.
However, in all the Suttas, the factors of the bright side are indeed mixed, both mundane (lokiya) and supramundane (lokuttara).
It has been explained. Although the word "heaven" (*sagga*) is mentioned in the nine suttas, nevertheless, the three paths and the three fruits are indeed obtainable there.
The second chapter, the Chapter on the Assembly (*Parisāvagga*), is concluded. (23) 3. Explanation of the Chapter on Bad Conduct (*Duccaritavagga*).
221–231. The first and subsequent sections of the third [chapter] have their meanings already explained.
In the tenth, one who composes poetry after having reflected is called a *cintākavi* (reflective poet). One who composes after having heard it is called a *sutakavi* (heard poet).
One who composes based on a single theme is called an *atthakavi* (thematic poet). One who [composes] at that very moment through his own inspired intuition, like the Elder Vaṅgīsa—
"He performs [this]—he is called a 'poet of inspired wit'.
The third chapter, on Misconduct, is concluded.
(24) 4. The Chapter on Karma.
1. Commentary on the Saṃkhittasutta 232.
In the first [sutta] of the fourth [chapter], "dark" (*kaṇha*) refers to the black, unwholesome action of the ten courses of unwholesome karma.

"Dark ripening" (*kaṇhavipāka*) refers to the dark ripening resulting from rebirth in the states of misery. "Bright" (*sukka*) refers to the white, wholesome action of the ten courses of wholesome karma. "Bright ripening" (*sukkavipāka*)...
Because it is reborn in heaven, it is a "white ripening. "Black-and-white" refers to mixed karma. "Black-and-white ripening" refers to the ripening of both pleasure and pain.

For having performed mixed karma, one who is reborn in the animal realm—such as in the position of a state elephant and so forth—experiences pleasure during its course through the power of the wholesome (kusala), while through the unwholesome (akusala) one is reborn even in a royal family.
In the course of worldly existence, one experiences suffering. By "neither black nor white," the knowledge of the four paths that brings about the destruction of karma is intended.
For if it were black, it would yield a black result; if it were white, it would yield a white result.
However, because it does not yield either kind of result, it is "neither black nor white"—this is the meaning here.
2. Commentary on the *Vitthāra-sutta* (233).

In the second [sutta], "with affliction" (*sabyābajjha*) means with hatred (*sadosa*). "Bodily formation" (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) refers to volition (*cetanā*) at the door of the body. "He forms" (*abhisaṅkharoti*) means he accumulates or compiles.
The same method applies to the other two [formations]. "The world with affliction" (*sabyābajjhaṃ lokaṃ*) means the world with suffering (*sadukkhaṃ lokaṃ*).

“Contact accompanied by affliction” means contact that has suffering as its result. “He experiences feeling accompanied by affliction” means he experiences resultant feeling that is fraught with distress.
“Entirely painful” means it is exclusively suffering, not mixed with pleasure.
Regarding the phrase “just as beings in hell,” here *seyyathāpi* is a particle used in the sense of illustration; by this, [it refers] exclusively to beings in hell.
He shows that there are no others equal to him. By this method, the meaning is to be understood everywhere.
In passages such as "Just as among human beings," first, among humans, pleasant feeling arises at one time and painful feeling at another.
Regarding "and some gods," here the sense-sphere deities (kāmāvacara-deva) are to be understood; for among them, those of greater influence...

For the devas, suffering arises at times through such events as rising from their seats upon seeing [the Buddha], the removal of their upper robes (*uttarāsaṅga*) when he has already put them on, and the raising of their joined palms;
whereas for those experiencing celestial success, happiness arises at times.
And as for "some in the states of loss" (*vinipātika*), here the *peta*s who dwell in various abodes (*vemānika*) are to be understood. For them, there is happiness at one time without interruption.
At one time they experience suffering. However, nāgas, supaṇṇas, elephants, horses, and so forth, like humans, possess a mixture of both pleasure and pain.

Regarding the phrase "the volition for abandoning," it should be understood here as the path-volition that leads to turning away from the round of existence (*vivaṭṭagāminī maggacetanā*). For that indeed conduces to the destruction of kamma.
3. Commentary on the Soṇakāyana Sutta.
234. In the third [sutta], "Sikhāmoggallāna" refers to a brahmin of the Moggallāna clan who possessed a large crest situated in the middle of his head.
"The former ones" should be understood as those from the immediately preceding day onwards, while "the earlier ones" are to be understood as starting from the second day onwards.
"Soṇakāyana" was his own pupil. "O sir, this world is subject to kamma."
"O, this world has the nature of kamma. 'Abiding by the undertaking of kamma' means it stands through the undertaking of kamma.
It shows that it stands only while piling up kamma; if one does not pile up kamma, one perishes. The rest is exactly as explained below. 4–9.
Commentary on the Sikkhāpada-sutta and others.

235. The fourth and subsequent sections are also clear in meaning. Regarding the factors of the path (*maggaṅga*), however, it is said that because one establishes mindfulness (*sati*) and then delimits [the object] with wisdom (*paññā*), both of these constitute action (*kamma*). The remaining factors are merely constituent parts (*aṅga*) and not action.

The same principle applies to the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*). In the Abhidhamma, however, all of this is described without distinction as simply action associated with volition (*cetanā*).
10. Commentary on the Samaṇa Sutta (241).
Regarding the tenth [verse], "right here" (*idheva*) means in this very dispensation (*sāsana*). This restriction, however, should be understood to apply to the remaining phrases as well;

for even the other types of ascetics (*samaṇa*) exist right here, and not elsewhere. "Empty" (*suñña*) means void and hollow. "The doctrines of others" (*parappavāda*) refers to the four [non-Buddhist schools].
The eternalists, the four partial-eternalists, the four proponents of the finite and infinite,
the four eel-wrigglers, the two fortuitous-originationists, the sixteen theorists of perception, the eight theorists of non-perception, the eight theorists of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
the seven annihilationists, and the five theorists of Nibbāna in this very life— all these sixty-two views are included in the Brahmajāla Sutta.
The doctrines of others outside of this [Buddhist teaching] are called "the doctrines of outsiders" (*parappavāda*). All of these are empty of these four types of fruit-abiding recluses;
for they do not exist here. Not only are they empty of these, but they are also empty of the twelve types of recluses:
namely, the four types of path-abiding recluses and those who have initiated insight-meditation for the sake of the four paths. Thus, they are indeed empty of all twelve types of recluses.
It was with reference to this very matter that the Blessed One said during the Mahāparinibbāna:
"Subhadda, it was at the age of twenty-nine that I went forth, seeking what is wholesome."
More than fifty years have passed,
Subhadda, since I went forth;
I am one who practices according to a portion of the true Dhamma.
“Outside of this [teaching], there is no ascetic.
“There is no second ascetic, there is no third ascetic, there is no fourth ascetic; the doctrines of others are empty of other ascetics.
For here, the term “one who dwells in a limited sphere” refers to one who has begun insight meditation (*āraddhavipassaka*).

Therefore, having combined the three—the one who has begun insight for the path of stream-entry, the one established on the path, and the one established in the fruit—he said, "There is not even a first recluse.

Having combined the three—the one who has begun insight for the path of once-returning, the one established on the path, and the one established in the fruit—he said, "There is not even a second recluse. The same method applies to the other two as well. The eleventh [section] is of obvious meaning.
The Fourth Chapter on Kamma.
(25) 5. The Chapter on Fear of Offenses. 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Schism of the Saṅgha.

243. Regarding the first [question] of the fifth [chapter]: "Ānanda, did that legal issue arise for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus as one of the legal issues such as a dispute-legal-issue (vivādādhikaraṇa)? The Teacher spoke thus, asking whether it had been settled.
"From where, Bhante? means: "Venerable Sir, from what source, how, and by what cause will that legal issue be settled?"
He speaks. "Kevalakappaṃ" means entirely and on all sides. "Standing for the schism of the Saṅgha" means he stands while merely replying to what was said by the Saṅgha for the purpose of debate.
"Therein, the Venerable One" refers to the Venerable Anuruddha while standing in that manner.
"He did not think even a single word should be spoken" means [he thought], "Friend, do not speak thus with the Saṅgha."
He does not even consider that a single word should be spoken. "He applies himself" means he devotes himself to practice.
"For the sake of the purpose" means for the sake of the reason. "They will cause him to disappear" means they will expel him by not allowing him to enter the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā ceremonies.
The rest should be understood according to the text itself.
2. Commentary on the Āpattibhayasutta 244.
"In the second [verse], 'having shaved him with a razor' means having shaved him with a razor while leaving five tufts of hair.
'With a harsh sound' means with a rough noise. 'With a drum' means with a drum for execution. 'Of one standing on dry land' means in a secluded place."
"Of one who stands. "Beheading" means deserving of beheading. "Yatra hi nāma" means "that indeed.

"So vatassāhaṃ" means "may I indeed be such that I would not commit such evil"—this is the meaning. "He will make amends according to the Dhamma" means he will make amends in accordance with the Dhamma;
the meaning is that he will stand upon the level of a novice monk (*sāmaṇera*). "Having put on black clothes..."
Having put on a garment of black cloth. "Mosalla" means deserving the blow of a pestle.
"Yathādhamma" means that one who, having emerged from an offense here and established himself in purity, is said to act according to the Dhamma. "Bhasmapuṭa" means a vessel of ashes.
"Gārayhaṃ bhasmapuṭa" means deserving to be struck on the head with a censurable vessel of ashes. "Yathādhamma" [means...]

Here, one who confesses an offense is said to make amends in accordance with the Dhamma. "Those who find fault" refers to those worthy of censure. "In the cases of offenses entailing confession" means in those matters that must be confessed.
By this, all remaining categories of offenses are included. "These, monks, are the four fears regarding offenses" means, monks, these are the four kinds of fear that arise on account of an offense.
3. Commentary on the Sikkhānisaṃsasutta 245.

In the third [verse], it is "possessing the benefits of training" (sikkhānisaṃsa) because the benefits of training are found therein. It is "with wisdom as the supreme" (paññuttara) because wisdom is the highest therein.

It is "having liberation as its essence" (vimuttisāra) because liberation is the core therein. It is "having mindfulness as the dominant factor" (satādhipateyya) because mindfulness exercises sovereignty therein. Of these...
For it is said that one "lives" for the sake of the benefits and so forth comprised by the training; thus, "pertaining to higher conduct" (*ābhisamācārika*) means pertaining to the highest conduct.
This is a designation for the virtue prescribed by way of formal duties (*vatta*).
"In such and such a manner, he [should train] in that training" means that in such and such a manner, that monk desiring training [should train] in that particular precept.
“Fundamental to the holy life” (*ādibrahmacariyika*) is a designation for the four great precepts that constitute the beginning of the holy life of the Path (*maggabrahmacariya*).

“In all ways” (*sabbaso*) means in every aspect. “Phenomena” (*dhammā*) refers to the phenomena of the Four Noble Truths. “They are well-observed by wisdom” (*paññāya samavekkhitā hontīti*) means they are clearly seen by means of the wisdom of the Path together with insight (*vipassanā*).
“They are touched by liberation” (*vimuttiyā phusitā hontīti*) means [they are touched] by the contact of knowledge through the liberation of the fruit of Arhatship (*arahattaphala-vimutti*).
"They are touched. "Mindfulness is well-established within oneself" means that mindfulness is properly established precisely within one's own internal domain.
"I will support with wisdom" means I will support with insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*).
"I will examine with wisdom"—here too, insight-wisdom is intended. "Or whatever phenomenon is touched, I will support it there with wisdom."
But here, it is specifically path-wisdom (*maggapaññā*) that is intended.
4. Commentary on the *Seyyasutta* (246):
"The dead" (*petā*) refers to those who have passed away. "They lie on their backs" means they mostly lie in a supine position.
Alternatively, those born in the realm of the hungry ghosts (pettivisaya) are called *petas*.
Because they have little flesh and blood, their bodies are so packed with masses of bone that they are unable to lie down on one side; they remain lying flat on their backs.
"He becomes dissatisfied" means that because of his intense heat, the lion, king of beasts, places two of his forefeet in one spot and his hind feet in another, and [extends] his tail...

Having placed [the body] between two posts and having observed the positions where the toes of the front and back feet were placed, he lies down with his head resting on top of the two front feet. Even after sleeping for a whole day, when waking up, he does not wake up in terror;
rather, he lifts his head, observes the positions of the front feet and so forth, and [arises].

If it stands having left some spot, it becomes displeased, thinking, “This is not worthy of your birth, nor is it befitting your courage,” and lies down right there; it does not set out for its feeding ground.
It is with reference to this that it was said: “It becomes displeased. But when it stands without leaving [its place], [thinking] “This is worthy of your birth and your courage...”
Thinking, "This is indeed appropriate," he rises up joyful and elated;
stretching himself like a lion, shaking his mane, and letting out a lion’s roar three times, he sets out for his feeding ground. Therefore it is said: "He becomes delighted.
5. Commentary on the *Thūpārahasutta* (The Discourse on the Worthy of a Stupa)

247. Regarding the fifth [case], "The Wheel-turning Monarch": why does the Blessed One here permit the construction of a stupa for a king who died while living in the midst of a household, but not for a virtuous worldling monk?
Because it would not be extraordinary. For if stupas were permitted for worldling monks, there would be no room for stupas even on the island of Tambapaṇṇi.

The same applies in other instances. Therefore, he does not permit [the building of a stupa], thinking, "They will become common. A Wheel-turning Monarch (cakkavatti-rāja) is born only once; therefore, his stupa is marvelous.

However, it is entirely appropriate to perform even great honors for an ordinary person (puthujjana) who possesses virtue, just as one would for a monk who has attained final Nibbāna. The sixth and seventh [sections] have meanings that are self-evident.
8. Commentary on the First Discourse on Modes of Speech (Paṭhamavohārasutta-vaṇṇanā) 250.
In the eighth [discourse], "un-Aryan modes of speech" refers to the talk of those who are not noble. The same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well.
This concludes the fifth chapter, the Chapter on the Fear of Offenses.
The Fifth Fifty is concluded. (26) 6.
The Chapter on Direct Knowledge (Abhiññāvagga). 1–3.
Commentary on the Discourses on Direct Knowledge, etc.

254–256. In the first [section] of the sixth [chapter], "having known" (*abhiññāya*) means having understood. "Calm and insight" (*samatho ca vipassanā ca*) refers to one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*) and the knowledge of insight that discerns formations (*saṅkhārapariggahavipassanāñāṇa*).
"True knowledge and liberation" (*vijjā ca vimutti ca*) refers to the true knowledge of the path-knowledge (*maggañāṇavijjā*) and the remaining associated mental states (*sampayuttakadhammā*).
In the second [section], "noble search" (*anariyapariyesanā*) is the seeking and questing of the ignoble. "Subject to aging" (*jarādhammaṃ*)...
The state of being worn out by old age. The same method applies to the remaining cases as well.
The third [section] is self-evident. 4.
Commentary on the Māluṅkyaputta Sutta: 257. Regarding "Māluṅkyaputta": he is the son of the brahmin woman Māluṅkyā. "In this" means in this request for your instruction.

By this, he both disparages and praises the Elder. How so? It is said that in his youth this man was attached to the requisites, but later, in his old age, desiring to dwell in the forest, he requested a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). Then the Blessed One said:
"What can we say here about this youth? Like Māluṅkyaputta, you too were attached to the requisites in your prime..."
By speaking with the intention, "You should enter the forest and practice the duty of a recluse when you are old," he is indeed disparaging the Elder.
However, because the Elder himself desired to enter the forest and practice the duty of a recluse precisely at the time of his old age, the Blessed One said:
"In this matter, what shall we say of the young? This Māluṅkyaputta of ours, even at the time of his old age..."
The construction is as follows: "Having entered the forest, desiring to practice the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*), he asks for a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
You, however, do not even exert effort during your youth"—speaking with this underlying intention, he is said to be "encouraging" the Elder.
5–10. Commentary on the *Kulasutta* and others.
258–263. “They appoint him to the fifth office” means they appoint him to the position of storekeeper (*bhaṇḍāgārika*).

In the sixth [case], “endowed with beauty” means endowed with the beauty of the physical body; “endowed with strength” means endowed with bodily strength. In the section on the bhikkhus, “endowed with beauty” means endowed with the beauty of virtuous qualities;
“endowed with strength” means endowed with the strength of energy (*vīriya*); “endowed with speed” means...
He is endowed with the speed of knowledge. The same method applies to the seventh [chapter] as well. The rest here is self-evident.
